'Russia does not consider Trump’s statements strong,' Zelensky pleads for help as Russia targets energy grid
A Ukrainian Defense Ministry adviser stated that SpaceX has capped Starshield’s military package at 100 miles per hour for terminals in motion. He said Ukrainian forces were not notified.
Russia struck Ukraine’s energy and critical infrastructure overnight with 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 attack drones and loitering munitions, leaving at least 600,000 people without power, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced in a post on X. The targets were in Kyiv, the Kyiv region, and Kharkiv.
Zelensky said 26 facilities of Ukraine’s power system and four facilities in the oil and gas sector were damaged, and that there were fatalities and injuries. He warned that outages could become even more widespread and thanked repair crews, Ukrainian energy workers and State Emergency Service personnel for their efforts.
Zelensky also pointed out that the ballistic missile strike hit energy infrastructure covered by the ceasefire announced by President Donald Trump. “The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale – Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States," the Ukrainian president said, adding, "Russia does not consider the American President’s statements strong.”
Zelensky then called for a forceful response. “We ask America and EVERYONE in the world who does not turn a blind eye to reality to respond – and to respond forcefully,” he said. “Russia has squandered the opportunity for de-escalation and has clearly chosen to continue its insane war of annihilation.”

In the post, the Ukrainian President specifically asked Trump to impose strong sanctions on Russia, noting that the Lindsey Graham bill, recently passed and signed into law, authorizes and regulates such measures. "The American President has all the effective and necessary tools to bring peace closer through strength, justice, and pressure on the aggressor. We ask for additional packages of Patriot missile interceptors for Ukraine."
Zelensky concluded his lengthy post by stating, “It is entirely fair for us to tell the United States, Europe, and all our partners that no country in the world should be left alone to face such a deranged and pro-war actor as Russia.”
Separately, Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Ukraine’s Defense Ministry, said SpaceX has partially restricted Starlink service in Ukraine, specifically its Starshield military package. The limit caps terminals at 100 miles per hour while in motion.
“I confirm that SpaceX has implemented speed limits for Starlink terminals while in motion, starting tonight,” Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram. “Currently, the restriction applies to the ‘military package’ of Starshield services and is set at a speed of 100 miles per hour. Our defense forces were not notified of this restriction, and it has resulted in the disruption of several missions. It is clear that this action is not coincidental and is related to the current political situation.”
He did not say which political situation he meant or offer evidence for the link.

Japanese Journalist Faces Up to 20 Years in Russia on Charges of Spying on Kuril Islands Mobilization
Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) has detained 34-year-old Japanese national Yuki Imai, a reporter for the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper, in Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk on espionage charges. Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk, the main city on Russia’s Sakhalin Island just north of Japan, on espionage charges. He was detained as he was preparing to leave Russia and was then flown to Moscow.
Moscow’s Lefortovo Court ordered the journalist held in custody on October 13, and he faces up to 20 years in prison if convicted, Meduza reported.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russian authorities allege that Imai was collecting intelligence on military personnel, specifically gathering data on volunteer fighters and the number of residents mobilized from the Kuril Islands for Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine on behalf of Japanese intelligence.
Imai, who has visited Russia since 2014, had arrived in the country most recently in the summer of 2026. He previously studied at Saint Petersburg State University and regularly posted photos from his travels across Moscow and Saint Petersburg.
He had expressed interest in Soviet military equipment, classical music, ballet, and Soviet cinema, and was traveling with a book by Ivan Bunin . His recent journalistic work covered the State Duma elections, the unveiling of a monument in Khabarovsk marking Soviet victory over Japan, North Korean citizens in Sakhalin, and Russia's strengthening relations with North Korea, according to Meduza.
During his latest trip, he also visited Vladivostok and Nakhodka in the Primorsky Krai region to cover local cultural centers, Far Eastern life, and historical Russian-Japanese relations. His most recent article was published on October 5.
Relationships between Russia and Japan deteriorated further following Vladimir Putin’s first-ever visit to the disputed Kuril Islands in August 2026, where he traveled to Iturup after observing Russian Pacific Fleet exercises. In response, Tokyo summoned Russia's ambassador to lodge a formal protest, with Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi reiterating that the islands remain an inherent part of Japanese territory.
Following the visit, Japanese Foreign Ministry officials indicated that Tokyo was evaluating additional sanctions against Moscow, while analysts noted the Kremlin likely intended the trip to deter Japan's increasingly assertive defense posture and discourage European actions against Russia’s shadow fleet.

US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have put their planned trip to Moscow on hold.
The visit has been put on hold indefinitely, according to a report by The New York Times on October 13.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Tensions between Ukraine and the US over President Donald Trump’s diesel agreement with Russian leader Vladimir Putin have escalated into the most severe strain in bilateral relations since last year’s Oval Office controversy.
An unnamed US official stated that Trump reacted with intense anger toward Ukraine, making it difficult to predict what subsequent steps might follow, according to The New York Times.
Reports indicate that Witkoff and Kushner have suspended their travel plans to Russia until Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy “improves relations with Trump.”
In September 2026, US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held a three-hour meeting in Moscow with Russian leader Vladimir Putin, which ended without a breakthrough as Putin remained committed to capturing the entire Donetsk region.
Bloomberg reported that Putin believed his forces could capture the area within six months, though calculations by the Institute for the Study of War estimated it would take until October 2032 at their current rate of advance.
Following the talks, Witkoff traveled to Kyiv to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European national security advisers, reporting “substantial progress” from those discussions. The diplomatic mission was preceded by an unannounced visit to Moscow by CIA Director John Ratcliffe, who presented Russian intelligence leadership with a grim assessment of the Russian military's battlefield situation and economy.

Daily Update: Russia Loses 1,650 Troops, 2 Tanks and 371 Vehicles in One Day

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Daily Update: Russia Loses 1,650 Troops, 2 Tanks and 371 Vehicles in One Day
Russia lost an estimated 1,650 troops, two tanks, and 54 artillery systems over the past 24 hours, Ukraine’s General Staff reported on October 14.
According to the latest Ukrainian military estimate, Russia’s total personnel losses since the start of its full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022, have reached approximately 1,557,350.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russian forces also lost one armored combat vehicle, bringing cumulative losses to 12,414 tanks and 25,535 armored vehicles. Another 54 artillery systems were recorded as lost, raising the overall estimate to 51,195, while one additional multiple-launch rocket system brought that total to 2,212.
Ukraine also reported 1,827 operational-tactical UAVs lost over the latest reporting period, pushing the cumulative figure to 563,589. Another nine unmanned ground systems were added to the tally, bringing estimated losses in that category to 2,951.
Russia’s estimated losses of air defense systems remained unchanged at 1,704, while aviation losses stayed at 443 aircraft and 356 helicopters. Cruise missile losses remained at 5,126, with naval losses unchanged at 35 ships and boats and two submarines.
Another 371 vehicles and fuel tankers were recorded as lost, raising the cumulative total to 162,789, while five additional pieces of special equipment brought that figure to 4,828.
Ukrainian and Russian forces clashed 229 times across the front during the latest reporting period.
Earlier, Ukrainian military intelligence operatives neutralized two groups of Russian special forces during a counter-sabotage operation in the Zaporizhzhia direction, capturing one Russian soldier after identifying the units’ movements and setting up an ambush.

SpaceX limits Starlink operations in Ukraine, disrupting military ops., missile defense capability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:09:07 UTC
17:09:07 KST

SpaceX has introduced a limit on some Starlink services in Ukraine, stopping the operation of its military-grade version above 100 miles per hour (160 km/h), disrupting combat missions, presidential adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov said on Wednesday.
"Our defense forces did not receive a warning about this limitation, and this led to the disruption of several missions," he wrote on Telegram, adding: "It is clear that this action is not coincidental and is related to the current political situation."
Ukrainian officials fear the move was made at Trump's request
Ukraine’s security services detected disruptions to Starlink terminals across the country overnight on Tuesday night, a source familiar with the matter confirmed to The Jerusalem Post. Ukrainian officials fear the move by the company, owned by Elon Musk, may have been made at the request of US President Donald Trump.
Starlink terminals are one of the key tools enabling Ukrainians to maintain internet access amid Russia’s invasion. The disruptions reportedly interfered with several critical operations.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said in a social media post that Ukraine had not received an alert about incoming Russian strikes. “This is already the second time this has happened,” Zelensky wrote.
“During the first wave of drone and missile strikes, no warning was received, but an alert was issued during the second wave,” a source familiar with the matter added in a statement to the Post.
Trump himself claimed on Tuesday that the United States had not halted intelligence-sharing cooperation with Ukraine. "We are helping them, and we are sharing intel," Trump told reporters. "We want the war to end, so we're working with them and Russia on getting the war to end."
Zelensky said Russia launched 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 drones overnight on Tuesday night, targeting energy facilities and critical infrastructure across Ukraine. According to the Ukrainian president, approximately 500,000 people were left without electricity following the attack.
Ukrainian negotiators traveled to the US on Friday and Saturday to urge US President Donald Trump to increase sanctions pressure on Russia.
Zelensky accuses US of inaction as Russian strikes kill over 70 in two days
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky accused the US of being unwilling to help Ukraine after a Russian bomb attack on Thursday killed at least 35 people in the east, sending the two-day death toll from Russian strikes to over 70.
Hours after the strike on the embattled city of Kramatorsk tore through two buses, Zelensky criticized Washington's effort to pursue economic ties with Russia while also seeking to mediate the more than four-year war.
Speaking to reporters in Pryluky, the Ukrainian leader urged the US to accede to his requests to expand Ukraine's access to the Starlink satellite service to help it target Russian ballistic-missile launchers.
"Open Starlink for Ukraine. You did open it when you were responding to Iran ... I’ve said quite openly — give it to us, help us defend our skies and dominate there. And then Putin will sit down at the negotiating table," he said in an emotional statement.
Ukraine has in recent months aimed to wrest the battlefield initiative from Russia, whose gains have slowed this year, but is still suffering from Moscow's increasingly brutal air war.
"So where's the truth here, where's the honesty? Where's the stalemate? ... That's called unwillingness," he said, referring to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio's assertion earlier on Thursday that the war is at a stalemate and that the United States would keep working toward a settlement.
"One cannot, on the one hand, negotiate with the Russians about future economic projects, whilst on the other hand say that we find ourselves in some sort of ... diplomatic stalemate," Zelensky added.

Iran tensions, Syria talks put Iraqi Kurdistan at the center of Middle Eastern diplomacy - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:09:07 UTC
17:09:07 KST

The Kurdistan Region of northern Iraq has played an increasingly important role, often behind the scenes, in reducing tensions in the region. At a conference of the 2026 Middle East Research Institute (MERI) Forum in Erbil, a number of Kurdish leaders described recent initiatives the region has undertaken.
The new comments at the MERI conference illustrate how the Kurdish leadership sought to navigate the recent conflict between the US, Israel, and Iran. Although the Kurdistan Region came under more than 1,000 Iranian missile and drone attacks, the Kurdish leaders sought to reach out to Iran and the US. They also worked to broker talks between Damascus and Kurds in eastern Syria.
Who were the key leaders involved? Kurdistan Region President Nechirvan Barzani and Prime Minister Masrour Barzani played a major role. The two men are related and lead the Kurdistan Democratic Party. In addition, the members of the Talibani family, primarily Bafel and Qubad Talibani, from the rival Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) party were instrumental.
'We are part of the solution'
“We are very pleased today to see that Kurds are part of the solution - whether in Syria, as marked by the presence of Comrade Mazloum [Abdi] here, or in Iraq, where we are part of the solution,” Qubad Talabani stated at the 2026 Middle East Research Institute (MERI) Forum in Erbil.
Qubad Talibani is Deputy Prime Minister of the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG). Rudaw reported that Talibani told MERI, “Erbil expressed readiness to facilitate discussions between Kurds and the countries where they live in the Middle East, including in Iran.”
He also said, “We are very pleased today to see that Kurds are part of the solution - whether in Syria, as marked by the presence of Comrade Mazloum [Abdi] here, or in Iraq, where we are part of the solution.”
The report at Rudaw noted that Nechirvan Barzani played a key role in talks in Syria and Turkey. Nechirvan is a unique figure in Kurdish politics today because of his long experience and his ability to navigate the complex politics of Iran, Turkey, Syria, and Iraq.
The Kurdistan Region is involved in a variety of discussions in part because of its geographic position. Northern Iraq borders Iran, Turkey, and Syria. It sits at the crossroads of major regional policies.
For instance, US forces were concentrated in the KRG before the left on September 30. Iran, as noted, has targeted the region 1,000 times. This is mostly because Iran is targeting Kurdish Iranian opposition groups that are based in northern Iraq. Turkey is dealing with peace talks with the PKK, and the PKK has forces also in the KRG.
Most importantly, the KRG helped smooth discussions in Syria. The US was leaving Syria in 2025, and the US-backed SDF, which is Kurdish-led, was expected to integrate with the new government in Damascus. The Kurdistan Regional Government sought to make sure Kurds would not be harmed in Syria.
“As political forces in the Kurdistan Region, we stand ready for any coordination and role assigned to us,” Qubad Talibani added. “Furthermore, the Kurdistan Region has significantly contributed to the advancement of the integration process of the now-dissolved Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) into the Syrian state system,” Rudaw noted.
SDF commander Mazloum Abdi praised the Kurdistan Region for its support. This is important because there are still many tensions in Syria and the role of the KRG is likely not over. The Syrian Kurdish political authorities, called the AANES, never built a prosperous region like the KRG. They were also linked to the YPG and the PKK, and as such were generally rivals of the KDP. This is internal Kurdish politics, but it matters. When the chips were down, the Kurdish leadership in Erbil went to help Kurds in Syria, despite past disagreements among the politicians.
Not everything has been smooth sailing. Nechirvan Barzani was critical of the Kurdish Iranian opposition groups. These groups have bases and camps in the KRG. Some of the Kurdish Iranian groups are closer to the KDP or PUK.
However, Iran has made it clear it will continue its attacks until the KRG is able to assure Tehran that these groups are not a threat. Earlier in the year, in March, media reports suggested the US was willing to arm the Kurdish Iranian groups. The idea of US arms moving through northern Iraq to Iran was certainly seen by Iran as a threat.
“Rojhelat’s [western Iran’s Kurdish region] opposition forces, unfortunately, behaved very irresponsibly,” Nechirvan Barzani said speaking at MERI. This was tough criticism for these groups.
Barzani’s comments shed light on the issues facing the Kurdish Iranian groups
The Amargi, a local grassroots media network, noted that Barzani’s comments shed light on the complexities the Kurdish Iranian groups have faced. At least six of these groups exist. These include the centrist KDPI and PAK, as well as the more left-leaning Komala and PJAK.
PJAK is often believed to be closely linked to the PKK. Another group, Khabat, is part of the Kurdish Iranian opposition alliance. The groups formed an alliance in January and February, right before the US and Israeli strikes began. Iran may have seen this development as alarming.
“Meanwhile, the parties had begun preparing. According to accounts circulating within their ranks, former peshmerga fighters returned from abroad, while light weapons and vehicles were acquired. These preparations do not substantiate Trump’s allegations that Kurds diverted or kept weapons intended for Iranian protesters. The parties concerned rejected those accusations, which have not been publicly substantiated,” the Amargi noted.
“For some Iranian Kurds, including activists, party supporters and observers, the 39-day war appeared to offer a long-awaited opportunity after what they considered a missed chance during the Jin, Jiyan, Azadi (Women, Life Freedom) movement. They hoped that a weakened regime would pave the way for a ground operation, but events did not unfold as they had expected.”
The Amargi added that “Iranian Kurdish parties explained their decision not to intervene by pointing to the absence of international guarantees and protection. Without air cover, external coordination and a broader uprising in Iran, they feared that an operation would fail and leave civilians exposed to retaliation.”
Barzani’s critique of the groups may not be everything it seems on the surface. He may be trying to reduce tensions with Iran by showing that the KRG is listening to Iran’s concerns. So long as Iran believes that the KRG will rein in these groups, or at least prod them not to send forces over the border, then Iran may reduce its attacks. A recent statement from KDPI, one of the Kurdish Iranian groups, also indicated that KDPI will not send its forces over the border. KDPI tends to be politically close to the KDP, and it will not want to cause the KRG any trouble. KDPI members have resided in the KRG for decades and their facilities near Koya have been frequently targeted by Iran.
Iran knows it can’t eliminate all the Kurdish opposition. It likely prefers the groups weakened and abroad, rather than fighting in Iran. For this reason, Iran is willing to wait and see if the KRG can make sure the groups’ activity is curtailed. Barzani’s comments were aimed at reducing tensions with Tehran in this respect.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

EU Opens Two More Accession Clusters for Ukraine After Rada Passes Minority Education Law
The European Union formally opened two more negotiating clusters for Ukraine on October 13 during an Intergovernmental Conference session in Luxembourg.
The announcement came at a press conference following the meeting, Transparency International Ukraine reported.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The newly opened negotiation areas cover Cluster 2, which addresses the internal market, and Cluster 3, which focuses on competitiveness and growth.
European officials confirmed that identical negotiation tracks were launched for Moldova on the same day.
According to Transparency International Ukraine, the advancement became possible after the Verkhovna Rada passed amendments to the national law on education across both readings in a single session, meeting conditions previously required by Hungary.
While calling the milestone an essential step for European integration, the NGO noted that the overall pace of progress still falls behind the targets set in June 2026.
“A significant part of the reforms from the Roadmap is still ahead, and this is a chance to show Europe that Ukraine is capable of fulfilling its obligations. Yesterday’s vote on the law on the educational rights of national minorities showed that when there is political will, the Rada can pass the necessary decision in the first reading and as a whole in one meeting,” stated Andrii Borovyk, Executive Director of Transparency International Ukraine.
The decision follows the agreement of all 27 member states on October 12. Ukraine has now opened four of six clusters, with Cluster 4 (Green Agenda) and Cluster 5 (Resources, Agriculture and Cohesion) still ahead.

France Opens Criminal Probe Into Captain of Suspected Russian Shadow Fleet Tanker
French prosecutors in Saint-Denis, Réunion, have opened a criminal investigation into the captain of DF Peak, a tanker suspected of belonging to Russia’s shadow fleet, Le Monde reported on October 13.
The case centers on the captain’s failure to justify the vessel’s nationality during an inspection at sea, which confirmed that its Beninese flag was irregular.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The offense carries potential penalties of up to two years in prison and a fine of €300,000 ($327,000), alongside the possible confiscation of the vessel.
Investigators are working to clarify the operating conditions of the tanker and identify both its owner and operator, who may also face criminal charges, according to the Saint-Denis prosecutor.
Currently, 21 crew members of various nationalities remain on board. They have been placed under restrictive measures limiting their movement for an initial period of 48 hours, which can be extended by a judge.
On the morning of October 12, the French Navy intercepted the crude oil tanker DF Peak in the Indian Ocean, more than 450 nautical miles south of Réunion Island.
Authorities detained the vessel over suspicions that it operated under a false flag to facilitate illegal fuel transport, an action French President Emmanuel Macron announced while emphasizing France's resolve to combat the shadow fleet globally.
According to Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence War&Sanctions portal, the tanker was linked to the sanctioned Russian carrier Sovcomflot and remained subject to sanctions imposed by the United States, Canada, the European Union, Ukraine, Switzerland, Japan, and the United Kingdom.

NEW DELHI: Senior AAP leader and Rajya Sabha member Sanjay Singh on Wednesday warned Prime Minister Narendra Modi against targeting young protesters after Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) activists Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das were sent to five days of judicial custody following their detention in an attempt to breach Jantar Mantar.In a post on X, Sanjay accused the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) of opposing the national flag. China-North Korea border bridge to open Oct. 15, Beijing announces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:01:51 UTC
17:01:51 KST

Faisal Mahmud
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
China announced Wednesday that a new bridge connecting the country with North Korea will officially open to traffic on Thursday, marking a further step toward strengthening cross-border connectivity between the two neighbors.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning made the announcement during a regular press briefing in Beijing.
“As agreed between China and the DPRK, the new Yellow River Bridge connecting the two countries will officially open to traffic on October 15th,” Mao said, adding that a joint inauguration ceremony would be held Thursday.
DPRK stands for the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea, North Korea’s official name.
Mao described China and North Korea as friendly neighbors connected by mountains and rivers.
She said the bridge would facilitate bilateral trade and people-to-people exchanges, bringing greater benefits to citizens of both countries.
The 3-kilometer (1.9-mile), bridge connects Dandong in China’s northeastern Liaoning province with Sinuiju in North Korea.
Its construction began in October 2011.
China remains North Korea’s largest trading partner, despite international sanctions imposed over Pyongyang’s nuclear weapons program.

Ex-President Yushchenko calls on Trump to abandon trade with Russia, concessions to Putin
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:00:58 EEST
17:00:58 KST

Third President of Ukraine Viktor Yushchenko addressed an open letter to President of the U.S Donald Trump, criticizing the authorization of trade in Russian diesel fuel and calling for the fulfillment of security commitments under the Budapest Memorandum, the politician published the appeal on Facebook on Wednesday.
"It looks wild and painful when calls are heard for Ukraine to 'stop,' instructions on whom we should elect and how to live, or when a green light is given to trade in Russian diesel. Every dollar from this diesel is a purchased missile that will strike our homes tomorrow," Yushchenko stressed in his appeal.
According to the former president, trading with an aggressor country during wartime directly finances its war machine, while talks by the U.S about the possibility of concessions or agreements with Vladimir Putin immediately provoke the Kremlin into new strikes with ballistic missiles and guided aerial bombs against residential neighborhoods in Kyiv, Zaporizhia, Odesa, Dnipro, and Kharkiv region.
Yushchenko reminded the head of the White House that following the collapse of the USSR, Ukraine voluntarily surrendered the world's third-largest nuclear arsenal in exchange for official guarantees of security, sovereignty, and the inviolability of borders, sealed by the U.S signature on the Budapest Memorandum in 1994.
In addition, the former Ukrainian head of state drew a historical parallel with Washington's policy in the 1930s, when the U.S supplied oil to Imperial Japan for the sake of preserving stability, which ultimately led to the Japanese air attack on Pearl Harbor using American fuel. At the same time, the politician pointed to the joint struggle of Ukrainians and Americans in World War II, mentioning Ukrainian-born Sergeant Michael Strank, who raised the US flag over Iwo Jima, and Ukrainian Alexander Silvashko during the historic meeting of allies on the Elbe on April 25, 1945.
Concluding the appeal, Yushchenko emphasized that the Ukrainian people will never yield their territory and will not succumb to Russian missile blackmail, summarizing that "one does not negotiate with tyrants – one stops them."

India remains a ‘natural partner’ for Russia – Jaishankar
India remains a natural partner for Russia as Moscow turns increasingly toward Asia amid its deteriorating relations with European nations, Indian Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar has said. Maintaining strong ties with Moscow serves the interests of both countries and the wider world, he added. 
Russia’s relationship with Europe has become “pretty much a broken, embittered relationship,” pushing Moscow to strengthen its ties with Asia, particularly China, Jaishankar told the Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi on Tuesday. 
He noted that Russia had historically considered itself a European country and valued its relationships with both Europe and the US, but that sanctions following the escalation of the conflict in Ukraine had pushed it toward Asia.

China's foreign trade maintains sound momentum in first three quarters
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:00:06 CST
17:00:06 KST

The State Council Information Office (SCIO) holds a press conference on China's import and export of the first three quarters of 2026 in Beijing, capital of China, Oct. 14, 2026. (Xinhua/Jin Liangkuai)
BEIJING, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- China's foreign trade maintained sound momentum in the first three quarters of 2026, with both exports and imports growing rapidly and the overall growth rate reaching its highest level for the same period in five years, official data showed Wednesday.
The country's total imports and exports rose 18.8 percent year on year to 39.94 trillion yuan (about 5.94 trillion U.S. dollars) in the January-September period, according to the General Administration of Customs (GAC).
Growth accelerated through the year, with the expansion rate rising from 15.3 percent in the first quarter to 18.3 percent in the second quarter and 22.3 percent in the third quarter.
Foreign trade growth in the first three quarters was the fastest for the same period in the past five years, with both quarterly and monthly growth rates generally accelerating, said Wang Jun, GAC's deputy head.
"Latest international data show that such a growth rate ranks among the top among major economies, and China remains the world's largest trader of goods," the official told a press conference on Wednesday.
Exports increased 16.4 percent year on year to 23.2 trillion yuan, while imports expanded by 22.3 percent to 16.74 trillion yuan, GAC data showed.
In September alone, China's total imports and exports reached 5.16 trillion yuan, up 27.5 percent from a year earlier and crossing the 5-trillion-yuan mark for the first time. This figure also marked the sixth consecutive month of double-digit monthly growth.
Exports rose 29.6 percent year on year to 3.03 trillion yuan, while imports grew 24.6 percent to 2.13 trillion yuan for the month.
The country's trade with more than 180 countries and regions expanded during the first three quarters. Trade with free trade partners reached 19.55 trillion yuan, up 30 percent and contributing over 70 percent of the total trade increment. Meanwhile, trade with other APEC economies rose 23.9 percent to 24.07 trillion yuan.
Trade with ASEAN grew 22.7 percent to 6.84 trillion yuan, that with the European Union rose 8.4 percent to 4.78 trillion yuan, and trade with the United States increased 4.1 percent to 3.18 trillion yuan.
Exports continued to shift toward new and higher-quality growth drivers. The equipment manufacturing sector contributed nearly 90 percent of the export increment, while intermediate goods accounted for more than half of total exports, underpinning global industrial and supply chains, according to the GAC. ■

China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:59:58 CST
16:59:58 KST

SEOUL, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's new jobless claims fell for a third straight month due to a sharp contraction in the construction sector, government data showed Wednesday.
The number of new applicants for job-seeking benefits dipped 2.5 percent from a year earlier to 87,000 in September, keeping a downward trajectory since July, according to the Ministry of Employment and Labor.
The statistical breakdown highlighted a significant reduction in claims from the construction industry that was offset by moderate increases in healthcare and retail sectors.
The construction sector recorded the steepest decline of 22.4 percent last month, and the manufacturing industry followed with a decrease of 6.8 percent.
New jobless claims in the healthcare and social welfare and wholesale and retail sectors grew 7 percent and 2.5 percent, respectively, in the cited month.
The government offers the job-seeking benefits to help the unemployed find work, accounting for the majority of unemployment benefits. It is financed by the state employment insurance fund.
The number of benefit recipients totaled 601,000 in September, down 3.7 percent from a year earlier.
It was driven by a substantial contraction of beneficiaries in the construction industry, the number of which dropped 26.8 percent last month.
The total payout for job-seeking benefits declined 3.4 percent to 1.03 trillion won (about 771 million U.S. dollars) in the cited month. ■

S. Korea's ICT exports hit record high in September amid AI boom
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:59:29 CST
16:59:29 KST

SEOUL, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's exports of information and communications technology (ICT) products hit a record high, driven by an unprecedented global boom in artificial intelligence (AI), government data showed Wednesday.
The ICT product shipments skyrocketed 195.8 percent from a year earlier to 75.15 billion U.S. dollars in September, topping 70 billion dollars for the first time in history, according to the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources.
The milestone surpassed the previous record of 59.98 billion dollars set just a month earlier in August, keeping an upward trajectory for 20 consecutive months since February 2025.
The ICT sector served as the primary driver of the country's export growth, accounting for 62.1 percent of South Korea's total exports last month.
Semiconductor exports spiked 262.8 percent to reach an all-time high of 60.33 billion dollars, marking a triple-digit increase for nine straight months.
The historic performance was propelled by expanding global AI infrastructure investments that led to higher demand and soaring prices for memory chips used in AI chipsets.
Display panel shipments shrank 11.5 percent to 1.70 billion dollars amid adjustments in release schedules for some smartphone models, but mobile phone exports jumped 28.2 percent to 1.90 billion dollars thanks to strong demand for premium models alongside rising exports of parts such as camera modules.
Shipments for computers and peripherals surged 393.0 percent to 7.16 billion dollars, fueled by robust demand for solid-state drives, while communications equipment exports fell 2.3 percent to 220 million dollars.
The country's imports of ICT products soared 55.3 percent over the year to 21.43 billion dollars in September, sending the trade surplus in the ICT industry to 53.71 billion dollars.
The ICT trade surplus exceeded 50 billion dollars for the first time in history. ■

	 Servicemen of the Combined Arms Army of the Central Military District (CMD) have arrived in the Republic of Belarus to take part in the command-and-staff exercise with the CSTO Peacekeeping Forces “Indestructible Brotherhood-2026” and the special exercise with the CSTO joint NBC protection and medical support formation “Barrier-2026”.
CSTO Peacekeeping Forces practice checkpoint procedures as part of the “Indestructible Brotherhood-2026” exercise
14.10.2026
At the Losvido training range in the Republic of Belarus, peacekeeping units practiced tactical procedures at a stationary checkpoint as part of the process of coordinating units and practicing joint actions during the command-and-staff exercise with the CSTO Peacekeeping Forces “Indestructible Brotherhood-2026”.
Checkpoints are designed to enforce access control, ensure security and maintain public order, prevent unlawful activities, and detain offenders.
The main tasks of peacekeepers at checkpoints are to demonstrate the presence of peacekeeping forces to all parties to the conflict and to the local population in the area of the operation, monitor the situation in their area of responsibility, inspect and control the movement of people and vehicles, and prevent the smuggling of weapons, ammunition, explosives and other prohibited items.
A standard checkpoint has been set up at the Losvido training range, demonstrating modern approaches to organizing security. The facility includes several fortified firing positions providing reliable protection for peacekeepers. Areas have been designated for personnel and armored vehicles, enabling a rapid response to changes in the situation. Special zones have been equipped for vehicle inspections, while gates on both sides of the checkpoint and warning signs around its perimeter enhance security and ensure orderly operations.
The actions of peacekeepers during the “Indestructible Brotherhood-2026” exercise demonstrate the high level of readiness of the CSTO Peacekeeping Forces to carry out peacekeeping and security tasks. The skills practiced at the Losvido training range will enable them to operate effectively in real-world peacekeeping operations.
The Republic of Belarus is hosting the command-and-staff exercise with the CSTO Peacekeeping Forces “Indestructible Brotherhood-2026” and the special exercise with the CSTO joint NBC protection and medical support formation “Barrier-2026”.
The exercises involve contingents of the CSTO Troops (Collective Forces) from the Republic of Belarus, the Republic of Kazakhstan, the Kyrgyz Republic, the Russian Federation and the Republic of Tajikistan. These include military contingents, units of internal affairs bodies (police) and the National Guard, as well as operational groups from the CSTO Joint Staff and Secretariat. The Russian military contingent is primarily composed of units of the Combined Arms Army of the Central Military District.
In total, more than 1,500 servicemen and over 300 items of weapons, military and special equipment are involved, including approximately 80 different types of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs).

Ministry’s statement
- Overnight, the Russian Armed Forces launched a massive strike using ground-based precision weapons and long-range attack drones against targets in Ukraine, the Defense Ministry reported.
- According to the ministry, the strike hit communication and energy infrastructure facilities in Kiev and the Kiev and Kharkov Regions used to support the military-industrial complex and the armed forces of Ukraine.
Targets hit
- The ministry later specified that the ATM Ukrsibbank data center in Kiev was hit. The facility handled Internet traffic exchange for gathering intelligence about the Russian Armed Forces.
- Russian forces also struck the Darnitskaya combined heat and power plant (CHP-4), powering military-industrial complex facilities in Kiev.
- In addition, the Kievskaya combined heat and power plant (CHP-5) was hit; it supplies electricity to military facilities and military-industrial enterprises in Kiev and the Kiev Region.

- Russian forces also struck the Kievskaya electrical substation, providing for the transmission and distribution of electricity from western Ukrainian regions to Ukraine’s military facilities in the Kiev Region.
- Furthermore, the Kharkov CHP-5 combined heat and power plant, powering military-industrial facilities in Kharkov and the western part of the Kharkov Region, was struck.
- The Russian Armed Forces also struck the Zmiyevskaya thermal power plant, supplying electricity to Ukrainian military facilities in the southeastern part of the Kharkov Region.

- Energy facilities in Kiev sustained damage following explosions, city mayor Vitali Klitschko reported.

- He provided no further details.

12th Kyiv International Economic Forum to Take Place on October 26, Focusing on Business and Economic Resilience Amid New Challenges
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:53:42 EEST
16:53:42 KST

Kyiv will host the 12th Kyiv International Economic Forum (KIEF) on October 26, bringing together more than 500 participants, including owners and executives of Ukrainian and international companies, government officials, investors, diplomats, and experts. This year’s theme, “People. Business. Economy. What’s Next?”, will guide discussions on how businesses and Ukraine’s economy can withstand mounting challenges, adapt to changing conditions, and return to growth.
Now in the fifth year of Russia’s full-scale invasion, Ukraine’s economy faces growing pressure. Russian attacks continue to target industrial facilities, energy infrastructure, ports, railways, logistics hubs, and other assets critical to business operations. According to Ukraine’s Ministry of Economy, direct damage from destruction could reach approximately $10 billion annually. Combined with the blockade of seaports, these losses have already cost Ukraine an estimated 1.5 percentage points of GDP in 2026.
In its October forecast, the World Bank projects that Ukraine’s economic growth will slow to 1.2% in 2026 and reach just 1.5% in 2027 if active hostilities continue. The Bank previously projected 4% growth in 2027, assuming hostilities would end by late 2026.
“While discussions previously focused on Ukraine’s reconstruction, the priority today is how to strengthen economic resilience here and now. Businesses need solutions that will help them protect their assets, maintain production, and continue investing even during wartime”, says Vasyl Khmelnytskyi, KIEF initiator, founder of UFuture holding.
Participant Registration
KIEF 2026 will feature 14 panel discussions addressing the most pressing challenges facing Ukraine’s economy. Key topics will include protecting business facilities, maintaining operations during air raid alerts, decentralizing logistics and energy supply, ensuring reliable communications, insuring against war-related risks, securing compensation for lost assets, accessing finance, and maintaining macroeconomic stability.
Discussions will also explore how Ukraine can adapt its industrial development strategy and energy policy to new realities, redefine national economic priorities, strengthen international cooperation, and advance European integration amid emerging challenges. Special attention will go to frontline cities and the practical solutions they have already implemented to keep their economies functioning.
Confirmed forum speakers include:
- Oleksandr Komarov, CEO and President of Kyivstar Group;
- Ruslan Shostak, President of TERWIN Corporation, founder of EVA and Varus;
- Francis Malige, Managing Director, Head of Financial Institutions, EBRD;
- Yuliia Svyrydenko, President of KSE Business School;
- Vyacheslav Klymov, Co-owner of NOVA Group;
- Dominykas Tuckus, Managing Director of the Amber Infrastructure Fund;
- Igor Nikonov, Founder of the Ukrainian development company KAN Development;
- Tomas Fiala, Founder of Dragon Capital;
- Inga Andreieva, Country Manager, Ukraine and Moldova, Mastercard;
- David Godfrey, Board Member, British-Ukrainian Economic Future, Former Chief, Executive, UK Export Finance (UKEF) | CBE.
Ukraine’s economy has already demonstrated its ability to adapt rapidly to major disruptions. In 2022, following the destruction of the Kremenchuk oil refinery and the resulting fuel shortages, the country rebuilt its fuel supply chains, while thousands of businesses relocated from frontline regions to safer areas further inland.
In 2023, Ukraine launched its own maritime corridor after traditional shipping routes were blocked. Following large-scale attacks on the power grid last year, businesses and the government also accelerated the development of distributed power generation.
Media Accreditation
“Today, any discussion about the future must start with practical decisions that businesses, the government, and international partners can make right now to sustain economic resilience and restore growth. This is precisely what KIEF 2026 is about”, says Yuriy Pyvovarov, CEO of KIEF.
Title Partners: UFuture, Mastercard, AEQUO, PrivatBank, Kyivstar
Forum Partners: Sense Bank, NEQSOL Holding, FUIB, DTEK, Ajax Systems, Uklon, TERWIN, Eclectic Talents Group, BALEX, CEO Club Ukraine
Interfax-Ukraine is the forum's media partner.

Complaints of nuisance behaviour on Hong Kong public transport hit 3-year high
Noisy and inconsiderate passengers who play loud music or put feet up on seats in the spotlight as government cites jump in complaints since 2023
Complaints about noisy and inconsiderate passengers on Hong Kong’s public transport have more than doubled over three years, with authorities recording a surge in reports of people playing loud music and putting their feet on seats.
The Transport Department and Environmental Protection Department received 66 complaints about noise nuisance and improper or unhygienic behaviour in 2025, up from 31 in 2023, according to figures released by the government on Wednesday.
“[Passengers] should be considerate and maintain mutual respect towards other passengers when using public transport services,” Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan said in a written reply to lawmaker Mark Chong Ho-fung.
Noise complaints, including those involving passengers playing audio at high volume on electronic devices, rose from 10 in 2023 to 11 in 2024, and then to 24 last year.

Ukrainian drones hit Russia's biggest data centre
MOSCOW, Oct 14 - Ukrainian drones hit Russia's biggest data centre, owned by the country's largest bank and technology company, Sberbank, but did not disrupt its operations, a senior company executive said on Wednesday.
The strike in the Saratov region on the Volga River followed three attacks in the past week on data centres owned by Russian tech group Yandex. Ukraine says it is responding to Russian attacks on its own data sites.
"We confirm that the data processing centre was attacked. At the same time, all of Sberbank's systems and services are operating normally and without disruption," Sberbank First Deputy CEO Alexander Vedyakhin told reporters.

Both companies have invested heavily in the development of their models but lag global leaders in the United States and China by up to nine months, partly due to Western sanctions which complicate Russia's access to the most advanced hardware.
Russia's state RIA Novosti news agency reported in 2024 that the Sberbank centre that was hit in Balakovo, covering an area of 55,000 square metres, will host Russia's biggest supercomputer, which is scheduled to go into operation in 2027.
The site is located next to the Balakovo nuclear power plant and the Saratov hydroelectric power plant.
Neither Yandex nor Sberbank have said whether supercomputers were damaged in the Ukrainian attacks. REUTERS

Saudi employee arrested for allegedly bugging OpenAI office
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:49:58 UTC
16:49:58 KST

Breadcrumb
FBI arrests Saudi employee for allegedly bugging OpenAI office
A Saudi employee of OpenAI was arrested after allegedly planting a recording device in one of the company's San Francisco offices, the AI firm and federal prosecutors said Tuesday.
"We discovered a sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices" and "referred the matter to the FBI," OpenAI told AFP in a statement.
OpenAI's security team found the device late last month and the employee, Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan, was arrested on 9 October, the US Justice Department said.
Alfozan, a 35-year-old engineer who had worked for OpenAI since July 2025, allegedly wrapped a USB device in toilet paper and inserted it into a television located in an "executive conference room," according to a Justice Department statement.
He was allegedly caught on camera "near" the conference room multiple times but was not authorised to participate in meetings located there.
He used a "productivity tool" to search for more information about OpenAI's office buildings, meeting rooms, calendars, schedules and people's locations, according to the statement.
A chatbot account connected to Alfozan's spouse also allegedly contained queries related to remote audio recording and encrypting memory cards.
"This serious situation underscores why winning the global super intelligence race is a national security prerogative," Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said in the statement.
"The intelligence community remains committed to safeguarding America's cutting-edge intellectual property from foreign threats," Clayton added.
The arrest and allegations come amid a fierce global race to dominate in artificial intelligence, which the Trump administration has pushed to be rebranded as "superintelligence."
Saudi Arabia's state-backed AI firm Humain invested $3 billion in Elon Musk's xAI shortly before the American billionaire's space company, SpaceX, acquired the AI division in February.
Now known as SpaceXAI, the division announced last year that it was teaming up with Humain to build a 500-megawatt data center in Saudi Arabia.
Multiple devices
It was not immediately clear what, if any information the recording device was able to collect.
"At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data," OpenAI told AFP in a statement.
A second device was found by OpenAI's security team when they searched an unattended bag that belonged to Alfozan, according to the Justice Department.
Alfozan was caught on security footage from inside the restricted conference room where he appeared to look behind the television where the recording device had been placed, the Department said.
A LinkedIn account matching Alfozan's name and resume show that he previously worked at Facebook-owner Meta, as well as an AI startup and a venture capital firm.
He was also a student at University of California at Berkeley and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
The Justice Department said Alfozen had been charged with "using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications," for which he could face up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine.
It did not accuse Alfozan nor Saudi Arabia, which is a close US ally, of spying activity in its statement on Tuesday.
Alfozan is expected to appear at a federal court hearing on 19 October.
In 2022, a former Twitter worker, Ahmad Abouammo, was found guilty of spying for Saudi officials keen to unmask critics on the platform.

U.S. moves leave Ukraine less able to defend itself
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:49:49 UTC
16:49:49 KST

- Ukraine received no partner warnings of Russian ballistic missile launches for two straight nights, the Ukrainian Air Force said, detecting missiles only minutes before impact.
- Starlink also stopped working above 160 km/h for Ukraine’s military, hitting tactical drones used in defense, as Russia’s strike left 600,000 without power.
Ukraine’s ability to defend itself against Russian strikes has been limited by two U.S. moves in a single night: the country went without early warning of Russian ballistic missile launches from its partners for a second time in a row, and Starlink, the U.S. satellite service its frontline units depend on, was cut back for the Ukrainian military just as Russia launched one of its heaviest missile attacks on Ukraine’s power grid.
The Ukrainian Air Force said Russia launched a ballistic missile attack on Kyiv at about 10:40 p.m. on Oct. 13, and that once again no information about the launches had come from Ukraine’s partners before the missiles were in the air. The Air Force said the reasons were being investigated.
“The situation is similar to yesterday’s. No information regarding launches from enemy territory had been received from our partners. The reasons are being investigated,” the Ukrainian Air Force said in an official statement.
Ukraine has relied heavily on early warning from the United States, whose satellites can spot the heat of a missile launch deep inside Russia within moments, giving Ukrainian air defense crews time to prepare and giving cities time to sound air raid sirens. Without those alerts, Ukrainian forces only detected the incoming ballistic missiles once they came within range of ground radars, a few minutes before impact, and tried to shoot some of them down. The lost minutes shorten the reaction time for interceptor crews and hit civilians hardest, leaving people in Kyiv and other cities less time to reach shelters and metro stations.
The attack that followed was massive. Zelenskyy said Russia fired 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 attack drones and loitering munitions overnight into Oct. 14 at energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, the Kyiv region and Kharkiv, damaging 26 facilities in the power system and four in the oil and gas sector and leaving at least 600,000 people without electricity. He said there were dead and injured and warned that outages could spread.
Zelenskyy said the missile salvo deliberately targeted the energy infrastructure covered by the ceasefire President Donald Trump announced on Oct. 11, which Moscow never confirmed accepting.
“Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States,” said Zelenskyy.
During the same night, Starlink terminals used by Ukraine’s military began losing their connection whenever they moved faster than 160 km/h (100 mph). Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Zelenskyy who is widely known by his call sign “Flash” and who has tracked Russian attempts to jam Starlink along the front, said the restriction hit the military StarShield package of the SpaceX service and that units received no notice before it took effect.
“Our defense forces did not receive any warning about this restriction, and it led to the disruption of a number of missions. It is obvious that this action cannot be a coincidence and is linked to the current political situation,” said Serhii Beskrestnov.
The restriction falls on Ukraine’s defense, not on its strikes inside Russia. SpaceX has never allowed Ukraine to use Starlink for strikes on Russian territory, and Zelenskyy said earlier this month that Kyiv was still asking for that permission, so Ukraine’s long-range drones and cruise missiles that hit targets in Russia do not rely on the service. Starlink has also been unavailable to Russian forces since February, when SpaceX and Ukraine’s Defense Ministry introduced a whitelist that cut off unregistered Russian terminals. Inside Ukraine, Starlink is used on tactical drones and uncrewed ground vehicles that operate over Ukrainian and Russian-occupied territory, so a speed cap above 160 km/h cuts the links of fast tactical strike and interceptor drones fighting Russian troops and drones along the front.
Ukrainian volunteer Serhii Sternenko, who first reported the change, said ordinary satellite terminals kept working and suggested SpaceX may have acted at the request of the Trump administration, while British analyst Jimmy Rushton noted that the limit does nothing to protect the Russian oil refineries Trump has criticized Ukraine for striking.
Ballistic missiles are the hardest part of Russia’s strike packages for Ukraine to stop, because they fly too fast and too high for most of its air defense systems, and Ukraine relies mainly on U.S.-made Patriot batteries to intercept them. Zelenskyy asked Washington and other partners for more Patriot interceptors and called on Trump to impose strong sanctions on Russia under the law sponsored by Sen. Lindsey Graham, which Trump signed in September.
“We ask for additional packages of Patriot missile interceptors for Ukraine,” said Zelenskyy.
The Ukrainian Air Force warned that further Russian attacks cannot be ruled out. Neither the White House nor SpaceX has explained why the missile launch warnings stopped or why the Starlink speed limit was introduced, or said whether either change is temporary.

Ukrainian OSINT channel: Russia turned a bare field into a Geran-5 launch site in a month—and drones are already arriving
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:49:28 UTC
16:49:28 KST

Russia has nearly finished the first section of a new launch site for jet-powered Geran-5 attack drones near the town of Millerovo in Rostov Oblast, anonymous Ukrainian OSINT channel Absolutely Reliable Source reported on 13 October. The channel’s bio says it covers Ukraine’s deep strikes and that its author belongs to a larger, unnamed structure. It says Russia rushed the build to scale up attacks after its September strikes on Kyiv.
The site is meant for the kind of drone Ukraine stops far less often than the older Shaheds. Ukraine downs 55% of jet-powered Shaheds, the class that includes the Geran-5, and more than 90% of the older propeller-driven ones, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 26 September. Russian industry makes about 3,000 Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones a month, Ukraine’s military intelligence (HUR) told Militarnyi in August. A new launch site is how Russia plans to fire more of them, the channel argues.
Built in weeks, by the channel’s count
The channel’s images from 1 September show no construction at the site. The latest ones show eight prepared positions for launchers and 32 places for preparing drones for launch, the channel wrote. Imagery from the day before its post shows drones being unloaded in one zone, it said.
The channel’s headline says the work took a month. Ukrainian outlet Militarnyi, comparing the channel’s own images from 1 September and 12 October, put it at about six weeks. Both readings rest on the same images, which have not been independently verified.
Built like Tsymbulova
The construction style is very similar to Tsymbulova, Russia’s jet-drone base in Oryol Oblast, the channel wrote. That base has separate positions for storing, preparing, and launching jet drones, Militarnyi said. By late May, less than a month into an expansion of Tsymbulova, Russia was already building 10 more launchers there.
Ukrainian drones have hit Tsymbulova repeatedly, though most of the damage imagery comes from Absolutely Reliable Source. Militarnyi reported strikes on the base’s bunkers and hangars in September. Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck it again overnight on 1 October, damaging two ground shelters and drone preparation areas, Absolutely Reliable Source said. On 10 October, OSINT channel Exilenova+ reported another drone strike there, saying several bunkers, one jet-drone launcher, and a drone storage area were hit.

Russian occupation forces over the past few days launched several dozen jet-powered Geran-4 drones from the territory of temporarily occupied Crimea into western Ukraine, with individual units covering a distance of 880 kilometre, reported presidential advisor Serhiy Beskrestnov (Flash).
"Thus, our adversary is exploring the possibilities of attacking western regions of Ukraine with jet-powered 'Shaheds' from various directions. The maximum flight range of the 'Geran-4' turned out to be slightly greater than expected," Serhiy Flash wrote on Facebook.
According to his data, the route of enemy drones ran from Crimea through Odesa and along the border with Moldova. Four jet drones reached Lviv, covering a distance of 820 kilometre, while several others reached Lutsk at a distance of 880 kilometre from the launch site.
To cover such a distance, the Geran-4 devices maintained an altitude of 5–6 kilometre and an average speed of 320–380 kilometres per hour m . Flash suggests that to increase the flight range, the Russian military may have reduced the drone's warhead weight.

Americans say Trump misusing presidency for personal wealth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:45:47 UTC
16:45:47 KST

More than half of Americans believe US President Donald Trump is placing his personal wealth ahead of the country’s interests, while roughly six in 10 think he is profiting from the presidency in ways they consider illegal or unethical.
According to a new survey by The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research, 56% of US adults believe Trump has placed “a lot” of emphasis on his personal business interests since returning to the White House.
By comparison, only about one-quarter said he had given the same level of attention to the interests of the country as a whole, while roughly one in 10 said he had focused heavily on people like them.
The survey also found that around 60% of Americans believe Trump is either illegally profiting from his presidency or engaging in unethical behavior that does not necessarily break the law.
About 40% said they believe he is doing something illegal, while approximately 20% considered his conduct unethical but not illegal. Only about one-fifth said he was doing nothing wrong.
“His wealth increases,” said Barbara Thaxton, an 87-year-old independent voter from Florida. “But the people in the country are just barely getting by.”
The findings come as Trump’s family business expands into new ventures, including cryptocurrency and overseas real estate deals, raising renewed questions about potential conflicts of interest between his private financial activities and his public responsibilities.
Trump has relaxed restrictions on his family’s overseas business activities that were in place during his first term and launched several cryptocurrency ventures since returning to office.
In a financial disclosure filed in June, the president reported receiving more than $1 billion from new cryptocurrency businesses, according to the report, according to Press TV.
One major venture received a $500 million investment from a United Arab Emirates business linked to the country’s royal family after Trump’s election victory.
The Trump Organization has also pursued eight foreign real estate deals during the first year of his presidency, including projects in countries where governments exert considerable influence over private business.

More than 200 firefighters and 49 vehicles and pieces of equipment were deployed to contain the blaze.

Kazakhstan reveals key spending priorities for 2027

Kazakhstan reveals key spending priorities for 2027
Kazakhstan’s Minister of Finance Madi Takiyev presented the draft law on the republican budget for 2027–2029 to members of the Qurultay, outlining the Government’s key spending priorities for the coming year, Qazinform News Agency reports.
According to the minister, the draft budget was developed in line with the Budget Code and the country’s socioeconomic development forecast through 2030.
For 2027, Kazakhstan projects budget revenues of 25.4 trillion tenge and expenditures of 30.2 trillion tenge, with a planned deficit of 4.6 trillion tenge, or 2.3% of GDP.
“In 2027, 6.9 trillion tenge will be allocated to social assistance and social security, while healthcare will receive 2.5 trillion tenge to fund guaranteed free medical services, medicines, and health insurance,” Takiyev said.
The Government also plans to allocate 60.4 billion tenge to scientific research projects in 2027, up 18.4 billion tenge from 2026.
Regional development is another key priority, with around 7.4 trillion tenge, or nearly a quarter of the annual budget, allocated to this area.
The funds will primarily go toward improving social and public utility infrastructure to enhance living standards.
Meanwhile, 3.7 trillion tenge has been earmarked for the real sector of the economy in 2027, with most of the funding directed toward transport infrastructure, agriculture, industry, entrepreneurship, and digital development.
“Another priority is security, public administration, and reserves, for which 4.9 trillion tenge has been allocated in 2027. The largest share, 3.3 trillion tenge, will go to law enforcement and security agencies, while 787 billion tenge is earmarked for public administration,” the minister said.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Economy Serik Zhumangarin had presented Kazakhstan’s socioeconomic development forecast for 2027–2029 during a plenary session of the Qurultay.

Kazakhstan to spend $2 trillion tenge on major construction projects from National Fund

Kazakhstan to spend $2 trillion tenge on major construction projects from National Fund
In 2027, Kazakhstan plans to spend 2 trillion tenge from the National Fund on implementing a program to construct social and infrastructure facilities. This is what Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Economy Serik Zhumangarin said at the Cabinet’s weekly meeting, Qazinform News Agency reports.
According to him, budget forecasting for 2027-2029 was based on fiscal rules and targets set by the Public Finance Management Concept through 2030.
Thus, in 2027, revenues are projected to reach 19.9 trillion tenge, or 10.0% of GDP. Compared with the estimate for the current year, this represents an increase of 2.8 trillion tenge.
The main increase in revenues is projected to come from:
- Economic growth - 1. 7 trillion tenge
- VAT refund amount reduction - 1.1 trillion tenge
- Other factors - 0.5 trillion tenge
At the same time, a revenue decline of 0.5 trillion tenge is expected.
Value-added tax (VAT) and corporate income tax account for the largest shares of tax revenues. Non-tax revenues are projected at 377 billion tenge, while special revenues are estimated at 18 billion tenge.
In accordance with fiscal rules, the guaranteed transfer from the National Fund is set at 2.43 trillion tenge in 2007 and 2008, and 2 trillion tenge in 2029.
At the same time, Zhumangarin noted that the Head of State had outlined a course for a "major construction" and authorized the use of National Fund resources. A task was set to implement a large-scale program for building social and infrastructure facilities.
"In this regard, a targeted transfer from the National Fund is envisaged, amounting to 2 trillion tenge in 2027 and 1.5 trillion tenge annually in 2028-2029," the Deputy Prime Minister said.
The funds will be allocated to finance critical facilities and projects of national importance.
The National Fund’s net foreign currency assets are projected at $65.2 billion in 2027, rising to $67.3 billion in 2028 and $70.6 billion in 2029.
Earlier, it was reported that Kazakhstan forecasts inflation at 7.5-9.5% in 2027.

Wildlife photographer of the year 2026 winners – in pictures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:41:54 UTC
16:41:54 KST

Wildlife photographer of the year 2026 winners – in pictures
A selection of the winning images from this year’s competition across topics ranging from underwater to urban wildlife, and photojournalism to mammal behaviour. The overall winner is Federico Veronesi of Italy for his powerful image of an elephant carrying a dead calf
Wildlife photographer of the year 2026 | The Aftermath by Federico Veronesi, Italy | Winner, Behaviour: Mammals
Veronesi witnessed a powerful moment of an elephant carrying a dead calf, a rare glimpse into complex animal behaviours. He was tracking elephants when he came across an unusual pattern of drag marks in a dry riverbed in Namibia. A female emerged with the calf, its leg wedged between her tusk and trunk. Behaviours centring on death have been observed in Asian and African elephants, including vocalisations, guarding the dead, inspecting and handling bones and carrying the deceasedPhotograph: Federico Veronesi/Wildlife photographer of the year 2026
Escape Artistry by Michał Michalski, Poland | Winner, Natural Artistry
Michalski uses a slow shutter speed to create the illusion of trees still swathed in autumn foliage. A field of unharvested sunflowers had attracted mixed flocks of birds, especially goldfinches and bramblings. As they took to the sky, startled by a sparrowhawk, Michalski blurred the movement against a backdrop of leafless birches. There is evidence that flocks containing multiple species forage more efficiently, partly because each brings different skills to the groupPhotograph: Michał Michalski/Wildlife photographer of the year 2026
The Great Divide by Alex Visbal, Colombia | Winner, Wetlands: The Bigger Picture
Visbal documents how a single engineered line can reshape an entire wetland. The distinctive pink colour on the left is caused by microbes that thrive in extremely saline water, which happens when an area is cut off from a supply of fresh water. The ecology of the lake in Utah is in sharp decline due to industrial use, upstream diversions and climate change. Since this image was taken, the state has brought the area under conservation managementPhotograph: Alex Visbal/Wildlife photographer of the year 2026
Shedding Light by Agorastos Papatsanis, Greece | Winner, Plants and Fungi
Papatsanis uses ultraviolet light to reveal the glowing yellow stems of ‘beautiful bonnet’ mushrooms growing from a decaying log. On the lower slopes of Greece’s Mount Olympus, he experimented with UV illumination until it revealed the strongest fluorescent response from the mushroomsPhotograph: Agorastos Papatsanis/Wildlife photographer of the year 2026
Night-Time Catch by Alex Lindbloom, US | Winner, Oceans: The Bigger Picture
Lindbloom finds a whale shark investigating the catch of a bagan, or mobile net-fishing platform, in the inky waters off Papua. He started searching for sharks around dawn when the nets were still in the water. Initially lacking natural light for his drone’s camera, he found these sharks illuminated by the bagan’s bright lightsPhotograph: Alex Lindbloom/Wildlife photographer of the year 2026
A Watchful Eye by Aaron Sanders, UK | Winner, Animal Portraits
Sanders glimpses a common octopus behind a curtain of kelp in the waters off Cornwall. Aaron had been diving off Porthkerris Beach when he noticed the footprints of octopus suckers through a thin blade of kelp, and a single eye slowly emerging. ‘We remained perfectly still, watching one another with a seemingly shared curiosity,’ he saysPhotograph: Aaron Sanders/Wildlife photographer of the year 2026
Shifting Sand by Sitaram Raul, India | Winner, Behaviour: Invertebrates
Raul encounters a scorpion burrowing into one of the shifting dunes of the Thar desert. Exploring the dunes at night, he saw many scorpions searching for prey. But as sunrise approached, they started burrowing to avoid the intense heat. Raul timed the exposure so that the excavated sand was suspended in mid-airPhotograph: Sitaram Raul/Wildlife photographer of the year 2026
The Meeting Place by James Lewin, UK | Winner, Animals in their Environment
Lewin watches a young bull elephant spray a group of zebra as they congregate in Kenya’s Chyulu hills. While there was no shortage of subjects and action around this waterhole, he had to deal with the harsh, unforgiving light. He chose to soften the light using a camera converted to infrared, creating this dream-like scenePhotograph: James Lewin/Wildlife photographer of the year 2026
Afternoon Snack by Alexis Tinker-Tsavalas, Germany | Winner, Rising Star Award
Tinker-Tsavalas reveals the exquisite beauty of the tiniest of animals in the finest of detail. When he spotted this robber fly, it had already impaled the flesh fly with its needlelike mouthparts. The bubbles forming in the victim’s eyes indicate that the robber fly has injected digestive enzymes that liquefy its internal tissues before they are sucked outPhotograph: Alexis Tinker-Tsavalas/Wildlife photographer of the year 2026
Secret Worlds by Kutub Uddin, Bangladesh/UK | Winner, Portfolio Award
Kutub Uddin reveals a magical and often surreal world of slime moulds that can barely be seen with the naked eye. In this image – Tiny Dancers – an immature Cribraria aurantiaca is at a tiny and often overlooked stage in its life. Uddin became interested in slime moulds in 2024, and devotes much of his time to revealing this hidden world – exploring his local woodlands in West Sussex, where fallen logs and damp forest floors provide opportunities for discovering these fascinating organismsPhotograph: Kutub Uddin/Wildlife photographer of the year 2026
Warning Sign by Francisco Negroni, Chile | Winner, Photojournalism
Negroni recorded this scene of a dead puma amid the rugged, windswept beauty of Patagonia – tied to the fence and presented as a hunting trophy. The province of Santa Cruz in Argentina banned the hunting of pumas in 2025, but illegal persecution continues. Livestock predation is one of the major causes of human–puma conflict, and it’s suggested that enclosing sheep at night and using guard dogs can significantly reduce the loss of livestock without resorting to huntingPhotograph: Francisco Negroni/Wildlife photographer of the year 2026
Birdsong Painted in Light by Konrad Gräeter, Germany | Winner, 15-17 Years
Gräeter highlights a male blackbird singing in a vineyard early one April morning. He had to crouch down low on the steep slope of the vineyard and point his camera through a gap in the foliage to frame the blackbird within its landscape. Blackbirds can be heard singing at different times of day, but their songs have the most complex compositions at dawnPhotograph: Konrad Gräeter/Wildlife photographer of the year 2026
Protective Pose by Anton Sorokin, US | Winner, Behaviour: Amphibians and Reptiles
Sorokin finds a California newt laying its eggs as it clasps vegetation that already holds another newt’s egg clutch. He waded along the edge of the pond, carefully dipping his camera and lighting beneath the surface to record this remarkable view of parental care. The newts interlock their back feet to protect the clutch, which is vulnerable to predation by other newts. They will stay like this until the gelatinous mass around the eggs has swollen too large to be eaten and has solidified on to the stemPhotograph: Anton Sorokin/Wildlife photographer of the year 2026
Young wildlife photographer of the year 2026 | Labour of Love by Oscar Whitfield, Zimbabwe/UK | Winner, 11-14 Years
Whitfield notices the arduous exertion of this dung beetle pushing its precious cargo. Using a fast shutter speed and high light sensitivity, he lay flat on the ground to photograph the beetle at eye level, with the sunshine and heat creating dry dust all around him. Breaking up dung and burying it prevents the conditions required for methane production, reducing the quantity of greenhouse gas emissions. Burying dung also helps it decompose fasterPhotograph: Oscar Whitfield/Wildlife photographer of the year 2026
Making Morays by Tony Wu, USA/Japan | Winner, Under Water
Wu provides a first-time glimpse into the mating ritual of two Abbott’s moray eels at the apex of their spawning arc. On the verge of swimming back down to safety, the larger male in the foreground has already released a diffuse cloud of sperm, while the female in the background has just commenced ejecting a stream of eggs. This is likely the first time the courtship and spawning have been documented, and observations from Wu’s work with biologists are feeding into published scientific studies. Kagoshima Prefecture, Kyushu, JapanPhotograph: Tony Wu/Wildlife photographer of the year 2026
Scenes from the Swamp by Isak Pretorius, South Africa Winner | Behaviour: Birds
Pretorius chanced upon two elusive shoebill storks among wetland vegetation, while exploring the swamp in a narrow canoe with a guide. The birds pulled out vegetation, dropped it and then repeated the process several times. It is likely this is a breeding pair gathering nesting material. Though often called the shoebill stork, these large birds are more closely related to pelicans, herons and ibises. Fewer than 5,300 mature shoebills survive across their entire range and their numbers are decreasingPhotograph: Isak Pretorius/Wildlife photographer of the year 2026
Wily Coyotes of San Francisco by Loren Elliott, US | Winner, Photojournalist Story Award
Elliott opens a window into the lives of the often-misunderstood coyotes living in the environs of San Francisco. About 100 of these urban-adapted wild canines live alongside more than 800,000 human inhabitants, and attitudes towards them are mixed. Coyotes sometimes prey on domestic animals, but they also bring benefits such as controlling disease-carrying rodentsPhotograph: Loren Elliott/Wildlife photographer of the year 2026
Urban Jungle by Seth Forestson | UK Winner, Urban Wildlife
Forestson spots a common water monitor carrying its fish supper in a Bangkok park. The challenge wasn’t finding the lizards, but catching them in action, as they spend most of the day basking in the sun. Common water monitors have successfully adapted to living in cities across south and south-east Asia. They will take whatever food source is available, such as the plentiful supplies of catfish and koi in the lakes of Bangkok’s Lumphini ParkPhotograph: Seth Forestson/Wildlife photographer of the year 2026
Flight of the Bumblebee by Amelie Davis, UK | Winner, 10 Years and Under
Davis highlights a common carder bee suspended in mid-air as it flies in to land and feast on a flower in Surrey. On this August afternoon the garden was ‘teeming with bees’. Without her camera, she borrowed her dad’s smartphone and was able to record the delicate detail of a single wingbeat. Bees perceive plants and flowers in many ways. Distinguishing one colour for nectar and another for pollen helps them make rapid decisions when foragingPhotograph: Amelie Davis/Wildlife photographer of the year 2026

More than 1,300 Taiwanese gain Siraya identity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:41:32 UTC
16:41:32 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — As of the end of September, 1,336 Taiwanese have obtained Plains Indigenous status as members of the Siraya people.
The Plains Indigenous Peoples Status Act passed its third reading in the Legislative Yuan on Oct. 17, 2025, and was promulgated by the president on Oct. 23, taking effect on the same day, per CNA.
The Cabinet officially recognized the Siraya as one of Taiwan’s Plains Indigenous peoples on July 31. Applications to be included in the official list of Siraya group members and Plains Indigenous status registration opened on Aug. 13, according to CNA.
The law aims to protect Plains Indigenous peoples’ demand for formal recognition and their right to identity.
According to a Council of Indigenous People’s (CIP) report, the council has accepted applications for recognition from nine Plains Indigenous peoples since the law took effect: the Siraya, Taivoan, Makatao, Taokas, Kaxabu, Pazeh, Papora, Babuza and Ketagalan, CNA reported.
The CIP said a panel of experts and scholars will soon review applications from the Pazeh, Kaxabu, and Taokas peoples. A draft proposal outlining membership requirements for the Taivoan people will be announced soon.
The council said it would expedite the procedures for official recognition and identity registration.
