Russia arrests Japanese journalist on spying charges
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:12:37 BST
16:12:37 KST

Russia arrests Japanese journalist on spying charges
- Published
Russian authorities have arrested a Japanese journalist on suspicion of espionage, accusing him of gathering information related to Moscow's defence capabilities for Tokyo.
The journalist, identified as Yuki Imai from the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper, was detained in the far-eastern Sakhalin region, a day before he was due to leave Russia. He was flown to Moscow where a court ordered he be placed in pre-trial detention, Russian reports say.
Japan says it is still seeking details about the arrest, and has not been able to contact Imai.
The arrest comes as tensions worsen between the two nations after Russian leader Vladimir Putin visited the disputed Kuril Islands, claimed by both countries, in August.
Russian authorities allege that Imai "acted on the instructions of [Japan's] national intelligence service" to gather information about people involved in a special military operation on the Kuril Islands, state news agency TASS reported.
The Kuril islands sit between Hokkaido in northern Japan and Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula. The archipelago is administered by Russia, but four of the southernmost islands are claimed by Japan, which calls them the Northern Territories.
Russia's FSB security agency published footage showing three masked men in black uniforms storming a hotel room and handcuffing a man. The video then shows him being accompanied onto a plane before appearing in a cage in a Moscow court. It did not say when he was detained or when the court hearing took place.
Imai will be remanded until 12 December, before his trial begins, according to Interfax, another Russian news agency.
Those convicted of espionage in Russia can be sentenced to up to 20 years in prison.
"Tokyo's attempts to use its correspondents in Russia, who hold foreign journalist status, to gather information aimed at undermining our country's security are regrettable," Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said in a statement on Tuesday.
"We cannot help but point out that today's incident is not an isolated one," she noted, but did not name other journalists or media outlets that are allegedly involved in similar activity.
Japan has not commented at length on the arrest. Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara told a press briefing that Japan did not know about the arrest until the announcement and had had no contact yet with the journalist.
Imai's published work has covered Russia's relations with North Korea and life in Sakhalin.
Hokkaido Shimbun ran a report on the arrest without naming the reporter. "We are still confirming the details. Ensuring the reporter's safety is our top priority," it said in response to the BBC's queries.
Russia and Japan have been locked in a dispute over the Kurils for decades, and it is the main reason Moscow and Tokyo did not sign a peace treaty after World War Two.
Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi sharply criticised Putin's visit – his first-ever to the islands – saying it "wounded the feelings of the Japanese people" and is "incompatible with Japan's consistent position on the Northern Territories".
Moscow dismissed her remarks as "politically inappropriate" and "legally unfounded".
Over the years, attempts to resolve the territorial dispute have made little progress. Bilateral ties have also remained frosty, with Japan imposing sanctions against Russia for its invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Last week, Moscow again angered Tokyo by requesting the extradition of the president of the International Criminal Court (ICC), who is Japanese.
The president Tomoko Akane, along with other ICC officials, has been placed on Russia's wanted list since 2023 after the court issued an arrest warrant for Putin over war crimes in Ukraine.
In 2023, Russia detained The Wall Street Journal's Evan Gershkovich on espionage charges and later sentenced him to 16 years in prison.
Gershkovich, a US citizen, was released in a 2024 prisoner swap, the largest exchange since the Cold War ended in 1991.
In 2019, Moscow detained an unnamed Japanese journalist from Kyodo News on suspicion of attempting to obtain military secrets. The journalist, who was picked up in Vladivostok, was ordered to leave the country within 72 hours.
Additional reporting by Chie Kobayashi

Pope Leo XIV recovering from lung cancer surgery: What happens next?

In the hospital chapel, dozens of faithful prayed for the pope's health during the operation.
Pope Leo XIV had a "calm" night after lung surgery, the Vatican said on Wednesday.
The pope is recovering at Rome's Gemelli Hospital after undergoing surgery to remove a cancerous tumour from his right lung on Tuesday.
In a statement, the Vatican said the surgery had been “successfully completed, as planned and within the expected timeframe,” adding that the pope had returned to his room on the hospital's tenth floor, in a ward next to the papal apartment where Pope Francis was hospitalised a year and a half ago.
The 71-year-old pope underwent the 90-minute operation, after which the Vatican said he "woke up normally."
Part of the pope's lung was removed during surgery, and he is awaiting test results to determine whether the cancer has spread.
The statement did not mention further treatment, with the Vatican saying doctors were not yet considering chemotherapy or other therapies pending additional test results.
Experts said much would depend on how advanced the cancer was and whether it had spread.
However, the Vatican said it was detected early and was localised, both important factors in determining the prognosis.
Will the pope's recovery affect his November trip to South America?
The surgery has raised questions about whether the US-born pontiff will be able to proceed with his planned 6–17 November trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.
The Vatican said the pope's recovery is expected to take around a week, with all his audiences cancelled until 20 October.
It remains unclear whether the pontiff will be able to proceed with his planned trip to South America next month.
Oncologists generally advise patients to avoid flying for three weeks after surgery, leaving the pope just enough time to recover before the trip.
The visit, set to be the longest of his papacy so far, would involve more than 31,000 kilometres of travel across 12 flights and two helicopter journeys.
"He has decided to undergo surgery soon in order to not change his plans for future overseas trips, so there is no need to worry, as it is not an emergency,” said Tokyo Cardinal Kikuchi Tsutomu, who saw the pontiff on Monday.
The surgery marks Pope Leo XIV's first hospitalisation since becoming pope on 8 May 2025.
The Vatican has traditionally been secretive about papal health, but became more transparent during the papacy of his predecessor, Pope Francis, who openly discussed his health problems.

Houthis strike Aramco headquarters; report: Chinese components used in missile production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:12:23 UTC
16:12:23 KST

Air raid sirens sounded Wednesday morning in Riyadh and the nearby city of Al-Kharj, a day after Yemen's Houthi rebels struck the headquarters of Saudi oil giant Aramco in Dhahran, eastern Saudi Arabia. The Saudi Energy Ministry confirmed that an administrative building at the company's headquarters was hit, causing what it described as a limited fire. There were no casualties, while international media reported that it remained unclear whether the building had been struck directly by a missile or damaged by interception debris or shrapnel. 
The attack followed Saudi airstrikes on oil facilities in Houthi-controlled areas of Yemen. Before the strikes, Saudi authorities issued an evacuation warning for facilities belonging to the Yemeni Oil Company, particularly the al-Sabaha station in the capital, Sanaa. The Houthis subsequently issued their own warnings to Aramco employees, identifying the company's headquarters in Dhahran, King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and Aramco's Riyadh refinery as potential targets. Like the Saudis, the Houthis included precise locations of the threatened facilities in their announcements. 
The exchange came after a devastating Houthi attack on Riyadh's international airport on Saturday, which killed at least 13 people and wounded 309. A regional official familiar with the details told the Associated Press that the missile struck an area containing passenger terminals 3 and 4, which serve domestic flights.
According to the Saudi aviation authority, the dead included foreign nationals from the United States, Egypt, Jordan, Syria, the Palestinian territories, Sudan and Bangladesh, as well as Saudi citizens. Reports said the airport was evacuated and numerous ambulances were dispatched to the scene. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio subsequently confirmed that an American citizen had been killed and strongly condemned the attack, calling for an immediate end to strikes that endangered innocent civilians. Saudi authorities deployed heavy security around the airport and warned against distributing footage of the Houthi attacks.
Saturday's strike came just two days after another deadly Houthi assault on the same airport, Riyadh's main international aviation hub. During the earlier attack, at least one passenger aircraft, reportedly empty at the time, was damaged, and three Saudi citizens, including a pilot, were killed. Three additional people were killed in previous attacks on airports in Riyadh and Abha last week.
The strikes mark a significant escalation in the long-running conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis. Fighting has continued inside Yemen between the Iran-backed rebels and forces loyal to the internationally recognized Yemeni government, which receives Saudi military support, including extensive airstrikes. The growing ability of the Houthis to disrupt Saudi aviation represents an especially serious challenge for Riyadh, exposing vulnerabilities in its defenses and undermining confidence in the kingdom's ability to protect vital infrastructure.
Repeated missile attacks have also severely disrupted international aviation, effectively restricting access to Saudi airspace and putting additional pressure on airlines already struggling with the effects of regional wars and soaring fuel prices. The damage to airports, combined with the threat to energy infrastructure, has heightened concerns about how long the kingdom can sustain such disruptions.
The Chinese connection
Meanwhile, a report published Wednesday by The Wall Street Journal revealed that the Houthis had obtained a range of components from Chinese suppliers to develop their own version of Iran's Kheibar Shekan ballistic missile. The findings, based on research by Conflict Armament Research, suggest that the rebels are working to manufacture more advanced weapons domestically rather than relying exclusively on complete missile systems smuggled from abroad. 
The Iranian missile, which has reportedly been used against US military targets during the war with Iran, is designed to maneuver toward its target and potentially evade air defense systems. According to US assessments cited in the report, certain versions feature a warhead that separates during the final phase of flight and uses a small propulsion system to adjust its trajectory. The technology could make interception considerably more difficult.
The Conflict Armament Research report described two shipments intercepted by Yemeni authorities in 2025, with missile-related equipment concealed among other goods. The seized material reportedly included metal components for missile bodies and engines, stabilizing fins, solid-fuel rocket motor components and heat-resistant materials designed to protect parts of the missile during launch.
According to UN reports cited by The Wall Street Journal, Chinese companies have become the largest source of goods destined for the Houthis. Beijing, however, maintains that it complies with restrictions on arms sales to the rebel group. The findings raise concerns about the Houthis' growing manufacturing capabilities and their ability to acquire increasingly sophisticated missile technology despite international restrictions.
The latest escalation is also raising fears of wider economic consequences for Saudi Arabia. The kingdom's real GDP is projected to contract by 3.6% this year, reflecting several factors, including declining oil activity. The attacks have added pressure ahead of major international gatherings scheduled for Riyadh this month, including the kingdom's flagship investment conference and the World Petroleum Council's energy congress. Several senior executives have reportedly canceled plans to attend.
The impact is extending beyond the suspension of operations at Riyadh's airport. Employees in the capital's financial district were instructed to work from home Wednesday amid continuing security concerns, illustrating how the Houthi campaign is increasingly disrupting the kingdom's economic and commercial life.

Europe should move into “war mode” in terms of arms production to keep up with Russia, Poland’s defense minister has said.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Russia spent an estimated 7.5% of its GDP on military expenditure in 2025, according to an analysis by the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, and produced around seven million artillery, mortar, tank and rocket munitions, data from the Estonian Foreign Intelligence Service show.

Russia Innovates for War, Not Prosperity
EU budget ‘unacceptable’
Speaking at a joint press conference with EU Commissioner for Defense and Space Andrius Kubilius, Kosiniak-Kamysz made the case for ramping up Europe’s defense industry capacity now to prevent greater costs later.
The defense minister said Warsaw is pushing for increased defense and security spending in the EU budget, describing current proposals by the Irish presidency as “unacceptable” to Poland.
“I understand that Ireland is a neutral country, situated far away on an island, and does not feel these threats [from Russia], but the role of the presidency is to hear the voice of those who do feel the threats, and our strong voice,” Kosiniak-Kamysz said, adding that the issue had formed the starting point of his talks with Kubilius.
Ireland, which holds the rotating six-month presidency of the Council of the EU, presented a budget proposal for 2028–2034 on Saturday that foresees an 8% cut in expenditure compared with the European Commission’s plan and trims the broader competitiveness, prosperity and security budget heading by around 13%.
Kosiniak-Kamysz pointed out that under Kubilius, EU-level defense financing had “grown radically,” but said it must be increased further, arguing that the “time has come” for Europe to multiply its defense production, as failure to do so would not only cost more in the future but also affect the prospects of future generations.
“Poland has already been through this,” he said. “So we know what we’re talking about.”

Trade between Russia and China up by 30.6% to $214.3 bln in January-September
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:09:37 UTC
16:09:37 KST

BEIJING, October 14. /TASS/. Trade between China and Russia rose by 30.6% year-on-year to $214.3 billion in January-September, according to the General Administration of Customs of China (GACC).
In the reporting period, Chinese exports to Russia grew by 33.1% to $98.06 billion, while imports of Russian products into China increased by 28.6% to $116.24 billion.
In January-September, Russia’s trade surplus with China reached $18.16 billion, which is 10.1% up year-on-year.
According to the GACC statistics, Chinese-Russian trade turnover in September rose by 13.5% compared to August, reaching $29.06 billion. In particular, Chinese exports to Russia totaled $13.39 billion (up 12.9%), while shipments from Russia to China increased by 13.9% to $15.67 billion.
In terms of value, the bulk of Russian goods supplied to China consists of oil, natural gas, and coal. Other key items include copper and copper ore, timber, fuel, seafood, and agricultural products. China exports automobiles, tractors, computers, smartphones, industrial and specialized equipment, and a wide range of consumer and industrial goods to Russia. Authorities in both countries are working to optimize the structure of bilateral trade, including through the development of e-commerce and primary processing projects.
In 2024, Chinese-Russian trade turnover reached a record high, exceeding $244 billion, but contracted by 6.9% to $228.1 billion in 2025. As Russian Ambassador to China Igor Morgulov said earlier, this annual figure could soon rise to $300 billion.

‘Massive’ Russian attack on Ukraine kills at least six, damages power sites
Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Ukraine’s partners failed to warn of Russian ballistic missiles attack on Kyiv.
Russian air attacks have killed at least six people in Ukraine and left hundreds of thousands without power, days after United States President Donald Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” in the more-than four year war.
The Russian Defence Ministry said on Wednesday that its forces had carried out a “massive” strike against communications and energy infrastructure facilities in Ukraine, the Interfax news agency reported.
In a statement, it said Russian forces targeted two heat and power plants in the capital Kyiv, another such plant in the wider Kyiv region along with a thermal power plant and an electricity substation.
Other targets included a heat and power plant in Kharkiv along with a thermal power plant which it said supplied the Ukrainian military in the southeast of the Kharkiv region.
The ministry said it had also hit a data centre in Kyiv which it said was used to gather intelligence on Russia’s armed forces.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko urged people to remain in shelters.
“Energy facilities in Kyiv and the surrounding region have come under a massive ballistic missile strike. There are power disruptions in the capital,” he wrote on Telegram.
DTEK, Ukraine’s largest private energy provider, said the attack had caused emergency power cuts in several urban districts of Kyiv.
A Russian strike on a multistorey building in the capital’s Desnianskyi district killed two people, while another attack in Golosiivsky district killed one, Ukraine’s state emergency service said.
The Ukrainian military also reported that two people were killed and six wounded in Russian attacks on the Dnipropetrovsk region. Another person was killed in the southeastern Zaporizhzhia region.
Further Russian missile attacks were reported in the Kharkiv and Zhytomyr regions, while other strikes hit Sumy and Chernigiv.
Al Jazeera’s Audrey MacAlpine, reporting from Kyiv, said a record number of hypersonic missiles were used in the attacks on the capital.
“Over half a million people in Ukraine are without power as a result of these strikes,” she said.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine received no warnings from its Western partners of a Russian ballistic missile attack on the capital, raising questions about intelligence sharing.
“A Russian ballistic missile attack on Kyiv. Once again, no early warning from our partners,” he wrote on Facebook. “This is absolutely unjust: when they are destroying our infrastructure, and Ukraine is not even receiving early warnings about ballistic missile launches.”
The president said Ukraine detected the missiles only as they neared Kyiv.
He also accused Russia of violating the “energy ceasefire” Trump announced on Sunday.
“A targeted Russian ballistic missile strike specifically against energy infrastructure – the very infrastructure covered by the ceasefire announced by the American President,” he wrote on X.
“The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale – Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States.”
A technology adviser to the Ukrainian president said the operation of some Starlink internet terminals appeared to have been restricted overnight, stopping the operation of its military-grade version above 160 kilometres per hour, disrupting combat missions.
“Tonight SpaceX introduced a speed limit for the Starlink terminals in motion,” Sergiy Beskrestnov said, referring to Elon Musk’s company, which owns Starlink.
“Our defence forces were not warned about this restriction, which led to the disruption of a number of missions. Obviously, this action cannot be a coincidence and is linked to the current political situation.”
Russia also reported Ukrainian drone strikes overnight. The governor of Russia’s Saratov region, Roman Busargin, said a Ukrainian drone strike had killed one person in the city of Balakovo.
Busargin said all infrastructure facilities were operating as usual. Balakovo is home to a data centre of Russia’s top lender Sberbank, a nuclear power plant and a hydropower station, whose dam spans the Volga River, among other facilities.
Sberbank later said its data centre in the Saratov region had been attacked by drones, but that all systems were operating as normal.
Moscow mayor Sergey Sobyanin said air defence forces had downed nearly 500 drones flying towards the Russian capital overnight. Russian authorities said about 160 more were brought down over the Rostov region, while others targeted Moscow.
Russia’s military later put the number of downed Ukrainian drones overnight at 902, of which 180 were shot down near the capital Moscow.

Tehran Auto Plaza seeks to turn the automotive world into a destination
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:06:26 UTC
16:06:26 KST

Tehran Auto Plaza seeks to turn the automotive world into a destination
TEHRAN – For many motorists, a visit to a car showroom has a specific purpose: to inspect a vehicle, discuss a price and decide whether to buy. Tehran Auto Plaza is being developed around a broader idea, one in which the automobile becomes the starting point for a day of discovery, specialist services, social encounters and new experiences.
Introduced to the media on October 12, the complex is planned as a large-scale automotive destination, bringing together vehicle showrooms, specialist facilities, commercial outlets and spaces for activities beyond buying and selling cars.
The development is designed to accommodate approximately 90 showrooms, alongside workshops, vehicle-tuning facilities, parts and accessories outlets, and services related to vehicle care. Its broader program also envisages cafés, restaurants, shopping opportunities, family-oriented amenities and events intended to attract people whose interest in cars extends beyond ownership.
The idea is to create a place where visitors can encounter different parts of automotive culture in one setting. Some may arrive to explore new models or specialist equipment; others may be interested in vehicle customization, automotive technology, photography or events that bring enthusiasts together.
By combining commercial activity with opportunities for leisure and participation, Tehran Auto Plaza aims to establish a more expansive role for the automobile in the urban experience.
A destination on Tehran’s western edge
Situated along the Lashgari Expressway, which connects Tehran with Karaj, the development occupies a substantial site in the capital’s western corridor. The project materials describe an eight-hectare complex, while other published descriptions refer to a larger combined area for its commercial and service functions.
The layout is intended to distinguish the principal vehicle-display areas from much of the technical infrastructure. The upper section is planned to accommodate the showrooms, while the lower section is intended for workshops, spare-parts businesses, tuning facilities and related automotive services.
This separation gives the project an organizational logic: visitors can explore vehicles in a dedicated display environment while technical work and specialist activities take place in designated areas.
The scale is also central to the concept. Rather than presenting a single brand or a narrow category of vehicles, the development is intended to accommodate a variety of automotive businesses and services. That breadth could make it relevant to first-time buyers, experienced motorists, collectors, families and people simply curious about new developments in the car industry.
Its eventual character will depend on the mix of businesses that become operational and the range of activities available to visitors. Nevertheless, the plan points toward a destination that seeks to bring together commercial, technical and recreational uses rather than treating them as separate experiences.
More than a place to look at cars
The showroom remains the natural starting point, but it is not intended to define the entire visit.
The planned facilities encompass services for different stages of vehicle ownership, including maintenance, repairs, detailing, paintwork inspection, car washing, parts supply and customization. These activities address different interests: a motorist may need a routine service, while another may want to improve a vehicle’s appearance, upgrade its equipment or learn more about specialist products.
Detailing and vehicle-care services, for example, can appeal to owners who take particular care of their cars’ interiors and exterior finishes. Tuning and customization facilities offer another dimension, allowing motorists to explore equipment and modifications suited to their vehicles.
The inclusion of specialist outlets also has the potential to bring together customers and professionals who might otherwise operate in separate parts of the city. For enthusiasts, this could provide opportunities to discover products, compare approaches and exchange knowledge with people who share their interests.
A spare-parts hypermarket is among the facilities planned for the complex, adding a retail dimension to its technical offering. The intention is to make it easier for visitors to find components and accessories while accessing related installation or maintenance services.
The broader proposition is convenience, but also variety. A visitor who arrives with one particular task may discover services or products that were not part of the original plan for the trip.
Where technology meets automotive culture
Technology is another part of the development’s identity. In addition to the proposed automotive super app, the complex envisages opportunities to introduce new technologies, demonstrate specialist equipment and organize activities that bring visitors closer to developments in the industry.
A digital platform could complement the physical experience by helping users discover services, arrange appointments and access information before arriving. It could also help connect visitors with businesses operating within the complex, making it easier to plan a visit around specific interests.
The planned intelligent features and vehicle-related digital services form part of a wider effort to connect the physical and digital sides of automotive activity. For a visitor, this could mean exploring a product in person, obtaining information through a digital service and arranging a related appointment without having to begin the process again elsewhere.
Technology demonstrations and specialist events could give the complex an additional educational role. They may offer opportunities for customers to learn about new equipment, compare products and understand how technological developments are influencing vehicle use and customization.
The effectiveness of this approach will depend on the quality of the content and services provided. Digital tools are most useful when they make information easier to understand and help people take practical action. Similarly, technology events will be more engaging if they provide demonstrations and useful explanations rather than simply displaying products.
A meeting point for enthusiasts
One of the more distinctive aspects of the plan is the intention to host automotive gatherings and specialist events.
Car culture encompasses more than the purchase of a vehicle. It includes the design and engineering of automobiles, the restoration of older models, customization, photography, motorsport-related interests and the communities that form around particular brands or types of cars.
The planned events at Tehran Auto Plaza could provide a setting for these interests to intersect. Gatherings of enthusiasts, specialist presentations and displays of new equipment could encourage people to exchange experiences and become acquainted with developments beyond their usual areas of interest.
Such activities can also create opportunities for automotive businesses to meet customers in a less transactional setting. A product demonstration, technical presentation or themed gathering allows participants to explore an idea before making a purchase or committing to a service.
The proposed program includes events related to emerging automotive technologies and opportunities for brands to introduce products and developments to interested audiences. Test-drive experiences are also part of the wider concept being promoted for the destination.
For the complex, a regular calendar of events could help establish reasons to return after an initial visit. Instead of depending entirely on people who arrive to buy or service a car, it could attract visitors interested in a particular exhibition, demonstration or gathering.
The success of this approach will depend on the variety, organization and regularity of the events. A lively automotive destination needs more than physical space; it needs activities that give people a reason to use it.
A place for families and leisure
The inclusion of cafés, restaurants, shopping opportunities and recreational spaces reflects the project's intention to welcome a broader audience.
For families, these facilities could make a visit more comfortable, particularly when different members have different interests. Someone comparing vehicles might spend time in the showrooms while others take a break in a café or explore other parts of the complex.
For automotive enthusiasts, food and leisure facilities could encourage longer visits and make it easier to attend events or spend time with fellow enthusiasts. For casual visitors, they could help turn the complex into an accessible destination even when there is no immediate intention to purchase a vehicle.
This approach places greater emphasis on the experience surrounding the automobile. The car remains the central theme, but the visit can include dining, social interaction, browsing and entertainment.
The quality of the visitor experience will depend on practical details as much as on the range of amenities. Clear wayfinding, convenient parking, comfortable shared spaces and effective coordination between commercial areas will be important to making a large complex easy to navigate.
Parking is a particularly significant consideration for a destination of this kind, where visitors may arrive in their own vehicles and spend time moving between different facilities. Published accounts of the project describe substantial parking capacity, although the precise figures vary across reports.
If the planned amenities and circulation arrangements work together effectively, the complex could accommodate visits of different lengths and purposes, from a brief stop at a specialist outlet to a longer outing built around a vehicle display or event.
A platform for automotive media and content
Tehran Auto Plaza also envisages a role in automotive media and content production.
The proposed capabilities include professional photography and video production, specialist automotive content, press gatherings and events designed to introduce new products and technologies. These activities could create opportunities for journalists, photographers, filmmakers, reviewers and other content creators to work in a setting that brings different vehicles and automotive services together.
For media professionals, a concentrated range of showrooms and specialist facilities can offer practical advantages. It can make it easier to arrange vehicle photography, record product demonstrations, interview industry representatives and produce material about equipment or services.
The complex could also provide a setting for public-facing content that helps audiences understand technical subjects. Automotive journalism, for instance, can explore not only a vehicle’s design and features but also maintenance, safety, ownership costs and developments in technology.
A dedicated environment for media activities could encourage collaboration among businesses, technical specialists and content producers. It might also give automotive brands additional ways to introduce products to potential customers, provided that promotional material remains clearly distinguished from independent editorial coverage.
The proposed facilities therefore have the potential to support both commercial communication and more informative coverage of the automotive sector. The range and quality of the resulting work will depend on the resources made available and the relationships developed with media professionals.
Employment and business opportunities
Beyond its appeal to visitors, the complex represents an effort to concentrate a range of automotive businesses within one commercial environment.
The planned activities could create opportunities for showroom personnel, mechanics, technicians, parts specialists, vehicle-care professionals, sales staff, hospitality workers, event organizers and media-production teams.
The project’s management has estimated that it could generate more than 2,000 direct jobs, potentially rising to around 2,300 to 2,400, alongside thousands of indirect jobs. These are projections rather than verified employment outcomes, and their realization will depend on the number of businesses that become operational and the scale of their activities.
The concentration of different services could also encourage cooperation among businesses that have traditionally operated separately. A customer purchasing a vehicle, for example, might subsequently use a detailing service, obtain accessories or attend an automotive event at the same destination.
For smaller specialist businesses, being part of a larger complex could offer access to visitors who might not otherwise discover their services. For customers, it could provide a broader choice of providers and make it easier to explore related offerings.
The commercial model will need to balance the interests of the businesses operating within the complex with the expectations of visitors. A successful destination must offer a compelling reason to visit, while providing its occupants with a viable environment in which to operate.
Building a lasting identity
Tehran Auto Plaza enters the market with an ambition that extends beyond assembling showrooms and service outlets. It seeks to establish an identifiable destination around the automobile, bringing together commerce, specialist knowledge, technology, leisure and community activities.
That ambition will be measured by what visitors can actually experience once the planned facilities and programs are operating. The variety of vehicles on display, the quality of specialist services, the accessibility of shared spaces and the regularity of events will all influence whether the complex develops into a destination people choose to revisit.
Its appeal could ultimately lie in the combination of these elements. A place that allows motorists to explore vehicles, obtain specialist assistance, discover new products, meet fellow enthusiasts and spend time with family offers a different proposition from a conventional showroom.
Tehran Auto Plaza is setting out to create such a place on the western edge of the capital. If its commercial, recreational and cultural plans are delivered in a coordinated way, it could give Tehran’s automotive community a new meeting point and offer visitors a more varied way to engage with the world of cars.
The longer-term challenge is to turn the scale of the development into a consistent experience. Its success will depend not simply on how many businesses occupy the complex, but on whether the combination of services, activities and visitor amenities gives people a clear reason to make the journey and return.

Nearly 200 Ukrainian drones flew toward Moscow, while a Sberbank data center came under attack in Russia’s Saratov region

‘Like we don’t exist’: Palestinians in West Bank denied say in Israel vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:05:31 UTC
16:05:31 KST

‘Like we don’t exist’: Palestinians in West Bank denied say in Israel vote
Palestinians in the occupied West Bank have no voice in the October 27 election, even as Israel’s government shapes their lives through settlement expansion, home demolitions and movement restrictions.
Jabal al-Baba, occupied West Bank – In Jabal al-Baba, a small Bedouin community east of Jerusalem, Israel controls almost every aspect of Palestinians’ daily life, from building homes and accessing water to moving freely.
Yet when Israelis head to the polls on October 27, the vast majority of the nearly three million Palestinians in the occupied West Bank will have no say in choosing the government that rules their lives under occupation – unlike the 700,000 Jewish settlers living in some 300 illegal settlements and outposts across the territory, including occupied East Jerusalem.
“They treat us like something that doesn’t exist,” said Atallah al-Jahalin, Jabal al-Baba’s community representative.
“You don’t have the right to vote. You don’t have the rights that you would have in a democratic state.”
About 450 people live in Jabal al-Baba, a community in Area C, which makes up about 60 percent of the occupied West Bank and remains under full Israeli military and civil control.
Many residents here raise sheep and goats beside homes made from corrugated metal. Most belong to the Jahalin tribe, whose families were expelled from the Naqab (Negev) desert region by Israeli authorities in the years after the Nakba, the violent ethnic cleansing of Palestine by Zionist militias in 1948.
“You are forbidden from building a house. You are forbidden from building a street. You are forbidden from building a school,” said al-Jahalin. “Everything is forbidden to us.”
Residents face constant pressure from Israeli soldiers and settlers, al-Jahalin said, on top of repeated demolitions.
“In the past few years, we have had more than 100 demolition operations in our community,” he said. “We were constantly rebuilding our homes.”
Israel says it demolishes Palestinian structures built without permits, which are almost impossible for Palestinians to obtain. Israeli rights group Bimkom found authorities rejected more than 99 percent of Palestinian building permit applications in Area C between 2021 and 2024.
While Palestinians are restricted from developing, Israeli settlements, which are illegal under international law, are expanding at a record pace. In April, Israel’s security cabinet was reported to have approved 34 new settlements in a single decision, including outposts legalised retroactively, according to Peace Now, an Israeli anti-settlement watchdog group.
For al-Jahalin, the aim is clear: to push his community out and make way for settlers.
“There is an Israeli plan to displace the people who are here,” he said. “All of this is a means of pressure. We have to leave these areas for the benefit of the settlement projects.”
E1 exposes limits of government change
In this month’s vote, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud Party and the far-right coalition it leads face a tight race against an opposition alliance consisting of an assortment of parties that are united in their stated aim to “preserve and strengthen Israel as a Jewish and democratic state”.
The opposition grouping has not declared an official leader, but former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, of the centrist Yashar party, is seen as its most likely candidate for prime minister.
Recent polls indicate the two blocs are running neck and neck, with neither side appearing on course to win a majority. Most leaders of the Jewish-led opposition bloc, meanwhile, have ruled out joining forces with the Arab-led parties that represent the Palestinian citizens of Israel who make up about 20 percent of its population.
But for many Palestinians, a change at the top would mean little.
Jamal Juma’, coordinator of the grassroots Stop the Wall campaign, said decades of occupation have taught Palestinians not to expect a new government to shift fundamental Israeli policies. He pointed out that it was Israel’s centre-left Labour Party – and not the right – that began building settlements in the West Bank after 1967.
For Jabal al-Baba, the clearest test of what a change in government would mean is E1, a strip of land between Jerusalem and the illegal settlement of Ma’ale Adumim, where the community sits.
The E1 project would link the settlement to Jerusalem, cutting the West Bank in two and threatening the forced displacement of some 18 Bedouin communities, including Jabal al-Baba.
In August 2025, Israel gave final approval to 3,401 settler homes in E1, which far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich said would “bury” the idea of a Palestinian state. A month later, Netanyahu vowed “there will be no Palestinian state. This place belongs to us.”
This year, the government put the land up for sale in two tenders, timed to advance before the election. Israel’s attorney general has since moved to delay parts of the process until after the vote, and Smotrich is challenging that in court.
In the lead-up to the election, Eisenkot rejected the idea of a Palestinian state as “delusional” while also expressing support for “strengthening” settlements. But asked about the E1 tenders in August, he said: “Not now.” He called advancing the project a mistake with an international cost, and said far-right ministers and settler violence were damaging Israel’s standing abroad.
That puts him at odds with the current government over the timing of E1 – but not over the idea of settling the West Bank.
“There may be a democracy, but only for Jewish people,” said Kareem Jubran, field research director at Israeli rights group B’Tselem, which describes Israel’s rule over Palestinians as apartheid.
“Even if the governments change, the system remains,” he said. “If the left exists, it is a Zionist left. It is not very influential in Israeli political life.”
In Jabal al-Baba, where settlement expansion threatens the community’s future, al-Jahalin has reached a similar conclusion.
“It may be Eisenkot, it may be Netanyahu,” he said. “Israeli policy is already on the table. It doesn’t matter who carries it out.”
A system no election will dismantle
Whoever forms Israel’s next government will continue to exercise decisive power over the lives of Palestinians in the West Bank, which was divided into three areas – A, B and C – as part of the Oslo Accords in the 1990s.
Israel’s control is most direct in Area C, but its restrictions reach across the West Bank.
“The Israelis are controlling everything in the West Bank, every single thing,” said Juma’, of the Stop the Wall campaign, citing Israel’s control of the movement between Palestinian cities and villages, as well as access to water and electricity and the territory’s borders.
“Every city and every village, they have constructed a gate at the entrance,” he added.
Juma’ also warned that continued fragmentation could turn the West Bank into isolated enclaves, cutting Palestinian communities off from one another.
“It will be like open prisons, like Gaza,” he said. “But here we have different Gazas.”
Jubran, of B’Tselem, said stopping that trajectory depends on international pressure, not the outcome of Israel’s election.
“If the international community were determined to take practical steps to stop the E1 project, it could,” he said. “As long as it is not, E1 will go ahead.”
Back in Jabal al-Baba, the threat of renewed forcible displacement is looming large.
Al-Jahalin said his family was expelled from the Naqab once already – but he will not leave again.
“I am not ready to live the life of my father,” he said. “I, as a Palestinian, will stay, whether I die or live on this Earth.”

Russia-linked bot networks kept their weekly rhythm after drone strikes on three Yandex data centers—disinformation monitor LetsData
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:03:21 UTC
16:03:21 KST

The claim that strikes on Russian tech giant Yandex thinned out social media bots finds no support in the networks tracked by Ukrainian disinformation-monitoring company LetsData, co-founder Ksenia Iliuk told Euromaidan Press on 13 October. She cautioned that the strikes may still have affected networks outside the company’s view.
At the Warsaw Security Forum, Lithuania’s prime minister suggested allies should ask Ukraine to strike more Russian data centers because that might help protect European elections from foreign interference. Bot networks are one tool of that interference, so whether the strikes mute them carries weight well beyond Ukraine.
No drop in the networks LetsData tracks
Drones hit Yandex data centers in Sasovo and Vladimir between 8 and 11 October. Ukrainian drone maker Fire Point said its FP-1 drones struck Yandex’s Kaluga site in between. On 12 October, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the Warsaw Security Forum that once Ukraine’s response reached Yandex, social media had fewer bots.
More than 500 drones by Moscow’s count: Kh-101 fuel plant, second Yandex data center, and a far-north refinery hit
LetsData checked X and Facebook, where bot networks usually stand out clearly, Iliuk said. Its analysts looked at networks attributed to Russia’s influence ecosystem. Among them are groups of X accounts spreading domains from what she called a new wave of Doppelgänger, a Russian campaign that clones real news sites.
Those networks look unaffected, Iliuk said. None of them has stopped posting or broken its usual rhythm, she added. Some are slightly less active, but LetsData’s analysts say that is typical for them. The networks run on a weekly cycle, and the check fell in the part of the week when they post less.
A network that jumped from Germany to Ukraine
LetsData worked with two samples. One covers accounts that systematically target Ukraine, Moldova, and Armenia. The other covers bot networks the company has followed for some time that keep changing their target audience, so they have no fixed country.
Ukrainian drones hit three of Russian tech giant Yandex’s data centers in four days. Ukraine’s president says the bots thinned out too
About two weeks ago, one network from that second sample wrote about elections in Germany and spread fake Die Welt sites, she said. It now posts about mobilization in Ukraine and shares a fake site of Ukrinform, Ukraine’s state news agency.
What the check can’t see
The company can compare only within networks whose usual behavior it knows, Iliuk said. Checking the whole internet is impossible because the scale is colossal, she said. A Cloudflare chart that circulated as evidence counted automated web requests from Yandex’s network, including its search crawlers, not social media posts, Cybernews reported.
So the networks LetsData follows show no impact, Iliuk said. That does not mean the strikes had no effect at all, she noted. They may have shown up in networks the company isn’t tracking now. LetsData will keep watching and report other signals if they appear.

Scale back on hake and coley, seafood charity tells shoppers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:00:48 UTC
16:00:48 KST

UK shoppers have previously been urged to avoid UK-caught cod and to buy European hake or coley instead – but now these fish are in trouble, too.
The Marine Conservation Society (MCS), an environmental charity, publishes its Good Fish Guide to help consumers and businesses make sustainable seafood choices. It uses a traffic-light system to rate seafood according to the health of fish stocks and environmental impact.
On Wednesday, the MCS downgraded the ratings for European hake caught in the North Sea, Celtic Seas, or Bay of Biscay from green to amber owing to declining stocks and increased fishing pressure.
Meanwhile, the rating on coley caught around the UK (North Sea, West of Scotland, Rockall and Skagerrak) has fallen from amber to red – the worst rating – meaning it is a “fish to avoid”. Of the 10 coley fisheries rated by the guide, two are still green while the other eight are amber.
Kerry Lyne, the Good Fish Guide manager, said the “status of fish stocks are continuously changing” and a “fish that was a good choice a few years ago is not necessarily a good choice everywhere today”.
Most of the seafood consumed in the UK is made up of just a few different species, known as the big five: cod, haddock, salmon, tuna and prawns. This puts a lot of pressure on a handful of wild stocks.
Cod populations have been in decline since 2015. The main cause is overfishing, although changing sea temperatures and other ecosystem pressures have affected breeding and juvenile survival.
“The best thing we can all do if we eat seafood is diversify our seafood choices and avoid those most under threat,” Lyne added.
With that in mind, the charity has suggested wild-caught sea bass from around the UK as a more ocean-friendly alternative to cod. Similar to cod, sea bass is a mild white fish with a flaky texture that can be swapped like-for-like in any recipe.
The guide is updated twice a year and of the 727 ratings, the latest review has 29 downgrades and 11 upgrades.
On the good news front, UK Atlantic bluefin tuna, which has shown huge signs of a population recovery, has a brand new green rating. Chris Graham, the charity’s head of ocean regeneration and sustainable seafood, said one of the factors behind the resurgence was better fisheries management brought in more than 20 years ago.
“We’re pleased to see a small, well-managed fishery in place, but caution must prevail, and this iconic species must be monitored closely so the health of the UK population can continue to improve,” Graham said.
Lyme Bay “disco-pot” scallops were another new entry, with an amber rating. LED lights inside the pots to attract scallops mean the new technology has a much lower impact on the seabed than traditional dredging.

This civil war on the British right is a charade – its politics are more united than ever | Jonathan Liew
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:00:48 UTC
16:00:48 KST

Kapow! In a warmly received conference speech, Kemi Badenoch turns her fire on Reform UK, describing it as “weird”, and ruling out an electoral pact. Slap! Not to be outdone, her former colleague Robert Jenrick derides Badenoch as a champion of the wealthy, which is quite rich for a guy who looks like he’s just accidentally ingested a bundle of £50 notes through his sphincter. Bosh! Reform’s Richard Tice and Restore’s Rupert Lowe clash online over the result of a council byelection in Derbyshire, in which the Greens profited from a split rightwing vote. “Vote Restore get Islamists,” Tice chides. “Vote Reform, get some random Bangladeshi bloke,” Lowe responds.
Meanwhile, the Conservatives are back. The Kemibounce is real. The Keminaissance is true. We’ve all got a severe case of the Kemirrhoids. And you may wonder why much of the media are talking about a Badenoch revival in a year where her party lost 563 councillors and 40% of its councils, remains about four points below its apparent nadir of 2024, and in which the leader herself appears incapable of doing a broadcast interview without looking like a restaurant diner who received exactly what she ordered and is inexplicably furious at it. The point is that the Conservatives are a serious party of government again, and the reason is that we all said so.
And even if we take into account Badenoch’s curiously resilient personal polling, this does feel like a largely arbitrary volte-face. There was a soft-focus interview in the Financial Times, a warm editorial in the Sun, and generally positive coverage of the Tory conference in the rest of the rightwing press. Tom Tugendhat, the new shadow foreign secretary and once regarded as a party moderate, had a sympathetic platform in the Observer to defend the party’s opposition to net zero and the European convention on human rights.
From a safe distance, it is possible to regard these realignments in a fairly optimistic light. The right is tearing itself to shreds, potentially allowing a leftwing alternative – or failing that, Labour – to clean up. And in the continuing scrap between Lowe and Nigel Farage, or the series of aggressive Telegraph editorials aimed at Restore Britain, it is tempting to glimpse a reassertion of basic, consensual values in which, for all our many disagreements, certain voices will always be beyond the pale.
Occasionally you will even hear it said on the progressive left that a strong centre-right is a necessary, welcome bulwark against the extremist far right. That while we can disagree strongly and vehemently with Badenoch’s party, we can also recognise the ways in which a moderate right can act as a kind of cordon sanitaire against the nativists, ethnonationalists and race theorists who may otherwise get their hands on the levers of government. All of which would probably be true, if that were actually what was happening. But is it?
Let’s start with the Tories, who appear to be rapidly pivoting towards a demographic that one insider has described as “Waitrose Woman”: affluent, socially liberal, turned off by culture-war rhetoric but laser-focused on tax and the economy. “We have done a ton of opinion research over the last 18 months,” a Conservative source told the Mail on Sunday. “You do have to appear reasonable.” Or, as one shadow cabinet minister told the Guardian: “We have outsourced our toxicity to Reform.”
But in the real world, beyond superficial branding, how different are the two platforms? Shadow cabinet member Nick Timothy called Islamic prayers in Trafalgar Square un-British, “an act of domination”, “straight from the Islamist playbook”, and Badenoch backed him. Badenoch advocates a ban on pro-Palestine marches, but argued Tommy Robinson should not receive the same treatment. Another shadow cabinet member, Katie Lam, advocated mass deportations of legally settled immigrants in order to make Britain a “culturally coherent group of people”.
The Conservative police and crime commissioner Donna Jones responded to the masked vigilante protests in Portsmouth by blaming the government for failing to control our borders. A former neo-Nazi activist was selected as a local election candidate for the Tories, and subsequently appointed as an adviser. In the Telegraph, Badenoch wrote that anyone committed to net zero targets is no longer welcome in the party.
As for Reform, Monday’s announcement that it would immediately suspend the UK asylum system brought the party further in line with Restore, both of whom advocate ICE-style raids, the stripping of citizenship from people who thought they were here permanently, and the cessation of aid and visas to countries who refuse to take back migrants. Suella Braverman, a former Tory, now says she can “understand why some people are drawn to Restore”, and suggests people of colour cannot be English.
Indeed, you can argue that net zero, welfare, tax cuts, Israel, Brexit, defence spending, trans rights, Donald Trump, the obsession with grooming gangs and Islam, immigration and, most importantly, their common enemies, there is barely a sheet of nori to separate the three parties. And yet at the same time we are expected to believe that these parties engaged in an eternal blood feud, rather than three heads of the same army, pursuing different strategies towards a common cause.
Naturally Westminster will fall for this narrative wholesale, focused as it is on divisions over alliances, personalities over ideas. The Conservatives will be allowed to carry on decontaminating their brand without decontaminating their platform. Farage will continue as flag bearer for the movement, sweeping up donor money and airtime. Meanwhile Restore serve an equally important role as the engine of change, the pressure group, the brains trust: shifting the rhetorical window to the right while allowing Badenoch and Farage to look reasonable in comparison.
The civil war on the right is in fact a charade, a fake fight being enacted for our benefit. The right bloc is now a single basic substance, responsive and carefully calibrated to the different audiences it needs to capture. Reform, already in informal talks with Restore, can now tailor its offering to the post-industrial north, Midlands and Wales, leaving the rehabilitated Conservatives – the acceptable face of the project – to concentrate on their southern and rural heartlands. And if, after all the bickering and infighting, a coalition should be required? Do we really expect a Conservative party founded entirely on the gain and exercise of power to suddenly turn it down?
To those on the left, the idea of a rightwing meltdown feels vaguely reassuring. But in reality nothing here is being repudiated. The personalities may butt heads for our entertainment, but the ideas and politics are largely common among them all. The parts are being divvied out, but ultimately the production remains the same.
- Jonathan Liew is a Guardian columnist

Pollinating insects flock to plants gardeners might think of as ‘weeds’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:00:47 UTC
16:00:47 KST

Ubiquitous urban plants often derided as “weeds” are the most attractive to pollinating insects.
The autumn blooms of common ivy, rich in pollen and nectar, are the most visited by insects including bees and butterflies, according to an eight-year study.
The next most popular are hogweed and bramble flowers, followed by non-native buddleia, which attracts four times as many butterflies and moths as other high-scoring flowers.
The popularity and importance of plants for insects that many gardeners might dig up or cut down are revealed by the UK Pollinator Monitoring Scheme, in which citizen scientists have recorded insect visits to flowers during 10-minute surveys since 2017.
Ivy received 22 visits by flying insects per 10-minute count with hogweed a close second (20) followed by buddleias, bramble, knapweeds and thistles, which received an average of 14 visits each.
Jo Milborrow, the butterfly monitoring officer for Butterfly Conservation, one of the partners in the pollinator monitoring scheme, said: “We already recommend ivy as a great plant to grow because it is an important resource for breeding holly blue butterflies and nectaring commas and red admirals, so the fact that this easy-to-grow native species is also the number one plant for pollinating insect visits is a fantastic discovery – we would recommend people to start growing ivy today!”
The survey, which is run by the UK Centre for Ecology & Hydrology (UKCEH) and the Joint Nature Conservation Committee (JNCC), found that hoverfly numbers had declined by about a third in both abundance and total number of species recorded across Britain over the past eight years.
There was better news for solitary bees, which increased in one survey. Honeybees, beetles and flies excluding hoverflies all increased in the survey, which covered mostly gardens, suggesting that these could be providing an important refuge for some pollinators.
Martin Harvey, a volunteer coordinator at UKCEH, said volunteers could contribute counts via the Pollinator Monitoring Scheme website next year between April and September. “Participants often say how much they have enjoyed spending time counting pollinators,” he said, “and it is always fascinating to observe the close association between insects and flowers”.

Personalised cancer vaccines take a leap forward – can Swiss pharma catch up?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

Personalised cancer vaccines take a leap forward – can Swiss pharma catch up?
Vaccines tailored to each patient’s tumour look increasingly promising after positive melanoma trial results. But a Roche-backed vaccine stumbled days later, raising questions about where the approach can succeed – and what it means for Swiss pharma.
For decades, the idea of a vaccine to treat cancer promised more than it delivered. That may be changing. This summer, the first successful Phase III trial of an mRNA vaccine designed around each patient’s own tumour was announcedExternal link by US-based Moderna and MSD (known as Merck in the US). It was given to people whose melanoma had been surgically removed, and it made the cancer less likely to return.
“It clearly has the potential to be a breakthrough,” said Olivier Michielin, head of oncology at Geneva University Hospitals. He was already working on experimental therapeutic cancer vaccines over 20 years ago. Back then, scientists could see that the vaccines were activating the immune system, but that wasn’t translating into notable health benefits for patients.
Cancer vaccines fall into two broad categories:
Preventive vaccines, such as those against HPV and hepatitis B, protect against infections that can later cause cancer; researchers are also testing vaccines to prevent cancer in people at high risk.
Therapeutic cancer vaccines are given to people who already have cancer or have been treated for it. They work as a form of immunotherapy, training the immune system to recognise and attack cancer cells.
This article focuses on therapeutic vaccines, and in particular on personalised ones designed around the mutations found in each patient’s tumour, and built with the mRNA technology that’s behind the Covid jabs.
But just nine days after Moderna and MSD’s announcement, Germany-based immunotherapy pioneer BioNTech and Genentech, a subsidiary of Swiss drug giant Roche, External linkstoppedExternal link a failing Phase II trial of their own personalised mRNA vaccine for colorectal cancer. The two companies are still testing the same vaccine in pancreatic cancer.
What do these contrasting results reveal about where personalised vaccines might work best? The answer has different implications for Switzerland’s two pharma giants: Roche has a stake through its long-term partnership with BioNTech, while rival Novartis hasn’t entered the field.
Encouraging results
Moderna and MSD’s vaccine, intismeran autogene, is personalised: each dose is made specifically for one patient, targeting their tumour’s mutations. Given alongside MSD’s immunotherapy pembrolizumab (marketed as Keytruda), the trial showed the vaccine significantly delayed the return or spread of melanoma compared with Keytruda alone, the companies said. They have yet to say whether it helps patients live longer.
Full results of the Phase III trial – the final stage of testing before the vaccine is submitted to regulators for approval – will be presented at the end of October. In an earlier, smaller study, the combination nearly halved the risk of the cancer coming back.
If the full Phase III results confirm the smaller study, it would be “clinically very significant”, said Michielin, especially because Keytruda on its own is already an effective treatment. He pointed out that this trial could validate several ideas at once: mRNA as a cancer treatment, mutations unique to each tumour as targets, and treatments made from scratch for individual patients.
Financial markets took noteExternal link: Moderna shares surged by as much as 60% in pre-market trading after the Phase III announcement. MSD shares also rose, although by a much more modest 6%. The gap is mainly a matter of size, said Stefan Schneider, senior equity analyst for pharma at Swiss investment firm Vontobel and a virologist by training. For Moderna, a successful cancer vaccine could be a major new source of income, while for MSD, one of the world’s biggest drugmakers, it would be a small addition to its business.
Why did one trial succeed and the other fail?
Michielin and Schneider point to several differences between the MSD-Moderna and Roche-BioNTech trials. The first is the cancer itself. Melanoma carries an unusually large number of mutations, giving a personalised vaccine plenty of targets, and it is one of the cancers in which immunotherapy already works best. By contrast, most colorectal cancers are “cold” tumours, which contain few cancer-fighting immune cells and often respond poorly to existing immunotherapies.
The second is how the vaccine was used. Moderna’s was combined with Keytruda, which stops tumours from switching off the immune cells that approach them. The vaccine by Roche and BioNTech, autogene cevumeran, was tested on its own in colorectal cancer.
But in an earlier trial Roche and BioNTech had also tested the same vaccine in melanoma, alongside Keytruda, and it failed to meet its main efficacy goal. Those patients had advanced disease that had spread, or the tumour could not be removed surgically, whereas Moderna’s trial treated patients after surgery.
Roche, however, is cautious about drawing conclusions . In a written response to Swissinfo, the company said its melanoma trial “was not designed to test whether the adjuvant setting is preferable to the metastatic setting” – that is, treating patients after surgery rather than at an advanced stage.
At this stage of research, no single factor can explain the different results – the colorectal patients were also treated after surgery. But together they suggest personalised vaccines may work best early, in cancers the immune system can recognise, said Michielin.
The main open question for Schneider is whether vaccines can also help in cold tumours, where immunotherapy currently does little. That is also where a vaccine could make the biggest difference, which – he suggested – may be why Roche is focusing on them.
Roche and BioNTech are testingExternal link their vaccine in pancreatic cancer, another cold tumour, in a trial that combines it with Roche’s own immunotherapy and chemotherapy after surgery. The outcome could help answer that question, but according to the trial registry, the results are not expected before 2031.
Personalised mRNA vaccines are being developed mainly by two partnerships.
Moderna and MSD are testing an mRNA vaccine (intismeran autogene) in nine mid- and late-stage trials, focusing on melanoma, lung, bladder, and kidney cancer. One large lung cancer trial tests the vaccine on its own.
Roche and BioNTech have tested an mRNA vaccine (autogene cevumeran) in four mid-stage trials. One continues, in pancreatic cancer, where it is combined with Roche’s immunotherapy and chemotherapy after surgery; results are not expected for several years. A colorectal cancer trial was stopped in August 2026 for lack of benefit, and an earlier trial in advanced melanoma failed in 2025. A trial in bladder cancer, combined with a rival company’s immunotherapy, was paused in 2025 after a safety issue and dropped in 2026.
Other personalised approaches, using technologies different from mRNA, are also being tested. French biotech Transgene, for example, is testing a personalised vaccine built on a modified virus, given on its own after surgery for head and neck cancer, now in a mid-stage trial.
Off-the-shelf vaccines, which target features shared by many patients’ cancers rather than being tailored to each individual, are also in late-stage testing. Among these, BioNTech is testing a vaccine in advanced head and neck cancer, and French biotech OSE expects Phase III results for a lung cancer vaccine in 2028. But it’s a highly risky business: Danish firm IO Biotech went bust this year after its melanoma vaccine narrowly missed its goal in a final-stage trial.
Overall, more than 2,000 trials of therapeutic cancer vaccines have been launched since 2000, according to a 2025 studyExternal link.
Two Swiss pharma giants, two different strategies
Big pharma has bet on RNA-based medicines before. Major drugmakers piled in some 25 years ago, then largely retreated around 2010 when progress proved slower than hoped, said Schneider. When they returned in the second half of the 2010s, they mostly did so through partnerships with specialists rather than by buying companies outright. Roche was among them: its US subsidiary Genentech teamed up with BioNTech in 2016 to develop personalised cancer vaccines, sharing the costs and profits.
For Schneider, Roche “has what it takes to be there”. Its diagnostics business can support the tumour testing needed to design personalised treatments; it has long experience matching therapies to the molecular features of a patient’s cancer; and its checkpoint inhibitor, Tecentriq, can be combined with a vaccine. The stakes are modest, though. Schneider does not include the vaccine in his valuation of Roche, and even a success would be a small addition to a company of its size.
Novartis, Switzerland’s other pharma giant, is not working on personalised mRNA cancer-vaccines, at least not publiclyExternal link, despite being active in both RNA technologies and oncology. In a written response to Swissinfo, it stated it “will pursue opportunities where we believe Novartis can make a differentiated contribution for patients”.
Schneider sees this approach as a business calculation: the company is focused on renewing products approaching patent expiry, and personalised vaccines would mean entering a new field, for a product whose profitability is still unclear.
The manufacturing bottleneck
Even if cancer vaccines obtain regulatory approval, there are still significant practical hurdles to overcome.
Each vaccine has to be made for one patient. “You have to take the tumour, sequence it, design the RNA, synthesise it, package it, send it back to the hospital and inject it,” Michielin noted. Today that takes around six weeks – for patients with a fast-moving disease, that wait alone can determine whether a personalised vaccine is a realistic treatment option.
Schneider said there are expectations the timeframe could drop to about four weeks, and Michielin hopes the process will become leaner, for instance by making vaccines on site at university hospitals rather than shipping everything to large factories.
The other issue is price. Most medicines get cheaper as production ramps up, but economies of scale are difficult to achieve for a product made for a single person. Michielin said cost must stay “very, very high among our priorities”. The treatment is likely to be expensive, Schneider noted, but he does not expect costs to sink the business case: cancer drugs already command high prices, and other personalised treatments, such as CAR-T cell therapies, have made it to market.
From trial success to the clinic
No personalised mRNA cancer vaccine has been approved yet, and Moderna and MSD have not yet applied for approval. Michielin advises interested patients to ask their oncologist whether a suitable clinical trial or access programme exists. Even with compelling final data, he cautioned, broader access would still take “many, many months”.
Cancer vaccines are not expected to replace existing treatments. Schneider sees them as “one additional option” for some patients. If they really deliver, Michielin expects vaccines to become an important tool for doctors, but not a cure-all. “In oncology, I think we have come to realise that it’s rarely just one strategy that wins,” he said.

A building in southern Tel Aviv that was unoccupied due to renovations partially collapsed on Wednesday morning.
The Tel Aviv-Jaffa Municipality said the building was slated for demolition prior to its unexpected collapse, and instructed residents to stay away from the scene.
No injuries were reported in the incident on Nahalat Binyamin Street.
Israel’s Fire and Rescue Authority said it was conducting searches at the site alongside Israel Police and Magen David Adom paramedics to rule out the possibility of additional people being trapped in the rubble.
The authority added that the five construction workers inside the building were able to escape the building moments before its collapse.
Footage from the scene shows people running from the site as the building came down, sending smoke billowing across the busy Tel Aviv street.
Some 80,000 buildings in Israel in danger of collapse
In 2021, a residential building in Holon collapsed after authorities evacuated 16 families out of safety concerns.
The evacuation was carried out after reports there had been an explosion in the building on Serlin Street. When firefighters and rescue workers arrived at the scene, they observed cracks in the building. Some residents who tried to leave their homes said they could not open doors because the building’s infrastructure had shifted, police said.
Following the 2021 incident, the Israel Builders Association warned that as many as 80,000 buildings in Israel, with about 300,000 apartments, are in danger of collapsing and must be reconstructed in the coming years to avoid calamity.
“We published this in a report that we submitted to the government in 2017, but this is something we have been saying for years,” said the association’s then-deputy director-general Shay Pauzner.
“The message is that Israel needs to start thinking strategically about this, because we are in the danger zone.”

Trump hails Greenland as 'second to none' for security of US and Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:59:41 UTC
15:59:41 KST

Trump signed a security deal with the leaders of Greenland and Denmark in September, which allows the US to build two military bases in the south and east of the island.
US President Donald Trump hailed Greenland as "second to none" for US and European security on Wednesday, saying any future attack on America would have to pass through the Arctic island.
Greenland "from a Security Purpose in the Defence and Offence of both the United States of America, and Europe, is second to none," Trump said in a post on Truth Social.
He added any future attacks on the US would have to come across Greenland, "where our Defence will routinely knock down drones, missiles, or any other form of weapon not yet even conceived."
Trump also said that oil, gas and mineral exploration was preparing to begin in Greenland.
Washington signed a security deal with the leaders of Greenland and Denmark after Trump threatened to take Copenhagen's strategically important Arctic Circle territory by force.
Greenland, which lies on the shortest route for missiles between Russia and the United States, represents a highly strategic location for Trump's desired "Golden Dome" defence shield.
It also has untapped rare earth deposits and could be a critical player as melting polar ice opens up new shipping routes.
"Massive Oil, Gas, and Mineral Exploration is getting ready to begin in our new and beautiful Greenland!" Trump said in a post on Truth Social.
Citing experts, Trump said "the amount of easily available Oil is far greater than that of almost...anywhere in the World."
He did not give details of prospective American involvement.
In August, media reports of a US oil company's preparatory operations in a remote region of eastern Greenland left locals and authorities on the island uneasy.
Trump signed a security deal with the leaders of Greenland and Denmark on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York in September.
Under the terms of the deal, shared online by the Danish Foreign Ministry, the US will be permitted to expand its military presence on Greenland through the modernisation and enlargement of its current Pituffik Space Base and the establishment of new defence areas at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig.
It will also allow the US "free access to and movement between" defence areas across Greenland, "including the Territorial Waters, by land, air and sea."
American aircraft may also fly over and land in any territory on the island, it states.
Both Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenland’s Premier Jens-Frederik Nielsen welcomed the agreement, which stopped short of Trump's wish to seize the territory for the US, a move he had argued was essential for the US' "national security."
In a statement, Frederiksen said the deal "strengthens our common security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic Area," while Nielsen said it was "to the benefit of us all."
The US is reported to have had 17 military facilities and over 10,000 troops on Greenland at the height of the Cold War.
It currently operates just one base on the island, the Pituffik Space Base, which is used for missile warning, missile defence and space surveillance missions, per the US Space Force.

Weekly regional transport strikes begin, to run until Christmas
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Regional bus and train services across most of the country are disrupted by strikes as of Wednesday morning, which trade unions CNV and FNV organised over pay and working conditions.
Staff at regional operators Arriva, EBS, Qbuzz, Transdev and Keolis are taking part. National rail operator NS is running a normal service.
City transport in Amsterdam and The Hague, run by GVB and HTM, is not affected because it falls outside the regional pay deal. In Rotterdam, RET trams and metro trains are running but its buses are not. Few or no buses and trams are expected to run in Utrecht.
The strikes could continue every week until Christmas unless the unions’ demands are met. They want higher wages, quicker access to permanent contracts for staff, and better working schemes for older employees.
They will announce each week’s strike day only shortly beforehand, assuming their demands aren’t met. They also plan to pick a different day each week, so operators can’t prepare emergency timetables and the same passengers are not hit every week.
