Sudan cannot afford to dismiss a chance for dialogue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
05:51:09 UTC
14:51:09 KST

Sudan cannot afford to dismiss a chance for dialogue
A new initiative faces serious questions about military influence, but its critics should not write it off prematurely.
More than three years into the war between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), Sudan is desperately in need of a political settlement. The fighting has caused immense suffering, and a military solution alone cannot rebuild the state or reunify its fractured society. Under such circumstances, any effort aimed at encouraging Sudanese-Sudanese dialogue deserves serious consideration rather than outright rejection.
In August, a self-appointed committee of 19 Sudanese public figures, chaired by Ahfad University President Qasim Badri, launched an initiative to prepare the ground for national dialogue inside Sudan. Its members had earlier met SAF chief General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and called for legal restrictions on opposition politicians to be lifted. The authorities subsequently issued a decree to drop certain politically motivated charges against Sudanese abroad returning for dialogue and grant participants temporary legal protections. These are limited but important confidence-building measures.
The initiative has nevertheless faced strong opposition. The civilian coalition Sumoud, led by former Prime Minister Abdalla Hamdok, and Ta’sis, an alliance that includes the RSF, have opposed the proposed internal dialogue. They question its independence and warn that holding talks in army-controlled areas could legitimise al-Burhan’s authority and entrench the country’s divisions. These concerns are legitimate and deserve serious attention. But the committee says it is not seeking to negotiate Sudan’s future or determine the agenda of a national dialogue. Its role is to help create the conditions for Sudanese political actors to engage one another directly. The question is whether it can fulfil that role without allowing one side of the conflict to dominate the process. Dismissing the initiative before it has had an opportunity to demonstrate its value would be premature.
The country’s political actors and civil society organisations remain deeply divided, previous mediation efforts have faltered, and the war continues to make comprehensive political engagement increasingly difficult. The committee’s initiative is an attempt to break the deadlock. Efforts to prepare for political dialogue should not be postponed until the fighting stops. Securing a ceasefire and ensuring humanitarian access are urgent priorities, but preparations for political dialogue can proceed alongside efforts to achieve them.
The committee’s members were not elected, and they do not represent every political constituency. Yet the committee’s legitimacy cannot be judged solely by how it was created. It must also be judged by whether it can help bring a broader range of political actors into a national dialogue.
Good intentions alone cannot resolve concerns about credibility. Political dialogue can succeed only if participants believe the process is fair and independent. The legitimacy required to facilitate a political opening is not necessarily the same as that required to negotiate a national settlement. But even a preparatory initiative must earn the trust of those it seeks to bring together.
The committee’s meeting with al-Burhan was a practical necessity. As army chief and head of the Sovereignty Council, he was in a position to respond to the committee’s demands for legal protections. Engaging with al-Burhan does not in itself amount to an endorsement of his authority. But if the initiative becomes too closely associated with the army, other political actors may view it as an extension of al-Burhan’s political agenda rather than an independent facilitator. The committee must therefore demonstrate that its engagement extends beyond the military authorities and that it is prepared to work with political forces that oppose them.
The initiative was launched in Khartoum, which is under army control. This raises a genuine concern about whether a process beginning in territory controlled by one side of the war can attract the confidence of political forces across the country. A national dialogue cannot be confined to one geographical or political constituency. Entire regions have experienced different realities of war, governance, displacement and insecurity. The committee must find ways to reach those living outside army-controlled areas, including Sudanese displaced by the fighting, and ensure they can participate freely and without intimidation.
Sumoud and Ta’sis’s decision to reject the initiative does not automatically invalidate the process. Their concerns deserve consideration, but outright rejection at this early stage risks closing off an opportunity for political engagement. At the same time, their absence matters. Sudan’s crisis is too deep and complex to be addressed by any single political current. The committee cannot expect every stakeholder to endorse its initiative immediately, but it must create conditions that persuade reluctant actors to participate. If it fails to do so, the initiative itself will have failed.
The African Union Commission and the Arab League have also welcomed the initiative, providing an important measure of regional support. Their endorsement lends weight to the effort to revive Sudanese-led political dialogue, although external backing cannot substitute for the confidence of Sudan’s own political forces.
The committee’s initiative should therefore be judged without excessive optimism or automatic suspicion. The legal measures announced following its engagement with al-Burhan are an encouraging first step, but the real test lies ahead. Does it help remove legal and political obstacles facing opposition actors in practice, not just on paper? Can it win the confidence of those who have rejected it? Can it ensure that Sudanese across the country’s political and geographical divides have an opportunity to participate freely?
What is clear, however, is that Sudan’s crisis will ultimately require Sudanese actors with profoundly different visions of the country’s future to sit together and engage one another politically. No committee can do that on their behalf. No external actor can do it for them. At best, a preparatory initiative can help create the conditions under which such engagement becomes possible. The concerns raised by its critics should not be dismissed, but neither should they be grounds for rejecting the initiative before it has had an opportunity to address them. Those who have rejected it should remain open to reconsidering their position if the committee demonstrates that it can build an independent and inclusive process. If it succeeds, it will have rendered an important national service.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Israel returns 22 artifacts to Greece in first antiquities repatriation between Jerusalem, Athens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
05:49:11 UTC
14:49:11 KST

Israel on Tuesday returned a collection of 22 artifacts illegally removed from Greece, in the first repatriation of its kind between the two countries, as Athens renews its push to recover illegally taken and stolen antiquities from around the world.
Among the artifacts returned are fifteen ancient Attic vessels, six vases from Corinthian workshops, and one bronze statue of a female figure, all dating to between the 8th and 4th century BCE.
Of the Attic vessels, eleven are black-and-white, three are red-and-white, and one is ambergris, dating to the ancient and classical periods. The six Corinthian vases date to the ancient period, while the authenticity of the bronze female statuette requires further investigation.
The antiquities had been seized in 2020 during a joint investigation into illegal antiquities trafficking conducted by the IAA's Theft Prevention Unit, Israel Police, and the Israel Tax Authority. As part of the operation, the forces raided a gallery, warehouses and apartments in the Gush Dan area, where thousands of illegally acquired archaeological items from Israel and around the world were found.
They were officially returned in a Tuesday handover ceremony at the National Archaeological Museum in Athens, attended by Greek Culture Minister Lina Mendoni, Israeli Ambassador to Greece Pninat Yanay, and Israel Antiquities Authority's (IAA) Theft Prevention Unit Amir Ganor.
Mendoni said Israel's return of the 22 antiquities is especially significant, "marking the first time Israel has returned antiquities to Greece, serving as the starting point for closer cooperation between the two countries in the protection of cultural heritage."
Combating illegal antiquities trade
"This return confirms that cooperation between states can make a substantial contribution to combating the illicit trade in antiquities," she stated, noting that "The return of any cultural asset to its place of origin carries a broader symbolic and ethical dimension. It serves as a reminder that the protection of cultural heritage is a collective responsibility."
"I am confident that the cooperation between Greece and Israel will continue to yield tangible results in the safeguarding of cultural heritage."
In her own speech at the ceremony, Yanay explained that "Antiquities are much more than historical objects."
"They are moments from the past, frozen in time through art. They tell us who the people who created them were, what they believed in, how they lived, and remind us how deeply the past remains part of who we are today."
"For more than 2,000 years, these ancient objects have witnessed the rise and fall of empires, wars, revolutions, and enormous changes in our world. And through it all, they have survived," she said.
Becoming links in the chains between generations
"This celebration is not only about returning antiquities to their rightful home. It is also a celebration of something much greater and deeper: the special, strong, and profound friendship between the State of Israel and Greece," she wrote.
"Two modern states, two ancient nations, and two great civilizations that deeply understand the meaning of history, the importance of heritage, and the responsibility to preserve it for future generations. These antiquities belong to Greece’s past. Today, through their return, they also become part of the shared future of Israel and Greece."
'"Let us try to imagine a child looking at one of these ancient vessels today and feeling a spark of wonder," added Yanay. "They see what another child might have seen and felt 2,000 years ago, and thus become another link in the chain of generations that had been broken."
"For me, there is also something deeply moving in the thought that I have the privilege, as Ambassador of Israel, of placing this ancient object into your capable hands, and that my country had the honor of contributing to this significant moment and mission."
"The illegal trade in antiquities knows no borders, neither the boundaries of the law nor the borders between countries,” said Ganor. “Antiquities that are looted in one country find their way to another, causing irreversible damage to the cultural heritage of the country of origin."
"The illegal trade in antiquities serves as a cover for the financing of terrorism and organized crime, and it serves as a means of money laundering. Cutting off smuggling chains and preventing continued illegal profiting on the back of antiquities helps to thwart and prevent various types of criminal activity, and certainly helps to protect cultural heritage assets.”
Heritage Minister Amichai Eliyahu added that "The State of Israel is well aware of the deep connection between a people and its heritage, and the importance of preserving the historical evidence that tells its story."
"The return of these antiquities to Greece expresses our commitment to protect cultural heritage assets, and to act resolutely against the illegal trade in antiquities, wherever it takes place."
He continued, congratulated the IAA and both Greek and Israeli law enforcement agencies for their actions that led to the return of the artifacts.
"The strengthening cooperation between the countries expresses a shared responsibility to preserve the treasures of the past, for the sake of future generations," he said.
Israel, Greece expected to sign heritage MoU
As result of the cooperation between the IAA's Theft Prevention Unit and the Greek Antiquities Police in this case, a joint international enforcement workshop was held for representatives of the two units last month.
During the workshop, the two units discussed the possibility of expanding information sharing, identify items suspected of being looted, and trace antiquities trade routes.
In her remarks at the handover ceremony, Mendoni noted that during her visit to Jerusalem in March 2025, she discussed the expansion of cultural cooperation between Israel and Greece with Culture and Sports Minister Miki Zohar.
According to Mendoni, the return of these antiquities is a practical expression of the commitment that the two ministers discussed at their meeting. As well, a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) is expected to be signed between the countries, which will anchor their cooperation in the field of protecting cultural heritage assets.

At the same time, operational and intelligence coordination between the IDF and the US military's Central Command (CENTCOM) is aimed at refining early-warning mechanisms against attempts to catch Israel by surprise and reducing the likelihood of unexpected attacks as much as possible.

Gigantic prehistoric snake discovered in India may have been one of the largest ever
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
05:44:39 UTC
14:44:39 KST

Gigantic prehistoric snake discovered in India may have been one of the largest ever
- Date:
- October 14, 2026
- Source:
- Scientific Reports
- Summary:
- A massive prehistoric snake discovered in India may have rivaled the largest snake ever known. Called Vasuki indicus, the 47-million-year-old giant could have reached up to 50 feet long, making it comparable to the legendary Titanoboa. Scientists believe its enormous body made it a slow-moving ambush predator, similar to a modern anaconda.
- Share:
A colossal prehistoric snake that lived in India about 47 million years ago may have been one of the largest snakes ever to exist. Known as Vasuki indicus, the ancient reptile could have reached an extraordinary 15.2 meters (50 feet) in length, putting it in the same league as Titanoboa, the enormous extinct snake long regarded as the largest ever discovered.
The remarkable discovery, described in 2024 in the journal Scientific Reports, came from fossils unearthed in Gujarat, western India. Researchers estimate that Vasuki measured between 10.9 and 15.2 meters (36 and 50 feet) long, although its exact size remains uncertain. Its enormous body and unusual evolutionary history offer a glimpse into a time when giant snakes inhabited the warm, tropical landscapes of ancient India.
Giant Snake Fossils Unearthed in India
Paleontologists Debajit Datta and Sunil Bajpai of the Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee identified the species from fossils recovered at the Panandhro Lignite Mine in Kutch, Gujarat. The remains date to the Middle Eocene, a period roughly 47 million years ago when Earth's climate was considerably warmer than it is today.
The researchers examined 27 fossilized vertebrae, the individual bones that make up a snake's backbone. Many were remarkably well preserved, and some remained connected in their original arrangement. The bones appear to have belonged to a fully grown animal.
The species was named Vasuki indicus in honor of Vasuki, the mythical serpent associated with the Hindu deity Shiva, who is traditionally depicted with the snake wrapped around his neck. The second part of the name refers to India, where the fossils were discovered.
How Big Was This Prehistoric Snake?
Although the scientists did not recover a complete skeleton, the preserved backbone provides important clues about the snake's enormous proportions.
Individual vertebrae measured between 37.5 and 62.7 millimeters (1.48 and 2.47 inches) long and between 62.4 and 111.4 millimeters (2.46 and 4.39 inches) wide. Their unusually broad shape suggests that Vasuki possessed a thick, cylindrical body capable of supporting tremendous weight.
To estimate its total length, the researchers compared the fossilized bones with vertebrae from living snakes whose body lengths are known. Two different methods produced estimates ranging from 10.9 to 12.2 meters (36 to 40 feet) and 14.5 to 15.2 meters (48 to 50 feet).
Those measurements place Vasuki among the largest snakes ever identified. Its estimated length rivals that of Titanoboa, the giant snake that inhabited what is now Colombia approximately 60 million years ago and is thought to have reached around 13 meters (43 feet).
However, the researchers caution that their calculations involve considerable uncertainty. Different methods can produce substantially different estimates, particularly when scientists must reconstruct an extinct animal using an incomplete backbone. It remains unclear whether Vasuki actually exceeded Titanoboa in length.
A Massive Predator That Likely Hunted by Ambush
Despite its intimidating size, Vasuki probably was not a particularly fast or agile hunter.
The researchers suggest that its enormous body and distinctive vertebral structure would have favored relatively slow movement. Rather than actively chasing prey, the snake may have relied on ambush tactics, remaining concealed until another animal came within striking distance.
Its hunting behavior could have resembled that of modern anacondas and large pythons, which can overpower prey through constriction. These snakes use their muscular bodies to tighten around captured animals, interfering with circulation until the prey dies.
Scientists suspect Vasuki may have hunted in a similar way, although its precise diet and hunting behavior cannot be determined from the surviving fossils.
Its anatomy also suggests that the snake may have spent much of its time on land or in shallow, swampy environments, rather than living exclusively in water. The ancient landscape surrounding the fossil site contained wetlands and marshes that could have provided suitable habitat for an enormous ambush predator.
Ancient India's Warm Climate May Have Helped Snakes Grow Enormous
The discovery also raises questions about why some prehistoric snakes reached sizes far beyond those of most species alive today.
During the Middle Eocene, the region where Vasuki lived experienced tropical conditions, with average temperatures estimated at approximately 28 degrees Celsius (82 degrees Fahrenheit).
Snakes are ectothermic animals, meaning they depend heavily on external sources of heat to regulate their body temperature. Warm environments can support the activity, digestion, and growth of large reptiles, potentially helping explain why exceptionally large snakes appeared during some of Earth's warmer periods.
However, temperature alone does not determine how large a snake can become. Food availability, suitable habitat, evolutionary history, and other environmental factors also influence body size.
A Lost Lineage of Giant Snakes That Spread Across Continents
Beyond its extraordinary size, Vasuki provides evidence of an ancient branch of snake evolution.
The species belonged to Madtsoiidae, an extinct family of snakes that survived for roughly 100 million years, from the Late Cretaceous to the Late Pleistocene. Members of this group occupied regions including India, Africa, Europe, South America, and Australia.
Unlike modern anacondas and pythons, Vasuki represented a separate evolutionary lineage within this long-extinct family.
The researchers found that its closest relatives included Madtsoia pisdurensis, a fossil snake from ancient India, and Gigantophis garstini, another large prehistoric snake known from North Africa.
These relationships suggest that a lineage of giant madtsoiid snakes originated on the Indian subcontinent before spreading into other parts of the world.
As India moved northward and collided with Asia around 50 million years ago, changing geographic connections may have allowed these snakes to disperse through southern Eurasia, including southern Europe, and eventually into Africa during the Eocene, approximately 56 to 34 million years ago.
Later Fossil Discoveries Reveal an Ancient World Filled With Snakes
Research published in 2025 has added important context to the discovery of Vasuki.
In a study published in the Journal of Paleontology, Datta and Bajpai described additional fossil snakes from Eocene deposits in western India. Their findings revealed a surprisingly diverse community of ancient reptiles, including aquatic snakes, another large member of the madtsoiid family, and other extinct snake groups.
Among the discoveries was Pterosphenus rannensis, an ancient aquatic snake species that adds to scientists' understanding of how these reptiles evolved and spread.
The researchers also identified another madtsoiid snake that appears to have shared a marshy environment with Vasuki. This suggests that the giant predator was part of a broader community of snakes occupying different ecological roles, rather than an isolated evolutionary oddity.
Evidence from the fossil deposits indicates that some of these snakes inhabited tidal environments, while others occupied swamps and marshes. Together, the discoveries paint a more detailed picture of the complex ecosystems that existed in India tens of millions of years ago.
What Modern Anacondas Reveal About Giant Snakes
Additional evidence about snake gigantism emerged from a separate 2025 study published in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology.
Researchers examining fossilized anaconda vertebrae from Venezuela found that these enormous snakes had already evolved large bodies by approximately 12.4 million years ago. Ancient anacondas reached estimated lengths of around 5.2 meters (17 feet), comparable to the size of many living anacondas.
The findings suggest that anacondas maintained their impressive size for millions of years, even as climates and ecosystems changed. They also show that prehistoric snakes did not necessarily grow larger simply because the planet was warmer.
Although anacondas are evolutionarily distinct from Vasuki, the research offers a useful comparison for understanding how different snake lineages became giants and adapted to their environments.
For Vasuki indicus, the full story remains incomplete. Its precise size, appearance, and behavior are still uncertain, but the fossil evidence establishes it as an extraordinary example of prehistoric gigantism.
Together with later discoveries from the same region, the ancient snake is helping scientists reconstruct a largely forgotten world in which massive serpents occupied the tropical landscapes of India.

Details
Counterpoint Research reports that global smartphone shipments fell by 20% in the third quarter of 2026, reaching their lowest level in 14 years. The last time smartphone shipments were this low was when Samsung released the Galaxy S3.
The decline affected not only overall shipment figures but also the market share held by major smartphone brands.
Chinese brands, including Xiaomi, Vivo, and Oppo, accounted for a smaller share of the overall market in the third quarter of 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier, while Samsung continued to hold the leading position with 23% of the overall market, and Apple held 22%, compared with 19% and 18%, respectively.
Counterpoint says that Samsung's overall shipments fell by only 3%, with the success of the Galaxy Z Fold 8 playing a major role in the company's performance this quarter. Meanwhile, a recent report claims that Samsung is currently not making a profit from selling Galaxy phones.
Meanwhile, Apple experienced a 22% year-over-year decline due to the absence of a standard iPhone 18. Oppo and Vivo declined by approximately 20%, while Xiaomi cut shipments by 30%.

Turkish prosecutors appoint government trustee to run pro-opposition Halk TV
ANKARA, Oct 14 - Turkish authorities appointed a government trustee to run pro-opposition broadcaster Halk TV, prosecutors said on Wednesday, as police raided the channel's Istanbul office in a case that has renewed concerns about media freedom in the country.
The Istanbul Chief Prosecutor's Office said its financial crimes unit had conducted an investigation into Halk TV Chairman Cafer Mahiroglu over "bribery, tender-rigging, and laundering of assets derived from crime", adding that evidence, witness statements and transaction records showed criminal activity.
The prosecutor's statement said it had issued detention orders for 17 people, including Mahiroglu, and 11 of them had been detained. Firms in which Mahiroglu is a partner or administrator have been seized and the Savings Deposit Insurance Fund (TMSF) has been appointed as trustee, the statement added.
Mahiroglu, who is currently outside Turkey, is being sought by the authorities.
"Hundreds of police have entered the building. Entry into the Halk TV building is not being permitted while a search is being conducted inside," the broadcaster said on its website.
The channel's live broadcast was cut at 6:30 a.m. (0330 GMT), after which pre-recorded material began airing.
Deniz Bayramoglu, a programmer at Halk TV, said on X that Editor-in-Chief Suat Toktas had tried to argue with the head of the trustee delegation to continue the broadcast but that this was not permitted.
CRACKDOWN ON PRESS FREEDOM
The move makes Halk TV the fifth major Turkish news outlet to have a trustee appointed, following similar legal decisions for Flash TV, Eko Turk, Haberturk and Tele1.
The government has often used the appointment of trustees in recent years to take over the administration of municipalities or to seize companies. It has long appointed political trustees to take charge of municipalities in southeastern Turkey, removing elected mayors from a pro-Kurdish opposition party.
Authorities have more recently appointed trustees to several major opposition-held municipalities as part of an unprecedented legal crackdown on the opposition, prompting some mayors to join President Tayyip Erdogan's ruling party.
Rights groups and Western countries have criticised Erdogan's government over its human rights record and crackdown on press freedom in recent years as it establishes tighter control over mainstream media. Several opposition or independent outlets have experienced access bans, fines, and other restrictions.
Ozgur Ozel, chairman of the main opposition New Party, condemned the move against Halk TV, saying it was an attempt by the government to prevent people from accessing news.
"Dawn raid on a television channel, appointing a trustee — only dictators would do such a thing," Ozel said on X.
"Those who appoint trustees to municipalities and trample the people's will have now appointed a trustee to Halk TV, watched by millions. Because THEY ARE IMPOTENT AND COWARDS!" REUTERS

From Cairo to Tokyo: Can you guess these twin cities?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
05:40:18 UTC
14:40:18 KST

From Cairo to Tokyo: Can you guess these twin cities?
As a London borough moves to cut ties with Haifa, test your knowledge of the world’s twin cities.
Hackney, a borough in east London, is consulting residents until October 14 on whether to end its twinning with Haifa, Israel’s third-largest city, a link that dates back to 1968.
The Green Party-led council voted on July 28 to end the partnership in principle, citing its values and human rights commitments amid Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. Councillors will make a final decision after the consultation and a review of the borough’s twinning policy.
What are twin cities?
Twin cities, also called sister cities, are places in different countries linked by formal friendship agreements. These relationships can support school exchanges, cultural events and civic visits, though many become inactive over time.
Can you guess which cities are twinned? Take our quiz below.
How twin cities began
Modern town twinning grew after World War II as a way to rebuild trust and foster peace. Coventry and Stalingrad (now Volgograd), both heavily bombed during the war, established a friendship link in 1944, often cited as the first modern city-twinning relationship.
The US city of St Paul and Japan’s Nagasaki established a sister-city partnership in 1955 to promote reconciliation after the atomic bombing of the latter in 1945. Cities have since formed links because of shared histories, similar roles as capitals or ports, or communities with roots in both places.
Why do cities cut ties?
Because twinning is often symbolic, ending a link can allow a council to make a statement. Several UK councils suspended or ended links with Russian cities after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
Prague’s relationship with Beijing also ended in 2019 amid a dispute involving Taiwan, after which the Czech Republic established a partnership with Taipei. Hackney’s proposal is the latest example of cities reassessing their international ties.

====================================================================================================

'You live from one deployment to the next': Israeli reservists struggle to rebuild their lives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
05:35:42 UTC
14:35:42 KST

On October 6, 2023, after 21 consecutive days on base, Gleb and his soldiers headed home for the weekend. The next day, just two days before he was due to begin his pre-discharge leave, his phone rang. It was his commanding officer: "Get here."
Three years later, Gleb has never really left military life behind. Although he officially completed his mandatory service in December 2023, he has since been called up for six rounds of reserve duty. His next deployment is already scheduled for January.
Noam, who completed his mandatory service almost a year after Gleb, has also been caught in the same cycle. He has already served more than 260 days in the reserves.
Both belong to a generation of young combat soldiers caught between military service and civilian life. They were discharged in the midst of the longest war in Israel's history, with no smooth transition or period of respite. As the reserve system struggles under an unprecedented burden, they are repeatedly called back to fight in the north and south, while their education, careers and personal lives remain on hold.
The two discussed the friends they have lost, the psychological toll they continue to endure and a discharge that exists largely on paper.
"I avoided starting school, taking a new job or getting involved in a project because I knew I'd be called back to reserve duty," Gleb says. "So why even start?"
'A zombie horror movie'
The two men came to the military from different backgrounds. Noam gave up a potential career as a professional soccer player and consulted his rabbi and father before enlisting. "We concluded that I would find a way to combine military service with my religious lifestyle." In March 2022, he enlisted in the Givati Brigade's Tomer Company, a unit for ultra-Orthodox soldiers.
Gleb enlisted a year earlier, in March 2021, joining the Paratroopers Brigade. He completed his mandatory service as a commander in the combat platoon at Havat Hashomer, an IDF training base. "I started my military journey at Havat Hashomer, so I went back there to come full circle," he explains.
After receiving that phone call, Gleb rushed to his base to collect equipment, then headed to the Jordan Valley to prepare his battalion.
"We stocked up on as much ammunition and water as we could, then headed into the unknown," he recalls.
From the Jordan Valley, his unit was sent directly south to Kfar Aza, Be'eri and Sderot.
"It was a shock," Gleb says. "The roads around Gaza looked like something out of a zombie horror movie. It was hard to believe this was happening, especially here, in our own home.
"The first week was one shock after another, mission after mission, and we still hadn't grasped the magnitude of what had happened. Then we started hearing about the soldiers killed in our battalion, in our team. The first friends we had lost. Only then did we understand that we were going to war and that we would be entering Gaza. This wasn't an operation in Nablus or a firefight in a refugee camp. This was about taking back control."
Noam: "Say you start studying. Then what? Before you know it, you're back in Lebanon with no reception, trying to connect to Zoom and falling behind. It just won't work."
Noam and his team were training at the Tsnobar military outpost in northern Israel on Oct. 7, where they were serving as the area's quick-reaction force.
"You don't even feel like you're part of what's happening. You're in shock," he recalls.
He describes how, the moment they learned of the attack on the Gaza border communities, the commanders and soldiers quickly gathered their equipment and boarded buses that took them south, to the front lines.
In those early days, when the full picture was still unclear, devastating messages began appearing in their WhatsApp groups.
"One of the guys I went through basic training with wrote, ‘Our unit is gone. Our team is gone.’" Noam says. "You read that and can't process the fact that it's happening so close to you."
Discharged from the military, called straight back to the reserves
The war made it clear to both men that completing their mandatory service was far from the end of their military obligations.
Gleb's mandatory service was extended by three months. Just six months after it ended, he was called up for his first reserve deployment.
"You never get your reserve call-up notice six weeks in advance, the way you're supposed to," Gleb says. "It's always just a few days beforehand. Once, I got a message from one of my officers at 4:30 a.m.: 'Report to the base in the north on Friday. We're entering Lebanon on Sunday.'"
Noam was discharged in November 2024, and just a month later he was back in uniform.
"The soldier I trained to replace me was killed," he says. "At that moment, I realized I had to find a way to go back and train someone else. I returned to my unit as a reservist, and this time I trained five soldiers instead of one."
Another emergency reserve call-up order, known in Israel as a Tzav 8, is already awaiting him in November.
For both men, every attempt to build a civilian life has been thwarted by the knowledge that another call-up is just around the corner.
"It's constant exhaustion, a steady downward spiral," Noam says. "You remain in the same place you were when you were discharged, living from one deployment to the next. In between, you start thinking about civilian life and realize it's not really possible.
"Say you start studying. Then what? Before you know it, you're back in Lebanon with no reception, trying to connect to Zoom and falling behind. It just won't work."
He was forced to postpone plans to improve his high school exam scores and register for the psychometric  exam, Israel's standardized test for university admission, after realizing he would be called up for another deployment midway through his first semester.
"Since my discharge, for two years and eight months now, I've been stuck in the same place: working in security, going on a reserve deployment, returning to security work and then another deployment," Gleb says.
"There's this feeling of being stuck that affects almost everything. I avoided starting school, taking a new job or getting involved in a project because I knew I'd be called up for reserve duty and wouldn't really be able to devote myself to it. So why even start?"
'Everyone I know is struggling emotionally'
But the deepest wounds do not appear on a resume, and recognizing the need to address them is only half the battle.
"There's a huge and difficult gap between understanding what needs to be done and actually doing it," Gleb says. "I realized during the first months of the war that I would need to process what I'd been through, but I didn't actually start until six months after completing my mandatory service."
Members of his team organized their own sessions to process their experiences. Every two or three days, they would sit together without professional guidance, simply to make sure no one was left behind.
"It gives me the feeling that I'm not alone. There are difficult moments, and I know who to turn to. My friends always keep an eye on anyone who's struggling, and I do the same."
Gleb: "The state and the Defense Ministry must pay much more attention to the mental health of discharged combat soldiers because what's being done today simply isn't enough. Everyone close to me has been affected psychologically."
But not everyone can talk about their distress or ask for help, and in the most extreme cases, the consequences can be devastating.
"When you don't process what you've been through, it can reach the point where a combat soldier takes his own life," Gleb warns.
"Sadly, I lost one of my soldiers and a friend who couldn't cope with what they'd been through. May his memory be a blessing. That's the price of failing to address these issues. The state and the Defense Ministry must pay much more attention to the mental health of discharged combat soldiers because what's being done today simply isn't enough.
"Everyone close to me has been affected psychologically, and there's no shame in that. We do difficult work that not everyone is willing to take on and not everyone is capable of handling. It comes at a cost, and that cost needs to be acknowledged.
"At the same time, treatment is available, and people must get help. Responsibility is shared by the state, the Defense Ministry and the military, but some of it also rests with the combat soldier himself."
Noam points to another failure: The system relies entirely on soldiers seeking help themselves.
"Some guys just can't bring themselves to ask for help. All they have are their friends, who come and sit with them, but we're not professionals. A mental health professional needs to reach out to them and provide ongoing support."
He believes friends and relatives should also be able to report when a soldier is in distress, rather than waiting until it is too late.
Alongside their psychological struggles, Noam and Gleb discovered that taking their first steps into civilian life was far from straightforward.
Both turned to Gav LaLochem ("Support for the Fighter"), a nonprofit organization founded in 2019 by Oria Isaak and Itamar Israelit that has helped approximately 2,000 discharged combat soldiers to date.
Through a series of meetings, the organization provides practical tools for managing finances, entrepreneurship and career development, as well as job placement assistance, a personal mentor and access to an alumni community.
"Combat soldiers think they'll be welcomed with a red carpet when they leave the military, but that's not how it works at all," Noam says. "You get out and you're in shock. At Gav LaLochem, there are mentors who guide you every step of the way."
"That transition is critical," Gleb explains, "because discharged combat soldiers don't have a sufficient safety net to ease their transition to civilian life, something to help them make sense of civilian life, even when it comes to the simplest things."

Forcing gas producers to sell to Australia won't 'crash' prices, King says
Unknown

2026-10-14
05:34:59 UTC
14:34:59 KST

Gas reservation laws won't cause wholesale price 'crash', King says
In short:
The resources minister has declined to detail how far she expects gas prices to fall under a proposed reservation law, saying the government's modelling is commercially sensitive.
Madeleine King has introduced legislation to create a gas reservation scheme she says will create a "modest" domestic oversupply.
What's next?
The Coalition has indicated it will work with the government to pass the laws, but says questions remain about how future supply and investment will be assured.
The resources minister says gas prices will not crash under national reservation laws, but refused to say how much they will fall as the industry warns the government is pushing too hard.
Madeleine King said she wanted the proposed laws to make prices fairer while ensuring new gas projects would still be profitable enough to proceed.
"Allow me to be clear: we need gas to support the rollout of renewables. We need gas to have a strong Australian manufacturing industry. We need gas to continue heating our homes," she said.
The legislation introduced to parliament this morning would force producers to sell up to a fifth of their gas slated for export to Australia, pushing down wholesale prices by sparing the country from having to compete with the international market for its own resource.
How much gas producers will be required to sell to Australia each year would be set by the energy regulator, with a target amount of 110 per cent of Australia's actual needs. The government says the "modest oversupply" will put downward pressure on prices for consumers.
But after being burned by its failure to meet a previous promise to cut home power bills by $275 through renewables, which was thrown off course by Russia's invasion of Ukraine driving up gas and fuel prices globally, the government has been reluctant to put a price tag on how much prices would be expected to fall under the scheme.
The resources minister told the National Press Club that the rules for gas producers had been carefully balanced, but that information was commercially sensitive.
"We have done a lot of study and a lot of analysis and, I might add, that so has just about everybody else in relation to this," Ms King said.
"A lot of the modelling that we have done, or the analysis that we have done, is commercial-in-confidence, so it is difficult."
She said the government would release an impact assessment related to its gas reservation laws, but did not commit to that including estimated impacts on wholesale gas prices.
"Our focus is on making sure there is this modest oversupply, and that demand calibration is really important, as well, in this," Ms King said.
"We all know having too little gas to firm renewables or provide for the manufacturing industry is as dangerous as having a massive oversupply which crashes the market, but also it can undermine investment in renewables, so it is a really fine balance we have got to achieve here."
The resources minister said the bill's focus was to make gas cheaper for heavy industry and energy generation, but added that an important element was ensuring cheaper gas prices "will be felt by the consumer".
'Sugar hit' will hurt in long-term, industry says
The gas industry has warned that the government's plan could force the sale of gas at rates that are cheaper than it costs to produce.
It says the scheme might provide a "sugar hit", but would make future gas projects unviable and dry up supply in the long-term.
"The government cannot expect industry to invest billions of dollars in new gas supply while introducing policies that fundamentally undermine the commercial viability of those investments," Australian Energy Producers chief executive Samantha McCulloch said.
"Any price impact is likely to be temporary because of the impact this is going to have on investment and future gas supply.
"The [Australian Competition and Consumer Commission] has said that the marginal cost of new supply is somewhere between $9.50 and $13 [per gigajoule]. You need a price within that range to encourage investment in new supply."
Australian Energy Regulator data shows wholesale gas prices have been between about $10 to $11.50 per gigajoule, depending on jurisdiction.
The Coalition has indicated it will work with the federal government to create a national gas reservation scheme, but says "numerous questions" remain about how future supply and investment will be assured.
"Reserving gas on paper is one thing. Ensuring we have the supply, investment, and infrastructure to deliver affordable, reliable energy to Australians when and where they need it, is another," Shadow Resources Minister Susan McDonald said in a statement.
The gas reservation scheme is meant to provide a long-term fix to issues that emerged after the invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Wholesale gas prices soared from their average of less than $10 per gigajoule to $60 per gigajoule amid the interruption to global supply.
The federal government rushed in temporary fixes, including a one-year cap of $12 per gigajoule on gas prices, but a government review of the gas market found those had not been "sufficient" to place downward pressure on prices, and longer-term answers were needed to give the industry confidence to continue investing.
It also noted that new production and infrastructure to get gas from the north to south-eastern Australia was "critical" to ensuring lower prices.

WASILLA, Alaska – With three weeks to go before the US midterm elections, President Donald Trump campaigned in remote Alaska on Oct 13, one of several conservative states where Democrats have a rare chance of flipping a Senate seat amid voter dissatisfaction with the cost of living and the Iran war.
Polls have shown Democratic candidate Mary Peltola tied with or slightly ahead of incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan in a state that Trump carried by about 14 percentage points in 2024.
In Alaska, as in much of the US, the President’s approval rating is underwater, hit by rising diesel and petrol prices and a conflict in the Middle East that has proven deeply unpopular with voters.
Energy shocks have an outsized impact on this vast Arctic state, where people depend on heating oil to brave the long winters and many products must be flown, shipped or trucked across vast distances.
Opening for Trump, Sullivan acknowledged that Alaskans face “challenges” when it comes to energy costs.
But “the conflict in the Middle East is temporary”, he said. “The true forever war is the national Democrats’ war against Alaska oil and gas and our jobs.”
The Republicans’ decision to hold a rally in Wasilla, a deeply conservative town of roughly 10,000 people about 45 minutes north of Anchorage, the state’s most populous city, fits an emerging pattern.
Trump has taken to campaigning in conservative-leaning parts of competitive states, rather than in more politically diverse areas with more votes potentially up for grabs.
The strategy could help turn out his most devoted supporters on election day, analysts say, while keeping Trump far from the independents and political moderates who have soured on his presidency.
Soon after taking the stage at a sports complex surrounded by birch, spruce and aspen trees, Trump vowed the Iran war would “end very soon... and prices will come tumbling down”.
“I’ve done more for this state than any other state in the union,” he said, highlighting his administration’s efforts to attract Asian investment in an Alaskan pipeline project, fund new power lines and expand high-speed internet access.
At one point, Trump pardoned two local repair shop owners convicted of violating the federal Clean Air Act for removing pollution controls from diesel engines.
He also encouraged Republicans to vote by mail – a process he has repeatedly sought to curtail and discredit.
Lance Million, 68, a retired foreman from Wasilla who showed up early for the Oct 13 rally, expressed dissatisfaction with the Iran war but said he would vote for Sullivan because “I’m a Republican, a staunch Republican”.
“I’m a little bit disappointed in Trump for not getting it (the war in Iran) over with in a timely manner,” Million said.
Still, he said, “we just don’t have any other choice at this point in time because it’s either Sullivan or Peltola”.
Polls lean towards Democrats
All 435 seats in the US House of Representatives and 35 of the 100 US Senate seats will be decided on Nov 3.
Public opinion polls suggest Republicans may lose control of one or both houses of Congress, which would likely limit Trump’s ability to enact his policies in the final two years of his presidency.
A New York Times/Siena survey released on Oct 3 showed Peltola, an Alaska native who served as the state’s sole US House representative from 2022 to 2025, leading by 7 percentage points, though some polls point to a much tighter race.
Suzanne Downing, the former communications director for the Alaska Republican Party, said fuel prices were weighing on every aspect of rural life and proving a major drag on Republicans.
She said Alaskan men in particular were apathetic about voting this cycle – a potential problem for Republicans as they tend to be conservative.
“They like Trump, but they feel like they’ve been let down,” Downing said.
Campaigning in Wasilla could help the President “reinvigorate” his base, she added.
Sullivan, a former Alaska attorney-general, has been a strong advocate for oil and gas drilling, including in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, and has emphasised the state’s strategic importance amid growing US competition with Russia and China over control of the Arctic.
Peltola made history in 2022 as the first Alaska native and first woman elected to represent the state in the House of Representatives.
She cultivated a pragmatic, bipartisan image and focused on local issues such as fisheries but lost her 2024 re-election bid to Republican Nick Begich III.
Responding to previous criticism from Sullivan over her record, Peltola has said she supports oil and gas development in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and that she is not a typical national Democrat.
Jo Bennett, a retired state worker from Anchorage in her 60s who said she has voted for both parties, was among a group of women on the afternoon of Oct 13 putting up placards on an overpass along the highway between Anchorage and Wasilla.
Together they read: “War is a pain in the ga$.”

Trump says "massive" oil, gas and mineral exploration in Greenland is "getting ready to begin"
President Trump said Wednesday that "massive" oil, gas and mineral exploration is preparing to begin in Greenland.
In a statement posted on his Truth Social platform, Mr. Trump said "Massive Oil, Gas, and Mineral Exploration is getting ready to begin in our new and beautiful Greenland," but did not give more details.
The president added that "there are Experts that are saying that the amount of easily available Oil is far greater than that of almost any land, anywhere in the World."
Mr. Trump also touted Greenland's role in the defense of the United States in Europe, saying that "any future attack" on the U.S. would have to come across the semi-autonomous island, "where our Defense will routinely knock down drones, missiles, or any other form of weapon not yet conceived."
"It gives us time, location, and sightline, like nowhere else in the World!" Mr. Trump added.
The announcement comes more than four weeks after the U.S., Greenland and Denmark, which oversees the territory, signed a new security agreement to bolster American military and security presence on the island.
That agreement, which gives the U.S. broad access to the island's airspace and territory, largely focuses on using Greenland for military purposes, but also mentions resource extraction and "minerals cooperation" between the two countries, without specifying any details.
The plan allows the U.S. to expand the existing Pituffik Space Base, the northernmost U.S. military installation which serves as an early-warning system for incoming missiles. The agreement also says the U.S. can establish additional bases at the sites known as Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig, which are roughly 950 miles apart. Any of the three parties can propose more "defense areas" as needed, subject to approval by the others.
The deal, which has no expiration date, also blocks non-NATO countries from establishing bases on the island without agreement from the parties.
Since his first term, Mr. Trump had cited Greenland's strategic location as one of the reasons for greater U.S. control over the semi-autonomous island, and even suggested purchasing the island from Denmark or using military force.
Some industry experts believe mineral resources in Greenland have only been lightly explored and up until now the cost of extraction has not made economic sense for private companies.

Fuuga, Turku's new, sprawling music centre along the Aura River is opening on 26 October.
The 90-million-euro project was approved back in 2020, and the facility is preparing to welcome its first visitors.
The name Fuuga is the Finnish term for ‘fugue’ - a musical composition in which different voices weave around a central melody.
At the heart of the building is the main concert hall, which seats around 1,300 people. A second smaller hall, Ateljee, can accommodate another 300.
Fuuga will become the home of the Turku Philharmonic Orchestra, but the centre is intended to be more than just a concert venue. Its restaurant and roof terrace offer views over the Aura River, while visitors can enter the building without buying a concert ticket or visiting the restaurant.
According to Turku Mayor Piia Elo, the space is meant for all of the city's residents, rather than a venue exclusively reserved for concertgoers.
Interest in the new venue is strong, with more than 80 percent of tickets for the autumn programme already sold.

====================================================================================================

Economic Watch: New wave of American fast-food chains bets on China's younger generation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:31:57 CST
14:31:57 KST

SHANGHAI, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- At noon on a September day, the line outside the newly opened Church's Texas Chicken, a fried chicken shop from Atlanta in the United States, wound back two or three times, filling nearly half the walkway on a downtown Shanghai food street.
After about an hour, two young women were nearing the end of the line. "It's a first store, so a bigger crowd is only normal," one said. Behind them was an eager buyer surnamed Shi, who had studied in Canada. The bone-in fried chicken felt like an old acquaintance, he said. "It's juicier."
Across the street, Gao, the owner of a herbal tea shop, had grown used to the long queue out front. She recalled the crowds were even bigger in the first few days after opening. "They lined up from 9 a.m. to 10 p.m."
This American fast-food chain is the latest to make high-profile inroads into the Chinese mainland market. While McDonald's and KFC, which entered China over three decades ago, have long been etched in the memories of Chinese millennials, a new wave of U.S. fast-food brands is once again betting on China's younger generation.
In early August, Virginia-based burger brand Five Guys opened its first two Beijing locations at two Joy City malls, following its 2021 Shanghai debut. The chain, which prides itself on using fresh ingredients and no freezers, charges around 100 yuan (about 15 U.S. dollars) per meal, pricier than expected. Even weeks after opening, customers still line up for their orders.
In addition, Popeyes, the well-known Southern-style fried chicken chain that set up shop in Shanghai's busiest commercial district in 2020, ventured into Beijing this April with a store in Wangfujing shopping district, where waits once exceeded an hour before foot traffic gradually leveled off. Popeyes now operates more than 100 stores in China.
And there's more to come. Wendy's, headquartered in the U.S. state of Ohio, announced in May a new franchise agreement to build up to 1,000 restaurants in China over the next 10 years.
"With U.S. fast-food brands increasingly entering China, the Chinese market is a top priority in our global expansion, underscoring our long-term commitment to the country," Steven Zhang, China CEO of Texas Chicken, told Xinhua. The chain has signed a development deal with a local team for at least 600 stores.
PAST GLORY, NEW BATTLE
Chinese consumers' craze for American fast food can be traced back to a few years after the country's reform and opening up.
In November 1987, KFC opened its first fried chicken restaurant in the Chinese mainland at Qianmen, Beijing. A piece of original recipe chicken cost 2.5 yuan at the time -- a premium price by Chinese consumption standards then. Even so, crowds still waited nearly an hour in line for a piece of fried chicken.
In October 1990, McDonald's opened its maiden Shenzhen store, where all 20 cash registers running at full capacity still weren't enough to meet demand, and all 500 seats inside were filled. Back then, eating American fast food was considered a status symbol for the newly emerging Chinese middle class.
Over the past four decades, the country's fast-food sector has gone from a blank slate to one of the most crowded markets in the world. Domestic fried chicken and burger brands, like Wallace Burger & Chicken and Tasiting, have rapidly expanded their store counts.
Now, a U.S. brand can no longer rely on local consumers' reverence for foreign labels to succeed. "In 1987, a KFC meal took up 7 percent of the average monthly salary, making it a luxury; in 2026, a per-customer spend of 30 to 40 yuan accounts for only about 0.5 percent," said Tang Jiansheng, deputy secretary-general of the Shanghai Consumer Council. The newcomers have to find their own value for Chinese consumers, he added.
Five Guys and Church's Texas Chicken are not targeting lower-tier markets for the time being and are instead pursuing a niche strategy, with food priced slightly above KFC.
"As one of China's most trendsetting and inclusive cities, Shanghai is highly receptive to new things, making it an ideal place for foreign brands to take root and a high-quality market sample for refining our products, services, and operating models in the early stages," said Zhang of Texas Chicken.
NICHE MARKET
Having queued for a quarter of an hour outside the Church's Texas Chicken store in Shanghai, a customer surnamed Zhou said, "In Shanghainese, this is called 'ga nao mang' -- it just means joining the fun."
Queuing is never the hard part, said Tang, an expert in consumer insights and business analysis. "The make-or-break test for foreign fast-food companies is to turn viral queues into everyday repeat business."
Before opening, the Church's Texas Chicken store ran taste tests with over 500 Chinese consumers, adjusting saltiness, seasoning, and crispiness to fix issues locals care about, according to Zhang.
The restaurant sits in a fashionable food district in downtown Shanghai that has seen a revival in recent years. "Three years ago, business on this street was nothing special, but now it's bustling again," Zhou said, pointing at the fried chicken shop's decor. "The planning team chose the location shrewdly -- even though the rent is expensive here, it has the largest foot traffic."
"The restaurant sector here is fiercely competitive, but most brands lean heavily on delivery and are highly homogenized," explained Zhang. "Fried chicken, by contrast, has a natural edge -- it works for both dine-in and delivery, making it more resilient."
To adapt to Chinese consumers' new fast-food habits, McDonald's has introduced drive-thru restaurants in China, with more than 80 already operating in Beijing.
Yum China, which operates KFC in the Chinese mainland, said in a written reply to Xinhua that Chinese consumers now care about both "value for money" and "emotional value." Last year, the company partnered with 70 top IPs spanning gaming, anime and sports to deepen engagement with local consumers.
INTERWOVEN CHAINS
The presence of American brands in China is going hand in hand with their deep integration into the country's industrial chain. McDonald's China, together with its core Chinese supply chain partners, participated in a supply chain expo held in Beijing this June.
Its potato supplier in China has launched precision fertilization pilots on three farms across north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. The program uses real-time petiole and soil testing, combined with dynamic fertilization decisions, to grow high-quality ingredients.
Yum China, which also owns Pizza Hut in the Chinese mainland, said it stays committed to a local-first approach, working to build a local supply chain system to world-class standards.
Church's Texas Chicken has chosen a local Chinese team to work with Yangtze River Delta suppliers and build a local supply chain, according to Zhang. "This model preserves the craft and brand identity of 74 years of American fried chicken while enabling quick, flexible responses to China's domestic market, avoiding cultural misfit issues."
In Tang's view, such a collaboration is now the popular approach used by foreign food brands entering China, thanks to the market's complexity, which requires deep localization and use of China's now highly mature local talent and capital.
China's supply chain depth and breadth mean "any brand producing and selling here can find ready and efficient support," said Tang.
"The resilience of China-U.S. trade ties over the past four decades rests on the value of China's market itself -- not just its vast consumer base, but its complete efficiency system," he added. ■

New Zealand extends strategic diesel reserve to August 2027

14:31:48 KST

WELLINGTON, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- The New Zealand government has extended an agreement for a 550,000-barrel strategic diesel reserve until Aug. 1, 2027, to strengthen the country's fuel security amid global uncertainty.
The reserve, held by Z Energy at Marsden Point in the country's Northland, is intended to protect domestic fuel supplies against potential disruptions, as diesel is critical to the economy, including key sectors such as agriculture and freight transport, Finance Minister Nicola Willis and Associate Energy Minister Shane Jones said in a statement on Wednesday.
Jones said that fuel supplies remain consistent, but the extension would help maintain domestic fuel resilience and protect against potential disruptions to diesel supply.
Diesel will continue to be stored in tanks at Marsden Point, and the storage capacity is about 90 million liters of fuel, equivalent to roughly nine days of typical national fuel consumption, the statement said.
Under the agreement, Z Energy will continue to own and manage the diesel, while the government will control its release into the domestic market.
If the diesel remains unused when the contract ends, it will progressively transition into Z Energy's regular stocks through November 2027. The agreement also limits the government's exposure to any long-term decline in fuel prices, the statement said.
The government is closely monitoring the impact of the Middle East conflict on energy security and has plans to respond if the global situation changes, Willis said. ■

Russia Destroys Ukrainian Troops’ Position as Encirclement Tightens in Kharkov Region
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
05:31:32 UTC
14:31:32 KST

Russia Destroys Ukrainian Troops’ Position as Encirclement Tightens in Kharkov Region

====================================================================================================

Russia Innovates for War, Not Prosperity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
05:31:00 UTC
14:31:00 KST

Russia excels at making things that destroy – at the expense of its own future.
Since Vladimir Putin launched his full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russia has concentrated its technological expertise, dwindling human capital, and oil-and-gas revenues on war, rather than on its people’s well-being.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
It has sharply increased production of missiles, glide bombs, and attack drones. Russian forces have improved their electronic warfare capabilities, learned to modify Iranian-designed Shahed drones, and incorporated Chinese jet engines into Banderol quasi-cruise missiles. Cheap first-person-view drones saturate the battlefield, and Russian engineers have devised increasingly sophisticated decoys to overwhelm Ukrainian air defenses.
Russia’s war machine is inflicting ever-greater death and devastation on Ukraine.
Four and a half years of war have created a war economy in which the Kremlin can concentrate money, engineers, imported components, and industrial capacity on its military priorities. That concentration of resources has imposed mounting costs that are becoming harder to conceal.
In September, the Bank of Russia kept its benchmark interest rate at 14 percent and forecast inflation of 6 to 7 percent for 2026. Russia is no longer experiencing the apparent wartime boom that followed the invasion. High interest rates make investment and modernization expensive, while military factories compete with civilian companies for engineers, machinists, capital and materials.
12 Senators Sign Bipartisan Letter Urging Trump to Rescind Russian Diesel Deal
In an article entitled “The Coming Crisis in Russia’s Political Economy,” published in May, Nigel Gould-Davies of the International Institute for Strategic Studies argues that Russia is approaching the limits of its productive capacity. Labor is an even tighter constraint. Oil-and-gas revenue can finance government spending but it cannot manufacture skilled workers or create factories, industrial equipment, and technological knowledge. As more resources are pushed into the military economy, each additional increment produces less.
Nowhere is Russia’s predicament clearer than in semiconductors. Mikron, part of the Rostec- and Sberbank-controlled Element Group, is a leading Russian chip manufacturer. It advertises production technologies ranging down to 90 nanometers; such mature semiconductors remain essential for automobiles, industrial equipment and many military systems.
By contrast, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) began volume production of its 2-nanometer technology late last year. Russia lacks the advanced chip-design capabilities, fabrication capacity, high-bandwidth memory, packaging, interconnects, cooling systems, and sophisticated software needed to manufacture processors competitive with those produced by TSMC and other leading semiconductor companies.
This matters because technological backwardness is not measured against where competitors stood five or ten years ago but where they are today. A Russian company that replaces an unavailable Western component may keep a factory operating but it has not narrowed the technological gap – it has merely reconstructed yesterday’s technology at considerable expense.
The pace outside Russia is accelerating further. On Sept. 30, 2026, OpenAI and Synopsys announced GPT-Synopsys, an artificial intelligence (AI) system being developed specifically to help design semiconductors. AI is increasingly being applied to the process of designing the next generation of technology itself.
Russian engineers, meanwhile, have a very different assignment – finding substitutes for unavailable software, maintaining aging equipment, and solving compatibility problems caused by sanctions. Russia calls this “technological sovereignty.”
One of its own most prominent businessmen has inadvertently exposed the weakness of that claim. In May, Sberbank CEO German Gref said Russia’s largest bank hoped eventually to operate its GigaChat AI system using Chinese processors. One of Russia’s showcase AI projects may depend on sophisticated chips Russia cannot competitively manufacture itself.
According to Bloomberg, citing people familiar with official assessments, more than 90 percent of Russia’s imports of sanctioned technology were coming through China by 2026. Before the war, Russian companies could participate, however imperfectly, in a diversified international technology economy. Putin has replaced much of that relationship with dependence on a single, more powerful neighbor whose interests do not necessarily align.
The deeper damage from this process is cumulative because industrial equipment and information systems require replacement parts, software updates, firmware, calibration, technical documentation and continuing support. A machine does not stop operating the morning its foreign manufacturer leaves Russia. It becomes progressively more difficult to maintain.
The results of Russia’s import-substitution campaign point in that direction. In a May 2026 study based on official documents, statistical data, and company surveys, Heli Simola of the Bank of Finland Institute for Emerging Economies (BOFIT) found that heavy investment in priority industries had produced only limited import substitution. In many sectors, output has declined and dependence on foreign inputs has increased.
The same problem appears in information technology. Russian technology company K2Tech reported this year that 70 percent of companies it examined remained dependent on Western backup systems. Russian replacements exist, but companies have been reluctant to abandon established foreign systems for critical operations.
Industrial deterioration is rarely instantaneous, but Ukraine has found a way to accelerate that process. Its deep drone strikes against Russian refineries and industrial facilities amount to what Ukrainians have aptly called “long-range sanctions.” Destroying a piece of equipment matters more when replacing it is difficult.
The Aug. 11, 2026 strike against the Orsk refinery illustrates the point. The refinery was forced to shut after a Ukrainian drone attack, and according to Orenburg Oblast Governor Yevgeny Solntsev, repairs are expected to take as long as six months because sanctions complicated the replacement of imported equipment.
Damage to one industrial facility consequently spreads outward – to fuel availability, transportation, military logistics, export revenues, and, ultimately, prices paid by Russian consumers.
None of the above makes Russia less dangerous. Russia has repeatedly demonstrated its ability to improvise, cannibalize commercial technologies, and solve particular military problems. This, however, is precisely the distinction that matters. A country can become exceptionally good at concentrating declining resources on weapons without becoming technologically stronger as a whole.
Putin inherited a country with considerable scientific talent, engineering traditions and industrial capacity. He has squandered that inheritance. Engineers are diverted toward weapons, civilian investment is crowded out, and Russian companies spend money reproducing technologies already available elsewhere. Dependence on Western technology has increasingly become dependence on Chinese technology. With every additional year of war, Russia risks becoming less capable of designing, building, and maintaining the technologies on which its future will depend.
Steven Fisher served as CEO of Citibank Ukraine from 2010 to 2018. He and Georgetown University’s Harley Balzer coedited Failure: Russia Under Putin (Brookings Institution Press, 2025). This op-ed was prompted in part by Balzer’s unpublished manuscript, “Technocide: How Putin’s Regime Stole Russia’s Future.”

Iran: Political infighting deepens as economic woes mount during war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
05:30:00 UTC
14:30:00 KST

Political infighting in Iran deepens as economic woes mount
October 14, 2026
Hardliners are piling the pressure on Iran’s government and calling for the removal of Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. Oil Minister Mohsen Paknejad’s resignation is also failing to ease the pressure on President Masoud Pezeshkian.
As the war continues and diplomatic efforts to find a solution make little headway, the internal power struggle is intensifying. President Pezeshkian’s government is the focus of mounting tension.
Hardliners in Iran's parliament are pushing for impeachment proceedings against Araghchi. A trigger for the discontent was Araghchi's meeting with US negotiators on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York. Critics accuse the foreign minister of holding the talks without official authorization.
In a letter, Tehran lawmaker Amirhossein Sabeti informed parliamentary speaker Mohammad-Bagher Ghalibaf that he had registered a motion to impeach Araghchi on parliament’s online portal. Lawmaker Hossein-Ali Haji-Deligani also said parliament could use its oversight powers, including impeachment proceedings.
A structural problem within Iran’s power system
"When the regime is forced to negotiate, as it is in the current situation and in talks with the United States, the supreme leader or the hardline core of power avoids taking responsibility and shifts it onto elected institutions and moderate forces within the government," political analyst Ali Afshari, who lives in the United States, told DW.
Hardliners can use this approach to attack moderate factions over decisions that were previously agreed upon within the power apparatus, Afshari said.
He added that hardliners serve an important function within the Islamic Republic.
"The role of hardliners in the Islamic Republic is to influence public opinion, the political system's traditional supporters and the values of the Islamic Republic in both domestic and foreign policy," he said.
Hardliners held a parliamentary majority during the implementation of the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), the 2015 nuclear deal, and voiced their political opposition. Their resistance, however, ultimately did not affect the signing of the agreement.
"The Foreign Ministry is not a decision-maker. It implements what the government asks of it — and Araghchi is operating within that framework," Afshari said.
Lawmakers must first collect a set number of signatures to move forward with impeachment proceedings.
The lucrative business of oil
The timing of the latest move is significant: Iran's government finds itself under enormous economic pressure. Meanwhile, oil exports, which are one of the country's key sources of revenue, have fallen sharply as a result of the US blockade.
The resignation of Oil Minister Paknejad adds to the pressure. Officially, he stepped down for personal reasons.
Umud Shokri, an energy strategist, geopolitical analyst and energy security expert, casts doubt that a change at the helm of the Oil Ministry would alter the situation. Iran relies on networks that enable it to export oil despite sanctions, Shokri said. Opaque structures have become entrenched, making it harder for the government to control key revenue streams.
Circumventing sanctions has become a lucrative business for certain factions within Iran's political system, he said.
"By law, these revenues should be under state control. But we know that has not been the case for years," Shokri said.
Economic opacity has deepened during the sanctions period, he added, under the pretext of national security and protecting the population.
Private actors with close ties to the country's centers of power, particularly the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), have developed methods to sell oil to the armed forces through hidden channels. Neither the prices nor the commissions charged or the total sums involved are transparent.
"The government has only limited influence over these transactions. The Revolutionary Guards, in particular, would organize and control such deals," Shokri said.
Analysts have signaled that political and economic situation could likely deteriorate further in the coming days and weeks.

CJP leaders said the action was taken to demonstrate against the brutal crackdown on youth protesters in Delhi over the weekend and the decision by the Delhi police to shut-down Jantar Mantar – a stretch of road surrounding an observatory in central Delhi – as the capital’s designated protest site, a status it has held for more than 30 years.

On Saturday, the CJP – a movement with a substantial following among India’s youth – called for a protest in Jantar Mantar to demand the resignation of the election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused of overseeing the mass disenfranchisement of millions of Indian voters.

It was also met with concern by a UK political delegation visiting Delhi, led by trade minister Jonny Reynolds who confirmed he had raised it with the Indian government.
