Money laundering failures land Bank of America with a $1.2 billion fine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
05:28:11 UTC
14:28:11 KST

US authorities have imposed a $1.2 billion (€1.07bn) penalty on Bank of America over failures to tackle money laundering. The bank also settled alleged sanctions violations involving Iran and Russia.
The US Treasury Department said on Tuesday that it had imposed a $1.2bn (€1.07bn) fine on Bank of America for anti-money laundering failures.
"When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire U.S. financial system to significant illicit finance risks," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement. "Today's actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law."
Treasury said Bank of America, the country’s second-biggest bank, also reached an $11.6 million (€9.9mn) settlement with the department's Office of Foreign Assets Control over "apparent violations of numerous sanctions programs, including on Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism."
In a statement, Treasury said its Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) imposed the $1.2bn penalty for Bank of America's "failure to mitigate and report priority national security risks, including Chinese Money Laundering Networks and illicit finance along the southwest border."
Treasury said the bank failed to report more than $5bn (€4.27bn) in suspicious transactions on time, including over $1bn (€853mn) linked to national security and other priority financial crime risks.
The penalty includes a $750 million (€640mn) fine imposed by the US Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the largest fine ever imposed by the federal banking regulator.
Treasury said that Bank of America "admits that it willfully violated" the 1970 Bank Secrecy Act, which requires banks to help the government detect and prevent money laundering.
"Financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right," Bank of America said in a statement. "We worked with regulators to reach these penalty resolutions stemming from violations cited in the previously reported 2024 (Comptroller of the Currency) Consent Order and FinCEN's investigation.
"We have invested billions of dollars in technology and dedicated thousands of employees to combat financial crime, and our team is far along with and committed to completing the work required to address the issues raised by our regulators."
The latest action is the third-largest penalty ever issued by the Treasury Department, behind a roughly $4bn (€3.41bn) settlement in 2023 with Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, and an approximately $3bn (€2.56bn) settlement with Canada-based TD Bank the following year.
Both settlements were part of the Biden administration's efforts to combat money laundering. Its broader push also aimed to improve compliance in the cryptocurrency industry.
In 2024, Binance founder Changpeng Zhao was sentenced to four months in prison after pleading guilty to failing to prevent money laundering on the platform. Prosecutors said criminals had used it to move money connected to child sex abuse, drug trafficking and terrorism.
US President Donald Trump pardoned Zhao in October 2025.

Global deforestation fell in 2025, but Congo Basin losses surged
Worldwide destruction dropped 15 per cent, though impending super El Nino threatens 2030 targets
Deforestation slowed worldwide last year, but the improvement is unlikely to last as the situation deteriorates in Central Africa and an exceptionally strong El Nino weather pattern intensifies, a new study said on Wednesday.
Seven million hectares of forest – roughly the size of the Republic of Ireland – were permanently destroyed in 2025, a 15 per cent drop from the previous year, according to the annual Forest Declaration Assessment.
The slowdown, however, is not enough to keep the world from missing a pledge to end deforestation by 2030, according to the report, which was drafted by a coalition of research groups and non-governmental organisations.
The 2025 figure is “encouraging but so far it’s the exception, not a new trajectory”, Erin Matson, the study’s co-author and lead consultant at advisory group Climate Focus, said in a media briefing.

Christa Pike survives two doses of lethal injection drug: can Tennessee try to execute her again?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
05:24:05 UTC
14:24:05 KST

How could a death row inmate survive two doses of a lethal drug and regain consciousness? The extraordinary case of Christa Pike has thrust the death penalty in the United States back into headlines around the world in recent days, reigniting debate over how executions are carried out.
Pike was sentenced to death for murdering a female friend at age 18 because she suspected the victim was trying to "steal" her boyfriend. On September 30, more than 30 years after the murder, the state of Tennessee attempted to execute her.
Pike received two doses of a drug that, in high concentrations, is supposed to stop breathing and heart function. But then something highly unusual happened: She did not die. Pike was taken to a hospital, recovered quickly and in recent days has begun walking and even speaking.
Death row inmates surviving execution attempts is uncommon, but not unprecedented. In almost every previous case, it happened because the procedure was halted midway, either because an electric chair malfunctioned or because the execution team was unable to find a suitable vein and insert an IV.
Pike's case, however, is particularly extraordinary. As far as is known, she is the first person in U.S. history to survive an execution attempt after the lethal drug had already been injected into her body.
Pike's was not even the only botched execution attempt in Tennessee this year. In May, the state attempted to execute Tony Carruthers, who had been sentenced to death for kidnapping and murder, at the same prison. The execution team spent about an hour and a half trying to insert an IV but failed, and the procedure was called off.
Pike's case, however, proved to be the final straw for Tennessee. In its wake, the governor suspended all executions through the end of the year, and the state's corrections commissioner resigned.
The injection designed to be 'humane' has the highest failure rate
But what happened in Tennessee was not merely an isolated failure. A study by Professor Austin Sarat, which examined nearly 8,800 executions in the United States between 1890 and 2010, found that the very method intended to make executions more efficient and less gruesome has an exceptionally high rate of complications.
According to the study, 7.2% of the 1,054 executions carried out by lethal injection since 1982 were botched. That is a higher failure rate than any other execution method and more than twice the overall average.
There are three main reasons for this. The first is physiological: The injection works only if the drug enters the bloodstream directly. But for some inmates, including older people and those with a history of drug use, finding a suitable vein can be extremely difficult. When the IV is not properly inserted, the drug may fail to reach its intended destination.
The second problem is a lack of properly trained personnel. According to research by Professor Corinna Lain of the University of Richmond, very few doctors across the United States participate in executions. Many physicians refuse to take part in the procedure on ethical grounds.
The result is a paradox: The procedure looks entirely medical, with syringes, IV lines and monitors, but those carrying it out do not necessarily have the necessary medical training or experience.
The third problem is the drugs themselves. Many pharmaceutical companies do not want their products used in executions and therefore refuse to sell them to states for that purpose. As a result, states are forced to obtain the drugs from small pharmacies and suppliers whose identities are sometimes kept secret. Under these circumstances, it is difficult to know who manufactured the drugs, how they were stored and how reliable they are.
This is where the economic absurdity comes in. Because almost no one is willing to supply the drugs, states pay exorbitant prices for them. Tennessee, for example, paid an average of approximately $95,000 for the drugs needed for each execution between 2017 and 2020, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.
Even so, the drugs account for only a small portion of the overall cost. The common assumption is that the death penalty is cheaper than life imprisonment, but in many cases the opposite is true. A University of Denver study found that cases in which prosecutors seek the death penalty take more than five years on average to reach sentencing, compared with less than a year and a half for cases involving life imprisonment without parole.
The real costs come afterward, during the appeals process, which lasts nearly 20 years on average. According to the Death Penalty Information Center, in some states a death penalty case costs $1 million to $3 million more than a case that ends in a life sentence.
Can Pike be executed a second time?
Despite the failed attempt, Pike's story is not over. Her death sentence remains in effect, and at least in theory, Tennessee could attempt to carry it out again.
But her case differs from previous botched executions. In Pike's case, the lethal drug had already been injected into her body. Her case could therefore present the courts with an unusual legal question: Would a second attempt to execute someone violate the Eighth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, which prohibits "cruel and unusual punishments"?
Another possibility is that Tennessee's governor could decide to commute her sentence to life imprisonment.
As of October 2026, the death penalty remains legal in 27 US states. Another 23 states have abolished it, while executions are effectively suspended by governors' orders in several states, including California.
Tennessee tried to close the case of Christa Gail Pike, but instead reopened the broader debate over the death penalty. Her case raises a question that is difficult to ignore: If the state cannot reliably carry out an execution, how much can it be trusted to decide who should be put to death?

Brian Cox awarded 2026 Stephen Hawking Medal for Science Communication
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
05:14:07 UTC
14:14:07 KST

British physicist and broadcaster Brian Cox has been awarded the 2026 Stephen Hawking Medal for Science Communication, recognising his work bringing complex scientific ideas to audiences around the world.
Cox was presented with the award at a private ceremony at the Royal Astronomical Society in London on 2 October, by co-founders of Starmus, Sir Brian May and astrophysicist Garik Israelian. STARMUS is a global platform for science, art, and human inspiration that brings together some of the most brilliant minds on the planet.
The medal, established by Starmus with Stephen Hawking a decade ago, honours outstanding science communicators across disciplines and creative forms – from literature and broadcasting to music, film and art – who are helping bridge the gap between science and society, spark curiosity and make science accessible to all.
“It’s a great honour to receive the 2026 Stephen Hawking Medal from Starmus, and particularly poignant for me because I was there with Stephen when the Medal was first announced 10 years ago,” Cox said at the ceremony.
“Astronomy is the oldest science, and in today’s fractured world I believe that striving to understand the Universe is more important than ever,” Cox added.
“The Stephen Hawking Medal was born from a shared belief that science should inspire people far beyond the scientific community,” May said. He also emphasised this message was particularly important at a time when “truth, evidence, and critical thinking are increasingly challenged”.
Stephen Hawking Medal recognises Cox’s accessible science
Cox is one of Britain’s best-known science communicators. He has presented television series including Universe and The Planets, written books such as The Quantum Universe and delivered lectures around the world. He currently serves as Professor of Particle Physics and Royal Society Professor for Public Engagement in Science at the University of Manchester.
His work attempts to enlighten the public on subjects ranging from the smallest building blocks of matter to the origins and eventual fate of the Universe – ideas that are not always easy to explain while keeping an audience engaged.
Alongside Cox, this year’s medal winners are filmmaker Ridley Scott, the Artemis II crew, Nobel Laureate Geoffrey Hinton, and 17-year-old Valeria Corrales, who receives the Stephen Hawking Medal Junior. Christiana Figueres, a key figure in brokering the 2015 Paris climate agreement, will also be awarded the inaugural Jane Goodall Earth Medal.
Previous recipients of the Steven Hawking medal include broadcaster David Attenborough, astrophysicist Neil deGrasse Tyson, marine biologist Sylvia Earle, filmmaker Christopher Nolan, composer Hans Zimmer and musician Brian Eno. The NASA communications office has also received the award.
The medal’s design reflects the unique mix of science and culture at the heart of Starmus’ vision. One side features a portrait of Hawking by Soviet cosmonaut Alexei Leonov, while the other depicts Leonov during his historic spacewalk, alongside an image of Brian May’s ‘Red Special’ guitar associated with rock band Queen.
During the London ceremony, Cox, May and Israelian discussed astronomy, humanity, music, artificial intelligence and Hawking’s enduring legacy. Cox was also presented with an OMEGA Speedmaster Moonwatch crafted in 18K Moonshine Gold.
‘The Search for Truth’ continues at the 8th Starmus Festival
The award will be celebrated as part of Starmus VIII Festival, which takes place on the Canary Islands from 17 to 22 October.
This year’s festival, themed ‘The Search for Truth’, will bring scientists, astronauts, Nobel Prize winners, artists and musicians together across Tenerife and La Palma. The location is fitting for such a celebration, with both islands recognised for the quality of their night skies and astronomic facilities, the latter protected as a Starlight Reserve.
Alongside lectures and discussions, the programme includes music, art, stargazing and a science camp, aiming to take the conversation beyond the lecture hall and inspire real-world curiosity.
Music from Andrea Bocelli, Rick Wakeman and Sarah Brightman will set the tone, alongside more than 40 speakers across the week, including Nobel laureates May-Britt Moser, Donna Strickland and Steven Chu, and astronauts Chris Hadfield, Victor Glover, Reid Wiseman and Jeremy Hansen.
The festival will close in La Palma with a free public performance of Ilan Eshkeri’s Space Station Earth. This live orchestral work is accompanied by footage from space, exploring how seeing Earth from above can reshape human perspective.
Ten years after Hawking helped launch the medal, Starmus is recognising Cox’s embodiment of its original ambition: not only to explain what we know about the Universe, but to inspire us all to look up and wonder.

Google Finland head apologises for forest clearances at data centre sites
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:10:02 EEST
14:10:02 KST

Google’s Finland country manager Antti Järvinen has apologised for extensive forest clearances at the company’s data centre sites in Muhos and Kajaani.
330 hectares of forest have been cleared in Muhos and just under 200 hectares in Kajaani.
Järvinen spoke to the media on Tuesday after the company had previously commented on the controversy through written statements.
"The reason I am only speaking to the media now is that there has been a lot to investigate. I understand that people have been looking for me, too," Järvinen said.
Google has faced criticism since the Finnish Association for Nature Conservation accused the company of illegally clearing forests in Muhos and Kajaani without the required environmental impact assessments.
Last week, the Finnish Supervisory Agency (LVV) ordered Google to suspend the work.
Järvinen said Google and its subsidiary had acted to the best of their understanding of the law at the time. He said the projects had been advanced in cooperation with authorities and experts.
Google has repeatedly maintained that authorities were aware of its plans for the forest clearances.
However, when asked which authorities it believed had been informed and how that understanding had arisen, Järvinen declined to name them.
"We don't think it would be useful to start debating this publicly. This is our project, and we take full responsibility for what has happened," he said.
Järvinen said he would leave it to the authorities to comment on their own involvement.
Building inspector alleges pressure from Google's lawyers
Muhos municipality's building inspector told newspaper Helsingin Sanomat that Google's lawyers had pressured him into granting permission for preparatory work. Asked whether Google had pressured municipalities, Järvinen denied this.
"I don't recognise this kind of behaviour. I've seen the memo from that meeting, after which the permit was granted. There were no lawyers from our side present at that meeting. Our representatives and our construction consultant's representatives were there, after which the permit was granted," Järvinen said.
He also denied that Google had rushed the clearances to get ahead of environmental assessments, saying the project had been "advanced quite swiftly" but "very openly, in good cooperation with all the different partners and local authorities."
He also denied receiving pressure to speed things up from outside Finland.
Google denies acting out of negligence
Questions have been raised about how Google could have proceeded without understanding the requirements of Finland's environmental impact assessment legislation.
Järvinen said the environmental assessment process had been part of the project's development throughout.
"All decisions were made based on the best understanding we had of the legislation at the time," he said.
He denied that the company’s actions were due to a lack of expertise, inexperience or negligence.
"I am extremely sorry that we are in this situation. I want to apologise for that," Järvinen said.
In addition to Muhos and Kajaani, Google is building data centres in Hamina and Vaala.
Last month it was announced that the tech giant was investing 13 billion euros in Finland.

"Betrayal of the people of Ukraine": 12 US senators write to Trump over deal with Putin
A bipartisan group of 12 US senators has written to President Donald Trump demanding that he scrap a recently reached agreement with Russian ruler Vladimir Putin to allow Russian-origin diesel fuel to be sold on global markets.
Source: a letter on the website of Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal, as reported by European Pravda
Details: The letter was signed by Democrats Richard Blumenthal, Chris Coons, Dick Durbin, Jack Reed, Jeanne Shaheen and Sheldon Whitehouse. They were joined by Republicans Alan Armstrong, Susan Collins, John Cornyn, Mitch McConnell, Lisa Murkowski and Thom Tillis.
"Granting Moscow the ability to sell Russian diesel freely in global markets damages American security interests and is a betrayal of the people of Ukraine, who continue to defend themselves from Putin's murderous, illegal war. This deal is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our Allies; it should be rescinded," the senators said.
They urged Trump instead to take swift action to implement the sanctions provided for under the recently passed Lindsey Graham Act.
"These authorities require you to apply economic pressure on Russia and the chief enablers of its war, in particular China, and thereby enhance your negotiating position to bring a swift end to this ruinous conflict," the senators wrote.
They stressed that peace in Ukraine must be achieved on just terms, safeguarding Ukraine's democratic values, sovereignty and security.
"For decades, America has stood as the bastion of freedom against tyranny, and American presidents have embodied our nation's resistance to tyrants. Putin is a tyrant. Withdraw from this agreement, rescind General Licence No. 135, and execute the authorities provided under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026," the letter said.
Background:
- On 9 October, Trump said he had spoken to Putin and reached an agreement with him on the supply of Russian diesel fuel to the US and global markets.
- The move has drawn sharp criticism from European allies and within the US, as has Trump's call for the appointment of a new president of Ukraine to replace Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — DPP New Taipei mayoral candidate Su Chiao-hui (蘇巧慧) leads KMT rival Lee Shu-chuan (李四川) by 13.1 percentage points, according to a new poll released Tuesday.
The survey, conducted by Beacon Market Research from Oct. 6-8, found that 43.1% of respondents supported Su, compared with 30% for Lee, per Liberty Times. Su also led Lee in perceived suitability for the mayor’s office and expectations of winning.
Asked who was most suitable to be New Taipei mayor, 48.6% chose Su, while 22.3% considered her unsuitable. For Lee, 35.9% considered him suitable, while 33.5% said he was unsuitable.
The poll also asked whether voters wanted the KMT to continue running the city or would prefer to give the DPP a chance, Liberty Times reported. While 27.9% favored keeping the KMT in office, 44.2% supported a DPP administration.
Regarding expectations for the outcome, 34.8% chose Su, compared with 32.8% who chose Lee. The poll’s modeled vote-share estimates put Su at 50.1% to 53.1% and Lee at 46% to 48.9%, based on voting intentions, strength of support, and previous election results.
The Taipei Trust in Democracy Association commissioned the survey, with polling expert Tai Li-an (戴立安) responsible for questionnaire design and analysis, and Beacon Market Research conducting telephone interviews. It surveyed 1,073 New Taipei residents aged 20 or older, including 750 by landline and 323 by mobile phone, with a maximum sampling error of 3 percentage points at a 95% confidence level.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s King Yuan Electronics Co. (KYEC) has signed a deal for Nvidia to pay up to NT$45 billion (US$1.4 billion) in advance for chip-testing services at its future US facility, the company announced Tuesday.
The deal will help KYEC and its wholly owned US subsidiary, AeternZ Semiconductor Testing Corp., develop testing capacity in the US reserved for Nvidia. When testing services begin, KYEC will deduct the cost of the services from the prepaid amount until it is fully used, the company said in a filing.
KYEC’s board greenlit the plan in July, citing demand from US customers and a shortage of local chip-testing capacity. “Not everyone wants to go, and not everyone can go,” said KYEC General Manager Chang Kao-hsun (張高薰), referring to the challenges of expanding into the US market.
KYEC has yet to disclose the facility’s location or construction timeline. As the firm expands in Taiwan, Chang has previously said each facility can take at least 24 months to build, and the company might need to build two to three facilities annually to meet rising demand for testing services.
In May, KYEC raised its capital expenditure budget to a record NT$50 billion from NT$39.4 billion, with spending focusing on high-power burn-in and advanced packaging testing services.
Taiwan’s semiconductor companies have been expanding their US operations as Washington seeks to strengthen domestic chip production. Following TSMC’s multibillion-dollar investment in Arizona, companies like Foxconn and Wistron are also establishing AI production facilities in Texas.
In May, KYEC also opened a testing facility in Singapore focusing on high-value services for AI chips, high-performance computing, and advanced packaging.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) on Tuesday urged architects to work with the government on urban renewal, age-friendly housing, and green buildings.
Speaking at a leadership handover ceremony for the National Association of Architects, Lai thanked architects for their contributions to urban development and public safety. He said their work helps shape cities and preserves the places where people live and raise families.
Lai said the country has about 5.16 million residential units more than 30 years old. More than 6,000 urban renewal and reconstruction projects for unsafe or aging buildings have been approved, but he said much more work remains, per a press release.
He urged the legislature to pass proposed amendments to the Urban Renewal Act and the Act for Accelerating Reconstruction of Unsafe and Old Buildings to help more communities improve housing safety.
The government is also implementing a NT$5 billion (US$158 million) building-renovation program to help eligible older homes upgrade plumbing, repair exterior walls and roofs, and install barrier-free facilities. The initiative aims to improve living conditions for older residents and allow them to remain in familiar communities, per CNA.
Lai recalled the 2016 collapse of the Weiguan Jinlong Building in Tainan following an earthquake when he was mayor. Architects and engineering professionals helped assess damaged buildings and support the city's disaster response and reconstruction, he said.
He thanked architects for conducting emergency safety assessments after earthquakes, helping authorities determine whether residents can safely return to damaged buildings.
Lai also called on architects to incorporate carbon-reduction measures into building design as the nation works toward its 2050 net-zero emissions target. For example, in 2025, he said the Interior Ministry issued 1,342 green building certificates, an annual record, per the press release.
The government is also encouraging newly built public buildings to meet Level 1 building energy-efficiency standards and move toward near-zero carbon emissions.
Lai said he hoped to maintain close communication with the architectural community to ensure government policies reflect industry needs and help make cities safer, more accessible, and more resilient.

Boat capsizes in Bihar, killing 13
A boat capsized in the river Ganges in the eastern state of Bihar, drowning at least 13 people, authorities said on Wednesday.
News agency Press Trust of India reported that all of the deceased were children under the age of 15. At least six others on board were rescued.

Jantar Mantar: What to know about Delhi's delisted protest site?
Jantar Mantar, in central Delhi, is an 18th century open-air astronomical observatory.
For over three decades, a stretch of road leading up to it was where Indians came to be heard, press their demands and hold those in power accountable. That was until last week when the Delhi Police delisted the iconic venue as a protest site.
What sparked the latest protests?
The move came days after a confrontation between thousands of police personnel and anti-government protesters led by India's Cockroach Janta Party (CJP).
The group, along with student organizations and activists, mobilized thousands to protest against a revision in electoral rolls which reportedly deleted 130 million voters.
While those deleted include dead and duplicate voters, critics argue the staggering number likely includes a vast number of eligible voters. India's poll body and the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party party have denied this.
Jantar Mantar has been the central rallying location for protesters demanding election Chief Gyanesh Kumar's resignation for overseeing the revision.
This is the same location that acted as a home base for the CJP-led youth protests in July over an exam scandal, which resulted in the removal of India's former education minister.
Why is delisting Jantar Mantar controversial?
Now, instead of Jantar Mantar, authorities have designated three alternative venues in Delhi. Campaigners argue those venues will reduce visibility and proximity to lawmakers as Jantar Mantar was surrounded by the nation's biggest institutions.
"Jantar Mantar is in the centre of the town, it is connected, it is next to parliament... it was a very important space for all protests," human rights activist Shabnam Hashmi told AFP. "This is nothing but a move to curb dissent," he said.
CJP leaders Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das were among about a dozen people who jumped barricades on Tuesday to enter the grounds of Jantar Mantar, despite the delisting a day earlier.
An Indian court has now sent Das and Ranka to five days in judicial custody over trespassing and other violations.
Student organization demands 'immediate release' of Cockroach leaders
Left-wing All India Students' Association (AISA) on Wednesday demanded the "immediate release" of Cockroach movement conveners Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka after the duo were sent to judicial custody over trespassing amid protests.
"Tihar Jail for raising the Tricolor at Jantar Mantar?" the organization questioned in a post on X, adding that they stood in solidarity with the political pressure Group Cockroach Janta Party (CJP).
AISA is one among several groups and opposition parties protesting in India's national capital against India's election chief Gyanesh Kumar.
AISA's National President Neha Bora has been at the forefront of the recent protests which saw Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling government deploy thousands of police and rapid action forces to detain protesters.
Cockroach party conveners Ranka, Das sent to 5 days in judicial custody
Three leaders of India's Cockroach movement — Co-Conveners Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka and organizer Ajinkya Shinde — have been formally charged with multiple violations by authorities in India's national capital.
It all comes amid their protest against India's election chief over mass deletion of voter names from electoral rolls.
The trio was detained early Tuesday after they allegedly "sneaked" past police barricades to enter the grounds of Jantar Mantar in central Delhi, which until recently was a designated protest site.
News agency PTI, citing sources, reported that police have now formally charged them with trespassing, violation of prohibitory orders, breach of a peace bond and obstructing a public servant from discharging officials duties.
Meanwhile, Cockroach Janta Party's Founder Abhijeet Dipke said Das and Ranka had been "sent to five days judicial custody."
"Their fault? Unfurling tricolor at Jantar Mantar," Dipke wrote on X on Wednesday morning, referring to the national flag.
"Show some guts, Narendra Modi. If you're so determined to crush dissent, have the courage to officially declare an Emergency instead of hiding behind these cowardly tactics," he said.
Dipke's post suggests the trio have already been produced in front of a magistrate. Under Indian law, a person arrested by police has to appear in court within 24 hours of the arrest. One can only be sent to judicial remand by a judge.
Defending advocate accuses police of making false claims in court
Advocate Abhisht Hela, who is representing Das and Ranka, questioned the grounds for sending the two into judicial remand and accused the police of making false claims in court, Times of India reported.
"They have been sent to five-day judicial custody because of the presumption of the police that they can commit a crime. Police lied in court that they had given a call urging people to come there," Hela said, adding that no such call was made.
Meanwhile, Shinde, who seems to have been released, told reporters that the government was misusing its powers to curtail people's rights. "If the government thinks that sending our two leaders, Ashutosh and Saurav, to jail for five days will frighten them, it is absolutely mistaken," Shinde said, as per PTI.
He further called on "everyone" to "come together to bring an end to this dictatorial government."

France’s emissions are falling as fuel prices soar. Why is it still missing climate targets?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
05:02:49 UTC
14:02:49 KST

Despite using less fossil fuels, France is still far short of the 5 per cent annual reduction in emissions it needs to meet its climate targets.
France is getting an unexpected boost in its efforts to cut greenhouse gas emissions, but it comes with a catch consumers are feeling at the fuel pump.
Soaring fuel prices caused by the war in Iran have prompted people to buy less diesel and cut down on their gas use at home. That has helped bring emissions down 4.1 per cent in the first half of 2026, according to Citepa, a French organisation that measures air pollution and greenhouse gases to track the country’s environmental impact.
France is now on track to cut emissions by 2.8 per cent this year, up from 2.1 per cent in 2025. That would amount to 10 million tonnes fewer emissions than last year.
Even so, it’s still falling short of the pace needed to meet its long-term climate targets. France is aiming to halve emissions by 2030 compared to 1990 levels, but meeting that goal will require annual reductions of around 5 per cent.
Fuel prices hit French consumers
Much of the emissions reduction boils down to the cost of filling up the car. Fuel prices have surged since the start of the year, with diesel climbing 45 per cent after the war in Iran choked off oil supplies through the Strait of Hormuz.
People have simply bought less fuel since then. Diesel sales fell 7.3 per cent in the first six months of 2026. In that same timeframe, transport emissions dropped 4.5 per cent.
Emissions from homes and commercial buildings fell even more, dropping 12 per cent in the first half of the year mostly due to less natural gas use for heating, water and cooking.
But the downward trajectory is unlikely to last. Citepa expects emissions to fall just 1.3 per cent in the second half of the year, partly because France is using more gas-fired power plants to produce electricity for neighbouring countries.
The energy industry’s emissions are expected to rise by 3.6 per cent over the full year, even as transport and other sectors continue to record reductions.
France’s Ecological Transition Minister Monique Barbut called the decline “encouraging” but acknowledged it was “not yet enough to meet our climate targets”, according to AFP.
Global emissions could fall for first time since 2020
Elsewhere in Europe, emissions are on a steady – if slow – decline.
Germany’s emissions fell about 2 per cent in the first half of 2026 as demand for oil dropped. However, the think tank Agora Energiewende has warned the country could still exceed its annual emissions limit by around 10 million tonnes – the first time it will have done so since passing its landmark climate law in 2019.
High energy costs have also encouraged European households to find more affordable alternatives to fossil fuels. Heat pump sales rose 25 per cent in France, Germany and Poland early in 2026, and EV sales have also spiked since the start of the war. Meanwhile, solar power has saved the EU an estimated €37.4 billion in gas imports since it broke out in February.
Outside of Europe, emissions are also going down. In China, oil use fell 9 per cent in the second quarter of 2026, while carbon emissions dropped 1 per cent – the first time a decline in China’s emissions had been linked to oil rather than coal.
A recent report by Carbon Brief based on forecasts from the IEA suggests global fossil fuel CO2 emissions could fall about 0.5 per cent this year, which would be the first annual decline since stay-at-home orders caused them to plummet in 2020.
While the IEA expects oil demand to climb when the war ends, the widespread embrace of solar and wind power, nuclear energy, electric cars and heat pumps could keep fossil fuel use down even after their prices stabilise. Those technologies helped to prevent an estimated 3 billion tonnes of CO2 emissions worldwide in 2025, the agency reports.

Cheese tart, corn salad, squash with ’nduja, radicchio salad: Joe Otway’s recipes for early autumn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
05:00:46 UTC
14:00:46 KST

Early autumn is one of the most generous and comforting times of year to cook with British produce: sweetcorn is at its peak, squash begins to sweeten as the weather cools and bitter leaves such as radicchio provide balance to the season’s abundance. Today’s recipes are simple celebrations of British ingredients, using just a handful of carefully chosen components to let each vegetable shine. Whether it’s a buttery cheese tart for sharing; a fresh, herby corn salad; sweet roast squash with warm, spicy ’nduja; or bitter leaves lifted with a floral dressing, they all rely on cooking with ingredients at their seasonal peak and allowing nature to guide the menu.
Cheese tart
Prep 10 min
Chill 30 min+
Cook 1 hr
Makes 4 individual tarts
90g unsalted butter, plus extra for greasing
120g plain flour, plus extra for dusting
110g mature cheddar, finely grated
70g whole eggs
25ml whole milk
10g ready-made English mustard, or to taste
110ml double cream
Sea salt and black pepper
First, make the pastry. Rub the butter into the flour until the mix resembles coarse breadcrumbs, then add 60g of the grated cheddar and knead gently until the mix comes together into a dough. Divide into four, wrap and chill for at least 30 minutes.
Meanwhile, make the custard. Blend the eggs, milk, remaining 50g grated cheddar and mustard until smooth, then stir in the cream by hand and season to taste.
Heat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4, and grease and line four individual 8-10cm tart tins. Lightly flour a work surface, roll out each piece of pastry, then use to line the tins. Line each pastry base with baking paper, fill with baking beans or similar, then blind bake for 15 minutes, until lightly golden. Lift out the paper and beans, then return the tarts to the oven for a further five minutes, until the bases are crisp and golden.
Carefully pour the custard into each tart case until they’re almost full, then bake for another 15-25 minutes, depending on your oven (the actual temperature of domestic ovens varies a fair bit, after all), until the custard is lightly browned and just set with a slight wobble in the centre.
Leave to cool to room temperature, then serve, either with a bitter leaf salad or with one of the following two sides.
Corn salad with soured cream and oregano
Prep 5 min
Cook 15 min
Serves 4
Sea salt and black pepper
4 fresh sweetcorn cobs, or 1 400g tin good-quality sweetcorn
150g soured cream
100ml extra-virgin olive oil
Juice of ½ lemon
Sea salt
20g fresh oregano leaves, plus extra to garnish
30g parmesan, shaved
Bring a large pan of salted water to a boil, drop in the corn cobs, cook for four or five minutes, until tender, then drain and refresh. Once the cobs are cool enough to handle, cut off the kernels and put in a bowl (if you’re using tinned corn, skip the blanching stage and simply drain the water from the can).
Mix the soured cream with 20ml of the olive oil, the lemon juice and a pinch of salt. Blend the oregano with the remaining olive oil until fragrant. Dress the sweetcorn with the oregano oil, then season generously with salt and a little more lemon juice, if needed.
Spread the soured cream mix over a platter, spoon the dressed corn on top, scatter over a few more oregano leaves and finish with generous shavings of parmesan and a final twist of black pepper.
Roast winter squash with ’nduja
Prep 10 min
Cook 45 min
Serves 4
1kg winter squash (uchiki kuri is ideal, although butternut works well too), halved, deseeded and cut into skin-on wedges
5 tbsp olive oil
Sea salt
20g pumpkin seeds
120g ’nduja
2 tbsp good-quality honey
150g Greek yoghurt
1 tbsp lemon juice
1 small handful flat-leaf parsley, leaves picked and roughly chopped
Heat the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7. Toss the squash wedges with two tablespoons of the olive oil and a generous pinch of salt, then arrange on an oven tray and roast for 30-40 minutes, turning every 10 minutes, until tender and caramelised. Add the pumpkin seeds to the tray for the final 10 minutes of cooking.
Meanwhile, in a small saucepan gently warm the ’nduja, honey and the remaining olive oil until the mix comes together into a loose dressing. In a small bowl, mix the yoghurt with the lemon juice and a pinch of salt.
Spread the yoghurt on a platter, arrange the squash wedges and toasted pumpkin seeds on top, then spoon over the warm ’nduja dressing. Finish with the parsley and serve.
Radicchio with elderflower vinaigrette
Yes, elderflower is an early-summer flavour, but that’s why they invented cordial, so we can enjoy that gentle fragrance all year round.
Prep 10 min
Serves 4
3 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
2 tbsp elderflower cordial
2 tbsp white-wine vinegar
1 tsp dijon mustard
Sea salt and black pepper
2 heads bitter leaves – radicchio, treviso, chicory or endive will all work well here
40g hard sheep’s cheese, or pecorino
In a small bowl, whisk the oil, cordial, vinegar, mustard, and salt and pepper to taste, until lightly emulsified.
Trim the bases off the radicchio heads, then separate the leaves and put them in a medium bowl. Dress the leaves generously with the vinaigrette, then season with a little more salt and pepper if needed. Leave to marinate for five to 10 minutes, so the leaves soften slightly and absorb the dressing, then arrange on a serving plate and finish with generous shavings of the cheese.
- Joe Otway is chef/co-owner of Higher Ground, Bar Shrimp and Flawd, all in Manchester.

Birdwatch: the paradoxical puffin – a comical bird with a fighting spirit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
05:00:46 UTC
14:00:46 KST

Few birds are as paradoxical as the puffin. It rivals the robin as Britain’s best-loved bird, yet most people have never seen one in the flesh. In spring and summer, they gather in large, noisy colonies to breed, but spend the autumn and winter far out to sea in the North Atlantic. And despite their small size, and gentle, clown-like appearance, puffins will fight to save their precious catch of sand eels from being seized by an opportunistic – and much larger – skua or gull.
Puffins, like penguins, have a very human quality, too. When the late Bill Oddie and I filmed puffins at a colony on Shetland, he memorably described them as “looking like old men in dinner jackets, waiting to go into supper at the club”, while the bird’s scientific name, Fratercula arctica, translates as “little brother of the Arctic”.
Their huge, colourful bill once earned them the name “sea parrot”, while “puffin” – meaning “fat” or “swollen” – was originally given to the young of another burrow-nesting seabird, the Manx shearwater. Confusingly, that species still retains the misleading scientific name Puffinus puffinus.
Now, like so many seabirds, puffins are in trouble. The sand eels, on which they rely to feed themselves and their single chick, are shifting north because of the climate crisis. Puffins are also threatened by avian flu, pollution and disturbance – ironically often caused by visitors to their colonies, over-eager to get closeup photos of these charismatic little birds.
The Puffin: A Biography, by Stephen Moss, is published on 15 October.

UK will not put tariffs on Chinese vehicles, says Jonathan Reynolds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
05:00:45 UTC
14:00:45 KST

The business secretary has hit back at European demands for British tariffs on Chinese imports, saying the government will not change its trade rules because of pressure from Brussels.
Jonathan Reynolds warned that the government would not bow to calls from other countries for the UK to hit Chinese vehicles with import taxes, despite political pressure to align with the EU in exchange for deeper future economic ties.
The EU imposed tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles in 2024 and last Friday agreed a 350,000 a year quota on Chinese hybrid cars amid fears cheaper alternatives are causing deindustrialisation and job losses.
Reynolds conceded that levying sanctions on Chinese goods was an option in the future, but he dismissed concerns from Brussels that the UK could provide a back door to the European market.
His comments highlight the divisions that remain between the UK and EU on trade and industrial policy, which could derail the prime minister’s attempts to move closer to Brussels.
“I just want to be clear: when we make any trade decision in terms of trade defence tariffs in relation to the EU, that’s based on the UK interest – it’s not based on any other country asking for that,” said Reynolds during a trade trip to India.
“In 2024, [we] looked at this issue carefully, and we keep it under review depending on what the needs of industry are … But it comes down to what is the fundamental nature of the UK automotive sector. It’s an export-led sector, so that’s what I’ve got to take into account.”
With Europe having imposed tariffs of up to 45% on Chinese electric cars, some believe that the UK has opened an alternative route into the EU for Chinese companies setting up in the UK to sell into the bloc.
Nissan, for instance, has agreed to look at building cars in northern England for the Chinese manufacturer Chery.
Reynolds rebutted those accusations, however, saying: “The UK currently has no major Chinese manufacturer based in its automotive sector, so we’re not making vehicles here and sending them to the single market through some sort of back door.”
His comments raise the stakes ahead of intense final weeks of negotiations before the long-awaited UK-EU summit, which Andy Burnham confirmed this week would be held in Brussels on 20 November.
The prime minister told the Commons on Monday he wanted a “serious dialogue” over the UK’s place in Europe, as he framed the summit as a possible first step to EU membership.
The new Made in Europe trade rules aim to protect European companies from subsidised Chinese imports, but British manufacturers worry they will also be shut out of supply chains.
The issue will not formally be on the agenda at the November summit, but British officials are hoping to use those talks to shape the European legislation.
Diplomats on both sides of the Channel say the summit will now be an early test of whether Burnham’s desire for a “real reset” in UK-EU relations is likely to bear fruit.
One EU official said this week that the UK’s negotiating position would determine whether it was worth pursuing more fundamental changes such as British access to the single market, a new customs union or re-accession.
Some in Brussels have been pushing for Britain to levy tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles in return for getting access to the European market under the new trade rules.
Reynolds has previously dismissed such an option in part because of the risk that Beijing could hit the UK with reciprocal tariffs, damaging British companies such as Jaguar Land Rover.
He said it would be to Europe’s detriment if it did not admit the UK into the scheme. “If you look at the impact analysis of such a policy, the consequences for the EU [of] excluding the UK are much more difficult,” he said.
“This is not just in the UK’s interest; it’s not in the EU’s interest because obviously we have integrated supply chains.”
Reynolds said the summit was an important milestone in EU-UK relations but also insisted that new trading terms for electricity, emissions and food and drink products would be a major achievement in themselves.
Speaking from a two-day trade delegation to Delhi and Mumbai, he acknowledged that the landmark free trade agreement he helped strike last year with India would become defunct if Britain does rejoin the EU.
“Obviously, if you enter those arrangements, you are doing things collectively. So there would be trade relationships with the UK that were based on Europe, the EU as a whole – that is how the European Union works in terms of its relationship.
“That’s why obviously when we were part of it, we didn’t have these separate bespoke arrangements.”
But he insisted that it remained worth continuing to push to broaden the scope of the agreement, as he unveiled a series of UK-India investments which officials say are worth over £1bn to the UK over the next 15 years.
The deal has already begun to reduce the price of Scotch whisky in Indian shops, after tariffs were reduced from 150% to 75%. Now British officials are keen to free up trade in services as well as goods, for example, pushing for both countries to recognise each other’s legal qualifications.
“There are some specific things regarding who can practice law and in which area,” Reynolds said. “I am confident over the medium to long term that this will improve over time.”
He added: “We’ve got to be cognisant of this long-term position with the EU. But frankly, there’s a job to be done here and now, which we’re doing.”

Global financial system is failing developing countries, says Ed Miliband
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
05:00:45 UTC
14:00:45 KST

The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, will claim the global financial system is failing developing countries, as he calls for a “new deal” for governments struggling under the burden of debt.
Promising to throw the UK’s diplomatic weight behind urgent reform, he will evoke the example of the Gleneagles summit under the last Labour government in 2005 – the culmination of the Make Poverty History campaign.
“The global financial system and indeed the global order is failing to serve developing countries on debt, on resilience and on climate. This is not just against our values but against our national interest,” Miliband is expected to say.
“In the interconnected world we live in, more than ever, the opportunities and challenges we confront are collective.”
Speaking in Bangkok on Wednesday, he will call for the World Bank and other multilateral development banks (MDBs) to use the resources they have available to lighten the load for governments trapped by hefty borrowing costs.
“We need action on developing country debt through the MDBs,” he is expected to say. “Action that leverages the balance sheets of the international financial institutions to support these countries to repay over longer time horizons, and crucially, refinancing, with better rates, to give them precious fiscal space.”
The foreign secretary will be in Bangkok to attend the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank annual meetings.
He opted to take up the UK’s seat on the bank’s board himself instead of leaving it to the development minister, Kirsty McNeill.
Labour’s manifesto in 2024 promised to restore the UK’s international reputation on development issues – but Keir Starmer subsequently slashed the aid budget to pay for defence.
Campaigners have long claimed the high interest rates paid by many developing countries mean the repayments crowd out vital public spending – including on tackling the climate emergency. In sub-Saharan Africa, more than three times as much is spent on debt servicing as on education.
Miliband will argue that making the global financial system work better for emerging economies will also help to attract more private investment – a key aim of the World Bank under the current president, Ajay Banga.
The UK is due to take up the presidency of the G20 group of nations next year – a key global forum for discussing global financial issues, including sovereign debt, which includes emerging economies such as China, India, South Africa and Brazil.
The chancellor, John Healey, will set out his own G20 priorities in Bangkok later this week, including mobilising more resources from the balance sheets of the IMF and the World Bank.
When the UK held the chair of the narrower G8 group in 2005, at the leaders’ summit at the Gleneagles hotel the UK secured agreements that eventually resulted in more than 30 countries receiving large-scale debt write-downs.
Miliband will say resources are now more constrained – but as well as debt refinancing for a large number of countries, he will demand an overhaul of the “common framework” for restructuring the debts of countries unable to pay.
The framework is widely criticised as too slow and cumbersome. Among other reforms, the UK wants to see changes to ensure private creditors cannot hold up negotiations – as has happened in recent cases including that of Ethiopia.
The foreign secretary will also call for overhauls to allow help to be made available more rapidly to countries in trouble. “We need finance teed up in advance of crises, so that governments get support in days, not months,” he will say.
Miliband will be speaking at the launch of a report by the Rockefeller Foundation thinktank, which calls for a “surge” in affordable financing from the IMF and the World Bank to debt-burdened countries.
Tim Jones, the policy director of the campaign group Debt Justice, welcomed Miliband’s focus on the issue but said a litmus test of any plan would be whether private sector creditors bear some of the costs. “Action on debt relief is urgently needed. That must include private lenders sharing in the cost. Otherwise public money will just bail out private lenders rather than be used for investment.”

Palantir is worming its way into the British state – it’s time to curb this controversial US company’s influence | George Monbiot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
05:00:44 UTC
14:00:44 KST

What a world we live in. Imagine: gangs dragging civil servants off commuter trains and beating them up because they handed government data jobs to the wrong contractor – and the government is changing its procurement decisions as a result. Well, OK, it might not have happened yet, but it’s only a matter of time. As the former Labour deputy leader Tom Watson asks: “Do you want to let the rule of law lead procurement practice, or do you want mob rule to lead procurement practices?” No, I absolutely don’t want the latter, and it’s always good to get ahead of trouble.
But then I remember there are two common meanings of mob rule. One is intimidation by crowds of thugs. The other is a pejorative term for democracy. And while I’ve yet to see government procurement practices in the UK determined by pitchforks and flaming torches, democratic transparency could be a genuine threat to certain contractors. One might have hoped that Watson, who once took on the Murdoch empire, would have recognised the distinction. But then again, one might have hoped that Watson would not have taken a job as a senior vice-president at Palantir.
Over the past few years, this US company has been worming its way into the British state. It has landed contracts worth hundreds of millions with the Ministry of Defence, several police forces, the Financial Conduct Authority, the atomic weapons establishment and the NHS. Its superpower, according to a deep investigation by Peter Geoghegan and Lucas Amin in the London Review of Books, is that it is “willing to spend more on securing political access than almost all of its British and continental competitors”. It made abundant use of Peter Mandelson’s company Global Counsel, which seems, in turn, to have made abundant use of the UK’s remarkably flimsy lobbying laws. Watson is one of more than 30 former UK ministers and officials Palantir now employs.
Palantir’s contracts might have been awarded lawfully, but some of us might question the ways in which doors were opened for it. These include an unrecorded meeting between Boris Johnson, Dominic Cummings and the co-founder of Palantir, Peter Thiel, in Downing Street in 2019. It was invited back to Downing Street when the Covid-19 pandemic began a few months later, and was working in the NHS within days, on a contract for which it charged only £1. The mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, has criticised such loss-leaders, which can quickly lead to reliance on a company, at which point it can name its price.
Another controversial meeting was brokered by Mandelson in 2025, when he was UK ambassador to the US. Keir Starmer visited Palantir’s showroom in Washington, where he met the company’s global and UK chief executives, Alex Karp and Louis Mosley. They talked about defence spending. No 10, Geoghegan and Amin tell us, “refused to say whether Starmer knew that Palantir was a client of Global Counsel, in which Mandelson still held a stake of around a fifth at the time. The meeting was never declared on transparency registers.” A few months later, Palantir secured a £241m contract with the Ministry of Defence, without an open tender.
Now we learn that Martha Dalton, a key player in Andy Burnham’s campaign to win the Makerfield byelection, enabling him to become prime minister, was on unpaid leave from the lobbying company she co-founded, Lodestone. Lodestone had done extensive work for Palantir. And the Financial Times reports that Samantha Jones, then the lead non-executive director on the board of the health department, was an adviser to one of Palantir’s partners when the company was bidding for its huge and controversial NHS contract. Now she is permanent secretary in the same department.
There have been repeated allegations that some of Palantir’s products are rubbish. But, as the House of Commons science, innovation and technology committee warns, government agencies can quickly succumb to “vendor lock-in”: once you start using them, it can be very hard to stop.
Thiel, has claimed that “the NHS makes people sick”, and that we should “just rip the whole thing from the ground and start over”. The company is deeply embedded in the Trump administration, where it supplies software that helps ICE find undocumented people. It also works for the Israeli government on identifying targets in Gaza. When Karp was confronted by a protester who told him that “Palantir kills Palestinians”, he replied: “Mostly terrorists, that’s true.”
This is the company handling our critical information. After official denials, it turns out that NHS England has granted Palantir “unlimited access” to patient data. This is a huge issue. Identifiable patient data is supposed to be visible only to people directly involved in a patient’s care, or who have received the patient’s informed consent. There are widespread concerns about how this and other datasets might be used.
So, as Palantir runs into ever-greater controversy, it’s not hard to see why it might have hired Watson, who, with Burnham, was a minister in Gordon Brown’s government. I wouldn’t presume to speculate about what attracted Watson to the multibillion-dollar company.
In July, the government’s ethics and integrity commission recommended a major shake-up, enabling us to see all the encounters between lobbyists and ministers, aides and senior officials. I’ve heard this call many times before. The pattern is always the same: a scandal, followed by a call to action, followed by … little or nothing.
Before he became prime minister, David Cameron noted that lobbying “has tainted our politics for too long”. He would shine “the light of transparency” on it. Instead, he oversaw an act that was “more loophole than law”. It did nothing to protect us from lobbying by people such as Cameron – pulling strings, once out of office, among his old colleagues, to try to drum up government business for the bank Greensill .
You could almost believe that the real purpose of government was to do the bidding of corporations, foreign states and the ultra-rich. You could almost believe that some government ministers may have an eye on future opportunities when they resist effective reform.
So this is another key test for Burnham. Will he allow the mob rule of private business to keep dominating our lives, or will he ensure that government is for the people?
- George Monbiot is a Guardian columnist

World's oldest shipwreck found off coast of Turkey
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:00:35 BST
14:00:35 KST

World's oldest shipwreck found off coast of Turkey
- Published
The world's oldest shipwreck has been discovered off the coast of Turkey, archaeologists say.
They have dated it to between 4,400 and 4,700 years old, which is the Early Bronze Age, and is around the same time that the Great Pyramid was being built.
The ship's wooden structure has not survived, but the ceramic storage pots it was carrying were lying on the sea floor and, remarkably, some still contain traces of what they held inside.
The archaeologists who found the ship say it was about 10m in length and was a trade vessel carrying cargo across the Mediterranean Sea.
"The shipwreck is a time capsule at the bottom of the sea," said Prof Hakan Öniz, from Akdeniz University in Turkey, who led the Mediterranean Archaeology Association expedition.
The wreck is close to the shore of Kekova Island in Antalya, Turkey. The artefacts lie scattered across an underwater slope, just 30m beneath the waves.
Three large stone anchors were found, as well as more than 30 ceramic storage pots, called amphorae.
The fact that none of the ship's wood remained meant techniques like radiocarbon dating - which measures a form of carbon in organic materials - could not be used to determine its age.
Instead, archaeologists analysed the shape of the amphorae. Because pottery styles have changed over time, differerent styles are linked to particular periods.
The Kekova ceramics are distinctive, with two handles, a ridge in the middle and a flat base.
Öniz said this design matched other amphorae unearthed in Egypt and the Middle East that were known to be 4,400-4,700 years old.
"Comparing the decoration techniques… we can definitely say our wreck is Early Bronze Age. This is 100%."
Divers from the expedition brought the pots up to the surface, where they are now being carefully conserved after so many thousands of years underwater.
Dr Karin Sowada, an archaeologist from Macquarie University, Australia, examined the amphorae after they were recovered. Some were intact and she was surprised to see they still contained a viscous, glossy residue.
"I looked inside and nearly fainted. I could not believe how much [residue] was visible. It wasn't just like spots…. a lot of this material was still remaining," she said.
The team is now working to find out exactly what was being carried in the amphorae.
"It could be olive oil, it could be wine, it could be tree resins," Sowada said.
"It's possible that [the residue] could actually be the result of reuse of the jars. I mean, these jars are huge - they're not things that you just ship away and then never see again. People would have emptied these jars on arrival and potentially used them for many, many, many years."
The wreck and its cargo are also shedding light on trade in the ancient world.
The archaeologists say the ship started its voyage from somewhere along the eastern coast of the Mediterranean.
They believe it was taking goods to either the ancient city of Troy, in what is now north-western Turkey, or to the Minoan people in Crete.
Travelling by sea was fraught with danger, particularly around Kekova Island, where the strong currents and winds have claimed many ships.
There are hundreds of wrecks in the area, and the Mediterranean Archaelogy Association specialises in finding and studying them.
Öniz says that when he is diving on the wreck his first thoughts are about the lives of the people who were connected to this vessel.
"We are the first humans who [have] touched these objects after 5,000 years.
"We are always thinking of the sailors... the producers of the amphora and the person who carried the amphora on their shoulders to the ship, and the women who were waiting for their husbands, and they unfortunately couldn't go back."
The Kekova discovery now tops the list of the world's oldest shipwrecks.
Previously, the record holder was a wreck off the coast of Dokos, an island in southern Greece, which dates to about 4,200 years ago.
The oldest known shipwreck where some of the wood is still preserved was found in the Black Sea off the coast of Bulgaria. It dates to about 2,400 years ago.

Missile alert interrupts Saudi minister mid-speech (VIDEO)
A missile alert interrupted a speech by a Saudi minister, Ahmed bin Sulaiman Al Rajhi, while he was addressing an economic forum in Riyadh on Monday, amid escalating Houthi attacks on the kingdom.
The incident occurred at the Riyadh International Convention and Exhibition Centre, when warning notifications sounded simultaneously on the minister’s phone and those of audience members.
Al Rajhi, the human resources and social development minister, briefly acknowledged the alerts before calmly continuing his speech.
“We are under the protection of the Lord of the Worlds. God willing, may God turn their plot back upon them,” he told the audience.
The interruption came after two consecutive Houthi attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh over the weekend, which killed more than a dozen people, including several foreign nationals.
Residents reported hearing several powerful explosions in the Saudi capital on Monday night, according to Al Jazeera. The Saudi military said its air defenses had intercepted at least one Houthi ballistic missile targeting Riyadh, along with two additional projectiles launched toward the southwestern city of Khamis Mushait.
Saudi Arabia’s aviation authority announced on Monday that Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport would remain closed until October 17 following the deadly strikes.
The Houthis claimed responsibility for Saturday’s attack. In an exclusive interview with RT, Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a spokesperson for the group, described the strike as retaliation for years of Saudi bombardment of Yemen’s civilian infrastructure.
He warned that the Houthis would continue targeting Saudi military facilities and critical infrastructure until Riyadh ended its involvement in Yemen, lifted its blockade and agreed to a “comprehensive and permanent peace.”
Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen’s civil war in 2015, leading a military coalition supporting the internationally recognized government against the Houthis.
Large-scale fighting largely subsided following a UN-brokered truce in 2022 but flared up again in July after Saudi-backed Yemeni forces struck the Houthi-held Sanaa Airport.
Last month, the Houthis seized large stretches of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and territory around the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait, including the port of Mocha.
Saudi-backed government forces have since launched a counteroffensive, claiming to have recaptured key positions near the vital shipping route connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.
Riyadh has stepped up its air support for the offensive, intensifying strikes on Houthi-held territory in recent days. According to the group, Saudi bombardments have killed nearly 400 people since early September, many of them civilians.
