When Truth Loses its Witnesses
Mohsen Askari on why not all political narratives should be treated as equal.
I am Iranian living in Istanbul, Turkey. In recent months, I have found myself sitting in rooms with other Iranians, all of us shaped in different ways by the same regime, the same history, and the same accumulated exhaustion. Yet when we speak about what’s happening in Iran, it often feels as if we’re describing different countries. One person sees resistance, another sees foreign manipulation. One sees the collapse of a dictatorship, another sees the danger of national humiliation. One sees war as the terrible price of liberation, another sees it as proof that liberation cannot come through bombs. One sees the Islamic Republic as defeated, another repeats its language of victory. One person speaks of ‘the people’, another asks, “Which people – and who gave anyone the right to speak in their name?”
This is not just ordinary disagreement. It produces a deeper shock. If people who speak the same language, who have lived under the same political order, have inherited the same wounds, and watched the same events unfold, cannot agree on what’s happening, what hope is there for historical truth? If even the present is already broken into incompatible accounts, can we possibly say we know the past?
Protest Gothenburg © Crannofonix News 2026 Creative Commons 4
Relativism Conceals Corruption
The apparently easiest answer to this problem is ‘relativism’: everyone has their own truth. Everyone speaks from their own pain. Every story is partial. Every account is constructed.
There is something right in this. Human beings do not experience history as raw data. We do not live through events as neutral recording machines. We remember through fear, loyalty, shame, class, exile, ideology, trauma, hope, and loss. The same event can enter different lives with different meanings. A person inside Iran may experience foreign pressure differently from a person in exile. A parent may hear ‘war’ differently from a young protester. Someone whose child has been killed will not speak in the same register as someone watching from a television studio. There is no ‘view from nowhere’.
But a dangerous mistake hides inside this truth. From the fact that all narratives are partial, it does not follow that all narratives are equal. Some narratives expose harm, some conceal it. Some help us understand a situation more fully, some make understanding harder. Some return agency to the wounded, some steal agency from them. Thus, a victim’s testimony, a regime’s denial, a propagandist’s justification, and a strategic analyst’s cold description of violence, are not simply four ‘perspectives’: they’re reports of four different relations to suffering, evidence, agency, and power, and some are better than others, in various ways. So the plurality of narratives should make us more careful in narrative assessment, not more relativistic.
This distinction matters because political violence does not only attack bodies; through the misinformation that attends the physical violence it attacks the conditions under which truth can be known, shared, trusted, and judged. It kills witnesses. It corrupts language. It destroys evidence. It floods public space with suspicion. It makes testimony sound partisan before it can even be heard. It turns grief into propaganda, and propaganda into ‘common sense’.
Hannah Arendt understood this danger clearly. In her 1968 essay ‘Truth and Politics’ she warned that factual truth is fragile because it depends on witnesses, records, and a shared public world. Mathematical truth can survive without public agreement, but factual truth cannot. If enough people deny that something happened, if records are destroyed, if witnesses are discredited, if language itself is made slippery, factual truth becomes politically homeless, and very short-lived.
Authoritarian regimes know this. Their greatest achievement is not making people believe the official story; it’s making people give up on the possibility of truth altogether. The dictator does not need everyone to say, “The regime is right.” It may be enough if people say, “Who knows? Everyone lies. Every side has its own story.” That is not skepticism. It is surrender disguised as sophistication.
The problem is not that politics contains narratives. It must. No society can remember everything, and no person can tell the whole of an event. The problem is that narratives do things: they classify actors, they assign motives, they distribute innocence and guilt. They decide whose pain counts as evidence, and whose pain becomes noise. Consider that in many authoritarian settings, protest is not described as protest. It is reclassified as infiltration, manipulation, rioting, sabotage, or ‘soft war’. This is not just a minor linguistic shift. Once protesters are seen as instruments of an outside power, they’re no longer seen as citizens with grievances. Their anger no longer has to be interpreted. Their suffering no longer has to be answered. Their deaths can be narrated as the restoration of order. The dead are no longer dead citizens, they are evidence that a conspiracy was defeated. This is a theft of agency. A person who risks their life to speak is transformed into a political puppet. A political demand from the opposition party becomes a security incident. State violence becomes management.
A narrative, then, is not merely a representation of reality, it is an intervention in reality. It can open moral attention, or close it. It can widen the space of responsibility, or narrow it. It can make the victim more visible, or make the victim disappear behind a theory. This is why the question ‘Whose narrative is this?’ is never enough. We must also ask: What does this narrative make possible? What does it make impossible? What facts must it deny? Whose suffering does it erase? Who becomes more powerful if this story is believed?
Bad Language
Miranda Fricker’s work on epistemic injustice gives us useful language for this problem. Testimonial injustice happens when a speaker’s credibility is unfairly reduced because the listeners have been prejudiced. Someone speaks, but their word arrives already discounted. In a political context this discounting can become systematic: the protester is treated as manipulated, the exile as hysterical, the grieving mother as emotional, the prisoner as unreliable. Meanwhile, the official is treated as serious because he speaks the language of order. This is not simply a mistake in listening, it is the political rearrangement of credibility.
Fricker’s second concept, hermeneutical injustice, is also relevant. This is the injustice people suffer when they don’t have the shared concepts needed to make sense of their experience. Something happens to them, but the available public language cannot yet name it properly. This problem is sharpened under authoritarianism because language itself is managed – killing becomes ‘restoring order’, disconnection becomes ‘security’, and so on. People are harmed, and then the language available to describe that harm is stolen or poisoned.
To recover truth, then, is not only to collect facts. It is also to recover the conditions under which testimony can be heard and experience can be named.
A similar linguistic problem appears when some people claim to speak for ‘the people’. In moments of crisis, everyone seems to invoke ‘the people’. Regimes claim to defend them. Opposition leaders claim to represent them. Foreign governments claim to help them. Media channels claim to show what they want. But under authoritarianism, the people are everywhere in speech and nowhere in power. That’s why ‘The people want [whatever]’ is often a dangerous political sentence. Sometimes it’s true, sometimes it’s wishful thinking, and sometimes it’s propaganda – the speaker’s own desire dressed in democratic clothing.
Hearing the People
This leads to a distinction that I have come to think of as ‘democratic audibility’. A population is democratically audible when people can form political judgments freely, communicate them without coercive distortion, and have them registered through credible public channels. This requires more than speech. It requires safety, access, institutions, trust, and the possibility of disagreement without terror.
This idea is close to the late Jürgen Habermas’s theory of communicative action and his concern with the conditions under which public communication can be rational and legitimate. But democratic audibility emphasizes something more basic, and more easily damaged in authoritarian contexts: the possibility of a people becoming hearable politically at all. A culture may be full of voices, and yet still be politically inaudible. This is especially true in the digital age, where visibility is easily mistaken for political audibility. A video can go viral or a hashtag can trend; but circulation is not political authorization, and loudness is not representation. The most visible voices are not necessarily the most legitimate ones – especially when fear, censorship, exile, wealth, algorithmic amplification, and unequal access determine who is heard.
In an authoritarian crisis this problem becomes severe. The person in the country may be unable to speak freely, while the person outside it may speak freely but not represent those inside it. The person with access to foreign media may be treated as the national voice, while the person without internet access vanishes from the record. And silence itself becomes unreadable, as the person who says nothing may be silent from fear, exhaustion, strategy, disagreement, or grief, or many other reasons.
This does not mean that no one can make political judgments. It means we must be honest about the damaged conditions under which such judgments are made. When a people has been deprived of free institutions, open media, secure communication, and basic safety, no claim to speak for them should be accepted without scrutiny.
Lost in the Woods of Rhetoric by Venantius J Pinto
Truth & Uncertainty
Truth also needs infrastructure. This may sound strange because we often imagine truth as a matter of mind or character: A truthful person is honest. A rational person follows evidence. A good historian checks sources. All this is right, but incomplete. Truth also depends on phones, cables, archives, courts, hospitals, journalists, witnesses, internet access, translation, memory, and trust. It depends on whether a mother can call her son, whether a video can be uploaded without being deleted, whether a doctor can record a cause of death honestly, whether a journalist can investigate without fear of imprisonment, and whether citizens have the same access to the outside world as officials and propagandists. When a state controls who can connect, it also controls who can testify. When only some people can speak, only some can upload, only some can bypass censorship, and only some can reach foreign audiences, then the public record is unequal before interpretation even begins.
A media blackout, then, is not merely an interruption of communication. It is an attack on the social conditions of truth. It not only stops people from speaking, it also prevents families from knowing, journalists from verifying, citizens from coordinating, and the outside world from hearing. It turns life into uncertainty.
In Persian, the word bī-khabarī means ‘being without news’. But in moments of political instability, this means more than just ‘lacking information’. It means not knowing whether your mother is safe, your brother is alive, your friend has been arrested, or whether the silence in your phone is technical, political, or final. For the philosopher, uncertainty may be a problem of knowledge. For the exile, it may be the sound of a phone that does not ring. And this kind of not-knowing is not empty; it is full of images, fears, guesses, rituals, and distress. People refresh apps. They wake in the night. They scan fragments of news. They interpret short messages as proof of life. ‘We are fine’ becomes both reassurance and a question generator: Fine how? Written freely? Sent under fear? Copied from someone else? Already out of date? The point is that bī-khabarī is not simple ignorance, it’s relational ignorance. It’s the absence of news from someone whose ordinary presence has helped hold your world together. A daily message from a parent is not just information. A photo, a message, a joke, a complaint about the weather, or a reminder to eat properly, may look trivial from the outside, but these small exchanges are how distance becomes bearable, as they’re how a person abroad continues to belong. When that rhythm disappears, the primary question is ‘Where am I in relation to those I love?’ So a blackout does not merely remove data, it removes the ordinary confirmations through which people remain real to one another. This is why the sentence ‘I am fine’ becomes semantically strange under an information blackout. In ordinary life, it may be enough. Under political oppression it becomes unstable: Are they fine, or protecting me? Are they speaking freely, or carefully? Are they safe now, or were they only safe when the message was sent? Does the word ‘fine’ describe reality, or is it a small act of mercy sent across danger?
Here truth becomes inseparable from trust. A message is not only judged by its content, it’s judged by tone, timing, background noise, delay, and the history of the relationship. People learn to interpret silence as evidence. But silence is a terrible witness. It can mean fear, sleep, arrest, technical failure, battery loss, injury, or nothing at all. The mind fills the gap because love cannot leave it empty. This is why not-knowing can be a form of suffering.
In ordinary epistemology, uncertainty is often treated as a lack – a missing proposition. But in political crises, uncertainty can be manufactured, weaponized, and prolonged. To cut communication is to force people into interpretation without grounds. It makes them search for signs while denying them reliable evidence. It makes the imagination do the work of the torturer. In such conditions, truth is not only a proposition, it is also reassurance. It is the daily confirmation that someone exists, speaks, breathes, and remains reachable. When that confirmation is removed, the world itself becomes less stable.
This is why political violence cannot be understood only through the visible act: the shooting, the arrest, the bombing, the lying speech, the bad law. It must also be understood through the damage done to relations. We depend on testimony not as an optional supplement to knowledge, but as a foundation of human life. Almost everything we know, we know because someone told us it, recorded it, preserved it, or made it available. To destroy trust in testimony is to destroy the world.
The work of Nobel Prize-winning Belarusian writer Svetlana Alexievich is important here. Her books do not give us one clear history of Soviet life, war, or disaster – they give us voices, often contradictory, wounded, self-deceiving, generous, bitter, confused, brave. She does not resolve them into a single official account. Yet she also does not treat all speech as equally truthful. The power of her work lies in preserving plurality without abandoning moral seriousness.
This is the balance we need. We must resist the fantasy of one story that explains everything. But we must also resist the lazy pluralism that treats every story as just another equally-viable angle.
Judging the Narrative
In his work on history and silence, Michel-Rolph Trouillot argues that silences enter history at many stages: when facts are created, when archives are assembled, when narratives are made, and when history is finally written. He means that the past is not only lost because time passes, but because power filters what survives. The same is true of the present. What we will later call history is being filtered now. Some voices are being recorded, others are being buried. Some deaths will become statistics, others will become symbols. Some testimonies will be translated, others will remain in private messages, family grief, or silence. Some narratives will travel because they are useful to powerful actors, others will remain morally true but politically weak.
So how should we judge narratives without pretending to be neutral gods? We can begin with a few tests:
First, what facts must this narrative deny? A story that survives only by refusing evidence deserves suspicion.
Second, whose suffering does it make visible? A narrative that notices only the pain of its own side is not necessarily false, but it is morally incomplete.
Third, whose credibility does it deflate even before listening begins? This is Fricker’s warning. If a person’s testimony is dismissed because they are a protester, an exile, a woman, a grieving parent, a prisoner, a refugee, or simply inconvenient to the preferred theory, then injustice is already underway.
Fourth, whose agency does it erase? If citizens become puppets, victims become tools, or protesters become instruments of powers, then something has gone wrong.
Fifth, who benefits if this story is believed? This does not automatically disprove the story, but it does reveal its political function.
Sixth, does the narrative allow complexity, or does it instead demand loyalty? Propaganda usually cannot tolerate mixed feelings. Human truth often begins with them.
Seventh, does the story help us judge, or does it exhaust judgment? Some narratives do not persuade us of a falsehood directly. They simply tire us intellectually until we no longer want to know the truth.
This last point is crucial. The crisis of truth in our time is not just that people believe false things, it is that many people become too exhausted to defend true things. They see an unending stream of competing videos, experts, accusations, corrections, countercorrections, and emotional rhetoric, and eventually they say, “I don’t know anymore.” Sometimes that sentence is intellectually honest. Sometimes it is the beginning of moral withdrawal.
The challenge is to keep judgment alive without making judgment simplistic. This is difficult because politics is complicated. Foreign intervention can be opposed without defending a dictatorship; a regime can be criminal without making every enemy of that regime virtuous; a protest movement can entertain many errors without losing its basic legitimacy; a person can fear war, yet understand why others welcome the weakening of an evil state. A person can be morally authoritative, yet still politically mistaken.
Complexity is necessary. But complexity should not become a hiding place for moral cowardice. (To say that things are complicated is sometimes the beginning of thought; sometimes, it marks the end of responsibility.)
Conclusions
The question is not whether we can escape political and historical narratives. We cannot. The question is whether we can develop the moral discipline of narrative judgment. Such a discipline requires humility, because no one sees everything. It requires courage, because some facts must be defended even when they’re inconvenient. It requires listening, because lived experience cannot be replaced by theory. It requires suspicion, because power often speaks in the language of reason. And it requires care, because behind every political narrative there may be someone whose grief is being used, denied, or forgotten. So in the end, the answer to propaganda is not merely counter-propaganda. It is also not the polite but misplaced relativism that says ‘Every side has its truth’. The answer is harder: it is to listen widely, judge carefully, and refuse to grant moral acceptability to narratives that depend on erasure.
The present will soon become history. But it will not easily become history fairly. Rather, it will pass through memory, media, archives, fear, translation, ideology, and power. Some of what matters most will be lost. Some of what is false will survive. Some of what is true will remain, but without witnesses. That is why we must strongly promote truth as a fragile public practice. In times of political oppression or instability, truth survives not by becoming simple, but by refusing to become indifferent.
© Mohsen Askari 2026
Mohsen Askari is an English instructor and interdisciplinary researcher at Boğaziçi University in Istanbul, writing on language, truth, testimony, education, and political thought.
Epistemic Injustice
Miranda Fricker © Edmond J. Safra Center for Ethics 2016 CC 2.0
Philosopher Miranda Fricker developed an influential analysis of what she calls epistemic injustice:
Testimonial injustice is when a speaker’s credibility is unfairly reduced because the listeners have been prejudiced against them.
Hermeneutical injustice is the injustice people suffer when they don’t have the shared concepts needed to make sense of their experience.
Find out more: Epistemic Injustice: Power and the Ethics of Knowing (Oxford Univ. Press, 2007)

In Defence of Hope
Sam Nuttall hopes to defend it with the help of Gabriel Marcel and Ernst Bloch.
The idea of ‘hope’ is a funny one for Western philosophy. It would be a little hasty to go as far as calling it a philosophical blind spot, as thoughts on hope can be found in Aristotle, Pascal, Kant, Nietzsche, and Heidegger, among others – but equally, it seems as if philosophy has never quite got comfortable with hope. And often, when one does find it mentioned in the great works of philosophy, it’s cast in a negative light. Perhaps it sits a little too close to optimism, leading to it being readily associated with naivety and a lack of critical thought – key enemies of the philosophical undertaking.
For a certain type of philosopher, optimism and hope are the poor relations of those trusty, regular philosopher’s companions, pessimism and cynicism. They think that the optimist is the child living in fairy tales, while the pessimist is the wise elder who has seen it all, and, more importantly, seen through it all: it’s Descartes seeing through the edifice of knowledge, tearing it down with a doubt-fuelled steamroller; it’s Marx, seeing through the bounty and pleasure of middle class society to find exploitation and alienation running rife underneath it; it’s Nietzsche killing God, leaving our very conception of values and morality in free-fall. The risk however is that a broader association of pessimism with intelligence starts to take hold. This proliferates in cinema and literature in the beloved archetype of the ‘tortured genius’, thus reinforcing the problematic idea that great insight must always come at the cost of happiness and comfort. This perhaps conditions a view of philosophy, and academia more broadly, as shackled to the realm of the critical.
The point of sitting down to write this is not to dismiss the works of Descartes, Marx, or Nietzsche. Nor is it to argue that philosophy should not be critical. Instead, I wish to show that the philosophical temperament need not lead to us throwing the baby out with the bathwater – the baby being hope, and the bathwater being, well, all that the philosopher dismisses as naïve! Hope can be compatible with a method of sober, critical thought.
The saving of hope from this dismissal will fall on the shoulders of Gabriel Marcel and Ernst Bloch, through whose works a more potent hope, rather different perhaps from the common understanding of it, will emerge – one that’s grounded in reality, that remains critical, and is thoroughly philosophical.
Artwork © Simon Ellinas 2026 Please visit caricatures.org.uk
Gabriel Marcel & Hope for the Individual
In his work Homo Viator: An Introduction to the Metaphysics of Hope (1962), French philosopher Gabriel Marcel (1889-1973) very quickly wants to sever the ties between hope and optimism. For Marcel, optimism is a non-critical blind faith, an assurance that things will turn out well. Hope, however, is an act of the will, a strenuous commitment that one must maintain in the face of challenges. In this Marcel is interested in a quite particular form of hope, dismissing what he terms ‘trivial’ hope – ends-based hope, the hope for specific things or events (such as a new car) – in favour of an ‘absolute’ hope that transcends particular aims. One may think of this as echoing Kant’s ethics, which isn’t concerned with particular effects or ends, but rather with the duty of the subject. Marcel’s hope is a character trait, and should be categorised alongside things such as courage, honesty and humility.
The key aspect of hope for Marcel lies in ‘availability’ – an openness to the future and the Other (person, or generally, the world beyond the subject). While the present is imperfect and may elicit feelings of despair, hope ensures that the subject remains available to the idea that their life and the wider world can be different from the present. This functions as an antidote to despair – in which the subject effectively closes themselves off from the potential of the future to be different. Despair isolates, turning us away from the world, which we view as statically bound to the negative. Hope, conversely, eases the grip of the ego. This can make a coming together and true communication between subjects possible.
Ernst Bloch & Hope for Society
The German thinker Ernst Bloch (1885-1977) investigates hope at the intersection of Marxism and Freudian psychoanalysis. He believes Western philosophy has failed to sufficiently interrogate this future-facing dimension of human subjectivity due to our preference for the past.
Bloch believes that a dissatisfaction with the state of affairs is part of the human condition. Insofar as it is impossible for any society to be perfect, there’s always some form of lack in the present, which leads to thoughts of a hypothetical, more utopian future. Bloch’s account is philosophically interesting due to the importance he places on certain emotions. He is less interested in what he calls ‘filled emotions’ – those drives such as envy, greed or ambition, that are aimed toward a specific object – and instead focuses on ‘expectant emotions’ – those drives that lack a specific present object. It is to this second category that hope belongs.
In the absence having of a precise object, expectant emotions deal generally with what Bloch calls ‘the not-yet’. Firstly, there is his idea of the ‘not-yet-conscious’, a modification of Freud that holds that there’s an element of the unconscious that looks to the future. While Freud conscribes the unconscious to recollections of the past, and takes night-dreams as illustrative of this, Bloch believes that the unconscious partially looks forward – citing daydreams as evidence. There is also the ‘not-yet-become’, which is the potential within the material reality of the present to be otherwise. Here Bloch is most clearly flying his Marxist flag. For Bloch the present is rife with potentiality, be it in the material conditions of society or within human subjectivity. Hope, consequently, is an almost inherent aspect of the human condition. As mentioned, for Bloch the present is always characterised by a certain lack; but the present can only be understood as ‘lacking’ in a temporal setting – as paling in comparison to the memory of a better past, or as an imperfect state that awaits a better future. Hope can be at its most potent and influential when the not-yet-conscious and the not-yet-become are brought together. When the future-facing consciousness of subjects comes together with elements of the present reality that can facilitate the change they are striving for, then hope becomes extremely powerful. This is the 'utopian function’ of hope.
Bringing Them Together
Marcel and Bloch both detail their accounts of hope with either explicit or implicit reference to the dismissive attitude of philosophy I mentioned earlier. Both take steps to rehabilitate the concept against any accusations of it being anti-philosophical. Marcel, does this by distinguishing hope from optimism and dismissing the idea that the two are necessarily connected. In Bloch, hope, far from belonging to the realm of wishful thinking or fantasy, is a concept grounded in material reality, is practical through-and-through.
Both thinkers also work on the basis of similar metaphysical assumptions concerning indeterminacy in both the present and the future. For Marcel, this is an adoption of the existentialist view that ‘existence precedes essence’, meaning that humans are born into (or in Heidegger’s term, ‘thrown into’) a world without a purpose or a path to follow. Similarly, Bloch, as a ‘process philosopher’, views the world as always incomplete, always changing.
Interestingly, similar assumptions have underpinned theories that have gone in a very different direction. The post-death-of-God realisations of the universe’s lack of inherent meaning and the subject’s lack of inherent purpose may seem to naturally lead to despair and pessimism. For Marcel and Bloch, therefore, to take the same base assumptions but still advocate for hope is an interesting turn. They notice that at the core of nihilism is nil, meaning nothing. So the lack of an inherent meaning does not mean that man or the universe crosses over into negative meaning, as this would mean there is some value – negative value, but still value nonetheless – and therefore not nothing. But instead, this nil, this lack, is there to be filled, showing that man and the universe are blank canvases. Yet what specifically comes to populate them is not predetermined. On this view, philosophy’s tendency to stray into pessimism is just as ungrounded as the flights into fantasy and blind optimism it so often critiques. While using the idea of hope – so often associated with optimism – Marcel and Bloch actually walk a tightrope between optimism and pessimism.
Beyond Optimism & Pessimism
Perhaps some will ask whether the hope given by Marcel and Bloch is a counterfeit hope. Perhaps some will feel that, in removing optimism from his theory, Marcel fails to offer the comfort or ease that people look for in hope. Likewise, Bloch’s picture of the world, despite the centrality of hope, may look rather bleak: a present that’s never satisfactory, human beings constantly looking to the horizon for something better. But to return to what I said earlier, ultimately, philosophy may have to shake its head and accept that it cannot satisfy a desire for a hope that’s staunchly optimistic, perpetually comforting, and completely reassuring. What use is a cosy hope that always comforts in the face of a world that will regularly contradict its reassurances?
I think what Marcel and Bloch muster is far more interesting and valuable. They tackle head on the forces that would make hope appear impossible. Hope survives the confrontation, and is far more vital for it. In fact, they highlight how hope must always be tied to that which seeks to destroy it – one simply cannot have hope without lack. The pair show that one can delve into the more abyssal aspects of philosophy, and of life, and still emerge head up, eyes on the horizon, ready to strive toward a future that’s still open.
Understood in these terms, hope can be a potent tool in response to a reality that, as much as ever, seems capable of extinguishing hope for good: a philosophy underpinned by hope, that seeks to affirm and create rather than cynically critique, holds the potential for bettering life on the individual level, and on the macro-scale, for bettering society as a whole.
© Sam Nuttall 2026
Sam Nuttall studied Philosophy at Newcastle University, where he developed a keen interest in post-Kantian European philosophy.

Albanian police fire tear gas at protesters as Education Ministry attacked
At least 23 protesters have been arrested in demonstrations in the capital.
Albanian riot police have fired tear gas and water cannons at hundreds of student demonstrators protesting over education and social conditions in the capital Tirana.
Protesters hurled bricks and concrete blocks at the Education Ministry on Tuesday, demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama.
Student organisers said the protest was over conditions at universities, higher education costs, financial support and employment prospects after graduation.
At least six officers and one female journalist were injured, according to a statement by police, and 23 people were arrested.
Police called on the protesters to stop attacking the ministry, but some attendees continued to assault officers with Molotov cocktails, firecrackers, stones and other hard objects, the statement said.
Protesters said they wanted to express frustration with inequality and government economic policies.
“What Albania needs is a revolution, a change, a complete overthrow of the system because it can’t go on like this,” protester Luljeta Kola said. She added that there was a deep social divide between the rich and the poor in the country.
Albania’s Deputy Prime Minister Albana Kociu wrote on Facebook: “Violence has not been, is not, and will never be a solution. Throwing stones, attacking institutions and the state police, as well as the senseless destruction of public property, are not how youth should express themselves.”
The Albanian capital has seen a series of anti-government protests since May, sparked by a luxury tourism project linked to US President Donald Trump’s family.
The project has fuelled anger over alleged corruption and a lack of transparency, with protesters demanding Rama’s resignation.
Students echoed those demands but told local media that Tuesday’s rally also aimed to decry university conditions, tuition fees and a lack of support for young people.
“Problems are not solved by pretending they do not exist. Students have questions, demands and plenty of reasons to be heard,” one of the organisers said on Instagram.

Commercial vessel strikes

Tehran has asserted control over maritime transit through the strait and warned ships against using unauthorised routes since the conflict erupted in late February following US and Israeli strikes, prompting Washington to impose a counterblockade on Iranian ports.
The heightened rhetoric coincided with fresh incidents at sea. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) confirmed on Tuesday that a commercial tanker and a container ship were struck by projectiles of unknown origin in the Strait of Hormuz.
The agency said an official inquiry is underway, but it did not disclose casualties or the extent of the damage.

The 71-year-old pontiff has lung adenocarcinoma, with tissue tests conducted during the operation confirming what doctors had suspected from preparatory examinations, the bulletin said.
The pope was admitted to Rome’s Gemelli hospital on Oct 13 for surgery to remove a growth on his lung that doctors found in a recent health checkup.
The Vatican had said earlier on the evening of Oct 13 that the surgery had been successful before providing a more detailed update from the pope’s lead surgeon, Professor Stefano Margaritora, the chief of thoracic surgery at the Gemelli.

An office tower in the Saudi Aramco complex in the eastern city of Dhahran was struck on the night of Oct 13 and the top three floors were damaged, the source said. The source and two other people with knowledge of the matter said the building was on fire.
The complex hosts a major operations centre for Aramco, which oversees a vast network of onshore and offshore oil rigs, pipelines, refineries and export terminals.
Allies failed to warn Ukraine of impending missile attack, Zelensky says
Ukraine received no prior warning from its Western partners about a Russian ballistic missile attack on its capital, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct 13, as Kyiv comes under intense US pressure to halt attacks on Russian refineries.
Russia hit no Ukrainian energy targets overnight for the first time since US President Donald Trump’s surprise Oct 11 announcement of an “energy ceasefire”, but hammered transport and logistics with ballistic missiles and drones.
Reuters and other media have reported that US officials have threatened to cut off intelligence sharing and weapons sales to Ukraine unless it stops attacking Russian refineries. Kyiv relies heavily on US intelligence for early warnings of missile strikes, experts and officials say.
Cornell bans fraternity parties for rest of academic year after alleged gang rape
Cornell University will ban parties and social events at fraternity houses until the end of the academic year, its president said on Oct 13, responding to the outcry over an alleged gang rape on campus in 2024.
The measure is the strongest reaction yet from Cornell’s leadership to a lawsuit filed by a former undergraduate, Jane Doe, alleging that seven men sexually assaulted her during a party two years ago.
Over the last several weeks, the Ivy League school in Ithaca, New York, and its president, Michael Kotlikoff, have come under heavy criticism from students, faculty and donors over its response to the allegations.
Gianni Infantino received undisclosed US$1.7 million World Cup payment: Report
Embattled FIFA president Gianni Infantino received a previously undisclosed US$1.72 million (S$2.2 million) World Cup payment, according to FIFA and IRS documents obtained by ESPN.
According to the report published on Oct 13, the lack of transparency surrounding the compensation is a potential violation of FIFA statutes.
Infantino received the compensation in 2024 from FWC2026, the official US-based organisation set up by FIFA to manage and operate the 2026 World Cup held this summer in North America, according to IRS records.

He added a disclaimer, saying the videos were obtained by him strictly for verification purposes and had not been authenticated. Solanki insisted that he was not endorsing the views and statements of any individuals or organisations behind the videos.
Seeking any genuine misconduct on part of the police/CAPF personnel to be addressed fairly, he said in case the allegations of inappropriate behaviour towards women protesters are substantiated, appropriate legal and departmental action may follow against the personnel and their supervisors. Alternatively, if the footage is found to be fabricated or manipulated, legal action and removal of the misleading content, should be pursued as per law.
He also requested gender sensitivity training for police personnel on the ground.A CRPF official told TOI that Solanki's act of directly approaching the rights watchdogs and Delhi Police against the conduct of CAPF/police officers, rather than raise the matter with his superiors, may be viewed as indiscipline as service conduct rules bar officers from filing public complaints against govt officers/depts. "The officer concerned was not even on the ground (where protests were held). If he was concerned, he would have raised the matter internally with his superiors," said an officer. The officer hinted that Solanki could face departmental proceedings over violation of conduct rules.

Public comments flood US government websites over proposed H-1B, OPT fee hikes
Chinese students and other graduates voice concerns over steep new costs that could threaten their prospects of working in America
Kana Liu, a Chinese Canadian living in the US on a work visa, felt compelled to speak up.
Faced with a Department of Homeland Security proposal to charge up to US$100,000 in fees for international students to work in the US after graduation under Optional Practical Training (OPT), she rushed to the government’s public comment portal.
“I firmly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fee,” she wrote on the federal comment site on October 12. “They create undue barriers for legitimate students and educational institutions while failing to effectively address the stated goals of preventing immigration fraud and protecting American workers.”
Liu is among thousands weighing in on two contentious proposals that could sharply raise fees for international students and employers of skilled foreign workers, fuelling debate and adding uncertainty for those hoping to study, work or remain in the US.

US trial begins for Rwandan-American accused of role in genocide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
22:15:44 UTC
07:15:44 KST

US trial begins for Rwandan-American accused of role in genocide
Eric Nshimiye, an American citizen, says the evidence against him consists of unreliable eye witnesses.
Boston, Massachusetts, United States – A United States federal court in Boston has begun hearing the case of a Rwandan-American accused of covering up his role in the 1994 genocide in Rwanda.
Prosecutors say Eric Nshimiye, a 55-year-old father of four and a US citizen, took part in a nationwide outbreak of genocidal violence against ethnic minority Tutsis by majority Hutu extremists in April 1994. More than 800,000 people were killed over about 100 days, in what has been called a genocide by the United Nations.
Investigators from the US Department of Homeland Security arrested Nshimiye at his home in Ohio in 2024, alleging he had lied to them in an interview about his time in Rwanda during the genocide. They also allege he committed perjury in a previous trial in 2019 in Boston when he testified on behalf of a friend who was also accused of perpetrating the genocide. Prosecutors say Nshimiye, a medical student at the time of the genocide in the town of Butare, himself took part in the killing and rape of Tutsis.
Hutus who took part in the violence “heeded calls by the government to terminate their neighbours,” Assistant United States Attorney Christopher Looney told the court on Tuesday, including Nshimiye in the group.
“He himself attacked Tutsis, and handed Tutsis over to be killed and raped,” Looney said.
During his 2019 testimony, Nshimiye denied being part of the genocide, and said he was not part of the pro-Hutu National Revolutionary Movement for Development and the Interahamwe, the paramilitary group blamed for most of the killings during the genocide.
Nshimiye faces charges of perjury and obstruction of justice for those denials. If convicted, the Trump administration could try to revoke Nshimiye’s citizenship.
Nshimiye, who is an ethnic Hutu, says he had gone to the capital, Kigali, on holiday before violence broke out. He says he never made it back to Butare because of the chaos engulfing the country in April 1994, and instead left the country as a refugee, eventually coming to the US and becoming a citizen in 2009.
At the opening of his case on Tuesday, Nshimiye, dressed in a dark blue suit, was calm and occasionally turned to smile at family and friends who came to support him. Since his arrest, authorities have kept Nshimiye without bail in a Boston-area federal jail.
Prosecutors plan to put more than a dozen witnesses on the stand, most flown in from Rwanda, who say they recall seeing Nshimiye participate in pro-Hutu political events before the genocide, and some who say they later saw him participate in genocidal violence in Butare.
His family says the events of 1994 are more complex than the simple narrative of Hutus killing Tutsis. Simply being an ethnic Hutu, Epa Bizimana, Nshimiye’s nephew, told Al Jazeera, should not be enough to convince a jury someone took part in the genocide.
“The jury is going to learn some things for the first time; Americans are going to learn something for the first time,” said Bizimana, who was 10 years old when he fled Rwanda with his family in 1994.
Defence lawyers told the court on Tuesday that Nshimiye was not part of the Hutus who participated in the genocide. They say the entire case against him is built on the accounts of eyewitnesses, some of whom were only able to identify him after repeatedly being shown his photo, and some of whom have a history of giving different testimony in trials of alleged genocidaires over the years.
Kurt Kerns, one of the defence attorneys, told the court that the prosecution’s case was based on evidence “that only reared its ugly head after Eric came to testify as a character witness, and 25 years after the genocide.”
Kerns said Nshimiye had never been implicated in domestic and international tribunals after the genocide, including the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda as well as an informal transitional justice system inside Rwanda, called gacaca, which tried more than a million people for their role in the atrocity.

Everyone Hates ‘Digger.’ It’s the Perfect Climate Movie
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
22:08:44 UTC
07:08:44 KST

Should you see a Looney Tunes–esque satire that stars Tom Cruise in prosthetics portraying a loud caricature of an American oilman, that’s currently on track to be one of the biggest box-office failures of all time?
Absolutely yes—and it’s a movie that rewired my expectations of what a movie about climate change should be. Digger, the critically panned, exorbitantly expensive new film from Alejandro González Iñárritu, calls into question the purpose of art and even the basic purpose of telling the truth in the face of a capitalist machine churning the world toward climate disaster. The deeply uncomfortable film forces audiences to confront what kind of characters we’re the most comfortable making into climate villains.
(Spoilers ahead—if you have any plans to see the movie, I really would encourage you to do so first before reading on.)
The film stars Tom Cruise as Digger Rockwell, an oil billionaire who only wears cowboy boots and lives in a mansion covered in antlers and polar bear skin rugs. At the start of the film, one of Digger’s oil-drilling platforms accidentally causes a massive iceberg to break loose, resulting in a huge methane leak. With catastrophe impending, he has to alert the president (John Goodman, putting in a performance reminiscent of his best work with the Coen brothers) as the iceberg barrels toward Europe.
The trailers play up the movie as a too-broad-it’s-painful satire of American oilmen and how a Trumpian-inspired religious-right administration would respond to a real climate disaster. Iñárritu, however, lets us in on the secret early: The farce we’re watching is actually a play within the movie, being performed in a theater with a leaky ceiling that keeps losing power. Tom Cruise is not playing Digger Rockwell, but rather an actor playing Digger Rockwell.
We eventually learn that the play, Fossil Fools, depicts events that actually happened some decades ago. From then on, you’re aware that every joke, every villainous portrayal of Digger and the president as Really Bad Guys, is for two audiences: moviegoers in 2026 and theatergoers living in a dystopian future.
From the trailers, I’d initially thought that the movie was going to be similar to Adam McKay’s blockbuster Don’t Look Up, a climate satire that drew record numbers of viewers on Netflix when it aired in 2021. Don’t Look Up puts scientists racing to inform the public about an impending asteroid collision and pushing to avert catastrophe against corporate and political interests that have other plans. McKay, at the time, said the film’s purpose was to make “people less tolerant of inaction from their leaders.” If the media—journalists, filmmakers, and the like—could correctly inform the public about the risks of climate change, the film (and its accompanying calls to action) posited, we would begin to see progress on cutting emissions.
Digger, similarly, deals with themes around climate misinformation. Digger admits he ignored alerts from his own company about the unfolding crisis on his drilling platforms. Goodman’s president and his cabinet decide to deploy a “firewall” that censors out all mentions of the climate crisis (including the phrase “Al Gore”) to control the narrative of what’s happening.
But where Don’t Look Up’s thesis is that action would happen if we just communicated the truth better, Digger takes a much more nihilistic view—that the truth has no value. Dr. Ganesh (Riz Ahmed), Digger’s long-suffering environmental expert, angrily tells the oilman that he is going to tell the truth about his company and climate change to a crowd of European Union leaders, and keeps his promise. (Ganesh makes the first reference to the “Exxon Knew” investigation I can recall in a major movie.)
Digger watches from a back room, then, in a ripping speech that forms the backbone of the movie, he tells the hostile European delegates that he, like other oilmen, knew that their product would cause runaway climate change. But that doesn’t matter, he crows. The world is hooked on oil, and the people in that very room have found a myriad of uses for it.
“You want energy to ask AI to solve the very same disasters that it’s fueling,” he says to the assembled delegates. “You want freedom to bask in the comfort of your unsustainable lives.” He ultimately leverages Ganesh’s truth-telling to avoid accountability—strolling out of parliament as members fight among themselves.
The bombastic portrayal of Digger Rockwell is, too, a rumination on what kind of truths we get as an audience and who the most palatable climate evildoers are. In between rehearsal takes of the increasingly outrageous Fossil Fools, we see Cruise grapple with how to play Digger, noting he watched hours of footage and found him not to be a finger-gunning shooting fool with a Texas drawl but a conniving, sharp businessman. But the play’s audience, watching Fossil Fools in a world Digger helped ruin, are not looking for truth—they’re looking for catharsis. Near the end of the film, an incredible late twist reveals the play has a wealthy benefactor with a vested interest in having it performed.
One of my big critiques of Don’t Look Up was the notion that a Hollywood movie could be an agent for change; that the movie’s star, Leonardo di Caprio, who parties on superyachts and takes private jets, could tell people to listen to scientists and just vote our way out of this mess. Digger essentially spits in the face of Don’t Look Up’s existence, pointing out that enjoying satire about climate change that paints specific villains like Digger Rockwell comes at the risk of ignoring forms of corporate power more palatable to liberal viewers.
This all may seem pretty nihilist, and I don’t think the movie is intended to be cheery. But I also don’t think it’s a message to not make art. Rather, Digger strives to be a reflection of our current reality, where truth often doesn’t matter, and art is often funded by the very powers it rails against. While Don’t Look Up was intended to be a call to action, Digger simply kicks back and says to viewers: This is where we are.
Five years after a record number of people watched Don’t Look Up, the Trump administration is back in power and has pulled the US out of the Paris Agreement again. The government is gleefully doubling down on “Drill, Baby, Drill.” Tech corporations that in the Don’t Look Up era were touting their goals to cut emissions and even reverse past damage are now walking those back, thanks to the AI boom—which, they promise, will help solve climate change someday. And here I am, typing on my computer, driving a car around that uses fossil fuels.
That Digger is the last film to come out of Warner Bros. before David Ellison’s purchase of the studio only underscores the role that wealthy, conservative individuals are increasingly playing in controlling the arts. In the end, I most appreciate Digger for pointing out the absurdity of the whole thing.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Tuesday confirmed reports that Egypt's former intelligence chief visited Israel before Hamas' attack on October 7, 2023, but denied he was present upon his landing and claimed he does not know which Israeli official met with him.
Speaking in an interview to pro-government Channel 14, Netanyahu said that "I know who he didn't meet. He didn't meet with me because I was attending a memorial ceremony for fallen IDF soldiers, so it was a lie from the outset," Netanyahu said. "He didn't meet with me, he didn't speak to me. Since when does an intelligence chief speak with a head of state?"
Netanyahu added: "Want to see the deep state? I'm the prime minister of Israel, and Egypt's intelligence minister was here. He spent 59 minutes on the ground. I want to know who he met with."
The interview follows several reports in global media about warnings Netanyahu purportedly received before Hamas' attack on October 7, 2023. Netanyahu has denied previous reports that he was warned by Kamel, saying it was "a claim that was already debunked at the beginning of the war" and calling it "fake news."
The Atlantic reported late September that Egypt's intelligence chief, Abbas Kamel, came to Israel 11 days before Hamas' October 7 massacre and delivered a warning that the armed group in Gaza was preparing for a major attack and that the window of opportunity to prevent a disaster was closing.
According to the report, which cites Israeli, Egyptian, Arab, U.S. and European officials briefed on his visit, Kamel recommended that Israel grant Hamas economic concessions to prevent a confrontation. He warned that if Israel did not change its course, "Gaza is going to blow up in your faces," the report said, citing a former Israeli official later briefed on the visit.
According to the report, Kamel arrived in Israel on September 26, 2023, the day the country's leadership marked 50 years since the Yom Kippur War. A plane linked to Egypt's intelligence service landed in an isolated area at Ben-Gurion International Airport and remained on the ground for 67 minutes before returning to Cairo.
According to The Atlantic, it is unclear with whom Kamel met during his brief visit.
The Atlantic's sources noted that the fact that Kamel personally came to Israel demonstrated the urgency of the situation. "The messenger was the message," a former Israeli official was quoted as saying, stressing that "there is no world" where Netanyahu is unaware of a meeting with Egypt's top intelligence official.
Also in September, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing officials in an Arab government, that Kamel called Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu days before Hamas' October 7, 2023 attack to warn him, after two earlier Egyptian warnings went unheeded.
According to the Journal, Egypt first warned Israel in June 2023 that the situation in Gaza was volatile and urged it to resume negotiations with Hamas.
The Yedioth Ahronoth daily reported on October 9, 2023, that Kamel spoke with Netanyahu in the days preceding October 7 and warned him of "something unusual, a terrifying operation" about to be launched by Hamas. An Egyptian intelligence official told Yedioth Ahronoth that Kamel was "amazed by the indifference" his warning was met with in Israel. According to the report, Netanyahu told Kamel, "In Gaza, we are in the picture, we are in control. Our problem is with the West Bank, and that's where we are also diverting forces."
Netanyahu also said in the Channel 14 interview on Tuesday that Iran and its allies are planning to attack Israel before the upcoming election, with opposition lawmakers warning that the prime minister may ignite an escalation for political purposes ahead of the October 27 vote.
Netanyahu said Iran is planning an attack, adding that Iran's leaders "want to do it either directly or through one of their allies."
Earlier on Tuesday, opposition frontrunner Gadi Eisenkot of Yashar, Yisrael Beitenu party leader Avigdor Liberman and the Democrats leader Yair Golan warned that Netanyahu may start a war ahead of the upcoming election in an effort to stay in power, with the latter saying that "the writing's on the wall, in letters of blood and fire."
Netanyahu said Iran and its allies want him to lose the election, listing Hamas, Hezbollah and the Palestinian Authority, alongside United Arab List party leader Mansour Abbas, who was part of former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett's coalition in 2021-2022.
Responding to a Channel 12 report that Netanyahu spoke with U.S. President Donald Trump last week about resuming the war against Iran, Netanyahu said he has "no intention of commenting on the many conversations I have with President Trump. ... As long as we haven't brought them down, they will come back. We first need to bring them down."
Netanyahu also said Israel must know how to go against U.S. interests when deciding on war. "You have to be able to act against the United States," he said.
Also on Tuesday, Defense Minister Israel Katz from Netanyahu's Likud party also warned that "Israel's enemies" may spark military conflict ahead of the October 27 election.
"We are identifying attempts by our enemies, led by Iran and its proxies, to carry out attacks that would influence the results of the election in Israel," Katz said, adding that the Netanyahu government will "make decisions according to security needs, without regard to any other consideration."

The Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) has found the missing head of an 11th-century Vishnu idol at Khajuraho, whose restoration became the subject of a recent controversy involving the Supreme Court, and plans to reattach it after expert examination. ASI has also introduced a three-year deadline for archaeological excavations to curb delays in research and cut approval times for most conservation projects to 15-20 days, director general Yadubir Singh Rawat told TOI in an exclusive interview. He also revealed plans for a preliminary excavation at Ujjain's Vaishya Tekri, where a Buddhist stupa could be larger than Sanchi's, although its actual scale and significance remain to be established.Controversy over the beheaded Vishnu idol at Khajuraho's Javari temple reached the Supreme Court last year when advocate Rakesh Dalal sought restoration, replacement or reconstruction of the seven-foot statue. While dismissing the petition, then CJI BR Gavai had said, "Go and ask the deity itself to do something now." Though Gavai later said he respects all religions and that his statement was taken out of context, a lawyer had tried to throw a shoe at him inside the courtroom.
Rawat said the missing head had been found in an ASI store. "During a visit to Bhopal for the Brics summit, I learnt that the statue's head - which had been kept in our store - had been found. The person in charge informed me that someone likely tried to break off the head to steal it but failed to do so. We are having experts examine it and will soon reattach it to the statue."
On encroachments at protected monuments, Rawat said "The root of this problem lies in the list prepared by British rulers in 1904 under the 'Ancient Monuments Preservation Act' - a list that the then govt adopted post-Independence without any review. The British had included cemeteries and graves of their obscure soldiers, horses and pets - which they deemed highly significant - among protected monuments." Rawat said a review in 1953 incorporated state monuments into a definitive list, but the central list remained unchanged. The resulting difficulties led to 17 monuments being removed from it.Regarding funding disparities, he said allocations depended on visitor numbers, maintenance requirements, security expenses and public facilities. Taj Mahal and Red Fort, he said, served as showcases for ASI, while Taj Mahal's maintenance required substantial expenditure because of its delicate structure and heavy tourist footfall. ASI paid around Rs 3 crore monthly for more than 200 CISF personnel deployed there.He said ASI circles had been instructed to prepare conservation and tourism development proposals for lesser-known sites like Bareilly's pyramid-like Bhim ki Gada structure.

An order issued by DGCA chief Vir Vikram Yadav said the "travelling public and airlines" were advised to ensure that the MOBIKINS MK-PB-04 powerbank was not carried or transported on board the aircraft."Airlines are further advised to take appropriate measures to identify and prevent the carriage of the aforesaid powerbank and to disseminate this safety advisory to the passengers through suitable communication channels," the order said.
Over the past year, several countries, including India, have started restricting powerbank usage on aircraft due to the possibility of them catching fire. Apart from limiting the number of powerbanks and their battery capacity, they can neither be used to charge personal electronic devices nor be charged via the in-seat power source on aircraft.
Instances of PED and powerbank fires have been on the rise globally. The biggest scare here remains airlines taking cabin bags from passengers at the boarding gate to be kept in the baggage hold. If a fire breaks out in the belly baggage hold, it may be a while before it is detected.

RABAT, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Ahmed Touizi, a member of the Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM), was elected on Tuesday speaker of Morocco's House of Representatives, the lower house of parliament, the official Moroccan news agency MAP reported.
Touizi received 220 votes out of 369 votes cast, against 59 for Driss El Azami El Idrissi, candidate of the opposition Justice and Development Party (PJD). A total of 90 ballots were declared invalid.
The election came a day after the announcement of the governing majority, which brings together the PAM, the Istiqlal, the Socialist Union of Popular Forces, and the Party of Progress and Socialism. The four parties hold 207 of the 395 seats, nine above the absolute-majority threshold of 198.

The PAM finished first with 97 seats in the 395-seat House of Representatives in the elections late last month. Under the constitution, Morocco's king appoints the prime minister from the party that wins the most seats, which then forms a government. ■

Roundup: African Energy Week opens in Cape Town with call for African energy cooperation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
05:46:03 CST
06:46:03 KST

Delegates attend African Energy Week (AEW) 2026 in Cape Town, South Africa, Oct. 13, 2026. AEW 2026 officially opened in Cape Town on Tuesday, with South Africa calling for stronger African energy cooperation to ensure affordable and abundant energy supplies amid global geopolitical tensions and market disruptions. (Photo by Xabiso Mkhabela/Xinhua)
CAPE TOWN, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- African Energy Week (AEW) 2026 officially opened in Cape Town on Tuesday, with South Africa calling for stronger African energy cooperation to ensure affordable and abundant energy supplies amid global geopolitical tensions and market disruptions.
South African Deputy Minister of Mineral and Petroleum Resources Phumzile Mgcina made the call at the opening ceremony, saying the current global situation highlighted the need for a more integrated and resilient African energy system.
"The ongoing conflict in the Middle East has once again demonstrated how developments in one region can have far-reaching consequences for countries and communities thousands of kilometers away," Mgcina said. "This development has contributed to rising fuel prices, rising cost of living."
She said these realities demanded decisive leadership from African leaders to strengthen the energy sectors of individual countries while collectively working toward building a more integrated, resilient and self-reliant African energy system.
"The current geopolitical environment has also underscored the strategic importance of Africa in the global oil and gas market. Our continent possesses substantial petroleum resources," Mgcina said. "This represents an enormous opportunity for strengthening energy security."
She also highlighted the importance of diversifying energy supplies and strengthening trade within the continent, citing South Africa's experience of sourcing petroleum products from different markets amid international supply disruptions.
"Our ability to source petroleum products through diverse markets reinforced the importance of diversifying supply and strengthening intra-Africa trade," Mgcina said.
She said no African country could achieve lasting energy security in isolation, as energy markets, infrastructure and resources were interconnected, making stronger regional cooperation essential.
Mgcina also called for a balanced approach to energy development, noting that many African countries continued to face energy poverty, limited industrial capacity and inadequate infrastructure.
Mgcina's call for greater regional energy cooperation was echoed by Senegalese Minister of Energy and Petroleum El Hadji Abdourahmane Diouf, who stressed the need for African countries to develop interconnected energy systems.
Diouf said Africa needed to shape its own energy development model and ensure that access to energy supported industrial growth and economic transformation. "Africa must be given the opportunity to develop its own energy model," he said.
The minister emphasized Senegal's openness to investment and long-term partnerships across the energy value chain, highlighting the importance of collaboration in advancing Africa's energy ambitions. "Senegal is open to ambitious partnerships across the entire energy value chain," he added.
Held at the Cape Town International Convention Center from Monday to Friday under the theme "Invest in African Energies: Affordable and Abundant Energy Additions," AEW 2026 is expected to attract more than 300 ministers and other senior officials, over 400 industry speakers, more than 10,000 global attendees and 1,500 companies.
First held in 2021, AEW serves as a platform for discussions on energy investment, market access and industrial growth, bringing together stakeholders to shape a shared vision for Africa's energy future. ■

UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Hostilities and displacement in Yemen are exacerbating pressure on civilians, who face food shortages and health risks, UN humanitarians said Tuesday.
"Basic supplies in Taiz City are becoming increasingly scarce and expensive," said the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA). "Petrol prices have tripled and cooking gas is largely unavailable. Food prices have reportedly risen by about 50 percent, and current wheat and flour supplies could run out in less than three weeks."
Fuel shortages are disrupting the city's water supply and putting water services at risk, said OCHA.
The office said that the basic health of families is increasingly at risk with overcrowded displacement sites, inadequate access to clean water and minimal health services.
The World Health Organization warned that suspected cholera cases in Yemen have surged. Of the more than 8,000 cases reported this year, a quarter were reported in the last four weeks. Children face a growing risk from measles, with more than 22,800 suspected cases and 128 deaths reported this year. Vaccination coverage remains critically low.
Meanwhile, the International Organization for Migration reported a sharp increase in the number of migrants arriving in Yemen despite the ongoing conflict. By the end of September, more than 130,000 migrants had entered the country since the start of the year.
OCHA said the United Nations and its humanitarian partners have provided emergency assistance to nearly 148,000 people across Yemen since hostilities began in August.
The office also reiterated the UN's call on all parties to adhere to international humanitarian law, protect civilians and civilian infrastructure, facilitate the safe movement of civilians and allow safe, rapid and unimpeded humanitarian access to people in need. ■

U.S. banks post mixed Q3 results

Unknown Publisher

NEW YORK, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Four of the largest U.S. banks reported mixed third-quarter results on Tuesday, with JPMorgan Chase posting a rare earnings miss while Goldman Sachs delivered a blowout quarter on surging equities trading.
JPMorgan, the largest U.S. bank by assets, reported earnings per share of 5.57 U.S. dollars, missing analysts' expectation of roughly 5.9 dollars. JPMorgan's revenue of about 50.2 billion dollars also fell short of estimates, as fixed-income trading disappointed and the bank took a 658-million-dollar loss on investment securities.
Goldman Sachs, by contrast, posted its second-best quarter ever for revenues at 18.68 billion dollars, nearly 2 billion above estimates, powered by a 72 percent jump in equities trading revenue.
Citigroup beat expectations with earnings per share of 2.85 dollars on revenues of 23.85 billion dollars, its best third quarter in a decade as net income jumped 40 percent.
Wells Fargo's results were more uneven. Its earnings per share narrowly beat estimates at 1.87 dollars, but both revenue and net interest income missed.
"The U.S. economy continued to be fueled by strong business investment and ongoing consumer spending," said JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon. But he also warned that large fiscal deficits, sticky inflation, elevated asset prices, rising interest rates and geopolitical tensions "continue to shift under the surface."
Bank shares reflected the split verdict. Goldman rose about 1 percent and JPMorgan was flat. Meanwhile, Wells Fargo fell more than 2 percent and Citigroup dropped about 4 percent despite its beat.
The broader banking sector has lagged badly recently, with the KBW Nasdaq Bank Index down more than 8 percent over the past three months as investors fretted over rates, AI disruption and geopolitics.
Analysts said the results did little to settle a bruising debate over bank stocks, which suffered their steepest quarterly decline since the 2023 regional banking crisis.
Barclays analyst Jason Goldberg argued the selloff went too far. "In our view, recent stock weakness has been driven more by fear than fundamentals, setting up a solid earnings season to re-anchor investors on underlying performance."
On credit quality, the news was reassuring. JPMorgan said it expects a net charge-off rate of about 3.2 percent in its card business, down from an earlier 3.4 percent forecast.
"The consumer is currently very healthy, primarily because of a healthy labor market," said JPMorgan CFO Jeremy Barnum, though he cautioned that an extended rate cycle would "almost by definition" bring higher unemployment and weaker credit.
Wells Fargo CFO Mike Santomassimo said credit is "really good" across consumer and business clients, with delinquency trends "a little better than we expected."
Bank of America and Morgan Stanley will report third-quarter results on Wednesday. ■

06:45:14 KST

ABUJA, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- The death toll from Lassa fever in Nigeria has risen to 268, with 1,138 confirmed cases reported so far this year, public health authorities said on Monday.
The case fatality rate stood at 23.6 percent between Sept. 21 and Oct. 4, up from 18.6 percent during the same period in 2025, the Nigeria Center for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) said in its latest situation report.
At least one confirmed case had been reported in 119 local government areas across 24 of Nigeria's 36 states so far this year, the NCDC said, adding that people aged 21 to 30 remained the most affected age group during the reporting period.
The hardest-hit states were Edo and Ondo in the south, and Bauchi, Benue and Taraba in the north. Together, they accounted for 88 percent of all confirmed cases in the country, the NCDC said.
The NCDC said poor sanitation, limited awareness in heavily affected communities and delays in seeking treatment continued to worsen the outbreak.
Lassa fever is an acute viral hemorrhagic illness mainly transmitted through food or household items contaminated with rodent urine or feces. Human-to-human transmission can also occur through direct contact with the bodily fluids of infected people. ■

Latest Trump administration proposal to change NIH research grant system draws scientists’ ire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
21:28:42 UTC
06:28:42 KST

The National Institutes of Health is weighing changes to the procedures it uses to allot scientific funding. Experts say the change—concealing scores on applications for grants—could reduce transparency around how federal money is spent on research.
Currently, applications for NIH grants are examined by at least three experts in the applicant’s field of research. That panel of peer reviewers then submits a written review that summarizes the likely outcomes of the proposed research, as well as the application’s strengths and weakness. The reviewers also each give the application a score between 1 and 9, with 1 being the highest. An average of these, called the impact score, is revealed to the applicant.
Under the proposed changes, grant applicants wouldn’t find out their impact score. Instead they would be told whether their application landed in one of three broad buckets: the top 25 percent, or “most competitive,” the next 25 percent, or “competitive,” and the bottom 50 percent, or “not discussed.” The latter category would mean an application did not even warrant extended discussion among the peer reviewers.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The proposal is designed to communicate “valuable information about the assessed scientific merit” and give program officers more flexibility on making awards, according to an NIH document outlining the rule change.
“Discussed applications would still receive a resume of discussion and all applications would still receive written critiques from the assigned reviewers, to include individual criterion/factor scores,” the document states. But some scientists and research organizations have criticized the change as potentially reducing transparency and accountability.
Joshua Weitz, a biology professor at the University of Maryland, said in a Substack post that the proposal could have disastrous results for the scientific community and lead to less transparency for both applicants and the NIH program officers charged with managing grant portfolios. Under the new system, he argued, an application that scored in the top 1 percent may be treated the same as one that scored lower but still within the top 25 percent.
“By concealing scores, the NIH proposal would make it harder for program officers to assess consensus, lead to greater uncertainty for applicants and undermine scientific peer review," Weitz tells Scientific American.
The proposal marks the latest way the Trump administration has tried to flex its muscles over scientific grants. Floated earlier this year, a separate bid to have political appointees, rather than peer review panels, decide grant recipients garnered significant backlash—and was put on hold until at least December after Congress rejected the change. “The NIH proposal should be interpreted in this broader context,” Weitz says.
“By reducing transparency and concealing quantitative feedback from experts serving on scientific review groups, the NIH proposal makes it harder for applicants and the public to understand the basis for grant award recommendations,” he adds. “In the absence of transparent data sharing, there is an increased risk that political priorities override scientific review in grant decisions.”
The proposal’s public comment period opened in August and ends today. Other comments on the proposal from research groups echo Weitz’s caution.
In a statement, the North American Vascular Biology Organization, which submitted a comment to the NIH, wrote that the proposed grant review system might “become significantly less transparent” and “will compromise accountability, and breed uncertainty, inefficiency, and distrust. It is also likely that the dearth of data regarding grant reviews will compromise the ability of Congress to exercise oversight and the agency’s own ability to assess and improve its funding choices.”
Meanwhile, Global Health Technologies Coalition (GHTC) wrote in a submitted comment that while it supports the NIH’s stated goal of ensuring funding decisions reflect the peer review process, any changes must “provide researchers with sufficient information to understand the scientific strengths and weaknesses” identified during peer review.
“Researchers and institutions have experienced significant changes to NIH funding policies, priorities, and grantmaking practices over the past year,” GHTC wrote. “Additional reforms should be implemented in a measured and thoughtful manner and clearly communicated to stakeholders to minimize unnecessary disruption to the research ecosystem.”
The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees the NIH, did not immediately return a request for comment.
