'Unapologetic Zionism' and the end of Israel's democracy myth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
18:38:35 UTC
03:38:35 KST

Breadcrumb
'Unapologetic Zionism' and the end of Israel's democracy myth
A Muslim woman on a Tel Aviv beach, a hijab in a crowded street, “Arabs and Jews” sharing public spaces. It is precisely this imagery of everyday coexistence that Israelis often invoke to rebut accusations of apartheid. Yet the country's electoral politics tell a more complicated story.
On 23 September, Israel's Central Elections Committee voted to disqualify Ra'am and the Joint List, seeking to exclude the principal vehicles of Israel’s Palestinian parliamentary representation from the upcoming end-of-October election. The petitions invoked provisions intended to protect Israel's Jewish and democratic character, including prohibitions on supporting armed struggle.
Furthermore, the Balad Party leader, Sami Abu Shehadeh, was banned from the upcoming Knesset elections.
The same elections committee that had issued all these decisions also rejected attempts to disqualify far-right Jewish parties, including Itamar Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit.
Although the Supreme Court overturned the decision, as it has repeatedly done over the past two decades, the irony remains hard to miss.
In 2021, against Arab consensus, Ra'am helped sustain an Israeli governing coalition, breaking a longstanding convention that kept independent Arab parties out of government. Yet five years later, the same party and its controversial leader, Mansour Abbas, found themselves fighting for the right to contest an election.
Exclusion
Today, as Israel swiftly shifts rightward, the boundaries of such participation are narrowing, bringing into sharper focus patterns of exclusion rooted in the state's earliest years, and potentially signalling a reversal in their political status.
Palestinians who remained after the 1948 Nakba, roughly 150,000, were incorporated into the electoral system while much of their population lived under military rule until 1966. They could vote for a parliament whose government restricted their movement, expropriated their land and treated them as a security and demographic threat.
The state wasn’t required to abandon the distinction between individual citizenship and nationality, which was reserved for Jews.
Therefore, Palestinian participation didn’t come with an equal claim to defining what Israel was, or the power to meaningfully improve their status. Nor did Palestinians have the right to return to the villages from which they had been expelled, while a Jew from Warsaw or Brooklyn could immigrate to Israel, acquire citizenship and enjoy preferential access to land and settlement opportunities.
Even in ethnic terms, they were reduced to merely “Arabs”, a generic label devoid of a distinct Palestinian identity, rendering them naturalised citizens in their own land. And simultaneously, or rather ironically, they were cast as an extension of the Arab World, while being severed from the wider cultural and linguistic environment to which they belonged.
Vote but not have a say
For decades, to maintain the state’s democratic image, the system managed this tension through legal restrictions, political bargaining, and institutional accommodation. It worked as long as institutions could absorb political challenges without fundamentally altering Jewish national primacy, while keeping the lid on the underlying conflict. This was, in effect, the achievement of what might be called suits-and-ties Zionism, largely associated with the Labour Party.
The occupation of the West Bank and Gaza in 1967 altered that environment profoundly. Territory that had occupied a central place in religious-nationalist imagination was now under Israeli control.
The impact on Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza was immediate, through military occupation and land seizures, whilst for Palestinian-Israelis the implications continued to be obscured by the longstanding arrangement that allowed them to “vote but not have a say”. A form of forced social bribe, so to speak.
Nevertheless, Israel has always had the power to withdraw the apparent “privilege” at its discretion. Over the past two decades, exclusionary politics have gradually gained freer rein. What has emerged, especially, is a more “unapologetic Zionism”. The religious-nationalist movements have moved from pressuring governments to exercising authority within them.
For Palestinian-Israelis, this convergence brought together ideological entitlement and the instruments of state power. What religious nationalism advanced as a matter of principle could brazenly be pursued through legislation, backed by the secular language of security and demography. This alignment found expression in electoral campaigns, such as “No loyalty, no citizenship” by the right-wing party Yisrael Beitenu in 2009, or a clip released on election day in 2015, in which Netanyahu warned that “the right-wing government is in danger. Arab voters are heading to the polling stations in droves.”
Protecting the Jewish state
Importantly, these campaigns coincided with, and were followed by, a growing body of discriminatory Israeli legislation, most notably the 2018 Nation-State Law, which reserved national self-determination exclusively for Jews and elevated Jewish settlement to a national value.
When the Arab party Balad submitted a proposed Basic Law entitled A Country of All Its Citizens, challenging the constitutional principle underlying the then-proposed Law, the Knesset Presidium refused to allow it to proceed to parliamentary debate. Supreme Court President Esther Hayut subsequently characterised Balad’s submission as crossing a red line, on the grounds that it negated Israel’s existence as a Jewish state.
Yet the significance of these proposals cannot be measured solely by their legislative success. From the perspective of “discursive institutionalism” and the political psychology of intergroup dynamics, political discourse both reflects and shapes collective attitudes.
Even unsuccessful bills, of which the Knesset has seen many, can signal a growing tolerance for exclusion, weakening social restraints on discriminatory behaviour and making previously contentious measures more politically conceivable. In this sense, the parliamentary arena becomes not merely a site of law-making, but a mechanism for renegotiating intergroup relations.
Such attitudes long predate the war in Gaza, although recent polling suggests they have intensified. A 2014–15 Pew Research Center survey found that 48% of Jewish Israelis supported expelling or “transferring Arabs from Israel”. Meanwhile, the 2025 Israeli Democracy Index found that support for government measures encouraging Arab citizens to emigrate had risen from 36% in 2019 to 53% in 2025. Only 16% of Jewish respondents believed Palestinian national identity was compatible with loyalty to Israel.
The irony is that Palestinian citizens have spent decades seeking to expand their influence within Israeli democracy, while movements determined to restrict that influence have gained power through the same institutions.
This contradiction has sharpened a longstanding Palestinian debate: whether electoral participation offers a way to change the system from within or merely legitimises its inequalities.
Mansour Abbas's entry into the governing coalition in 2021 tested the former proposition and yielded very few results. And today’s attempt to disqualify the principal Arab electoral lists, albeit overturned by the judiciary, marks a further step backwards.
Apartheid does not necessarily require the disappearance of democratic institutions; it can coexist with elections, courts and parliamentary representation when those institutions operate within an entrenched hierarchy of collective rights.
What Israel effectively operates on is a normalised two-tier conception of democracy. It is where political equality is recognised at the level of individual suffrage, however contested in practice, while remaining constrained by the institutional privileging of one national group over another, a principle treated as fixed and non-negotiable.
The legal significance, let alone the everyday implications for Palestinian-Israelis, lies not in individual instances of discrimination, but in whether they form part of an institutionalised system of domination, within which further exclusion can be pursued without fundamentally altering the existing political order. In other words, this version of ethno-democracy becomes the means of administering and perpetuating that hierarchy rather than a mechanism for overcoming it.
The late-October election may reveal just how far that transformation has gone, although the growing vulnerability of Palestinian-Israelis is already more apparent than ever.
Dr Emad Moussa is a Palestinian-British researcher and writer specialising in the political psychology of intergroup and conflict dynamics, focusing on MENA with a special interest in Israel/Palestine. He has a background in human rights and journalism, and is currently a frequent contributor to multiple academic and media outlets, in addition to being a consultant for a US-based think tank.
Follow him on Twitter: @emadmoussa

Pope Leo XIV undergoes successful lung surgery, Vatican says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
18:36:00 UTC
03:36:00 KST

Pope Leo XIV, 71, has been diagnosed with lung cancer after undergoing surgery in Rome on Tuesday, with doctors confirming that the lower lobe of his right lung was removed following the discovery of a malignant tumor.
The 71-year-old Leo returned to his room after the surgery at Rome’s Gemelli hospital, according to a statement from the Vatican spokesman, who promised further information at a later time. He had a scheduled operation to remove a nodule from his lung on Tuesday, which the Vatican said had gone smoothly.
Subsequent examination confirmed that the nodule was an adenocarcinoma, a form of lung cancer, the Gemelli medical team said.
The pope had announced his planned surgery on Sunday, saying the nodule had been detected during checks at a "very early stage" and was "well localized."
Leo had walked into Rome's Gemelli hospital through the main entrance earlier in the day and waved to dozens of well-wishers who had gathered to greet him. The Vatican said the surgery would be performed by a team led by Gemelli’s chief thoracic surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora.
The operation got under way as medical staff recited the Rosary prayer in the hospital chapel Tuesday evening. "Let us join together in prayer, asking the Lord to sustain our bishop, Pope Leo, and to comfort all those who are hospitalized here,” said the Vicar of Rome, Cardinal Baldassare Reina, at the start of the prayer.
The American pontiff has offered a rare level of transparency about the first publicly disclosed major health problem of his 17-month papacy. He revealed the discovery of the small, localized nodule during his Sunday noon prayer and announced that he would have it removed.
Oncologists say even if the nodule turns out to be cancerous, Leo’s prognosis is "excellent” since it will have been removed at an early stage.
The surgery, which is usually performed under general anesthesia, will require a weeklong hospital stay and the Vatican on Monday canceled all Leo’s audiences through Oct. 20.
"These are things that can be treated very well, if the words he used reflect the clinical situation,” said Dr. Lorenzo Spaggiari, director of thoracic surgery at the European Institute of Oncology, or EIO, in Milan, who is not involved in the pope’s care but knows the team at Gemelli.
But the decision clearly came as a surprise: While Gemelli has a specific papal apartment that past popes have used, complete with a private chapel on the 10th floor, Leo will actually be staying in a nearby room since the papal apartment is currently undergoing renovations, according to the Vatican press office.
Spaggiari said he expected the team at Gemelli would perform a biopsy to determine whether Leo has lung cancer followed by the removal of a section or lobe of the lung where the nodule is located.
Both could be done using robotic techniques, and could be performed consecutively, under the same anesthesia, with different specialist teams, Spaggiari said.
A sophisticated robotic bronchoscopy technology called ION allows a biopsy on nodules as small as 3 millimeters (1/10 inch), Spaggiari said. Both the Gemelli and the EIO have the technology, which has been available in Italy for just two years.
Gemelli also has robotic surgical technology, allowing the operation to remove the nodule to proceed "using a minimally invasive technique,” he said.
The technique involves the surgeon making four small incisions in the chest through which the instruments of the so-called da Vinci robot are inserted, he said. The surgeon then controls the robotic arms looking at a screen providing high-definition, 3D views of the surgical site.
"It’s a very well-established technology. This is something we have been doing for 20 years,” he said.
It wasn't known for certain what technique would be used on Leo. Gemelli has documented using both robotic procedures to diagnose and operate in under four hours.
The biopsy risk is "virtually zero,” while the surgical risk is very small, carrying a 0.6% to 0.8% mortality rate for patients in otherwise good health with good heart and lung function, Spaggiari said.
During the surgery, doctors would also remove lymph nodes that drain the segment or lobe. "If all those lymph nodes turn out to be negative, so stage one, then the outlook is very good,” he said, adding that no other treatment would be necessary.
The nodule was discovered during regular checks, the Vatican has said.
"I think he has had a bit of luck. They found something that was asymptomatic - a lung nodule, possibly a tumor. He might call it something else; we call it luck,” he said.
EIO advises patients not to fly for three weeks after surgery - which would give the pope just the interval needed to make his planned Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, depending on his recovery. The current itinerary for the trip is ambitious and the longest of his papacy to date, calling for Leo to clock just over 31,000 kilometers (19,000 miles) on a dozen flights and two helicopter rides, and a significant altitude change in Peru.
"He has decided to undergo surgery soon in order to not change his plans for future overseas trips, so there is no need to worry, as it is not an emergency,” said Tokyo Cardinal Kikuchi Tsutomu, who saw Leo on Monday.
A lung nodule is a small abnormal area measuring less than 3 centimeters (1.2 inches) that sometimes appears on a CT scan of the chest or abdomen. Often, the scans are done to investigate trauma or a lung infection, unrelated to a lung cancer screening. A nodule can be benign or malignant, and oftentimes surgical removal is recommended both to establish whether it is cancer and to treat a malignancy while it is still localized.
This is believed to be the second hospitalization for Leo, who is known to be sporty and in good shape, with weekly tennis games and swimming.
As a young missionary priest, he came down with typhoid fever in 1985, soon after arriving in Chulucanas, Peru. The illness and hospitalization were a cathartic moment for him to decide to stay in the poverty and discomfort of Peru after living in relative comfort in Rome - a decision that ultimately paved the way to his papacy, according to an interview Leo gave to Elise Ann Allen in 2025 for "Pope Leo XIV: The Biography.”
According to the book, Leo said he prayed to God to let him die rather than suffer the "horrible” pain of the fever. "I was hooked up to an IV, and I said, ‘If this is your sense of humor, Lord, I think you could do a little better.’
"Obviously, I survived; I recovered, but it turned out to be a very significant moment for me, because it was like, ’Well, you’ve already dealt with the illness; you already see what the needs are here - the order, the Augustinians, the church are telling you, ‘We need you here; go for it.’ I never looked back.”
___
Barry reported from Milan.

Drones and Missiles Are Rewriting the Military Balance on the Korean Peninsula
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
18:35:00 UTC
03:35:00 KST

The two Koreas have been close observers of the wars in Ukraine and Iran – not least because aspects of the conflicts mirror how both sides think they will win a potential war on the peninsula. The ongoing exchange of long-range drones and missiles, in particular, resembles the type of war both Koreas envision for themselves: a deep strike contest. To this end, both have recently begun developing low-cost, long-range attack drones, with some systems slated to be operational in the near term.
Long-range artillery, ballistic missiles, and nuclear weapons have, so far, shaped each side’s view of the military balance and whether deterrence holds on the peninsula. Armed drones will soon enter the picture.
These drones will exacerbate the South Korean military’s existing gaps in surveilling the North. Pyongyang’s growing missile and nuclear arsenal and diversified launch platforms have made the problem acute. With cheap attack drones, North Korea’s ability to disperse, conceal, and employ offensive firepower will further outpace South Korea’s capacity to destroy it.
This trend is at odds with the Lee administration’s ambitious timeline for gaining wartime operational control from the United States. South Korean forces will need additional capabilities to meet the qualitative conditions previously established by the two allies.
Drones on the Korean Peninsula
Long-range drones – unarmed aerial vehicles with operational range far beyond the forward edge of battle along the armistice line – have been a feature of the inter-Korean military competition for the past two decades. The first known operational use was in 2010 when a North Korean reconnaissance drone was spotted during the Yonpyeong Island shelling. Since then, periodic drone incursions have been a feature of the inter-Korean low-intensity skirmishes.
In 2014, South Korea recovered the wreckage of three North Korean drones less than 50 miles from the border. In December 2022, five North Korean drones overflew Seoul, including the presidential office, and returned North. In response, then-President Yoon Suk-yeol floated the idea of South Korean forces conducting reciprocal drone incursions into North Korea. North Korea claimed South Korean drones overflew Pyongyang in October 2024. While officially denied, public analysis of North Korean-released images visually matched developmental South Korean reconnaissance systems.
Rudimentary platforms – small, fixed-wing, turboprop, and unarmed – have featured in these largely symbolic aerial incursions so far, alongside unpowered balloons. There is no evidence that either side has employed armed drones in cross-border operations. Drones that had been operationally used on the peninsula, however, represent only a small subset of a broader inventory that includes systems with greater range and capability.
North Korea has been importing Chinese and Soviet drones and has been developing indigenous models for reconnaissance missions since the 1980s. In 2023, North Korea unveiled a high-altitude, long-endurance (HALE) reconnaissance drone and a medium-altitude, long-endurance (MALE) multi-role drone. Both are qualitatively different from its existing unmanned aircraft – the latter, for example, is capable of firing a missile – though limited numbers are in the inventory.
For South Korea, abortive development efforts in the late Cold War resumed in the 1990s with a focus on the tactical surveillance drones supporting the Army’s ground operations. Interest in long-range systems came in the late 2000s when the Agency for Defense Development (ADD) started developing a domestic MALE, KUS-FS, and the Republic of Korea Air Force procured Global Hawks from the United States. Four Global Hawks were delivered by 2020, and the KUS-FS is expected to enter service in 2027.
The wars in Ukraine and Iran have catalyzed the two Koreas’ interest in massed, cheap, and armed long-range drones while they continue to invest in large, sophisticated unmanned systems. In 2024, Kim Jong Un ordered officials to “establish a mass-production system and begin full-scale operation” of “suicide attack drones.” Thousands of North Korean laborers, and possibly engineers, have also reportedly been sent to the Yelabuga factory in Russia producing copies of Iran’s Shahed one-way attack (OWA) drone.
For South Korea, the ADD is developing the KUS-LM – dubbed the “K-LUCAS” with reported range and payload figures comparable to the American OWA drone called LUCAS – with plans to deploy it before 2030. The system has started trials on land and sea.
Theories of Victory
These investments by both Koreas in long-range unmanned systems, for both strike and surveillance, will alter the terms of the inter-Korean military competition. In the past few decades, the main domain of the inter-Korean military competition has become a deep strike-centric contest. The ability to wage a strategic air campaign – one not directly connected to the ground fight – is now central to how each side assesses the balance. Both sides appear to believe loitering munitions fit into this air power paradigm.
North Korea has pursued missile and nuclear weapons technology to hold at risk its neighbor and its ally, the United States, with long-range fires. South Korea’s Ministry of National Defense assessed that, in a contingency, North Korea plans a surprise massive firepower attack to create favorable conditions and force a rapid end to the war. Even absent an offensive intent, the threat of catastrophic damage from nuclear missiles and conventional munitions that bypass defenses creates a powerful deterrent intended to prevent attack and ensure regime survival.
Under Kim Jong Un’s rule, North Korea has expanded its missile force to deliver both conventional and nuclear warheads deep into South Korea and, increasingly, beyond the peninsula. The nuclear arsenal, too, has increased both numerically and in centrality to North Korea’s security policy. The KPA Ground Force also operates thousands of artillery pieces – with sufficient range to reach Seoul – out of hardened sites concentrated south of the Pyongyang-Wonsan line.
North Korea appears to see drones as a complementary element of its deep strike strategy, enabled by mass, concealment, and dispersal. Indeed, Kim Jong Un noted three attributes that make OWA drones a needed investment for the Korean People’s Army: low production cost, simple manufacturing process, and ease of integration into existing firepower. Drone salvos launched in conjunction with ballistic and cruise missiles could overwhelm South Korea’s air and missile defenses. Their relatively low cost also reduces the economic burden of procurement on North Korea’s constrained economy.
In response to a nuclear-armed adversary and fear of abandonment from its ally, South Korea has pursued a counterforce “Three Axis system” to serve as a non-nuclear deterrent. This idea has seen iterative conceptual updates over the past decade. Today, the approach rests on a three-pronged framework that combines preemptive strikes on North Korean nuclear and missile facilities (“Kill Chain”), multi-layered missile defense (Air Force-operated “Korea Air and Missile Defense” against ballistic missiles and the Army’s in-development “Low-Altitude Missile Defense” against artillery and short-range rockets), and overwhelming retaliatory firepower against military and leadership targets (“Korea Massive Punishment and Retaliation”).
Efforts in the past five years have sought to integrate drones into the strategy. The Yoon administration established the Drone Operations Command in September 2023 with an explicit mission to develop an offensive concept of operations – before that, South Korea’s military had only used drones for reconnaissance and surveillance. Despite initial criticism of the command as redundant, and its subsequent disestablishment for its implication in Yoon’s 2024 self-coup attempt, the South Korean defense community appears to acknowledge the need for this function. The mission continues in the Defense Drone headquarters, the recently formed successor body that focuses on force development, manning, and equipping – albeit shedding any operational role to the services.
South Korea’s Surveillance Problems
Deterrence on the peninsula holds today as both sides possess long-range strike assets that impose what, for now, are unacceptable risks and costs if the shooting starts. While ground forces remain important in both Koreas’ force structures, the main arena of the inter-Korean competition today lies in deep strike. The drone incursions in the past decade and a half introduced an additional low-intensity element to this competition. The development and eventual deployment of armed drones will create new requirements for South Korea to operationalize its Three Axis strategy and for the United States to defend its treaty ally.
South Korea’s limited intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) capacity stands out as a glaring vulnerability in anticipating this future. All three “axes” of its strategy depend on a near-perfect and near-persistent intelligence picture over North Korea, to monitor leadership movements, locate concealed facilities, track mobile missile launchers and submarines, identify incoming missiles – and now, detect drone launch sites and their launches. This is a tall order. South Korea’s ISR capabilities have long been identified as a weakness, as it historically has relied on U.S. capabilities.
ISR drones and additional ISR satellites are intended to supplement existing gaps to operationalize the Three Axis strategy, but even with systems expected to come online in the next five years, mobile targets will remain difficult to find, fix, and track. South Korea’s space-based ISR layer, in development since 2023, leaves roughly 2-hour windows between observation opportunities over potential launch sites. The South Korean Army’s Low Altitude Missile Defense, expected to come online in 2029, was designed to counter artillery threats and may be constrained by insufficient interceptors and sensor networks against drone salvos.
Thus, in the near to medium term, North Korea’s ability to disperse, conceal, and employ its drones, missiles, and nuclear weapons will outpace South Korea’s capacity to destroy them. In fact, North Korea’s rapid operationalization of OWA drones may require greater dedication of U.S. ISR assets to the peninsula.
The added challenge to South Korea’s defense strategy thus poses questions about the Lee administration’s ambitious push for wartime operational control transfer by the end of his term in 2030. The proposed change to the command structure of U.S. and South Korean forces has been tied to improvements in South Korea’s capabilities to lead the Combined Forces Command, including the capacity to operate its own ISR assets to meet operational requirements. The Lee administration has insisted on “no additional conditions” being placed on the transfer requirements. Yet, the deteriorating military balance in this domain will necessitate additional capability to meet the established qualitative conditions for making major changes to the Combined Force.

Airport attacks put aviation in crosshairs of geopolitical conflicts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
18:33:42 UTC
03:33:42 KST

Deadly attacks on Saudi Arabia's second-busiest airport over the past week are highlighting how conflicts in the Middle East are upending air travel on a larger scale.
Aviation is increasingly in the middle of these sprawling clashes as threats and outright attacks have forced airlines to quickly cancel flights throughout the Middle East for days, weeks and, in some cases, months. Some carriers might redeploy planes that would be going to some Middle East destinations like Dubai, United Arab Emirates, and Doha, Qatar, to other locations altogether.
"It's a new paradigm. Civil aviation is being directly targeted and it has not been the case in the last couple of decades," said Mark Zee, founder of OpsGroup, an independent aviation safety group whose members include pilots, dispatchers, airline employees and others.
The Saudi airport attacks, claimed by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis, were the deadliest in the country in more than a decade. Over the weekend, at least 13 people were killed and more than 300 injured when a projectile hit terminals at King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh, officials said. Other attacks have included drones.
"Historically, airport security is focused on preventing unauthorized access to aircraft and the airport, not defending airspace," said Jeff Price, a professor at the Metropolitan State University of Denver's Department of Aviation and Aerospace Science and an airport management consultant.
The threats to aviation are forcing officials to rethink how to protect blind spots in these major public spaces.
"There is this established way to deal with kind of more conventional weapons such as missiles. It's very expensive, but there is a way," said Gulnaz Ukassova, UAE-based security director of information and analysis at risk management firm International SOS. "There is still no sort of foolproof way to deal with the threat posed by drones. The technology, obviously, is constantly evolving."
King Khalid International Airport has been shut down for much of this week, and some carriers suspended operations there, citing safety concerns. CEOs of major oil companies also pulled out of an energy conference in the country.
Delta Air Lines, meanwhile, was less than two weeks away from launching an Atlanta-Riyadh route, the first nonstop commercial flight between the the two countries operated by a U.S. airline, according to the carrier.
But late Sunday, the Federal Aviation Administration warned U.S. carriers about safety-of-flight risks when flying in or over Saudi Arabia. On Monday morning, Delta said it would postpone the route's debut until March.
The new Delta route comes as Saudi leadership seeks to boost tourism to the country, part of the kingdom's Vision 2030 plan to diversify the economy from oil and attract international investment.
Air traffic in Saudi Arabia had been increasing rapidly. Scheduled growth in airplane seats in the market is up more than 23% this year from 2023, though the rise has recently slowed, according to aviation-data firm Cirium.
Whether travelers come back to the region depends on risk appetite. Ukassova said energy companies, which can depend on in-person visits to large projects, tend to have higher risk tolerance, while academics have a low bar for potential risks.
Longer routes, cut flights
The conflicts have cut off big parts of airspace in the Middle East, mainly over Iran. The outbreak of the Iran war in February set off massive aviation, travel and safety crises.
For example, Australian carrier Qantas has changed its Perth, Australia-to-London route to avoid Iranian airspace. Because that flight is then longer, the carrier has added a stop in Singapore to refuel.
For four years, Western commercial passenger and cargo planes have already had to fly longer routes to avoid Russian airspace. Carriers started detouring away from Russia after its 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
Taking longer routes to avoid potentially dangerous airspace has been adding to airlines' fuel bills, which got even more expensive this year due to those same Middle East conflicts.
While much of the traffic to Dubai and Doha has rebounded from the first days of the war since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28, it remains below 2025 levels, according to flight-data firm OAG. Capacity by seats across the Middle East is down 5.7% in October from last year, 2.2 million fewer seats, OAG reported.
Some airlines are opting to stay away from the region altogether.
"We will not fly to Dubai and Doha, and we need to wait until the situation gets settled," Finnair CEO Turkka Kuusisto told reporters last month in New York.

Pope Leo's lung nodule surgery was completed successfully, Vatican says
Update: The Vatican said Pope Leo was diagnosed with lung cancer during the surgery. Read the latest here. Our earlier coverage is below.
Pope Leo XIV underwent a successful surgery Tuesday to remove a lung nodule, according to the Vatican.
"The procedure was completed successfully, within the expected timeframe and as planned, and the Holy Father has returned to his room," the Holy See Press Office said. The office promised further information at a later time.
The 71-year-old Leo had walked into Rome's Gemelli hospital through the main entrance earlier Tuesday and waved to dozens of well-wishers who had gathered to greet him. The Vatican said the surgery would be performed by a team led by Gemelli's chief thoracic surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora.
The operation got underway as medical staff recited the Rosary prayer in the hospital chapel Tuesday evening. "Let us join together in prayer, asking the Lord to sustain our bishop, Pope Leo, and to comfort all those who are hospitalized here," said the Vicar of Rome, Cardinal Baldassare Reina, at the start of the prayer.
The American pontiff has offered a rare level of transparency about the first publicly disclosed major health problem of his 17-month papacy. He revealed the discovery of the small, localized nodule during his Sunday noon prayer and announced that he would have it removed.
The nodule was discovered during regular checks, the Vatican has said. It is not known if it is cancerous. In most cases, this kind of lung nodule is benign, doctors say.
Oncologists say even if the nodule turns out to be cancerous, Leo's prognosis is "excellent" since it will have been removed at an early stage.
The surgery, which is fairly low risk and usually performed under general anesthesia, will require a weeklong recovery at the hospital, the Vatican said. All Leo's audiences through Oct. 20 were canceled.
"These are things that can be treated very well, if the words he used reflect the clinical situation," said Dr. Lorenzo Spaggiari, director of thoracic surgery at the European Institute of Oncology, or EIO, in Milan, who is not involved in the pope's care but knows the team at Gemelli.
The procedure comes just weeks before Leo is scheduled to take a trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru at the beginning of November. Doctors typically suggest about three weeks to recover without any flying, giving Leo just the interval needed before the trip.
The current itinerary for the trip is ambitious and the longest of his papacy to date, calling for Leo to clock just over 19,000 miles on a dozen flights and two helicopter rides, and a significant altitude change in Peru.
"He has decided to undergo surgery soon in order to not change his plans for future overseas trips, so there is no need to worry, as it is not an emergency," said Tokyo Cardinal Kikuchi Tsutomu, who saw Leo on Monday.
A lung nodule is a small abnormal area measuring less than 1.2 inches that sometimes appears on a CT scan of the chest or abdomen. Often, the scans are done to investigate trauma or a lung infection, unrelated to a lung cancer screening. A nodule can be benign or malignant, and often surgical removal is recommended both to establish whether it is cancer and to treat a malignancy while it is still localized.

French lawmakers unanimously back bill to protect sexual violence victims

Unknown Publisher

18:23:17 UTC
03:23:17 KST

Şeyma Erkul Dayanç
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
France’s National Assembly on Tuesday unanimously approved a bill to strengthen protection for victims of sexual and gender-based violence.
The bill passed its first reading in a 503 – 0 vote, following six days of debate. It will now go to the Senate and is not yet in force.
The legislation would require investigators to interview victims and suspects, preserve evidence and look for other potential victims within one year.
It also provides for specialized police units and courts dealing with sexual and domestic violence.
Victims would be entitled to 10 days of leave to attend medical appointments or take legal steps.
The bill would require schools to hold regular interviews with students to help identify violence, with full implementation planned by 2032.
Other measures include expanded incest-related offenses, medical care for child victims and stronger consent requirements for invasive medical procedures.
The bill would also strengthen penalties for sharing sexual content without consent and sending unsolicited sexual images.
Lawmakers rejected several provisions intended to protect foreign victims, including a ban on issuing deportation orders against sexual violence victims who have filed complaints.
The reform gained momentum after the death of an 11-year-old girl, Lyhanna, who was found dead after being raped in southwestern France in June.
The suspect had previously faced several complaints alleging sexual violence against minors.
The government has pledged to assess the cost of the measures and present a budget plan after the Senate examines the bill.

US Supreme Court agrees to hear watchdog case on Elon Musk’s DOGE records

US Supreme Court agrees to hear watchdog case on Elon Musk’s DOGE records
The Trump administration argues that DOGE is exempt from freedom of information requirements.
The United States Supreme Court has agreed to hear arguments in a watchdog’s lawsuit seeking public records about trillionaire Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE).
The high court is intervening on Tuesday for a second time in Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics (CREW) in Washington’s case, which seeks access to DOGE records from its operations in the early days of US President Donald Trump’s second term. The Trump administration asked the court to hear the case.
Last year, the high court reined in a district court’s order for the government to produce DOGE-related records to CREW. The high court’s conservative majority concluded in June 2025 that US District Judge Christopher Cooper ruled too broadly in ordering documents to be turned over to the group.
CREW claims DOGE is a federal agency and therefore is subject to the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA).
The Trump administration argues that DOGE is exempt from FOIA’s requirements as a presidential advisory body.
Cooper ruled in CREW’s favour and ordered expedited processing of the group’s records request. An appeals court panel also sided with CREW.
The Trump administration claims the panel ignored the Supreme Court’s direction to consider separation-of-powers concerns and intruded on the “autonomy and confidentiality” of presidential advisers.
“Subjecting advisory bodies to intrusive discovery triggers the very concerns that Congress sought to avoid by excluding presidential advisory bodies from FOIA’s reach,” US Department of Justice lawyers wrote.
The administration also says the appeals court impermissibly authorised the plaintiffs to take a sworn deposition of DOGE acting administrator Amy Gleason.
CREW says the appeals court fully complied with the Supreme Court’s previous order. The group also asserts that the public has a right to know how DOGE helped the administration carry out a sweeping overhaul of government operations in 2025.
“Undisputed facts in the public record — including the President’s statements — confirmed that (DOGE) was wielding enormous independent authority across the federal government,” CREW lawyers wrote.
In a statement Tuesday, CREW lawyer Nikhel Sus said the lower courts have uniformly ruled that it is entitled to records that could help the court determine whether DOGE wields the type of authority that would make it subject to the Freedom of Information Act.
“We will continue to pursue transparency for the American people, who deserve to know the details of the Trump Administration’s efforts to unilaterally remake the federal government,” Sus said in the statement.
DOGE said it had slashed tens of billions of dollars in expenditures, but its claims were difficult for outside financial experts to verify.
Federal auditors found that some of DOGE’s reported savings across contract, grant and lease terminations were incorrect, lacked supporting evidence or included terminations that were already under way when DOGE was established, according to a report by the Government Accountability Office.

Give Riyadh a mirror

Give Riyadh a mirror
TEHRAN - In an article published on Monday, the editor-in-chief of the Saudi daily Asharq Al-Awsat used the Ansarullah strike on Riyadh airport as a pretext to level a series of sweeping — and at times bizarre — accusations.
The strangest claim comes where he writes of the attack: “Rarely in the history of warfare has a civilian airport crowded with passengers been the target of an attack.” One has to ask: Is Mr. Charbel suffering from memory loss, or is he deliberately seeking to conceal and distort the facts?
It would be possible to compile an extremely long list of Saudi airstrikes on civilian targets in Yemen since Riyadh launched its invasion of its southern neighbor in 2015. Even mourning ceremonies and wedding celebrations of the oppressed people of Yemen were not spared from bombardment, time and again turned into bloodbaths — in some cases with up to 150 victims killed in a single strike.
Let us examine just one case in greater detail. At midday on August 9, 2018, a bus full of schoolchildren stopped at the local market in Dahyan, in Saada province. The students were returning from a picnic — likely experiencing the happiest day of their lives.
Your country’s fighter jets had been circling in the sky above the area for nearly an hour. They were armed with MK-82 laser-guided bombs — bombs you had purchased from the United States just a year earlier. The missiles were fired, and moments later, the happiest day in the lives of 40 children became the last day of their lives. Most of them were under the age of 10.
Have you ever considered that almost everything about the war you unleashed on Yemen bears a striking resemblance to America’s wars? You named your operation “Decisive Storm”; America had “Desert Storm” on its record. The war launched in partnership with Israel against Iran was dubbed “Epic Fury.” You struck Yemeni civilians again and again — and America has never fought a war without repeated attacks on civilian targets. Does the chilling parallel between the Dahyan atrocity and the Minab school not give you pause? And there is one final, telling similarity: Riyadh, too, tried to manufacture a veneer of legitimacy for its aggression by assembling a nominal coalition — precisely what Washington does in most of its military adventures.
Have you ever asked yourselves why, despite possessing such modern and advanced weaponry, you have been unable to defeat Ansarullah? Your problem from the very beginning was that you never properly understood Yemen and its faithful, resilient people. You branded them an “Iranian proxy” — and you continue to do so. Strangely, you insist on denying the reality that Yemenis are independent, and that on matters of both war and peace, they decide for themselves. Until you accept that reality, you will never escape this self-made quagmire, and no mediator will be able to help you.
We, as Iranians — your Muslim brothers and your neighbors — want you to stand with dignity. We take no pleasure in seeing America treat you as a “cash cow,” plundering your wealth through colossal arms and security contracts. How can an America incapable of protecting its own bases and troops in the region possibly protect you and bring you security? Do you remember what Trump said in 2018? He declared openly that without us, Saudi Arabia would not survive two weeks. A year later, he boasted that with a single phone call, he took 500 million dollars from them.
In today’s world, money may solve many problems, but it certainly does not buy authority or respect. You have surely not forgotten what Trump said about your Crown Prince at the summit hosted by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF) in Miami this March, before some 1,500 prominent businessmen and investors: “He didn’t think he would be kissing my ass. He really didn’t. He thought it’d be just another American president that was a loser where the country was going downhill. But now he has to be nice to me. You tell him he’d better be nice to me.”
Have you ever wondered why Trump feels entitled to insult your leaders so brazenly?
Whatever the solution to Saudi Arabia’s problems today may be, it does not lie in Washington or Tel Aviv. They harbor a civilizational and existential hostility toward Muslims — a hostility that will not be resolved with bribes worth hundreds of billions.
And finally, I suggest that when you suffer a painful retaliatory blow on the battlefield in Yemen, instead of pointing the finger of blame at others, you take a good look in the mirror first.

Yemen’s leader vows to continue military operation until Houthi coup ends, state institutions restored
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
18:11:09 UTC
03:11:09 KST

The military operation against the Houthis will continue until their coup is ended and state institutions are restored, said the head of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council on Tuesday.
In an address marking the 63rd anniversary of the Oct. 14, 1963 revolution, which led to Yemeni independence, Rashad al-Alimi said the “Dawn of Yemen” operation was advancing toward its ultimate objective of “ending the coup” by Iranian-backed Houthis, restoring state institutions, and placing weapons and decisions on war and peace exclusively in the hands of constitutional institutions.
“This decision is now in effect, and there is no turning back, whatever the sacrifices,” he said.
He said the operation was launched “after exhausting opportunities for de-escalation,” accusing the group of insisting on continuing the war and expanding attacks on cities, villages, neighboring countries, and international waterways.
The operation’s purpose, he said, is to restore state institutions, protect citizens, and ensure that no armed group can override the popular will or threaten neighboring countries and international shipping routes.
Addressing developments in the province of Taiz, al-Alimi pledged that the state would continue working “with all its capabilities” to protect the province, reopen its roads, and ease residents’ suffering.
He said he had instructed the government, local authorities, and relevant agencies to mobilize available resources to meet urgent humanitarian needs, provide food and medicine, assist displaced people and affected families, and secure supplies and vital roads.
He added that protecting the south’s security and stability, and safeguarding its residents’ rights and aspirations, are an integral part of the state’s national responsibility. 
Message to residents of Houthi-controlled areas
Al-Alimi told residents of Houthi-controlled areas that they are “not a target” of the operation, saying their security, rights, and dignity are among its principal motivations.
He urged them to protect their children from recruitment campaigns, avoid sending them into the group’s wars, and avoid military sites and combat zones.
He also called on them to take advantage of announced safe-return and amnesty measures, subject to their legal conditions.
Al-Alimi reaffirmed the council’s commitment to the “justness of the southern cause” and its support for the outcome of dialogue among southern parties under Saudi sponsorship.
He called for “a just and comprehensive solution that addresses past grievances, respects the popular will, and guarantees rights, partnership, and a secure future for all.” 
Condemnation of attacks on Saudi Arabia
Al-Alimi condemned Houthi attacks on neighboring Saudi Arabia, particularly the strike on King Khalid International Airport, which he said killed and injured civilians and Umrah pilgrims of several nationalities.
He also condemned attacks on civilian and vital facilities and threats to the security of holy sites.
Saudi Arabia’s security and stability are “closely linked to Yemen’s security and the interests of its citizens,” he said, adding that attacks on the kingdom’s security and civilian facilities constitute attacks on the Yemeni people’s vital interests and the stability of the entire region.
He thanked Saudi King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman for supporting Yemen’s state institutions, armed forces, and security agencies.
Al-Alimi also praised Saudi assistance to Yemen’s economy and public budget, support for services and salaries, humanitarian relief, mine clearance, reconstruction, and development projects.
The statement came as a part of a military escalation that began in July, the most extensive since the relative calm that followed a UN-brokered truce that began in 2022.
Yemen has been engulfed in war since the Houthis seized Sanaa and several of the country’s 22 provinces in 2014, prompting an Arab coalition led by neighboring Saudi Arabia to intervene in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.

US sanctions Mexican cartel CDN's horse-racing, business network
MEXICO CITY, Oct 13 - The US Treasury Department on Tuesday sanctioned four people and 11 entities tied to the Cartel del Noreste (CDN), targeting a business network spanning horse racing, construction, trucking and the energy sector that Washington says helped finance the Mexican criminal group.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called it the agency's largest action to date against CDN's financial machinery, highlighting the cartel's persistence in using horse racing to launder money.
• Designated individuals include Pablo Cesar Guajardo Alvarez, alias "Takia," the accused CDN plaza boss in Nuevo Laredo and a former leader of the cartel's sicarios.
• Nuevo Laredo businessman Gamaliel Garza Garcia, involved in horse racing in both the US and Mexico, and his son were sanctioned alongside nine companies, including a quarter-horse racing stable, construction firms and fuel and gas businesses that Treasury said operated in support of the cartel.
• The action comes as US officials have raised concerns about cartel-linked horse smuggling across the US-Mexico border. Reuters reported last month that trafficked horses, which are often destined for racing in the US, continue moving through illegal crossing routes also used for drugs and migrants.
• Also targeted was Club La Molienda, a horse racetrack, restaurant and bar in Mexico's Tamaulipas state, that Treasury said is controlled by CDN and serves as a hub for the group's horse-racing activities.
• Tamex, a Nuevo Laredo-based trucking company, was sanctioned after authorities seized two cocaine shipments totaling 52 kg hidden in trailer brake drums linked to the firm.
• Treasury said cartel-linked front companies spent $16 million on US quarter-horse racing operations and laundered more than $22 million between 2008 and 2012, leading to the seizure of 455 horses.
• CDN was founded by brothers Miguel Angel and Oscar Omar Trevino Morales, who were transferred to the US in 2025 to face drug trafficking, racketeering and money-laundering charges. The group is a successor to Los Zetas. REUTERS

These Infections Are Linked to 12% of New Cancer Cases
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
18:07:34 UTC
03:07:34 KST

Cancer can seem random. It’s often the result of many factors, including genetic mutations that build up over a lifetime of exposure to sun, pollution, and other sources of DNA damage, combined with a person’s genetic predisposition. DNA damage accumulated over time can weaken the body’s ability to suppress out-of-control cell growth, which is how tumors form.
But infections are another significant cause of cancer. Uncovering the links between certain infections and cancers raises the hope that by preventing infection, one could prevent certain malignancies. A recent report from the World Health Organization’s International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) published in the Lancet Oncology found that 12% of new cancer cases in 2024—the most recent year for which data were available—were caused by 12 infections.
Which infections are associated with cancer?
Certain human papillomaviruses, or HPV, are behind the majority of cervical cancers and a number of head and neck cancers as well, says Harriet Rumgay, an epidemiologist at IARC who is an author of the new report. About 4% of new cancer diagnoses in 2024 could be attributed to HPV infection.
Doctors and researchers have known for decades that hepatitis B and hepatitis C infections also drive many cases of liver cancer, linked to 2% and less than 1% of new diagnoses respectively, according to the report.
There is also strong evidence linking Helicobacter pylori, a bacterium that infects the stomach and small intestine, with gastric cancers. This infection was calculated to be behind about 4% of new diagnoses. And Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV), which causes mononucleosis and affects more than 90% of the world’s population, was involved in around 1% of new diagnoses, including lymphomas, nasopharyngeal cancers, and gastric cancers. Seven other infections, including HIV, were also flagged as carcinogens in the study.
Most people who have these infections will not develop cancer. It’s not also immediate—there may be a years-long delay. And infection is often only one of a number of factors contributing to a given cancer. For instance, when it comes to the relatively high rates of EBV-driven nasopharyngeal cancers in China, researchers believe that some genetic predisposition and environmental factors are also involved.
Why do some infections cause cancer?
It depends on the infection. In the case of HIV, the virus suppresses the immune system, making it easier for other carcinogenic viruses to replicate. H. pylori causes tissue damage and produces toxins that destabilize the body’s natural control of cellular growth and division, which can lead to cancer.
With EBV, says Claire Shannon-Lowe, a virologist at the University of Birmingham in the U.K. who studies EBV and cancer but was not involved in the research, it has to do with how the virus hides within immune cells called B cells. “It's a whole host of things that the virus itself is doing to the B cell to make it continually grow,” she says. That includes blocking normal cellular housecleaning procedures that would both root the virus out and arrest cancer development.
How can these cancers be prevented?
Some of these infections have treatments. H. pylori can be cleared with antibiotics, for example, reducing the risk of gastric cancer, and treating HIV reduces cancer risk from the infection as well. Some other infections on the list have vaccines.
In fact, for some of these vaccines, cancer prevention was a major goal driving their development. “The hepatitis B virus vaccine was the first vaccine that was developed against cancer,” says Rumgay. Likewise, the HPV vaccine, which was approved 20 years ago, is intended to prevent cervical cancer. Cancer epidemiologists may start seeing the effects of widespread HPV vaccination in future analyses, Rumgay says. “More and more people who have been vaccinated are starting to reach the age where we would potentially see the impact on cervical cancer rates or other cancer rates,” she says.
However, these vaccines aren’t making it to everyone who might benefit from them. In the U.S., hepatitis B vaccination rates in newborns have declined steeply over the last two years.
For other infections, no vaccines are available. For EBV, a nearly ubiquitous virus with a long, clearly documented history of contributing to cancer, “we don't have an effective vaccine yet, or an effective way of preventing it,” says Rumgay. “This is something that we want to highlight with our study.”
Historically, it was difficult to interest pharmaceutical companies in vaccines for viruses like EBV that are common and nonlethal, says Lawrence Young, a virologist and emeritus professor of molecular oncology at University of Warwick in the U.K. who has spent his career studying cancer and EBV. (Young was not involved in the IARC research.)
But thanks in part to research suggesting EBV might be involved in multiple sclerosis, an autoimmune disorder, “they've all become very interested,” he says. A number of vaccine candidates are now being studied, with some in clinical trials.
For some of the infections implicated by the latest study—the Kaposi-sarcoma associated herpes virus, in particular—there’s need for much more research into prevention, says Rumgay. The hope is that “these new findings might stimulate more development in that area,” she says.

How partisan hatred shapes American views of the Black Lives Matter protests and January 6
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
18:00:51 UTC
03:00:51 KST

Americans interpret major political events through a deeply polarized lens, where hostility toward the opposing political party shapes whether they view protests as legitimate or dangerous. A new study published in Political Research Quarterly reveals that this divide is driven not just by party labels, but by intense dislike of political opponents, loyalty to specific party factions, and differing beliefs about what threatens democracy.
The research was conducted by Rongbo Jin at The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen, and Spencer Lindsay at the University of Arizona. They set out to investigate how preexisting political attitudes structure the way Americans evaluate two highly contentious events in recent history. Specifically, they looked at the 2020 Black Lives Matter protests and the January 6 attack on the United States Capitol.
The researchers emphasize that comparing public reactions to these two events does not mean the events are morally or qualitatively equivalent. One was a decentralized protest movement seeking racial equality, while the other was a violent attempt to halt the certification of a presidential election. Instead, the comparison serves to illustrate how the American public cognitively processes moments of intense political conflict.
In modern American politics, identifying with a political party is a deeply held social identity. This dynamic has led to a rise in affective polarization, a term describing the phenomenon where Democrats and Republicans not only disagree on policy but actively distrust and dislike each other.
People rarely analyze political information like objective scientists. Instead, they rely on mental shortcuts called heuristics to quickly judge new information. This reliance feeds into motivated reasoning, a psychological process where people readily accept information that flatters their political group while finding reasons to reject facts that make their side look bad.
These cognitive shortcuts are heavily influenced by a person’s core values. The researchers point out that Republicans often prioritize social order and conformity, meaning they might view protests that disrupt the social order as inherently threatening. Democrats, on the other hand, tend to place a higher value on individual rights and inclusion, meaning they are more likely to view protests by marginalized groups as a necessary democratic function.
To understand how these psychological forces shaped views of the recent protests and riots, the researchers first analyzed an original survey of 1,000 adult participants. Conducted in late 2023, the survey asked respondents to evaluate the Black Lives Matter protests and the January 6 event on several dimensions, such as whether they were legal, empowering, or dangerous.
The researchers measured affective polarization by asking respondents to rate their feelings toward both major political parties on a scale from zero to one hundred, with zero being the coldest possible feeling. They also asked participants to place themselves within party factions, such as identifying as a MAGA Republican or a progressive Democrat.
The survey results demonstrated severe partisan splits, with Democrats viewing the Black Lives Matter protests favorably and January 6 negatively, while Republicans exhibited the opposite pattern. Affective polarization amplified these views, as participants who expressed the coldest feelings toward the opposing party held the most extreme evaluations of both events.
The researchers even looked at pure independents, individuals who do not formally align with either party. They found that independents who simply expressed warmer feelings toward the Democratic Party still viewed the Black Lives Matter protests more favorably. This suggests that emotional attachments shape political views even in the absence of a strict party label.
Differences also emerged within the parties themselves. Progressive Democrats evaluated the Black Lives Matter protests much more positively than establishment Democrats. On the political right, MAGA Republicans viewed January 6 much more positively and the Black Lives Matter protests much more negatively than establishment Republicans.
The survey also asked whether participants believed American democracy was currently under threat. Both Democrats and Republicans who perceived a high threat to democracy held more polarized views of these events, but they did so in opposite directions.
For Democrats, believing democracy was threatened was linked to supporting the Black Lives Matter protests and condemning January 6. For Republicans, perceiving a threat to democracy was linked to condemning the Black Lives Matter protests and viewing January 6 more favorably.
The researchers describe this as a “saving democracy” frame. When citizens believe the political system is in danger, they use that belief to justify their evaluations of controversial political actions. Depending on a person’s preexisting political loyalties, the exact same event can be interpreted as either a defense of democracy or a direct attack on it.
Next, the researchers examined data from the American National Election Studies, looking at large surveys from 2016, 2020, and 2024. This included panel data, which tracks the exact same individuals over several years to see how their attitudes shift over time. Because this secondary data set did not include questions about January 6, the researchers focused solely on evaluations of the Black Lives Matter movement.
The panel data revealed that as Republicans grew warmer toward the Democratic Party between 2016 and 2020, they also developed warmer feelings toward the Black Lives Matter movement. Conversely, when Democrats grew warmer toward Republicans, they tended to view the movement less favorably.
The researchers suggest this indicates a shift toward more moderate political positions. When individuals soften their stance toward political opponents, they may also moderate their views on highly polarizing social movements associated with the political left.
The authors note that the study relies on observational data, meaning it can only identify associations rather than establish direct cause and effect. It is possible that evaluating these historical events in a certain way actually causes people to dislike the opposing party more, rather than the other way around.
Additionally, participants were asked in 2023 to evaluate events that took place in 2020 and 2021. Their memories and interpretations may have been shaped by years of political messaging and media coverage in the interim.
Future studies might use experimental designs to better understand the exact sequence of how political identity shapes the immediate processing of breaking news. Tracking public reactions in real time could help researchers map how competing narratives take hold before partisan lines fully solidify.
The study, “Inhabiting Different Worlds: How Partisan Attitudes Shape Americans’ Evaluation of the Black Lives Matter Protests and the January 6th Insurrection,” was authored by Rongbo Jin and Spencer Lindsay.

Trump sees equally tough fight for Republicans to retain Senate and House in midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
18:00:21 UTC
03:00:21 KST

US President Donald Trump has said that Republicans face an equally difficult fight to retain control of the House of Representatives and the Senate in November's midterm elections, despite forecasts showing a considerably tougher contest in the House.
"I would say equal," Trump told reporters on Tuesday at the White House when asked which chamber would be harder for Republicans to defend in the November 3 vote.
Trump acknowledged the historical disadvantage facing the party of a sitting president, although he insisted that enthusiasm among Republican voters was surging.
"When you have a sitting president... no matter how good they seem to be, they're at a big disadvantage, tremendous disadvantage," he said.
"But I'm doing a tour right now, and I'm doing rallies. The level of enthusiasm for the Republican Party is way up."
Trump's assessment was striking because Republicans have been widely seen as particularly vulnerable in the House, while the Senate's electoral map had initially offered them greater hopes of retaining control.
Election forecaster Decision Desk HQ gives Democrats a 77 percent chance of winning the 435-seat House, projecting that they will take 235 seats to the Republicans' 200.
It also narrowly favours Democrats to capture the 100-seat Senate, giving them a 56 percent probability of victory and projecting a 51-49 majority.
Trump on campaign blitz
Losing either chamber on November 3 would complicate Trump's ability to push his agenda through Congress during the final two years of his presidency, while handing Democrats greater power to investigate his administration.
Trump has embarked on a campaign blitz in the closing weeks of the election, including rallies in traditionally Republican states where his party faces unexpectedly competitive Senate races.
History offers little comfort to the president.
The party holding the White House has almost invariably lost seats in midterm elections, with just three exceptions in the House since 1934, according to figures compiled by the American Presidency Project.
Franklin D. Roosevelt's Democrats gained nine House seats in 1934, while Bill Clinton's party picked up four in 1998 and George W. Bush's Republicans gained eight in 2002.
The worst modern midterm drubbing came in 1938, when Roosevelt's Democrats lost 72 House seats, followed by Barack Obama's Democrats losing 63 in 2010.
Trump himself presided over a split verdict in his first midterms in 2018, when Republicans lost 41 House seats but gained two in the Senate.

Police have opened investigations into 34 allegations of violence against demonstrators.
Some 147 teaching staff have been injured in the protests, the Education Ministry said.
On Monday, Macron urged restraint from protesters, saying the issues “deserve time, consultations, discussion and respect”.

13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026

Handing over the desks to Mahad Primary School, Mustafa Giray Jezel, program coordinator in South Sudan of the Turkish Cooperation and Coordination Agency (TIKA), said the donation is part of the agency's ongoing efforts to support education in the country.
"We are here handing over 150 desks for school pupils. We hope it will help create an even more conducive environment for the learners. The Turkish agency is ready to support education in South Sudan," said Jezel.
TIKA's projects primarily focus on vocational training, alongside numerous other initiatives including strengthening administrative and social infrastructure, healthcare services, and providing clean water and borehole drilling.
Jezel said his visit to the school was part of an ongoing education support project, adding that he would visit the school again when other projects undertaken by TIKA are implemented.
"One cannot stress enough the importance of education. We appreciate Mahad Primary School for opening their doors. We are providing school desks to help achieve success in school; we want individuals to serve themselves and the country," he said.
Al-Nur Kur, director of the Mahad Institute, based in South Sudan’s capital Juba, emphasized the importance of the support provided by TIKA for achieving educational success, saying that such projects help create a conducive learning environment.
Kur said the Mahad Primary School includes learners whose families have been buffeted by persistent economic shocks, leading to a shortage of desks for primary school learners.
"We are supported with school desks, and that eases the burden for the parents. We are not charging money; we want children to learn. We provide an opportunity for every child to learn," he said.

“This pattern raises serious concerns that Israel is directing attacks against civilians not directly participating in hostilities – a war crime,” the press release partly states. Is this pattern really raising concern now? Iran focused on attacking "harder targets," U.K. spy chief warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
17:46:02 UTC
02:46:02 KST

Iran shifts focus to "harder targets, like military sites" with mounting sabotage attacks, U.K. spy chief warns
London — Iran has made a "major shift" in its efforts to attack the United Kingdom, including going after harder targets such as military bases, the head of Britain's domestic spy agency MI5 warned Tuesday.
In his annual threat update at MI5 headquarters in London, Sir Ken McCallum outlined the growing challenges facing the country, from hostile foreign governments and terrorism to the potential misuse of AI. Iran, he said, has demonstrated that it is "keen on subcontracting its U.K. violence … using criminal proxies to try to intimidate oppositionists, Iranian media organizations, and Israeli sites."
"Sadly, much of this aggression has been aimed at British Jewish communities, with whom I want to express solidarity," he said.
"The other major shift this year has been Iranian ambitions to come at harder targets, like military sites," he added.
All of these alleged activities led to more than 50 Iran-linked arrests in the U.K. over the past year alone, McCallum said.
His comments come after a series of arson and sabotage incidents targeting Jewish communities and other sites in the U.K. and across Europe, which McCallum described as "sickening acts."
He declined to provide details about the military installations targeted, including the alleged plot against the U.K. air base RAF Fairford that was thwarted in late September, citing "ongoing investigations."
The U.S. moved all of its long-range bombers off the base in the wake of the incident.
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Monday that the incident near the base, which was used by U.S. bombers to target Iran, was "almost certainly" directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
But as McCallum noted Tuesday with his reference to "subcontracting" and "criminal proxies," not all of Iran's suspected nefarious activities are easy to attribute to the regime in Tehran.
"Knowingly or unknowingly" working for Iran?
Britain's counterterrorism police unit said it was possible that the RAF Fairford incident "may be activity committed by proxies, or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly, working on behalf of a foreign state."
Iran, like Russia, has been accused repeatedly of using individuals who may be unaware they are even working for a foreign state to conduct sabotage attacks across Western Europe.
The Iran-aligned group Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamia — or The Islamic Movement of the Companions of the Righteous (IMCR) — claimed responsibility for a string of incidents earlier this year, including attacks on synagogues in the Netherlands and Belgium, and multiple attacks on north London's Jewish community.
A representative for the group told CBS News in March that it would "keep threatening U.S. and Israeli interests worldwide until we've avenged every child in Gaza, Iran, Lebanon, and the resistance nations," and it urged people "to stay away from Zionist and American interests."
Russia is "aggressor number one"
In his wide-ranging address, McCallum said the number of state-threat cases being handled by MI5 had quadrupled over the past decade.
"Since I started in this role in 2020, there has been another generational shift. We have again entered a new era of national security – requiring a new response," he said.
MI5 is devoting more resources to countering state threats in 2026 than it did during the Cold War, he said, highlighting the scale of the challenge posed by hostile foreign actors, and he said among those actors, Russia remains "aggressor number one."
McCallum said Moscow has escalated its attempts to wage "hybrid warfare" against Britain and its allies. That can include a wide range of cyberattacks, sabotage and other hostile activities that fall short of conventional military action, he said.
The intelligence chief suggested Russia's increasingly aggressive approach was linked to its difficulties on the battlefield in Ukraine, arguing that Moscow was seeking to unsettle other European countries "at a time when its military progress in Ukraine remained limited and came at a high cost."
He acknowledged longstanding conventional threats still exist, but were being "sort of well managed by military or other colleagues," while Russia, Iran "and others are seeking to do things beneath the level of conventional armed conflict."
Artificial Intelligence
Artificial intelligence was also a central theme of McCallum's address. He warned of the technology's rapid development amid the equally rapid changes in the security landscape, crediting AI with "supercharging the cybersecurity contest between attackers and defenders."
He said AI could be used to generate propaganda and radicalization material tailored to individuals, potentially making it easier for hostile actors to manipulate people and spread extremist ideologies.
Among the greatest concerns McCallum voiced was the possibility that AI could help people make existing biological weapons more dangerous, or help malicious actors develop entirely new ones.

Spain's royals visit Ceuta enclave amid friction with Morocco after border surge
CEUTA, Spain, Oct 13 - Spain's King Felipe and Queen Letizia visited Ceuta's Muslim cemetery on Tuesday where most of more than 100 migrants who died in July's mass crossing into the North African enclave from Morocco were buried.
The visit, the first by Spain's head of state since 2007 and in Felipe's 12-year reign, followed rising friction between Madrid and Rabat, which claims the tiny territory of Ceuta and Spain's other North African enclave, Melilla, as its own.
The streets of the 84,000-person territory, which covers less than 20 square km, were packed with thousands of Ceutans waving Spanish flags to greet the royal couple.
"I am a Spaniard, Spaniard, Spaniard," they chanted.
The Moroccan government has historically opposed Spanish royal visits to the two cities, which Madrid considers part of its territory since the 17th and 15th centuries, respectively.
The two kingdoms have traded barbs over border management following the crossing by more than 72,000 migrants from Morocco.
Addressing civilians in Ceuta, the king said Morocco's relationship to Spain and the EU must be grounded in respect, "while always adhering to the principle that Ceuta is Spain; Ceuta is Europe."
In a speech to parliament last Friday, Morocco's King Mohammed did not mention the royals' planned visit but said the current migration cooperation model with Spain had reached its limits.
While most of the migrants who managed to get into Ceuta later returned, at least 10,000 remain, straining local resources and fuelling some Spaniards' criticism of the central government ahead of a November 29 general election.
The leftist government has sought to present the royal visit as a gesture of support for Ceuta and its residents but right-wing opposition parties accuse Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez of failing to defend Spanish sovereignty over the enclave.
“It’s a real treat that they’re coming to Ceuta for the first time, and they really ought to come more often, because Ceuta is part of Spain and His Majesty the King doesn’t need to ask permission to visit any city in Spain," said Ceuta resident Isabel Bermejo, 57.
At the cemetery, the royal couple stood solemnly in front of the graves, most of which were marked only with numbers as the victims were never identified.
The couple were accompanied by Jewish, Hindu, Muslim and Christian religious leaders, representing the four religions present in Ceuta.
On Wednesday, the royal couple will visit Melilla, 370 km (230 miles) southeast of Ceuta. REUTERS
