Breadcrumb
Houthis warn of fresh attacks on Saudi Arabia after Sanaa strike
Yemen's Houthis said Saudi Arabia struck an oil facility in Sanaa on Tuesday, after the Riyadh-led coalition told civilians to leave the surrounding area in its first evacuation order for the Yemeni capital since the war flared up again.
After a series of strikes on the kingdom's airports and energy sites, the coalition's spokesman said people should leave an oil facility belonging to the Yemen Petroleum Company on the western outskirts of Sanaa before it was attacked.
An AFP correspondent in Sanaa reported hearing an explosion, while a breaking news alert on the Houthi-affiliated Al-Masirah TV channel said "Saudi aggression targets the oil company in Al-Sabaha, west of Sanaa".
The Saudi-led coalition is yet to confirm the reported strike.
Swiftly responding to the earlier coalition warning, the Houthis had issued a threat to target Riyadh's international airport, a refinery, and an Aramco facility in Dammam if the strike went ahead.
"The Yemeni Armed Forces urge all citizens to immediately evacuate and move away from targets that our forces will strike should the Saudi enemy target," military spokesman Yahya Saree wrote on X, identifying the three targets.
An attack at Riyadh's airport on Saturday left 13 people dead and operations suspended, rocking the world's top crude oil exporter and deepening the war in Yemen, where the kingdom backs the internationally recognised government.
An AFP correspondent reported that many civilians in Sanaa fearing shortages rushed to queue in front of fuel stations after the coalition warning.
The Yemen Petroleum Company sought to reassure the public, saying it had taken all necessary precautions in the event of an emergency to "meet people's needs".
Petroleum stocks were "available in safe facilities and locations, and in sufficient quantities" to meet demand for long periods, it said.
Saudi Arabia was still weathering fresh attacks on Tuesday, with the coalition saying its forces intercepted three drones north of the kingdom's capital Riyadh.
Many countries have issued travel warnings to their citizens in Saudi Arabia, most recently France, which told its citizens to avoid the airports in Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam on Tuesday.
The Saudi coalition has supported Yemen's government militarily against the Houthis since 2015 in a long-running civil war that has created a humanitarian crisis.
Economic woes
Traffic in perennially gridlocked Riyadh was noticeably lighter this week, as remote learning for all schools and work-from-home orders for some companies took effect, according to AFP journalists.
Saudi Arabia faces a major economic contraction this year with GDP expected to shrink 3.3 percent, the International Monetary Fund said on Tuesday, predicting a regional drop over Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.
The kingdom was already facing headwinds from Iran's chokehold on the Hormuz strait, vital for oil and gas trade, since the start of the Middle East war in February, when the US and Israel attacked Iran.
But the restart in July of Yemen's frozen war has further roiled the kingdom and brought the fight to its own soil.
Houthi attacks have also targeted oil tankers in the Red Sea - Saudi Arabia's alternative export route.
In Yemen, the renewed fighting was fuelling the risk of infectious disease outbreaks.
Suspected cholera cases tripled there in three weeks, the World Health Organization said Tuesday, warning that the growing disease burden was straining hospitals already treating war casualties.
Houthi warning
Blasts were heard over the Saudi capital again late Monday, with the Saudi coalition saying it intercepted a Houthi missile and the group announcing it had again targeted the airport.
On Monday evening, Human Resources Minister Ahmad bin Sulaiman Al Rajhi remained defiant.
"We're not going out," he told the crowd at the Riyadh Economic Forum. "We are safe. With God's will. May God turn their plots back against them."
The Riyadh airport attack prompted US President Donald Trump to say he was considering joining Saudi strikes against the Houthis, after having reportedly rebuffed previous Saudi requests.
The Houthis warned the US against intervention, with political bureau member Mohammed Al Bukhaiti telling AFP they would target American interests in the region.
Bukhaiti said the purpose of the campaign against Saudi targets was to send a message to the crown prince "that he can no longer wage aggression against Yemen from a safe position".

English football faces major financial risks, regulator warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
17:43:25 UTC
02:43:25 KST

Efe Özkan
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
nglish football’s finances are “dangerously exposed,” with most clubs operating close to financial collapse, according to a landmark report by the Independent Football Regulator (IFR) that was released on Tuesday.
The State of the Game report found that 94% of clubs in England’s top five leagues had losses in the 2025-26 season, while more than 60% of clubs in the English Football League (EFL) and National League were technically insolvent.
The IFR warned that a “dangerous cocktail” of rising debt and increasing reliance on owners to provide funding is putting clubs and their supporters at risk.
The report found that 66% of clubs could not survive for more than 90 days without new funding from their owners, while 29% said they could not survive beyond 30 days. It also found that 60% of clubs had no business plan.
“Seventeen clubs are now trading in such a way that if their players played for free, their non-playing costs would mean they would go bust,” IFR chairman David Kogan told BBC Sport. “Thirty-two clubs are operating on only 30 days’ cash. If the owner chooses not to pay cash at the end of the month, those clubs go bust.”
He said the findings showed that reform was needed before clubs faced an even greater financial crisis.
The report also highlighted widening financial disparities in the English football pyramid. The average Premier League club now earns more than eight times the average Championship club.
The IFR said the existing parachute-payment system for relegated Premier League clubs creates incentives for Championship teams to overspend and contributes to rising player wages.
It also warned that increasing net transfer debt, deferred transfer payments and transfer financing were creating financial links between clubs, owners and lenders, increasing the risk that financial problems could spread across the game.
“Nobody in football for 100 years has believed that football was trading in a solvent and effective state,” said Kogan. “But I think now where there’s so much more money involved, the extremes get more extreme.”
The IFR said the foundations of the English football pyramid were under “intense strain” and required urgent reform

Can Saudi Arabia find a viable path out of Yemen?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
17:41:51 UTC
02:41:51 KST

Can Saudi Arabia find a viable path out of Yemen?
TEHRAN – Saudi Arabia is once again testing its options for dealing with Ansarallah, hoping that what failed the first time might succeed the next.
It tried a war in March 2015 under the banner of the “Arab Coalition,” and the result was a brutal conflict that devastated everything in its path. The war dragged on for eight years before the guns fell silent, without achieving its objectives. Today, it seems decision-makers in Riyadh have fallen prey to the belief that whatever force fails to achieve can be accomplished by using even more force. The war is being reignited, this time with greater intensity and ferocity.
For more than a decade, Saudi Arabia tried blockade, isolation, and sanctions. When these measures failed to break Ansarallah’s resolve, it went a step further on July 13, bombing the runway at Sanaa International Airport to prevent an Iranian aircraft from landing.
On board was a Yemeni delegation returning from Tehran, where it had paid its respects following the martyrdom of the Leader of Iran’s Revolution, Ayatollah Sayyed Ali Khamenei.
The attack was intended as a reminder that the airport remained under blockade. Instead, it became the spark that reignited an unprecedented confrontation between the two sides, with hostilities now unfolding on land, in the air, and at sea, striking deep into both Saudi and Yemeni territories.
The option the Kingdom has refrained from trying is sustained negotiations and genuine dialogue with Ansarallah, whether face-to-face or through trusted intermediaries aimed at a lasting solution. By its very nature, a truce is temporary. It does not address the roots of a crisis or produce the necessary settlements between the conflicting demands and interests of the parties involved.
The collapse of de-escalation
The second extension of the truce agreement expired on October 2, 2022, without an agreement on a third extension, as the parties remained too far apart in their positions. Nevertheless, the ceasefire largely held, and the past four years saw a reduction in hostilities that was disrupted only by isolated incidents, none of which amounted to a significant breach or escalation, until the attack on Sanaa airport three months ago.
In April 2023, a Saudi delegation visited Sanaa. The trip lasted six days. In September 2023, an Ansarallah delegation visited Riyadh to explore the possibility of advancing a political process that could produce lasting solutions. That trip lasted five days.
However, three factors left everything unresolved: first, the widening gap between the two sides; second, Riyadh’s insistence that it was a “sponsor and mediator” rather than a party to the Yemeni crisis; and third, the outbreak of the Al-Aqsa Storm operation, which reshaped regional maps, balances of power, and priorities. As a result, matters remained unresolved, leaving both the intra-Yemeni and Yemeni-Saudi crises open to any number of possibilities and scenarios.
Ansarallah became preoccupied with its military campaign in support of Gaza, achieving tangible results that worked in its favor rather than against it. It subsequently evolved from a local actor into a regional player, particularly after reaching an understanding with the Trump administration under which the U.S. would halt its attacks on Yemen in exchange for ending attacks on American vessels and assets in the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandab Strait. Meanwhile, relations with Riyadh appeared to have been pushed to the back burner.
Some Ansarallah officials say the war now raging should have erupted two years ago, given the deadlock in efforts to find a solution and the worsening consequences of the blockade. However, the Gaza genocide postponed the entire matter.
There is also a reductive and misleading narrative that portrays the renewed war and confrontation as a response by Ansarallah to an Iranian order. Beyond being false and superficial, this narrative harms those who genuinely believe it, rather than those who repeat it out of spite or to demonize their adversaries.
Misjudging Ansarallah’s position and standing leads to some of the most erroneous and damaging conclusions. Ansarallah indeed makes no secret of its close ties to Iran and its regional axis. It is also true that the Sanaa government did not hesitate to support Gaza in the past and may not hesitate in the future to join a campaign in support of Hezbollah and Iran.
But above all, Ansarallah is an integral part of Yemen’s social and political fabric and one of the country’s fundamental constituencies. All of Yemen may not be governed by Ansarallah alone, but it cannot be governed without it.
Following the July attack on Sanaa airport, it became clear that a fundamental shift had taken place in Ansarallah’s language and preparations. Its leader announced a new equation: “blockade for blockade, ports for ports, and airports for airports.”
Few took these threats seriously until the confrontation on the ground escalated, with Ansarallah extending its control along the coast toward Taiz and the Bab al-Mandab Strait, while reciprocal strikes intensified in the heart of both Saudi and Yemeni territory.
The Kingdom has sought to absolve itself of accusations that it is directly involved in military operations, maintaining its position under the theory that it is a “sponsor and mediator, not a party” to the war.
The path Saudi Arabia has yet to try
The eight-year war failed to achieve its objectives, while Ansarallah emerged stronger and is now expanding its reach.
Nor can Saudi Arabia continue to deny the damage and consequences of its blockade on Yemen, which affects three-quarters of the population. It cannot credibly claim that the limited and restricted flights available, or the reduced flow of goods are sufficient to compensate the Yemeni people for shortages of food and medicine. Neither can it maintain that its measures target only Ansarallah and are directed exclusively at arms supplies.
The realities of Yemeni life and the daily experiences of ordinary Yemenis tell a different story. Reports by international organizations document poverty, deprivation, shortages of medicine and food, and the interruption of salary payments. Such conditions might be endured for another year or two, but allowing them to persist much longer seems untenable.
The option Saudi Arabia has yet to try, with the seriousness it demands, is to open the door to dialogue and negotiations, either directly or through a trusted mediator, such as Oman, in pursuit of solutions and settlements to all outstanding disputes.
Such a dialogue would begin between Sanaa and Riyadh, but it would not end with them. Instead, it would bring all Yemeni parties to the negotiating table, based on the principle that Yemen cannot be governed by a single Yemeni faction. The talks should not be tactical, intermittent, and ceasefire-focused. Dialogue must be a sustained, strategic commitment to a comprehensive negotiated settlement that addresses the root causes of the conflict, the blockade, the humanitarian crisis, and Yemen’s political future. The Kingdom has not genuinely embraced negotiation as a primary strategy, instead treating it as a pause between rounds of military pressure.
Experts believe the time has come to try this approach. It would not be costly and offers the shortest and least expensive path forward for all parties, especially Saudi Arabia, which has much to lose. Has the time finally come to stop repeating failed experiments and take a new path, one that might, at last, lead to a different ending?

China sentences three people to death for running Myanmar scam centres
Dozens more were imprisoned for their involvement in crimes including telecommunications fraud, trafficking and murder.
A court in eastern China has sentenced three members of a criminal gang to death for operating a network of scam centres in Myanmar.
In a statement released on Tuesday, Quanzhou Intermediate People’s Court, a high court in southeastern Fujian province, said it had sentenced Wei Huairen, Chen Dawei and Liao Jingfang for their involvement in the “Wei family criminal gang”.
The syndicate was involved in crimes including drug trafficking, organised prostitution, illegal casino operations, telecommunications fraud and the murder of at least two Chinese nationals.
The court said Wei was one of the group’s leaders and was found guilty of several crimes, including murder.
Three other members were jailed for life, while 55 others were handed sentences ranging from three years and three months to 24 years in prison.
The court said the gang’s operations netted more than $1.8bn.
Chinese state broadcaster CCTV on Tuesday described the gang as operating 14 “large-scale” compounds and having lured “thousands” of Chinese nationals with promises of high wages to Myanmar.
The verdict comes as Beijing intensified its crackdown on cross-border scam networks operating in southeast Asia, where scam parks have become an industrial-scale business.
The International Organization for Migration in July warned that scam centres in southeast Asia employ as many as 300,000 workers and use online schemes to defraud people in the West, many of them elderly.
Many of those conducting the online scams are trafficked foreign nationals forced to work in prison-like compounds.

‘EC should regain credibility’: Ashok Lavasa says poll panel must regain public trust amid SIR controversy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
17:37:34 UTC
02:37:34 KST

NEW DELHI: Former election commissioner Ashok Lavasa on Tuesday said the Election Commission of India (ECI) was facing an unprecedented level of controversy and urged the poll body to regain public trust amid protests over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.Drawing a parallel with cricket, Lavasa said the credibility of an election depended on people believing that the poll panel was impartial.
“If people feel that the umpire is not neutral, they will question the winning team's victory as well,” he said while addressing a citizens' convention in Kolkata virtually, according to news agency PTI.Lavasa's remarks came as opposition parties intensified their protests against alleged “vote chori”, demanding the resignation of chief election commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over the SIR exercise.Opposition leaders have taken to the streets in recent days and clashed with police in New Delhi.“The EC should regain its credibility and people's trust. The Election Commission of India, whose position is very high and possibly the highest among all public institutions, is today mired in controversies and people are taking to the streets to protest,” Lavasa said.
Questions over dissent within Election Commission
The former election commissioner referred to an Indian Express report that election commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had objected on record at least 14 times over the past 10 months to decisions and orders they said had been issued without their knowledge.
The objections reportedly came even as the nationwide SIR exercise was being overseen by the full commission.Lavasa questioned the lack of publicly available meeting minutes, saying it was difficult to establish whether decisions had been taken unanimously or by a majority.“This casts a doubt in the minds of the people whether the decisions of the Election Commission, including on the SIR, were unanimous or taken by majority,” he said.He also said the Election Commission had not provided an authentic clarification on the reported differences between its members.“Some press statements have been issued, but those create more questions and generate more doubts than they answer,” Lavasa said.The poll panel has maintained that differing views and observations are a normal part of deliberations in any institution. It has also said that all its orders carry full legal sanction and follow established statutory procedures.The EC added that all three commissioners, as well as its officers, were authorised to offer suggestions to improve the electoral system.
Lavasa flags concerns over SIR
Lavasa said the SIR exercise had triggered widespread anxiety over voting rights, adding that people had not been as concerned about protecting their right to vote in the preceding 16 months.“The EC's decision to conduct the SIR took everyone by surprise,” he said.He noted that the Election Commission had conducted special revisions of electoral rolls in the past under the Representation of the People Act and the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, but argued that the current exercise had created an unprecedented level of public concern.Lavasa also questioned the approach of categorising electors into three age groups based on their dates of birth under the Citizenship Act.The Constitution, he said, requires the Election Commission to enrol all those who meet the eligibility criteria under Article 326, which provides for voting rights for Indian citizens aged 18 and above who are not of unsound mind or disqualified under any law.“But unfortunately, with the tactics deployed this time, the goal is not to include. Possibly the priority is to exclude people from the voter list on the suspicion that they are not Indian citizens and not on evidence,” he said.Referring to West Bengal, Lavasa said nearly 60 lakh people's voting rights had gone under adjudication during the SIR, apart from those excluded from the draft electoral rolls. He said the EC had not adequately considered the proximity of the Assembly elections and the difficulty of adjudicating such a large number of cases in time.Lavasa added that around 33 lakh names had been restored to the voter list after adjudication.
Prakash Raj joins criticism of SIR
Actor-activist Prakash Raj, who also addressed the convention, described the SIR as the “most dangerous disease” and alleged that it was undermining democracy.“Even before Gyanesh Kumar came (as the CEC), they broke parties in Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Telangana, and Bihar,” he said, accusing the BJP leadership of seeking to divide people through the SIR into those who could vote and those who could not.Raj also alleged that the West Bengal Assembly elections were conducted in an “illegal” manner following the revision exercise, claiming that voter names had been selectively deleted. He said opposition parties had come to believe they were contesting “fixed” elections.
The convention was organised by CPI(M) leader Bikash Ranjan Bhattacharya and retired bureaucrat Jawhar Sircar.The protests over the SIR have also prompted a wider political confrontation between the opposition and the ruling BJP.Congress leader Rahul Gandhi has vowed to continue the INDIA bloc's campaign against alleged electoral irregularities, while Union home minister Amit Shah has accused the Congress of trying to shield infiltrators by opposing the exercise.

Ukraine takes step forward in EU membership talks after Hungary drops objections
BRUSSELS, Oct 13 - Ukraine took a step forward in its European Union membership bid on Tuesday, opening talks with the bloc on internal market and competitiveness standards, Irish Minister of State for European Affairs Thomas Byrne said, after Hungary dropped its objections.
The Hungarian government backed the move after Ukraine's parliament passed legislation on Monday expanding the rights of Hungarian speakers and other minorities to receive education in their native language.
The EU accession process normally involves years-long complex negotiations, further complicated in the case of Ukraine by the ongoing war.
As part of the process, candidate countries negotiate policy "chapters" which are grouped into six thematic clusters, including fundamental rights, the bloc's internal market and external relations.
The EU opened negotiations with Ukraine on the first set of policy issues — such as the judiciary and functioning of democratic institutions — in June. The two sides opened negotiations on the external relations cluster in July. REUTERS

Polish court to rule on custody of man suspected of plotting attack on PM
WARSAW, Oct 13 - A Polish court will decide on Wednesday whether to keep in custody a man suspected of planning an attack on the prime minister and defence minister after improvised explosive materials were found in his apartment, prosecutors said.
The 66-year-old man, identified only as Krzysztof N. under Polish privacy law, was detained on Sunday on suspicion of planning an attack on Prime Minister Donald Tusk and Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz.
He has been charged with nine offences, Warsaw regional prosecutors' spokesperson Piotr Skiba told reporters on Tuesday.
The man did not admit to the alleged offences and refused to provide an explanation.
"The most serious charge concerns plotting to forcibly overthrow state authorities — including the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers — using explosives stockpiled by the man," Skiba said. He added that the suspect faces a prison sentence of 2 to 15 years for the offence if found guilty.
The other charges relate to recordings published online and include promoting an ideology advocating the violent seizure of power in Poland, promoting war including the one in Ukraine, and inciting crimes motivated by nationality, ethnicity, race or political views.
Skiba said the man had been seeking people to join his plans and had created a group comprising several hundred people, according to a recording reviewed by investigators.
While violent crime is relatively rare in Poland, the country is politically polarised and has faced heightened security concerns because of its proximity to the Russian war in neighbouring Ukraine.
The suspect was planning an attack on members of the current government, though he also criticised politicians from previous governments, Skiba said. REUTERS

Philippine House prosecutors dropped three of the four impeachment articles on Tuesday against Vice President Sara Duterte, leaving only a charge of unexplained wealth to be tried by the Senate impeachment court, according to media reports.
The dropped charges include alleged misuse of confidential funds and an alleged assassination plot, the English newspaper Phil Star reported.
The Senate impeachment court accepted the withdrawal of the charges, leaving Duterte’s trial to proceed on a single charge of unexplained wealth.
"Today, the prosecution respectfully manifests that it will no longer pursue three of them,” lead prosecutor Jinky Luistro told the court. “It will stand on one, and that is article two on unexplained wealth.”
It means Duterte can only be acquitted or convicted based on Article II, which accuses her of unexplained and undeclared wealth.
The withdrawal is viewed as major scaling back of the impeachment case, as the dropped charges included two of the most prominent allegations against Duterte: the alleged misuse of confidential funds, and alleged grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr, first lady Liza Araneta-Marcos and former House Speaker Martin Romualdez.
Duterte may be disqualified from running for public office, including the presidency in 2028, if she is convicted.

- Russia hit transport and logistics instead of energy sites overnight, killing four in Kharkiv and wounding many, as Ukraine warned that US early-warning intelligence is vital to save lives.
AI generated
KYIV - Ukraine received no prior warning from its Western partners about a Russian ballistic missile attack on its capital, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct 13, as Kyiv comes under intense US pressure to halt attacks on Russian refineries.
Russia hit no Ukrainian energy targets overnight for the first time since US President Donald Trump’s surprise Oct 11 announcement of an “energy ceasefire”, but hammered transport and logistics with ballistic missiles and drones.
Reuters and other media have reported that US officials have threatened to cut off intelligence sharing and weapons sales to Ukraine unless it stops attacking Russian refineries. Kyiv relies heavily on US intelligence for early warnings of missile strikes, experts and officials say.
Speaking to reporters on Oct 13, Trump said Washington continues to share intelligence with Ukraine and is working with both Kyiv and Moscow to bring an end to the war. “We are helping them, and we are sharing intel,” he said.
Trump was asked whether Russia had violated the ceasefire and answered: “I’ll let you know about that later.”
Asked if Russia could use proceeds from the diesel deal to purchase more bombs, Trump sidestepped the question. “That’s a diesel deal, not for us. That’s being released into the world. That’s not being released to us.”
Zelensky said Ukraine had not targeted Russian refineries since Trump’s announcement on Oct 11.
He said Kyiv had not received the usual warning from allies of ballistic missile launches before a “particularly vile” attack on Kyiv overnight, in which five missiles hit civilian infrastructure.
“Intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches helps save lives,” Zelensky said on X, “and this is one of the most critical issues.” He stopped short of linking the lack of warning to any US threats.
Air raid alerts sound in Kyiv only after blasts are heard
Air alerts sounded in Kyiv on the night of Oct 12 only after several explosions had already ripped through the city.
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha tried to calm anxiety by saying Ukraine was still receiving US military intelligence. Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum, he said the delay had been due to the specifics of the weaponry that Russia had used.
As Ukraine fights a larger, richer and better-equipped enemy, Kyiv sees the strikes on Russian oil refineries as one of its few instruments to reduce Moscow’s ability to fight.
Yet Trump has repeatedly blamed Ukrainian attacks - which prompted Moscow to suspend diesel exports - for a sharp rise in US fuel prices this year, a headache for his Republican party ahead of Congressional midterm elections in three weeks.
Most analysts, however, say Trump’s war in Iran has had a far greater impact on the price rise.
Russia had struck six Ukrainian energy sites on Oct 12. It was unclear whether Moscow had deliberately avoided energy infrastructure overnight and on Oct 13.
A Kremlin spokesman, asked about the energy ceasefire, would only say that contacts were ongoing, but declined to provide any further details.
In his nightly video address posted on X, Zelensky said he had sent proposals to US officials with a view to new meetings in coming days with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner on ways to resolve the conflict.
He said Ukraine supported Trump’s announcement of an energy truce provided that Russia observed it.
“We need to work for peace, we need to look for ways to do the proper actions. Ukraine is ready for meetings,” he said.
Earlier, Zelensky reiterated Ukraine’s position, saying that Kyiv was ready for reciprocal steps to de-escalate, calling on partners to pressure Russia.
A Ukrainian delegation held talks in the United States last week and people familiar with the meeting said Witkoff and Kushner told them that a deal to allow Russian diesel exports was part of a bid to draw Russia back to negotiations.
Ukraine says it now has cards to play
Russian strikes killed four people in Ukraine’s second city, Kharkiv, and dozens were wounded across the country, Ukrainian officials said.
The Ukrainian air force said it was investigating the failure to receive surveillance warnings before the attack.
Fabian Hoffmann, missile expert at the Norwegian Institute for Defence Studies, said Ukraine’s European allies had “very limited” ability to replace US early-warning intelligence about Russian missile strikes:
“Ukraine relies on the so-called Space-Based Infrared System which the US deploys - and the US system is really second to none and only the United States can provide that.”
Sybiha said the US request to halt attacks on Russian refineries showed how Ukraine’s position had strengthened, alluding to Trump’s comment to Zelensky in a tense Oval Office meeting in 2025 that “you don’t have the cards”.
“In less than two years, we have gone from ‘having no cards’ to ‘not playing your cards’. That is an achievement,” Sybiha said.

02:24:02 KST

FUZHOU, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- China on Tuesday handed out death sentences to three leading members of a criminal gang led by the Wei family, which carried out criminal activities, including telecom fraud and gambling, in Myanmar.
Three others were sentenced to life imprisonment, while another 55 face jail terms ranging from three years and three months to 24 years, according to rulings made by the Intermediate People's Court of Quanzhou and People's Court of Nan'an, both in Fujian Province in east China.
The courts also correspondingly imposed supplementary punishments including fines, confiscation of property and deportation.
The courts found that the criminal gang led by the Wei family used its influence and set up multiple scam compounds in Kokang, Myanmar, where it exercised armed control and carried out various crimes starting from 2019, including telecom fraud, gambling, blackmailing, organized prostitution, drug trafficking and illegal border crossings.
Their gambling and fraud crimes involved 12.2 billion yuan (around 1.81 billion U.S. dollars), according to the court rulings.
Two Chinese nationals were killed as a result of the criminal gang led by the Wei family during its handling of disobedient personnel involved in telecom fraud, in collaboration with other scam rings, the courts said.
A member of the Wei family gang abused the militia force it controlled in wanton killings, causing the deaths of two Chinese nationals, the courts added.
The defendants were convicted of seven charges including murder and fraud, according to the court rulings. Lawmakers, political advisors, and family members of those involved, among others, watched from the public gallery as the verdicts were announced. ■

Guo, the Wimbledon doubles champion, progressed to the second round after a 1-6, 7-6(6), 7-5 victory against Cirstea, marking her first win over a top-20 player in her career, as well as her first victory in Wuhan's main-draw singles match.
"It was a very tough match. Honestly, I never imagined I would win until the match was actually over," Guo said. "Especially after losing the first set 1-6, I just wanted to stay on court a little longer and enjoy the feeling of playing on the center court."
"I didn't expect my level to get better and better. Even when facing match point, I just told myself not to give the match away easily and to keep trying. I held on to that mindset, and I'm very happy I could win in the end."
Guo will next play Katie Volynets of the United States, who ranks 88th in the world.
Wang dropped the opening set against the 17-year-old Pohankova despite clawing back from 0-3. Both players held serve to 6-6, and Pohankova took the tiebreak 7-2. The second set followed the same script to 6-6, but Wang erased a 2-5 deficit in the tiebreak to win it 9-7 and level the match.
Pohankova broke twice in the decider, raced to a 5-1 lead and converted her first match point on serve to close out the match in two hours and 55 minutes.
Elsewhere, Zhang Shuai struggled with illness in the match against Ashlyn Krueger of the United States before losing at 6-3, 6-0.
"It's a pity to end my Wuhan singles campaign this way. To be honest, I was completely drained today. This was the best I could do," Zhang said. "I'm sorry I couldn't do better given my condition, but I didn't want to give up the chance to play in front of you, so I tried my best to finish the match."
Zhang also expressed gratitude to local audiences. "I am so grateful for your love of tennis. It's the passion of the people of Wuhan that has made Chinese tennis history," she said. It's because of your love of the sport that tennis in Hubei is so strong."
In other matches, Daria Snigur of Ukraine stunned 14th-seeded Elise Mertens 6-4, 7-5; Maria Sakkari of Greece came from behind to beat 8th-seeded Marta Kostyuk 4-6, 6-2, 6-2. Ann Li of the United States progressed to the next round when Camila Osorio of Colombia retired while trailing 6-1, 3-0. ■

China, Botswana establish comprehensive strategic cooperative partnership
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
01:23:50 CST
02:23:50 KST

Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife Peng Liyuan hold a welcome ceremony for Botswana's President Duma Gideon Boko and his wife Kaone Boko in the Northern Hall of the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, capital of China, Oct. 13, 2026. Xi held talks with Boko, who is on a state visit to China, after the welcome ceremony in Beijing on Tuesday. (Xinhua/Xie Huanchi)
BEIJING, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- During their talks in Beijing on Tuesday, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Botswana's President Duma Gideon Boko announced the elevation of bilateral relations to a comprehensive strategic cooperative partnership.
Noting that this year marks the 105th anniversary of the founding of the Communist Party of China and the 60th anniversary of Botswana's independence, Xi said the two countries' ruling parties should strengthen cooperation and deepen exchanges on governance experience.
China supports Botswana in pursuing a development path suited to its national conditions, Xi said. He called on both sides to further improve the framework for economic and trade cooperation, and tap into new opportunities created by China's zero-tariff policy for African countries that have diplomatic ties with China.
China is ready to strengthen cooperation with Botswana in the digital economy, agriculture, animal husbandry and other sectors, and to carry out the smart education project, Xi added.
On promoting China-Botswana and China-Africa mining cooperation, Xi said Africa's resources belong to Africa, and this is the premise for cooperation.
China is willing to share its own experience and help African countries formulate mining development plans tailored to their national conditions, and China will encourage Chinese enterprises to transfer green technologies suited to African conditions, Xi said.
He said China will continue to promote China-Africa mining cooperation to move up the value chain and explore affordable, sustainable and innovative financing models.
Noting that Africa's resources should not become a tool for geopolitical rivalry, Xi said China welcomes all parties' genuine contributions to Africa's development and stands ready to work with Africa to create a more enabling environment for investment and business operations.
China has lifted all its poor population out of poverty and forged a successful development path with Chinese characteristics, from which Botswana has much to learn, Boko noted.
He said that Botswana highly values its ties with China, and will firmly adhere to the one-China principle and oppose any separatist moves toward "Taiwan independence" and any external interference in China's internal affairs.
Botswana is willing to strengthen development strategy alignment with China and welcomes more Chinese enterprises to invest and do business in Botswana, said Boko.
He added that the country stands ready to maintain close coordination and cooperation with China, uphold multilateralism, strengthen the solidarity of developing countries, promote Africa-China solidarity and cooperation, and make the global governance system more inclusive and representative.
After their talks, the two heads of state jointly witnessed the signing of multiple cooperation documents covering such areas as implementing the Global Security Initiative, Belt and Road cooperation, green minerals, health, and human resources.
During Boko's state visit to China, the two sides issued a joint statement on establishing a China-Botswana comprehensive strategic cooperative partnership.
Prior to the talks, Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan held a welcome ceremony for Boko and his wife Kaone Boko in the Great Hall of the People. Xi and Peng also held a welcome banquet for them in the evening. ■

SpaceX launches resupply mission to ISS for NASA
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
01:23:30 CST
02:23:30 KST

LOS ANGELES, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- NASA and SpaceX launched a new commercial resupply mission to the International Space Station (ISS) on Tuesday, carrying scientific equipment and supplies to the orbiting laboratory.
A SpaceX Dragon spacecraft carrying about 2,860 kilograms of cargo lifted off at 6:33 a.m. Eastern Time (1033 GMT) from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in the U.S. state of Florida.
After stage separation, the Falcon 9 rocket's first-stage booster returned to Earth and landed at the Space Force station.
The Dragon spacecraft is expected to dock autonomously with the ISS at about 11 a.m. Eastern Time (1500 GMT) on Thursday, according to NASA.
The spacecraft is delivering supplies for the station's crew and a range of scientific investigations, including the final set of ISS Roll-Out Solar Arrays, hardware for manufacturing artificial retinas in microgravity, and three-dimensional heart tissue models to advance large-scale drug testing, according to NASA.
The spacecraft is scheduled to remain at the space station until mid-November before departing the orbiting laboratory and returning to Earth with time-sensitive research and cargo, splashing down off the coast of California.
The mission marks SpaceX's 35th commercial resupply services mission to the ISS for NASA. ■

15 states elected as members of UN Human Rights Council
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
01:23:23 CST
02:23:23 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- The General Assembly on Tuesday elected 15 states as members of the UN Human Rights Council.
Through secret ballot, Burundi, Ghana, Nigeria, Zambia (for Africa); Japan, Jordan, Kuwait, Nepal (for Asia-Pacific); Moldova, Ukraine (for Eastern Europe); Brazil, the Dominican Republic, Uruguay (for Latin America and the Caribbean); Germany, Ireland (for Western Europe and other states) were elected.
The 15 states will serve three-year terms starting Jan. 1, 2027.
All 15 candidates were running unchallenged this year.
Burundi, Ghana, Japan, Kuwait, Brazil, and the Dominican Republic were re-elected.
The Geneva-based Human Rights Council is an intergovernmental body responsible for promoting and protecting all human rights around the world. It comprises 47 member states, with about one-third of its membership replaced each year through staggered three-year terms to ensure continuity.
To ensure equitable geographical representation, the council's seats are allocated among five regional groups: 13 for African States, 13 for Asia-Pacific States, six for Eastern European States, eight for Latin American and Caribbean States, and seven for Western European and other States. ■

Chinese President Xi Jinping meets with President of the Council of Ministers of Togo Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé, who is on an official visit to China, at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, capital of China, Oct. 13, 2026. (Xinhua/Li Xiang)
BEIJING, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping met with President of the Council of Ministers of Togo Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé in Beijing on Tuesday, during which the two leaders announced the elevation of bilateral relations to a China-Togo community with a shared future for the new era.
Xi pointed out that the traditional China-Togo friendship was personally forged by leaders of an older generation of both countries, enjoying a solid foundation and growing ever stronger with the passage of time. China and Togo share aligned visions for friendly cooperation and enjoy broad prospects ahead, Xi said.
Xi called on the two sides to further enhance exchanges at all levels between the two parties and the two countries, deepen the sharing of experiences in governance, and firmly support each other on issues concerning core interests and major concerns.
China welcomes Togo to effectively utilize measures such as China's zero-tariff policy and the "green channel" for products exported to China, further enhance its role as a regional hub for trade and logistics, and facilitate the entry of more distinctive local and regional products into the Chinese market, Xi added.
Xi noted that China appreciates Togo's efforts to expand the cross-border use of the RMB and is willing to strengthen cooperation with Togo in new energy, digital intelligence and other fields to support Togo's industrialization process.
Noting that China and Togo share similar positions on international and regional affairs, Xi also called on the two sides to enhance multilateral coordination.
Xi put forward four principles for the constructive participation of all parties in the settlement of hotspot issues in Africa.
First, adhering to the principle of "Africa-led." The African people are the true masters of Africa and should play a central role in regional affairs, Xi said.
Second, upholding fairness and justice. All participating parties should abide by the purposes and principles of the United Nations Charter and respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the countries concerned, he noted.
Third, promoting ceasing hostilities for peace. Wars and unilateral sanctions cannot fundamentally resolve conflicts between countries. It is imperative to uphold mutual respect, conduct extensive consultations, seek common ground while shelving differences, and practice mutual understanding and accommodation.
Fourth, addressing both symptoms and root causes. Efforts should focus on immediate security while planning for long-term development, Xi said.
Faure, who is on an official visit to China, said that during his visit, he personally witnessed the remarkable achievements of Chinese modernization and the extensive promotion of fine traditional Chinese culture under the leadership of President Xi, and gained a deeper understanding of China's governance philosophy and the key to success.
Noting that next year marks the 55th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations between the two countries, he said Togo is willing to enhance mutual trust with China, strengthen dialogue and communication, deepen enduring and mutually beneficial cooperation to jointly build a Togo-China community with a shared future for the new era, and better benefit the two peoples.
The Togolese side fully agrees with the important principles proposed by President Xi for the constructive participation of all parties in the settlement of hotspot issues in Africa, Faure said.
He expressed Togolese appreciation for China on its significant role in maintaining world peace and stability and jointly addressing global challenges, as well as the willingness to strengthen multilateral cooperation with China, jointly uphold multilateralism, and safeguard the interests of developing countries. ■

Israel bans fiber-optic drones in its airspace over security threats
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
01:23:13 CST
02:23:13 KST

JERUSALEM, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Israel announced Tuesday a ban on the operation of drones controlled by fiber-optic cables or cellular SIM cards throughout its airspace.
The decision was approved by Defense Minister Israel Katz and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the security cabinet, a statement by Katz's office said.
The statement said the move was prompted by "specific intelligence and growing threats from enemies from within and outside," including drone attacks, attempted attacks on senior officials, intelligence gathering and smuggling.
The directive is set to take effect on Sunday and remain in force for six months, providing a temporary security measure while additional solutions are developed, it added.
The ban includes specific exemptions for drones operated by security agencies or on their behalf, as well as ground-tethered fiber-optic drones and SIM-controlled drones that have received the necessary authorization from Israel's Civil Aviation Authority.
The move is part of a broader series of Israeli measures aimed at countering drone-related threats, including import restrictions and regulatory measures. ■

QINGDAO, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- China won one gold and one bronze medal as the 2026 World Rowing Coastal Championships concluded Tuesday in Qingdao, Shandong Province.
Zhang Yuanyuan and Sun Luping claimed gold in the women's double sculls, while compatriots Long Zhentao and Yang Yujiao took bronze in the mixed double sculls.
Zhang and Sun made a strong start in the women's double sculls final, establishing an early lead before maintaining their advantage to the finish. The pair avoided collisions involving rival crews around the turning buoys to secure the title.
"The waves were really big during the race, and at one point I wasn't sure how things would turn out. But we performed well throughout, and I'm proud that we were able to win for our country," Sun said.
Zhang said the race demanded quick decisions when navigating the turning buoys, adding that winning a world title in her home province of Shandong made the achievement particularly special.
Americans Kory Rogers and Christopher Bak won the men's double sculls, overcoming challenging wind conditions.
"You can't tell on camera, but the wind is really strong today; the surface of the water is pretty flat, but you really felt that heavy, heavy wind," Bak said.
"We kept pushing. You never know what can happen on a buoy."
France's Alexis Fortier produced a late comeback to win the men's solo title, edging Bak by just 0.79 seconds after recovering from an early setback.
"I was involved in a clash at the second buoy and I lost some ground, then I managed to catch up person by person and got past," Fortier said. "I never gave up and carried on to the finish. It went well and I'm very happy."
The United States also won the women's solo and women's coxed quadruple sculls titles, while Italy took gold in the men's coxed quadruple sculls and Finland prevailed in the mixed double sculls.
The United States topped the medal table with three golds and two silvers and received the national federation trophy.
Qingdao will next host the World Rowing Beach Sprint Finals, beginning October 18.
Beach sprint rowing, which combines a running start on the beach with a short rowing course, will make its Olympic debut at the 2028 Los Angeles Games. ■

Americans urged to reconsider travel to Saudi Arabia over Iranian, Houthi attack threats

02:22:34 KST

The US Mission in Saudi Arabia on Tuesday urged Americans to reconsider travel to the kingdom, citing risks from Iranian and Houthi missile and drone attacks, armed conflict and terrorism, Anadolu reports.
In a post on US social media company X, the mission shared a travel advisory maintaining Saudi Arabia at Level 3, or reconsider travel, while designating the area along the Yemen border Level 4, or do not travel.
The US travel advisory system has two lower levels: Level 1, which calls for normal precautions and Level 2 for increased caution.
Under the advisory, US government employees working in Saudi Arabia require special authorization to use any airport in the country and are prohibited from traveling within 20 miles (32 kilometers) of the Yemeni border. They also require special authorization to travel to the provinces of Jizan, Asir and Najran, as well as the cities of Qatif, Taif and Yanbu.
The mission advised Americans in Saudi Arabia to take similar precautions.
The advisory said that since the outbreak of hostilities between the US and Iran on Feb. 28, there has been an ongoing threat of drone and missile attacks from Iran. It said commercial flights remain operational from Saudi Arabia but have at times faced significant disruptions.
It said Iran and the Iran-backed Houthis have launched missile and drone attacks into Saudi Arabia, targeting cities, infrastructure, airports, military bases, diplomatic sites and energy facilities.
The advisory said falling debris from intercepted missiles and drones also poses a risk and warned US citizens against photographing, filming or sharing information about interceptions or affected sites.
READ: Saudi-led coalition launches airstrikes on Houthi positions in Yemen’s Sanaa
It cited terrorism, exit bans and the enforcement of Saudi laws governing social media activity among the risks facing travelers.
The advisory follows security alerts issued by the US Embassy in Saudi Arabia in recent days amid attacks and threats targeting the kingdom.
The embassy renewed its security alert on Monday for a third consecutive day following attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and an attack targeting King Fahd International Airport in Dammam.
The embassy warned of possible flight cancellations, airspace closures and other travel disruptions and urged US citizens to exercise caution at major airports.
Saudi authorities have reported missile and drone attacks targeting airports and other sites in the kingdom in recent days, while the Houthis have threatened further attacks on Saudi airports and oil facilities.
A Saudi-led coalition, meanwhile, has intensified military operations against Houthi positions in Yemen, including airstrikes in the capital, Sanaa.

Cholera cases surge in Yemen as conflict intensifies, WHO says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
17:18:45 UTC
02:18:45 KST

Cholera cases surge in Yemen as conflict intensifies, WHO says
Yemen has reported 8,034 suspected cases and 27 deaths this year, with a quarter of cases from the last four weeks.
Suspected cholera cases in Yemen have tripled in the past three weeks, the World Health Organization (WHO) warns, as civilians continue to escape renewed fighting and seek safety in unsanitary camps.
Ramped-up combat, which has pushed more than 200,000 people to flee their homes, drove suspected cases from 217 in the week of September 6-12 to 647 in the week of September 27 to October 3, the WHO said in a report on Tuesday.
“Families fleeing conflict are now facing another threat from diseases that can be prevented and treated,” said Annette Heinzelmann, the UN agency’s emergency director for the region.
“Without urgent funding and unimpeded access to safe water, vaccination and essential health services, outbreaks could spread rapidly among already vulnerable communities.”
Yemen had reported 8,034 suspected cases and 27 deaths this year, with a quarter of the suspected cases occurring in the last four weeks, the WHO said.
Five governorates hosting large numbers of displaced people in the southwest – Abyan, Lahij, al-Dhalea, Taiz and Aden – account for 92 percent of reported cases. The disease has also reached remote displacement camps in Hadramout in the country’s east that are particularly difficult for medical teams to access.
Emergency response underfunded
Cholera has ebbed and flowed for years as the conflict in Yemen has continued. In 2024, the WHO warned that the country was facing the “highest burden” of a global cholera outbreak. In 2017, a wave of the disease infected hundreds of thousands and killed at least 2,000.
Yemen was already suffering one of the “world’s worst humanitarian crises” and has seen an escalation of food insecurity and disease since fighting reignited between the Houthis and the government in July, shattering four years of fragile calm.
Cholera is an acute intestinal infection that spreads through food and water contaminated with the bacterium Vibrio cholerae, often from faeces. It causes severe diarrhoea, vomiting and muscle cramps.
Contracting the illness can be deadly when not treated with oral rehydration or antibiotics for more severe cases.
The Geneva-based WHO said it had only secured $3.78m of the $31m needed for its 90-day emergency response in Yemen.
The funding is intended to help expand disease surveillance in displacement sites, deploy rapid response teams, strengthen cholera treatment and improve infection prevention in health facilities and cholera treatment sites.

Greta Thunberg joins French student protests amid police clashes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
17:18:00 UTC
02:18:00 KST

Swedish activist Greta Thunberg joined French high school students protesting poor learning conditions Tuesday, as largely peaceful demonstrations were disrupted by clashes with police, who used tear gas to disperse crowds amid reports of thrown projectiles.
Four weeks into nationwide protests over teacher shortages, classroom overcrowding and dilapidated school buildings, more than 161,000 people took to the streets of major cities, according to interior ministry figures. That was down from 266,000 on a similar day of action a week ago.
The government has pledged to address the protesters' grievances, but with public finances already strained and borrowing costs at decades-high levels, it has limited options to invest in public services despite pressure from the streets.
The day started with pupils clustered outside schools with placards and megaphones. In Saint-Denis, a working-class suburb north of Paris, Thunberg joined one of the gatherings.
"We are inspired by the young people who are demanding their basic rights," she told reporters outside Lycee Paul Eluard, one of the schools where the protest movement first gained traction.
"Whether it's not funding schools enough, or the climate crisis, or social injustice crises ... it's about time that young people are stepping up and reclaiming that future."
In front of Paris City Hall, a youth orchestra played Antonin Dvorak's "New World Symphony." Some musicians had protest stickers on their cellos and violins.
The education ministry said 214 schools were closed, down from 800 on a similar protest day a week ago. It said 94.2% of high schools were open.
Six months out from a presidential election that polls suggest could usher in the first far-right government since World War Two, the youth protests, which have been supported by the left, have added to a sense of uncertainty and polarisation.
While most demonstrators marched peacefully on Tuesday, riot police charged and fired tear gas in locations in Paris, Lyon, Strasbourg and Nantes, while a fringe of protesters lit fires, vandalised property and hurled objects at police.
In central Paris, at least one car was set on fire during running confrontations between police and protesters down a central, tree-lined avenue.
In Lyon, the local authorities asked organisers to call off a march after a group of "hostile individuals" preceding the main procession vandalised shops and a petrol station and clashed with police.
While there was no immediate information on who was involved, it is not uncommon in France for street protests to attract so-called "casseurs", a fringe of rioters who seek to confront police and destroy property.
The protest movement and the police response have elicited polarised responses from leading contenders to replace Emmanuel Macron in next year's election.
Hard-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon, who has a chance of reaching the runoff according to polls, joined one of the marches in Paris, where young protesters chanted his name.
"The police are losing their breath running after young people to beat them up and injure them," he said in a post on X.
"The only ones not losing their breath are the young people bravely protesting," he added, accusing the media of failing to show the extent of police brutality.
Far-right leader Marine Le Pen, the frontrunner in the presidential race according to polls, has denounced violence by protesters and called for those who have damaged schools - or their parents if they are minors - to pay for repairs.
The government has already introduced a bill that would allow precisely that. It is going through parliament.

Mass rallies across France back students protesting school conditions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
17:18:00 UTC
02:18:00 KST

Tens of thousands of demonstrators took to the streets across France on Tuesday in solidarity with high school students demanding better learning conditions, intensifying pressure on President Emmanuel Macron as he approaches the end of his term.
Some 161,500 people turned out, according to the interior ministry – more than double the 71,500 it gave for the last nationwide demonstrations on Thursday last week.
Unions helping organize Tuesday's rallies put the countrywide turnout at 480,000.
The numbers suggested snowballing street opposition to the government just six months before France votes for a successor to Macron, who is completing his maximum second mandate.
On Saturday, national demonstrations against the spiralling cost of living are to take place, and unions and student groups see the two protest currents fusing together.
The agitation comes as Macron's centrist government struggles to get a cost-cutting budget through parliament, in the teeth of worsening debt that has spooked the bond market.
Although most of Tuesday's demonstrations were peaceful, violence occurred on the sidelines of one of two marches in Paris, where the interior ministry said 41,500 people participated.
AFP journalists saw some cars set on fire and police fired tear gas as masked youths tried to erect barricades across roads and threw objects. Tear gas was also fired during a demonstration in Lyon.
Among those taking part in a demonstration in the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis was Swedish activist Greta Thunberg. She said she was there because "our future is being robbed".
University students were prominent in Tuesday's demonstrations, alongside teachers and union leaders.
They were also backed by far-left opposition France Unbowed (LFI) party, whose chief, presidential hopeful Jean-Luc Melenchon, was seen among crowds in Paris.
Thousands also marched in the cities of Nantes, Lyon, Lens, Strasbourg, Toulouse, Bordeaux and Marseille, according to police and AFP reporters.
"We stand in solidarity with the high schools that are worse off. We need real measures and proper dialogue, not repression," said 16-year-old Emeline, outside a Marseille school.
"We're here because we really feel we're not being heard by the government," said Nina, 17.
The student movement sprang up last month, with teenagers at France's lycees – high schools for those aged 15 to 18 – blocking the entrances to many schools to demand better classroom conditions.
Perceived heavy-handed reactions from police against the students drove many to join Tuesday's demonstrations.
One teen lost his hand when he picked up a police stun grenade during the protests, while another lost an eye, and another teeth when an officer fired a tear gas canister in his face.
Police have opened internal investigations into 34 allegations of violence against demonstrators.
Some 147 teaching staff have been injured in the protests, the education ministry said.
"We're not giving up the fight, whether it's for the high school students who were hit with a harsh crackdown, or for denouncing police violence," said Patricia, a 20-year-old university student in Paris who did not give her last name.
Some Indian tourists who wandered into the Paris demonstration said they were unnerved.
"Initially we were terrified," said Snehil Jain, a 45-year-old visiting Paris for a week with his wife.
"We had seen the media images of violence around these protests. But then we saw it was a peaceful protest, so we were OK then."
France's education ministry said 214 schools, mostly high schools, were closed Tuesday.
University student union l'Union Etudiante reported 90% of universities had closed nationwide to show support.
French students say they are determined to press their demands over absent teachers, dilapidated buildings, overcrowded schedules and other grievances.
They have dismissed a government pledge – made after last week's demonstrations – to send 3,000 substitute teachers to the 114 worst-affected schools.
"We are continuing the blockades. We are not budging," said Naouel, a high school student in Brest. She said she hoped the protests would continue after the half-term holidays, in late October.
Mariolino, a 16-year-old in Nantes, concurred. "Those who think the anger will disappear with the holidays just don't get it," he said.
On Monday, Macron had urged restraint from protesters, saying the issues "deserve time, consultations, discussion and respect".

English football regulator chief vows to resign if there is political interference in Manchester City case

Efe Özkan
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
The chairman of England’s Independent Football Regulator (IFR), David Kogan, said on Tuesday that he would resign if he faced political interference over the future of Manchester City.
Kogan, who has the authority to assess the suitability of football club owners and executives, stressed the regulator’s independence amid scrutiny about the Premier League club’s ownership.
An independent commission is considering allegations that Manchester City breached Premier League financial rules. If the findings are upheld, the IFR could be required to determine whether the club should be forced to change ownership.
Kogan was asked about Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s comments that he would be “really concerned” if Manchester City’s Abu Dhabi owners decided to sell the club.
"We are independent. That is in the name. I am the chairman of the Independent Football Regulator and independence absolutely runs through everything we're doing,” said Kogan.
"And no politician has tried to influence and would try to influence anything we do on that,” he said, adding that he would resign in such a case.
An independent Premier League commission found Manchester City guilty of serious financial rule breaches between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons, including arranging "sham" contracts with commercial partners to artificially inflate revenue.
The club appealed the ruling, rejecting the allegations and maintaining innocence. Sanctions have yet to be determined.

Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani on Tuesday accused Israel of supporting armed militias operating outside state authority in the southern city of Suwayda, providing them with weapons and money to carry out an “agenda of chaos” in the region.
Al-Shaibani made the remarks at a joint news conference in Damascus with Sabrina Dallafior, director-general of the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW), according to the Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA).
He accused Israel of seeking to destabilize Syria since December 2024, when the Assad regime was toppled, through attacks on infrastructure and the occupation of additional Syrian territory.
The minister also accused Israeli forces of forcibly displacing Syrians and carrying out arbitrary arrests, saying the fate of dozens of Syrian detainees remains unknown.
Al-Shaibani called on the international community to halt Israeli actions threatening to plunge the region into chaos, and urged a return to the 1974 disengagement agreement, allowing UN forces to implement it.
He urged Israel to engage seriously in US-sponsored negotiations that he said have been underway for a year and a half, stressing Damascus’ commitment to reaching an agreement that respects Syria’s security and sovereignty.
Israel has occupied most of Syria’s Golan Heights since 1967. Following the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s regime, Israeli forces seized the demilitarized buffer zone and expanded their presence in southern Syria.
The 1974 disengagement agreement established a UN-monitored buffer zone between Syrian and Israeli forces.
Syria and Israel have held several rounds of US-mediated talks aimed at reducing tensions, halting Israeli military operations and reaching a security agreement.
In August, Syrian and Israeli delegations met in Jordan under US mediation to discuss measures to halt Israeli attacks, arrests and military operations, as well as the withdrawal of Israeli forces to positions held before December 2024.

Votes without power: What future for Palestinians in Israel?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
17:11:56 UTC
02:11:56 KST

Breadcrumb
Votes without power: What future for Palestinian citizens in Israel?
East Jerusalem - Israel's general election on 27 October, which will fill all 120 seats in the Knesset, is widely seen as a referendum on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
But it is also a contest over the political standing of Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up about a fifth of the population, the descendants of those who stayed on their land during the 1948 Nakba.
Their votes may decide which coalition bloc eventually governs, yet nearly every major Israeli party is working to keep them out of any future government.
“In the dominant political discourse, Israelis often address Arab citizens as subjects, not as equal citizens,” Raafat al-Jawabra, a researcher on Israeli affairs, tells The New Arab.
Most Israeli parties, he argues, do not see Palestinian citizens as a natural political partner, instead using them in their campaigns as a subject for fear and mobilisation.
Ahmad al-Safadi, a Jerusalem-based analyst of Israeli politics, says the problem goes beyond the Israeli right and far-right parties and their electoral campaigns.
Israeli parties, including those on the left, treat the Palestinian vote as a way to strengthen their own electoral base rather than as the voice of a community whose crises of crime, poverty, unemployment, and discrimination need clear policy answers.
The numbers explain why their vote matters. A recent poll by local Channel 12 puts the bloc led by former army chief Gadi Eisenkot and Netanyahu's coalition level at 52 seats each, with Palestinian parties on 12.
Salim Brik, a political scientist who researches Israeli parliamentary and party politics, argues that if Palestinian turnout rises above 65 percent, it could reshape the distribution of seats, possibly to the point where a list allied with Netanyahu fails to cross the electoral threshold.
That arithmetic has shaped the campaign. Netanyahu's Likud and Bezalel Smotrich's Religious Zionism have largely dropped conventional persuasion on the economy, the cost of living, and post-war reconstruction.
They are instead campaigning on the fear of Palestinian citizens and a promise of territorial "Judaisation" in the Galilee and the Negev (Naqab).
If Palestinian participation could decide the outcome, then delegitimising Palestinian citizens and casting any government that relies on them as a security risk serve the same goal.
An election built on exclusion
The clearest expression of this logic was the attempt to remove Palestinian parties from the ballot. In September, the Central Elections Committee, made up of lawmakers, voted to disqualify the United Arab List (Ra'am) and the Joint List.
Likud and its far-right allies backed the move, accusing both parties of supporting armed struggle and rejecting Israel's status as a Jewish state.
Last week, the Supreme Court unanimously reversed the decision, as it has done with similar disqualifications before. But the campaign still produced a result.
Sami Abu Shehadeh, leader of Balad, withdrew his candidacy after justices signalled they were ready to disqualify him over an article he wrote on 8 October 2023. He denied supporting Hamas or the attack.
Itamar Ben-Gvir, who led the case against him, called the withdrawal a victory. Adalah, the legal centre for Palestinian citizens, called the whole effort an attempt to delegitimise Palestinian citizens and their representatives.
According to al-Safadi, the attempts by Netanyahu and his religious right allies to push Palestinian parties out of politics have failed. He also sees a risk for the right. Continuing this rhetoric may lead Palestinian citizens to see the election as a direct confrontation with policies aimed at their political presence.
“Anti-Arab rhetoric could end up increasing turnout among people who now believe their exclusion will affect their daily lives and their place in their own towns,” he argues.
This would reverse a recent trend. Al-Safadi says the racism that followed 7 October, the war on Gaza and military operations in the West Bank depressed Palestinian participation in earlier votes. The same pressures, now accumulated, may push voters the other way.
This is where the right's strategy becomes risky. Recent polling has shown Smotrich's party struggling to clear the threshold, and he has moved further to the fringe by announcing a joint slate with Zehut (Identity) chairman Moshe Feiglin. Netanyahu has warned that a divided right in 1992 led to "the Oslo disaster", Yasser Arafat, and Hamas.
Brik's analysis shows why these warnings matter. In a race this close, a far-right list falling just below the threshold would remove a block of seats from Netanyahu's camp. Higher Palestinian turnout is one of the few factors that could cause that.
“Influencing which lists survive,” Brik says, “is one of the main electoral tools available to Arab parties”.
Al-Safadi adds in this regard that “Arab parties have also strengthened their position through joint electoral frameworks and surplus-vote agreements, which can give them more weight when seats are allocated”.
The fear campaign is therefore aimed at two audiences. To Jewish-Israeli voters, it presents Palestinian citizens as a threat to be contained. Its effect on Palestinian voters is less certain: it could discourage them from voting, or it could mobilise them.
The demographic battle for land inside Israel
The second pillar of the campaign turns long-standing state policy into a campaign pledge. Judaisation programmes, land allocation to Jewish communities, and demolitions in unrecognised villages have a long institutional history, and since 7 October they have been recast as security measures.
With Smotrich in control of settlement-related portfolios, the line between ministerial policy and campaign promise has largely disappeared. The rhetoric of settling "inside the Green Line" brings the logic of West Bank settlement into Israel proper.
The Green Line refers to the 1949 armistice demarcation line drawn after the Arab-Israeli War.
Brik places these issues at the centre of Palestinian citizens' concerns, especially in the Negev, where unrecognised Bedouin villages face problems of planning, land, and demolitions.
He points to the positions of Smotrich and Ben-Gvir, tensions in Palestinian towns such as Majd al-Kurum, and rhetoric about strengthening the Jewish presence in the Galilee and taking control of land owned or used by Palestinian citizens.
These issues, he says, will be on the agenda of any government that includes Netanyahu, Smotrich, and Ben-Gvir.
Al-Safadi ranks land as “the issue gaining the most importance among Arab voters”. Many Palestinians, he says, see what is happening inside Israel, in Jerusalem and in the West Bank as part of the same struggle over land, presence and control.
He argues that the targeting of Palestinian homes and continued planning restrictions and demolitions may strengthen collective action within the community to hold on to the land.
In this framing, land stops being a matter of planning and becomes a question about the limits of citizenship.
How different is Israel's opposition?
The Israeli opposition offers no real alternative. Ra'am made history in 2021 as the first independent Palestinian party to join an Israeli governing coalition, in the government that briefly removed Netanyahu.
Al-Jawabra's reading of the current field suggests the alternative is narrow. Most Jewish-Israeli parties, he says, still reject a government that depends on Palestinian parties, and 7 October marked a turning point in rhetoric that delegitimises Palestinian political participation.
Netanyahu's camp is the most hostile, but al-Jawabra sees no fundamental difference between Avigdor Lieberman and Netanyahu, Smotrich or Ben-Gvir on alliances with Palestinian parties.
Eisenkot has said he does not want such an alliance, though his tone is softer. He has also not ruled out working with Ra'am, while denying reports that he promised it a place in government.
Al-Jawabra names only Yair Golan, leader of the Democrats, as a prominent Israeli politician openly willing to cooperate and ally with Palestinian parties.
The result is that one camp campaigns against Palestinian citizens, and the other campaigns around them.
Votes without power
Even a strong Palestinian result may not translate into power. Brik argues that Palestinian parties have so far failed to turn their parliamentary weight into real bargaining power on land, settlements, and civil rights.
With most Jewish parties refusing to rely on them as direct coalition partners, they may end up as "a partner from outside" rather than a central part of government.
Al-Safadi warns of a return to marginalisation if competing Jewish parties can build coalitions that do not need Arab support, however many seats Palestinian parties win.
That is the central contradiction of this election. Palestinian votes may be needed to block one camp from reaching 61, while the government that forms keeps Palestinian parties at a distance.
Higher Arab turnout increases the community's potential influence, but it does not ensure that Jewish parties will treat it as a coalition partner.
For Palestinian citizens, the vote is a test of their position inside Israel's political system: whether their electoral weight becomes political influence, or whether their votes remain a number in the calculations of Jewish parties.
For residents of the Galilee, the Negev, and Jerusalem, the answer will depend less on the results than on what the next government does about land, demolitions, and planning, and on whether issues of rights and equality reach its agenda or are again postponed behind security and demography.
Monjed Jadou is a Palestinian journalist and founder of Palestine News Network (PNN), an independent Palestinian media network. He has contributed to international and regional media outlets. His work focuses on Palestinian affairs, independent journalism, media freedom, and promoting the principles of editorial independence and professional journalism in Palestine
