Energy security a question of time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:39:16 UTC
01:39:16 KST

On Oct. 5, Saudi Aramco chief executive officer Amin Nasser warned that the world’s oil stocks were “scarily thin.”
For most countries, that means higher prices. For Taiwan, which imports almost all of its fuel, it raises a more basic question: How long can it keep its power on if supplies are cut?
Taiwan holds more than 140 days of crude oil, but its natural gas, which generated 47.8 percent of its electricity last year, would last about 11 days. Japan, by comparison, holds roughly two months of gas.
After the US-Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb. 28, shipping through the Strait of Hormuz collapsed and Qatar, Taiwan’s second-largest gas supplier, stopped production. In April and May, no gas cargoes reached Taiwan from Qatar or the United Arab Emirates. Refiners rerouted oil through Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea ports and bought more from the US.
To keep the power on, Taiwan bought gas on the spot market, where single cargoes are sold to the highest bidder. Spot purchases rose from about 30 percent of supply to between 60 and 65 percent, and the price Taiwan paid rose by about 70 percent. Electricity prices for large industrial users rose 41.58 percent, while the government absorbed three-quarters of fuel cost increases for households.
It worked, at a high cost to industry and public finances, but it might be harder to repeat.
For one thing, a tight oil market also makes gas more expensive. That might seem odd, as oil and gas are different fuels, but most of the long-term contracts that supply gas to Asia, including those from Qatar and Australia, do not fix a price in advance. Instead, the price of each gas shipment is set by a formula tied to the price of crude oil: When oil rises, gas bought under those contracts rises with it. Taiwan is no exception. CPC Corp, Taiwan, the state-run importer, has said its gas import price formulas are “traditionally linked to crude oil prices,” using Brent crude or the average price of crude imported into Japan as the benchmark.
Australia and Qatar, which together supplied two-thirds of Taiwan’s gas last year, sell mainly on such oil-linked terms.
Aramco estimates that refilling the world’s oil stocks will add about 2 million barrels a day to demand for at least 18 months, keeping oil prices high. Taken together, that means Taiwan will pay more even for gas it has already secured under contract, adding to costs that CPC cannot pass on to consumers.
The Hormuz crisis is not over. Qatar has extended its suspension into early December and its main export plant at Ras Laffan, damaged in March, is still running at reduced capacity. Even when the strait reopens, supply will take time to recover.
Taiwan is entering winter without the supplier that provided one-third of its gas last year.
The short gas buffer matters for Taiwan in three ways:
The first is economic. Gas generates nearly half of Taiwan’s electricity, so a shortage would quickly become a power problem for industry, including the chipmakers at the heart of its economy. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC) alone uses about 9 percent of Taiwan’s electricity.
The second is fiscal. This year’s shortfall was covered by paying more, and the bill has landed on CPC and the treasury: a projected NT$56 billion (US$1.75 billion) loss for CPC this year and a request for supplementary public funding.
The third is political. The 11-day figure has already been used against Taiwan. In March, posts on Chinese social media claimed that Taiwan was about to run out of gas and officials replied with general assurances rather than figures.
A thin buffer is a vulnerability that others can exploit, even when supply holds.
The government knows the problem. It set a target of 14 days of gas reserves in 2018 and Qatar’s share of CPC’s gas supply has fallen to 11 percent this year.
However, three obstacles have slowed efforts to build a larger gas buffer.
The first is storage. Gas tanks need a port terminal, land, distance from homes, local consent and environmental approval. Planners moved the third terminal, at Guantang Industrial Port (觀塘工業港) in Taoyuan’s Guanyin District (觀音), offshore to protect the Datan algal reef, and it began commercial operations only last year. The fourth faces land contamination problems and the fifth is behind schedule.
Because Taiwan can store so little, it needs about 30 gas carriers to arrive every month, so any delay at sea quickly eats into its reserves.
The second is money. CPC must hold down domestic prices and secure fuel abroad. It expects its seventh straight annual loss this year, with debts above 90 percent of its assets. That makes cheaper, more secure long-term contracts harder to sign.
The third is competition from neighbors. In March, Minister of Economic Affairs Kung Ming-hsin (龔明鑫) said gas swaps with Japan and South Korea were difficult because “everyone is scrambling for cargoes.” Japan and South Korea have since expanded swaps with each other. The Energy Administration has said that Taiwan is open to holding gas reserves in Japan or South Korea, provided the gas can still reach Taiwan when needed.
Three steps could help. The first would be to explore whether CPC’s two roles can be separated. It means funding household price support openly from the budget, as the supplementary funding CPC has requested would partly do, so that the company can focus on securing supply.
The second would be to give storage projects a clear timetable. Environmental and local concerns are legitimate, but regulators could review terminal projects within a fixed time limit, reducing costs and delays.
The third would be to publish the gas reserve regularly. A regularly published figure for days of gas held would make claims like those in March easier to answer and let the public follow progress toward the 14-day target.
Mihir Shete is an academic at National Chengchi University.

Nangang Station leading source of emissions: TRC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:39:14 UTC
01:39:14 KST

Taipei Railway Corp (TRC) has disclosed its latest greenhouse gas emissions report, with Nangang Station — not Taipei Railway Station as many assumed — listed as its largest source of emissions.
TRC launched its sustainability program in 2024, establishing a greenhouse gas inventory as the first step toward achieving net zero emissions, it said on Tuesday last week.
The company conducted an initial inventory of 32 major stations, established an emissions management system and obtained carbon-footprint labels for three of its passenger services: the Tze-Chiang Limited Express, the Chu-Kuang Express and local trains.
Photo: CNA
Last year, TRC expanded the inventory to cover all 613 operating sites, maintenance facilities, offices and ancillary facilities.
Train operations accounted for 75.1 percent of its total carbon emissions, while station operations contributed 15.6 percent, Sustainability Development Section chief Peng Hsien-fu (彭賢富) said.
TRC’s emissions reached 428,400 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (tCO2e) last year, with train and station operations accounting for about 90 percent of the total, he said.
All five stations with the highest emissions are in the six special municipalities.
Nangang Station ranked first with 6,923.95tCO2e, followed by Taipei Station ranked second with 6,859.48tCO2e, Kaohsiung Station with 5,793.22tCO2e, Banqiao Station with 5,362.84tCO2e and Songshan Station with 4,268.61tCO2e.
Among maintenance facilities, Fugang Maintenance Depot in Taoyuan had the highest emissions at 3,474.97tCO2e, followed by Hsinchu Maintenance Depot at 2,491.51tCO2e, Qidu Maintenance Depot in Keelung at 2,473.9tCO2e, Taipei Maintenance Depot at 1,986.78tCO2e and Kaohsiung Maintenance Depot at 1,814.75tCO2e.
TRC is introducing more energy-efficient trains, regenerative braking systems, smart maintenance and digital management to reduce emissions, Peng said.
The company is also integrating operating and equipment data through its SOPHIA cloud platform to improve energy and equipment management, he said.
From 2019 to last year, TRC issued 55.36 million mobile tickets, reducing emissions by a cumulative 341tCO2e and saving NT$55.36 million (US$1.73 million) in printing costs, Peng said.
TRC has also installed solar power facilities at its stations, maintenance depots and rolling-stock bases. It has leased out 73 sites for solar installations, with a combined capacity of 40.6 megawatts.
The facilities generate about 60.44 million kilowatt-hours of electricity annually, enough to supply about 16,200 households, it said.
The company has set a target of reducing its carbon emissions by 3 percent by 2028.

====================================================================================================

Reject the merger of Grab and Foodpanda
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:39:12 UTC
01:39:12 KST

Southeast Asian food delivery platform Grab Holdings Ltd in March applied to acquire Delivery Hero SE’s Foodpanda operations in Taiwan, with the Fair Trade Commission (FTC) scheduled to announce its decision on Oct. 27.
On the surface, the deal is a business merger — but in substance, it involves personal data, national geospatial information and digital sovereignty. It cannot be assessed solely in terms of market share and price competition.
Grab has extensive and long-standing connections to Chinese capital. In 2015, Chinese ride-hailing firm Didi Chuxing and China Investment Corp, a sovereign wealth fund, invested in Grab. Grab invested in Chinese autonomous-driving firms WeRide and Momenta, and formed a joint venture with Ping An Good Doctor in 2018, integrating artificial intelligence (AI), identity, medical and payment data.
Grab signed a memorandum of cooperation with Huawei Technologies Co’s Petal Maps last year, and integrated electric vehicle systems with BYD Co and Guangzhou Automobile Group Co. It has worked with Ant Group Co on cross-border payments since 2016, deepening the partnership in 2023 through travel assistant Alipay+ Voyager.
Map data have national security implications. Through delivery workers’ GPS locations and images, Grab accumulates detailed, real-time local data that are far more valuable than static maps. Articles 7 and 14 of China’s National Intelligence Law require organizations and citizens to support and assist intelligence work. Even if Grab claims that its partnership with Huawei does not cover Taiwan, the nation has no way to verify whether data could be fully isolated from China following the acquisition.
Storing data overseas could render oversight ineffective. Grab claims that Taiwanese user data are stored in Singapore, but once data leave Taiwan, the government’s inspection powers under Article 22 of the Personal Data Protection Act (個人資料保護法) become difficult to enforce.
The government cannot verify whether data have been transferred to a third country, leaked or reused. Grab has suffered data breaches in Singapore involving account balances, license plates and home addresses. If the acquisition proceeds, the security of approximately 6 million consumers’ spending and mobility records, as well as transaction data, would be at stake.
Digital sovereignty is the foundation of a nation in the AI era. South Korea has restricted the export of high-precision map data on national security grounds since 2007, only beginning to ease the restrictions under some conditions in the past few years. Europe and the US have also strengthened controls on cross-border data flows. Those developments show that data sovereignty has become the core of national governance.
As a major tech power, Taiwan should do more to support domestic businesses rather than allow critical data to flow to overseas platforms with complex ties.
The acquisition poses risks to personal data, national geospatial information and digital sovereignty, outweighing any possible economic benefits. Article 13 of the Fair Trade Act (公平交易法) stipulates that “the competent authority may not prohibit any of mergers filed if the overall economic benefit of the merger outweighs the disadvantages resulted from competition restraint.”
The provision applies when a merger’s overall economic benefits outweigh the harm caused by reduced competition — a condition this case fails to meet.
The FTC should carefully weigh the risks and reject the acquisition.
Hsueh Hua-yuan is a professor in National Chengchi University’s Department of History and chairman of the Taiwan Association of University Professors.

The government yesterday condemned a series of attacks last week targeting King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh that resulted in deaths and civilian casualties, adding that one Taiwanese was injured in one of the attacks and hospitalized in Saudi Arabia.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs did not disclose when or where the Taiwanese was injured or their identity, citing privacy concerns.
Officials from Taiwan’s representative office in Saudi Arabia visited the person at the hospital, the ministry said.
Photo: Taipei Times
The ministry slammed the Houthis in Yemen for the series of attacks targeting civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and urged the group to immediately cease its attacks.
The ministry on Monday raised its travel alert for Saudi Arabian border regions, with Yemen on the highest level of “red,” urging people to leave the country immediately.
On Sunday, it raised the travel alert for the rest of Saudi Arabia to the second-highest level — “orange” — advising Taiwanese to avoid unnecessary travel to the country.
Taiwan’s representative office in Saudi Arabia on social media urged Taiwanese in the country to avoid travel to King Khalid International Airport.
It also urged Taiwanese to remain vigilant in the event of further attacks, follow safety instructions issued by local media and Saudi Arabian authorities, and maintain open lines of communication so the office can contact them when necessary.
In an emergency, Taiwanese in Saudi Arabia can call the representative office for assistance at +966-505-223-725, or ask family members in Taiwan to contact the ministry’s all-hours emergency hotline at 0800-085-095, the ministry said.
A missile strike by the Houthis in Yemen hit the airport on Saturday, killing 13 people and wounding hundreds. A day later, another attack killed one person and injured nearly a dozen others, said Saudi Arabian authorities, who have since announced that the airport would remain closed until Saturday.

Ministry expanding preschools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:39:11 UTC
01:39:11 KST

The Ministry of Education is allocating more than NT$500 million (US$15.58 million) this year to expand public preschool capacity amid growing demand for affordable childcare among dual-income families.
The measure is part of government efforts to alleviate the burden of parents with young children and boost the nation’s birthrate.
As of last month, Taiwan’s population had declined for 33 consecutive months, official statistics showed.
Photo: Lee Wen-te, Taipei Times
In the past, kindergartens in Taiwan accepted only children aged three or older. After the government changed the preschool system by integrating kindergartens and daycare centers in 2012, children can attend preschools from age two until they start elementary school.
However, a preschool must have a dedicated class for two-year-olds to enroll children of that age.
The Early Childhood Education and Care Act (幼兒教育及照顧法) stipulates that each preschool class for children aged two to under three may enroll no more than 16 children.
Classes with eight or fewer children must have at least one childcare and education services personnel, while those with nine or more must have at least two.
The law also stipulates that two-year-olds should not be placed in the same class as those in other age groups.
The curriculum should focus on daily care, developing self-care skills, and learning through play and exploration, while reading, writing and arithmetic instruction aimed at achieving proficiency is prohibited.
The enrollment of two-year-olds in preschool classes rose from 14.7 percent in 2016 to 64.1 percent last year, ministry data showed.
The ministry has established 600 public and quasi-public preschool classes for two-year-olds, three times its original target of adding 200 classes from 2024 to this year.
Since 2017, the government has subsidized more than 4,100 preschool classes nationwide, while the number of preschool teachers has reached 270,000, the education ministry said.
The ministry added that it is investing more than NT$500 million to increase the availability of preschools and preschool classes this year.
Wang Hui-chiu (王慧秋), a section chief of the ministry’s K-12 Education Administration, said that local governments are in charge of assessing and planning how to increase the number of preschools or preschool classes based on the number of children and teachers in each district, as well as actual enrollment, while the ministry offers subsidies to fund the increases.
“We are not asking all preschools to offer a dedicated class for two-year-olds or change the classes for children aged three to five to accommodate them. Local governments should make adjustments based on parents’ requests and other factors and consider offering classes for two-year-olds at elementary schools that have childcare facilities first,” Wang said.
Monthly fees at public preschools are capped at NT$1,000 for the first child, with second children and subsequent siblings attending for free.
At nonprofit preschools, the monthly cap is NT$2,000 for the first child, NT$1,000 for the second and free for subsequent children.
At quasi-public preschools, the caps are NT$3,000, NT$2,000 and NT$1,000 respectively, while children from low- and lower-middle-income families are exempt from fees.
Eligible families whose children do not attend public or quasi-public preschools can instead receive monthly childcare subsidies of NT$5,000 for the first child, NT$6,000 for the second and NT$7,000 for subsequent children.
Public preschools also offer extended care on weekdays and additional childcare services during winter and summer vacations, with 95 percent currently offering extended care.
Since 2021, the government has also encouraged government agencies and state-owned enterprises to set up childcare facilities for employees, with about 166 such facilities established as of this year.

INTERVIEW: Techman positive about robots’ long-term prospects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:39:08 UTC
01:39:08 KST

Techman Robot Inc (達明機器人) remains positive about humanoid robots over the long term, despite near-term hurdles that lie in technological maturity and real-world application capability, company vice president William Wang (王偉霖) said in an interview with the Taipei Times last week.
“I believe the long-term prospects for humanoid robots are very good, but there are still many challenges that need to be overcome at this stage,” Wang said at the company’s headquarters in Taoyuan’s Guishan District (龜山) on Wednesday last week.
The challenges include safety, precision, stability, cycle time, quality and payload capacity, while costs remain significantly higher than those of conventional robotic arms, he said.
Photo courtesy of Techman Robot Inc
Humanoid robots also need to be integrated with higher-level factory systems, such as manufacturing execution systems or warehouse control systems, to receive instructions on where to go and what tasks to perform, Wang said.
The company’s TM Xplore I humanoid robot, first showcased last year, can perform material handling and picking tasks, he said.
Techman plans to provide its second-generation model to some research institutions by the end of this year, Wang said.
The company looks to begin on-site trials with partners as early as the first quarter of next year, while also testing the robot at its own factories, he said.
Several semiconductor, automotive components, consumer electronics and logistics companies have expressed interest in the robot, he added.
For Techman, a robotic arm partner of Nvidia Corp, technologies developed for humanoid robots can be applied to and enhance its existing single-arm and dual-arm robotic systems, Wang said.
The company aims to use learning-based technologies to enable humanoid robots to adjust their grasping methods and trajectories according to changing environments, he said.
“After we build up these technological capabilities, we will look back and consider whether they can also be applied to certain single-arm collaborative robot applications to make them perform better,” he said.
Techman expects its collaborative robot business to grow by at least 20 percent this year from last year, supported by rising automation demand and solid market momentum, Wang said.
With continued collaborative robot demand from the semiconductor, electronics manufacturing, automotive and warehousing sectors, Techman expects revenue this year to exceed last year’s NT$1.82 billion (US$56.7 million) and is targeting double-digit growth next year, he said.
Besides strong interest from the semiconductor sector, the company is also targeting growing robot demand for artificial intelligence (AI) server assembly and inspection, Wang said.
Robot applications in AI servers include loading and unloading for surface-mount technology processes, back-end assembly and inspection, Wang said.
The company plans to start deliveries of its TM45S heavy-payload dual-arm collaborative robot unveiled in August for AI server assembly and semiconductor handling in the first quarter of next year, he said.
As the number of inspection items and quality requirements in AI server assembly processes increases, the company expects more opportunities to deploy its machine vision and AI recognition technologies, he said.
The company’s robot and vision inspection solutions are already deployed at Quanta Computer Inc’s (廣達) factories, Wang said.
It also supplies solutions to Jinpao Precision Industry Co (經寶) for rack-related operations and Accton Technology Corp (智邦) for assembly, inspection and surface-mount technology-related production processes, he said.
China accounts for about 30 percent of Techman’s total sales, followed by Taiwan and Europe at about 20 percent each, while Japan and Southeast Asia each account for about 10 percent, Wang said.
Beyond robot sales, Techman is also upbeat about the growth prospects of its in-house system integration business over the next few years, as the business provides production-line and factory-wide automation solutions, he said.

ENGLISH DIGEST 實用美語(空中美語)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:39:07 UTC
01:39:07 KST

Have you ever bought a product simply because everyone around you seemed to own one? Or have you ever supported an idea after seeing many classmates agree with it? If so, you have experienced the bandwagon effect, a psychological phenomenon in which people adopt certain behaviors, attitudes, or beliefs because others are doing the same.
The term originates from 19th-century American politics. Campaign managers would hire a bandwagon, a decorated wagon carrying musicians, to parade through towns, attracting crowds and signaling popular support. Over time, “jumping on the bandwagon” came to mean following whatever was fashionable or popular.
At its core, the bandwagon effect is driven by conformity and social pressure. Humans are inherently social creatures who seek acceptance and fear exclusion. In psychologist Solomon Asch’s well-known conformity experiments, about 75% of participants gave an obviously wrong answer at least once, simply to align with the group. The results showed how easily people may doubt their own judgment when surrounded by a confident majority. When we observe that a large number of people favor something, we tend to assume it must be correct or worthwhile. This assumption, however, is logically flawed. Popularity does not equal quality or truth.
Photo courtesy of Wikimedia Commons / 照片：維基共享資源提供
The consequences of this bias can be significant. In financial markets, it contributes to speculative bubbles, as investors rush to buy assets simply because prices are rising. In politics, polling data can sway undecided voters toward the leading candidate, making election outcomes partially self-fulfilling. In everyday consumer culture, trends spread rapidly through social media, convincing millions to purchase items they may not genuinely need. A product may appear more attractive simply because influencers, friends, or online reviews make it seem widely approved.
Resisting the bandwagon effect requires conscious effort. Before making a decision, pause and ask yourself: am I making this choice based on evidence and personal values, or am I simply following the crowd?
你是否曾經只是因為身邊所有人似乎都有某樣商品而跟著購買它？又或者你是否曾經在看到許多同學都贊同某個想法後也開始支持它？如果有，那麼你已經體驗過「從眾效應」了，這是一種心理現象，指人們因為其他人都在做同樣的事，而採納某些行為、態度或信念。
「從眾效應」一詞源自十九世紀的美國政治。當時，競選經理會雇用一輛花車（也就是載著樂手裝飾馬車）在城鎮中遊行，以吸引群眾並展現廣泛支持。久而久之，「跳上花車」逐漸演變成追隨流行或熱門事物的意思。
從根本上來說，從眾效應是受到順從心理與社會壓力驅動。人類天生是群居動物，渴望被接納且害怕被排斥。在心理學家所羅門·阿希著名的從眾實驗中，大約有75%的參與者至少曾經一次給出明顯錯誤的答案，只是為了與團體保持一致。實驗結果顯示，當被充滿自信的多數人包圍時，人們是多麼容易懷疑自己的判斷。當我們觀察到大量的人偏好某件事物時，往往會假設它必定是正確或具有價值的。然而，這樣的假設在邏輯上存在謬誤。受歡迎並不等於品質或真理。
這種偏見所造成的後果可能相當嚴重。在金融市場中，它會助長投機泡沫的形成，因為投資人僅僅看到價格上漲便爭相買進資產。在政治領域中，民調數據可能促使搖擺選民傾向於支持領先的候選人，導致選舉結果在某種程度上成為自我實現的預言。在日常消費文化中，潮流則透過社群媒體迅速傳播，說服數百萬人購買自己其實未必真正需要的商品。某項產品之所以看似更具吸引力，可能只是因為網紅、朋友或網路評論讓它看起來廣受好評。
要抵抗從眾效應需要有意識地付出努力。在做出決定之前，暫停片刻並自問：我是根據證據與個人價值觀來做出這個選擇，還是我只是單純地跟隨大眾的腳步？

這位候選人想要看起來有才智，然而他的評論顯示他對這些議題只有膚淺的了解。

Leo was reluctant at first, but his friends finally convinced him to go camping with them.
里歐一開始不願意，但他的朋友最後說服他跟他們去露營。
9. purchase v. 購買
Before the storm, the family went to the store to purchase supplies.
暴風雨來臨前，這家人到商店購買補給品。

The US Mission in Saudi Arabia on Tuesday urged Americans to reconsider travel to the kingdom, citing risks from Iranian and Houthi missile and drone attacks, armed conflict and terrorism.
In a post on US social media company X, the mission shared a travel advisory maintaining Saudi Arabia at Level 3, or reconsider travel, while designating the area along the Yemen border Level 4, or do not travel.
The US travel advisory system has two lower levels: Level 1, which calls for normal precautions and Level 2 for increased caution.
Under the advisory, US government employees working in Saudi Arabia require special authorization to use any airport in the country and are prohibited from traveling within 20 miles (32 kilometers) of the Yemeni border. They also require special authorization to travel to the provinces of Jizan, Asir and Najran, as well as the cities of Qatif, Taif and Yanbu.
The mission advised Americans in Saudi Arabia to take similar precautions.
The advisory said that since the outbreak of hostilities between the US and Iran on Feb. 28, there has been an ongoing threat of drone and missile attacks from Iran. It said commercial flights remain operational from Saudi Arabia but have at times faced significant disruptions.
It said Iran and the Iran-backed Houthis have launched missile and drone attacks into Saudi Arabia, targeting cities, infrastructure, airports, military bases, diplomatic sites and energy facilities.
The advisory said falling debris from intercepted missiles and drones also poses a risk and warned US citizens against photographing, filming or sharing information about interceptions or affected sites.
It cited terrorism, exit bans and the enforcement of Saudi laws governing social media activity among the risks facing travelers.
The advisory follows security alerts issued by the US Embassy in Saudi Arabia in recent days amid attacks and threats targeting the kingdom.
The embassy renewed its security alert on Monday for a third consecutive day following attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and an attack targeting King Fahd International Airport in Dammam.
The embassy warned of possible flight cancellations, airspace closures and other travel disruptions and urged US citizens to exercise caution at major airports.
Saudi authorities have reported missile and drone attacks targeting airports and other sites in the kingdom in recent days, while the Houthis have threatened further attacks on Saudi airports and oil facilities.
A Saudi-led coalition, meanwhile, has intensified military operations against Houthi positions in Yemen, including airstrikes in the capital, Sanaa.

Why we should be worried about the suspected Russian plague victim
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:39:06 UTC
01:39:06 KST

In pandemic preparedness work, scientists like to focus on the technical challenges: identifying pathogens, diagnosing infections, understanding their effects and developing vaccines and treatments. Each step promises progress through human innovation, investment and planning. The WHO, for example, brings experts together to identify and prioritize emerging disease threats and collect the evidence needed to prepare for them. But preparedness depends on more than scientific innovation.
As the past week has shown, politics is the elephant in the room in all of this. No one could have predicted we would be talking about pneumonic plague, and that the death of a single lab worker in Russia would cause global headlines. It might feel like an overreaction: the WHO deals with thousands of potential disease signals worldwide every month. But the circumstances of this case are unusual given the lack of transparency from Russian authorities on what happened — and ongoing concern about biological weapons research.
The 28-year-old lab worker died after developing severe pneumonia. She worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute, established in 1934, which studies plague and other dangerous pathogens including anthrax and cholera, and is rumored to be involved in biological weapons research. Ashish Jha, who was the US White House COVID-19 response coordinator, and who co-chaired an Ebola commission with me, wrote on social media: “US intelligence assess that Russia’s scientists continue developing biological weapons capabilities. Those programs operate in secret. Nobody outside inspects them and nobody inside has much incentive to admit when something goes wrong.”
Photo: AFP
On top of that, initial local media coverage suggested that she had died from pneumonic plague after a lab accident, possibly a broken test tube. Pneumonic plague is caused by a bacterium (Yersinia pestis), and can spread through respiratory contact and is always fatal if untreated. If antibiotics are given in the first 24 hours after symptoms, or even before onset of symptoms post-exposure, it is largely treatable. If she knew she had been exposed, why was treatment not given in time? (Pneumonic plague is a different disease to the more common bubonic plague, which transmits through flea bites.)
Despite Russian health authorities denying that it was a case of plague and insisting it was pneumonia of unknown origin, they quickly placed about 200 contacts of the lab worker under quarantine. The authorities reported that no high-threat pathogens were detected and monitoring had ended. The WHO released a statement noting a potential second linked case, but Russia denied this. The cause of death remains unconfirmed.
INSUFFICIENT INFORMATION
The WHO has pushed the Russian government for more information — including confirmation of the diagnosis and details of the investigations, the reason why it put so many people in quarantine and more information on the second case — but it has not yet received this information.
On the one hand, if this infection was spreading further, additional cases would have emerged by now. The lab worker died on Oct. 2, and the testing of contacts and release of those in quarantine indicates that any spread has been contained so far. However, given that the incubation period can be one to three days, continued monitoring is important.
There are three hypothetical scenarios if we assume the illness was pneumonic plague. The first is that the lab worker was accidentally exposed to the bacterium while doing research, and either didn’t know, or didn’t tell anyone out of fear — and therefore didn’t ask for treatment immediately. So when she became sick, her window of treatment had been missed.
Photo: Reuters
Second, the lab worker was exposed to an antibiotic-resistant strain. This may sound like a conspiracy theory, but senior academics have raised concerns given the history of the Soviet biological weapons program and the potential for pathogens to be engineered for hostile purposes.
Third, Dan Singer (the former White House director for countering biological threats) has suggested that this lab worker might have been given an outdated vaccine, which is only available in Russia as it is not approved by the WHO or most other countries. This is a live-attenuated vaccine, meaning a weakened version of the bacteria is given, but it doesn’t always provide protection and sometimes can cause disease.
ACCESS NEEDED
In short, we don’t know what happened because there is insufficient information from the Russian authorities. To understand what happened, investigators would need access to laboratory and clinical evidence, including genomic sequencing, pathogen identification and details of the worker’s research. Without this, we are left with speculation when only scientific certainty will do.
As a member of the WHO, Russia has an international legal obligation to share information with the agency. The WHO’s health regulations specifically cover “unusual and unexpected” events, as well as those with serious public health impact and with significant risk of international spread, or that risk affecting trade or travel. But unfortunately, as with most international law, there’s no real enforcement mechanism. There is a reliance on broad cooperation across countries, with the understanding that sharing information on disease spread is in all nations’ best interests.
The US government has also put pressure on Russia for answers, with US President Donald Trump saying he would speak to Putin about the situation. The US state department also formally requested further information under the international health regulations — the irony being that the US withdrew from the WHO in January, but is now invoking the international framework it left behind.
As a scientist watching this unfold, I’m reminded that while we can have research and expert conferences into better diagnostics, faster genomic sequencing, more effective vaccines and accessible treatments, none of these advances can compensate for a failure to share the information needed to identify a pathogen in the first place. Preparedness is a political challenge as well as a scientific one. And without transparency, it will be a case of one step forward, two steps back.

Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) yesterday pledged to impose heavier penalties on people who ride light electric vehicles (LEVs) while under the influence of alcohol or drugs after their driver’s license has been revoked.
Unlike electric bicycles, which rely primarily on pedaling with electric assistance, LEVs are powered mainly by electricity and can operate without pedaling.
In Taiwan, LEVs must be registered and display a license plate, and riders are required to wear helmets, but no driver’s license is needed.
Photo: Wu Cheng-ting, Taipei Times
They are subject to a maximum speed limit of 25kph and a weight limit of 40kg, excluding the battery.
Electric scooters, by contrast, require registration and a valid driver’s license, and generally offer greater speed and power for longer commutes.
Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) Legislator Yang Chiung-ying (楊瓊瓔) said in a plenary session that while the public welcomes the government’s efforts to curb alcohol or drug-impaired driving through higher fines and stricter criminal penalties, a loophole remains: Drivers whose licenses have been revoked for driving under the influence could switch to LEVs, which do not require a license.
Some people have jokingly referred to LEVs as vehicles for drunk drivers, she said.
Statistics compiled by the Tainan Police Department showed that in the first seven months of this year, nearly 3,000 traffic contraventions involving LEVs were recorded, with about 10 percent involving drunk or drug-impaired riders.
“These are not isolated cases, but a systematic circumvention of traffic laws that undermines tougher penalties for drunk or drug-impaired driving,” Yang said.
Although LEVs are limited to 25kph, many riders tamper with their vehicles to reach speeds of 50kph to 60kph, nearly as fast as motorcycles, she said.
However, the fine for riding an LEV while under the influence is only NT$1,200 to NT$2,400, which might not be enough to deter offenders, she added.
Cho said he had been briefed on accident rates involving LEVs at a Cabinet road safety meeting last month.
One major problem is that LEV riders often exceed the speed limit, he said.
He said tougher penalties should be imposed on LEV riders whose driver’s licenses had been revoked for drunk or drug-impaired driving.
Minister of Transportation and Communications Chen Shih-kai (陳世凱) said the ministry plans to address the problem at its source and would submit a report on the issue within three months.

China is this year’s APEC host, with a leaders’ summit scheduled for next month in Shenzhen. Chuang would, “as is customary,” attend the APEC meeting in Hong Kong on Tuesday and Wednesday next week, the ministry said. Minister of Labor Hung Sun-han (洪申翰) traveled to China’s Nanjing last month, also for an APEC event. Taiwan has yet to announce who would attend the leaders’ summit.
Photo: Chu Pei-hsiung, Taipei Times
WEATHER
Northern Taiwan to see rain
The greater Taipei area and eastern Taiwan should see sporadic showers today, with rainfall potentially intensifying along the north coast and in Yilan County tomorrow, the Central Weather Administration (CWA) said. Elsewhere, skies would be mainly cloudy to sunny, although afternoon showers are possible in southern mountainous areas. From Friday through Monday, cloudy to sunny weather is forecast for most parts of the nation, while eastern Taiwan and the Hengchun Peninsula (恆春半島) might see scattered showers, CWA forecaster Wang Pin-hsiang (王品翔) said. Temperatures in southern Taiwan would remain relatively steady throughout the week, with daytime highs of 30°C to 33°C. Nighttime lows would range from 22°C to 25°C. In northern Taiwan, daytime highs today are to hover between 27°C and 29°C before gradually rising from Friday, reaching 30°C or higher over the weekend, he said. Radiative cooling could cause nighttime temperatures to drop below 20°C today and from Friday through Monday.
TRAVEL
Taipei to hold travel fair
Taipei is to host the Taiwan International Travel Fair from Nov. 6 to 9, with discounted early-bird tickets going on sale starting yesterday, the Taiwan Visitors Association said. The exhibition at Taipei Nangang Exhibition Center Hall 1 features 1,600 booths representing 123 countries and cities, the association said in a statement. Previously called the Taipei International Travel Fair, the fair has revised its name to “Taiwan” as it enters its 40th year. Japan’s pavilion is hosting a record 252 booths, while tourism authorities from South Korea, the US, Thailand, Malaysia, France and the Czech Republic would take part, it added. Twelve airlines are participating, including first-time exhibitors Etihad Airways and Sun PhuQuoc Airways, while All Nippon Airways would return after several years of absence. Early-bird tickets are on sale today for NT$150 — 25 percent off the regular price of NT$200. Advance tickets would then be sold for NT$180 from tomorrow to Nov. 5.
CRIME
Man’s life sentence upheld
The High Court yesterday upheld a life sentence and lifetime deprivation of civil rights for a man who murdered his ex-girlfriend by stabbing her 19 times in public. The ruling upheld a Shilin District Court verdict that found Su Shih-hsin (宿世新) guilty of homicide. The ruling can be appealed. According to the district court’s verdict, Su had repeatedly injured his ex-girlfriend, surnamed Tsai (蔡), after she ended their relationship, the district court verdict said. On Nov. 25, 2024, he went to her workplace to confront her. After the two argued near a building’s arcade, Su pulled out a switchblade, pushed Tsai against a nearby wall and stabbed her several times in the chest and abdomen, the court found. After stabbing Tsai 19 times in total, Su stabbed himself in the left side of the chest, the verdict said. Tsai died later that evening despite receiving medical treatment, the court said.

Starlux Airlines posts almost 70 percent year-on-year sales growth in September
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:39:02 UTC
01:39:02 KST

Starlux Airlines Co’s (星宇航空) revenue last month rose almost 70 percent from a year earlier, bolstered by strong demand for passenger travel and for cargo shipments of tech devices amid the artificial intelligence (AI) boom.
The carrier generated NT$4.98 billion (US$155.21 million) in consolidated sales last month, up 69 percent from a year earlier, it said on Monday.
Passenger revenue rose 70 percent from a year earlier to NT$3.72 billion, while cargo revenue rose 59 percent to NT$706 million, the carrier said.
Photo: CNA
In the first nine months of this year, Starlux’s consolidated sales totaled NT$44.84 billion, up 37 percent from a year earlier, it said.
Fourth quarter is a peak season for international trade, and foreign buyers are expected to keep building inventories of AI servers, semiconductor equipment and electronic components, Starlux said.
Citing that trend and year-end shopping demand, the carrier said it is optimistic about its cargo business this quarter.
Starlux also expects growth in its passenger business to continue after it launched new routes this month, including Taipei-Bali, Taichung-Sapporo and Taichung-Nagoya, it added.
As the carrier takes delivery of new aircraft, Starlux said it would increase flights and deploy larger planes in its winter schedule, including Airbus A330neos on its Taipei-Hakodate and Taipei-Chiang Mai routes. Starlux said it would also deploy A350-1000s on its Taipei-Los Angeles and Taipei-San Francisco routes later this quarter.
Last week, Taiwan’s other major international carriers also reported solid sales for last month.
China Airlines Ltd (CAL, 中華航空) said its consolidated sales totaled NT$20.93 billion, a record for September and up 31.86 percent from a year earlier. Passenger revenue rose 30.73 percent to NT$11.46 billion, and cargo revenue rose 41.82 percent to NT$7.62 billion, CAL said.
EVA Airways Corp (長榮航空) reported consolidated sales of NT$20.75 billion, up 32.86 percent from a year earlier. Passenger revenue rose 28.09 percent to NT$11.94 billion, and cargo revenue rose 42.55 percent to NT$6.17 billion, it said.
CAL and EVA cited strong passenger demand during the Mid-Autumn Festival holiday, while their cargo businesses benefited from global demand for AI servers and consumer electronics.
In the first nine months of this year, CAL and EVA Air posted NT$185.92 billion and NT$194.38 billion respectively in consolidated sales, up 20 percent and 19.48 percent from a year earlier.
Tigerair Taiwan Ltd (台灣虎航), the country’s only low-cost carrier, said its average load factor — the percentage of seats filled — topped 90 percent last month, helping it lift revenue 36 percent from a year earlier to NT$1.74 billion.
Tigerair Taiwan’s consolidated sales for the first nine months totaled NT$15.62 billion, up 24 percent from a year earlier.

China-linked hackers hit Fiji: US embassy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:39:02 UTC
01:39:02 KST

Hackers with links to China compromised a regional organization in Fiji, the Pacific nation’s US embassy said yesterday, warning that governments and telecommunication networks in the region were also being targeted.
Fiji is emerging as a major telecommunications hub in the Pacific islands, as Google expands a network of subsea cables connecting the US military outpost of Guam, US defense ally Australia, French Polynesia and the mainland US, via Fiji’s capital, Suva.
Fijian Minister of Police and Communication Ioane Naivalurua said he was reviewing the situation after the US embassy announced that a “regional organization in Suva” had its network hacked between July and August.
Photo: AFP
“Hackers with links to China maintained access to the organization’s network over several days,” the embassy said in a statement posted on Facebook, without identifying the organization.
US officials have previously urged cable host Fiji to boost cybersecurity to guard against data risks from China.
Naivalurua said that police were investigating the reported attack and urged governments, organizations and the private sector to “take preventative action and harden the security of their respective digital systems.”
In Beijing, Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokeswoman Mao Ning (毛寧) said the ministry was not aware of the case, but that it “firmly opposes hacking activities and cracks down on them in accordance with the law.”
“At the same time, we also oppose using cybersecurity issues to smear China,” Mao told a regular briefing.
Fiji’s government on Friday asked the US to provide evidence for its claim last week that a Chinese state agency employee living in Fiji had paid bribes on behalf of Beijing.
The US Department of State accused the man living in Suva of “significant corruption.”
The US embassy yesterday pointed to action taken by the FBI in August to combat China-sponsored hackers targeting critical infrastructure in the US.
The FBI action “matters directly for the Pacific,” the embassy said.
A group of hackers called QTFY included former members of China’s military, working for a company paid by the Chinese Ministry of State Security, had targeted NASA, the US Department of Energy and power companies, an FBI affidavit said.
China-linked hackers were targeting foreign governments, organizations and telecommunications networks in the Pacific islands, the embassy wrote on Facebook.
The region’s political bloc, the Pacific Islands Forum, said it was not the organization that had been hacked.
“While the Pacific Islands Forum Secretariat is not affected, cybersecurity is increasingly important to the Pacific as the region’s digital security is closely linked to its economic resilience, national sovereignty, regional security, and wellbeing of Pacific communities,” a forum spokeswoman said.

The CPBL Taiwan Series is to begin at Taipei Dome on Saturday after the CTBC Brothers beat the Uni-Lions 8-2 on Monday to claim the last spot in the championship.
The Brothers face the Wei Chuan Dragons in the best-of-seven championship series, the first Taiwan Series to be played entirely at Taipei Dome. A champion could be crowned as early as Wednesday next week.
Wei Chuan are the home team for games 1 and 2 and, if necessary, games 5 through 7. The Brothers host games 3 and 4.
Photo courtesy of CTBC Brothers
CTBC reached their third consecutive Taiwan Series by winning the playoff series 3-2, a tally that includes the one-game advantage it received as the second-half regular-season champion.
The Brothers won Friday’s opener to move within one win of advancing, but the Uni-Lions took the next two games to force a deciding fourth game on Monday at Taichung Intercontinental Baseball Stadium.
Brothers starter Cheng Hao-chun earned the win and was named game MVP, allowing one earned run on five hits over 5-2/3 innings. He struck out two and walked three, throwing 98 pitches.
CTBC pulled away with three runs in the fifth inning, all forced home by bases-loaded walks. Chang Jen-wei and Chan Tzu-hsien added solo home runs in the sixth and seventh innings, respectively.
Cheng credited his teammates and recalled his coaches’ pregame message that to win, the team had to want it more than their opponents.
“We’re almost there. Hang in there a little longer,” he told supporters.
The game was the end of a long career for seasoned Uni-Lions player Chen Yung-chi.
The 43-year-old, who had announced his retirement this season, entered at first base in the sixth inning and singled to right field in his final plate appearance in the ninth.
Chen removed his cap to acknowledge the crowd before being replaced by a pinch runner and embracing Uni-Lions manager Lin Yueh-ping.
Although the game was played at the Brothers’ home stadium, fans of both teams chanted Chen’s name afterward. He embraced Brothers players and coaches before leaving the field to cheers.

PAKISTAN
Train derailment kills five
A passenger train early yesterday derailed in Punjab Province, killing five people and injuring 35 others, police and a Pakistan Railways spokesman said. The train was traveling from the southern port city of Karachi to the northwestern city of Peshawar when it derailed in Sher Shah, railway spokesman Kaleem Akhtar said. Rescuers recovered four bodies and evacuated the injured from the train’s 14 cars, he said. The injured were taken to a hospital for treatment, but one died before he could be transported, rescue officials said.
Photo: EPA
SOUTH KOREA
Eight wounded in stabbing
Eight people were yesterday wounded in a stabbing at a supermarket in Incheon, with one person going into cardiac arrest, police said. Officers responding to the scene arrested a male suspect and were investigating the motive and circumstances of the attack, a police spokesperson said by telephone. A witness cited by Yonhap news agency said the suspect appeared to have knives tethered to both hands and moved through several floors of the shopping complex, attacking people as he went before being subdued by bystanders and handed over to police. Local media reports described the suspect as a man in his 60s who was wearing an electronic monitoring ankle bracelet. The victims included six women and two men, with a woman in her 20s in cardiac arrest, the reports said.
THAILAND
Government mulls exit fee
Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul’s government is considering an outbound tax of about 1,000 baht (US$29.80) on Thai and foreign travelers leaving the country, while separately planning a 450-baht fee for foreign visitors arriving by air. The country needs to raise more revenue after years of budget deficits of about 3 to 4 percent of GDP have eroded its fiscal space. The Thai Travel Agents Association warned the outbound tax could sharply reduce passenger numbers and ultimately hurting inbound tourism.

Investment deal with Poland on agenda: minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:38:56 UTC
01:38:56 KST

Taiwan and Poland are working on signing an agreement before the end of year to facilitate investment in the European nation, Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) said on Monday.
Lin is leading a delegation to Poland, which visited a site in Miekinia in southwestern Poland where the Taiwan Electrical and Electronic Manufacturers’ Association has proposed building a technology park.
The delegation is working toward signing a memorandum of understanding with Poland to create a favorable investment environment for Taiwanese enterprises.
Photo courtesy of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs
The delegation, which departed Taiwan on Saturday, attended the two-day Warsaw Security Forum, at which Lin yesterday delivered a speech titled “The Taiwan Model: A Trusted Partner for Europe’s Reindustrialization.”
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement that the delegation on Monday visited Miekinia to see the proposed Technology Park site.
The International Cooperation and Development Fund would collaborate with entities to acquire the site, Lin said in the statement.
He said the he goal is to provide comprehensive policy support and a cooperative framework, creating an investment environment with robust infrastructure for Taiwanese enterprises to invest in the region.
Lin attended briefings by the Polish Investment and Trade Agency, local government authorities and representatives from the special economic zone on infrastructure planning, including roads, and water and power supply for the site, the ministry said.
Poland is the largest economy in central and eastern Europe, with a strong industrial base, well-developed infrastructure and quality talent, making it an excellent gateway for Taiwanese companies to enter the European market, Lin said.

The Gulf has entered 
a new era of instability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:38:53 UTC
01:38:53 KST

On Saturday, Houthi rebels launched a shocking and deadly attack on Saudi Arabia’s capital city, Riyadh. At the time of writing, the missile strike and another one on Sunday on King Khalid International Airport have killed at least 14 people and left 300 injured, marking a significant turn in a regional conflagration that is only getting more intense. It was the single most deadly attack on any Gulf country since the US and Israel launched their war on Iran in February. In Saudi Arabia, a country that is unaccustomed to such fatalities, the death toll is bewilderingly high and likely to prompt a bloody response.
Over the past year, the Gulf has entered a new era of instability that is not temporary and cannot be reversed. This might feel like an overstatement — casualties have been relatively low, after all, compared with Gaza and Iran — but the gradual erosion of peace and security in places such as Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) has changed the region more dramatically than its leaders would like to acknowledge.
The first audacious and unthinkable thing happened just more than a year ago, when Iran fired missiles at an airbase in Qatar that hosts US troops, in retaliation for US strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities. Lighting up Doha’s skies and scattering shrapnel, it was a dismaying moment for the Qataris, who have tried to maintain good relations with Iran. However, even then there was a degree of warning and coordination that signaled this was a face-saving measure on the part of the Iranians. Yet later last year, with no similar warning or choreography, Israel struck Doha, targeting Hamas members and killing five Palestinians and one Qatari. That was the beginning of the end of a longstanding norm and expectation — that there was a sanctity to Gulf lives and sovereignty, one secured by the management of the relationship with Iran and alliances with the US.
Illustration: Mountain People
Then came US President Donald Trump’s and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s war on Iran, which drew the Gulf once and for all into the fray. In retaliation for what Iran perceives to be political, military and logistical support for the offensive against it, Tehran struck Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman. Iran targeted military sites, energy facilities, desalination plants — an entire infrastructure that underpins the economies of these countries. Much damage was inflicted by the suspension of normal life, the shuttering of schools for months, the closure of airports and airspace.
The most disastrous consequence of all, from the perspective of Gulf rulers, has been the way the attacks have disrupted the integration of these countries into the cosmopolitan international community as places for tourism, entrepreneurs, sports and entertainment. They spent billions in securing Formula One, golf and boxing franchises and tournaments, only for a flurry of cheap drones to put it all at risk.
The result is a fractious unraveling that has reactivated hostilities that had laid dormant. Yemen’s civil war began in 2014 when Iran-backed Houthi rebels, in aspiration to greater autonomy in the minority Shiite homelands, took over the capital city, Sana’a. In 2015, a coalition of countries led by Saudi Arabia led a brutal campaign to dislodge the Houthis from territories they had gained, intensifying a grinding civil war that killed hundreds of thousands and triggered a humanitarian catastrophe. The war de-escalated in 2022 with a de facto but unformalized division of the country between the Houthis and an internationally recognized, Saudi-backed government; the ceasefire was followed by rapprochement between Saudi Arabia and Iran.
However, the war against Iran opened up strategic opportunities and stirred political loyalties, triggering a surge of Houthi advancement in Yemen. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz, for example, shifted more commercial traffic along Yemen’s coastline, prompting the Houthis to make advances and seize territory to gain control of the now crucial Bab al-Mandab Strait in the Red Sea. Tensions came to a head five months after the start of the war, with Saudi Arabia escalating strikes against the Houthis, and the Saudi-backed government bombing its own airport in Sana’a to prevent an Iranian plane from landing.
These developments are not just the result of a mischievous group seizing the moment, acting as spoiler in a bigger contest between Iran and the West. The Houthis are backed by Iran, but they are not empty proxies for Iran; they have domestic ambitions and sharp regional animosities, particularly against the House of Saud, which they see an imperious and arrogant master to whom they shall never submit. A senior Houthi official said that Saturday’s attack took place “so that the world understands” that Yemeni civilian infrastructure has been, and is being, targeted by the Saudis, gesturing toward that sense that Riyadh treats Yemeni lives as cheap.
From another perspective, what we are witnessing in the region is another consequence of Hamas’ Oct. 7 attacks on Israel, and what followed in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran. The final piece that was stabilizing the region’s tense equilibriums fell away when Trump decided that the safety and security of the US’s Gulf allies was secondary to his Iran “excursion,” as he called it. The limits of relying on the US security umbrella became clear to allies and enemies.
Last month, the Trump administration refused to extend military assistance to Saudi Arabia to fight the Houthis, after a meeting of US officials with the Houthis, who assured them that they would not attack US ships in the Red Sea, only Saudi vessels. What is upon Saudi Arabia is a long, intractable war with a resourceful and impassioned antagonist, one willing to sustain a high degree of pain in ways that Riyadh cannot match without orienting itself entirely toward war. If the 2015 campaign is anything to go by, it would claim thousands of lives with only a remote possibility of a decisive outcome.
So Saudi Arabia, and the entire Gulf, are pulled further into the relentless storm. Trump cannot bring the Iran war to an end, Gaza remains an open wound, Israel continues to strike and occupy parts of Lebanon. The Houthi resurgence represents a new reality in a region that is bewildered and losing lives and capital, stuck between old alliances that no longer work and new hostilities that are too calamitous to confront.
Nesrine Malik is a Guardian columnist.

Belize and Paraguay on Monday condemned Beijing sanctions over their countries’ ties with Taiwan, saying China’s actions create unnecessary tensions.
Earlier on Monday, Beijing announced sanctions against Paraguayan Minister of Information and Communication Technologies Gustavo Villate and Belizean Minister of Foreign Affairs Francis Fonseca.
The Paraguayan Ministry of Foreign Affairs said it rejected the sanctions, writing on X that they created unnecessary friction.
Photo: AFP
It added that it reaffirmed its support for Taiwan and its commitment to democratic values and principles.
Villate told the Spanish-language Paraguayan daily ABC Color the sanctions were “predictable” and linked them to several cooperation projects between Taiwan and Paraguay.
The projects include a planned data center in Nueva Asuncion that incorporates security standards to prevent foreign interference in the companies involved in the project, he said.
Photo courtesy of Administration for Cybersecurity, MODA
He also said that Hon Hai Precision Industry Co (鴻海精密) had been invited to establish operations in Paraguay and participate in the “Yguazu Digital” project, an artificial intelligence-focused technology hub.
Meanwhile, the Belizean Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement that the sanctions would not alter Belize’s foreign policy and the government could continue to stand behind Fonseca.
“Measures directed at an individual for carrying out the lawful duties of his office are unwarranted, and we reject them,” it said.
Under the UN Charter, “every state has the right to conduct its foreign policy free from external pressure,” it added.
Belize’s relationship with Taiwan “was established by a sovereign decision of our country,” and the partnership has delivered in development, healthcare, education, infrastructure, the environment and agriculture for the benefit of Belizeans, it said.
In Taipei, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs earlier condemned China’s sanctions, calling them an attempt to interfere in other countries’ internal affairs and pressure them over their foreign policies.
The sanctions violated the principles of international law and infringed on other countries’ sovereignty and foreign policy, while highlighting Beijing’s attempts to use intimidation and transnational repression to force other nations to submit to its political agenda, it said.
The ministry reiterated that the Republic of China is a sovereign and independent country, and that it and the People’s Republic of China are not subordinate to each other.
This is an internationally recognized fact and reflects the objective reality across the Taiwan Strait, the ministry said, adding that Beijing has no right to interfere in Taiwan’s diplomatic relations.

2026-10-13
16:38:52 UTC

Tax revenue from securities transactions rose 71.2 percent year-on-year to NT$53.4 billion (US$1.66 billion) last month, a new September high, even as it marked the third consecutive monthly decline as market turnover continued to fall.
This year’s overall trading volume remains higher than last year, and securities transaction tax revenue last month still posted positive year-on-year growth for the 14th consecutive month, Ministry of Finance data released yesterday showed.
The stock market declined last month before rebounding later in the month and consolidating at high levels, the ministry said.
Photo: CNA
The TAIEX closed at 47,940.13 points at the end of the month, gaining 1,811 points or 3.93 percent, it said.
The average daily turnover of the local stock market was NT$1.032 trillion, down 5.8 percent month-on-month and marking the third consecutive month of decline. However, compared with the same month last year, it increased 71.8 percent, the ministry said.
The TAIEX yesterday closed down 960.65 points, or 1.95 percent, at 48,341.31, as investors took cues from overnight weakness on Wall Street amid escalating geopolitical unease and a sell-off of chip stocks across Asia.
In the first nine months of this year, cumulative tax revenue from securities transactions totaled NT$506 billion, rising 1.6-fold year-on-year and marking the highest level for the same period, the ministry said, adding that average daily stock turnover surged 160 percent year-on-year to NT$1.146 trillion over the period.
Overall, the nation last month collected NT$496.5 billion in tax revenue, up NT$81.3 billion, or 19.6 percent, from a year earlier and the highest September figure, the ministry said.
The growth was due to increases of NT$29.7 billion in business tax revenue, NT$25.4 billion in corporate income tax revenue and NT$22.2 billion in securities transaction tax revenue, it said.
Commodity tax revenue posted the largest decline of NT$1.1 billion in the month, it added.
In the first nine months of this year, cumulative tax revenue grew NT$700.4 billion, or 24.4 percent, to NT$3.571 trillion, as increases in corporate income, personal income, securities transactions and business taxes offset the decreases in revenue from commodity and land value increment taxes, the ministry said.
The January-to-September figure was 15 percent above the government’s budget for the first nine months and was 78.8 percent of its full-year target, it said.
It remains to be seen whether the tax revenue collected this year could exceed the government’s budgeted figure, as it must consider factors such as the stock trading volume in the coming months and the recovery of the local housing market, the ministry said.

Taiwan’s GDP to reach 10.7%, IMF says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:38:50 UTC
01:38:50 KST

The IMF has sharply raised its forecast for Taiwan’s GDP growth to 10.7 percent this year, the highest projected rate in the Asia-Pacific region, amid the ongoing artificial intelligence (AI) boom.
In its latest World Economic Outlook report released yesterday at its annual meetings in Bangkok, the IMF raised its forecast for Taiwan’s growth from the 5.2 percent it projected in April, making Taiwan the only economy in the world projected to post double-digit percentage growth this year.
Taiwan’s projected growth far outpaces that of neighbors in the Asia-Pacific region, including Japan at 0.7 percent, South Korea at 3.3 percent, Singapore at 5 percent and Hong Kong at 3.8 percent, the report says.
Photo: Ann Wang, Reuters
China’s economy is expected to grow 4.5 percent this year, while the US is forecast to grow 2.3 percent, the report said.
Despite the significant upgrade, the IMF’s latest forecast remains below the 11.05 percent growth projection released by the Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics in August.
Global AI development has remained highly concentrated, both upstream, in the computing hardware required for AI training and inference, and downstream, in developing and operating frontier AI models, the IMF said.
Upstream, only a few economies produce advanced semiconductors on a large scale, it said, adding that Taiwan and South Korea account for 62 percent of net trade in AI-related computing hardware.
“Given the structure of supply chains for technology exports from these two economies, a handful of commodity exporters and other manufacturing hubs in East Asia are likely to see spillovers from this activity,” the IMF said.
Reflecting the nation’s robust export performance, the IMF projected Taiwan’s current account surplus would reach 22 percent of GDP this year, among the highest of any major economy.
The IMF also forecast Taiwan’s consumer price index would rise 2 percent this year, up from its April estimate of 1.5 percent, while the unemployment rate was projected to remain largely unchanged at 3.4 percent.
The IMF raised its global growth forecast by 0.1 percentage points to 3.1 percent for this year, compared with 3.5 percent growth last year.
“Two major transformative forces — geopolitics and technology — are reshaping the global economy, with their short-term impact gradually coming into view and their longer-term impact still largely unknown,” the IMF said in the report.
However, “technology is most recently playing out as a positive demand shock powered by investment in AI and related hardware and infrastructure,” the IMF said. “Trade flows show this most strikingly.”
While many advanced economies have been buoyed by rising investment in AI technology, poorer countries that are not benefiting from that boom face stark choices as they deal with high energy prices caused by the Iran war, it said.
“The global economy has been resilient, but that resilience is under strain, with risks tilted to the downside,” IMF chief economist Silvana Tenreyro told journalists in Bangkok.
The US’ war on Iran, launched in February, has plunged the Middle East into violence and seen global energy prices skyrocket as a result of Tehran’s retaliation.
The IMF report detailed that the twin economic forces of the war in Iran and the AI technology boom had created a “fragmented” world economy.
“Headwinds from a prolonged war and persistent geopolitical tensions could revive inflationary pressures, strain fiscal and external positions, and hit energy-importing and low-income countries hardest,” it said.
“At the same time, the current technology tailwind could stop abruptly if expectations about AI-related profits and productivity gains are reassessed, weakening investment and tightening financial conditions,” the IMF report said.

Lightmatter reveals plans for its new technologies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:38:48 UTC
01:38:48 KST

Lightmatter Inc, a US-based optical interconnect solution start-up, yesterday said it plans to ship its first near-packaged optics (NPO) engines and high-density laser network-interface cards (NICs) next year, adding that this would pave the way for full-scale copackaged optics (CPO) engine production in 2028 and 2029.
The company’s liquid-cooling and high-density laser NIC, called Guide NR, is light-source engineered to power next-generation CPO and NPO architectures in artificial intelligence (AI) data centers.
One of the CPO engines with detachable fiber array units is assembled in Taiwan by ASE Technology Holding Co (日月光投控), Lightmatter chief executive officer Nick Harris told a virtual media conference yesterday.
Photo courtesy of Lightmatter Inc
Lightmatter also counts Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電), chip designer Global Unichip Corp (GUC, 創意電子) and passive fiber optic components maker Browave Corp (波若威) as its silicon photonics ecosystem partners in Taiwan.
Asked about the company’s commercial launches of new products, Harris said NPO and Guide DR could be launched next year and CPO in 2028.
“On the CPO side, we work with GUC, and there are others in Taiwan and elsewhere,” he said.
Initial, low-volume shipments of CPO are scheduled for next year, while high-volume deployment is expected start in 2028, Harris said.
The company’s photonic interposer technology, which is considered the most advanced and ultimate stage of CPO, will roll out on a very similar timeline, he said.
Silicon photonics is the next big breakthrough in artificial intelligence scalability, as it enables huge speedups for inference and training workloads, while traditional copper transmission reaches its physical scaling limits, he said.
The transition to photonics would coincide with the arrival of 224Gbps and 448Gbps copper-based SerDes technologies, he said.
Some Taiwanese companies have developed their first 400Gbps designs, but it remains highly unlikely that a standalone 896Gbps SerDes technology would ever materialize, Harris said.
Lightmatter already has technology capable of handling 1,600Gbps per optical fiber, which provides a scalable roadmap spanning from 400Gbps to 10Tbps per optical fiber, doubling the speed offered by traditional Ethernet technology, he said.
As the optical industry is facing acute laser and optical fiber shortages, Lightmatter uses bidirectional technology to halve optical fiber consumption, Harris said.
The company also uses a diversified supply chain and its proprietary Guide platform to mitigate laser shortages, he said.
The Guide platform relies on silicon-level integration known as Very Large Scale Photonics to drastically reduce laser usage, he added.
In the face of semiconductor capacity tightness, Lightmatter works with multiple foundries such as Intel Corp and Tower Semiconductor Ltd and packaging houses including Amkor Technology Inc to provide flexible options for customers ordering standard products such as Passage L20 and Guide, Harris said.
For custom product orders, clients secure their own semiconductor capacity, and Lightmatter builds on top of their allocated supply, he said.
Those clients are mostly industry giants, including hyperscalers and major semiconductor firms, he added.

Accountability in use of clinical AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:38:48 UTC
01:38:48 KST

Artificial intelligence (AI) is already reshaping Taiwan’s hospital wards. Squeezed by an aging population, nursing shortages and grueling paperwork, major medical centers are rapidly deploying algorithms. National Taiwan University Hospital uses large language models for medical records and International Classification of Diseases (ICD). Chang Gung Memorial Hospital integrates machine learning into disease prediction and triage.
Meanwhile, Taipei Veterans General Hospital has set up dedicated clinical review panels to audit algorithms throughout their lifecycle.
Most hospital AI tools in Taiwan still handle paperwork and triage, but that administrative line is already blurring. Systems are moving directly into diagnostic assistance and treatment pathways. Algorithms might not issue oncology diagnoses on their own, but they already prioritize which people gets urgent CT scans, flag suspicious lesions and suggest chemotherapy regimens.
When an algorithm errs, where does the liability fall? On the attending physician who trusted the screen? The hospital that procured the software? Or the vendor that wrote the black-box code? The danger in clinical AI is not only bad calculations; it is also the diffusion of responsibility.
Healthcare has paid dearly for overestimating software before. The Therac-25 radiation accidents in the 1980s killed and maimed people precisely because human oversight gave way to blind faith in automated code. The failure of IBM Watson for Oncology proved that sophisticated software collapses in real clinics when recommendations depart from clinical context and proven practice.
As legal academic Frank Pasquale wrote in New Laws of Robotics, AI must augment clinical judgement, not supplant it.
Pasquale’s core insight is straightforward: attribution must precede autonomy. In a hospital, an algorithm cannot be cross-examined and a providers cannot hide behind a proprietary model. Legal and moral responsibility must stay tethered to recognizable institutions and clinicians.
Aviation solved a similar dilemma years ago. When the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) introduced SMART — an automated tool for rerouting air traffic around severe weather — commercial airlines pushed back hard. Their concern was not whether the software worked, but who was on the hook if an automated route steered an airliner into a storm.
The FAA responded with a deliberate “start, crawl, walk, run” deployment: keeping human controllers firmly at the center of final routing choices until the operational logic was proven.
Clinical medicine needs the same posture.
The newly passed Artificial Intelligence Basic Act (人工智慧基本法) sets down broad principles: human oversight, transparency and accountability. However, broad statutory text does not tell an intensive care unit how to handle a conflicting drug alert.
Because fully autonomous clinical AI is not yet the standard of care in Taiwan, policymakers have a brief window to get the rules right.
Translating rules into clinical reality requires three concrete shifts:
First, tiered, risk-based oversight. Administrative tools for hospital bed tracking should not face the same regulatory friction as diagnostic algorithms that recommend surgery or radiation doses. Regulators must require rigorous clinical validation on local patient populations, transparent training datasets and an unobstructed right for clinicians to question and override recommendations.
Second, unbundled lifecycle liability. Responsibility must be divided by role, not blurred together. Developers must answer for model integrity and dataset bias. Hospitals must take ownership of local deployment and clinician training. Clinicians remain responsible for final treatment decisions within the software’s validated scope.
Third, post-market surveillance: Governance cannot stop at regulatory approval. Algorithms suffer from “data drift” as clinical protocols shift. Hospitals need multidisciplinary committees to track real-world errors, review patient outcomes and audit systems after vendor updates.
The transition toward healthcare AI is not an engineering race. It is a test of institutional credibility. The societies that thrive in the age of algorithmic medicine would not be those with the fastest processors, but those with the discipline to demand human accountability before automation outpaces oversight.
Hanson Wu is a healthcare policy professional with experience in pharmaceutical policy, health security and public affairs. He is a graduate healthcare policy researcher at National Taiwan University.
