MI5 chief lists Iran, Russia, AI and terrorists among threats to UK
LONDON, Oct 13 - MI5 spy chief Ken McCallum delivered his annual speech on Tuesday outlining his view of the threats to Britain, from hostile states such as Iran and Russia to the development of artificial intelligence.
Here is a summary of the main threats and issues he detailed in his speech and subsequent questions from media:
RUSSIA
McCallum called Russia, which denies involvement in hostile acts in Britain and other Western countries, "aggressor number one". He said it was escalating "hybrid" warfare, staying below the threshold that would trigger a direct NATO response.
He said Russia's capabilities had been reduced by the expulsion of 1,000 officials from embassies since the invasion of Ukraine, which meant it had to rely on native volunteers and criminal proxies.
IRAN
Tehran is also using criminal proxies - to target opponents, Iranian media organisations and Israeli interests in Britain - and has expanded its hybrid campaign in the last year, McCallum said.
He said operations connected to Iran had yielded more than 50 arrests in the UK, and that many had been aimed at Jewish communities.
The other shift had been "Iranian ambitions to come at harder targets, like military sites", he said.
Tehran also rejects accusations of malign activity in Britain.
ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
McCallum said AI was "supercharging the cybersecurity contest between attackers and defenders", producing tailored propaganda and material for individuals.
MI5 has caught potential attackers using it to try to improve reconnaissance and attack methodologies. AI-enabled drones added a new challenge, he said.
McCallum said the greatest concern about the misuse of AI was terrorists developing bioweapons or even creating new pathogens.
AI also presented a risk in itself.
"Put at its simplest, human history has given us no experience of facing an actor which is smarter than we are, is capable of out-thinking us. This is genuinely novel and deserves the serious attention it is getting."
TERRORISM
Britain in April raised its national terrorism threat level to "severe", meaning an attack within the next six months is highly likely.
McCallum said Al Qaeda and Islamic State continued to inspire plots, and MI5 was still having to respond to attempts to carry out mass-casualty attacks.
He said the most marked trend of the last year had been the increase in cases where extreme anti-immigration and anti-Muslim grievances were tipping over into terrorist intent.
An investigation into one 13-year-old who had been radicalised by extreme right-wing ideology had led to an unnamed foreign partner thwarting a lethal attack on its soil, he said.
BREXIT
On Sunday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Russia had interfered in Britain's 2016 referendum vote to leave the European Union, something Moscow has denied.
Asked about such interference, McCallum said it was public knowledge that Russian media such as Russia Today "came in pretty strongly around the time of the referendum", and there had been a certain amount of activity from trolls and bots.
But he said Russian online trolling had been comparatively unimpressive. REUTERS

IMF warns AI market correction could threaten global financial stability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:20:54 UTC
00:20:54 KST

Mücahithan Avcıoğlu
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
The International Monetary Fund warned on Tuesday that a correction in artificial intelligence-related markets could threaten global financial stability if investment and profit expectations disappoint, with existing financial vulnerabilities potentially amplifying the shock.
Presenting its October Global Financial Stability Report during the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, the fund said financial stability risks remain elevated despite the resilience of markets to repeated shocks and heightened uncertainty.
Athanasios Vamvakidis, an official in the IMF’s Monetary and Capital Markets Department, said stronger-than-expected economic growth, robust corporate earnings and optimism about AI had helped support global markets.
That resilience, however, should not be interpreted as evidence that the financial system is safe, he cautioned.
The IMF identified an AI-related market correction as one of three major risks that could spark financial stress, alongside rising sovereign bond yields and cyber incidents capable of disrupting financial services or undermining confidence.
An AI correction could emerge if expectations for investment or profitability are not met. Meanwhile, inflation pressures, fiscal imbalances and large volumes of government and private-sector borrowing are contributing to risks in sovereign bond markets.
Although the threats could be manageable individually, weaknesses already present in the financial system could magnify their effects, the fund warned.
The IMF said its banking-sector stress test, incorporating severe shocks related to AI, bond markets and energy, showed that banks remained broadly resilient.
Nevertheless, a group of weaker banks would face insufficient capital under that scenario, and the share of vulnerable institutions has been increasing.
The fund also highlighted risks in nonbank financial institutions, including insurers, pension funds, private credit providers and hedge funds.
Insurers and pension funds hold more illiquid assets, which could expose them to greater difficulties during a downturn. Private credit faces rising borrower leverage and liquidity pressures that could constrain lending.
Hedge funds can help support markets, but their borrowing and concentration in similar trades could amplify stress when conditions deteriorate.
Emerging markets have also demonstrated resilience, although weaker policy buffers in some economies and less transparent alternative financing sources in certain frontier markets remain concerns.
The IMF urged policymakers to strengthen financial resilience before further shocks materialize, noting that high public debt and limited policy space could complicate their response.
Its recommendations included placing public debt on a sustainable path, preserving central bank independence, maintaining a commitment to inflation targets and communicating policy clearly.
The fund also urged stronger cyber resilience and close monitoring of risks across banks and nonbank financial institutions.

Omair Ahmad on Love, Loss and the Lingering Spirit of Lucknow

Omair Ahmad is the author of ‘Encounters’, ‘The Storyteller's Tale’, ‘Tall Tales by a Small Dog’, ‘The Kingdom at the Centre of the World: Journeys Into Bhutan’ and ‘Jimmy, The Terrorist’, which won the Crossword Award for Fiction and was shortlisted for the Man Asian Literary Prize. He is also a prominent columnist and a political and social commentator. In this conversation, he discusses his latest novel, ‘Homecoming’. Excerpts:Q: How did this book come about? A: The genesis of this was when I was in DC. I just finished my second master's and I was missing home. Being a brown guy with a Muslim name in America, just when the war on terror was at its apogee leaves you a little off the place. And I hadn't been able to travel home since I’d gone, which was in 2001. So I met this person, a friend, and she invited me to a book club and everyone was writing little bits and they asked me to write something. And so I wrote the beginning of this novella, which is no longer the beginning. Much has changed, everything has changed. But there is a strong emotion behind it and I think that has carried through even now... My wife says it's about love, loss and Lucknow. I've gone very much for mood and the feel of a place.
So there's a bit of history, there's. But it's largely about people. So there's characters I've known, characters I've imagined, bits of stories that I've heard about Lucknow. Q: It is a form of storytelling which is disappearing as we are moving more and more into very nuclear and urban families. A: This was one of those things that I really struggled with. The novel as a form is very much a product of the European enlightenment pathway. It has the individual at the centre... If you pick up most novels, it's a very narrow thing of who they are. But for me, as a product of this country, of this culture, I always wanted to know what's behind them. Because we always understand people as being part of this family, this mahalla, this web of relationships. No person just is a person standing on their own... They are so much more than a person. They're also part of the past. They're also part of the relationship in their environments... The idea of the novel as a European construct and the way that we communicate is sometimes different, and we think that that's wrong. But I think one of the things which I have improved on is I'm no longer very apologetic about that. This is who I am. This is who we are. This is how we tell our stories... We are multilingual people. We talk in lots of languages. Even like, say, the Urdu or Hindi that I use at home and on the street and with elders versus young. These are all almost different languages. The way we use them, trying to transpose that into any language.. you're really struggling, because the forms aren't there. There's no correct way to go about it... I know that while I'm writing in English, I'm not necessarily thinking in English when I'm writing. And I'm writing about people who will be only partially thinking in English, if at all, or speaking in it. And so it's guesswork. It's just trying to bully my way through somehow to make this language work like that.
Q: There's a sentence you use: Memories are such flimsy things. A: Things are clearer in our memories than they were in real life. And if you ever had an argument with anybody, you know this true. Because in your memory, your argument is very clear. And in their memory, the argument is very clear. The reality is it was never clear. It was always messy.
But there is truth there. And memory is important for us, especially as a country where so much of our history is actually oral history. And so much of our history has been badly reinterpreted by colonial administrators for their own design, and that we have swallowed wholesale. And then we spend our whole time... like how you take fish bones out once you've taken a bite... But I struggle with this because I don't know what is true in all of this. And I wanted to register that little thing that, yes, we think our memories are clearer than what is recorded, but should we be that trusting of our own memories or other people's memories as well?

Lassa fever kills 268, spreads to 119 local governments in 24 Nigerian states
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:10:38 UTC
00:10:38 KST

Kabir Adeniyi
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
Nigeria has recorded 268 deaths from Lassa fever, with 1,138 confirmed cases reported in 24 states and 119 local government areas in 2026, according to the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) on Tuesday.
The figures were contained in the agency’s latest situation report covering Sept. 28 to Oct. 4, corresponding to epidemiological week 40. The case fatality rate stood at 23.6%, compared to 18.6% during the corresponding period in 2025.
The NCDC said confirmed cases increased from 924 during the same period in 2025 to 1,138 in 2026, while deaths rose from 172 to 268.
Nigeria recorded 8,414 suspected cases during the first 40 weeks of the year, compared to 8,041 in the corresponding period last year.
Despite the rise in cumulative infections and deaths, new confirmed cases declined to three in week 40, down from 13 in the preceding week. The latest cases were reported in Bauchi and Benue states, with one death recorded during the week.
Five states: Ondo, Bauchi, Taraba, Edo and Benue accounted for 88% of confirmed cases recorded in 2026. Ondo had the largest share, at 36%, followed by Bauchi with 23%, Taraba with 12%, Edo with 11% and Benue with 6%, according to the NCDC.
The agency attributed the high fatality rate partly to late presentation at health facilities, high treatment costs and poor health-seeking behavior in affected communities.
Lassa fever is an acute viral illness primarily transmitted to humans through contact with food or household items contaminated by infected rodents. Human-to-human transmission can also occur through contact with infected bodily fluids, particularly in health care settings without adequate infection-prevention measures.
The NCDC has urged residents to keep their surroundings clean, store food in covered containers and dispose of waste properly to reduce contact with rodents. It also advises those experiencing symptoms such as fever, weakness or headache to seek medical attention promptly.

15:09:51 UTC
00:09:51 KST

Karnataka deputy chief minister G Parameshwara announced a 2030 target for the state to emerge as a national leader in disaster prevention and preparedness.
Karnataka deputy chief minister G Parameshwara on Tuesday announced a 2030 target for the state to emerge as a national leader in disaster prevention and preparedness, stressing the need to make risk reduction an integral part of governance and development planning.Speaking at the inaugural meeting of the state platform for disaster risk reduction, held on the International day for disaster risk reduction, he said preventing disasters, safeguarding livelihoods and building long-term resilience must be key priorities for the state.
Parameshwara said development should not be judged merely by investment, infrastructure creation or economic growth, but also by the extent to which people's lives and livelihoods are protected. Floods, droughts and landslides can wipe out homes, agricultural produce and livelihoods built over many years, he pointed out.“For a government, a disaster may be an administrative emergency. For an affected family, it can mean a lifetime of hardship,” he said, calling for a shift from post-disaster relief and rehabilitation towards preventing avoidable damage and loss.
Focus on risk assessment and resilient infrastructure
Referring to the United Nations' sendai framework for disaster risk reduction 2015-2030, Parameshwara said Karnataka must improve risk assessment, early warning mechanisms, disaster preparedness and investment in resilient infrastructure.
He noted that the state faces multiple hazards, including droughts, floods, landslides across the Western Ghats and threats to coastal communities. Rapid urbanisation, changing land-use patterns and growing pressure on natural drainage systems have further heightened disaster risks, he added.The deputy chief minister called for comprehensive disaster risk assessments of major public infrastructure projects. He urged government departments to identify vulnerable assets and incorporate risk-reduction measures into their annual plans and budgets.He said the revenue department, working through the Karnataka state disaster management authority and district administrations, should strengthen disaster planning, vulnerability assessments, coordination of early warnings and measures to protect livelihoods.
Departments urged to strengthen coordination
Emphasising the need for coordinated action across departments, Parameshwara said the urban development department should prioritise flood prevention and drainage management, while the rural development department must improve disaster preparedness at the village level.The agriculture, education and health departments, he said, should focus on protecting farmers, schools, hospitals and essential services during emergencies.He also called for wider adoption of technology, including satellite imagery, geospatial data, artificial intelligence and predictive analytics, to strengthen risk assessment and improve early warning systems.Merely issuing alerts would not be enough, he said, emphasising that warnings must reach vulnerable communities in time for people to take appropriate protective measures.Parameshwara advocated a people-centred disaster preparedness network linking scientific institutions, district administrations, gram panchayats and households.He stressed the importance of developing local preparedness plans, building community volunteer networks, identifying safe shelters and evacuation routes, and conducting regular mock drills, particularly in areas prone to disasters.
Children, senior citizens, persons with disabilities and economically vulnerable households must receive special attention in disaster planning, he added.
Livelihood protection to remain a priority
Highlighting the economic consequences of disasters, Parameshwara said disaster management efforts must account for the losses suffered by farmers, fishermen, small traders and daily-wage workers, rather than focusing only on damage to physical infrastructure.He said the Karnataka state disaster risk reduction roadmap 2025-2030 must be implemented through measurable targets, time-bound action plans, clearly assigned responsibilities for departments and regular monitoring.The state platform for disaster risk reduction, he added, should concentrate on tangible improvements, including stronger infrastructure, uninterrupted essential services and timely assistance for families affected by disasters.

Türkiye, EU must strengthen cooperation amid global trade turbulence: Trade minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:09:09 UTC
00:09:09 KST

Mücahithan Avcıoğlu
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
Türkiye and the European Union must act with a shared understanding of competitiveness and economic security amid global trade turbulence, Turkish Trade Minister Omer Bolat said Tuesday. 
In a post on Turkish social media platform NSosyal following a Türkiye-EU Business Summit in Brussels, Bolat said he addressed business leaders alongside EU Commissioner for Trade and Economic Security Maros Sefcovic at the event, which drew broad participation from Turkish and EU business circles. 
Bolat said bilateral trade exceeding $233 billion and European capital accounting for approximately 70% of foreign direct investment in Türkiye showed the depth of their economic partnership and mutual interdependence. 
He said Sefcovic stressed the strategic importance of Türkiye-EU economic and trade relations and highlighted the key role of the High-Level Trade Dialogue mechanism in advancing those ties. 
Bolat stressed that the EU's new industrial and competitiveness policies should take into account the strong production and supply chains established through the Customs Union. 
"Türkiye is not only an important trading partner for Europe; it is also a strong production base, a reliable supply chain partner, and a strategic partner in global competition," he said. 
Türkiye's potential to strengthen Europe's industrial capacity, supply security, and competitiveness in global markets is becoming increasingly important, Bolat added. 
Deepening economic relations on the basis of existing achievements would therefore serve both sides' long-term interests, he said. 
Bolat reaffirmed their determination to strengthen cooperation in the green and digital transitions, make more effective use of the opportunities offered by the Customs Union, and reinforce ties between their business communities to boost joint competitiveness and bilateral trade. 
He also said the Century of Türkiye vision, pursued under President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's leadership, aims to expand the country's production, export, investment, and technological capabilities while strengthening its position in the global economy. 
Türkiye will continue working to advance its role in international trade by drawing on its strategic location, industrial infrastructure, skilled workforce, and manufacturing capabilities, he added. 
'Solution should not be to exclude trusted partners' 
In his speech at the Türkiye-EU Business Summit, Bolat called on the European Union to include Türkiye as a trusted partner in its proposed "Made in EU" initiative, warning that excluding the country from the bloc's industrial framework would undermine decades of economic integration and established supply chains. 
"We respect the (EU’s) ideal Industrial Accelerator Act, which is normal, and we suffer from the same grave concerns about huge imports from third countries. But the solution should not be to exclude trusted partners or Customs Union," he said. 
"The solution which we strongly request and expect from our member countries, European Parliament and European Commission and EU Council of Ministers, is that Türkiye should be a trusted partner with the 'Made with Europe' project," Bolat said, adding that Türkiye is working closely with its European counterparts on the issue.
He stressed that Türkiye's inclusion would serve the interests of both sides, particularly their auto, ye industries and wider manufacturing sectors, given the deep integration of their economies. 
Bolat added that high-level trade dialogue last year had already helped reduce the number of outstanding trade-related issues within the Customs Union from 29 to 14, with further progress expected. 
Visa difficulties 
Bolat also said Turkish citizens continue to face difficulties obtaining visas despite Türkiye's status as an EU candidate country and its longstanding institutional ties with the bloc. 
He acknowledged that recent European Commission measures had eased visa procedures somewhat, but said significant obstacles remain.
Procedures were eased, “but not enough," he said, referring to the difficulties faced by Turkish businesspeople, academics, transport operators, and students.
He stressed that visa-related barriers are incompatible with the objective of strengthening ties between Türkiye and the EU, while welcoming what he described as the constructive and sincere approach of European counterparts.

China builds a lighter cousin of the U.S. HIMARS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:04:45 UTC
00:04:45 KST

- China has developed a light rocket launcher on an upgraded Dongfeng Mengshi MV3 truck with a modular 20-round pod for 122 mm rockets.
- The launcher can fire guided or unguided rockets out to a maximum range of 40 km.
China has developed a new light, highly mobile rocket launcher built on an upgraded version of the Dongfeng Mengshi MV3 tactical truck, carrying a 20-round launch pod that can fire guided or unguided 122 mm rockets out to 40 km (25 miles), according to images and details shared by Chinese military commentator DS北风 on X.
The launcher uses a modular, box-shaped launch pod mounted on the rear of the truck, a design that lets crews swap out a spent pod for a fresh one instead of reloading individual tubes.
The 20 rockets in each pod can be a mix of guided and unguided types, and the maximum range of 40 km puts it in the same class as the 122 mm rocket launchers that make up much of China’s tactical rocket artillery.
The Mengshi, built by Dongfeng Motor, is China’s equivalent of the Humvee, a four-wheel-drive tactical vehicle used across the People’s Liberation Army, and the MV3 is the third generation of the family. Putting a rocket launcher on a light truck lets airborne, air assault and light infantry units take their own rocket artillery into terrain where heavier trucks cannot go, and lets crews fire and move away quickly before enemy counterfire arrives.
The concept is similar to the U.S.-made HIMARS, which mounts a pod of six 227 mm GMLRS guided rockets on a five-ton truck and has been widely used in Ukraine. China’s new launcher carries more but smaller rockets with a shorter range, trading reach for volume of fire at shorter distances. The PLA already fields 122 mm rocket launchers on larger trucks and tracked vehicles, as well as the PHL-16, a long-range modular system that fires heavier rockets and missiles from interchangeable pods.

UnitedHealth Group tops estimates, hikes profit outlook as insurer manages high medical costs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:04:35 UTC
00:04:35 KST

UnitedHealth Group on Tuesday posted third-quarter earnings that blew past estimates and raised its full-year profit outlook, as the company continues to manage high medical costs and sees investments in value-based care and artificial intelligence take hold.
The nation's largest private insurer said it expects fiscal 2026 adjusted earnings of at least $20.50 per share, up from a previous outlook of $19.50 to $20 per share.
The healthcare giant's turnaround plan is gaining momentum after three consecutive strong quarters this year. UnitedHealth is working to stabilize margins by shrinking membership, exiting unprofitable contracts, and ramping up investments in artificial intelligence and value-based care, which tie doctor and facility compensation to patient health outcomes, quality of care and cost effectiveness rather than the volume of medical services provided.
"You'll see in the quarter that we continue to execute not only on the financial aspects of our business, but really doing them with a simpler approach and an approach that's really focused on investing heavily in value-based care," CFO Wayne DeVeydt said in an interview.
Here's what the company reported for the third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
- Earnings per share: $4.69 adjusted vs. $4.14 expected
- Revenue: $112.69 billion vs. $111.40 billion expected
The company posted third-quarter net income of $4.11 billion, or $4.56 per share, compared with $2.35 billion, or $2.59 per share, in the same period a year ago. Excluding items like business divestitures, restructuring and the expected reduction of reserves for unprofitable contracts, UnitedHealth earned $4.69 per share.
Revenue fell to $112.69 billion from $113.16 billion a year earlier. The company's insurer, UnitedHealthcare, and its Optum healthcare unit both topped analysts' operating earnings estimates for the quarter, according to StreetAccount.
Managing high costs
Notably, UnitedHealth's medical cost ratio — a measure of total medical expenses paid relative to premiums collected — came in at 88.4% for the third quarter. Analysts were expecting a ratio of 89.9%, according to StreetAccount. A lower ratio typically indicates the company collected more in premiums than it paid out in benefits, resulting in higher profitability.
Still, DeVeydt told CNBC that medical costs in the quarter "continue to be elevated versus historical norms" — an issue that has plagued insurers, particularly those operating privately run Medicare Advantage plans, for more than two years.
"I think it's something we should keep an eye on. I think you'll see that our medical care ratio has improved quite a bit, but I don't want that to be misleading in terms of [medical cost trends]," DeVeydt said.
He said the independent dispute resolution, or IDR, process under the No Surprises Act is adding at least 100 basis points, or 1 percentage point, to total medical costs. That federal law, which took effect in 2022, aims to protect consumers from unexpected medical bills.
The IDR process allows providers and insurers to resolve disputes over out-of-network payments. DeVeydt said those changes are driving up the company's claims costs, which can ultimately be passed on to consumers through higher premiums.
DeVeydt added that costs for inpatient services and pharmacy, particularly costly specialty pharmacy drugs for cancer and rare diseases, remain elevated.
Still, he highlighted the company's value-based care efforts, which he said are helping control medical costs by steering patients toward the right providers and emphasizing preventive care, DeVeydt added.
He said acute hospital admissions among UnitedHealth members fell 15% year over year through the third quarter, while home health admissions rose 10%, suggesting more patients are receiving care in lower-cost settings.
"You're finding more members are actually getting into a lower-cost care environment, but more importantly, they're getting into the care environment they actually want to be in," he told CNBC. "So we think we're really balancing both the quality and the cost."
UnitedHealth is also rolling out AI-powered ambient listening tools to reduce physicians' administrative burden and free up time for patient visits. Appointment scheduling done by patients rather than with the assistance of a provider increased 27% year over year, DeVeydt said.
He expects those initiatives to have a compounding effect on medical cost management through the fourth quarter and into 2027 as the programs expand.

Authorities responded to a fire caused by the attack on Tuesday, the ministry said in a statement. No injuries or fatalities were reported.
The attack on the headquarters of Saudi’s national oil company came after Yemen’s Houthis warned all employees and civilians near Saudi Arabia’s oil facilities to evacuate, calling the sites “a legitimate target” earlier on Tuesday.
The warning from the group’s spokesman, Yahya Saree, was prompted by an evacuation order from the Saudi-led coalition urging civilians to evacuate Yemeni Oil Company’s al-Sabah central station in the Houthi-controlled capital Sanaa.
Saree responded to the coalition’s evacuation order, warning that any strikes on Sanaa would meet a “harsh and painful” reprisal on the Saudi Arabian capital Riyadh.
Saudi Arabia also intercepted missiles launched by the Houthis towards Riyadh, SPA reported. Four people were injured and 15 homes were damaged by the debris from two intercepted missiles, said the Civil Defense spokesperson, according to SPA.
Attack on Sanaa oil facility
Shortly after the Saudi-led coalition’s evacuation order, Al Jazeera’s team on the ground reported hearing explosions in Sanaa. Media outlets affiliated with the Houthis said air strikes by the Saudi-backed forces struck an oil facility in the al-Sabah area of the capital.
Shortly after the warning, Saree said on Telegram that any Saudi attack on Sanaa would be met with a “firm and painful” response in the Saudi capital, Riyadh.
Houthi officials appeared to have anticipated the attack. The oil company said its storage facilities were empty and that a Saudi strike would not affect oil reserves or supplies for residents.
Still, witnesses in the city said lines of cars formed at some gas stations amid fears of a shortage.
“We heard the explosion upon Saudi Arabia targeting the Yemeni oil al-Sabah central station here in the capital Sanaa,” Al Jazeera correspondent Yousef Mawry said.
Saudi Arabia also conducted two other air strike campaigns on the Ras Isa port, targeting Yemeni oil storage tanks and on an oil station in the Houthi-controlled Hodeidah province, according to Mawry.
Saudi-led coalition spokesman Major General Turki al-Maliki accused the Houthis of using the facility and its underground fuel depots for their arsenal of missiles and drones.
Following the reported explosions, Saree said Houthi fighters were confronting Saudi-backed forces in Sanaa.
In a statement on X, Saree said the Houthis would target the sites that were ordered to be evacuated if the Saudi-led coalition proceeded with an attack on Sanaa.
Civilians were told on Tuesday to evacuate the Aramco company headquarters in Dhahran, Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport and a refinery affiliated with Aramco in Riyadh.
Airport attacks
An attack on Riyadh’s airport on Saturday left at least 13 people dead and more than 300 injured, rocking the world’s top crude oil exporter. Another person was killed, and 11 were wounded on Sunday after a projectile struck the airport in Riyadh.
Many international airlines have since suspended flights to Saudi Arabia and neighbouring countries following the deadly weekend attacks by the Houthis, including Air France-KLM, Air India, Etihad, Lufthansa, Delta, Gulf Air and Qatar Airways.
The kingdom, which backs Yemen’s internationally recognised government, was still weathering new attacks on Tuesday, with the coalition saying its forces intercepted three drones north of Riyadh.
Saree also reiterated the Houthis’ warning to airports in Saudi Arabia following recent attacks on multiple airports and oil facilities across the country since last week in a spillover from the wider regional conflict between the US and Iran.
Saudi Arabia’s cabinet, chaired by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, said on Tuesday the Houthis would face “consequences” for their attacks across the kingdom, according to the Saudi Press Agency.
US President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that the Houthis were “behaving very badly” and told reporters he “might” ask Turkiye’s President Recep Tayyip Erdogan to intervene and support Saudi interests.
“President Erdogan, I think, would do as I ask,” Trump said.
Speaking at the IMF-World Bank meetings in Bangkok, IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva said the attacks could have negative spillover “everywhere”.
Dawn of Yemen
Saudi Arabia has in recent weeks launched strikes against the Houthis and is backing a Yemeni government counteroffensive known as the “Dawn of Yemen” after the group seized strategic territory last month.
Yemeni forces loyal to the internationally recognised government said they launched a series of air strikes on Houthi positions and equipment in the country’s southwest on Tuesday.
A total of nine air strikes were conducted in Taiz governorate, including five in Dhubab district and four in al-Masrakh district, the government said.
According to the Taiz Military Axis Media Center, affiliated with the Ministry of Defence, fighting is ongoing between government forces and the Houthis in al-Shaqab, south of Taiz.
The Yemeni Network for Rights and Freedom said on Tuesday that the Houthis had killed at least five civilians, including a five-year-old girl in Taiz during the previous 24 hours and injured 17 others.
The organisation accused the Houthis of shelling residential neighbourhoods, damaging at least seven homes. It also alleged that the group had fired more than 180 projectiles across Taiz during the previous 24 hours.
Houthi offensive
In September, the Houthis carried out a lightning ground offensive on Mocha, pushing back forces loyal to Yemen’s government from the strategic port city. The same month, the group’s forces again swept through and seized territory along the western coast and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, including the strategically located Mayyun Island in the strait.
As the fighting in Yemen continues to rage, the president of the International Committee of the Red Cross, Mirjana Spoljaric, warned that civilians across the Middle East are bearing the brunt of escalating hostilities and has called for all parties to de-escalate.
“In Yemen, the scale of death, displacement and damage to civilian infrastructure, including in Aden and Sanaa, is mounting at an alarming rate. Across the Middle East, civilian infrastructure has repeatedly been hit and lives have been lost,” Spoljaric said in a statement.
At least 46 civilians have been killed and more than 130 others injured in Yemen since August, many of them children, and more than 200,000 people have been displaced since September, according to the United Nations.

Is this the best time for US strategists to push for abandoning ambiguity on Taiwan?
Trump’s quiet approach to Taiwan opens door for debate on ending decades-old US policy of strategic ambiguity
For nearly five decades, the United States’ Taiwan policy has centred on strategic ambiguity by not declaring whether it would intervene militarily in a potential Taiwan conflict.
This policy – designed to deter Beijing from using force while preventing Taipei from formally declaring independence – is being challenged by realist US strategists amid a broader debate over America’s role in the world, growing constraints on US military might and a shifting regional balance of power driven by China’s military rise.
A small group of realist US strategists is pushing for the US to rule out military intervention over Taiwan to avoid the possibility of a catastrophic war between mainland China and the US. Experts said this idea, despite still being a minority view, was at least opening debate on the long-standing one-sided policy.
“When US officials first adopted strategic ambiguity over Taiwan, China’s military was no match for that of the US. This is no longer the case,” wrote Jennifer Kavanagh, director of military analysis at the Washington-based think tank Defence Priorities, in an opinion piece late last month.

A duo goes against the tide to explain an origin of human endurance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

A duo goes against the tide to explain an origin of human endurance
Perhaps it was diving, not just chasing prey on the African savanna, that made us marathoners
Two researchers may have opened floodgates on the debate over why humans can run marathons, swim the English Channel or dive a hundred meters and back on a single breath and their ape cousins can’t.
Humans evolved endurance for feats like these not just by running down prey on the African savanna, but also by diving for food in lakes or coastal waters, the duo propose September 17 in PaleoAnthropology. The hypothesis adds complexity to a decades-old theory that puts the drivers for evolution exclusively on land. But it coexists with a history of pushback for any water-related ideas.
The work is causing ripples among anthropologists. “I could not work out [at first] if this was groundbreaking or dumb,” says Christian Tryon, a paleoanthropologist at the University of Connecticut in Storrs.
In 1960, researchers came up with what’s been called the aquatic ape or waterside hypothesis, which suggested that our ancestors evolved longer legs and other adaptations from swimming for their suppers in watery habitats. Popularized in media accounts but not adequately vetted in peer-reviewed journals, the idea was shunned by the scientific community as additional fossils pointed away from a life in water. More recently, the dominant theory has been that it was landlocked human ancestors who gradually developed our remarkable endurance. “There’s been this reluctance to really think about anything sort of water-related as important in human evolution,” Tryon says.
Yet evolutionary anthropologist Josephine Joordens, a self-professed “water person” who trained as a marine biologist, had long wondered whether coastal life was vital to the evolutionary process, because it provides easy access to both water and land resources. Joordens combined forces with Erika Schagatay, a physiologist at Mid-Sweden University in Östersund, to formulate what they call the “dive first, run later” hypothesis.
Schagatay — herself a freediver — has spent decades observing and monitoring modern sea foraging people such as the Ama in Japan and the Sama-Bajau in Southeast Asia. Joordens studied fossil evidence and combed the literature about aquatic activities. Our evolution “was likely a very complex and very dynamic process,” says Joordens, of the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig, Germany.
They propose some Homo species wound up shallow-water diving repeatedly about 2 million to 3 million years ago, much the way the Sama-Bajau do today. These people spend four to six hours per day repeatedly diving several meters deep to catch fish and collect shellfish and other food. They evolved bigger spleens than their non-diving counterparts and, it seems, enhanced respiratory and cardiovascular capacity. They have the ability to “pace” breathing periods and breath-holding to avoid fatigue. In our ancestors, that could have paved the way for the cardiorespiratory stamina needed in modern endurance running, Schagatay says.
These Homo divers evolved heavy bones to help stay underwater and downward facing noses to keep water out, the two suggest. They eventually passed those endurance-boosting traits on to other populations with lighter bones and a more terrestrial lifestyle.
The study “shows there is a lot of evidence” for forage diving as an early evolutionary driver, says Leslea Hlusko, a paleobiologist at the Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana in Burgos, Spain.
This idea is not a retread of the aquatic ape theory, says Christopher Ruff, a biological anthropologist at Johns Hopkins School of Medicine. “Occasional aquatic foraging is quite a different proposal“ from the discredited theory’s primarily aquatic existence and should be taken seriously, Ruff says.
Not everyone thinks the dive first idea holds water.
Multiple factors work against the idea that diving could have helped humans become better endurance runners, says Daniel Lieberman, a paleoanthropologist at Harvard University. He argues that endurance diving does not require an enhanced aerobic capacity: It slows the heart rate, whereas running speeds it up. He disputes how and why heavy bones arose; they could have developed in people who used their bodies for heavy work and not because such bones helped divers with buoyancy issues. Nor is the downward pointed nose meaningful given that many diving mammals have forward facing noses. Other reasons, such as keeping the air in nostrils moist, were probably more important in selecting for this feature, he says.
What’s more, many people around the world have long relied on running down game for food, says archaeologist Eugène Morin of Trent University in Peterborough, Canada. “Diving is costly and the [caloric] returns are low,” so early humans would not choose to dive if other foraging opportunities existed, he argues.
Critiques aside, “the simple ‘ape walked out from forest to savanna’ story clearly does not cut it anymore,” says Pascal Gagneux, a biological anthropologist at the University of California, San Diego. Coastal routes around Africa, along Africa’s lakeshores and out of Africa “must have played a huge role” in human evolution, Gagneux says.
The pair knows they risk the ire of their peers in presenting this “dive first”  hypothesis, but Joordens says, “we are both in our early 60s and we both have beautiful careers, so we thought ‘whatever happens, happens.’”
And Tryon ultimately found the paper worth the read. “If nothing else, it gets people thinking and it gets people looking.”

In a separate incident on Tuesday, four Palestinians from the same family were injured after settlers stormed their home in the village of Talfit, south of Nablus in the northern West Bank, according to a medical source and a family member.
Trump says Yemen's Houthis are 'behaving very badly'
US President Donald Trump on Tuesday said Houthi militants who control vast swaths of Yemen were "behaving very badly" as consequences of the US-Iran war spill into the broader Middle East.

It said it will target the Aramco oil facilities in Dhahran, east of the kingdom, and the capital Riyadh, as well as the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. The airport has been hit several times already, killing more than a dozen people.

How Iran made the Houthis into such a problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:55:47 UTC
23:55:47 KST

How Iran made the Houthis into such a problem for the U.S. and its allies
Yemen's Houthi rebels have morphed over the last decade from being a little-known group in northwest Yemen, to Iran's most potent ally in the region and a central opponent of the United States and its allies across the Middle East.
While Iran's other proxy forces have been depleted in recent years, the Houthis have taken center stage in the Middle East, offering yet another example of how a smaller, guerrilla-style force that's dug in on the ground can cause asymmetric damage through hard-to-repel aerial attacks.
In support of their Iranian benefactors, the Houthis launched initial attacks on Israel not long after the U.S. joined the Jewish state in strikes across Iran on Feb. 28, sparking the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.
Saudi Arabia, one of the world's richest nations and a key American ally, is now bearing the brunt of the Houthis' attacks, which have killed at least 20 people at Saudi airports over the last week. Along with other allied groups, the militants have also attacked Saudi oil infrastructure, helping drive up global energy prices by threatening the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which, like the Strait of Hormuz, is a key maritime chokepoint for oil and gas shipments.
The Saudis have asked the U.S. to join its military operations against the Houthis, and President Trump, who initially rejected the request, said over the weekend that he's considering it.
Iran's "most powerful proxy"
The Houthis are backed financially and militarily by Iran, officials from the U.S. and Israel, as well as many regional analysts, have said for years.
They were once a relatively marginal group within what Iran calls its Axis of Resistance — a loose alliance of anti-Israel, anti-U.S. militant groups that includes Hamas in Gaza and Hezbollah in Lebanon. Both of those U.S.-designated terrorist organizations have been severely weakened by Israeli operations launched in the wake of the Hamas-led attack on Oct. 7, 2023.
The Houthis joined Hamas and Hezbollah's attacks on Israel and became the target of an Israeli counteroffensive, as well as military operations by the Biden and Trump administrations. But unlike Hamas and Hezbollah, the group has rebounded and emerged better armed, battle-hardened and confident.
"The Houthis are the most powerful proxy within the Iranian network, hands down," said Mohammed Al-Basha, founder of the Basha Report, a U.S.-based risk advisory group. "Any U.S. military strategy planning a campaign on Iran will have to take into consideration what the Houthis will do next."
After the 2023 attack on Israel, with help from Iran, the group really started gaining capacity and momentum.
"Before Oct. 7, we didn't see them getting the newest equipment from Iran. After Oct. 7, they got the best," al-Basha told CBS News, adding that Tehran not only armed the Houthis, but also helped the group hone its skills in penetrating air defenses.
The Houthis started adopting new tactics, including targeting Israel with layered attacks using drones, cruise missiles and then ballistic missiles to overwhelm the country's significant defenses.
Now the Houthis are using the same tactics against Saudi Arabia.
In the age of asymmetric warfare, the group has also used Yemen's ranking as one of the poorest countries in the world as something of a strategic advantage: They rely on a strongly ideological support base willing to suffer economic pain and isolation if the tradeoff is inflicting great damage to the Saudis and the global economy, said Yoel Guzansky, a senior research fellow focused on Persian Gulf politics and security at the Institute for National Security Studies.
"All you need is a not very sophisticated surface-to-surface missile to strike Riyadh airport. They can assemble those in small factories in the mountains," Guzansky said.
What do the Houthis want?
Houthi military spokesman Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said recently that the group's attacks on Saudi Arabia are in response to a "brutal Saudi aggression against our country and our people."
But al-Basha said the Houthis' real objectives are not retaliation, but power and recognition.
They want to seize control of all of Yemen, and to get the Saudis to both recognize their legitimacy, and help bankroll their expansion, he said, which is why he believes they have coupled their campaign inside Yemen with the attacks on Saudi Arabia.
The Houthis' Iran-powered evolution
The Houthi movement grew out of the Zaydi Shiite Muslim sect, which has roots that date back centuries in northern Yemen. They are a minority in the country, which is predominantly Sunni Muslim, but the number of Zaydis is significant, representing as much as a third of Yemen's overall population.
The Houthi movement originally emerged as an effort to protect Zaydi culture within Yemen, but it evolved into a group that has as its slogan: "Allah is the Greatest; Death to America; Death to Israel; A Curse upon the Jews; Victory to Islam."
Analysts estimate that the armed Houthi force consists of hundreds of thousands of combat-ready fighters. The group itself claims to have trained more than a million militants.
Their march to real power began in 2012, when the then-much-smaller group, consisting of thousands of fighters, capitalized on unrest in Yemen following the Arab Spring ouster of longtime authoritarian President Ali Abdullah Saleh to build a loyal following in the north of the country.
In 2014, they seized the capital Sanaa, sparking a civil war with the Western- and Saudi-backed government. The government was forced to relocate to the southern port city of Aden, where it is still based, and it has also retained control of the less-populated eastern portion of the country.
The Houthis quickly took control of key state military and civilian powers, including missile brigades and special forces, and the ability to levy taxes, explained al-Basha.
The group survived a first round of fighting with the Saudi-led military coalition from 2015 until 2022. During that time, military advisers from Hezbollah and Iran helped train Houthi commanders and combatants — and built up the group's ability to manufacture its own weapons, including drones and missiles, according to analysts.
The Houthis may also be using AI software to fine-tune their weapons. U.S. tech firm Anthropic released a report in September saying it had identified "threat actors" based in northern Yemen using their Claude Code software "in place of human software engineers to develop the guidance, navigation, and control (GNC) software that steers and stabilizes a flying vehicle."
The weapons the unnamed actors were attempting to develop included guided rockets and multi-stage ballistic missiles, according to Anthropic, which said it did not have evidence of the actors successfully fielding an operational device.
While they can produce some of their own weapons, however, Fabian Hinz, a weapons analyst with the International Institute for Strategic Studies, wrote last year that the Houthis "remain dependent on Iran for key technologies and advanced capabilities. While Tehran's support has, in some areas, evolved from the direct provision of complete systems to enabling localized manufacturing, it remains a critical enabler of Houthi military activity."
But it is not a one-sided relationship.
"With Hamas and Hezbollah severely weakened, the Houthis have become an increasingly indispensable pillar of Iran's regional strategy, providing Tehran with a relatively resilient and cost-effective means of threatening Saudi Arabia, Israel, and international shipping while projecting power far beyond Yemen," Guzansky told CBS News. "Their strategic value to Iran has arguably never been greater, even if the Houthis retain considerable autonomy in their decision-making."
Yemen's devastating war
Situated at the southern end of the Arabian Peninsula, the Houthis are geographically isolated from any outside ground force, with the exception of the Saudis, who don't have the manpower to take on such a well-entrenched enemy, analysts say.
Domestically, in Yemen's vicious civil war, the well-coordinated group faces opposing forces that, while largely aligned with the Saudi-backed government, are themselves divided and operating under separate command structures.
Since Yemen descended into war in 2015, the United Nations estimates that some 377,000 people have died, more than half due to indirect causes such as starvation and disease amid the fighting.
More than 201,210 people have fled from their homes, according to data from the United Nations' International Organization for Migration, including more than 3,700 who have fled by sea to Djibouti.
According to figures published by the World Health Organization last week, Yemen's Ministry of Health and Population had reported 959 deaths and 4,207 injuries attributed directly to the fighting across 10 provinces between the beginning of September and Oct. 2.
The Houthi-run Ministry of Health said Tuesday the death toll from the recent escalation of fighting, during the same period, stood at 107, with 278 more wounded.

Israel raids Ramallah medical complex and Palestinian NGO offices
Israeli forces stormed the courtyard of the Palestine Medical Complex in the occupied West Bank city of Ramallah on Tuesday and raided the offices of several prominent Palestinian human rights organisations, including Addameer, seizing equipment and files.
Israeli forces deployed snipers at the entrances to the medical complex during the incursion, according to Palestinian news agency Wafa. They also blocked people from entering and leaving the facility.
The Palestine Medical Complex, considered the largest government medical facility in the occupied West Bank, has previously been targeted by Israeli forces.
In July, local reports said soldiers stormed the area surrounding the complex and fired tear gas canisters extensively, causing suffocation injuries among Palestinians.
The latest developments came as Israeli forces also raided the offices of several Palestinian non-governmental organisations (NGOs) in Ramallah on Tuesday, including Addameer, which advocates for Palestinian prisoners, as well as the Union of Palestinian Women's Committees and the Human Rights Association, according to Al Jazeera English.
Israeli forces confiscated equipment belonging to Addameer, which Israeli authorities have previously designated a "terrorist organisation".
Israeli forces have previously raided the offices of several Palestinian human rights groups across the occupied West Bank, accusing organisations advocating for Palestinian rights of having links to armed groups.
Israel has claimed that several of these organisations have ties to the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP), a secular, left-wing movement with political and armed wings.
However, the organisations have disputed the allegations, and the claims have been challenged over the lack of publicly substantiated evidence supporting them.
On Tuesday, Israeli forces, accompanied by two tow trucks, also entered Al-Bireh, the Al-Tireh neighbourhood and the town of Sarda, north of Ramallah, patrolling the streets in military vehicles, Wafa reported.
Israeli forces also stormed the Legislative Council Roundabout, a prominent junction in central Ramallah, firing live ammunition, rubber-coated metal bullets and tear gas canisters while targeting journalists in the area, according to Wafa.
Local media reports said Firas Lutfi, a journalist with Sky News Arabia, sustained a shrapnel wound to his leg after being directly struck by a tear gas canister.
After the war in Gaza began in October 2023, Israel also increased its attacks in the occupied West Bank, with repeated Israeli military raids and settler attacks which have killed hundreds of people.

Trump Has Asked Guilfoyle to Resign, Says New White House Press Secretary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:52:45 UTC
23:52:45 KST

Kimberly Guilfoyle on Tuesday announced her resignation as President Donald Trump's Ambassador to Greece, amid a deluge of negative press including allegations that she asked a political donor to handle her $100,000 personal American Express bill. 
"Serving as the United States Ambassador to Greece has been the honor of a lifetime," Guilfoyle wrote in a lengthy statement posted to X. "From my first day as Ambassador, I have worked tirelessly to advance President Trump’s America First agenda, strengthen our strategic alliance with Greece, and deliver meaningful victories for the American people."
Guilfoyle's announcement came soon after Katie Zacharia, the White House’s new press secretary, confirmed at her first briefing that Trump had asked for the resignation of Guilfoyle. 
“We have asked Ambassador Guilfoyle to resign. She has been a wonderful asset to the team and we wish her well,” Zacharia said in an unusually brief debut in the briefing room.
Along with recent allegations about her dealings with a campaign donor, Guilfoyle, who was once engaged to Donald Trump Jr. and a major player in the MAGA movement, racked up a reputation for hard partying in Athens and living large as Trump’s personal rep in the region.
Allegations about Guilfoyle's conduct
The controversy began in late September, when The Wall Street Journal published a series of reports about Guilfoyle’s conduct before and during her tenure in Athens. The reports included allegations that she promoted a Greek construction company’s business interests, traveled on private jets and stayed in luxury accommodations paid for by businessmen, and sought money from a Trump donor to cover her personal credit card debt.
In one of the most serious allegations, the Journal reported that Guilfoyle exchanged text messages with businessman Eric Deters, a Trump donor, ahead of her Senate confirmation hearing in July 2025, asking him to wire $100,000 to clear her American Express bill. According to the report, Guilfoyle offered to use her connections to the Trump Administration, including her relationship with Trump Jr., to help Deters gain access to administration officials. Deters told the Journal that he did not pay her.
The Journal also reported that she promoted the Greek construction firm Aktor Group and that its lobbyist, Christos Marafatsos, attended diplomatic meetings across Balkan countries. It reported that Guilfoyle encouraged governments in the region to work with the company. Lawyers for Guilfoyle and Aktor Group disputed allegations that she acted improperly in promoting its business interests.
In another report, the Journal cited an audio recording in which Guilfoyle allegedly discussed luxury travel paid for by businessmen, including a private jet trip to the January 2026 World Economic Forum with Aktor Group CEO Alexandros Exarchou.
Guilfoyle’s lawyers have denied wrongdoing. Her attorney, Jesse Binnall, disputed the authenticity of the reported messages and said the money she sought was payment for earlier unpaid services, including travel and appearances at events before her nomination.
"These allegations are false, and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity," Guilfoyle said in her post on Tuesday announcing her resignation. "I have dedicated my professional life to fighting for justice, standing up for what is right, and defending the values that make America exceptional. I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service."
The allegations prompted scrutiny from lawmakers in both parties. Rep. Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, sought answers from Secretary of State Marco Rubio in a September letter, saying the reports suggested potentially corrupt influences on U.S. foreign policy. Rep. Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, later requested financial and communications records from Guilfoyle, citing public corruption and national security concerns. Senate Republican Majority Whip John Barrasso called the reports “very troubling” and said the Senate Foreign Relations Committee would examine the matter.
Guilfoyle's history with Trump's family
Guilfoyle’s departure comes as the controversy has drawn attention to her relationship with the Trump family and her transition from conservative media personality to diplomat. A former prosecutor in San Francisco and Los Angeles, Guilfoyle rose to prominence as a co-host of Fox News’ The Five, which she joined in 2011. She left the network in 2018 and helped raise funds for Trump’s 2020 presidential campaign. She was also a witness to events leading up to the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol and met with the House committee investigating the insurrection in 2022.
Trump announced his intention to nominate Guilfoyle as ambassador to Greece in December 2024, amid reports that she and Trump Jr. had split. The Senate confirmed her nomination in 2025, and she was sworn in that September, becoming the first woman to serve as U.S. ambassador to Greece.
Guilfoyle was previously married to California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat widely viewed as a potential 2028 presidential contender. The two were married from 2001 to 2006, before Newsom became governor.
“Kimberly Guilfoyle was not a member of my family. I guess she dated my son a long time ago,” Trump told reporters outside the White House, shortly after Guilfoyle announced her resignation.
The President suggested Guilfoyle’s ouster was driven by recent negative stories about her coming to light. “We didn’t like what we were reading,” he said.

‘Block, blunt, break’: What’s in NATO’s new Russia war plan?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:52:22 UTC
23:52:22 KST

‘Block, blunt, break’: What’s in NATO’s new Russia war plan?
NATO’s top commander says he is revealing the plan to stop a Russian invasion of Europe, even though the threat is not ‘imminent’.
NATO’s top general has unveiled a new war plan for countering a Russian attack on members of the alliance, embedding lessons learned from the front lines in Ukraine.
Speaking about NATO’s so-called “theory of victory” at the Warsaw Security Forum on Monday, General Alexus Grynkewich, who has served as head of United States European Command and the Supreme Allied Commander Europe since 2025, said the plan rests on three strategies designed to stop an invasion in its tracks: “block, blunt and break”.
The announcement comes amid mounting warnings from European intelligence agencies of rising threats from Russia, including both the prospect of conventional military action and “hybrid warfare”, which can include tactics from cyberattacks to tampering with undersea cables.
In a bid to ease the alliance’s growing concerns, Grynkewich said: “What I want to do is assure the one billion citizens of our alliance that we’ve got this. We know what we need to do. We know how we would do it.”
But the new plan from NATO comes at a time when the alliance itself appears divided on how to deal with Russia, following a series of recent overtures from US President Donald Trump to Russian President Vladimir Putin, including his latest controversial plan for Russia to release stocks of diesel to global markets despite sanctions on Russian oil.
So, what’s in the new NATO plan, and what are European agencies warning about? How has Russia reacted? And is the alliance even on the same page on all of this?
What’s in the new NATO plan?
General Grynkewich told the Warsaw Security Forum that NATO does not view a military confrontation with Russia as “imminent or inevitable”, but that it will nevertheless be ready for one.
“Implementing the theory of victory I’ve described today would require me to issue orders that I hope to never give,” he said. “But let there be no doubt: should war come, we will block, blunt any attack, and then if it does not cease, we will break the forces conducting aggression against us.”
The “block, blunt and break” strategy, he explained, is aimed at stopping an attack rather than taking enemy territory.
Drawing directly on lessons learned on the front lines in Ukraine and from conflict in the Middle East, Grynkewich said the plan relies on the use of precision weapons with “affordable mass”, like drones, and other autonomous systems.
In the plan, he said, the alliance’s forces would “block” an attack at the border to halt enemy advances on the battlefield, then “blunt” the attack by hitting incoming troops from the air, sea, and land. Then, at last, they would aim to “break” the enemy by targeting the supply chain and command networks.
“If required, we will break the enemy’s forces and the operational warfighting system that is arrayed against us,” he said. “Enemy formations will be starved of replenishment. Enemy commanders will be unable to control their forces. Enemy forces and support capabilities will be reduced and destroyed.”
Are Russian threats in Europe on the rise?
Germany’s foreign intelligence chief, Martin Jaeger, warned last week that the country risked being drawn into a “violent conflict” with Russia, saying Moscow increasingly viewed Berlin as a principal adversary.
He cited an attempted drone attack on a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig airport in August as an example of the escalating threat. Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt has also warned of a Russian-linked “shadow war” involving sabotage, cyberattacks and other covert operations.
In France, President Emmanuel Macron warned last month that the Russian hybrid threat facing France and other European countries had intensified in recent weeks, and ordered the preparation of plans to protect critical infrastructure.
The United Kingdom’s Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said that he had received confirmation upon entering office that Russia interfered in the 2016 Brexit referendum, although he did not publicly detail the evidence behind that assessment. Last week, he travelled to Berlin to meet with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, in part to discuss plans to combat Russian hybrid warfare.
Russia issued a nuclear warning to NATO late last month, saying it was prepared to use its arsenal, including nuclear weapons, if the alliance attempted to isolate Kaliningrad, a Russian exclave bordering Poland and Lithuania.
In July, Romania’s Defence Ministry said it had recorded 33 instances of Russian drones entering its airspace since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022. Eighteen of those incursions had occurred this year, and Romanian F-16 fighter jets had shot down three drones during the year.
Poland has also accused Russian intelligence services of orchestrating an arson attack on a Starlink satellite-internet station in Wola Krobowska last month. Warsaw described the incident as part of Russia’s hybrid warfare campaign against countries supporting Ukraine.
Norway, too, has issued similar warnings. Beate Gangas, head of the country’s Police Security Service, said this week that Europe is facing its most serious security situation since World War II, echoing concerns over suspected Russian sabotage and covert operations across the continent.
What has Russia said?
In August, Russia warned the UK that it could face “consequences” for supplying drones to Ukraine that have been used in long-range attacks inside Russian territory.
“London’s actions will inevitably carry consequences for which it will have to answer,” the Russian embassy in London said in a statement on August 17. “The deeper its involvement in the conflict and the greater its support for Kyiv’s terrorist machinery, the higher the price it will pay.”
Despite this, Russia is not preparing for “any kind” of conflict with Europe, President Vladimir Putin said last month. He added that Russia had “no real motive” to escalate tensions and criticised European countries that have suggested otherwise.
“Many in Europe talk about expecting an attack from Russia and therefore believe they must themselves prepare for hostilities, for a war with Russia,” Putin told reporters in St Petersburg.
“I want to emphasise once again: we are not preparing for any kind of hostilities with Europe,” he noted.
Putin added that Russia was considering its stance on whether to resume peace talks with Ukraine following recent Ukrainian attacks on Russia, particularly on energy infrastructure.
“On proposals to resume negotiations, yes, they are all on the table, and it is all possible. But after everything they’ve done, we will give careful thought to what steps we need to take in response,” Putin said.
Is NATO united?
Since taking presidential office in the US, Trump has repeatedly attacked other NATO members for not shouldering enough of the financial burden for defence. He has also been angered by NATO members’ general refusal to join in the US-Israel war on Iran.
As a result, there are fears that Trump cannot be relied on to provide support if it is needed within the NATO alliance, analysts say.
In August, after the Russian consulate in London warned of “consequences” for the UK for providing Ukraine with long-range drones, former Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Andrei Fedorov told the BBC that could include the possibility of attacks. He said many of the military experts currently advising the Kremlin are “convinced” that NATO would not respond forcefully if Russia were to hit the UK. “Trump will not allow NATO to answer,” he said.
The alliance is facing a deepening divide over Russia, as Trump pursues engagement with Moscow while European governments insist that Russia must remain under pressure if the war in Ukraine is to come to an end.
Last month, Washington invited Putin to December’s Group of 20 (G20) summit in Miami, in a move that was seen as potentially ending Moscow’s diplomatic isolation since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The European Union responded that Russia remained a G20 member but said it would continue condemning the invasion regardless of whether Putin attended.
The divide deepened last week when Trump announced a deal allowing Russian diesel exports into US and global markets, temporarily easing sanctions on Russian fuel. His administration said the move could help lower energy prices and encourage Putin to return to peace negotiations.
Critics have warned that it would generate revenue for Russia while undermining Western efforts to constrain its war effort.
Meanwhile, Trump has also escalated his criticism of Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and suggested that Ukraine should elect a new leader willing to make a deal with Russia. Zelenskyy had called Trump’s diesel agreement with Putin “not fair and not honest”, arguing it would benefit Russia.
EU foreign ministers also insisted that European sanctions against Russia would remain in place despite Washington’s deal with Moscow.
On Sunday, Trump claimed in a Truth Social post to have instigated an “energy truce” between Russia and Ukraine, under which both sides would refrain from targeting each other’s energy facilities with long-range strikes. However, Zelenskyy said such a deal was “news to me” – although he also said Ukraine would respect such a truce if Moscow honoured it as well. Regardless, Russia, which also has not confirmed agreeing to an energy truce, continued striking Ukraine’s facilities on Monday, according to Ukrainian officials.

US threatens restrictions on military aid to Nigeria over child soldier concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:49:51 UTC
23:49:51 KST

Kabir Adeniyi
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
The US has placed Nigeria on its Child Soldiers Prevention Act blacklist, which could restrict military assistance, weapons sales, and defense cooperation unless President Donald Trump grants a waiver.
The designation was detailed in the US State Department’s 2026 Trafficking in Persons Report, which accused armed groups operating in Nigeria of recruiting and using children in their activities.
The report identified Boko Haram and the Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP) as groups that recruit, abduct and use children, including as combatants, spies, porters, messengers and guards. It said some children were as young as 12.
Countries on the list may face restrictions on international military education and training, foreign military financing, excess defense equipment and certain commercial licenses for military equipment. The restrictions are subject to presidential waivers and other legal exceptions.
The report said the restrictions would apply from Oct. 1 for the fiscal year unless a waiver or other applicable exceptions were granted.
The designation comes amid continued security cooperation between Washington and Abuja, including efforts to combat extremist groups in northeastern Nigeria.
The report also criticized Nigeria’s broader anti-trafficking record, saying Abuja had failed to meet minimum standards for eliminating human trafficking for the 15th consecutive year.
It said Nigerian authorities investigated 1,341 trafficking cases during the reporting period, but recorded 94 prosecutions and 97 convictions. Of 2,004 identified trafficking victims, 675 received government-supported assistance, according to the report.
The State Department also raised concerns about alleged corruption and official complicity in trafficking crimes, saying the government had not reported investigations, prosecutions or convictions of officials allegedly involved.
Despite the criticism, the report acknowledged some progress, including increased government funding for victim services and prevention programs, cooperation with foreign governments on trafficking investigations and the repatriation of Nigerians exploited abroad.
Nigeria has previously appeared on the Child Soldiers Prevention Act list, including in 2015 -2018 and 2020 - 2021. Previous US administrations waived restrictions, allowing military assistance and arms sales to continue.
The latest designation could complicate aspects of the security partnership, although the extent of any restrictions will depend on the application of the law and whether the US president grants a waiver.

14:49:44 UTC
23:49:44 KST

- Kim Jong Un opened a new underground-style defense museum displaying the Hwasong-20 ICBM, new missiles and drones.
- Among the exhibits is a new 4x4 armored vehicle closely resembling the Canadian Roshel Senator used by Ukraine in Kursk.
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has opened a new national defense museum packed with the country’s missiles, rocket launchers and drones, and among the exhibits is a previously unseen 4×4 armored vehicle that closely resembles the Canadian-made Roshel Senator used by Ukraine.
State news agency KCNA reported on Oct. 13 that Kim attended the opening of the Defense Revolution Museum, run by the Second Economy Commission that oversees North Korea’s arms industry, on Oct. 11 and vowed to keep developing the country’s weapons. KCNA quoted him calling the museum a “precious monument” and did not give its size or location, though photos suggest at least part of it was built underground, with weapons lined up in long, tunnel-like halls.
The new armored vehicle shown in KCNA photos shares the overall layout and several hull details of the Senator, a Canadian armored car built on a Ford F-550 truck chassis that Roshel has supplied to Ukraine in large numbers. The North Korean version appears to have a lengthened body, suggesting it has been adapted to carry more troops in the back. KCNA did not name the vehicle or give any details about its protection, engine or how many are in service.
North Korean troops know the Senator from the battlefield. Ukrainian units used Senators during their incursion into Russia’s Kursk region in August 2024, where thousands of North Korean soldiers later fought alongside Russian forces to push Ukraine out. Russian troops have captured several Senators intact or lightly damaged, including one taken by naval infantry in the Kursk region that month, and a captured vehicle may have been handed to North Korea, which now appears to be building its own version. Roshel has delivered more than 2,000 Senators to Ukraine since Russia’s full-scale invasion, and open-source tracking project Oryx had documented 182 in Mrap version and 83 Senator IMV of them destroyed, damaged or captured by the end of 2025.
The museum’s largest exhibit is the Hwasong-20 intercontinental ballistic missile, which North Korea has displayed but not yet flight-tested, shown with a world map suggesting it could reach the United States and beyond. Visitors also see a new submarine-launched ballistic missile, the 600 mm super-large multiple rocket launcher and a range of drones developed under Kim’s rule.
Kim opened the museum a day after North Korea test-fired what KCNA described as a tactical ballistic missile, which state media said brought “an important change” in improving all of the country’s weapons systems. Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi condemned the launch. The museum opening also came as U.S. President Donald Trump said he might meet Kim during a planned trip to Asia in mid-November.

The UK has urged Interpol to reject Argentina’s requests for the arrest of individuals involved in a major offshore oil project near the Falkland Islands, known in Argentina as the Islas Malvinas, warning that the moves could be politically motivated, according to a report by The Guardian.
British officials sent a letter to Interpol’s headquarters in Lyon, France, calling for caution in handling Argentine requests for detentions, including those targeting British nationals involved in the Sea Lion oil project.
The development comes amid rising tensions over the sovereignty of the British overseas territory, with UK officials describing Argentina’s actions as the most serious since the 1982 war.
The Sea Lion project, located in the North Falkland Basin in the South Atlantic, could triple the islands’ gross domestic product (GDP).
Argentine President Javier Milei has vowed to block the project, while his government has initiated criminal proceedings against Israeli company Navitas and its British partner, Rockhopper Exploration.
The UK government is concerned that Argentina is seeking to intimidate individuals and companies involved in the project and discourage future investment, according to the report.
Andrea Clausen, chief executive of the Falkland Islands government, confirmed that Argentina’s use of Interpol posed a threat.
“One would hope that Interpol wouldn’t necessarily take action,” she told The Guardian.
She added: “Certainly those of us who have an interest have had a look at certain sections of Interpol’s constitution to see what we think it could mean.”
Interpol reportedly responded to the UK’s letter by reaffirming its commitment to Article 3 of its constitution, which prohibits intervention or activities of a political character.
Red notices are requests to locate and provisionally arrest individuals pending extradition. Interpol screens such requests, but member countries independently decide whether to act on them.
UK officials remain concerned that Argentina could persuade member states that its requests are based on domestic law rather than political motives.
Argentina continues to claim sovereignty over the Falkland Islands, where 99.8% of residents voted to remain a British territory in a 2013 referendum.
The 1982 conflict lasted 74 days and killed 649 Argentine military personnel, 255 British military personnel and three islanders.
