All trains between Odense and Fredericia replaced by buses after cable fault
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:51:32 UTC
22:51:32 KST

The Danish government has presented a proposed budget for 2027 that prioritizes national security, with more money allocated to defence amid an increasingly tense international security situation.
The proposal, titled “A stronger defence of Denmark – a strengthened Denmark to defend”, was presented by Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard of the Social Democrats (S) at the Ministry of Finance on Friday morning.
The government wants to ensure that defence spending reaches 3.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2030.
Hummelgaard said the proposal reflected the need to make “hard priorities” in response to the current security situation. He also described the Danish economy as being “in top shape”.
“The government’s proposal for the finance bill shows that we take responsibility upon ourselves, and that we lead the way in working for a greener, freer, and more equal Denmark,” Hummelgaard said.
Pia Olsen Dyhr of the Socialist People’s Party (SF), the minister for economic and interior affairs, also highlighted the security situation.
“We do not solve all the challenges we have in Denmark with this finance bill. But we are well on our way,” she said at the press conference.
“I also think everyone must remember that we are in an escalated security policy situation,” Olsen Dyhr said.
Much of the proposed budget had already been announced, either in the government’s policy platform or through statements by ministers in recent weeks.
The proposal allocates 1.2 billion DKK to children’s services and education in 2027, including Denmark’s public primary and lower secondary schools, known as folkeskole.
It also sets aside a total of 10.1 billion DKK in 2030 for tax cuts. These include abolishing the intermediate income tax and the top-top tax, as well as reducing corporation tax.
“We are simplifying the tax system,” said Taxation and Growth Minister Jakob Engel-Schmidt of the Moderates (M).
The tax measures will be negotiated separately as part of a tax reform. While the budget proposal includes tax cuts, the government also plans to freeze several tax thresholds, which would increase the tax burden for some taxpayers as incomes rise.
The liberal think tank Cepos estimates that the government’s various plans will result in a net tax cut of 2.2 billion DKK in 2030.
Business and Competitiveness Minister Martin Lidegaard of the Danish Social Liberal Party (R) highlighted investment in young people and education.
“We are significantly strengthening knowledge, general education, and formal education in Denmark, from ABC to PhD. It is good for the individual young person, but it is also good for Denmark’s future,” Lidegaard said.
Unlike in recent years, when the government’s fiscal room for manoeuvre helped fund much of its budget plans, this proposal includes several measures to find additional savings.
These include cuts to the Danish student grant (SU), savings on senior pension payments, a proposed tax on cruise ships and further reductions in state administration costs.
The government must now negotiate with other parties in the Danish Parliament, the Folketing, to secure a majority for the 2027 budget.
The proposal includes a negotiating reserve of 500 million DKK annually from 2027 to 2030, which other parties can seek to use to fund their own priorities.

China, Botswana elevate relations to 'comprehensive strategic cooperative partnership'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

22:50:49 KST

Amir Latif Arain
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
China and Botswana announced on Tuesday the elevation of relations to a "comprehensive strategic cooperative partnership," Chinese media reported. 
The announcement was made during a meeting between Chinese President Xi Jinping and his Botswanan counterpart Duma Gideon Boko in Beijing, state-run Xinhua News reported.
Boko arrived in Beijing for a six-day visit to China on Monday.
Xi and Boko held "extensive and constructive* discussions on the state and future direction of China-Botswana relations, China-Africa relations and regional and international developments of mutual interest and concern.
The two sides reaffirmed their shared commitment to promoting international peace and security, sustainable development, multilateralism, respect for international law and the purposes and principles of the Charter of the UN. 
The two presidents decided to elevate relations to a Comprehensive strategic cooperative partnership between the two countries, opening a "new chapter in the longstanding and evolving relationship between the two countries."
The two agreed to support each other’s efforts to safeguard sovereignty, independence, territorial integrity, national dignity, security, development and prosperity.
They reaffirmed their staunch support for each other on issues concerning their respective core interests and major concerns.
Botswana reaffirmed its longstanding commitment to the one-China principle, recognizing that "there is but one China in the world, Taiwan is an inalienable part of China’s territory, and the government of the People’s Republic of China is the sole legal government representing the whole of China."
The two sides also agreed to promote exchanges of experience and mutual learning in governance, public administration, institutional development, sustainable development, economic transformation, modernization, poverty reduction and other areas of mutual interest.

China Focus: China builds nationwide green hydrogen hubs for low-carbon shift
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
21:50:48 CST
22:50:48 KST

HOHHOT, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- For decades, Inner Mongolia's windswept steppes fueled China's heavy industry with coal. Now this same land generates green hydrogen from wind and solar -- a sharp shift as China's hydrogen sector moves from pilot demos to commercial scale, with hubs spanning Baotou's mining belt to Shenzhen's tech coast for the global low-carbon transition.
This push has received significant policy backing since late 2025, when the National Energy Administration released the first batch of hydrogen pilots in the energy sector, covering nine regions and 41 projects. Among them, Baotou in north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region is one of the key pilot sites.
Supported by abundant wind and solar resources and a strong industrial base, the city is building an integrated hydrogen value chain that spans green hydrogen production, storage, transport and diversified applications.
Nearly 20 leading industry players have established a presence in Baotou, helping to develop several benchmark projects in the hydrogen sector. Among them, a 200,000-kW renewable hydrogen demonstration project operated by a hydrogen subsidiary of China Huadian is producing 7,800 tonnes of green hydrogen annually. Construction of a 195-kilometer hydrogen pipeline linking Bayan Obo to downtown Baotou is also underway.
On the application side, hydrogen heavy-duty trucks are already operating in mining areas, while hydrogen buses have entered urban routes in Baotou.
In May, a hydrogen-powered two-wheeler developed by a local company was launched for public use in the city, with an initial batch of 1,000 units intended for public-use and convenience services. The project aims to expand the application of solid-state hydrogen storage in civilian transport.
Baotou's drive reflects a wider effort in Inner Mongolia to use hydrogen as a lever for energy transition. In 2025, the region's green hydrogen output reached 12,694 tonnes, a 3.6-fold year-on-year increase. To date, eight green hydrogen projects have been completed, giving the region an annual production capacity of 80,000 tonnes, among the highest in China.
Similar momentum is visible in other parts of the country. In north China's Shanxi Province, the city of Lyuliang is building a full hydrogen value chain ranging from production to end use. The city has achieved an annual hydrogen production capacity of 135,000 tonnes, built 14 refueling stations with a daily capacity of more than 30 tonnes, and deployed 1,315 fuel-cell vehicles.
Shenzhen, in south China, meanwhile, is a national pioneer in this sector and is home to nearly 200 companies active across the hydrogen and fuel-cell industry. Covering hydrogen production, storage and transport, refueling, fuel cells, system integration and end-use applications, the local industry has surpassed 50 billion yuan (about 7.4 billion U.S. dollars) in scale, with fuel-cell vehicles holding the largest market share among Chinese cities.
These regional developments reflect a broader national expansion. According to a report from the National Energy Administration, China's hydrogen output topped 39 million tonnes in 2025, marking continued industry expansion and keeping the country a global leader in both production and consumption.
Demonstrations across multiple scenarios are also speeding up. In transport, long-haul heavy-duty applications and low-altitude operations are being actively tested. In 2025, almost 8,000 fuel-cell vehicles were deployed, more than 10 hydrogen-fueled vessels entered service, and over 30 hydrogen-powered drones were released or test-flown.
China has also approved five city clusters for comprehensive hydrogen applications, spanning multiple regions -- a move aligned with the 15th Five-Year Plan for building a new energy system, which calls for coordinated development across the entire hydrogen value chain.
"China's green hydrogen capacity now accounts for more than half of the global total, and the hydrogen industry is moving from demonstration applications to scaled-up development," said Zhang Lin, a senior official at the China Electricity Council.
Zhang added that the next five years would be a critical period for China's hydrogen sector to shift toward market-driven growth, with the rise of a full value chain covering production, storage, transport and use, creating significant opportunities for the country's green transition and a market worth trillions of yuan. ■

Chinese President Xi Jinping meets with President of the Council of Ministers of Togo Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé, who is on an official visit to China, at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, capital of China, Oct. 13, 2026. (Xinhua/Li Xiang)
BEIJING, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping on Tuesday put forward four principles for the constructive participation of all parties in the settlement of hotspot issues in Africa, during his meeting with President of the Council of Ministers of Togo Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé, who is on an official visit to China.
First, adhering to the principle of "Africa-led." The African people are the true masters of Africa and should play a central role in regional affairs, Xi said.
Second, upholding fairness and justice. All participating parties should abide by the purposes and principles of the United Nations Charter and respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the countries concerned, he noted.
Third, promoting ceasing hostilities for peace. Wars and unilateral sanctions cannot fundamentally resolve conflicts between countries. It is imperative to uphold mutual respect, conduct extensive consultations, seek common ground while shelving differences, and practice mutual understanding and accommodation.
Fourth, addressing both symptoms and root causes. Efforts should focus on immediate security while planning for long-term development, Xi said. ■

Feature: Chinese Wu Opera bridges cultures in Zimbabwe
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
21:50:06 CST
22:50:06 KST

An artist performs on stage during the "Wu Opera in Africa" showcase in Harare, Zimbabwe, on Oct. 12, 2026. (Xinhua/Tafara Mugwara)
HARARE, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Wu Opera performers in vibrant costumes brought centuries-old Chinese operatic traditions to life in Harare, the capital of Zimbabwe, on Monday, captivating the audience with expressive gestures, soaring vocals and martial arts.
The showcase featured a vibrant selection of classic Wu Opera repertoire, including the elegant "The Goddess of Heaven Scatters Flowers," the witty and expressive "The Sedan Ride," and the action-packed "Three Fights Against the White Bone Demon," a beloved narrative from the Chinese literary classic "Journey to the West."
Originating in east China's Zhejiang Province, Wu Opera, also known as Jinhua Opera, is a traditional performing art that seamlessly weaves together singing, acrobatics, and stylized movements to convey timeless stories rooted in Chinese history and folklore.
Beyond its striking attire and intricate choreography, the art form explores universal human themes of love, courage, justice, and devotion, offering local audiences a vivid window into China's rich cultural tapestry.
The "Wu Opera in Africa" showcase, presented by the Zhejiang Wu Opera Research Center, was hosted by the Chinese Embassy in Zimbabwe, the Zhejiang Provincial Department of Culture, Radio, Television and Tourism, and the municipal government of Jinhua.
The performance forms part of a series of cultural events taking place across Zimbabwe this year to celebrate the China-Africa Year of People-to-People Exchanges, designed to deepen cultural ties and foster mutual understanding between the two sides.
Tang Xiaoping, minister counselor and charge d'affaires ad interim of the Chinese Embassy in Zimbabwe, described the show as a highlight of bilateral exchanges.
"Through closer people-to-people and cultural exchanges, we can deepen mutual understanding, build more consensus, and inject new momentum into global peace and development," Tang said. "Tonight's Wu Opera performance is undoubtedly one of the most remarkable highlights of this year's people-to-people exchanges."
Tsitsi Gezi, deputy speaker of the National Assembly of Zimbabwe, echoed Tang's sentiments. "A performance can express what words sometimes cannot, allowing deeper connections between our peoples," Gezi said. "Though governments may formalize relations, it is events like this that make friendships personal and enduring."
Gong Jianjun, director of the Management Center at the Wu Opera Theater of China, said he was proud to share Chinese cultural heritage with local audiences.
"Through the bridge of Wu Opera, we hope to leave our finest artistry in Zimbabwe and allow local audiences to feel the profound charm of traditional Chinese culture," Gong said. "We use opera as a medium to foster mutual learning among civilizations."
Experiencing Chinese opera for the first time, audience member Inaty Sibanda noted how the performers' elaborate costumes and evocative movements conveyed profound emotions, bringing the narrative unfolding on stage vividly to life.
"I found it very amazing. I love the colors and the attire. To me, it was more like a fairy tale story that they were telling us about their culture. And it was beautiful and lovely," she said.
Sibanda added that witnessing the opera offered a unique opportunity to learn about China's heritage, expressing hope that similar cultural events could be held regularly to enhance local awareness.
Another viewer, Vheneka Roy, said he was impressed by the artists' dedication and skill, as well as the richness of Chinese cultural heritage. He said the showcase deepened his appreciation of the common ways Zimbabweans and Chinese express themselves.
"What caught my attention was that the performers were truly enjoying themselves. They didn't look rigid at all," Roy observed. "They were very much in flow, allowing themselves to become the piece and naturally convey its meaning."
For Roy, the immersive experience highlighted the powerful potential of cultural diplomacy in cementing genuine people-to-people bonds between China and Zimbabwe.
"If there is one takeaway today, it is to be proud of where we are from while appreciating others for where they are from," Roy said. "We can appreciate each other in all aspects without superseding each other." ■

Feature: Kenyan youth explore climate finance to promote green agriculture
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
21:49:57 CST
22:49:57 KST

NAIROBI, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Coffee plants grow among taller trees on a farm in Murang'a County, central Kenya, where the leafy canopy provides shade and helps retain soil moisture. In the fields, farmers are replacing some synthetic fertilizers with organic alternatives to improve soil health and reduce production costs.
These practices are part of efforts by local smallholder farmers to adapt to changing climatic conditions and rising agricultural costs.
Kenyan entrepreneur Godfrey Noel is exploring how digital technology and climate finance can help make such changes more accessible to farmers.
In September, Noel and his team won gold at the final of the Global AgriInno Challenge 2026 in Hangzhou, east China's Zhejiang Province, with their AgriKonnekt project, which seeks to connect smallholder farmers in East Africa through digital agricultural services.
The project provides measurement, reporting and verification services to cooperatives, farmer organizations and financial institutions. By collecting and verifying data on farming practices, the team aims to assess their environmental benefits and help link those benefits to climate finance.
For Noel, the challenge is not simply encouraging farmers to adopt more sustainable practices, but also ensuring they have the resources to do so.
Noel noted that smallholder farmers face mounting pressure from unpredictable rainfall, extreme weather events, rising input costs and deteriorating soil conditions, all of which can undermine agricultural productivity and household incomes.
"Climate finance has a lot of money, but to get that money into agriculture, you have to demonstrate the environmental benefits of these practices and show that the data is credible and verifiable," Noel said.
His team has developed a digital platform to collect and analyze farm-level information and generate reports. Internet of Things (IoT) devices installed on farms gather basic data, including soil pH and moisture levels, while satellite data provides an additional means of monitoring and verification.
By combining ground-based measurements with satellite observations, the system seeks to establish a more reliable picture of farming practices and their environmental impact.
The verified data is then submitted to climate finance providers for assessment. Once approved, funding is channeled to provide farmers with inputs such as organic fertilizers, seedlings and seeds at no cost to them, according to Noel.
The arrangement is intended to ease farmers' financial burden while encouraging practices that can improve soil conditions and support more resilient agricultural production, Noel added.
The project currently covers about 2,000 farmers in Kenya. Noel said the team works with cooperatives and community-based organizations to reach more farmers and strengthen local accountability. It aims to expand its reach to at least 12,000 farmers across Kenya, Uganda and other areas over the next 12 months.
For Irene Kabochi, chief executive officer of Murang'a Farmers Cooperative Union, helping farmers adapt to changing weather patterns has become an increasingly important priority.
"We want to proactively help farmers prepare for changing climatic conditions and take measures to mitigate the effects of climate change," she said.
Kabochi said the team's data services and agricultural technology support could help cooperatives collect and analyze farm information, laying the groundwork for accessing climate finance.
The cooperative is working with Noel's team to diversify agricultural production beyond coffee by introducing crops such as macadamia and avocado. It is providing seedlings to farmers and plans to establish a demonstration farm to explore farming methods better suited to local climatic conditions.
For Simon Macharia, a farmer who has grown coffee for more than a decade, access to quality seedlings has offered a practical incentive to improve production.
The coffee seedlings he received free of charge through the project have encouraged him to consider how better planting materials and improved cultivation methods could raise yields.
He added that farmers participating in the project had begun trying more scientific and environmentally friendly cultivation practices, seeking to reduce chemical use, improve farm ecology, and lower production costs.
"For us farmers, we need to protect the land while also making farming more profitable," he said.
During Noel's visit to Hangzhou for the competition, Noel toured agricultural technology exhibitions and visited institutions including Zhejiang University.
A visit to a greenhouse particularly caught his attention. He saw a specialized growing medium containing multiple nutrients to support plant growth, which led him to think about the challenges facing Kenya's arid and semi-arid regions.
Large areas of northern Kenya, including Turkana, face difficult conditions for crop production, Noel said.
He believes that exploring suitable protected-farming systems and cultivation technologies could offer additional options for food production, provided they are adapted to local environments.
His team is also following developments in Chinese agricultural IoT technology, with an eye toward solutions that can function in remote Kenyan areas where electricity supplies and network connectivity are unreliable.
Noel added that linking environmental protection with tangible economic benefits for farmers is key to encouraging the wider adoption of sustainable agricultural practices and ensuring their long-term viability. ■

Trainees attend the South Africa workshop under the Global Female Entrepreneurs Empowerment Program (GFEEP) in Johannesburg, South Africa, Oct. 8, 2026. (Xinhua/Chen Wei)
JOHANNESBURG, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- After nearly two decades in business and several work-related trips to China, South African entrepreneur Beauty Sonny found herself back in a classroom, learning to look at her business in a new way.
At the closing ceremony of a China-supported entrepreneurship workshop in Johannesburg on Monday, Sonny described the two-week course as a "14-day MBA."
"We thought we knew our businesses," said Sonny, a director of Monenebe Maintenance and Projects, a company involved in equipment rental.
She said the course introduced practical tools, including the Business Model Canvas, that helped her identify weaknesses in her business model and rethink how to make her business more sustainable.
Sonny was among 61 South African women entrepreneurs who completed the two-week workshop under the Global Female Entrepreneurship Empowerment Program, led by Beijing Foreign Studies University (BFSU). The initiative aims to strengthen women's entrepreneurial skills through business education and practical training while fostering business cooperation.
For other participants, the lessons addressed challenges that had emerged as their businesses grew. Years ago, Naomi Mashigo and her husband started a small shop in a rural community.
Their shop has since grown into a supermarket employing 14 people. But for Mashigo, a small business owner, expansion has brought new challenges, particularly in managing finances and staff.
She said the training offered practical insights into these challenges, with assignments encouraging participants to examine their own businesses rather than work only with hypothetical cases.
The role of small businesses in creating employment was also highlighted by South African First Lady Tshepo Motsepe, who attended a workshop-related event on Oct. 8. She thanked China for providing training opportunities and encouraged participants to grow their businesses, create more jobs and contribute to their communities.
Gui Bo, a program leader and instructor, said the workshop focused on business model analysis and innovation, helping participants identify weaknesses in their existing operations and explore ways to improve them.
The workshop also brought participants together with Chinese businesses operating in South Africa. According to Gui, more than a dozen entrepreneurs had been connected with Chinese business resources or introduced to potential technical and product solutions.
Beverly Matoro, 46, founder of Bev's Kids Transport in Johannesburg, operates three vehicles carrying more than 60 schoolchildren each day.
She hopes to collaborate with Chinese technology companies to develop an app under her own brand, which she could eventually offer to other school transport operators.
"I would love to sell it to other people who are doing the very same business that I'm doing," she said.
BFSU President Jia Wenjian said the program sought to connect entrepreneurship education with practical business needs while fostering closer ties between Chinese and African communities. He said the university planned to deepen cooperation with enterprises to help translate training into business growth and job creation.
For Sonny, who has already built business ties with China, the two weeks of learning were also a chance to explore what further cooperation might bring.
"The relationship is not ending today," she said, expressing hope for continued support from Chinese partners in strengthening business cooperation in South Africa. ■

Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Aysu Biçer
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
Climate campaigners staged a demonstration outside the UK Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) in London on Tuesday, calling on the government to halt development of the controversial Rosebank oil and gas field in the North Sea.
Organized by activists from groups including Fossil Free London, the protest called on the UK government to reject new oil and gas licenses and accelerate the transition to renewable energy.
A public consultation on the Rosebank project concluded in August 2026, following a landmark legal challenge that found the previous approval of the development unlawful.
The Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled that the previous Conservative government had failed to fully consider the project’s downstream emissions when approving the development.
Rosebank, estimated to contain more than 480 million barrels of oil, is the UK’s largest undeveloped oil and gas field.
The project is primarily owned by Norwegian state-backed energy company Equinor and Ithaca Energy through a joint venture.
Opponents, including the #StopRosebank campaign, argue that developing the field would prolong the UK’s dependence on fossil fuels and undermine international climate targets.
Supporters of the project, meanwhile, have argued that domestic oil and gas production is necessary to safeguard the country’s energy security during the transition to cleaner energy sources.
The UK government is considering whether to approve the Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gas projects, which were initially approved by the previous Conservative administration.
Although Labour pledged to ban new drilling in the North Sea in its 2024 election manifesto, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has vowed to take a “pragmatic” approach to decisions on new developments.

Tajikistan, Turkmenistan to Import Indian Surface-to-Air Missile Systems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:48:00 UTC
22:48:00 KST

India’s growing defense industry has set sights on Central Asia for new customers. In early October, Indian Defense Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh, speaking to Asian News International (ANI) held up the indigenously designed and produced Akash medium-range mobile surface-to-air missile (SAM) system as a “success story.” He highlighted exports of the system to Armenia, Tajikistan, and Turkmenistan.
“The first customer was Armenia, which has taken multiple batteries,” Singh said. “Thereafter, we’ve also exported it to Tajikistan and Turkmenistan. Production has stabilised. We have additional orders for our own services, and I’m sure there will be many more from various parts of the world…”
Singh’s comments confirmed a report from July, published in Indian business magazine BW Businessworld, which cited official data as listing Tajikistan and Turkmenistan as export destinations for the Akash system.
Although ANI reported that both India’s Defense Research and Development Organization (DRDO) and the Ministry of Defense had confirmed that “Tajikistan and Turkmenistan have joined the buyer list,” neither of the Central Asian countries has commented publicly on the reports.
Central Asia’s militaries have been diversifying suppliers, but the bulk of region forces remain Soviet and/or Russian in design and procurement, with newer additions of Chinese, Turkish, Indian, and Western equipment.
RFE/RL’s Zamira Eshanova recently explained the variety on display:
Recent military parades show just how much Central Asian armies are diversifying their equipment. At its Independence Day parade in Ashgabat on September 27, Turkmenistan displayed a newly acquired Chinese FK-2000 air-defense system, adding to its existing arsenal of Chinese-made missile systems. Also on parade were a Brazilian-made A-29 Super Tucano attack aircraft and Italian-made Leonardo M-346 training jets.
Tajikistan, meanwhile, has displayed China’s HQ-17AE air-defense system, along with Chinese-made armored vehicles used to transport and protect troops. During its 2026 Independence Day celebrations, Uzbekistan also showcased Chinese J-10CE fighter jets. And, in recent years, Kyrgyzstan has acquired several types of Turkish military drones.
Essentially nothing is known publicly about the Indian defense exports to Tajikistan and Turkmenistan: the number of systems, the delivery timelines, or the prices.
More is known about the Armenia exports, which may provide some insight for Central Asia watchers. Armenia signed a $720 million deal with Bharat Dynamics Limited in 2022 for an unknown number of Akash SAMs and 15 Ashwin ballistic missile interceptors. Although deliveries were pushed back, in November 2024 Yerevan took delivery of its first Akash battery, which included four launchers a Rajendra radar. A second delivery reportedly took place in July 2025.
As the Oxus Society noted in an October 2024 report on Tajikistan’s military, “India’s military involvement in Tajikistan dates back to the early 1990s and early 2000s, beginning with the refurbishment of Tajikistan’s Ayni Airbase.” But after the base was refurbished, Tajikistan pivoted back to Russia, walking back plans for India to station its own military assets at the site. Instead, Dushnabe signed and agreement with Moscow to allow Russian forces to use the base. India has had access to, though not a permanent presence, at the Farkhor Airbase near the Afghan border.
Prior to the apparent Akash deals, India hadn’t sold any defense equipment to Tajikistan or Turkmenistan.
The export of one type of system, if and when they arrive into Central Asian hands, won’t fundamentally alter the military supplier balance in the region. But it underscores that regional governments are looking for additional partners and pathways out of strict dependence on Russia for defense materials. Such a move introduces new problems, specially regarding interoperability – the ability of different systems to work together effectively.

Yemeni government launches air strikes on Houthi positions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:47:14 UTC
22:47:14 KST

Yemeni government launches air strikes on Houthi positions
Yemeni rights group accuses the Houthis of killing five civilians and injuring more than a dozen others.
Forces loyal to Yemen’s internationally recognised government say they have carried out a series of air strikes on Houthi positions and military equipment in the country’s southwest.
A total of nine air strikes were conducted in Taiz governorate on Tuesday, including five in Dhubab district and four in al-Masrakh district, the government said.
According to the Taiz Military Axis Media Center, affiliated with the Ministry of Defence, fighting is ongoing between government forces and the Houthis in al-Shaqab, south of Taiz.
The Yemeni Network for Rights and Freedom said on Tuesday that the Houthis had killed at least five civilians, including a five-year-old girl in Taiz during the previous 24 hours and injured 17 others.
The organisation accused the Houthis of shelling residential neighbourhoods, damaging at least seven homes. It also alleged that the group had fired more than 180 projectiles across Taiz during the previous 24 hours.
The war in Yemen erupted in 2014 when the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), seized the capital Sanaa and forced the government to flee.
An international military coalition led by Saudi Arabia intervened in support of the internationally recognised government in 2015, leading to years of fighting between the warring sides.
A 2022 UN-backed truce halted most fighting, but tensions have been high in Yemen since the Iran-aligned Houthis declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabian ports and shipping passing through the Bab al-Mandeb strait in July.
In September, the Houthis carried out a lightning ground offensive on Mocha, pushing back forces loyal to Yemen’s government from the strategic port city. The same month, the group’s forces again swept through and seized territory along the western coast and the Bab al-Mandeb strait, including the strategically located Mayyun Island in the strait.
As the fighting in Yemen continues to rage, the president of the International Committee of the Red Cross, Mirjana Spoljaric, warned that civilians across the Middle East are bearing the brunt of escalating hostilities and has called for all parties to de-escalate.
“Civilians are paying an unacceptable price as a result of military operations in the Middle East,” Spoljaric said in a statement.
“In Yemen, the scale of death, displacement and damage to civilian infrastructure, including in Aden and Sanaa, is mounting at an alarming rate. Across the Middle East, civilian infrastructure has repeatedly been hit and lives have been lost,” she said.
At least 46 civilians have been killed and more than 130 others injured in Yemen since August, many of them children, according to the United Nations.
More than 200,000 people have been displaced in Yemen since September, according to the UN’s migration agency (IOM).
As the fighting in Yemen has escalated, the Houthis have carried out a series of attacks on Saudi Arabia’s airports and oil facilities. At least 14 people were killed in separate Houthi missile attacks on King Khalid airport in Riyadh over the weekend, drawing widespread international condemnation.
Saudi Arabia’s energy minister promised the kingdom would carry out a “serious response” to the attacks.
Several airlines have cancelled flights to Saudi Arabia and neighbouring countries in response to Houthi attacks. These carriers include Qatar Airways and Emirates, the United Arab Emirates’ flagship carrier.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz spoke to Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) on Tuesday about regional issues. Merz told MBS that Iran must engage in serious negotiations and accused Tehran of destabilising the region.
Meanwhile, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty has met Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) Secretary-General Jasem Mohamed AlBudaiwi. Abdelatty said in a post on X that “Gulf security is integral to Egypt’s national security”.
Abdelatty also spoke to his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, and urged an immediate halt to Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. Although Tehran provides the Houthis with crucial financial and military support, several analysts suggest that Iran holds little sway over the group.

EXPLAINER - What to know about Nord Stream sabotage trial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:44:10 UTC
22:44:10 KST

Kanyshai Butun
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
- Incident triggered competing accusations over who was responsible, with several countries rejecting allegations of involvement
Germany is preparing to put a Ukrainian national on trial over the September 2022 explosions that damaged the Nord Stream gas pipelines in the Baltic Sea, with prosecutors alleging that Ukrainian state authorities ordered the operation.
The suspect, identified as Serhii K., is accused of helping lead a group that carried out the sabotage. His indictment marks the first time German prosecutors have formally brought the Nord Stream sabotage case before a court.
Another suspect, identified by Germany as Vladimir Z., is in custody in Croatia and is fighting extradition. He was earlier detained in Poland.
What happened to Nord Stream?
Nord Stream is a network of offshore natural gas pipelines connecting Russia and Germany beneath the Baltic Sea. The four lines of Nord Stream and Nord Stream 2 had a combined annual capacity of 110 billion cubic meters.
Construction of the first Nord Stream pipeline was completed in 2011, and it began operating in 2012. Nord Stream 2 was completed in September 2021 but never entered service.
In September 2022, Nord Stream AG, the operator of the pipelines, confirmed damage to both systems as Danish and Swedish authorities reported explosions and gas leaks in sections passing through their respective waters.
Pipeline pressure stabilized, and the gas leaks stopped several weeks after the incident, with Russia opening a criminal case on charges of international terrorism.
Russian President Vladimir Putin later described the US and countries with alternative energy supply routes to Europe, including Ukraine and Poland, as “beneficiaries” of the disruption.
Which countries have been accused of involvement?
While Western officials initially suspected Russia, German investigators later focused on possible Ukrainian involvement. The US, Poland and the UK have also faced allegations, but have denied involvement.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov dismissed claims of Russian involvement as “quite predictable and also predictably stupid,” stressing Moscow lost a route for gas supplies to Europe.
The US rejected the allegations as “Russia's disinformation,” while Poland called the claims “completely groundless insinuations.” 
In August, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Germany should not prosecute suspects accused of blowing up the Nord Stream pipeline, adding that those who built the project “should be ashamed, not those who disabled them.”
The UK also rejected allegations, saying Russia was “resorting to peddling false claims of an epic scale.”
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy denied Kyiv's involvement, saying the government has officially never taken part in any operation related to the Nord Stream blast.
He said Ukraine held high-level talks with Germany on the issue, and that German officials knew Kyiv was not involved in planning or carrying out the operation.
What do German prosecutors say?
Serhii K. was detained in Italy near Rimini in August 2025 on suspicion of involvement in the sabotage. He was extradited to Germany three months later and has remained in pretrial detention in Hamburg.
The suspect is charged with causing an explosion, damaging property, disrupting public services and being an “accomplice to war crimes” for targeting civilian objects, prosecutors said.
German prosecutors allege that Serhii K. was an officer in the Ukrainian army at the time, and helped plan the operation with other military personnel “acting on behalf of state bodies in Ukraine.”
Prosecutors allege the objective was to destroy both pipelines, permanently halt Russian gas deliveries and prevent Moscow from using energy revenues to finance its war against Ukraine.
Investigators claim the suspects traveled to Germany using forged Ukrainian passports and hired a yacht, the Andromeda. Traces of the explosives HMX and RDX were found aboard the vessel.
According to prosecutors, the explosives were attached to the pipelines near Denmark’s Bornholm island using timers by Sept. 22, 2022. They detonated four days later, causing extensive damage and rendering the pipelines inoperable.
Serhii K. denies the allegations.
The high-profile trial opens in a Hamburg court on Wednesday.

Iraq faces six-month air defence gap after US-led coalition exit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:41:36 UTC
22:41:36 KST

Breadcrumb
Iraq faces six-month air defence gap after US-led coalition exit
Iraq faces a potential six-month gap in its air defences following the withdrawal of US-led coalition forces, with new systems not expected to arrive until early next year.
The coalition completed its military withdrawal at the end of September, removing air defence systems that had helped protect parts of the country, including the Kurdistan Region.
Baghdad says agreements have been reached to purchase new equipment, but the first systems could take up to six months to arrive.
The transition has taken on added urgency after two drones targeted a camp for Iranian Kurdish refugees near Erbil last week.
Sabah al-Numan, spokesman for the commander-in-chief of Iraq's armed forces, said Baghdad had made "tangible progress" in acquiring new air defence systems.
He said the first batch would arrive within six months and be deployed across the country.
The package would include advanced radar systems, interceptor weapons and aircraft, he said, as part of a wider plan to strengthen Iraq's control over its airspace.
Numan said the country's security situation remained relatively stable and that Iraqi forces were maintaining a high level of readiness.
However, the announcement leaves questions over Iraq's ability to detect and intercept aerial threats before the new systems become operational.
Iraq has long struggled with limited and ageing air defence capabilities, while drones and missiles have become an increasingly prominent security threat.
A Defence Ministry official nevertheless played down the prospect of an immediate security vacuum.
"The available Iraqi air capabilities are not at a high level, and there is no denying that, but the security situation in the country is relatively calm," the official told The New Arab on condition of anonymity.
The official said Iraq retained "reasonably good capabilities" and that there were currently no expectations of major security breaches.
Concerns are particularly acute in the Kurdistan Region.
Kurdistan Region President Nechirvan Barzani said on Monday that both federal Iraq and the autonomous region required effective air defence coverage.
"Let us be realistic. The Kurdistan Region and Iraq as a whole need an air defence system," he told the MERI Forum in Erbil.
Barzani said an earlier agreement negotiated under former prime minister Mohammed Shia al-Sudani with the United States had included plans to provide air defence capabilities covering Kurdistan.
"Air defence is not only a need for the Iraqi state. The Kurdistan Region also needs it," he said.
He also stressed that weapons should remain under state control.
Military expert Aqil al-Shammari warned that the process could take longer than the six months announced by the government.
He said another three months could be required to integrate the equipment, establish command-and-control systems, train personnel, arrange maintenance and complete deployment.
"Owning the system does not mean providing complete air coverage," the former brigadier general told The New Arab.
Shammari said the transition period would be a major test of Baghdad's ability to protect Iraqi airspace.
Kurdish officials had warned before the coalition withdrawal that removing foreign forces and their air defence systems without an immediate replacement could leave the region vulnerable.
The withdrawal forms part of a wider transition towards a new security relationship between Baghdad and Washington focused on training, technology and military co-operation without a direct US combat presence.
They have argued that protecting Kurdistan's airspace is ultimately the responsibility of the federal government because it forms part of Iraq's national airspace.
Those concerns intensified after two explosive-laden drones targeted a camp housing Iranian Kurdish refugees near Erbil last week.
No casualties were reported, but the attack renewed fears that gaps in Iraq's air defences could leave the Kurdistan Region vulnerable to further drone strikes.
The withdrawal has also raised wider questions over whether Baghdad can manage its security without the coalition's military presence.

US Supreme Court to hear asylum fight involving Nigerian cook
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:40:35 UTC
22:40:35 KST

US Supreme Court to hear asylum fight involving Nigerian cook
Oct 13 - The US Supreme Court agreed on Tuesday to hear a bid by President Donald Trump's administration to deny asylum to a man who was forced to prepare meals for an apparent separatist group in Nigeria, in a case that could expand what officials may deem terrorist activity under American immigration law.
The justices took up the Justice Department's appeal of a lower court's ruling in favor of Nigerian citizen Izuchukwu Ozurumba, who was denied US asylum due to his work cooking for a group known as the Unknown Gunmen that US officials considered to be a terrorist organization. The lower court ruled that cooking did not qualify as "material support" for terrorism under the immigration statute.
The Supreme Court is expected to hear arguments and rule in the case by the end of June.
The administration, in appealing the case to the Supreme Court, said that if the lower court's ruling were allowed to stand, it would "substantially increase the burden on the government in excluding aliens with links to terrorism."
The case centers on whether Ozurumba's work for the group fell under provisions of US immigration law that bar the entry of non-US citizens who have "engaged in a terrorist activity," including actions that provide "material support" for such activity or "to a terrorist organization."
"At stake in this case is whether the government can use an overly broad reading of the law to shut the door on people seeking asylum," said Aimee Mayer-Salins, an attorney with the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, which is helping to represent Ozurumba.
The lower court "correctly recognized that asylum should not be denied to immigrants who provided no meaningful support to a terrorist group," Mayer-Salins added.
Following a job tip in 2022, Ozurumba took a van to a remote camp outside of Lagos, according to court papers. After he was hired, he eventually learned the camp was run by the Unknown Gunmen, a group likely associated with Nigerian separatists, according to court papers.
Ozurumba soon "observed that the young men's movements from the camp coincided with news reports of murder and arson," his lawyers said in a court filing. Ozurumba sought to leave but was forced to stay without pay, they added.
After six months he escaped while on an outing for supplies, eventually making his way back to Lagos, they said.
Ozurumba then faced beatings and threats of death, prompting him to flee to Venezuela, where the threats continued, his lawyers said. Ozurumba then traveled to the southern US border and entered the country illegally in July 2023. Ozurumba eventually applied for asylum and other protections from deportation.
'BASIC HUMAN NEEDS'
During Democratic former President Joe Biden's administration, an immigration judge deemed the Unknown Gunmen a terrorist organization and found that Ozurumba's cooking for the group rendered him inadmissible, and denied him any protections from deportation.
The judge concluded that the cooking helped the group accomplish its goals by satisfying their "basic human needs," and that it was irrelevant that he had worked under duress.
Ozurumba was deported back to Nigeria last year while his case was on appeal.
The Richmond, Virginia-based 4th US Circuit Court of Appeals sided with Ozurumba in September 2025, ruling that he was a captive laborer and his cooking did not constitute material support.
Ozurumba's work "provided nothing that the organization could use or readily divert to plan or carry out its terrorist activities," the 4th Circuit ruled, but declined to order the government to return him to the US while the case proceeds.
"Providing meals to a terrorist organization's members is no less a material form of support than providing gasoline for its vehicles," the Justice Department told the Supreme Court in its appeal. REUTERS

“American wheat was expensive due to the stronger dollar, driving up the dollar cost of wheat, which is among the factors that made European wheat more attractive,” he added.

The new embassy will be built at 9 Sapir Street in the commercial district of Herzliya Pituach, on a plot measuring approximately 2,500 square metres.

Under the approved plans, up to 20% of the permitted floor space will be allocated to residential accommodation for the Emirati ambassador and diplomatic personnel, located on the upper floors.
The development will also include a separate entrance to an underground car park, an expanded access road and improvements to surrounding public facilities and pedestrian walkways.

He said the embassy's location near international companies and advanced technology firms would make it a prominent landmark in Herzliya's commercial district.
The UAE embassy currently operates from temporary offices in Tel Aviv and Herzliya, with the new complex intended to become its permanent diplomatic headquarters.
No date has been announced for the start of construction or the building's opening.

The approval comes at a sensitive time in UAE-Israel relations, following reported disagreements over an attempted hijacking involving a Flydubai flight last month.
Israeli economic news website Ice linked the timing of the approval to recent tensions between Abu Dhabi and Tel Aviv following the incident, which saw a Flydubai aircraft make an emergency landing at Saudi Arabia's Tabuk airport in late September.

On the universality of Gazan resistance: A century-long struggle for human rights
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:33:58 UTC
22:33:58 KST

The struggle of Gaza’s people is frequently interpreted through the competing languages of security, nationalism, religion and geopolitics. Each illuminates part of the conflict, yet each can obscure its most fundamental question: are Palestinians entitled to the rights every human being possesses simply by being human? Viewed through the history of human rights, Gazan resistance acquires a significance extending beyond one people or territory. It exposes the distance between humanity’s proclaimed commitment to universal dignity and its willingness to protect those whose rights are repeatedly denied.
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights, adopted in 1948, rejects hierarchies of human worth. Rights belong to people regardless of nationality, religion, political allegiance or recognition by a sovereign state. Palestinians therefore need no special justification for claiming life, liberty, education, property and security. Their entitlement precedes the political arrangements through which these rights should be protected.
Gazan resistance, understood as the broader struggle against dispossession and for individual and collective freedom, makes this principle concrete. It encompasses political mobilisation, civic action, cultural continuity and the work of sustaining society under destructive conditions. Its universal significance arises from the rights being defended and the insistence that Palestinians must be able to exercise them.
A Century of Dispossession and Resistance
Beginning this history on 7 October 2023 reduces an extended struggle over rights to the aftermath of one event. It obscures the experiences shaping successive Palestinian generations: dispossession, displacement, occupation and the frustration of political freedom.
The century-long dimension emerges from the imperial arrangements preceding Israel’s establishment. The 1917 Balfour Declaration supported a Jewish national home in Palestine while describing the existing non-Jewish population through safeguards for civil and religious rights. Incorporated into the British Mandate, this formulation recognised one population’s national aspirations without equivalent recognition of the other’s.
The violence surrounding Israel’s establishment transformed political exclusion into mass dispossession. The April 1948 attack on Deir Yassin by Irgun and Lehi became an enduring expression of Palestinian civilian vulnerability.
During the Nakba, approximately 750,000 Palestinians were uprooted. Gaza became a major refuge for people separated from their homes, livelihoods and communities.
The coincidence of the Nakba and the Universal Declaration in 1948 reveals a profound historical dissonance. As the international community articulated universal dignity, Palestinians lost essential conditions for exercising their rights. Their subsequent struggle has continually exposed the gap between recognition and protection.
Israel’s occupation of Gaza in 1967 added further layers of control. Its withdrawal of settlements and permanent ground forces in 2005 did not establish Palestinian sovereignty. The International Committee of the Red Cross continued to regard Gaza as occupied because Israel retained effective control over key dimensions of access and movement. The Israeli blockade imposed in 2007 further constrained economic and social life.
Recurring violence intensified these conditions. The United Nations recorded 2,251 Palestinian deaths during the 2014 hostilities, including 1,462 civilians. A UN commission investigating the 2018 Great March of Return found that Israeli forces killed 183 demonstrators with live ammunition. Gaza’s insecurity thus long preceded October 2023.
The three generations of human rights illuminate this experience. Civil and political rights protect against violence and arbitrary power; socioeconomic rights sustain dignified life; collective rights concern a people’s future. In Gaza, their interdependence is unavoidable.
READ: UN verifies 1,076 Palestinian deaths in Gaza since ceasefire, warns of possible war crimes
First-Generation Rights: Life, Liberty and Security
The right to life is fundamental. By October 2026, Gaza’s health authorities reported over 74,000 Palestinian deaths since October 2023, according to Reuters.
Genocide directly concerns this right.
In September 2025, the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel concluded that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza.
It identified four genocidal acts, including killing, serious bodily or mental harm, destructive living conditions and measures intended to prevent births, alongside genocidal intent. Separately, in January 2024, the International Court of Justice ordered binding provisional measures requiring Israel to prevent acts prohibited by the Genocide Convention and enable urgently needed humanitarian assistance.
Liberty and security also require protection against arbitrary detention and torture. A July 2024 UN report documented detention without charge or trial and accounts of ill-treatment. Freedom of association likewise matters: UN experts condemned Israel’s 2021 designation of six Palestinian civil society organisations as terrorist organisations. These findings connect physical survival with safeguards against arbitrary power and the defence of dignity.
Property Rights: The Foundations of Freedom
Property connects individual protection to the history of dispossession. Article 17 of the Universal Declaration recognises ownership and prohibits arbitrary deprivation of property. A Palestinian home or agricultural plot also sustains family continuity, independence and attachment to place.
OCHA’s September 2025 humanitarian snapshot reported that 92 per cent of Gaza’s housing units were destroyed or damaged. Such devastation simultaneously removes shelter, accumulated savings and the physical foundations of community life. Rebuilding therefore concerns the restoration of social continuity as well as material assets.
Settlement policies elsewhere in the occupied Palestinian territory reveal a related connection between property and political exclusion. In its July 2024 advisory opinion, the International Court of Justice found Israel’s continued presence unlawful and identified obligations concerning settlement cessation, evacuation and reparation. Its findings connected Israeli policies to the denial of Palestinian self-determination.
Property links individual rights to collective freedom: people cannot meaningfully control their future while repeatedly losing the material foundations of their existence.
Second-Generation Rights: Education, Health and Livelihoods
Economic and social rights deepen this understanding. People may survive bombardment while losing everything needed for a viable future. Education, healthcare, food and employment give dignity practical substance. Their destruction produces injuries that outlast immediate violence.
In August 2025, famine was formally confirmed in Gaza Governorate. The joint announcement by UN agencies linked starvation to conflict, repeated displacement, severe restrictions on humanitarian access and the collapse of essential systems. Hunger thus exposes how the destruction of social infrastructure can threaten life as directly as armed violence.
Healthcare illustrates the same interdependence. In September 2026, OCHA documented shortages of cancer medicines, dialysis supplies and insulin, linking disruption to underfunding and obstacles to the entry of available medicines. Interrupted treatment can cause irreversible harm even after supplies resume.
Education reveals the consequences across generations. A November 2025 assessment presented by UNESCO found that 95 per cent of Gaza’s higher education campuses were damaged or destroyed, with 22 of 38 completely destroyed. OCHA reported approximately 200,000 children without structured learning in September 2026. These losses threaten the knowledge and professional capacity essential to future recovery.
Yet the defence of education continues.
UNESCO reported providing temporary learning spaces for 10,000 university students. Such efforts embody resistance through the preservation of learning: students and educators sustain capacities on which rebuilding their society depends.
Livelihoods connect these examples. UNRWA has documented how restrictions on fishing constrain families’ incomes. Under blockade, access to the sea becomes a question of economic survival. Restoring rights therefore requires opportunities to work and produce alongside emergency assistance.
Humanitarian relief is indispensable, but a durable response must restore the ability to sustain an independent life. Otherwise, assistance risks becoming the permanent means of supporting people whose freedom remains unresolved.
OPINION: Gaza’s displaced face a deadly choice: collapsing buildings or flooded tents
Third-Generation Rights: Self-Determination and Cultural Continuity
Self-determination brings these dimensions together. Frequently discussed alongside collective or third-generation rights, it is expressly recognised in the common first article of the two principal international human-rights covenants. It encompasses peoples’ ability to determine their political status, pursue development and control their natural wealth and resources.
For Palestinians, this reaches into daily life. Who determines access to land and water? Who decides whether people can move, rebuild or establish economic connections? Self-determination concerns the capacity to influence these conditions instead of remaining permanently subject to decisions made elsewhere.
Restrictions on fishing demonstrate how collective and socioeconomic rights overlap. Access to natural resources supports livelihoods, food security and development. Control over those resources therefore affects both individual welfare and a people’s capacity to shape its future.
Cultural continuity belongs within the same struggle. By 24 March 2026, UNESCO had verified damage to 164 cultural sites in Gaza, including religious buildings, monuments, museums and archaeological sites. These losses affect the places through which communities locate themselves in history and transmit belonging. They diminish Palestinian collective life and humanity’s shared inheritance.
Maintaining family records, preserving cultural knowledge and documenting violations consequently carry political significance. These practices defend claims that displacement and impunity might erase. They assert that Palestinians possess a history and the authority to help determine their future.
Gaza and the Universal History of Emancipation
The significance of this assertion becomes clearer within the broader history of emancipation. The American struggle for independence advanced government by consent. The French Revolution gave enduring force to liberty and equality. South Africa’s anti-apartheid movement challenged institutionalised racial inequality. Their importance lies partly in how particular struggles expanded the reach of principles presented as universal.
These histories also expose a persistent tension. Movements and states can proclaim universal rights while excluding people from their enjoyment. Progress depends on those excluded demanding that the principles apply to them. Universality gains practical meaning through resistance to the claim that some people must indefinitely await protection.
Gazan resistance belongs within this history through its assertion of rights whose validity extends to everyone. National character and universal significance are compatible: Palestinians seek to exercise freedoms that cannot coherently be reserved for others. Their struggle demands that human rights apply even when protection challenges powerful interests.
This places responsibility on institutions and governments invoking universal principles. Recognising Palestinian suffering must translate into protection, accountability and the restoration of conditions necessary for freedom. Palestinian voices and choices must inform reconstruction and political arrangements; treating people solely as aid recipients overlooks their agency.
If protection depends on geopolitical importance or diplomatic alliances, rights become privileges distributed through political favour. Defending Palestinian rights therefore also defends the equal application of standards that governments claim to accept as universal.
Gaza therefore tests whether human dignity generates obligations when fulfilling them carries political costs. Sympathy alone cannot resolve that question. Universal rights acquire credibility through consistent protection, especially where power makes their enforcement difficult and inconvenient.
The rights Palestinians defend emerge from their particular history, but their validity does not stop at Palestine’s borders. Life, liberty, a home, education, healthcare and the freedom to shape a collective future belong to the common substance of human dignity.
The universality of Gazan resistance lies in its insistence that Palestinians must be able to exercise the rights humanity has already declared to be universal.

France's national Anti Terrorism Prosecutor’s Office (PNAT) has taken over the investigation into the Aubagne school shooting after initial findings suggested a possible link between the 14-year-old suspect and the “True Crime Community” movement, Franceinfo reported.

The ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Filmmakers Terrified Bystanders With Their Monster Sounds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:30:00 UTC
22:30:00 KST

Actor Seth Green—yes, that one—has seen Godzilla Minus Zero and says it’s awesome.
While introducing the New York Comic Con panel for the 39th film in the Godzilla franchise, Green stressed that the filmmakers behind the movie “have created kaiju that feel physically real and, trust me, emotionally terrifying.”
While a lot of that terror came from the work of Oscar-winning visual effects artist Tatsuji Nojima, some it came from the shrieking of Godzilla and his three-headed nemesis, King Ghidorah. Those roars were the work of sound designer Natsuko Inoue and her team, who created the monsters’ outsize vocalizations by rolling speakers to the top of an outdoor dam—much to the horror of people nearby.
“There were people having a picnic, maybe people just taking a stroll,” Hisafumi Takeuchi, who also worked on sound for the film, said during the panel. “The person walking their dog, though—they had the worst time, because the dog was freaking out and barking back at us.”
Since the creatures are imaginary, getting their screams to sound realistic is essential to making them seem believable—and genuinely scary—onscreen. At first, Inoue wasn’t sure if the idea of recording at the dam would work. Those fears were quickly put to rest.
“The first time we sent that roar out on the speakers, I could see the relief and confidence in everyone's eyes,” Inoue said. “By using speakers and projecting it into the real world, capturing the reverb, the echo, the reflection of the sound back with the mic, it manifests it in our world.”
For other kaiju sound effects, Inoue’s team took an analog foley approach. To simulate Ghidorah’s dragon-like wings, for example, they flapped a rubber fisherman’s suit and mixed that noise with the sounds of an accordion-like air duct.
Getting two of Toho’s most famous monsters right was a huge undertaking, especially after the success of Zero’s predecessor, Godzilla Minus One, which brought home $114 million worldwide at the box office. Following that 2023 film’s harrowing mix of post–World War II malaise and bracing kaiju destruction will be tough, but a new trailer shown during the film’s panel at NYCC promised a sequel full of aerial dogfights and a punch-’em-up for the ages between Godzilla and Ghidorah.
Like the previous film, Godzilla Minus Zero is directed by Takashi Yamazaki and features visual effects from Tatsuji Nojima, whom Green called “the first Gen Z Oscar-winner” for his work on One.
Nojima began doing visual effects as a hobby while he was still a teenager before joining animation house Shirogumi as a compositor. After Yamazaki noticed a crude animation of waves that Nojima was working on, the director tasked the budding animator with developing the idea. Nojima turned around a fully rendered shot of ocean water over rocks that looked indistinguishable from reality. After that, Nojima recalled, Yamazaki said, “OK, I think you’re ready to animate and do VFX for Godzilla now.”
During the panel, Nojima broke down how he created a shot from the trailer showing Godzilla bursting out of the ocean while chasing a seaplane. “I simulated 200 million particles to get the whitewater effect correct in Godzilla Minus One,” he said. “With this shot in Godzilla Minus Zero, the scale is absolutely different with the new Imax aspect ratio, plus there was no live-action plate, so we're dealing with a lot of CG on screen. We required 2 billion particles.”
Godzilla Minus Zero is set to hit US theaters on November 6 and Japanese theaters on November 3, which has become known as Godzilla’s birthday since it marks the date in 1954 that Ishirō Honda’s original film was released in Japan.

The European Commission president has urged EU leaders to adopt tougher measures against irregular migration, including an emergency response framework and expanded powers for the bloc’s border agency, Politico reported Tuesday.
In a letter to the leaders of all 27 member states ahead of this week’s European Council summit in Brussels, Ursula von der Leyen called for measures to respond when migration is used as a tool to destabilize the bloc.
“We must prevent such threats and make clear that we will never compromise the protection of our external borders: no state or non-state actor will be allowed to exploit our rules or our values to destabilise the Union,” she wrote.

The letter follows a migration crisis in Spain’s North African exclave of Ceuta over the summer, when around 70,000 migrants arrived from Morocco, according to the report.
Von der Leyen’s letter will inform discussions on migration scheduled for Friday, day two of the summit.

'Absence from draft SIR doesn't mean deletion': EC to Bombay HC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:28:59 UTC
22:28:59 KST

The Election Commission of India clarified that missing names from the draft electoral roll during the Special Intensive Revision do not imply their deletion.
The Election Commission of India (ECI) on Tuesday told the Bombay high court that a voter's name missing from the draft electoral roll prepared during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) does not automatically imply deletion. The court reserved its judgment on a writ petition filed by a Goa resident.Senior Advocate Ashutosh Kumbhakoni, appearing for the ECI, told the Goa bench that the SIR involves preparing the electoral roll afresh, unlike a Special Summary Revision (SSR), which focuses on updating an existing list.
The bench, comprising Justices Valmiki Menezes and Amit Jamsandekar, reserved its verdict after hearing arguments in the matter. The hearing took place amid an ongoing controversy over the SIR exercise and the functioning of the ECI.Paresh Salgaonkar and five members of his family, who live in the St Cruz constituency of North Goa district, had approached the court alleging that their names were removed from the electoral roll during the revision process.
ECI clarifies the nature of the SIR exercise
Kumbhakoni submitted that an SIR is a comprehensive, de novo exercise in which the electoral roll is prepared from scratch.
In contrast, a summary revision updates the existing electoral roll on the basis of information received through the prescribed procedure.“Absence from the draft SIR roll does not automatically amount to deletion,” the ECI lawyer said, maintaining that a name missing from a draft list being prepared afresh could not technically be described as deleted.The lawyer further argued that the petitioner had allegedly not lived at the address recorded in the electoral rolls before the SIR for eight to 10 years. He also contended that the petitioner had not applied for an address change before the revision exercise began.“In fact, my lord, this is a classical case which shows the effectiveness of SIR,” Kumbhakoni told the court.According to the news agency PTI, the judges observed that they had made it clear from the outset that the petition did not challenge the SIR process itself.
Petitioner’s lawyer recounts timeline of events
Advocate Vivek Rodrigues, representing the petitioner, detailed the events surrounding the enumeration exercise and the subsequent absence of the petitioner's name from the draft electoral roll.Rodrigues said the enumeration process began on November 4, 2025. The Booth Level Officer (BLO) visited both the petitioner's former and current addresses on November 8.On November 12, the petitioner contacted the BLO to request an enumeration form. However, the officer declined, saying the form had to be delivered to the address listed in the electoral roll, which was the petitioner's previous residence.The petitioner later submitted Form 8 to seek a change of address. The ECI acknowledged receipt of the application on December 8, 2025. However, the petitioner's name was absent when the draft electoral roll was published on December 16, Rodrigues told the court.The BLO subsequently informed the petitioner that the Form 8 application was still being processed and had not been rejected.
Rodrigues said the petitioner received a letter from the ECI on January 17, 2026, informing him that his address-change application had been forwarded to the Electoral Registration Officer (ERO).The final date for submitting objections to the draft electoral roll was January 19. However, the petitioner's application was rejected on January 21, after the deadline had passed.“On January 21, my application is rejected. So I am neither in the boat nor in the canoe, left in the sea,” Rodrigues argued before the bench.

Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman attends a welcome ceremony at the Hotel des Invalides in Paris, as part of a two-day official visit to France, August 24, 2026. (AP File Photo)
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has rejected an Israeli push to join the military campaign against Yemen’s Houthi group, despite efforts to secure Riyadh’s approval through U.S. mediation, the Israeli media has reported.
The daily, citing an unnamed diplomatic source, said the crown prince was not interested in Israeli military assistance, fearing that cooperation with Israel could provoke a negative reaction among the Saudi public.
Another source familiar with the matter said Israel hoped military cooperation with Saudi Arabia would strengthen bilateral ties and pave the way for a future normalization agreement.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities on the report.
Saudi Arabia has no diplomatic relations with Israel and has maintained that normalization depends on resolving the Palestinian issue, including the establishment of a Palestinian state.
The report comes amid escalating Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, including repeated strikes on airports that have caused casualties and disrupted flights.
An attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Oct. 10 killed 13 people and injured more than 300 others.
Another attack on the same airport on Oct. 11 killed a Pakistani resident and injured 11 others, according to Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation.
The escalation began in July following a period of relative calm after a U.N.-brokered truce took effect in April 2022.
Yemen has been at war since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and several provinces in September 2014 before a Saudi-led coalition intervened in March 2015 in support of the country’s internationally recognized government.
Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia has launched an investigation to determine how its air defenses failed to intercept a barrage of missiles and drones fired by Iran-backed Houthi rebels, including an attack on Riyadh airport that killed at least 13 people and wounded over 300.
The officials said the initial probe showed that Yemen’s Houthis first fired multiple drones to pave the way for a mix of cruise and ballistic missiles to reach Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport.
The Houthis possess ballistic missiles and advanced systems fitted with warheads that can change direction during flight and pose a challenge to Patriot interceptors and other defense systems used by the Saudis.
One of the officials said the investigation also aims to find out why air defense systems did not provide earlier warning of the attack in which the Houthi missiles and drones flew over 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) to reach Riyadh.

BRUSSELS, Oct 13 - The European Union has signed an additional €25 million ($29 million) in funding to expand migration cooperation into eastern Libya, according to a letter from European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to EU leaders seen by Reuters.
The funding will support border management, search-and-rescue and anti-smuggling activities in eastern Libya. It is a further sign of deepening EU engagement with the region controlled by military commander Khalifa Haftar as Brussels seeks to curb irregular migration across the Mediterranean.
Libya, where control is split between rival western and eastern administrations, has been a major transit route for migrants attempting the dangerous sea crossing to Europe since the 2011 NATO-backed uprising that toppled Muammar Gaddafi.
The EU and its member states have long supported and trained the Libyan coastguard, which intercepts migrants at sea. While the EU formally recognises only the Tripoli-based government, it has stepped up contacts with authorities in eastern Libya since last year as migrant departures from areas controlled by Haftar in eastern Libya have risen.
The move follows the July announcement by the EU that it would establish a Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre in the eastern Libyan city of Benghazi, further expanding cooperation with authorities in the east.
"Libya remains the top country of departure for illegal crossings to the EU," von der Leyen wrote, describing an upcoming EU-Libya meeting as a way to keep cooperation going.
She said the EU and the International Organization for Migration were supporting voluntary returns from Libya to countries of origin.
"We are equally focused on reducing the number of migrants arriving to Libya with the sole intention to cross illegally into the EU," she added. REUTERS

Activist Greta Thunberg joins France student protests
