Deadly Houthi attacks in Yemen’s Taiz as government forces advance in Marib
Government troops launch major offensives across multiple fronts, while Houthi bombardments kill civilians in southwestern Yemen.
Yemeni government forces say they have made strategic advances into the Marib governorate in north-central Yemen as they push on with operation “Dawn of Yemen”.
The offensive by the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces, launched just over a week ago, comes after major gains by the Iran-backed Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah or Supporters of God, in September, when it swept along the country’s Red Sea coast, capturing the strategic port city of Mocha and territory around the Bab al-Mandeb, one of the world’s most important shipping routes.
Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, said operation Dawn of Yemen aimed to retake all remaining Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa, which the group has controlled since 2014, when the war first started.
Meanwhile, intense clashes and Houthi shelling on residential neighbourhoods in Taiz in the southwest of the country have caused dozens of civilian casualties.
Operation Dawn of Yemen
In the northwest of Marib governorate, a military source told Al Jazeera that government troops have successfully taken control of strategic, commanding heights surrounding the strategic Maas camp facility in the Medghal district. The source noted this followed intensive attacks that had breached the Houthi group’s fortifications.
On the southern front, forces from the Saba and Bayhan axes announced the capture of the al-Muqailat and Jabal Zajjar positions north of the Harib district. Government forces claimed the fierce clashes resulted in the Houthis retreating and suffering human and material losses.
This field progress coincided with continued violent battles along the front lines in the north and south of Marib. Government forces launched concentrated strikes using warplanes, drones, artillery and rocket launchers, targeting Houthi military positions and reinforcements.
The armed forces’ media centre published footage it said documented drone attacks on Houthi military barracks and vehicles within the scope of the third military region’s operations, noting the destruction of multiple combat vehicles and equipment.
Above: Footage from the battles within the operational theatre of the seventh military region north of Marib: Media centre of armed forces.
Military spokesperson Colonel Majid al-Nuzaili announced on Monday that operations have involved 1,879 precise strikes, neutralising 950 Houthi fighters and destroying 380 military vehicles.
Meanwhile, Houthi-affiliated media reported that air strikes targeted Kamaran Island and the al-Qanawis district in the coastal Hodeidah governorate along the Red Sea and the Harf Sufyan district in Amran, western-central Yemen.
Escalation in Taiz
In the southwestern governorate of Taiz, where the Houthis have the city of Taiz under siege, government forces and popular resistance fighters are engaged in fierce battles across multiple major axes amid a wide-scale field escalation.
On the western fronts, heavy fighting has flared in al-Dhabab, Hathran and Jabal Han as government troops have sought to thwart infiltration attempts and repel Houthi attacks. Sources within the government forces told Al Jazeera that troops captured 81 Houthi fighters in al-Dhabab on Monday afternoon.
In the southern and southwestern countryside, battles have intensified in the al-Shaqb, al-Aqroud and al-Misrakh areas. A field military source told Al Jazeera that government forces are involved in fierce clashes from all directions in the al-Shaqb area of Taiz, with confrontations extending to areas the Houthis seized on Monday in Sabir.
Also in the southwest, a field military source from the Southern Giants Brigades told Al Jazeera that Houthi forces had fired a ballistic missile at the highly strategic mountain range of Jabal Kahboub at midnight. The source confirmed there were no human or material casualties, with damage limited to the missile’s distant impact zone.
Civilian toll rises
The military escalation has severely affected civilian populations. Al Jazeera correspondent Abdullah Qatran reported seeing Houthi mortar shelling targeting the al-Ikhwa residential neighbourhood in the centre of Taiz, resulting in an undetermined number of deaths, injuries and property damage, causing widespread panic.
With Taiz under Houthi siege, civilians there are also suffering severe shortages of fuel and other essential supplies. Yemen’s Ministry of Public Health and Population said on Saturday that medicines, intravenous fluids, medical supplies and fuel at the city’s health facilities were “nearing depletion”.
Compounding this, the Yemeni Network for Rights and Freedoms has documented 43 violations by Houthi forces in Taiz over the past 24 hours, which have killed five civilians and wounded 17. According to a report by Yemen’s state-run Saba news agency, casualties included five-year-old Ahlam Abdulsalam, who died when shelling struck her family’s home in the al-Misrakh district.

Saba also reported that a Houthi attack early on Tuesday struck al-Safwa Hospital, shattering windows, injuring at least one person, and triggering panic among patients and medical staff. This followed earlier Houthi shelling in which five people, including three children, were injured in the al-Dhahra residential area and the nearby Beer Basha district.
The Yemeni Network for Rights and Freedoms warned that continuous shelling and restrictions on supplies are worsening humanitarian conditions, calling on the United Nations and the international community to take urgent steps to protect civilians.

BEIJING, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping has called for efforts to firmly follow a path with Chinese characteristics in developing the country's health programs, to secure decisive progress in the Healthy China Initiative over the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030).

Xi stressed that people's health is a key benchmark of a nation's prosperity and strength.
Since the 18th CPC National Congress in 2012, the Party has made a major decision to launch the Healthy China Initiative, promoting the establishment of the world's largest systems of medical services, traditional medicine, disease prevention and control, and healthcare security, said Xi, noting that the country has achieved historic accomplishments and made all-round progress in healthcare.

China unveils railway sci-tech innovation plan for 2026-2030
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
20:56:17 CST
21:56:17 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- China, which operates the world's largest high-speed rail network, has issued a railway science and technology innovation plan for the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030).
This innovation plan outlines key tasks in basic research and frontier technologies, engineering construction, technical equipment, transport services, digital and intelligent railways, safety, and green and low-carbon development.
The plan, recently released by the National Railway Administration (NRA), proposes to basically establish a science and technology innovation system that leads railway modernization by 2030.
During the 2026-2030 period, China plans to build about 30 new railway industry science and technology innovation bases under the NRA, achieve breakthroughs in no fewer than 100 key core technologies, and produce no less than 500 major scientific and technological achievements.
It will also plan no fewer than 20 typical application scenarios or demonstration projects in areas such as the 400 km/h high-speed train operating system.
Regarding technical equipment, the plan proposes to steadily and orderly advance research on 600 km/h high-speed maglev technology as well as testing and verification of key technologies for domestic production.
In the case of transport services, the plan will promote upgrading the official 12306 ticketing platform from a single ticket-buying service to whole-journey intelligent services, providing one-stop intermodal travel solutions that precisely match passengers' "personalized, differentiated and diversified" needs.
China will accelerate the building of large models, datasets and computing power infrastructure in the railway industry, and will establish a minimum of 20 high-quality industry datasets and more than 20 typical artificial intelligence application scenarios, according to the plan.
Concerning green and low-carbon development, the plan calls for promoting demonstration operation of low-emission and low-fuel-consumption diesel locomotives as well as locomotives and rolling stock with multi-source power such as battery and hydrogen, establishing and improving a carbon management system, and helping total railway carbon emissions peak by 2030.
In contrast to the railway sci-tech innovation plan for the 14th Five-Year Plan period (2021-2025), the new plan places greater emphasis on basic research and frontier technologies, thereby better advancing high-level scientific and technological self-reliance and strength in the railway sector.
By the end of 2025, the country's total operating railway mileage had reached 165,000 km, including more than 50,000 km of high-speed rail.
On Sept. 28 this year, China opened four high-speed rail sections, connecting Xiong'an in north China's Hebei Province with Shangqiu in Henan Province in central China, Xi'an with Ankang in Shaanxi Province in northwest China, Yichang with Xingshan in central China's Hubei Province, and Harbin with Yichun in Heilongjiang Province in the country's northeast.
During the National Day holiday, which lasted from Oct. 1 to Oct. 7, these new lines made it easier for people to visit relatives and brought new vitality to tourism along the routes.
China's high-speed rail network is projected to hit 70,000 km by 2035, featuring eight north-south vertical lines and eight east-west horizontal lines. Once complete, the network will connect major cities, city clusters and key economic zones across the country. ■

France to miss target for reducing greenhouse gas emissions in 2026: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
20:56:15 CST
21:56:15 KST

PARIS, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- France's greenhouse gas emissions are projected to fall by 2.8 percent in 2026 from the previous year, but this reduction would remain less than that required to meet the country's climate goals, according to a report released Tuesday.
The Interprofessional Technical Center for Studies on Air Pollution (Citepa), an independent body responsible for monitoring the country's emissions, said in its latest barometer that France's greenhouse gas emissions, excluding carbon sinks, totaled an estimated 179.7 million tons of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO2e) in the first half of 2026. This was down 4.1 percent from the same period in 2025.
The decline was mainly driven by the buildings and transport sectors, where emissions fell by 12.0 percent and 4.5 percent, respectively, according to Citepa.
However, the downward trend is expected to slow in the second half of the year, with emissions projected to fall by 1.3 percent year on year, the report said.
For the whole of 2026, France's greenhouse gas emissions are projected to reach 349.4 million tons of CO2e. This represents a reduction of 2.8 percent, slightly below the 3.1 percent decline envisaged for 2026 under France's third National Low-Carbon Strategy (SNBC 3). It would also remain well below the average annual rate of emission cuts needed to meet the country's climate targets by 2030.
Citepa said France's emissions reductions will need to accelerate in the coming years to comply with its carbon budgets and meet its climate targets for 2030. Under the SNBC 3 roadmap, annual emissions cuts are expected to accelerate to 5.7 percent in 2027 and 6.1 percent in 2028 from the previous year. ■

Researchers develop new X-ray tech mapping elements in 3D with far less data
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
20:56:12 CST
21:56:12 KST

JERUSALEM, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Researchers have developed a new X-ray method to map elements inside a sample in three dimensions without scanning every tiny point, Israel's Bar Ilan University said in a statement on Tuesday.
The technique, called X-ray fluorescence ghost tomography and detailed in the journal Optica, could help scientists study materials, batteries, rocks and biological tissues faster and more efficiently.
X-rays make atoms glow at element-specific energies, or "colors," allowing researchers to identify them.
Instead of copying an image pixel by pixel, the new method projects patterns of X-rays through the sample and collects the combined glowing signals with a detector. Then a computer solves one large mathematical problem to rebuild the 3D element map.
In tests, the researchers mapped nearly 2.8 million 3D pixels using only 400 pattern measurements per angle. Across 276 angles, that totaled about 110,000 measurements, versus 4.75 million for the old point-by-point scanning. That is roughly 97 percent less data, while retaining useful detail.
They explained that the method exploits the fact that most real samples are "sparse," or mostly empty or made of only a few materials.
The researchers caution that denser samples will require corrections, and the computation is heavy. Still, the approach could make 3D chemical imaging faster, cheaper, and practical for large or delicate samples, they said. ■

====================================================================================================

Chinese study finds global urban land subsidence uneven but generally slowing
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
20:55:54 CST
21:55:54 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Global urban land subsidence varies widely but has generally slowed in recent years, according to a study by a Chinese research team published Oct. 12 in the journal Nature Cities.
Researchers from Peking University, South China Normal University and other institutions systematically assessed land subsidence between 2014 and 2023 in 465 cities worldwide, each with a population of over one million.
Land subsidence is a global issue that poses a major challenge to urban infrastructure safety and sustainable development.
According to the research, subsidence is most severe in Southeast Asia, West-Central Asia and North America, with representative cities including Mexico City and Toluca in Mexico, and Medan and Bandung in Indonesia. Mexico City recorded the most intense localized subsidence, with rates exceeding 0.2 meters per year.
Although land subsidence remains widespread, global urban subsidence has generally slowed in recent years. The research team detected marked deceleration in many cities across Southeast and East Asia.
This indicates that water resource allocation and groundwater management measures in the two regions are effective, said Hu Xie, a researcher of the team at Peking University.
"In China's Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei urban agglomeration in particular, large-scale water diversion projects such as the South-to-North Water Diversion Project and stronger groundwater management have helped replenish groundwater in some areas, significantly easing subsidence," Hu said.
The team also built an open platform for global urban land subsidence, offering the dataset in a searchable and visual format to the public.
As geological and groundwater big data accumulate and artificial intelligence and complex models advance, the analysis of subsidence causes and risk assessment will have a stronger data and methodological foundation, said Tao Shengli, a researcher at Peking University. ■

Anaerobic digestion uses microorganisms to break down organic matter, such as kitchen waste, livestock waste, or compost, in sealed, airtight settings. Biogas can generate electricity around the clock, unlike weather-dependent solar and wind power.
Yeh toured the facility and explained its installation maintenance cycle and material management process. Center staff demonstrated how organic matter is converted into biogas.
The center said the biogas is fed into a network of generators with a capacity of up to 800 kWh. It is expected to generate 6.4 million watts by late 2026 while cutting runoff sludge by 40%. Shen said he hopes the ministry will introduce the technology to other industries to help eliminate agricultural and kitchen waste.

Argentina seeks tribunal order against UK oil activity near Falklands
Oct 13 - Argentina's government said on Tuesday it had filed a request for provisional measures with the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea seeking to halt British-authorized hydrocarbon activity near the Falkland Islands.
The request aims to prevent the United Kingdom from exploiting hydrocarbon resources on the continental shelf of the Northern Falklands Basin, the government added in a statement.
The filing "seeks to preserve Argentina's sovereign rights over its continental shelf and prevent activities authorized unilaterally and illegally by the United Kingdom," the government added.
Addressing Britain's parliament after Argentina's move, Uma Kumaran, parliamentary under-secretary for the foreign office, said that "legitimate commercial activity in the Falkland Islands remains lawful, and the British government stands behind those engaged in it."
Kumaran added that the UK would engage with the tribunal process but would not provide a running commentary on the proceedings.
"The notification does not constitute a judgment by an international court or tribunal. It does not invalidate licenses issued by the Falkland Islands government, alter the islands' regulatory authority, or require lawful hydrocarbon development activities to cease," Kumaran said. Britain also announced it was taking legal measures to protect businesses from pressure to comply with Argentine domestic measures.
Tensions between Argentina and the UK over the territory that is controlled by Britain but claimed by the South American country have escalated. Last month Milei's government presented legislation to crack down on companies drilling for oil off the Islands.
The government's proposal would toughen penalties on companies and individuals who participate in activities linked to natural resources in the Falklands, and in Argentina's maritime spaces without authorization from Argentine authorities. The new bill, which has yet to be approved by Congress, aims to revamp 2011 legislation with a tougher framework.
Argentine Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno said on X that the latest request aims to prevent the start or continuation of hydrocarbon development on the Sea Lion project.
Oil companies Navitas Petroleum and Rockhopper Exploration, owners of the Sea Lion offshore project north of the Falklands, have previously indicated they do not expect Argentina's actions to derail development.
Navitas Petroleum Chief Executive Ian Ramsey on Tuesday welcomed Britain's support for the project.
"In the face of Argentina's increasingly aggressive efforts to pressure companies associated with the development, we are grateful that the UK Government has made its position clear; that it will robustly defend the Falkland Islands' right to pursue lawful economic development," Ramsey said in a statement to Reuters. 13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
A Chinese delegation has visited Russian-held islands claimed by Japan to conduct feasibility studies for joint projects, Kyodo News reported Tuesday.
The delegation’s visit followed Russian President Vladimir Putin’s trip to the island of Etorofu in August, his first visit to the Russian-controlled but Japanese-claimed island chain off Hokkaido, which prompted protests from Tokyo.
Russia calls the islands the Southern Kuril Islands, while Japan refers to them collectively as the Northern Territories.
The Chinese delegation from the northeastern province of Heilongjiang, which included businesspeople, visited the largest of the disputed islands, Kyodo reported, citing the government of Sakhalin Oblast, a Russian Far Eastern region that includes the islands.
Sakhalin authorities said the visit focused on international cooperation, with Gov. Valery Limarenko highlighting the area’s potential for tourism and other businesses.
Tokyo maintains that the Northern Territories, consisting of Iturup, Kunashiri, Shikotan and the Habomai islet group, were “illegally” seized by the now-defunct Soviet Union soon after Japan’s surrender in World War II on Aug. 15, 1945.
Russia argues that the seizure was legitimate.
The territorial dispute has prevented the two countries from signing a peace treaty since World War II. Tensions have deepened in recent years amid Japan’s sanctions against Moscow over the Russia-Ukraine war.
The Japanese government summoned Russian Ambassador to Japan Nikolay Nozdrev to lodge a “strong protest” over Putin’s visit, while Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said the islands were an inherent part of Japanese territory “both historically and under international law.”

Scientists wonder: Is my AI stealing my ideas?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:48:08 UTC
21:48:08 KST

Recently, controversy and accusations have followed artificial intelligence companies flexing their models’ research capabilities. When OpenAI claimed an internal model had solved one of math’s seven million-dollar problems, a mathematician at New York University insinuated that the company had stolen his progress, which he had shared with one of their chatbots. Weeks later, the New York Times reported a similar story unfolding between Anthropic and a biologist at the University of Copenhagen regarding a group of enzymes.
Despite this, scientists from all disciplines are opting to use these companies’ large language models. Some use them as a soundboard or a tool for literature review, others for cleaning up nearly finished work. And mathematicians and theorists are tapping their new, powerful models to generate entire proofs for their research. But as researchers feed more of their data and ideas into these models, concerns are growing about how that content is getting used.
Both OpenAI and Anthropic stated unequivocally that they did not train their models on the mathematician’s and biologist’s uploaded data, respectively. But the companies—which have not consistently met academic norms—don’t have every scientist’s trust. Some suspect they may not even have the full picture themselves. Their agents could be accessing data in ways the companies don’t even realize. After all, it took three months for the public to learn that OpenAI’s models had breached containment and hacked into foreign government databases.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
With these conspiracy theories swirling, some researchers are now seeing the models more as competitors than tools—and the use of them as a betrayal. “I’m not encouraging it, and I’m not doing it myself,” says Clément Canonne, a theoretical computer scientist at the University of Sydney. “I’m not using them.”
Ahead of taking their companies public, OpenAI and Anthropic are increasingly stepping into math and science to show how capable their products are. But AI has sometimes felt less like a guest over for dinner and more like an unwanted visitor breaking and entering. If scientists feel that these companies are rifling through their every interaction, they may start locking them out entirely.
The lack of transparency invites these sorts of fears. “Right now, these systems infer things about you without telling you that they’re inferring things about you,” says Jennifer King, a fellow at the Stanford University Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence, who researches data privacy and policy.
King says the only way for researchers to really ensure their safety when using large language models at the present moment is to look at their account settings carefully. According to her, “enterprise” accounts—which represent a special deal worked out between a client company and the AI’s owners—seem to be safe. “But if you are on a personal account, all bets are off,” she warns. She describes how users on personal accounts need to explicitly opt out in many cases to prevent their information being used from training.
Plus, even if a company isn’t intentionally using your data to train their models, one of their many agents could always go rogue, infiltrating company data and hoovering up individual users’ conversations with their chatbots. While there is no evidence this happened in the case of any of the AI companies’ scientific discoveries, rogue events over the summer have left some extra concerned about who they trust with their data.
The trouble is, it’s hard to get much evidence at all out of the tech giants. “The companies are not transparent about these practices, so it’s really hard to pin down,” King says. That means experts can’t speculate about any particular case. But in general, “the companies spy on you and use that information against you,” says Bruce Schneier, a security researcher and activist.
The new AI models are very capable, including for research, and many believe they will help researchers find new results faster. So scientists may feel they face a choice: either use the models and risk leaking a discovery or don’t and risk someone who does publishing it first.
All this has created an uneasy landscape in which many scientists are left feeling they have to give up their privacy and work to keep up. “There is definitely a pressure,” Canonne says. “If you’re not using them, are you going to be irrelevant?”

Egypt's Baha'i minority is running out of space to bury their dead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:45:47 UTC
21:45:47 KST

Egypt's Baha'i minority is running out of space to bury their dead
CAIRO, Oct 13 - In a Cairo cemetery shaded by palms and tangled shrubs, pale graves are packed so tightly that in some places only narrow strips of sand and broken pavement separate one family’s plot from the next.
This is the last remaining burial place of Egypt's Baha'i community, a religious minority long on the margins of official life, and it is quickly running out of room.
As it fills, the cemetery has become a symbol for the community of the bureaucratic obstacles and restrictions they say complicate everything from school enrollment to pensions and marriage registration.
"God forbid that this area becomes completely full. If that happens, we would have no other places where we can bury," said Joumana Labib, a 25-year-old architect whose extended family is buried there.
The Baha'i faith, whose members are scattered across different continents and believe their 19th century founder Baha'u'llah is a prophet, was brought to Egypt by merchants in the 1860s, not long after it originated in Iran. With current numbers in Egypt estimated in the thousands, they are a tiny minority in a mainly Muslim country of about 110 million.
The Egyptian constitution guarantees religious freedom, though mainstream Islamic scholars view the Baha'i faith as heretical and officials are often reluctant in practice to recognise religions outside the main Abrahamic faiths.
BURIAL REQUIRED WITHIN ONE-HOUR JOURNEY
While Islamic tradition requires burial within a day, Baha'i practices allow a body to be moved no more than one hour from the place of death, creating particular challenges.
Burial grounds once used by Baha'is in the port cities of Alexandria and Port Said have been filled or reassigned over the years, leaving many families to transport bodies to Cairo, according to the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), a leading Cairo-based rights group.
Community members say requests for new burial grounds in Alexandria and Port Said — where much of Egypt's Baha'i community lives — have been rejected without clear written explanations, said Marina Samir, who heads EIPR's freedom of religion and belief work.
"Death becomes, instead of a time when people are trying to comprehend their loss, a logistical process," Samir said.
Egypt's government information agency and the governorates of Alexandria and Port Said did not respond to requests for comment.
Last year, in a response to a UN human rights report, Egypt's government said it "does not impose any restrictions on personal belief or religious affiliation, including adherence to the Baha’i faith".
Based on government data, there were "sufficient burial sites to meet the needs of all citizens", it said.
President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi has repeatedly stressed the need for religious coexistence and said the state works tirelessly to fight discrimination and promote tolerance.
MARRIAGE WITHOUT RECOGNITION
A landmark 2009 court ruling allowed those who do not follow Islam, Christianity or Judaism to leave a dash in the religion field on their identity documents.
The change allowed Baha'is to avoid declaring a faith they do not follow, but still left them facing practical difficulties.
One of the biggest is establishing Baha'i marriages in official records. Baha'i couples are often registered as "single" even after decades together, which can complicate child registration, inheritance, pensions, health insurance and family records.
Hanan Kamal El-Din, 65, said her identity card describes her as single, although she married in a Baha'i ceremony 45 years ago and has two children in their 40s.
"What harm would recognising this marriage do to society?" she said.
Like other Baha'is, she won an individual court ruling recognising her marriage in 2020. But that decision was overturned by a higher court in January this year, a ruling other Baha'i couples now fear could affect them as well.
Ahmed Helmy, 49, also won a court ruling allowing his documents to show he was married, but said his wife has already been removed from the family section of his account on the government’s digital services platform.
He worries his status on his identity card will revert to "single" when he next renews it.
"If I do not have proof of marriage, I cannot add my wife to health insurance," he said. "Anything I own, my wife won't be able to inherit. Anything she owns, I won't be able to inherit."
For Labib, the community's shrinking burial space and the bureaucratic hurdles are connected by the same demand: to be treated as an equal citizen.
"I am not asking anyone to accept my religion," she said. "I am asking them to accept me as a person in this country." REUTERS

Stating that in war conditions we must accept responsibility, make decisions, and courageously defend those who work, he said: "Do not doubt that if we move forward in coordination in this gathering, we can, through synergy, place the parliament and the government on a single axis in the economic field and move forward."
Qalibaf, stating that currently the most important priority in all decision-making is the livelihood of the people and the armed forces, said: "We must act in such a way that the people's livelihood is the last place harmed by the pressure of war and sanctions, and the first positive result of decisions is on the people's table. This view must also exist in economic growth, reconstruction, and providing liquidity to the industrial sector."

The great Indian scam trap: More aware, yet still vulnerable
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:45:18 UTC
21:45:18 KST

A 79-year-old woman in Mumbai recently tried to buy dry fruits worth Rs 248 after seeing an advertisement on WhatsApp. Instead, she lost Rs 11.7 lakh after a caller posing as a company representative persuaded her to make 13 UPI transfers. She was warned that her bank account could be closed due to a technical error.Her experience brings together several findings in the GSMA India Consumer Scam Report 2026, based on an online, English-language survey of about 500 Indian adults conducted from July 29 to August 3. Online shopping scams were cited by 33% of Indian victims, more than any other type. Among surveyed victims who lost money, two in three recovered nothing.The survey compares Indian respondents with those in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, the Philippines and Vietnam. Three in four Indians surveyed (75%) said they were very concerned about online data privacy, against 48% across those six countries. Yet two in three (66%) were comfortable sharing personal details with “conversational apps” when buying, against 40% across the region. A third (33%) said they were "very comfortable" doing so, against just 7%. The report does not name the apps or establish whether respondents actually shared their details.
Privacy fears high, but Indians willing to share data
Trusting the channels scammers use
Indians also rate everyday communication channels as more trustworthy than respondents in the six Southeast Asian countries. These are also channels regularly used by scammers. Among Indian victims, 42% were scammed through messaging apps, 37% through social media and 33% through email. The email figure is almost double the regional 17%. And 64% of Indian victims were scammed through multiple channels, against 43% across the Southeast Asian countries.
Messaging apps lead scam routes, with 42% exposure
After online shopping, prize, lottery or inheritance scams were cited by 31% of Indian victims (remember the Nigerian prince emails?), and job or income scams by 30%. QR-code or payment-link scams were cited by 27%, against 18% across the region.Scammers also apply psychological pressure. Urgency featured in 39% of Indian victims' experiences, while secrecy or confidentiality featured in 33%, against a regional average of 22% for secrecy. In the Mumbai case, the alleged fraudster created a fear of losing banking access by warning that a technical problem could lead to account closure. Digital-arrest scams often play on the secrecy angle by leveraging potentially sensitive information.Technology adds another layer. Nearly half of Indian respondents (48%) said they had encountered AI-written scam messages, the same share reported fake AI images, and 42% said they had seen deepfake videos of real people.
The changing behaviour pattern
Indians are gradually becoming more guarded against scams. Seventy-two per cent of Indian respondents said their own experience, or that of someone close to them, had changed how they behave. Sixty-one per cent avoided some incoming contacts or online transactions because of scam concerns, and 26% had cut back on or changed how they shop online, up from 20% in 2025.There is healthy scepticism about platforms too. Sixty per cent associated Facebook with scams, up from 51% in 2025, and Instagram's figure rose from 50% to 57%.But only 49% had strengthened their account security, against 58% across the region. Among victims, 93% said that, in hindsight, they had done something they should not have, and 91% felt confident they would not fall for a similar scam again.Indians are relatively willing to let institutions use their data to detect fraud. Of the respondents, 87% were comfortable with banks or financial providers doing so, 82% with the government, 81% with mobile operators and 73% with digital platforms, each higher than the corresponding regional figure.
Recovering losses is difficult
Twelve per cent of Indian respondents said they had been scammed in the previous year, against 8% across the region. Of the 165 Indian respondents who had ever been scammed, 86% approached at least one organisation, against 69% across the region. The share going to the police rose from 37% in the 2025 survey to 49%.However, a third of reported cases remained unresolved, and in 35%, no organisation took primary responsibility in the victim's experience. Among those who lost money, 67% recovered nothing. India's recovery outcome was nevertheless better than the six-country average. Some 33% recovered some or all of their money, against 18% across the region.
India's record is better than countries in Southeast Asia
The home ministry told Parliament that the Citizen Financial Cyber Fraud Reporting and Management System had "saved" more than Rs 11,158 crore across over 32.80 lakh complaints by June 30, 2026, but that figure does not show how much victims got back. In a separate disclosure, the ministry reported more than Rs 206 crore refunded over the three financial years from 2023-24 to 2025-26. The National Crime Records Bureau does not maintain data on money lost or recovered in cyber fraud cases, Rajya Sabha was informed.
Scam, a global menace
GSMA, which represents mobile operators, calls for closer coordination among banks, platforms, telecom companies and authorities after scams are reported, and for greater transparency from government and police.Scams are a global business. The Global Anti-Scam Alliance estimates that consumers across 42 surveyed markets lost about $442 billion to scams in a year. In the US, the FBI recorded $20.877 billion in cybercrime losses in 2025, more than $2.9 billion of it from two forms of call-centre fraud: fake tech support and government impersonation. The FBI's 2025 Internet Crime Report recorded 5,879 complaints from India, the second-highest among countries outside the US, after Canada.
Since 2022, the FBI and CBI have run 27 joint operations against such fraud in India, leading to more than 475 arrests. One of them, Operation Chakra, broke up a Noida-based network in December 2025 accused of duping more than 600 Americans of over $48.7 million.If you are conned, call 1930 immediately. It may help save your money.

TEHRAN- The ceremony commemorating World Standards Day was held on the morning of October 13, under the slogan "Shared Vision for a Better World" and focusing on "Clean and Affordable Energy." The ceremony also emphasized the necessity of developing clean energy, increasing productivity, and upgrading standards related to energy consumption in energy-intensive industries. Optimizing production processes, developing renewable energy infrastructure, and reducing environmental pollution are among the areas in which these standards play a role.
The implementation of energy management standards in the agricultural and food industry value chain is also particularly important. The use of clean and low-consumption technologies in sectors such as cold storage, processing industries, and industrial greenhouses, in addition to helping manage production costs, can help maintain product quality after harvest and reduce agricultural waste.
Standardization of energy-intensive equipment and processes in agriculture and the food industry also provides the basis for increasing productivity, optimal use of resources, and strengthening sustainable food security infrastructure. From this perspective, the development and implementation of energy-related standards, in addition to economic effects, are also important in protecting natural resources and reducing the environmental consequences of production activities.
In another part of the ceremony, top production and service units at both national and provincial levels, conformity assessment bodies including inspection companies and partner laboratories, corresponding technical committees, quality control managers, sample drafting secretaries, and pioneers in the field of quality were honored.
This ceremony was held with the aim of explaining the role of standards in improving the quality of products and services, enhancing productivity, and supporting sustainable development.

African Union holds Kigali talks as fighting continues in eastern DRC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:40:26 UTC
21:40:26 KST

African Union holds Kigali talks as fighting continues in eastern DRC
Three former African presidents discussed security commitments, refugee protection and regional cooperation.
Kigali, Rwanda – The African Union (AU) has held consultations in Kigali, Rwanda, as part of efforts to advance the peace process in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), where fighting continues despite diplomatic initiatives to end the conflict.
The consultations, held on October 6, focused on implementing the Washington Peace Agreement, security arrangements, the disarmament, demobilisation and reintegration of fighters, refugee protection and regional economic cooperation, the AU said in a statement.
The delegation comprised former Ethiopian President Sahle-Work Zewde, former Kenyan President Uhuru Kenyatta and former Botswana President Mokgweetsi Masisi. Zewde is the deputy chairperson of the AU Panel of Facilitators for the eastern DRC peace process.
From Goma to Kigali
The Kigali consultations followed meetings in Goma, eastern DRC, on October 5. According to the AU, the delegation met representatives of the United Nations Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (MONUSCO), the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), the Expanded Joint Verification Mechanism Plus (EJVM+) and the Alliance Fleuve Congo/March 23 Movement (AFC/M23).
Following the Goma meetings, the AU panel called for respect for ceasefire commitments, cooperation with verification mechanisms and restraint from actions that could undermine the peace process. It also stressed the need to protect civilians, ensure safe humanitarian access and prevent sexual and gender-based violence.
In Kigali, the facilitators held separate consultations with Rwandan officials and representatives of regional institutions. The AU said the discussions covered security commitments, the protection of refugees and returnees, and regional economic cooperation, including mineral traceability, cross-border trade, energy and infrastructure.
The facilitators said they would continue their engagements in Kinshasa as part of efforts to support dialogue and advance the peace process.
Two agreements, separate negotiations
The consultations come amid parallel diplomatic efforts to address the conflict. The Washington Peace Agreement, signed by the DRC and Rwanda on June 27, 2025, includes security commitments intended to address concerns over armed groups and the presence of forces in eastern DRC.
Implementation remains a central issue. At a meeting of the agreement’s Joint Oversight Committee in June 2026, the parties expressed concern over escalating fighting and called for the agreement to be fully implemented, including commitments concerning the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR) and the disengagement of forces.
The Washington agreement is separate from the Doha Framework for a Comprehensive Peace Agreement, signed on November 15, 2025, by representatives of the Congolese government and AFC/M23 under Qatar’s mediation.
The Doha framework provides a basis for negotiations between the two sides on outstanding issues, including security arrangements and ceasefire monitoring. Subsequent discussions have focused on implementing existing commitments and negotiating remaining protocols.
The two processes address different aspects of the conflict: the Washington agreement deals with relations and security commitments between the DRC and Rwanda, while the Doha process addresses negotiations between the Congolese government and AFC/M23.
Kinshasa and Kigali remain at odds
Kinshasa accuses Rwanda of supporting AFC/M23, an allegation Kigali denies. Rwanda, in turn, accuses the Congolese government of supporting and arming the FDLR, which it considers a threat to its national security.
The Washington agreement includes commitments by the DRC to address the FDLR and by Rwanda concerning the disengagement of its forces and the lifting of defensive measures. The parties have continued to discuss how those commitments will be implemented and verified.
The continued diplomatic engagement reflects the challenges facing efforts to resolve the conflict, with security commitments and negotiations involving different parties proceeding on separate tracks.
The AU’s consultations in Goma and Kigali form part of its wider mediation efforts. Whether those efforts contribute to improved security will depend on the implementation of commitments by the parties and continued engagement in the respective peace processes.

The Apple HomeView Is Like a Giant Apple Watch for the Home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:38:32 UTC
21:38:32 KST

It’s a big year for Apple firsts. The company launched the first MacBook Neo, unveiled its first folding iPhone in September, and installed a new CEO for the first time in 15 years. Now comes the Apple HomeView, Apple’s first smart display.
Rivals like Google and Amazon have made countless screen-enabled smart speakers since voice assistants invaded the home a decade ago. But Apple stuck with a smaller smart home ecosystem centered on its HomePod speakers, even removing the iPad as a hub device a few years ago, which forced users to buy an Apple TV or HomePod to get started. Maybe that’s why it hasn’t found much success in the home.
Announced Tuesday at an event in New York City, the 7-inch smart display arrives alongside several other new smart home devices as part of Apple’s bid to revitalize its lagging ecosystem. The HomeView costs $299 and comes in two versions—a speaker base and a wall-mounted display—both priced the same. Preorders are live, with sales kicking off on November 13.
A Big Apple Watch
The first thing I thought of after seeing the Apple HomeView in action is that it looks like a blown-up Apple Watch. The 7-inch square screen has multiple “faces” you can swipe through, exactly like the smartwatch. You can even customize the face’s colors and add different complications for more glanceable information.
The faces can range from a clock, your favorite photos of friends, family, or pets (you can even use shared albums) to weather updates and, yes, Snoopy animations. Swipe up for the home screen, which is more like an iPhone or iPad, with apps neatly arranged alongside widgets. Except the HomeView doesn’t run iOS or iPadOS—it runs the generically named HomeView software.
It doesn’t have an App Store. Instead, Apple has a curated selection of apps, including FaceTime, Messages, and Safari. A handful of third-party media apps like Spotify are available, and developers can bring over existing CarPlay apps. If your iPhone already has one of these CarPlay apps installed, it can automatically appear on the HomeView after setup. (There are no video streaming apps like YouTube, Netflix, or Disney+, but if those companies choose to make their apps available on the CarPlay framework, they will show up on the HomeView; for now, you'll have to consume videos by using the Safari browser.)
To get the most out of the HomeView, you need an iPhone with Apple Intelligence support (an iPhone 15 Pro or newer)—you can’t set it up with an iPad. Apple says you can still set it up with an older iPhone and access some of Siri AI's smarts (like broad world knowledge), but smarter app actions and personal context queries require an iPhone with Apple Intelligence.
The aluminum hardware, powered by Apple’s A18 chip, comes in four colors: silver, starlight, rose pink, and space gray (Apple color-matches the woven cable, too). The standard HomeView has a speaker base with a screen that tilts manually up or down for angled viewing, but you can also buy a wall-mountable version. The latter offers three mounts to choose from, one of which is DIY-friendly and has a visible power cord that needs to run to an outlet. The other two are designed for professional installers, either hardwired or connected via Power over Ethernet (PoE).
Technically, the primary speakers—two full-range drivers—are built into the screen. But the standard HomeView has a base that houses a down-firing woofer and two force-canceling passive radiators for stronger bass. It sounds pretty good based on a very limited listening experience, and can fill a large room quite well. The wall-mounted variant won’t have that extra oomph but Apple claims it tunes the audio for wall placement.
The 7-inch Liquid Retina display has familiar elements, like True Tone, which adjusts the screen’s color temperature to match the room’s lighting. The ambient light sensor can also reduce display brightness from 500 nits to 0.3 nits, which is the lowest brightness Apple has ever engineered on a screen. That’ll be helpful if you place the HomeView on the nightstand.
That is, if you're comfortable placing a camera-equipped display in the bedroom. A 12-megapixel Center Stage camera and four-microphone array sit on the front, but they aren’t just for FaceTime calls. The camera handles facial recognition, allowing the software to adapt to whoever is looking at the screen. Apple says all of this data stays on device.
“Trust is becoming increasingly important with rising consumer expectations around privacy and security,” writes Anshika Jain, principal analyst at Counterpoint, in an email to WIRED. “In fact, Apple could actually benefit from its privacy-first approach.”
You can add up to six iCloud accounts, and the user interface will adapt to each person, like Google’s Pixel Tablet. That means your wife can tint every app icon green and have no widgets on her home screen, but if you stand in front of the HomeView, it’ll switch to your setup. You won’t be able to view other household members’ sensitive messages and personal information. For this personal content to show up, you don’t just have to stand in front of the HomeView—your iPhone needs to be on the same Wi-Fi network and must have been recently unlocked.
The HomeView can also recognize voices, which helps if Dad asks Siri AI to “Play music.” It will play from Dad’s music library and his preferred music app, rather than another iCloud user’s music. If you have multiple HomePods or HomeViews, you can manage your speaker groups in the HomeView’s interface.
The HomeView also supports Apple’s Handoff tech, so you can bring your iPhone close to send a Safari recipe to the smart display, or have it continue the podcast you were listening to on your commute. In the middle of a FaceTime or phone call? Put your iPhone near the HomeView, and it’ll transfer it over.
Betting on Siri AI
Like any smart display or smart speaker, Siri AI powers the HomeView. It is, after all, the main way to interact with the device (though yes, there’s a keyboard you can pull up to type). Apple spent a great deal of time revamping Siri this year, finally launching a more capable assistant in iOS 27.
Siri AI on the HomeView understands your personal context from your iPhone, so if you ask it to play a song your friend Eric recommended, it’ll know right away what you mean by looking at your Messages history. You can ask when your brother Jeff will likely arrive at your home from the airport on Thursday, then set a schedule for Siri to turn on the coffee maker 15 minutes before his estimated arrival. All of this can be done with natural language, meaning you don’t have to say specific commands for Siri AI to understand you.
One neat trick is the HomeView’s ability to convert recipe pages from Safari into digestible content. Load a recipe, and it will let you view the ingredients or “Start Cooking,” no need to read three paragraphs of the author’s relationship to the stew. It automatically converts the recipe into step-by-step instructions, even auto-populating timers for relevant steps so you can start individual timers as you progress.
Naturally, the HomeView is also designed to control all of your smart home devices, too. You can create a widget for any device you have added in the Home app to quickly control it on the HomeView. And if you swipe to the left from the home screen, you’ll see the “Camera” face, which shows a live stream of connected security cameras (you can view nine feeds at once).
Much like the upcoming iPhone Duo folding phone, Apple is late to market. The company is betting on tight iPhone integration, glanceable Watch-like software, and a more context-aware Siri to make the HomeView feel more like a screen you’ll actually want on your counter. Everything hinges on whether Siri can hold up its end of the bargain—and the voice assistant doesn’t exactly have the best track record.
“The greater challenge is to make AI useful for everyday interactions,” Jain says. “Apple must provide a more capable Siri experience and ensure seamless control across its entire product range in order to stand out from the competition.”

‘Help non-native speakers with Dutch!’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:36:17 UTC
21:36:17 KST

Flemish Economy Minister Hilde Crevits (Flemish Christian democrat CD&V) launched the ‘Spreektaal’ or ‘Spoken Language’ campaign at the Albert Heijn supermarket in Rumbeke (West Flanders) today. During Dutch Language Week, she is asking customers to help non-native speakers who ask for explanations in broken Dutch by communicating with them in Dutch. From today, all shop staff will be wearing a badge bearing the words “We’re open to a chat”.
“Today we are making a very special appeal,” says the minister. “If you go shopping and there are people asking for explanations about a product in broken Dutch, please help them in Dutch. Every year, hundreds of thousands of people start taking Dutch lessons. They are looking for places to practise.”
A small corner of the shop has been set aside where people can have a coffee and have a natter. According to Crevits, some people don’t dare to ask for help because they’re afraid of making mistakes. “But if you pluck up the courage, you’re guaranteed always to be helped in Dutch,” she says.
Crevits was initially surprised herself that a department store could play a part in this. Until she heard the story of a woman who, 20 years ago, could barely speak Dutch. She asked another woman where the aubergines were. A friendship grew out of that. “Now, 20 years later, they are best friends.”
Making mistakes is all part of the process
Jean-Paul Fraeyman is the manager of the supermarket on Koestraat. He notices that many non-native speakers apply for jobs when he is looking for new staff. “The better they learn the language, the easier it is for them to integrate, both into the running of the shop and in their personal lives,” he says.
He wants customers to know that making a mistake whilst learning Dutch is all part of the process and “is absolutely not viewed negatively”.
The same goes for the West Flemish dialect!
Carolina Sergant is the shop’s marketing manager and says she often discusses Dutch language courses with staff.
“Our shop has many staff members with an integration background. They started via local social services, via work-based learning or a VDAB training course they’ve completed.”
She believes staff can even learn the idiosyncratic West Flemish dialect - that many Flemings from outside the coastal province struggle to comprehend - on the job too, as customers will speak to them in broad West Flemish.

France seizes another 'shadow fleet' tanker; Russia decries 'piracy'
PARIS/MOSCOW, Oct 13 - France's military was taking a tanker suspected to be part of Russia's "shadow fleet" skirting Western sanctions to Reunion island on Tuesday in what Moscow called another act of "piracy".
Sanctions on Russia for invading Ukraine and aimed at cutting its oil revenue have spawned a fleet of often ageing and unregulated vessels helping Moscow keep its crude exports flowing.
The DF Peak, previously named the Kaliningrad and flagged from Benin, is at least the fifth Russian-linked tanker to be seized by France since 2024.
"We had doubts regarding the flag under which this vessel was sailing, so we carried out an inspection," French army spokesperson Colonel Xavier Rival told a news conference.
"Those doubts remain, and therefore the vessel is currently proceeding to Reunion Island by decision of the public prosecutor, so that we can examine the matter in detail."
The US on Monday temporarily eased sanctions on the sale of Russian diesel as the Middle East war disrupts oil supplies and boosts prices.
Europe has been taking tougher action against tankers using false flag registries to transport Russian oil, including boarding vessels at sea.
Russia's embassy in France was quoted by the state RIA news agency on Tuesday as saying that the seizure of the DF Peak was "piracy" and a blatant violation of international law.
RIA cited the embassy as saying it was trying to determine if any Russian citizens were among the crew. France had also not notified Russia about the tanker's seizure, it said.
DETERMINED TO TACKLE SHADOW FLEET
In a post on X on Monday evening, President Emmanuel Macron showed French military personnel intercepting and boarding the tanker from helicopters in what he said was some 450 nautical miles south of Reunion, a French territory in the Indian Ocean.
"France is determined to combat the shadow fleet, wherever it may be in the world," he said, adding that it was suspected of sailing under a false flag and being involved in illicit fuel transportation activities.
The vessel’s Hong Kong-based manager listed in shipping databases, Zheng Xin Marine, could not be reached for comment.
The vessel has been hit by US, UK and EU sanctions in 2024.
It was partially loaded and last seen off the coast of Madagascar on October 12 at 0429 GMT with its previous port listed as Guanta in Venezuela, LSEG ship tracking data showed.
Russia has used such tankers, which typically lack mainstream insurance or safety certification, to skirt sanctions by sailing under the flags of various nations to obscure their true ownership, cargo and movements. REUTERS

As Houthis approach Yemen's Taiz locals flee fear of another siege
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:33:00 UTC
21:33:00 KST

As Iran-backed Houthi rebels push to capture the strategic city of Taiz in Yemen's 12-year civil war, fear gripped the locals with many deciding to flee.
Weam Abdullah and her family are among the war-displaced population leaving Yemen’s third largest city. They had survived a yearslong siege by the rebels earlier in their country’s civil war and they didn’t want to endure that again.
They made it out just in time. Shortly after Abdullah, her husband and two young children left, the rebels captured a key town on Oct. 4, largely encircling Taiz and cutting off most supply routes from government-held areas.
"We already feel dead, there was already despair” in the city, Abdullah told The Associated Press by phone from a province farther south. "We feel as if we are cursed. Everyone is conspiring against us even though we’re not affiliated with any party or politics.”
The assault follows a lightning offensive last month in which the rebels seized Yemen’s Red Sea coast, strengthening their ability to attack Saudi oil shipping and plunging global energy prices further into turmoil.
The advance has triggered fear among Taiz's more than 1 million residents, who live in the rugged mountains of southwestern Yemen. On a recent day, crowds mobbed groceries in the city center to buy up food and other essentials, fearing they will soon run out. Diesel fuel and cooking gas supplies are running low, residents said.
Some residents are collecting cardboard and wood to burn for cooking, while merchants are raising food and water prices, said Shaif al-Gabiri, a child protection consultant at the Civic Center for Advocacy and Support, a local nonprofit group.
"If the siege continues, then these stocks will run out," he said.
Explosions from fighting between Houthis and pro-government forces echo from the surrounding mountains. Some strikes have hit the city itself, reminding residents of an ordeal they hoped might be over.
Taiz has been on the front line of Yemen’s civil war since 2014 when Houthi rebels seized the north and much of the country’s west, including the capital, Sanaa. Saudi Arabia later entered the war at the head of a coalition backing the internationally recognized government, which had been forced to flee south.
A strategic gateway to the south, Taiz is also one of Yemen’s most important historical and cultural centers. It once served as the capital of several Islamic dynasties and a major center of religious learning.
Al-Qahira Castle, a monumental fortress more than 800 years old, overlooks the city from a hill. To the south rises Mount Sabir, more than 3,000 meters (9,800 feet) high, its slopes carved into agricultural terraces.
For much of the war, Houthi forces surrounded most of Taiz and blocked its main roads. Bombardments regularly struck the city center, power cuts were frequent, and residents struggled to find food.
The only routes to government-held areas were steep, winding mountain back roads. Bringing in supplies or getting people to hospitals in the southern port city of Aden took hours.
Taiz was "a jungle" at the time, Abdullah said. If people didn’t die "from artillery, then they would die from the siege, malnourished because of lack of food," she said. After nightfall, "many streets were deserted and looked scary."
A truce reached in 2022 eased fighting across Yemen and brought some life back to Taiz. Many who had fled returned, and homes were rebuilt. But prices remained high, and residents struggled to get by, Abdullah said. Houthi forces still controlled areas north, east and west of the city and charged "customs” duties on supplies passing through.
The truce ended in August when the Houthis launched a new assault. Last month, they seized the Red Sea coast, capturing the port city of Mocha and several strategic islands. They then began advancing around Taiz.
Abdullah said her family feared a new siege would be worse than the last. Her children were afraid to go outside to play.
"This is why we left," she said. "The situation was terrible, you couldn’t get essentials, and there’s a shortage in everything ... There is no diesel to work water pumps."
As they fled Taiz, they saw government reinforcements heading toward the city and heard explosions and gunfire, she said. They passed through Turbah, about 40 kilometers (25 miles) south of Taiz, before reaching the government-controlled province of Lahj.
Days later, the Houthis captured Turbah, encircling Taiz and a pocket of government-held territory.
As well as the main roads out of Taiz, some of the alternative mountain routes used in the past are now closed, causing "some confusion and panic," according to Abdelrahman al-Qaliaa, director of the Taiz branch of the Industry and Trade Ministry.
He urged residents crowding stores to only buy what they immediately needed to prevent shortages.
Pro-government forces are fighting Houthis in the mountains southwest of Taiz, trying to break the rebels' hold.
Ahmed Abdel-Jaber said shelling near his house in a mountain village wounded his 7-year-old grandson in his stomach. The boy was taken to a hospital in Taiz.
Abdel-Jaber moved his family of nine to another village farther from the fighting. "If we decide it’s unsafe there, we’ll flee to another area," he told the AP by phone.
Growing numbers of government soldiers, women and children wounded in the fighting have been brought to hospitals in Taiz.
"Hospitals could run out of diesel at any point," said Dr. Fahd Nazary of the Taiz provincial health office. Delivering medical supplies has also become more difficult, he said. "This is a huge catastrophe."
Al-Gabiri, the child protection consultant in Taiz, described fears that the fighting could worsen.
"Here I am sitting in a coffee shop," al-Gabiri said, "knowing that at any moment a shell could fall on me or an explosive could come from any direction, hitting any house and any street."

Why the TTP Remains the Central Fault Line Between Pakistan and Afghanistan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:29:00 UTC
21:29:00 KST

On October 11, Pakistan’s military reported that security forces had killed 12 militants and Afghan Taliban personnel during an attempted crossing from Afghanistan into Pakistan’s Kurram district. A Pakistani soldier was also killed in the exchange of fire. The Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), the military’s media wing, said Afghan Taliban border posts had opened fire in support of the attempted crossing.
The incident came 10 days after Pakistani airstrikes in Afghanistan, which Islamabad said targeted militant camps and hideouts. Pakistan reported that the strikes killed 22 militants. At the same time, the United Nations Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA) confirmed that at least 10 civilians, most of them children, were killed and nine injured in Kunar and Helmand provinces. The U.N. mission called for de-escalation and greater protection of civilians, underscoring the humanitarian risks of continued cross-border hostilities.
These incidents reflect a wider deterioration in Afghanistan-Pakistan relations, driven in part by Islamabad’s concerns about militant groups operating from Afghan territory.
On September 18, a suicide car bombing at a mosque inside the Kohat Police Lines complex in Pakistan’s Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, followed by an armed assault, killed at least 31 people, including 16 police personnel, and injured more than 100, according to local police officials. Ittehadul Mujahideen Pakistan (IMP), a militant alliance linked to the Hafiz Gul Bahadur faction, claimed responsibility for the attack. The IMP operates within the broader network of militant groups active along the Afghanistan-Pakistan border and has had links with the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), a militant umbrella organization waging an insurgency against the Pakistani state.
The scale of the threat is reflected in the 2026 Global Terrorism Index, which ranked the TTP as the world’s third-deadliest terrorist organization in 2025. The index identified rising violence by both the TTP and the Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA) as contributing to Pakistan’s worsening security environment. Islamabad has maintained that the Afghan Taliban authorities are allowing the militant outfits, including the TTP and the BLA, to maintain sanctuaries in Afghanistan, an allegation Kabul denies.
The Kohat attack was just one manifestation of a broader security dispute that has strained Afghanistan-Pakistan relations for years. In 2022, shortly after the Taliban returned to power in Afghanistan, Pakistan negotiated with the TTP through mediation by Afghanistan’s Taliban authorities. They reached a ceasefire in June 2022, but the agreement collapsed in November, when the TTP announced a resumption of attacks across Pakistan.
A February 2023 U.N. Security Council monitoring report cited assessments by several member states that the Taliban’s return to power in Afghanistan had emboldened the TTP and contributed to an escalation in its attacks against Pakistan. The report also examined links between the TTP and other armed groups. Subsequent U.N. Security Council monitoring reports have provided further support for Pakistan’s security concerns. A July 2024 report noted that the TTP continued to operate from Afghanistan and conduct attacks inside Pakistan, citing member states’ assessments of Taliban tolerance and support for the group. The December 2025 report went further, describing the continued harboring of TTP leaders in Afghanistan and the facilitation of the group’s operations by the Taliban authorities.
As concerns about cross-border militancy persisted, Islamabad pursued a parallel response at home. In June 2024, the government approved Azm-e-Istehkam, a national framework intended to strengthen intelligence-based operations and law enforcement. However, domestic counterterrorism measures have not resolved the cross-border dimension of the threat.
Regional diplomacy has struggled to bridge the divide between Islamabad and Kabul. The eighth Moscow Format Consultations on Afghanistan, held on October 5, offered a recent example of this impasse. The meeting brought together Afghanistan and regional powers, including Pakistan, China, India, Iran and Russia, to discuss security and regional cooperation. It ended without a joint statement after the Pakistani and Afghan delegations struggled to agree on the language concerning terrorism. Pakistan’s Special Representative for Afghanistan, Mohammad Sadiq, emphasized the threat posed by militant groups operating from Afghan territory, while the Afghan Taliban delegation resisted the proposed wording. The disagreement illustrated a fundamental obstacle: the two sides have yet to agree on how to define and address the security problem itself.
The Moscow impasse followed earlier attempts to ease tensions through direct negotiations. After the October 2025 fighting, Qatar and Turkiye hosted talks that produced a ceasefire, followed by further rounds of negotiations in Istanbul, Doha, and Riyadh. These efforts did not resolve the central dispute. Pakistan seeks verifiable action against the TTP, while the Afghan Taliban authorities deny that the group operates from their territory in the manner Islamabad alleges. Without agreement on the underlying security concerns, diplomatic engagement has struggled to produce a durable settlement.
Economic ties have suffered as a result. In January 2026, Pakistani and Afghan traders agreed to establish a joint committee to discuss reopening border crossings. However, commercial negotiations could not overcome the wider security impasse. Since the October 2025 clashes, Pakistan has kept its border crossings with Afghanistan closed to trade – by far the longest closure in recent decades, disrupting a key transit route into Central Asia. The economic burden has fallen on traders and transporters on both sides, while Afghanistan has sought to diversify its trade through Iran, India, and other regional partners.
The costs of confrontation are therefore not confined to the security domain. Prolonged border closures disrupt livelihoods and commercial networks, while airstrikes and armed clashes expose civilians to further harm. The biggest challenge is to prevent the security dispute from becoming a self-reinforcing cycle in which militant violence prompts punitive measures, those measures deepen bilateral hostility, and deteriorating relations make cooperation against militancy even more difficult.
Breaking this cycle requires practical measures rather than competing declarations. First, Pakistan and the Afghan Taliban authorities could establish a verification mechanism, facilitated by a mutually acceptable third party such as Qatar, Turkiye, or China, to investigate specific allegations of militant activity and assess compliance with security commitments. Second, trade routes could be reopened gradually against measurable security benchmarks, linking economic recovery to demonstrable progress. Third, regional powers could support a sustained counterterrorism dialogue focused on information-sharing, specific incidents, and border management. Such targeted cooperation may offer a more realistic starting point than broader diplomatic forums where disagreements over the nature of the threat continue to prevent consensus.

Around 650 prisoners to be released early in England, Wales
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:28:16 UTC
21:28:16 KST

Aysu Bicer
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
Around 650 prisoners are set to be released early from jails in England and Wales on Tuesday in the second phase of a government scheme aimed at tackling overcrowding in the prison system.
The scheme allows eligible offenders serving sentences of up to 2 1/2 years to leave prison after serving one-third of their sentence, rather than half, according to the BBC.
The second wave follows the release of around 700 prisoners on Oct. 1, all serving sentences of less than 19 months.
The government plans to release around 5,000 prisoners in stages, with the process extending to June next year for those serving sentences of more than 12 years.
The number of eligible prisoners was reduced from an initial estimate of 6,000 after officials excluded rapists and the most serious child sex offenders. Those convicted of manslaughter are also ineligible, along with offenders convicted of several other offenses, including indecent assault involving members of child grooming gangs.
The scheme has raised concerns among victims’ groups and probation officers over public safety and the capacity to supervise offenders after their release.
Alice Russell-Harris of domestic abuse charity Refuge told the BBC that releasing perpetrators could put survivors at serious risk of harm. She said license conditions, including electronic tagging and exclusion zones, were frequently breached by perpetrators.
Concerns have also been raised about delays in fitting electronic tags, which are used to monitor curfews and other release conditions.
Meanwhile, probation service union Napo said its members were overwhelmed by workloads and the need to provide intensive supervision to released offenders.
Union General Secretary Ian Lawrence warned that the number of prisoners being released was placing significant pressure on the service, calling for additional resources.
The developments come as the government prepares to present plans to overhaul criminal courts to Parliament, while probation officers prepare to vote in a ballot that could lead to strike action over pay and workloads.

Generative AI transforms internet marketing, ushers in ‘citation economy’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:28:10 UTC
21:28:10 KST

Enes Ege and Emir Yildirim
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
Search engines and virtual assistants powered by artificial intelligence (AI) are reshaping digital marketing by replacing click-driven metrics with a “citation economy,” as experts say producing original and verifiable content has become increasingly important for brands to stand out amid the oversaturation of generative AI content.
Digital visibility across AI platforms like ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google AI Overviews hinges on “generative engine optimization,” or “GEO,” according to a report by Princeton University and partner institutions.
Researchers developed a test dataset called “GEO-bench,” which includes over 10,000 different queries to analyze the data processing architecture of generative search engines.
The test showed that digital content with verifiable statistics, credible citations and expert opinions increased its visibility in AI-generated answers by up to 40%.
With more and more users relying on AI-generated summaries rather than clicking through search engine query results, marketing agencies worldwide are reshaping their strategies to adapt to the changing trend.
Experts say this transition will usher in a new era where brands that produce high-quality original content will prevail over those that boast massive ad budgets.
Bunyamin Sarac, co-founder and CEO of Indexa, told Anadolu that brands appearing in AI chatbot answers and AI-generated search engine summaries are more successful as internet traffic shifts away from the simple click-based system.
Sarac stated that AI engines evaluate real-time search results using trust signals like “source authority,” “timeliness” and “extractability.”
“Developers of these models do not fully share the details of their source selection mechanism, so we can’t really say that there’s a definitive formula, but research and observation showed certain signals that these models look for,” he said. “AI responses are trained by two sources: the data set used to train the model and web search inquiries at the moment that the answer is generated to a prompt.”
Sarac noted that click-through rates drop when users receive an AI summary, citing Pew Research Center findings that showed that while 8% of users who read an AI summary on Google clicked on one of the resulting links, this rate was nearly double among those who did not see a summary.
“We expect a decline in web traffic from information-seeking inquiries, as visitors who click on a website will be those who have already read the AI summary or done their research through AI and are closer to making a purchase – the metric for success will shift from the number of clicks to the number of times that a product or brand was recommended for critical search inquiries,” he added.
Erdem Dagdemir, co-founder and CEO of Analythick, told Anadolu that conventional search engine optimization (SEO) focused on technical code and voluminous data, which is no longer sufficient. He urged brands to embrace a newer approach that highlights human context, real-world customer satisfaction and organic digital footprints.
“AI does not look at the volume of data but at its qualitative accuracy and depth, synthesizing information by cross-referencing a brand’s digital footprint and asking if the source is trustworthy and whether customers are satisfied,” he said.
“Brands must plan their operations, establish effective communication, and build trust by prioritizing customer satisfaction,” he added, noting that if these digital footprints do not corroborate a brand’s corporate promises, AI might completely remove the brand from recommendations.
Dagdemir stated that large language models (LLMs) go through online forums and review sites to reveal persistent consumer complaints to decide whether a brand or product can be recommended to users. He added that marketing teams clinging to outdated methods, like oversaturating superficial content, will lose ground to competitors who offer verifiable information.
“The clear and fast responses AI chatbots are made to deliver force people and industries to adapt to this new pace, and Türkiye’s ecosystem stands at this threshold of adaptation – while some brands are still using outdated methods to cling to their prominence, the fundamental rule of the new era is no longer about visibility but about reliability, and amid the clutter of information and scarcity of quality content, I think brands that abandon ad-driven strategies in favor of offering genuine and accurate information will gain a significant edge over competitors in AI-generated search responses,” he added.
