Investigators hunt French supermarket fridge hackers, no claim of responsibility
- French investigators are hunting hackers after a cyberattack took control of supermarket fridge systems at hundreds of stores, with no group claiming responsibility.
- The attack hit chains including Carrefour, Monoprix, Intermarche and Cooperative U, and left staff throwing spoilt meat and frozen food into rubbish bins.
- Experts blamed outdated Danfoss software and poor cyber hygiene, warning that thousands of fridge interfaces are still exposed online and remain at risk.
AI generated
PARIS – French investigators on Oct 13 were hunting the hackers who seized control of cooling units at hundreds of supermarkets in a cyberattack that underlined the vulnerabilities of connected systems, with no group publicly claiming responsibility.
The investigation comes as Dutch supermarket company Ahold Delhaize grapples with a separate cybersecurity incident that disrupted online services, although the Dutch authorities said they saw no connection between the two events.
The absence of a claim of responsibility by hacktivists or a ransom demand by cybercriminals has puzzled investigators, according to a source with knowledge of the probe. Typically, such groups tend to quickly seek to monetise their hacks or claim credit for them for political ends.
The cyberattack, which manually overrode the temperatures at fridges in supermarket groups including Carrefour, Monoprix, Intermarche and Cooperative U, appears to have been easy to pull off, three cyber experts told Reuters.
Staff at some Paris supermarkets threw boxes full of perished meat and frozen goods into giant rubbish containers on Oct 13. At least 350 supermarkets – a small fraction of the total number in France – were caught up in the strike.
Firm blames outdated software
France’s cybersecurity agency has said the breach affected fridges that relied on software by Danish firm Danfoss, as well as Copeland and Dixell software.
Danfoss said on Oct 12 that many of the affected units had “reached end of life and no longer receive software or security updates” or were “running outdated firmware.”
It said it had “advised customers to keep supported systems updated with the latest firmware and to migrate legacy systems to current-generation solutions”.
The company declined further comment on Oct 13.
Copeland, which owns Dixell, acknowledged the “vulnerability.”
“We are currently working with impacted customers to mitigate the risk,” the company said, adding that it would strengthen cybersecurity.
In Danfoss’ case, the serious vulnerabilities present in older versions of its firmware have been known for months.
On Aug 9, cybersecurity firm Claroty detailed weaknesses – since patched – in the Danfoss AK-SM 800A controller that could have allowed intruders to bypass authentication and run code on compromised devices.
‘Basic cyber hygiene’
Although the precise mechanism by which attackers compromised the refrigerators has not been publicly disclosed, cybersecurity experts said all signs pointed to a basic stunt enabled both by the failure to adopt Danfoss’ updates and by exposing device interfaces to the internet.
“This is about basic cyber hygiene,” said Ken Munro, a partner at the British cybersecurity firm Pen Test Partners. “Get it wrong and you get a smelly mess of defrosted food.”
He said the well-known vulnerabilities meant the attackers were essentially pushing at an open door, something that meant the hack could easily be “kids messing around”.
“If this was a nation state, why affect only a subset of French fridges? There are plenty of other nations with fridges on the internet,” he said. “No ransom or demand suggests a lack of appreciation of the potential commercial losses that the fridge owners may experience.”
Problem still exists
Plenty of fridges remain reachable via the internet. Using the internet scanning service Shodan, Reuters found at least 4,500 Danfoss interfaces still viewable on Oct 13.
Reuters could not independently establish how many of them were running vulnerable software, but French internet scanning company Onyphe said only a small minority of the devices appeared to be running the latest version of the software.
Outdated and vulnerable versions were “still widely represented among publicly accessible interfaces”, Onyphe said.
Dutch disruption
Separately, Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize said on Oct 13 that it had begun “starting a controlled re-launch of certain systems” following a cybersecurity issue that began on Sunday evening.
The Dutch cybersecurity watchdog NCSC said it did not believe the incident was linked to the French supermarket hack.
Ahold operates the Albert Heijn chain in the Netherlands and several major US chains including Stop & Shop and Giant Food. Websites for stores in both countries remained offline late afternoon on Oct 13, with online ordering and delivery services unavailable. REUTERS

People who ghost tend to feel worse about it than the people they ghost realize
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:00:13 UTC
21:00:13 KST

When someone stops responding to your messages, it is easy to assume they simply do not care. But new research suggests that people who leave messages unanswered tend to feel worse about their silence than their conversation partners realize. The findings, published in Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, also indicate that even a brief reply can narrow this emotional misunderstanding.
Ghosting occurs when one person abruptly stops responding to another person’s messages without an explanation. In the context of digital communication, it happens when at least one person in the exchange believes the silence might be permanent. Ghosting can range from an intentional decision to end a romantic relationship to a temporary lapse where someone reads a message but gets distracted and forgets to reply. The researchers call the person who stops responding the “ghoster” and the person left waiting the “ghostee.”
Prior studies suggest that cutting someone off emotionally takes a toll on the person doing the rejecting. For example, a 2013 study found that socially excluding someone actually causes emotional distress for the person enforcing the exclusion. Building on this idea, a 2022 study of people who had both ghosted and been ghosted by romantic partners found that ghosters were more likely to describe feeling guilty, but also relieved, while those who were ghosted more often described sadness and hurt.
The research was led by Sophia Li of the Haas School of Business at the University of California, Berkeley, and Coral Zheng, a PhD candidate in organizational behavior at the University of Cambridge’s Judge Business School, who contributed equally to the work. They wanted to expand on this psychological dynamic.
“Ghosting has been a very common, popular, but also annoying phenomenon to many people nowadays. So I think, first of all, we’re definitely motivated to study ghosting as a real-world problem,” Zheng told PsyPost.
“At the same time, the past literature usually defines it as a breakup strategy in the romantic context, while we think there’s more than that,” Zheng explained. “In addition to an intentional strategy that aims to permanently dissolve a relationship, there are situations where people accidentally forget to respond, simply do not see the message, strategically postpone a response (which the other person might already interpret as ghosting), etc. Thus, we want to include a broader definition of ghosting that includes unintentional, temporary ghosting and across different contexts as well.”
To capture this, the researchers designed a series of studies to see if the victims of ghosting actually recognize the internal distress experienced by the people ignoring them. If ghostees fail to notice this guilt, they might falsely assume the other person is entirely cold or hostile.
In the first study, they recruited 195 adults and asked them to recall a specific time they communicated online with someone they knew who wasn’t a close friend or immediate family member. Half of the participants recalled a time they ghosted someone, while the other half recalled a time they were ghosted. The participants then rated how bad they felt about the situation and predicted how bad the other person felt on a scale from 1 to 5, where 1 meant “not bad at all” and 5 meant “extremely bad.”
The researchers found that the people who ghosted others reported feeling worse (an average score of 2.27) than the victims predicted they would feel (an average score of 1.56). The victims underestimated how much guilt and sadness the ghosters felt, but also how relieved they were. The gap was wider when the ghosting was unintentional, such as when someone simply forgot to text back: these ghosters felt particularly bad, but the people they ghosted did not anticipate this. Interestingly, ghosters were accurate in predicting how bad the ghostees felt (averaging 2.11 for both actual and predicted feelings).
In the second study, the researchers tested 601 adults using imagined scenarios. Participants pictured texting back and forth with a friend they did not know very well. Half imagined being the one who stopped replying, and half imagined being the one left waiting. Each participant considered two versions of the scenario: one in which no reply came at all, and one in which the friend sent a short message reading, “Sorry, but I can’t talk right now.”
Once again, those imagining being the ghoster expected to feel worse (an average score of 3.23) than the people imagining being ghosted predicted (1.94). Sending a short reply narrowed this gap: responders expected to feel less bad (2.33), and receivers’ predictions (1.82) came closer to the mark. The brief message also reduced self-blame. When ghosted, about a third of receivers assumed they had been annoying their friend, compared with about one in five after a short reply, with most assuming the friend was simply busy.
For the third study, the researchers paired up adults in an online chatroom for an eight-minute text conversation designed to help them get to know each other. Afterward, one person in each pair was given a choice to either participate in a second five-minute conversation or skip it entirely. If they chose to skip it, their partner was left waiting alone in the chatroom without any explanation. Of the 229 pairs who completed the study, the researchers analyzed the 175 in which one partner chose to skip.
In the live experiment, the overall pattern did not hold. On average, the people left waiting did not underestimate how bad their partners felt (3.26 for those who skipped versus 3.35 predicted, on a scale where 5 meant “extremely bad”), though they did overestimate how negatively the skippers felt toward them (3.41 predicted versus 2.29 actual). Part of the explanation may be that the two sides did not always agree on what had happened. People who skipped the chat rated their behavior as less like ghosting (2.56) than their waiting partners did (3.06).
“The affective misperceptions between the ghosters and ghostees also show that the experience and subjective perceptions are sometimes asymmetric,” Zheng noted. “Therefore, the current work also argues that ghosting is a subjective experience – if at least one of the communication parties perceives their experience as ghosting, it is ghosting to this particular party. It could either be the ghoster actually wants to ghost but the ghostee doesn’t feel so, or the ghostee feels ghosted albeit the ghoster does not mean to.”
In an analysis that was not planned in advance, the researchers looked only at participants who rated the behavior as ghosting (a 4 or 5 on the 5-point scale). In that group, the original pattern reappeared: those who skipped felt worse (3.93) than those left waiting predicted (3.51). Across all pairs, the people left waiting also underestimated how much their partners wanted to develop a friendship.
These results offer a new perspective on why communication breakdowns happen and how they are perceived by both sides. The findings align with research covered by PsyPost in 2024, which found that people who are ghosted tend to underestimate how much the person who ignored them still cares about their well-being. That earlier work focused on ghosters’ concern for the other person rather than on how bad ghosters themselves feel. Together, these studies suggest that the quiet side of a digital conversation may be more conflicted than it appears.
“If you’ve been ghosted, it may help to know that the person who hasn’t responded probably feels worse than you expected. If you’re the one who hasn’t responded, maybe consider sending a short reply before going silent,” Zheng said. “We hope to help both parties understand the other person’s perspective, reduce misunderstandings, and increase well-being for both sides.”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The live experiment, the most realistic of the three, did not find the overall effect; it emerged only among participants who saw the behavior as ghosting, an analysis the researchers had not planned in advance. People left waiting were also told their partner might not return, which may have reduced the uncertainty that usually comes with being ghosted.
The interactions also involved short online chats between complete strangers, which might not capture the intense emotional weight of being ghosted by a long-term romantic partner or a close friend. Another limitation is that all the participants were based in the United States. In cultures where avoiding direct confrontation is considered polite, people might not feel as guilty about ghosting, and victims might interpret the silence differently.
There is also an ongoing debate among psychologists about how to precisely define ghosting. As the third study showed, two people can experience the exact same conversation and disagree on whether ghosting actually took place. As digital communication continues to evolve, researchers will need to keep exploring where people draw the line between a delayed response and a permanent digital exit.
Looking ahead, Zheng pointed out that complete silence is only one part of a larger puzzle. “Besides the complete silence, which is ghosting, there are many other aspects in online communication that are still underexplored,” she told PsyPost. “For example, how do people feel and predict the other person’s feelings based on the speed of a response, the length of a message, the tone of a message, whether there are emojis/punctuation or not, whether the tone is positive vs. neutral, etc. The elements in online communication dynamics are fascinating.”
The study, “The Pain of Ghosting? People Underestimate How Bad Their Conversation Partners Feel About Not Responding,” was authored by Sophia Li, Coral Zheng, and Juliana Schroeder.

Global action to end violence against children is lagging behind risks: UN expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Global action to end violence against children is lagging behind risks: UN expert
The UN Special Representative on Violence Against Children has called for stronger global action to protect boys and girls caught up in a growing number of crises, as current efforts fall short.
“Almost 45 million children are displaced because of conflict, but also because of natural disasters, because of the climate crisis,” said Najat Maalla M’jid, briefing journalists at UN Headquarters in New York on Monday.
Food insecurity and the rapid spread of technology are also hampering efforts to reduce violence against children, Ms. M’jid noted, after delivering her final report to the General Assembly, which she described as “a wake-up call” for greater mobilization.
Her presentation to Member States coincided with the 20th anniversary of the first-ever UN global study on violence against children. Although the world has changed since then, she highlighted “ongoing complex multiple crises” facing the international community in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic.
Young lives caught in crises
Today, one in five children lives in extreme poverty “and not only in the poor countries but also in the wealthy countries despite all the money put in cash transfers, cash benefits, and so on”, she said.
Other issues of concern include rising prices globally and food insecurity, while some countries are seeing a pushback against human rights.
Added to this is what she called “the wonderful, very, very quick spread of technology, including AI, that offers opportunity but opens huge avenues for child sexual exploitation, but also cyberbullying, deepfakes and enrollment in criminal activities”.
A clear message
Ms. M’jid began her remarks by reflecting on the 2006 UN study, which showed that violence against children occurs in every country and across all settings, whether at home, school, in the community and beyond.
She recalled the years of work and engagement – including with children and young people – to produce the document.
“This landmark study really highlights two big principles: violence is always preventable and violence is never justifiable,” she said, noting that these messages were also reiterated in the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.
Efforts falling short
The Special Representative said the past two decades have brought legal and policy reforms, but also “many difficulties to effectively ensure their implementation and to make services accessible to children and their caregivers”.
She pointed to “lessons learned”, such as the importance of having strong political commitment that translates into services that uphold child protection and well-being, with a dedicated budget.
She also hailed the increasing participation of children and youth at all levels, as well as stronger integrated services in all regions.
“But the problem is that it is not put at scale, that we are not going fast,” she said. “The problem is our solutions are always lagging behind the risks.”
‘Children are not waiting’
Twenty years after the first UN General Assembly report on child violence, success in combating it still depends on effective multilateralism, Ms. M’jid said, specifically, how can children again unite the world to ensure their protection and well-being.
She announced that 55 countries have joined the Pathfinding Global Alliance on Ending Violence against Children, “and more are coming”.
Launched in 2024, the State-led platform aims to support countries in translating political commitments into concrete actions through measures such as peer learning, strengthening co-operation, and sharing practices.
Ms. M’jid concluded her remarks by stressing that children and young people are part of the solution to ending the violence they suffer.
“Children are not waiting,” she said. “Children are already taking action.”

Disasters cost $228 billion in housing losses every year
$228 billion is a staggering amount of money to find, but that’s exactly what communities around the world are faced with every year, to rebuild housing after disaster strikes.
Highlighting the need for greater investment in stronger homes and better preparedness, UN Secretary-General António Guterres said that millions of homes are damaged or destroyed annually “displacing families and deepening poverty”.
Marking the International Day for Disaster Risk Reduction, the UN chief stressed that “as climate and disaster risks multiply, building safer dwellings is the shared responsibility of governments, developers, engineers and communities”.
Echoing that message, the UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction – UNDRR – noted that damage to housing alone accounts for 43 per cent of the direct cost of cyclones, floods, tsunamis and earthquakes.
Difference between life and loss
Spokesperson Jeanette Elsworth stressed that reducing the impacts of disaster depended on building resilient homes and households that had prepared for the worst.
“Among those people who had received an advance warning during a disaster, only 27 per cent of those who had neither a household disaster plan nor confidence in their ability to protect themselves…were able to act on that warning,” she said, citing data from the Lloyd’s Register Foundation World Risk Poll 2026.
“By contrast, 83 per cent of those who had both a plan and confidence in their ability to respond were able to take action.”
Ms. Elsworth noted that progress in reducing disaster deaths over the last 11 years has not been matched by reductions in their economic impact.
All households should have access to risk information, early warning alerts and the resources they need to protect themselves, she maintained, in a call to put housing resilience at the centre of disaster risk reduction efforts.
Safer and stronger
Governments, the private sector and community authorities could do this by “building in safer locations, enforcing resilient building standards, retrofitting existing homes and empowering households with the knowledge and tools they need to prepare for disasters”, she continued.
The UN International Organization for Migration (IOM) helped 1.4 million people in 2025 across 39 countries with disaster risk reduction programmes, supporting nearly 1,200 communities.
Maria Moita, Director, Department of Humanitarian Response and Recovery at IOM, said that for many people, the end of a disaster is “only the beginning of a much longer struggle to return home, restore livelihoods and rebuild their lives”.
The agency also helped extend early warning coverage to more than 1.2 million people.
Lessons in recovery
Recent emergencies in Nepal, Venezuela and Colombia have demonstrated how planning for disaster and data gathering can have a significant bearing on recovery.
In Nepal, where devastating flooding caused by a glacier collapsing in August affected more than 84,000 people and damaged approximately 7,500 homes, IOM assessments across 48 displacement sites identified 3,650 displaced people and 28 sites still operational.
In Venezuela, following the June earthquakes, the agency assisted 50,600 people, providing temporary accommodation, essential supplies, health care and protection.
Surveys indicated that more than half of affected households identified housing repairs as a priority. “The lesson was clear: recovery planning had to begin early, before temporary displacement became prolonged,” Ms. Moita stressed.
In Colombia, an earthquake in August reportedly affected nearly 500,000 people and damaged more than 200,000 homes, leaving an estimated 20,000 families displaced in Cali.
“Rebuilding homes alone is not enough, communities also need functioning services and opportunities to rebuild their lives,” the IOM official noted.
“We need sustained investment in early warnings, local preparedness, safer housing, and recovery efforts that begin from the outset and build resilience. Disasters may strike suddenly. Displacement can last much longer,” Ms. Moita said.

800 million young people face a future without jobs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

800 million young people face a future without jobs
Approximately 800 million young people entering the labour market in developing economies over the coming years will not find jobs unless countries act, the head of the UN Development Programme (UNDP) warned on Tuesday, as the agency launched two initiatives to boost investment and employment.
“If you look at the next 15 years, there will be 1.2 billion young people graduating from school, going into the labour market,” UNDP Administrator Alexander De Croo told a press briefing in New York from Bangkok, where he is attending the World Bank Group-International Monetary Fund (IMF) Annual Meetings.
“Unfortunately, for only 400 million of these, there will be jobs. For 800 million of these, there will not be jobs.”
Mr. De Croo said the gap was driven by demographics – in many developing countries, the median age is between 18 and 25 – and that the job projections were based on the current state of technology.
“That is not going to go by itself. This is the result of policy,” he said.
From investment to jobs
Of the two initiatives, the Investment Accelerator will help governments improve investment policies and legal frameworks, build pipelines of investment-ready projects and move them from preparation to implementation.
The Jobs for Prosperity Facility will help countries identify sectors with strong job-creation potential, align skills with what employers need and tackle barriers to business investment and hiring.
Asked whether artificial intelligence (AI) was a factor, Mr. De Croo said the projections could change through active labour policies, noting that sectors such as care, agriculture and tourism would still create many jobs even as AI accelerates.
“Job creation is actually the only real sustainable way for people to grow out of poverty,” he said.
Both initiatives are backed by expanded partnerships with the World Bank Group, the European Investment Bank and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, with pilot initiatives already underway in Nepal, Yemen, Haiti, Lebanon and Ghana.
A ‘triple shock’
The launch comes as many developing countries face what Mr. De Croo called a “triple shock”: high energy costs, one of the most pronounced El Niño events since 1950, and very high borrowing costs.
According to a new UNDP report, No Time to Recover, the median developing country now spends 9.5 per cent of total government income on interest payments alone.
For the first time since 2010, the number of people living in multidimensional poverty – which measures not only income but also access to electricity, water, health care and education – has risen.
“Those numbers should absolutely be a wake-up call to all of us,” Mr. De Croo said.
While the global economy has proved more resilient than expected, that resilience is not shared equally, he added.
“Some countries have still quite strong economic fundamentals. Others do not have the fundamentals to withstand further shocks.”

World News in Brief: West African migrant crossings, Argentina takes UK to maritime tribunal, farming in Gaza, mental health update
Fewer people from West Africa are reaching Europe by sea, but the journey has not become safer, the UN migration agency (IOM) said on Tuesday.
Arrivals from Mali, Senegal, Guinea and The Gambia fell by 59 per cent in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period last year, to 4,566 people.
But the drivers of migration persist. West Africans made up a growing share of arrivals on the Mediterranean routes, accounting for 21.9 per cent on the Western route, up from 15.6 per cent, pointing to a shifting landscape.
Longer journeys, same dangers
On the Atlantic route to the Canary Islands, arrivals fell 62 per cent between 2024 and 2025, yet recorded deaths and disappearances barely changed – 1,172 compared with 1,215.
Tighter controls in Morocco, Mauritania and Senegal are pushing departures south, adding up to 750 kilometres to crossings of around 2,200 km.
“No single country can solve this alone,” said IOM Director General Amy Pope. “We need to protect migrants wherever they are.”
Argentina asks maritime tribunal to halt Falklands oil project
Argentina has asked the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS) to order the United Kingdom to halt an offshore oil project near the Falkland Islands (Malvinas), the Hamburg-based court said on Tuesday.
Buenos Aires wants the Sea Lion development in the North Malvinas Basin stopped while an arbitration case launched by Argentina on 28 September is under way.
It also wants London to refrain from steps that could aggravate the dispute, such as granting new permits.
A hearing date will be announced shortly.
Long-running dispute
The UN lists the Falkland Islands (Malvinas) as a non-self-governing territory and has long urged both sides to negotiate.
Britain has administered them since 1833; Argentina claims sovereignty and the two countries went to war over the islands in 1982. Buenos Aires seeks to resume bilateral negotiations over the islands.
London says the islanders have the right to determine their own future and no discussion over sovereignty can occur without their consent.
Tensions have risen in recent weeks, after President Javier Milei gave London a two-week ultimatum over the project, announcing tougher measures against any companies involved in oil and gas exploration around the islands.
Gaza: increasing dangers confronting war-torn enclave’s farmers
Farmers in Gaza are facing increasing risks as they try to return to their fields.
In an update on Tuesday, the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), warned that the so-called Yellow Line of demarcation controlled by the Israeli military continues to expand into western Gaza.
This has increasingly limited access to agricultural land and prevented farmers from planting new crops.
‘Farming is my life’
FAO highlighted the case of 39-year-old grower Maryam, who described her small vegetable farm as a “lifeline” for her family of eight in southern Gaza.
Maryam is one of 1,700 farmers supported by FAO to purchase seeds, water and the other inputs they need to grow crops. The agency also helps herders and fishing families in Gaza
In her first season, Maryam harvested approximately three tonnes of okra.
“Farming is my life and my family’s life. It is the income source I depend on. Being able to farm again means that I am alive and that I can live with dignity with my family,” she told FAO.
WHO supports call for mental health care in the community
There’s a new call from the UN World Health Organization (WHO) to reform mental health services by developing community-based models.
According to WHO, about half of all those living in psychiatric hospitals and other institutions around the world had no choice when they were admitted.
This is despite the fact that people living with mental health conditions “can flourish in their communities when given the right support”, the agency insisted.
Mark van Ommeren, Head of WHO’s Mental Health and Substance Use Unit, said large numbers in need of services “are forced to live beyond closed doors. About half were brought in against their will, stripped of basic daily choices like what to wear, when to eat and cut off from the outside world.”
Pioneering Sri Lanka
Who said on Tuesday that many countries still rely heavily on psychiatric institutions and that across the world, nearly half of all public mental health funding is spent on maintaining them.
This leaves millions of people unable to get the care they need in general hospitals or in the community.
The WHO applauded Sri Lanka for replacing its isolated mental health institutions with community-based services.
Today, the country delivers care through inpatient and outpatient units in hospitals, clinics and rehabilitation units.
“When care is characterized by coercion, rigid control, or social isolation, it risks becoming a form of confinement rather than care,” WHO stressed.

‘Need for UN has never been greater,’ UN chief says, proposing slimmer $3.3 billion budget for 2027
Key points
- The proposed 2027 programme budget is 1.2 per cent below the 2026 approved level
- UN80 Initiative reforms will continue, with more cuts, staff relocations and the abolition or downgrading of some posts
- Predictable cashflow and timely payment of dues are essential as efficiency gains will not be sufficient to resolve the liquidity crisis
Divisions deepening
“The challenges before us are profound,” Mr. Guterres told the General Assembly’s Fifth Committee, comprising all 193 UN Member States that handle administrative and budgetary matters at UN Headquarters in New York.
“Geopolitical divisions continue to deepen, conflicts persist across regions and humanitarian needs are soaring, international law is trampled, climate disruption is hitting every continent and artificial intelligence is reshaping economies and societies,” said the Secretary-General.
Moreover, the planet’s collective Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), aimed at leaving no one behind, “are slipping further from reach”, Mr. Guterres said.
“And yet, in this era of uncertainty and fragmentation, the need for the United Nations has never been greater,” he declared.
Read the full statement here.
UN80 reforms: From proposal to practice
Reminding the committee that more than a year has passed since the UN80 Initiative was launched, the UN chief said “with your support, we set in motion far-reaching changes guided by a clear objective: to make the Secretariat more efficient, more effective, and better equipped to serve in a rapidly changing world.”
Taking stock of UN80 achievements, he said the Secretariat had already “moved from proposals to implementation”:
- The number of underrepresented Member States fell from 28 to 26 between August 2024 and August 2026
- Gender parity has been reached among internationally recruited staff
- Payroll operations have been consolidated
- Phase one of common administrative platforms had launched in New York and Bangkok
- Some functions have moved to lower-cost duty stations
- The UN Secretariat has absorbed a reduction of 3,116 regular budget posts
Through a voluntary early separation programme and reassignments, he said the impact on staff was “much smaller than what could be imagined” because planning began a year and a half in advance in the anticipated shortfalls.
Watch the Secretary-General’s introduction of the proposed 2027 budget:
Next phase
For 2027, the Secretary-General proposed additional post relocations across 12 entities, with the largest going to the Kenyan capital, Nairobi.

At the same time, he pointed out that the proposed budget incorporates standard-cost adjustments from the outset for the first time, so there will be no separate recosting later in the year.
Liquidity warning
However, the Secretary-General stressed that “efficiency alone cannot compensate for an unstable financial foundation”.
“Member States must fulfil their financial obligations in full and on time, as required by the UN Charter,” he said.
The Secretary-General also stressed that the world body needs predictable financing and timely payments of national dues to implement the mandates the Member States themselves have approved.
“Taken together, these measures will help address the liquidity challenges of the Organization and support the effective implementation of mandates,” he said.

Yemen: Houthi siege, cholera outbreak and aid cuts put civilians in the crosshairs
Yemen’s southwestern city of Taiz is facing a “devastating” humanitarian crisis as escalating tensions are dramatically driving up food prices and causing shortages of supplies, the UN Spokesperson said on Tuesday.
Taiz, Yemen’s third largest city, has been a major battleground between the Iran-backed Houthis and the internationally recognised Saudi-backed Yemeni government since the start of the war in 2014.
The Houthis have besieged the city since 2015 but tightened their blockade at the start of this month when they took control of the last main road between Taiz and other government-held areas.
The development is part of a broader offensive the Houthis launched in early September to seize key territory along Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast.
Supplies plummet, prices rocket
Current wheat and flour supplies in Taiz could run out in less than three weeks, while food prices have reportedly risen about 50 per cent and cooking gas has become largely unavailable, the UN warns.
Petrol prices have also tripled and fuel shortages are putting water supply and health services at risk.
“We continue to urge [the parties] to…uphold their obligations under international humanitarian law and to refrain from direct attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure and take constant care to spare both civilians and the infrastructure they use,” The UN’s Stéphane Dujarric stressed on Tuesday.
Disease outbreaks
At the same time, across the country, escalating conflict and mass displacement have disrupted health services and pushed people into overcrowded shelters with inadequate access to safe water.
As a consequence, Yemen is seeing a surge in cholera – an acute and potentially fatal intestinal infection, which mostly spreads through water or food contaminated by human faeces.
The country has reported 8,034 suspected cholera cases and 27 deaths this year, with a quarter of them occurring in the last four weeks.
Since August, 200,000 people have been displaced, which the UN’s health organization WHO notes coincides with a sharp increase in cholera transmission.
Children also face serious risks from measles, with more than 22,800 suspected cases and 128 deaths reported this year.
Vaccination coverage, at an estimated 45 per cent for each of the two recommended doses, is critically low in Yemen, increasing the risk of outbreaks of vaccine-preventable diseases.
Health services under strain
Health facilities, which are already treating thousands of people injured in the fighting, are struggling to keep up with the growing disease burden.
Approximately 500 health facilities across nine affected governorates lack partner support, the WHO found.
The agency is working with the Yemeni government to strengthen surveillance, testing and treatment, but its 90-day emergency response is critically underfunded. It needs $31 million and has received just $4.3 million, less than 14 per cent of the total.
“Without urgent funding and unimpeded access to safe water, vaccination and essential health services, outbreaks could spread rapidly among already vulnerable communities,” said WHO official Dr Annette Heinzelmann.

How protests have shaped India: From anti-Hindi agitation to farm laws
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:57:51 UTC
20:57:51 KST

How protests have shaped India: From anti-Hindi agitation to farm laws
Activists challenging India’s government over electoral roll controversies have a long legacy of protest to draw on.
New Delhi, India – Central parts of the Indian capital have been flooded in recent days with thousands of armed personnel, chasing down young protesters demanding the resignation of the country’s chief election commissioner (CEC) and struggling to secure a place to stage a sit-in in New Delhi.
Since last week, several student organisations and a wide spectrum of opposition parties have been engaged in a tactical tug-of-war, with tens of thousands turning up on Monday, far outnumbering police personnel.
Protesters are demanding sweeping reforms and the resignation of CEC Gyanesh Kumar after revelations of election irregularities. The agitation marks the latest challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s grip on power, after his education minister was forced out by the same group of demonstrators less than three months ago.
The Modi government has tried to portray protesters as representing antinational interests, working to slow down India’s growth or even to enable its breakup.
But India, the world’s most populous country, has had a long history of street protests, from its freedom struggle against the British Empire to waves of movements during the 79 years of the Indian republic that have shaped its modern identity.
“Time and again the government [of the day] has opposed these protests, [and] at times engaged with them critically,” Rasheed Kidwai, a political analyst in New Delhi and former journalist, told Al Jazeera. “But protests have run centrally through India’s story all along.”
Here is a look at major street protests in India and how they often forced powerful governments and leaders to yield.
Anti-Hindi agitations (1965)
India’s newly-formed constitution envisaged Hindi replacing English as the central government’s official language after a 15-year transition, ending on January 26, 1965. Many people in southern India, particularly Tamil speakers in the then Madras state (now Tamil Nadu), feared that this would sideline them in government employment, civil service examinations and dealings with the central administration.
For the federal government of a vast and diverse country, the idea of one common official language of communication was attractive as a tool of unification. But for many of the ancient societies that had agreed to come together under the Indian Union, this led to fears of cultural domination by the Hindi-speaking north of the country.
Demonstrations by several student organisations, opposing the imposition of Hindi, broke out, often leading to clashes with the police.
The Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK), a regional political party advocating Tamil nationalism, led by CN Annadurai and M Karunanidhi, spearheaded the protests. In January 1965, Annadurai was arrested on the eve of an anti-Hindi agitation. Two young supporters immolated themselves, and Hindi books were burned.
Then-Prime Minister Lal Bahadur Shastri assured protesters that English would continue to be used alongside Hindi. The DMK won Tamil Nadu’s state election in 1967, ending the until-then dominant Congress party’s rule in the state.
It was one of the defining moments of Indian federalism and regional identity in a young nation. English has remained one of India’s two official languages — and the Congress party has never returned to power in Tamil Nadu on its own.
The JP Movement (mid-1970s)
The JP Movement — named after its socialist leader, Jayaprakash Narayan — began amid student protests against corruption, inflation and government mismanagement in the states of Gujarat and Bihar in 1973-74.
Soon, it evolved into a nationwide challenge to then-Prime Minister Indira Gandhi and her Congress government’s dominance over Indian politics. Students, civil society groups, trade unions and opposition parties subsequently joined the agitation.
Narayan famously called for “Sampoorn Kranti”, or “Total Revolution”, a slogan that still rings in India.
The movement set the stage for a national emergency, declared by Gandhi on June 25, 1975, suspending civil liberties and censoring the press. After the emergency ended, opposition parties united and defeated Congress in the 1977 general election, ending Gandhi’s uninterrupted reign and giving India its first non-Congress government.
The Total Revolution did not come to pass, as Narayan had envisioned, but the movement fundamentally altered opposition politics — showing no leader was beyond the electoral consequences of mass dissent. Many of the leaders who emerged from this movement went on to become state chief ministers and leading federal ministers.
Mandal Commission protests (early 1990s)
In August 1990, then-Prime Minister Vishwanath Pratap Singh announced that his government would implement recommendations of a panel that had been set up more than a decade earlier under a member of parliament, Bindeshwari Prasad Mandal. The Mandal Commission, as it was known, recommended that 27 percent of central government jobs be reserved for people from Other Backward Classes (OBCs), communities identified as socially and educationally disadvantaged.
The decision triggered nationwide protests against reservation by students of privileged castes, who feared losing out on their dominance over government jobs. At the time, OBCs only held a little over 12 percent of government jobs — though they represented 52 percent of the national population.
Supporters of reservations argued that concrete actions were needed to address entrenched caste discrimination and unequal access to opportunities.
More than 100 students tried to die by suicide by setting themselves alight, and more than 60 succeeded, during those protests.
In 1992, the Supreme Court upheld the 27 percent OBC reservation in central government employment, excluding the relatively financially better-off “creamy layer” within communities. The move marked one of the largest affirmative action initiatives in independent India.
Protests against liberalisation, globalisation (early 1990s)
Rather than a unified campaign, the protests arose from a series of labour protests and strikes against India’s economic reforms, launched in 1991 under then-Prime Minister PV Narasimha Rao and Finance Minister Manmohan Singh, who would go on to become prime minister in 2004.
The reforms reduced restrictions on private enterprise and opened more sectors to foreign investment. Trade unions feared that privatisation and easier business closures would cause job losses, weaken collective bargaining and erode workers’ protections.
Left-aligned political parties supported many of these protests. But the protests could not prevent the reform programme from proceeding.
Successive governments have continued to expand private sector participation, pursue disinvestment in state-owned enterprises, and modify labour regulations.
Anna Hazare’s anticorruption movement (2011)
The movement erupted amid public anger over major corruption scandals involving the Congress-led coalition government, including a controversy around licensing of the country’s 2G spectrum and allegations surrounding preparations for the 2010 Commonwealth Games, held in New Delhi.
Activists demanded a strong law with an independent anticorruption ombudsman empowered to investigate and punish corruption involving public officials.
Social activist Anna Hazare led the movement through hunger strikes, also featuring activists such as Arvind Kejriwal, Kiran Bedi and Prashant Bhushan. Its demonstrations attracted large crowds across the country.
Parliament passed a law in December 2013, establishing a statutory framework for an anticorruption watchdog. But more than a decade later, its impact is minimal.
The movement was divided over whether activists should enter electoral politics. Kejriwal broke away to establish the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) in 2012 and went on to become a two-time chief minister of Delhi state.
The legacy of the movement remains largely in the shadow of Kejriwal today, who is now in opposition after Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) won the Delhi state election last year.
Protests following the ‘Nirbhaya’ gang rape (2012)
On December 16, 2012, a 23-year-old paramedical student was gang-raped and brutally assaulted on a moving bus in New Delhi. She died on December 29 while receiving treatment. Victims of sexual assault cannot be named publicly under Indian law. So she was widely referred to as “Nirbhaya”, meaning fearless in Hindi.
The crime triggered mass demonstrations against sexual violence, unsafe public spaces, inadequate policing and the treatment of women in the country. Protesters demanded justice for the victim and fundamental changes to how authorities handled sexual assault cases.
Students, young people, women’s rights activists, and common residents mobilised in Delhi, including around India Gate and other key locations.
Four adult defendants were convicted and sentenced to death; their executions took place in 2020.
Parliament passed the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2013, broadening the legal recognition of sexual offences, criminalising offences including stalking and voyeurism, and strengthening penalties for several crimes.
Activists continue to argue that stronger laws alone cannot address entrenched misogyny and inadequate policing. And crimes against women, including sexual crimes, remain rampant across most parts of India, including the capital.
Anti-CAA protests (2019-20)
India’s Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA), passed in December 2019, offers an expedited path to Indian citizenship for Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi and Christian migrants from Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Pakistan who arrived before December 31, 2014. Muslims were excluded from this provision.
Critics argued that making religious identity a basis for preferential citizenship undermined India’s secular constitutional principles. Millions feared the law could work alongside a proposed National Register of Citizens (NRC) to place Muslims at greater risk of exclusion and possible expulsion from India.
The movement was decentralised. Students at Jamia Millia Islamia and Aligarh Muslim University led major demonstrations, while women-led sit-ins, especially at Shaheen Bagh in Delhi, became national symbols of resistance against Prime Minister Modi’s Hindu majoritarian politics.
In February 2020, large-scale mob violence primarily targeting Muslims broke out in northeastern Delhi. More than 50 people, mostly Muslims, were killed.
Meanwhile, the sit-in in Shaheen Bagh lasted 101 days before police cleared the site on March 24, 2020, soon after imposing the COVID-19 lockdown. Dozens of Muslim activists were arrested and charged under antiterrorism laws. Student leaders such as Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam remain in jail, six years on, with no trial.
The protests could not secure repeal of the law, but delayed its implementation. The government notified its implementation in March 2024, bringing the citizenship process into operation.
Farmers’ protests (2020-21)
In 2020, the Modi government introduced three agricultural laws intended to liberalise farm markets and facilitate direct sales to private buyers.
Many farmers, particularly in northern India, feared that the changes would weaken the government-regulated wholesale markets through which much of their produce was sold. They also worried that the reforms would undermine the minimum support price (MSP), a government-set price for certain crops.
Numerous farmer unions surrounded and shut down roads leading up to Delhi under the Samyukt Kisan Morcha, a coalition formed to coordinate the agitation. Thousands of farmers camped on Delhi’s outskirts for months.
More than 700 farmers died amid extreme weather, road accidents, suicides and clashes.
In November 2021, Modi announced that the government would repeal the laws.
It marked the first such moment when protesters had wrestled a significant concession from Modi, who built his political currency as a leader who does not compromise.
‘Cockroach’ protests (2026)
It was a dig at India’s Chief Justice Surya Kant’s remarks, equating the country’s unemployed youth with “cockroaches” and “parasites”, sparking fury in the backdrop of a decade of sliding in multiple democratic indices.
Student Abhijeet Dipke doubled down on the viral joke, creating a pressure group – the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) – and led protests against irregularities in the national medical school entrance examination. The newbie protesters of the CJP movement were held together by left student organisations, choking Parliament Street and the popular protest site Jantar Mantar in New Delhi.
The Gen Z protests eventually forced out the education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, in July 2026.
The CJP protesters have again come together, along with opposition parties, this time demanding CEC Kumar’s resignation.

Barrett to build Northrop’s 25mm smart grenade launcher
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:57:26 UTC
20:57:26 KST

- Northrop Grumman and Barrett Firearms signed a teaming agreement under which Barrett will build the 25 mm Precision Grenadier System launcher in Nashville.
- Barrett will also integrate the inductive setter that programs Northrop Grumman’s 25 mm airburst and proximity rounds.
Northrop Grumman has teamed up with Barrett Firearms to build the launcher for its Precision Grenadier System, a shoulder-fired 25 mm grenade launcher meant to let infantry squads hit enemies hiding behind cover and shoot down small drones, the companies announced on Oct. 12 at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington.
Under the agreement, Barrett will manufacture the weapon at its plant in Nashville, Tennessee, and integrate the inductive setter, the device that programs each round with the distance at which it should detonate before it leaves the barrel. Northrop Grumman will continue to lead development of the overall system and of its family of 25 mm ammunition, and says it is offering the weapon to both U.S. and international customers. The companies say pairing Northrop Grumman’s ammunition and military programs experience with Barrett’s commercial and military firearms production will let them move quickly from prototype to delivery for U.S. and allied forces.
The Precision Grenadier System is designed to give an infantry squad a precise way to reach targets in defilade, meaning enemy soldiers sheltering behind walls, trenches or terrain that direct rifle fire cannot hit, as well as to fight at close quarters and engage small drones. Northrop Grumman’s 25 mm ammunition family includes a high-explosive airburst round that detonates above or beside a target at a programmed distance, a proximity round that senses a nearby drone and explodes without needing to be programmed, a close-quarters battle round, and a training round ballistically matched to the combat rounds. The weapon feeds from detachable box magazines.
The design builds on Northrop Grumman’s experience with the XM25, a 25 mm airburst weapon the company inherited through its 2018 purchase of Orbital ATK, which U.S. Army units tested in combat in Afghanistan before the program ended in 2018. The U.S. Army launched its Precision Grenadier System effort to replace the M203 and M320 40 mm grenade launchers carried by infantry squads today with a semi-automatic, magazine-fed weapon that combines the launcher, smart ammunition and a digital fire-control sight.
Several teams are working on solutions for the U.S. Army requirement in calibers from 25 mm to 40 mm. Barrett and MARS Inc. won the Army’s xTech Soldier Lethality competition in May 2025 with a 30 mm grenade rifle, and FN America has continued testing its MTL-30 launcher under a separate Army prototype award. Northrop Grumman earlier developed its 25 mm launcher with Colt before selecting Barrett to manufacture the weapon.
The U.S. Army plans to turn the Precision Grenadier System into a formal acquisition program and award a prototype agreement, and Northrop Grumman says it is continuing prototyping and ammunition development with Barrett to meet that requirement and interest from international buyers.

SpaceX launches resupply mission to International Space Station
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:54:17 UTC
20:54:17 KST

Yasin Gungor
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
US aerospace company SpaceX launched its 35th commercial resupply mission to the International Space Station (ISS) on Tuesday morning, sending scientific research, critical hardware and operational cargo into orbit.
Loaded with more than 6,300 pounds (2,860 kilograms) of supplies, the SpaceX Dragon spacecraft launched aboard a Falcon 9 rocket from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida.
The rocket lifted off at 6.34 am local time (1034GMT), marking the fourth orbital trip for the Dragon cargo vehicle and the eighth flight for the first-stage booster.
 
Solar arrays, medical research
The cargo manifest includes the final pair of roll-out solar arrays designed to expand power capacity for station operations, upcoming research and eventual controlled deorbit procedures. Astronauts will install the units during spacewalks planned for late autumn.
The Dragon is carrying experiments to manufacture artificial retinas in microgravity to support vision restoration on Earth, alongside three-dimensional heart tissue models and brain organoids aimed at evaluating potential therapies for neurodegenerative conditions, including Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s diseases.
The spacecraft is expected to complete an autonomous docking with the station’s Harmony module around 11 am local time (1500GMT) on Thursday.
The resupply mission comes as the International Space Station prepares for its final phase of operations, with the orbiting facility scheduled to conclude its orbital duties at the end of 2030.

In India, a Dark Shadow Falls on Its Vaunted Elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:45:00 UTC
20:45:00 KST

On Saturday, New Delhi, the Indian capital, was under siege. The Indian government deployed more than 20,000 police and paramilitary personnel, barricaded the city center, and suspended internet access. By evening, more than 7,000 people were detained by the police, including leaders from India’s opposition parties, lawyers, and journalists. Despite the crackdown, thousands turned out in Delhi on Monday to protest with even greater vigor.
The repressive effort sought to deter a planned protest at Jantar Mantar, a traditional protest site in New Delhi. The protest centered on two core demands: the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner and the rollback of a nationwide process known as Special Intensive Revision (SIR).
The chief election commissioner heads the national electoral body and is appointed on the recommendation of a committee headed by the prime minister. The SIR ostensibly seeks to clean up and update the electoral rolls but has removed 130 million Indians from the rolls—more than half the number of Americans eligible to vote in the midterm elections.
The troubles truly began in the summer of 2025. Several Indian states were about to hold elections for their state legislatures. Ahead of those elections, the Election Commission announced an electoral revision in those states, citing the need to “clean up” electoral rolls. Numerous voters would be required to prove that they were citizens and entitled to be on the rolls by producing one or more documents from a select list. Election Commission officials would scrutinize the documents and either accept or reject them.
Judicial avoidance
Civil society groups and political activists promptly challenged the proposed electoral revisions before the Supreme Court of India in June 2025. They questioned the power of the Election Commission to undertake electoral revisions at such a scale. India’s election law does authorize the commission to undertake a revision of electoral rolls in specific electoral constituencies, provided it records its reasons in writing. The petitioners argued that it does not grant the Election Commission overarching power to require voters already on the rolls to prove their eligibility afresh.
The petitioners also argued that Election Commission’s list of acceptable documents was exclusionary and would result in large scale disenfranchisement. In India, access to documents issued by the government depends heavily on caste, class and gender. Many people simply lack necessary documents or the ability to navigate the bureaucracy to obtain them.
For months, the Supreme Court did not rule on the legality of electoral revisions on such a vast scale, allowing the exercise to become a fait accompli. Instead, it engaged in prolonged courtroom negotiations with the Election Commission over which documents Indian voters would have to provide to remain on the electoral rolls. There was an extended debate on whether Aadhaar, India’s national digital identity document, would be accepted.
But even as the legal debates continued, exclusions from electoral rolls mounted. In the eastern Indian state of West Bengal, where Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) had never won a state election, nine million people—around 12% percent of the electorate—found themselves excluded from the rolls.
Faced with these exclusions, and still unwilling to rule on the legality of the SIR, the Supreme Court took the extraordinary step of creating an entire administrative machinery: tribunals staffed by judicial officers to hear appeals from excluded voters. When the petitioners warned that these tribunals would take years, if not decades, to resolve all the appeals, the Supreme Court judges effectively said that it was fine for excluded people to note vote in the upcoming election as long as they would eventually be put back on the rolls.
The West Bengal election went ahead using the new electoral rolls and the BJP won. One indication of how flawed the SIR may have been was that around 90% of the voters in West Bengal, whose appeals were decided, were eventually restored to the rolls. Nine out of every ten excluded voters had been wrongfully removed. Yet even as exclusions numbered in the millions in each state, the Supreme Court noted that the data did not indicate “systemic disenfranchisement.”
Unchecked bureaucrats
Eventually, when the Supreme Court finally issued its judgment in the summer of 2026, it upheld the entire exercise. It affirmed the wide powers of the Election Commission to conduct the electoral revisions as it saw fit.
A central argument against the exercise was that by requiring every elector, including those already on the electoral rolls, to prove their eligibility afresh, the Election Commission was treating each individual as presumptively ineligible to vote. This was a grossly disproportionate exercise of power, particularly because more proportionate methods were available to the election commission.
The court rejected this argument too and, I believe, effectively immunized the commission from the requirement to act in a proportionate manner. As the legal scholar Vasudev Devadasan noted, the judgement had the effect of creating a "permanent class" of disenfranchised persons who simply cannot participate in political life.
The consequences soon became apparent: the new BJP government in West Bengal threatened, on more than one occasion, to cut off welfare benefits for people excluded from the electoral rolls through the SIR. Although the Supreme Court noted that the SIR was not meant to determine citizenship, by the summer of 2026, that distinction was becoming difficult to sustain.
Beyond the threat to people’s welfare entitlements, there were widely reported cases of passport renewals being denied because applicants had been excluded from the electoral rolls through the SIR.
In 2020, the Indian government’s attempts to create a National Register of Citizens (NRC) had been widely criticized because of how it would force every individual to prove their citizenship to state authorities, and lead to widespread exclusion. After widespread protests across the country against it, the NRC was shelved. The SIR now appeared to be a way of introducing the NRC through the backdoor.
As the SIR proceeded across multiple states—with large-scale exclusions in each—patterns began to emerge: disproportionate exclusions among vulnerable and marginalized people and of religious minorities, especially Muslims; and the use of algorithms to exclude even voters who possessed the required documents, citing "logical discrepancies" such an arbitrary age gap between parent and child, judged by arbitrary criteria that varied from state to state.
Other disturbing facts also came to light. In certain neighborhoods, people had submitted pre-filled forms in bulk, seeking to have Muslims removed from off the electoral rolls by questioning their citizenship. India’s electoral law allows third parties to object to anyone’s inclusion on the electoral rolls.
In Delhi, the omission of some prominent people from the rolls provoked public outrage. The Election Commission then introduced a “VIP portal” through which their names could be restored, creating a two-tier system of class privilege.
A tenacious reporter
Against this backdrop, an investigative report by Ritika Chopra, a journalist with the Indian Express newspaper in the last week of September, landed like a bombshell. Her report showed that although the Election Commission’s decisions were supposed to be taken by consensus among its three commissioners, the chief election commissioner had been taking them unilaterally, often over the objections of, and sometimes without involving, the other commissioners. (The Election Commission responded by describing differing “views and observations” as part of “deliberation in any institution.”)
More reports followed, documenting more unilateral decisions, opaque algorithms built by private corporations, and the increasing centralization of authority within the Election Commission to add or remove voters. It was a clear departure from India’s decentralized electoral system, which is designed to guard against decisions made in bad faith.
These reports crystallized latent anger, particularly against the chief election commissioner. Under Indian electoral law, election commissioners are appointed by a committee in which the political executive holds a two-to-one majority; they are, in effect, executive appointments. The Supreme Court’s 2023 attempt to reform this system was bypassed by subsequent legislation. The court then left a challenge to that legislation on the back burner. All of this explains why the chief election commissioner became the primary focus of public anger.
The story of the SIR is both an account of large-scale voter disenfranchisement in India and one of institutional crisis. Two failures converged: the failure to entrench the Election Commission’s independence in law and in the Constitution, and the failure of the Supreme Court to intervene despite evidence of disenfranchisement placed before it. Together they culminated in the furious popular protests in Delhi and the Indian government’s crackdown.
It is difficult to see how this story ends. The right to vote is hard won and its loss keenly felt. History shows that once people lose confidence in the institutions meant to protect that right, restoring their trust is exceedingly difficult. A long shadow hangs over electoral integrity in India. Lifting it will require urgent, systemic reforms. Whether those reforms will come remains uncertain.

Iran shakes with 67 earthquakes in a week
TEHRAN – A total of 67 earthquakes have been recorded across the country in a week from October 2 to 9, according to the seismological networks of the Institute of Geophysics of the University of Tehran.
Statistically, 64 earthquakes with magnitudes smaller than 3, three earthquakes with a magnitude between 3 and 4, and no earthquake with a magnitude above 4 have occurred in the country, irsc reported.
Of the total quakes, two had a magnitude of 3.6 on the Richter scale, the first occurred on October 4 in West Azarbajian, and the other one hit Semnan province on October 6.
Among the provinces of the country, Khorasan Razavi experienced the highest number of earthquakes with 12, followed by Yazd with 8, and South Khorasan with 7 earthquakes.
During the same period, one earthquake hit Tehran. No earthquakes were recorded in Ardabil, Alborz, Ilam, Bushehr, Chahrmahal-Bakhtiari, Zanjan, Sistan-Baluchestan, Qom, Qazvin, Kordestan, Gilan, Markazi, Hormozgan, and Hamedan provinces.
A total of 2,380 earthquakes with a magnitude of more than 2.5 on the Richter scale were recorded across the country over the past calendar year (March 2025–March 2026), according to the Seismological networks of the Institute of Geophysics of the University of Tehran, Mehr news agency reported.
Out of recorded earthquakes, 910 had a magnitude greater than 3, 130 had a magnitude greater than 4, and 15 had a magnitude greater than 5 on the Richter scale.
 
The Iranian plateau is located in a very seismically active region of the world and is known not only for its major catastrophic earthquakes but also for the disasters relating to natural hazards, especially earthquakes.
About 2 percent of the earthquakes in the world occur in Iran, but more than 6 percent of the victims of the world’s earthquakes during the 20th century are reported from Iranian earthquakes.

For his part, Moradkhani highlighted technology transfer and specialized training as the key pillars of the two countries’ collaborations, and called for the Vice Presidency for Science and Technology to play an active role in Iran-Africa joint commissions.
He also underscored the importance of establishing a network of experts and strengthening exchanges in the oil and energy sectors.
The official added that a draft memorandum of understanding (MoU) had been finalized and was expected to be signed during a visit to Tehran by senior Senegalese officials in January 2027.
Tehran hosts meeting of African envoys to boost science, health cooperation
On December 7, 2025, Iranian officials and the ambassadors of 19 African countries to Tehran discussed ways to enhance cooperation in the fields of science, education, research, and health.
Addressing the meeting, held in Tehran, Nader Tavakoli, the Chancellor of Iran University of Medical Sciences, said despite coercive sanctions, the country has managed to make great strides in the health sector, from education and treatment to technology and production of medicines, relying on committed and creative human resources, IRNA reported.
“Now, we are ready to share these achievements with Africans through establishing a strategic health alliance between Iran and African countries,” Tavakoli highlighted.
Elaborating on the core areas of the strategic alliance, he said that researchers will focus on addressing real-time illnesses, such as tropical and endemic diseases, drug shortages, and health service delivery in rural areas.
Admitting African students and developing joint educational courses, with dual accreditation, as well as dispatching professors for training of trainers, will be another part of the alliance.
Other main components of the strategic alliance will include sharing technical knowledge in fields such as manufacturing vaccines, biosimilar drugs, and medical equipment by establishing a collaborative production line in African countries, Tavakoli added.
The expansion of scientific interactions between Iranian and African scientists was the last point mentioned by the official. The strategic alliance will lay the basis for boosting scientific collaborations between over 60 universities and hundreds of top research centers across the country, he further noted.
On December 8, the ministries of health and foreign affairs, in a virtual meeting with Iranian ambassadors and attachés in Africa, discussed the potential for promoting cooperation with African countries in the health sector.
During the meeting, Alireza Biglari, the deputy health minister for international affairs, highlighted the country’s capabilities in areas related to health. Referring to the existing capacity as a valuable opportunity for the expansion of health diplomacy and the favorable condition for cooperation with African countries, the official announced the readiness of the health ministry to implement decisions and operational plans, IRNA reported.
For his part, Akbar Khosravi Nejad, Assistant to Iran’s Foreign Minister and Director General for Africa, underlined the importance of Africa in Iran’s foreign policy, and said that the country’s health system is one of the main sectors for enhancing collaborations with these countries.
Tavakoli, for his part, presented an account of the current activities and programs of the university in Africa, as well as future plans to meet African ambassadors in Tehran.

Iraqi students taking Persian Language Proficiency Test more than triple
TEHRAN – A total of 268 Iraqi students have taken the Persian Language Proficiency Test at six centers across Iraq, marking a more than threefold increase from the 78 participants recorded last year.
The test was organized with the support of Iran’s scientific counselor in Iraq and administered in Baghdad, Najaf, Wasit, Karbala, Basra, and Erbil.
Proficiency in Persian helps international students communicate more effectively with professors and classmates, pursue their studies at Iranian universities, and access academic resources in the language. These capabilities can also contribute to strengthening educational and academic ties between Iran and Iraq.
 
The Persian Language Proficiency Test is held three times a year both in Iran and in the countries that have Persian Language chairs, concurrently. The test has general and academic modules.
Apart from university students, foreign nationals who want to live, work, run businesses, and establish international offices in Iran, or study in Iranian schools are required to take the test.
On January 24, Abbas Qanbari-Baghestan, an official with the Organization of Student Affairs, said: “Attaining a specified score in learning the Persian language will be a key requirement for foreign students to be admitted to Iranian universities from the next academic year, which will start in fall 2026.” The test includes listening, speaking, and writing sections, he added.
Highlighting the importance of providing quality education for international students, the official said Persian language teaching centers play a key role in attracting foreign students and preparing them to major in universities. So, they should do their best to employ experienced professors to provide the best educational courses to help foreign students learn the Persian language.
Nearly 60,000 foreign students are currently studying in Iranian universities, compared with 35,000 students in the past Iranian academic year, which started on September 22, 2024.
Despite existing challenges, Iran has managed to attract students from 101 countries, Saeed Habiba, the head of the Organization of Student Affairs, said in October 2025.
The scientific capacity of the country’s universities and their positive record in international cooperation are a valuable opportunity that must be seized to transform the presence of foreign students into a national discourse and strategic planning, the official said, adding that the students are mainly from Afghanistan, India, Iraq, and Pakistan.
Attracting 320,000 intl. students by 2028 on agenda
According to the Seventh National Development Plan (2023-2028), the country is projected to increase the number of international students to 320,000 from currently around 60,000.
To this end, the higher education system needs to adopt some institutional and developmental approaches in organizations associated with foreign students, Mehr news agency reported.
In this regard, the parliament research center has evaluated Iran’s situation in attracting international students and measures that need to be taken into account.
According to the report, the number of foreign students in the country has grown from 13,767 in Iranian year 1394 (2015 – 2016) to 68,563 in 1403 (2024 -2025). The number of educational institutions that are allowed to accept foreign students has noticeably increased from 45 to 206 over the past decade.
The report also shows that 13 acts, such as providing short-time sabbaticals, granting visas, establishing a center for foreign student graduates, and holding remedial courses, have been developed and officially accepted by the parliament as part of educational charter for foreign students; however, they have not been implemented in time.
Also major organizations and institutions of the country have no participation in planning cultural programs for foreign students.
A lack of strategic comprehensive marketing skills, and bureaucratic and time-consuming correspondence were among other recognized problems.
The parliament research center has put forward some proposals to help attract more international students. The most important one highlights adopting an approach that focuses on generating income, soft cultural power, and expanding science.
The other suggestion emphasizes the importance of boosting south-south international relations, that is developing political and economic interactions with highly populated countries like Pakistan, India, Egypt and some countries in Central Asia.
Ongoing evaluation of other countries’ policies in attracting students, developing software and hardware infrastructures, stable and secure network, as well as increasing the number of scholarships are among other suggested solutions.
Before the US-Israeli war against Iran, nearly 60,000 foreign students from 101 countries, mainly from Afghanistan, India, Iraq, and Pakistan, were studying in Iran.
The Ministry of Science has announced that educational programs for foreign university students present in the country will continue despite the unfavorable conditions caused by the imposed war.
All universities have been asked to ensure that all international students benefit from the educational facilities and capacities of the universities by adopting innovative measures, including preparing offline educational packages, developing intensive summer training courses, and anticipating the possibility of completing practical courses in the coming years, in addition to continuing online education, IRNA reported.
These measures and plans should be implemented in a way that ensures that international students do not suffer academic, training, or even financial losses due to the conditions resulting from the imposed war.
Science Minister Hossein Simaei-Sarraf has said over 30 Iranian universities had been directly attacked by the United States and Israel since the war began in late February.
Five university professors and more than 60 students had been killed in the strikes, added Simaei-Sarraf, describing attacks on Iranian infrastructure as “crimes against humanity.”
“The main reason the enemy targeted this sensitive infrastructure was that they did not want us to gain access to this technology,” he said, adding that many Iranians abroad have contacted the university, offering to help fund its restoration.
