Visits to Ceuta
The appearance followed the pair’s visit Monday to Ceuta, the Spanish enclave bordering Morocco that has become a political flashpoint since mass migrant crossings in late July.
Bardella linked those arrivals to Spain’s regularization program and said a National Rally government would seek changes to the Schengen travel area so that migrants granted legal status or residence permits by one country could not travel freely to others.
Bardella also called for a tougher role for the EU border agency Frontex, including the ability to carry out migrant returns.
Abascal likewise argued that Spain’s migration decisions concerned the wider bloc. He said Bardella’s visit to Ceuta sent a message that Spain’s southern border was also the southern border of France and Europe.
The Vox leader also demanded migrant expulsions and a greater militarization of the border.
King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia are also due to visit Ceuta on Tuesday, their first official visit to the city since Felipe became king in 2014. Their itinerary includes a tribute to people who died at sea during the July crossings.
An estimated 80,000 people entered Ceuta from Morocco during the crisis, with at least 141 deaths, according to a European Parliament research briefing. Spanish authorities returned most of those who crossed within days, but thousands remain.
The crisis became a rallying point for the international far right, with Germany’s Alternative for Germany attacking Spain’s migration policies and US-based billionaire Elon Musk portraying the crossings as an “invasion.”

five prado masterpieces cross the atlantic for a free-roam virtual tour in brooklyn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:25:42 UTC
19:25:42 KST

five prado masterpieces cross the atlantic for a free-roam virtual tour in brooklyn
debuting at powerhouse arts, acciona cultura and the museo del prado transform classical masterpieces into a 30-minute free-roam VR tour, blending curatorial rigor with spatial storytelling.
[FEATURED]
PRADO MASTERPIECES ARRIVES AT POWERHOUSE ARTS
Making its US debut at Brooklyn’s Powerhouse Arts until December 20, 2026, Masterpieces: A Virtual Experience of the Museo del Prado transforms classical paintings into three-dimensional, navigable environments. Created by ACCIONA Cultura in exclusive collaboration with Madrid’s Museo Nacional del Prado, the 30-minute free-roam virtual reality installation invites visitors to step inside the canvas and explore classic art together. Driven by academic curatorship and faithful replication, the experience combines original storytelling, meticulous spatial design, and immersive soundscapes, turning passive viewing into an intimate, shared sensory journey.
ACCIONA CULTURA BRIDGES CURATORSHIP AND IMMERSIVE NARRATIVE
Marking its latest international iteration following presentations in Madrid, Buenos Aires, Tokyo, and Shanghai, the project expands ACCIONA Cultura’s portfolio of immersive spatial environments, which includes the Grand Egyptian Museum and New York’s Hip Hop Museum. Curated by Alejandro Vergara, Head of Conservation of Flemish Painting and Northern Schools at the Museo del Prado, the experience draws on original archives to balance historical accuracy with digital innovation. Transporting visitors inside the worlds of the paintings through an original narrative, Masterpieces offers audiences a new way to engage with their stories, symbolism, and detail.
REFRAMING THE SPECTATOR AS ACTIVE PARTICIPANT
Guided by the voice of a fictional security guard on his final night shift before retirement, visitors travel through an imaginary museum where the canvas opens into a multi-user digital environment. Because several of these masterpieces rarely travel or cannot leave Madrid, the physical-digital installation at Powerhouse Arts acts as a live architectural laboratory that redefines traditional art viewing. ACCIONA Cultura and the Prado address this shift by weaving five pivotal works, including Peter Paul Rubens and Jan Brueghel’s The Sense of Sight, Diego Velázquez’s Las Meninas, Paolo Veronese’s Venus and Adonis, Francisco de Goya’s Witches’ Sabbath, and Hieronymus Bosch’s The Garden of Earthly Delights, into a continuous, fluid spatial narrative.
Without presenting these historic canvases as silent relics isolated behind glass, thoughtful exhibition design dissolves cold museum distance to let the underlying stories breathe. Expanding allegorical cabinets, royal studios, classical myths, haunting shadows, and surreal worlds into interconnected 3D spaces builds an atmosphere of genuine wonder and personal discovery. Visitors no longer stand back in passive crowds, they move through the physical space together, engaging in an intimate dialogue with the art. Allowing audiences to feel the human behind the canvas shifts the traditional dynamic of viewing, reframing the spectator as an active co-creator within the spectacle.

curator: Alejandro Vergara

Yemen: Taiz faces humanitarian disaster as Houthis tighten siege
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:21:29 UTC
19:21:29 KST

Breadcrumb
Yemen's Taiz faces humanitarian disaster as Houthis tighten siege
Yemeni government forces are managing to stall the Houthi offensive on the besieged city of Taiz, analysts told The New Arab, as residents increasingly fear a repeat of previous sieges earlier in the war.
Ameneh Mehvar, Senior Analyst for the Middle East at ACLED, told The New Arab that, despite the recent encirclement by the Houthis and continued gains, "government forces, backed by Saudi airstrikes, appear to have stalled further significant Houthi advances in recent days."
Fighting around the city's suburbs and hills has continued in recent days, with Houthi attempts to advance along the western and southern approaches, including around al-Misrakh, where government-aligned fighters reportedly fended off a Houthi infiltration attempt, according to Yemeni analyst Muhammad al-Bashar.
However, the Houthis tightened their siege on Monday after closing all four exits from the government-held city, according to military sources cited by AFP.
A Yemeni government field officer said Houthi forces had established fire control over the exits and were shooting at vehicles attempting to pass through them.
The Houthis also attacked government positions defending the city's southern and western approaches, seizing new positions despite Saudi airstrikes.
Government-aligned forces lost 22 fighters in 24 hours of fighting, while the Houthis lost at least 40, according to AFP, citing military sources from both sides.
Mehvar noted, however, that the battle for the city highlights the limits of the government's recent offensive on the coast, which has been offset by the Houthis' stranglehold on Taiz.
"The Houthis do not need to capture Taiz outright to weaken government control, as prolonged isolation could erode the defenders' ability to sustain their positions while further deepening a humanitarian crisis."
The Houthi encirclement of Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city, was effectively completed after the group took the town of al-Turbah, severing the supply road to Aden, on 4 October.
It is not the first time the Houthis have occupied and encircled the city. The group previously captured Taiz in 2015 and laid siege to it until 2016, when government forces pushed them out, although the Houthis retained positions around the city.
Baraa Shiban, an Associate Fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), told The New Arab that the Houthis' strategy in Taiz is informed by their previous attempts to capture the city, with fighting now focused on its surrounding suburbs and hills.
"The Houthis had before tried to take control of the city itself, and then it proved to be very costly," he said, noting that urban fighting eventually forced the group out.
"What they did instead is that they then placed snipers and artillery on the hills overlooking the city, and that was what the situation [was like] when I was there. So, the bombing of the city was constant."
With urban fighting proving costly, Houthi advances have concentrated on the hills and peaks surrounding the city and the wider province, eventually leading to its encirclement.
“There's fighting literally from one hill to the other, from one road to the other,” he said, adding, “the fight is really concentrated on trying to take control of the main road, because if you control the main road, then you effectively are in control of the district."
Humanitarian crisis deepens as Taiz is cut off
The encirclement has triggered a worsening humanitarian crisis, with the Studies and Economic Media Center (SEMC), a Taiz-based civil society group, warning in a recent report that the city is "facing near-total isolation from food, medicine, and energy supplies."
SEMC said petrol stations had run out of fuel, while wheat and flour stocks were sufficient for just 19 days of consumption.
Saeed Saif, the UN Population Fund's (UNFPA) West Coast and Taiz Coordinator, told The New Arab that roads into the city had been completely cut off, with prices for basic commodities doubling and fuel prices tripling.
He warned of critical shortages of medical supplies, with only two of the eight UNFPA-supported health facilities inside the city still operational.
"High transportation costs prevent women, girls, and vulnerable populations, particularly pregnant women from accessing essential services," Saif said.
The deteriorating security situation has forced UNFPA to suspend some of its activities, leaving vulnerable residents with even fewer options for healthcare.
Saif, who returned to his hometown of Taiz in April after 25 years away, was himself forced to flee as fighting intensified.
He left the city on 13 September, travelling at night to al-Turbah along deserted roads and through military checkpoints.
During his six days there, he visited displacement sites just five kilometres from the front lines, where artillery shelling could be clearly heard.
On 18 September, following an emergency relief distribution, security warnings prompted him to evacuate again, this time with his family to Aden.
The journey took more than five hours through difficult terrain amid heavy rain and flash flood warnings, with the sound of bombardment along the way.
Saif said the experience was particularly distressing for his 13-year-old daughter and brought back memories of the family's evacuation from Sanaa during intense airstrikes in 2018.
"There is widespread fear and anxiety," he said, warning that a further wave of displacement could affect up to 100,000 households.
According to the UN's migration office, 57% of the more than 200,000 people displaced by the recent fighting across Yemen have come from Taiz province.
Yemen's Human Rights Ministry also warned on Monday that the tightening siege threatened to disrupt life-saving medical services, including emergency surgery, intensive care, dialysis and neonatal care.
In a statement carried by the official Saba news agency, the ministry held the Houthis responsible for blocking supply routes and called on the United Nations and international humanitarian organisations to intervene urgently to secure access to food, medicine and fuel.
Shiban said conditions in the city were reminiscent of earlier sieges during the war.
"There is a genuine fear, and that reflects itself on the prices of goods, food, and other main materials."
Can government forces break the siege?
Although Houthi advances have slowed, government forces lack the firepower needed to reverse the group's gains around Taiz.
Government troops and newly formed local resistance forces are largely equipped with unarmoured pick-up trucks and Kalashnikov rifles, while the Houthis possess drones, artillery and tanks.
Shiban said "the situation doesn't play in their favour."
He argued that the government's best chance of breaking the siege could depend on the success of its parallel offensive along Yemen's western coast.
"If their [government] operation on the West Coast succeeds, pushing from the Bab al-Mandab up and then to the Mokha port, then they can enter [the city] using the same road that the Houthis entered into Taiz districts," Shiban said.
Such an advance could allow government forces to bring heavier weaponry into the city and challenge the Houthi encirclement.
"Other than that, it's going to be difficult because now the city is encircled."

Riyadh has faced repeated Houthi attacks in recent days, with strikes on King Khalid International Airport over two days forcing the temporary suspension of operations.
Despite the attacks, the World Petroleum Congress opened Sunday in Riyadh with broad international participation. Saudi Arabia is hosting the event for the first time, with proceedings scheduled to conclude Thursday.

“Riyadh today is one of the cities whose transformation you can most clearly see as you travel along its roads: in transport activity, urban expansion and the growth of projects, through to its global presence as a capital for business, investment and decision-making,” he said.
Since 5th October, five Saudi airports have been targeted in 10 attacks carried out by the Houthi group, killing 20 people and injuring hundreds, according to an Anadolu tally. The attacks have also caused material damage and disrupted air traffic.

DNA recording system reveals how a single cell becomes a body
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:17:08 UTC
19:17:08 KST

DNA recording system reveals how a single cell becomes a body
Scientists have recorded how a single fertilized egg becomes a complex body, uncovering hidden patterns of development that could shed light on birth defects and cancer.
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- University of Washington School of Medicine/UW Medicine
- Summary:
- Scientists have traced the development of a mouse embryo from its first two cells to the formation of organs, using a remarkable DNA recording system that reveals the family history of individual cells. Their findings uncover how different cell types emerge on their own schedules and could help explain what goes wrong in birth defects, genetic disorders, and cancer.
- Share:
Scientists have reconstructed a remarkably detailed family tree of cells in a developing mouse embryo, tracing their origins back to the moment a fertilized egg first divided into two cells. Using an innovative DNA recording technology, the researchers followed how those early cells multiplied, developed specialized roles, and eventually helped form a body with distinct organs and tissues.
The recording covered the first 13.5 days of embryonic development, providing an unusually detailed look at how a complex mammalian body takes shape. (Full gestation in mice is 19 to 21 days.)
The findings, published on October 8, 2026, in the journal Science, could help scientists better understand normal development and what happens when that process goes wrong.
"We are interested in tracking how cells' early ancestry in an embryo influences their later fates. Exploring cell lineages helps decode normal development. Such research could eventually advance knowledge about congenital malformations, neurodevelopmental conditions, genetic disorders or cancer," said Dr. Jay Shendure, a professor of genome sciences at the University of Washington School of Medicine in Seattle and a Howard Hughes Medical Institute Investigator.
Shendure led the research alongside Dr. Chengxiang Qiu, a molecular and systems biologist at Dartmouth College in New Hampshire. Both served as senior authors of the study.
A DNA Typewriter Records the History of Living Cells
The achievement was made possible by a technology called DNA Typewriter, developed by Shendure and Junhong Choi, who is now at Sloan Kettering Cancer Center.
Rather than simply observing cells as they divide, the system allows scientists to preserve a record of their history directly within their DNA.
To accomplish this, the researchers inserted a redesigned recording sequence, which they call a tape, into the genome of a fertilized mouse egg. The updated design made it easier to recover the information stored in individual cells.
As the embryo developed, the DNA Typewriter remained embedded in the genetic material of its cells, recording their divisions in a way that could later be used to reconstruct their ancestry. The result was something like a biological logbook, documenting the sequence of events that gave rise to different cell populations.
"Think of it like an actual typewriter, except it types onto a cell's own DNA instead of paper," explained Haedong Kim, a co-first author of the study and a postdoctoral scientist in genome sciences at UW Medicine, the Seattle Hub for Synthetic Biology and the Howard Hughes Medical Institute. "Every time a cell divides, it strikes one new character onto the next blank line -- always in order, never overwriting what's already there. Because the characters are always filled in sequence, that sequence itself spells out the cell's division history."
Because these markings are passed down to daughter cells, researchers can examine the recorded sequences and identify which cells descended from a shared ancestor. Cells carrying matching portions of the record can be linked together, allowing scientists to reconstruct branches of the embryo's family tree.
"Writing the record is only half the problem. You also have to read it back out of each cell, so we redesigned the tape to make that easier," said Kim.
Overcoming a Major Challenge in Developmental Biology
Reconstructing the entire history of a developing mammal has long been a formidable challenge. As an embryo grows, its cells divide repeatedly and begin taking on specialized functions. Following those relationships becomes increasingly difficult as the number and variety of cells expand.
Scientists accomplished a similar feat decades ago in a tiny roundworm, but that animal has a relatively simple body with far fewer cells. Its transparency also makes development easier to study.
Mammals are considerably more complicated. Earlier technologies provided important insights into mouse embryonic development, but they generally captured only portions of the larger cellular family tree.
Some traditional recording techniques also have significant limitations. They work by cutting DNA to create identifying marks, which can damage cells and erase information left by earlier divisions. Their recording capacity is limited, and because the marks are not necessarily created in a fixed sequence, scientists must attempt to reconstruct the order of events afterward.
"DNA Typewriter avoids all of this," said Kim. "It writes without fully severing the DNA, keeps recording relatively steadily, and writes everything in strict order, so we can record cell lineages at much higher resolution for a longer time."
Tracing an Embryo Back to Its First Two Cells
The researchers began by attempting to record development in 100 fertilized mouse eggs. Of those, 10 embryos were ultimately available for examination.
One specimen, identified as Embryo No. 3, stood out because its DNA recording system had functioned particularly well and preserved the most extensive developmental history. The scientists therefore concentrated their detailed analysis on that embryo.
One of the most important discoveries came from a recording made at the very beginning of development, immediately after the fertilized egg divided for the first time.
"Our recording captured a clear, permanent mark distinguishing the two very first cells, letting us trace nearly every cell we profiled from the embryo back to one or the other," said Kim. "One of these two founding cells did go on to produce more descendants than the other, but they produced diverse cell types at almost equal ratios."
This meant that although one of the original cells contributed more descendants overall, both founding cells gave rise to a remarkably similar mix of specialized cell types.
The finding illustrates how scientists can now investigate the earliest stages of development with a level of detail that was previously difficult to achieve.
Scientists Discover When Cells Choose Their Roles
The DNA recordings also revealed important information about when cells begin committing to their eventual roles in the body.
Early embryonic cells can give rise to many different types of tissue. As development progresses, their descendants gradually become more specialized, eventually forming structures such as the nervous system, skin, blood, and eyes.
By reconstructing the branches of the embryo's cellular family tree, the researchers could determine when different groups of cells began following distinct developmental paths.
Their observations were consistent with conclusions drawn from decades of previous research, but the new approach allowed them to examine these patterns within a single developing mouse.
"Blood cells and the retina committed relatively early, while the skin's outer layer didn't commit until noticeably later," the researchers explained. "Cell fate wasn't locked in all at once. Different cell types settled into their identity on their own separate schedules, some early and some late."
These findings show that the transition from a flexible, unspecialized cell to one with a particular biological function does not happen at the same time throughout the embryo.
Instead, different tissues follow their own developmental timelines. Some cells begin narrowing their possible futures early, while others remain flexible for a longer period before becoming committed to a specific role.
What This Could Mean for Birth Defects, Cancer, and Stem Cell Therapies
Understanding exactly how cells acquire their identities could eventually have important implications for medicine.
Many developmental disorders arise when the normal process of cell specialization or tissue formation is disrupted. Cancer also involves abnormal cell behavior, including failures in the mechanisms that ordinarily regulate cell growth and division.
By tracing cellular ancestry and identifying when different developmental pathways emerge, scientists may gain a clearer understanding of how these problems begin.
"This kind of large-scale developmental recording gives scientists a map of how one cell becomes a whole body -- which helps explain how organs form correctly, how that process can go wrong in birth defects, and how abnormal cell growth drives cancer. As stem cell engineering advances, this kind of recording can also help guide how we engineer cells for therapeutic use."
Although the work was conducted in mouse embryos and does not yet represent a direct medical treatment, it demonstrates a powerful way to study the biological decisions that shape a developing organism.
The approach could also support future stem cell research, particularly efforts to guide cells toward specific identities for regenerative medicine and other therapeutic applications.
Research Team and Funding
Additional co-first authors included Qi Yu and Sophie Seidel, both affiliated with the University of Washington School of Medicine's Department of Genome Sciences and the Seattle Hub for Synthetic Biology.
Shendure serves as the lead scientific director of the Seattle Hub for Synthetic Biology. He is also scientific director of the UW Medicine Brotman Baty Institute for Precision Medicine and the Allen Institute for Cell Lineage Tracing.
The research received support from the Seattle Hub for Synthetic Biology, a collaboration involving the Allen Institute, BioHub, and University of Washington School of Medicine (CZIF2023-008738); the Paul G. Allen Frontiers Group's Allen Discovery Center for Cell Lineage Tracing; the UW Medicine Brotman Baty Institute for Precision Medicine; the Washington Research Foundation; the National Institutes of Health (R00HG012973 and P30CA008748); the Damon Runyon Cancer Research Foundation (DFS-64-24); the Searle Scholars Award (SSP-2025-101); Dartmouth's Center for Quantitative Biology through a National Institute of General Medical Sciences grant (P20GM130454); and the Swiss National Science Foundation (239394).

Hezbollah outlines financial aid plan for Lebanese with destroyed homes
Oct 13 - Lebanon's Hezbollah will provide up to $14,000 in financial assistance to families whose primary homes have been destroyed or rendered uninhabitable during this year's war with Israel, the chairman of the group's Executive Council said on Tuesday.
Reuters reported last week that Hezbollah had received $200 million from Iran to help displaced Lebanese families, citing two people with direct knowledge of the transfer, though the US disputed Tehran's ability to provide such financial assistance.
Under the plan presented by Executive Council chairman Ali Damoush, eligible families in Beirut and its southern suburbs will receive $14,000, including $8,000 for furniture and $6,000 for rent. Families elsewhere in Lebanon will receive $12,000, comprising $8,000 for furniture and $4,000 for rent, maintaining the same rates as in 2024.
Damoush said the assistance would cover families whose homes were destroyed, deemed uninhabitable following technical assessments or severely damaged, as well as those displaced from Israeli-occupied areas or nearby locations.
The aid will be restricted to families who used the affected properties as their primary residences and do not own a second home, excluding summer homes and abandoned properties.
Payments will be made in four instalments over one year, starting with $3,500 for families in Beirut and its southern suburbs and $3,000 elsewhere.
Damoush said eligibility and the type of assistance would be determined according to a set of criteria assessing the extent of damage to each property.
HUNDREDS OF THOUSANDS OF PEOPLE UPROOTED BY THE WAR
Israel’s bombardment and invasion of Lebanon uprooted hundreds of thousands of Hezbollah’s Shi’ite Muslim constituents after the group entered the regional war in support of Iran on March 2, days after the US and Israel began attacks on Iran.
Israeli attacks have killed more than 4,300 people, according to Lebanon's health ministry, which does not distinguish between civilians and combatants.
Hezbollah received the cash last month despite tightening US economic pressure on Iran and increasing difficulties in getting funds to Tehran's Lebanese ally, according to the two people who spoke to Reuters.
At the time, a Hezbollah official said an amount had been secured and a plan for distributing it would be announced in the coming days, without elaborating on the source of the funds.
The United States disputed the Reuters report, saying the money was "not there". Iran has not commented.
Damoush on Tuesday declined to comment on either the Reuters report or the US reaction, and declined to provide a figure for the total amount Hezbollah would dedicate to shelter support. REUTERS

If the Congress believes elections are rigged, the Election Commission is not functioning properly and SIR is flawed, Goyal asked whether Congress chief ministers should resign in states governed by the party.

Gaza water crisis fuels rise in disease amid sewage pollution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:10:50 UTC
19:10:50 KST

Breadcrumb
'We are constantly getting sick': Gaza's contaminated seawater fuels disease among displaced families
Forty-year-old Suhair Ramzi lives with her five children in a tent near the beach in the Wadi Gaza area, after being displaced from Beit Lahia in northern Gaza when her family home was bombed by Israeli forces on October 18, 2023.
Suhair says choosing to live there was not a preference for being near the sea, but the result of having no alternatives.
The most densely populated areas for displaced people, including Al-Mawasi, can no longer accommodate new tents, while the family cannot afford to rent a plot of land in the city because of high rental costs.
Her husband, Mahmoud, worked as a driver before the war and is now unemployed, leaving the family unable to afford another place to live.
Suhair lives with her children Muath, 15, Mohsen, 12, Rami, 8, Rana, 5, and Dina, 3, far from areas regularly reached by water trucks.
Unable to afford to buy water, the family has come to rely on seawater in their daily lives, using it to wash dishes and clothes, bathe, clean, and perform ablution, despite knowing it is contaminated with sewage and waste.
"We spend a large part of the month in hospitals. The water is contaminated and causes us stomach problems and skin diseases, and my children are constantly getting sick," Suhair tells The New Arab.
She adds that the cost of treatment is an additional burden on the family, which cannot afford medical expenses every time one of the children falls ill.
Moving elsewhere has also become financially out of reach, as she says the cost of transporting their tent and belongings to another area is too high.
"If we could move somewhere with clean water, we would. But even moving to another place costs money that we do not have," Suhair says.
Suhair and her family’s experience is not isolated. According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), 70 percent of Gaza’s sewage pumping stations were out of service in September 2026, while all six wastewater treatment plants were non-operational.
As a result, more than 150,000 cubic metres of untreated wastewater are discharged into the environment every day, increasing the risk of water contamination and posing a threat to public health.
Children at risk
On the same shoreline, the sea has become one of the few spaces available to children living in tents to play and escape the realities of displacement.
Ten-year-old Abdul Rahim Sultan lived with his family in a tent near the sea and would go swimming there, like many children who have few other places to play.
His mother says seawater has become part of their daily lives, not just a place for children to swim.
"We use seawater every day for washing, cleaning and bathing because we don’t have another water source that is enough for us," she says.
After one trip to the sea, Abdul Rahim’s health began to deteriorate later that day. That night, he began vomiting repeatedly and eventually had to be taken to the hospital, where he was diagnosed with gastroenteritis that led to dehydration.
Abdul Rahim remained in the hospital for treatment, while his mother says shortages of medicines and medical supplies made treating sick children more difficult.
For the family, his illness was not simply a medical emergency, but an experience that highlighted the risks they face every day while having few alternatives to the water they use.
Dr Hamza Al-Astal, an emergency physician, says treating patients exposed to unsafe water has become a recurring part of emergency care amid Gaza’s ongoing water and sanitation crisis. He says symptoms can include gastroenteritis, vomiting and diarrhoea, as well as skin problems associated with exposure to contaminated water.
"Contaminated water is not only a problem when it is consumed. Using it for bathing, washing clothes and dishes, or even swimming can expose people to a range of health problems, particularly children," Dr Hamza tells The New Arab.
He adds that children suffering from diarrhoea and vomiting are particularly vulnerable to dehydration, and delayed access to treatment can make their condition more serious.
"We see children arriving dehydrated after losing large amounts of fluids. Under normal circumstances, these cases can be treated more easily, but the current situation makes it harder because families lack access to clean water, while health facilities themselves are under enormous pressure," he says.
Dr Hamza says the problem cannot be addressed through medical treatment alone, because treating patients without addressing the source of contamination leaves them exposed to the same risks.
"If a patient returns to using the same contaminated water after receiving treatment, they remain at risk of becoming sick again. Prevention starts with providing safe water and sanitation services, not simply treating the patient in the hospital," he adds.
Health surveillance data reflects the scale of communicable diseases in Gaza.
Among reported disease cases, acute respiratory infections accounted for 52 percent, while skin infections and diseases represented 28 percent and acute watery diarrhoea 20 percent.
Health workers continue to monitor these diseases amid limited access to safe water and sanitation services.
Sewage pollution
Ali Al-Kahlout, a water and sanitation specialist, says contamination sources extend beyond household wastewater to include solid waste, leaks from sewage networks, and wastewater treatment facilities operating below capacity.
He says some of this wastewater ultimately reaches the sea without adequate treatment, increasing pollution levels in coastal areas where displaced people live.
"The problem is that wastewater has no safe route for disposal or treatment, so some of it ends up in the sea. As infrastructure remains damaged or out of service, large quantities of wastewater are reaching the marine environment either directly or indirectly," Ali says.
He adds that the volume of wastewater discharged each day makes the sea one of the areas most affected by the crisis, particularly around areas where displaced people have gathered near the coast.
"We are talking about tens of thousands of cubic metres of wastewater that need to be treated before they reach the environment. When that treatment is unavailable, pollutants enter the sea, affecting water quality and increasing the risks for people who use it for swimming, washing or other daily needs," he adds.
Ali says the risk is not limited to direct contact with contaminated water, but also includes the accumulation of pollutants in the surrounding environment.
"When sewage mixes with the water people use every day, it becomes difficult for them to avoid exposure, particularly in displacement sites where there are not enough alternatives to clean water. Addressing the problem therefore starts with preventing wastewater from reaching the sea and improving water and sanitation services, rather than only treating people after they develop symptoms," he says.
As Gaza’s water and sanitation systems continue to deteriorate, the sea remains a destination for growing amounts of wastewater and waste, while damaged infrastructure's capacity to contain and treat pollution continues to decline.
The consequences extend beyond seawater quality to the coastal environment and public health, making access to safe water and wastewater treatment essential to containing further pollution and its risks.

Greta Thunberg joins French teens on new day of school protests

Greta Thunberg joins French teens on new day of school protests
SAINT-DENIS – Swedish activist Greta Thunberg joined a demonstration outside a high school in a working-class suburb of Paris on Oct 13 as French pupils took to the streets for another day of protests against poor conditions.
Now in its fourth week, the nationwide movement to highlight teacher shortages, classroom overcrowding and the dilapidation of facilities has involved marches, blockades of hundreds of schools and, in some cases, clashes with police.
Students clustered outside the doors of several schools in Paris and other cities in the morning hours, brandishing placards and megaphones and chanting slogans, and marches were planned later in the day.
Education Minister Edouard Geffray told France Inter radio that about 200 schools were closed, although he suggested some of the closures were due to safety precautions as they were on the routes of planned marches.
Greta Thunberg ‘inspired’ by French school protests
Thunberg, who rose to fame as a teenage protester against climate change but has since broadened her activism, said the French students deserved wider support.
“They should know that all over the world, we are following these developments. We are inspired by the young people who are demanding their basic rights,” she told reporters outside Lycee Paul Eluard in Saint-Denis, north of Paris, one of the schools where the protest movement first gained traction.
“Whether it’s not funding schools enough, or the climate crisis, or social injustice crises... it’s about time that young people are stepping up and reclaiming that future.”
Thunberg also criticised the police response, which has been fiercely debated, as an “extremely violent” sign that the authorities were protecting the status quo and ignoring young people’s demands.
Riot police have used tear gas and charged at protesters in numerous incidents, injuring hundreds and arresting thousands.
The government suspended the use of stun grenades last week after one teenager lost a hand.
While left-wing politicians have criticised the police, far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen and others have blamed violent protesters and highlighted damage inflicted on schools and injuries to staff and police officers.
The protest movement has added to a sense of uncertainty and crisis engulfing France six months ahead of a presidential election that could usher in the first far-right government since World War II, led by Le Pen's National Rally.
The cash-strapped government has promised to act to address the pupils’ concerns, but has little room for manoeuvre at a time when concerns over the national debt and the budget deficit are pushing up borrowing costs to the highest level in years.
Le Pen, the front runner to replace French President Emmanuel Macron according to opinion polls, has said she would slash spending to bring public finances under control. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

Sofia summons Moscow envoy after drone sinks vessel off Bulgaria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:07:00 UTC
19:07:00 KST

Bulgaria summoned Russia’s ambassador Tuesday after 11 sailors went missing when a drone attack sank their ship off the Bulgarian coast, marking the second possible deadly sinking of a cargo vessel in the area within a week.
Two cargo ships were hit by drones overnight and one was sunk, Bulgarian officials said. Bulgaria stopped short of explicitly accusing Russia of carrying out the attacks but Prime Minister Rumen Radev said their outcome "benefits the Russian Federation."
There was no immediate comment from Moscow on the incidents.
"This is absolutely unacceptable – another attack in the immediate vicinity of Bulgarian territorial waters," Radev said in a televised address.
The attacks were also condemned by Ukraine and the EU.
"The Black Sea has become another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on X. "Those responsible should be held accountable."
Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on X Tuesday that the strike "once again demonstrates Moscow's deliberate disregard for civilian lives."
"The Black Sea is a lifeline for global food security. Russia is attacking it to weaponise hunger and hold the world hostage," he said.
Speaking with von der Leyen and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte by telephone Tuesday, Radev urged their support to bolster his country's maritime and airspace surveillance, the Bulgarian government said in a statement.
NATO will continue to adjust its military presence on its eastern flank "as needed," Rutte said.
Bulgarian officials said five crew members had been rescued but 11 were still listed as missing from the ship which sank off the coast of the village of Krapets.
President Iliana Iotova identified the vessel as the Guinea-Bissau-flagged cargo ship HS Dignity and said a search and rescue operation was ongoing.
Another ship, the Chelsea 3 sailing under a Maltese flag, was also hit by three drones overnight, Bulgarian officials said. All crew from that ship – seven Ukrainians and eight Azerbaijanis – were rescued and none seriously injured.
A week ago nine Syrian sailors and one Egyptian were lost at sea from a ship that sank when hit by drones in Bulgaria's Black Sea exclusive economic zone. Another ship was also hit that night but the crew was rescued.
After meeting Radev in Sofia, Russian Ambassador Eleonora Mitrofanova said she had no information from the Russian Defense Ministry about attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea but did not rule out they could be a provocation by a third party, the Bulgarian government said.
More than four and a half years into the war that Moscow launched with its full-scale invasion in 2022, Black Sea shipping has increasingly been drawn into a prolonged battle of economic endurance.
Ukraine and Russia are both among the world's largest exporters of grain.
Russia has been bombing Ukraine's Black Sea ports, forcing Ukraine to rely increasingly on river ports on the Danube and shipping routes close to the coasts of NATO members Bulgaria and Romania.
Ukraine, for its part, has increasingly targeted Russian grain-exporting ships in other parts of the Black Sea and the Azov Sea at the mouth of the Don River.

====================================================================================================

Kyiv declares 2-day halt in Russian refinery strikes, Kremlin mum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:07:00 UTC
19:07:00 KST

Donald Trump's "energy cease-fire" finally unfolded Tuesday when Moscow did not hit any Ukrainian energy targets and Kyiv revealed it had not hit Russian refineries for two days.
Russia's Defense Ministry, in its daily summary of overnight strikes, made no mention of Ukrainian energy facilities. A Kremlin spokesperson, asked about the energy cease-fire, would only say that contacts were ongoing, but declined to provide any further details. However, one missile came down just over a kilometer from a plant providing heating to much of the city of Lviv, in the west.
Trump's cease-fire announcement Sunday came two days after his declaration of a deal that lifted U.S. sanctions on Russian diesel exports to allow Russia to supply almost 2 million metric tons of diesel, a bid to lower U.S. fuel prices.
Reuters and other media outlets have reported that U.S. officials have threatened to cut off intelligence sharing and weapons sales to Ukraine unless it halts its strikes on Russian oil refineries.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Tuesday that Ukraine had not hit Russian refineries for two days, since Trump announced the cease-fire, but that Russia had continued attacks on energy and critical infrastructure during that time. Russia struck six Ukrainian energy sites Monday.
It was not clear whether Russia had deliberately avoided targeting energy infrastructure overnight into Tuesday.
Trump has repeatedly blamed Ukrainian attacks – which prompted Moscow to suspend diesel exports – for a sharp rise in U.S. diesel prices this year, a headache for his Republican party ahead of Congressional midterm elections in three weeks.
Most analysts, however, say Trump's war in Iran has had a far greater impact on the price rise.
Four people were killed by Russian strikes in Ukraine's second city, Kharkiv and at least a dozen were injured across the country, Ukrainian officials said.
The Ukrainian air force said it had not received prior surveillance warnings before Russia fired six ballistic missiles at Kyiv late Monday, prompting widespread anxiety in online comments from residents. "The causes are being investigated," it said in a statement.
Intelligence about preparations for ballistic missile attacks has been part of the information that the U.S. provides to Ukraine, Ukrainian officials say.
Zelenskyy's office did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Tuesday that Kyiv continues to receive intelligence data from the United States.
Speaking at a Warsaw security conference, Sybiha said the U.S. request to halt attacks on Russian refineries showed how Ukraine's position had strengthened, alluding to Trump's comment to Zelenskyy in a tense Oval Office meeting last year that "you don't have the cards."
"In less than two years, we have gone from 'having no cards' to 'not playing your cards.' That is an achievement," Sybiha said.
Zelenskyy has said Ukraine supports the idea of an energy truce, but he has accused Moscow of violating the cesaefire – which Moscow has not acknowledged signing up to.
"This winter, if Russia does not agree to an energy cease-fire, we will respond," Zelenskyy told a security conference in Warsaw on Monday.
The Ukrainian air force said Tuesday that damage had been recorded at 17 locations overnight. Air defense units downed 88 out of 108 Russian drones, it said.
A cargo terminal in the southern Mykolaiv region and transport infrastructure in the southeastern Dnipropetrovsk region were damaged.
In Kharkiv, four people were killed and at least 11 injured in a residential building. In the western Khmelnytskyi region, a hospital was damaged, regional officials said.

Doctors warn of physical limits as China viral ‘flash step’ dance sends imitators to hospital

They were especially taken with three moves featured in the video: the “flash step”, “prodigal kicking the ball” and “black bear shaking fur”.
As its name vividly suggests, the flash step is a rapid, side-to-side dodging movement. “Prodigal kicking the ball” involves a rather bendy hopping kick with the arms outstretched, while “black bear shaking fur” features the dancer shaking vigorously, literally like a bear shaking its fur.

As diesel prices soar, Bolivian farmer turns trash into tractor fuel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:05:25 UTC
19:05:25 KST

As diesel prices soar, Bolivian farmer turns trash into tractor fuel
LAJA, Bolivia, Oct 13 - In the Bolivian Altiplano, where rising fuel costs are threatening farmers' livelihoods, local resident Etson Machaca built a small plant that turns plastic bags, old tires and used oil into energy for his tractors.
Though the operation is small, producing only between 80 and 150 liters of gasoline and diesel a day, the savings are a lifesaver for Machaca after Bolivia's centrist government last month ended state diesel subsidies in a bid to shore up public accounts.
The plant produces fuel at a cost of between 7 and 10 bolivianos ($0.60 to $0.86) per liter. Prices for diesel on the open market are about double, at 18 bolivianos ($1.54) per liter.
"We transform plastics, bags, tires, used oil. All of that has become raw material for us to produce fuel in the highlands," said Machaca, whose plant is located in Ancocala, a community in the rural municipality of Laja, about 35 kilometers (22 miles) from La Paz.
The plant uses a process known as pyrolysis, which heats materials to high temperatures in the absence of oxygen to break them down into products that can be processed into fuel.
Machaca said he does not sell the fuel, but uses it for his tractors and other farm equipment.
The savings matter as many families in the Altiplano have replaced livestock with tractors to plow their fields more efficiently, making farms reliant on diesel.
"If we don't sow today or tomorrow, there is no production here on the Altiplano. So diesel is very important for us," Machaca said.
Bolivia for years relied on natural gas exports to earn foreign currency, but has seen its liquid hydrocarbon output fall and its reliance on foreign purchases grow.
The landlocked South American nation imports 95% of the diesel and 60% of the gasoline it consumes, according to official data. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

Expert Insights: Thank You for the Question
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:05:14 UTC
19:05:14 KST

The author: Signe Biering Röpke is an executive coach, trained in psychology, with a background in diplomacy. She is also a career columnist for The Copenhagen Post.
A few days ago, my co-author Anatolie Cantir and I held a book launch of our new book, ‘The (Un)Happiest Expats in the Happiest Country in the World’.
We had been talking for perhaps twenty minutes about what life in Denmark can feel like for the people who move here: the loneliness, the invisible codes, the closed networks. Then a hand went up and the question was simple. “After hearing about all these difficulties with moving to Denmark, what are your solutions?”
I wish I could tell you that I gave a brilliant answer. I didn’t. I mumbled something about this not being a how-to book, Anatolie said something similar, and we moved on.
But the question stayed with me. Not because it was a bad question. On the contrary, it was a very reasonable question. But also a revealing one.
What I would have liked to say was this: “Thank you for your question. It is the reason we wrote this book.”
When we hear about something that is difficult, our first instinct is often to find a solution. What can we do? How can we fix it? I understand that instinct. I’m a practical person myself. And I know how powerless we can feel when we hear about problems without finding a solution.
But what if there isn’t a solution? What if our need to fix things prevents us from asking questions? Because if I cannot do anything about the answer, perhaps it is easier not to ask in the first place.
One of my hopes for our book is that it will make it easier for Danes and internationals to talk about things that are difficult, even when neither has a solution.
And perhaps that is especially important when what we are talking about is culture.
Denmark is a wonderful country. I have lived and worked in many parts of the world, and I appreciate and love Denmark deeply. Our trust in each other, our equality, our independence, our strong networks.
But some of these characteristics can make life difficult for people who arrive from elsewhere.
Our strong social networks are wonderful if you are part of them. Less wonderful if you are not. Our flat hierarchies give us freedom, but they also come with unwritten rules. Our respect for independence can feel like indifference.
So what is the solution? Should Danes stop being independent? Should we abandon our flat hierarchies? Should we give up the friendships we have had since school?
Of course not.
Danish culture is not ‘a problem’. It is a culture, with strengths and limitations, like every other culture. And it is not going away.
Neither are the internationals.
They are here, many of them to stay, and they are here as whole human beings. They are as different from one another as any two Danes are. Some came for love, some for work, some because they had no choice. Some thrive, some struggle, and many do both at the same time. That is also what the brackets in our title are trying to say.
Of course, some things can and should be fixed. We can make bureaucracy easier to navigate, help accompanying partners find employment, and make it easier to learn Danish.
But we cannot remove all the difficulties of living in Denmark. And some of the burdens – and insights – come from discovering that the things we take for granted are not universal.
And that goes for Danes as well.
I think we sometimes underestimate how difficult it is to see our own culture. To us, it is simply the way things are. We don’t notice the rules because we learned them so early that we have forgotten they are rules.
That is one of the reasons we wrote the book. Not to provide a list of things Denmark needs to fix, but to make the experiences of internationals visible – because we cannot overestimate the importance of being heard.
And perhaps we can find better solutions, where solutions are needed.
I am grateful for the question at our book launch. It made me think about what we are trying to achieve.
We don’t need to fix Danish culture. But we do need to understand it – and play a part in evolving it, including the parts that make life difficult for people who didn’t grow up here.
Before we reach for the solutions, we could pause – and ask: “What is it like for you?”
Even when we know we might not be able to fix it. Perhaps especially then.

Copenhagen has far more municipal savings per resident than poorer municipalities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:04:41 UTC
19:04:41 KST

The Danish government has presented a proposed budget for 2027 that prioritizes national security, with more money allocated to defence amid an increasingly tense international security situation.
The proposal, titled “A stronger defence of Denmark – a strengthened Denmark to defend”, was presented by Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard of the Social Democrats (S) at the Ministry of Finance on Friday morning.
The government wants to ensure that defence spending reaches 3.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2030.
Hummelgaard said the proposal reflected the need to make “hard priorities” in response to the current security situation. He also described the Danish economy as being “in top shape”.
“The government’s proposal for the finance bill shows that we take responsibility upon ourselves, and that we lead the way in working for a greener, freer, and more equal Denmark,” Hummelgaard said.
Pia Olsen Dyhr of the Socialist People’s Party (SF), the minister for economic and interior affairs, also highlighted the security situation.
“We do not solve all the challenges we have in Denmark with this finance bill. But we are well on our way,” she said at the press conference.
“I also think everyone must remember that we are in an escalated security policy situation,” Olsen Dyhr said.
Much of the proposed budget had already been announced, either in the government’s policy platform or through statements by ministers in recent weeks.
The proposal allocates 1.2 billion DKK to children’s services and education in 2027, including Denmark’s public primary and lower secondary schools, known as folkeskole.
It also sets aside a total of 10.1 billion DKK in 2030 for tax cuts. These include abolishing the intermediate income tax and the top-top tax, as well as reducing corporation tax.
“We are simplifying the tax system,” said Taxation and Growth Minister Jakob Engel-Schmidt of the Moderates (M).
The tax measures will be negotiated separately as part of a tax reform. While the budget proposal includes tax cuts, the government also plans to freeze several tax thresholds, which would increase the tax burden for some taxpayers as incomes rise.
The liberal think tank Cepos estimates that the government’s various plans will result in a net tax cut of 2.2 billion DKK in 2030.
Business and Competitiveness Minister Martin Lidegaard of the Danish Social Liberal Party (R) highlighted investment in young people and education.
“We are significantly strengthening knowledge, general education, and formal education in Denmark, from ABC to PhD. It is good for the individual young person, but it is also good for Denmark’s future,” Lidegaard said.
Unlike in recent years, when the government’s fiscal room for manoeuvre helped fund much of its budget plans, this proposal includes several measures to find additional savings.
These include cuts to the Danish student grant (SU), savings on senior pension payments, a proposed tax on cruise ships and further reductions in state administration costs.
The government must now negotiate with other parties in the Danish Parliament, the Folketing, to secure a majority for the 2027 budget.
The proposal includes a negotiating reserve of 500 million DKK annually from 2027 to 2030, which other parties can seek to use to fund their own priorities.

Iran fortifies nuclear sites, prepares for renewed war: report
Unknown

2026-10-13
10:01:34 UTC
19:01:34 KST

Breadcrumb
Iran fortifies nuclear sites as it prepares for renewed US war: report
Iran is strengthening its nuclear and military facilities, mobilising supporters and threatening a wider regional conflict as it prepares for the possibility of renewed war with the United States, according to a report by The Wall Street Journal.
Iranian leaders believe US President Donald Trump could launch fresh attacks after the 3 November midterm elections, prompting Tehran to reinforce sensitive sites and warn Washington that another offensive would trigger a more devastating response, the newspaper reported on Tuesday.
Citing Iranian officials and people familiar with regional communications, the WSJ said Tehran had issued both public and private warnings that renewed US strikes could lead to attacks on American interests and Gulf allies.
Satellite imagery has shown Iran strengthening defences around nuclear facilities and border areas, while authorities have stepped up pro-government rallies and promoted military training for civilians.
Iran's limited ability to counter advanced US fighter jets, high-altitude bombers and cruise missiles has pushed Tehran to rely increasingly on threats of wider retaliation to deter Washington, according to the report.
Sanam Vakil, director of the Middle East and North Africa programme at London-based Chatham House, said the prospect of war also served Iran's leadership as it grappled with diplomatic, economic and political deadlock.
Iran threatens Gulf infrastructure and US warships
Iranian officials have raised the possibility of launching ground incursions into neighbouring countries in response to further US attacks, according to people familiar with Tehran's warnings.
Senior Iranian national security official Mohsen Rezaei warned on Sunday that the United Arab Emirates could be targeted, along with regional data centres and internet cables.
Tehran has also warned Arab officials that critical infrastructure, including Saudi oil facilities, could come under attack if fighting resumes, the WSJ reported.
The threats come as Saudi Arabia faces mounting attacks from Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi movement.
A Houthi missile strike on Riyadh's airport on Saturday killed at least 13 people and wounded hundreds, according to the newspaper, which described it as the deadliest attack on the US or its Gulf allies during the conflict linked to the war with Iran.
Iran has also told intermediaries that it could respond more forcefully against American military personnel, including by attempting to sink US warships and inflict casualties among their crews.
The warnings highlight the risks to the Gulf's vital economic infrastructure if Trump orders another round of strikes.
US sends more military assets to Middle East
The US military is also preparing for a possible resumption of hostilities, with a third aircraft carrier strike group and an additional Marine unit heading towards the region according to the outlet.
The Pentagon is considering sending more air defence systems and ammunition to American bases across the region.
Trump ruled out launching an attack before the midterm elections last week but publicly raised the possibility of striking Iran's Mount Pickaxe nuclear site.
US officials said the military was developing several options for renewed strikes.
Direct fighting between Washington and Tehran has eased considerably since late July, when Trump backed away from plans for a major escalation, partly over concerns about dwindling interceptor missile stocks needed to protect American and regional targets.
The lull has nevertheless allowed both sides to prepare for another confrontation.
Iran has used the period to rebuild missile and drone production facilities and replenish its weapons stockpiles, while Washington has intensified economic pressure on Tehran.
Meanwhile, attacks on commercial shipping and tankers in the Gulf and Strait of Hormuz have increased.
At least three merchant vessels came under attack over the weekend, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency.
A drone strike on the Emirati tanker Petro Dolphin near Oman on Sunday sparked a fire aboard the vessel and left two Indian sailors missing.
Iran reinforces nuclear sites and mobilises civilians
Satellite images taken by Vantor and analysed by the Washington-based Institute for Science and International Security show Iran constructing new defensive barriers around its Pickaxe Mountain and Natanz nuclear facilities.
The measures, introduced last month, include makeshift earthworks designed to obstruct potential ground raids.
Iranian officials have also sought to demonstrate the country's readiness for another war.
Brigadier General Gholamreza Jalali, who oversees Iran's contingency planning, said in late September that airports, seaports and power plants had been equipped with shelters and emergency supplies to maintain operations during a conflict.
State media have meanwhile intensified coverage of pro-government demonstrations, with residents reporting that rallies have grown larger and spread to more locations in recent weeks.
Billboards in Tehran have advertised civilian training courses in the use of shoulder-fired anti-aircraft missiles and sniper rifles.
Last month, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps released footage of women undergoing training in guerrilla warfare, firearms and drone operations through its Basij paramilitary force.
In the northeastern city of Sabzevar, Revolutionary Guard personnel visited a kindergarten to recount stories of earlier fighting and display a US-made Tomahawk missile they claimed to have intercepted.
Behnam Ben Taleblu, senior director of the Iran programme at the Washington-based Foundation for Defense of Democracies, said Tehran's political rhetoric and military preparations indicated it was actively preparing for another confrontation.
He described the measures as serving both deterrence and war planning.

====================================================================================================

lightweight systems prove that more material does not mean better performance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:00:18 UTC
19:00:18 KST

lightweight systems prove that more material does not mean better performance
from heavy mass to high-performance envelopes, the shift toward lightweight architectural membranes explores how surfaces filter light, guide airflow, and redefine the space around us.
[FEATURED]
In the story of the Three Little Pigs, the choice of material determines the fate of each house. The wolf’s breath brings down the structures made of straw and wood, while the brick house remains standing. The moral is that the more solid the construction, the greater its ability to resist. A building, however, has to respond to much less straightforward questions. Remaining standing is still essential, but heat, light, air, and sound are not forces that necessarily need to be blocked. Sometimes sunlight needs to be kept out; at other times, daylight needs to be let in. Retaining heat may be desirable in winter and counterproductive in summer. Air needs to circulate, sound may need to be absorbed, and the conditions that determine these responses change throughout the day, across seasons, and over the life of the building itself. More material does not necessarily mean better performance. In some cases, it can simply add complexity without improving how the building responds.
This relationship between mass and performance was at the center of Serge Ferrari Architecture‘s recent reveal of the 7TH MATERIAL, a category currently centered on technical membrane. The category is framed around what materials can do: filtering light, modulating solar gain, guiding airflow, treating sound, or combining several of these functions within a single surface. Membranes do not replace concrete, metal, stone, or glass; they complement them by performing different functions.
For Nic Goldsmith, Founding Director of the Lightweight Structures Group at TYLin and author of Mass to Membrane, this discussion forms part of a much longer architectural trajectory. During the reveal, he described the history of architecture as ‘one long attempt to do more with less,’ tracing a shift from massive structures toward increasingly lighter ways of enclosing space. Along that trajectory, new material systems have expanded what architects can ask an envelope to do, a process that, in his view, is still unfolding. As he puts it: ‘We may not know the precise form future membranes will take. The direction is clear.’
Structural stability is only one measure of how well a building performs. Heat, light, air, and sound place different demands on a space, and the goal is not always to block them, but to control how they move through the building. A roof, for example, can be evaluated by the shade it provides, the daylight it allows through, the air that circulates beneath it, and the resources required to perform those functions over time. Its thickness or weight describes only part of the solution. Its properties, geometry, and relationship with the building’s other elements also matter.
At The Camp in Aix-en-Provence, this logic can be seen in the organization of the complex itself. Designed by Corinne Vezzoni & Associés, the 11,000-square-meter campus is covered by approximately 7,000 square meters of membrane, beneath which some circulation areas remain open to the air. The surface filters daylight, while its double curvature contributes to the roof’s stability, air circulation, and rainwater collection. Under the project’s specific conditions and fire safety approval, this configuration also removes the need for mechanical ventilation and smoke extraction within that volume. Its properties and geometry work together to provide shade, daylight, airflow, structural stability, and rainwater collection.
THE MATERIAL HELPS DEFINE THE FORM
Another example can be found at Hazza Bin Zayed Stadium in Al Ain, where BDP Pattern began with the conditions of a hot, dry climate to develop the enclosure. In this case, the path of the sun, rather than protection from rain, shaped its geometry: a 40-meter cantilever on the west side shades the field and stands at 4:00 p.m. on game days, while the porous façade encourages air to circulate through the envelope. Before settling on the final solution, the team built a full-scale prototype on site using three geometries and, over the course of development, reduced the number of panel types from 320 to 86, making it possible for a local manufacturer to produce them at an acceptable cost. Climate, material behavior, geometry, and fabrication all contributed to defining the form.
Architect and computational designer Nick Tyrer describes this relationship more directly: ‘Do not specify the material to fit a form you have already decided on. Let the material and the geometry find the form together, in response to the actual conditions of that place.’ Across projects responding to a headwind, a desert sun, and a coastline, Tyrer returns to the same point: ‘You don’t specify it. You design with it.’
At Al Ain, solar exposure, ventilation, geometry, material, and fabrication were therefore treated as parts of the same problem, changing when materials enter the design conversation. A technical data sheet can describe how a product performs under specific test conditions, but a design team still needs to understand how those properties behave within a particular configuration while the geometry can still be adjusted.
WHAT ENTERS THE COMPARISON
Serge Ferrari uses the idea of performance density to describe a comparison that begins with equivalent functions rather than equivalent quantities of material. Shading, daylighting, acoustic treatment, structural requirements, carbon emissions, and the additional systems needed over time can all become part of the equation. The comparison also considers what a solution makes unnecessary, from additional layers to heavier structures or greater mechanical capacity. There is not yet a single standardized metric that combines all of these variables.
A simulation for an office in Lyon helps illustrate the complexity of this calculation. With Type D glazing and automated external solar shading, cooling demand fell from 60.2 to 29.8 kWh/m²/year, while heating demand rose from 11.4 to 13.4 kWh/m²/year because of reduced solar gains in winter. Overall, combined heating and cooling demand decreased by 39.59%. The result applies to this specific configuration, reinforcing the need to read performance figures alongside the conditions that produced them.
PERFORMANCE OVER TIME
Comparing only the amount of material installed on day one also leaves out maintenance, replacement, and end-of-life considerations. In the methodology being developed around the 7TH MATERIAL, the assessment accounts for the materials and carbon mobilized over the entire period analyzed, including replacements, as well as the additional layers and systems each solution requires to deliver equivalent functions. The calculation therefore extends beyond the material itself to everything needed to install, operate, maintain, and eventually replace it.
For anyone specifying materials or systems, this means reading properties such as weight, light transmission, and resistance in context. Their significance depends on supports, adjacent layers, climate, conditions of use, and maintenance over time. Performance is ultimately shaped by how a material works with the rest of the architectural system.
The practical consequence is that material decisions need to happen earlier in the design process, while form, geometry, and system relationships can still be adjusted. Solidity becomes only one part of the equation. A solution also needs to be understood in terms of the functions it can combine, what it requires from the building, and what it may make unnecessary. Resisting the wolf’s breath remains a perfectly effective measure for a fairy tale, but in architecture, performance involves a much larger set of variables.
Guest Feature by Eduardo Souza / Archdaily
