What Flock Actually Costs Cities Across the Country
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

In 2020, the police department of picturesque Covington, Georgia, paid Flock Safety, the surveillance technology company, $40,000 to maintain 20 cameras around the city. The next year, it paid the same amount.
In 2022, that cost went up to $81,250. Fifteen new “Falcon” cameras, which Flock says have more sophisticated technology for reading license plates, accounted for $37,500. Another $3,750 went toward installing the new cameras, and the rest was spent maintaining the initial fleet.
Then, in 2024, the department paid Flock $113,225. Of that, $87,500 was to maintain its existing 35 cameras, a rate it agreed to pay for the next five years, and the remainder went toward eight new Falcon cameras. The next year, Covington paid Flock $159,000 for a combination of camera maintenance and enrollment in its Drone as First Responder program, which uses drones to fly to emergency scenes and stream footage back to the police station.
It’s unclear how much Covington will wind up paying Flock in 2026, but through August, it has paid $201,000—$100,000 to maintain its existing cameras, $800 to replace one, and another $100,200 for new software products. The Covington Police Department did not respond to a request for comment.
Overall, Flock is a small fraction of the Covington police department’s $12,488,733 budget for June 2025 to July 2026. But amid fierce blowback about Flock’s surveillance practices, contracts with the company are now being scrutinized in cities across the country. Flock did not provide a comment for this story.
WIRED obtained documents via public record request from a dozen Flock customers across the country and compared them to publicly available information from more than a dozen others. The documents shed light on how much Flock can actually cost communities, the way many of those deals are structured, and how the deals can expand over several years—leaving taxpayers on the hook year after year, with no end in sight.
“Once you let police officers try a tool,” says Matthew Guariglia, a senior policy analyst at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, “it becomes really hard to get the political will and motivation to take that tool away from them.”
How Flock Gets in the Door
When Flock was founded in 2017, it originally sold its license plate readers to private homeowner associations (HOAs). By the time the company decided to sell to police departments in 2019, it had an in: Rather than starting a camera network from scratch, police could start by accessing the cameras that HOAs were already using.
A version of this story played out in Alpharetta, Georgia. In 2020, the city’s police department paid Flock $17,680 for five Falcon cameras and logins for Flock software called Wing, which can extract vehicle and license plate data from off-brand camera footage. The next year, when Alpharetta bought a few more Flock cameras, a payment justification noted that “several” local private homeowner associations had already purchased Flock and granted them camera access.
“We are looking to add more city cameras into the Flock system,” the justification read. According to the city, “other vendors” would “not integrate with our existing Flock system.”
Over the next several years, Alpharetta expanded its work with the company significantly. By 2025, the city’s annual Flock bill had ballooned to $381,000.
As in other industries, companies that sell technology to police often use financial incentives to get customers in the door. Clearview AI, Ring, and Taser have all ponied up enticing offers to agencies around the country.
“A lot of these police surveillance vendors have learned the lessons of general old salesmanship,” Guariglia tells WIRED. In other words, deals and discounts work.
In some cases, this looks like new and increasingly expansive Flock products. In 2025, for instance, Alpharetta paid for an upgrade to the Elite Package of FlockOS, which Flock describes as a real-time crime-center platform. Other products are first offered with a free trial; Alpharetta took advantage of one 90-day window last year to try a new product dubbed Nova.
Flock also expands its contracts by offering discounts if departments sign a multiyear contract. In 2024, Alpharetta locked into a five-year contract with Flock that would cost $254,250 the first year and $238,000 for each successive year. The agreement was $232,500 less than five one-year agreements, which could be subject to higher rates.
The Alpharetta Police Department declined to comment.
Five-year agreements are common among Flock customers, which the company has sometimes marketed as a “price-lock promotion.” In a November 2023 email, Flock customer success manager Gwen Saltal used this framing to offer a five-year deal to New York’s Albany County Sheriff’s Office.
“As you may be aware, on April 1st, the cost of new Falcons went from $2,500 to $3,000, which will apply for future renewal terms on existing cameras as well,” Saltal wrote. “If you would like to lock in your current camera rates, Flock is offering a 5-year contract to hold that pricing.” The Albany County Sheriff’s Office did not respond to a request for comment.
In other cities, Flock won long-term contracts because it offered a convenient product bundle. (This is far from exclusive to Flock; Motorola, for instance, recently inked a $54 million agreement with Louisiana for a slate of policing technology.)
Guillermo Mixer, the police chief of the central California city of Greenfield, reported in a January city council meeting that the annual cost of the city’s surveillance system was $112,900, spread across five contracts with three companies: Flock, the surveillance camera company SurveillanceGrid, and the drone company Paladin.
Mixer proposed ditching SurveillanceGrid and Paladin and instead locking into a five-year contract with Flock. The annual cost would be $136,940—about $24,000 more than its level of spending at the time. He noted, however, that the price included three new cameras and access to Flock911, which transmits 911 call data to responding officers, as well as drones from Aerodrome, a company Flock acquired in 2024.
A proposed order form listed dozens of other Flock products and services included in the contract, though it’s unclear how many of those were new additions.
In the end, Greenfield’s city council unanimously approved Mixer’s repackaged Flock contract. Mixer and the Greenfield Police Department did not respond to a request for comment.
What Your Money Gets You
WIRED reviewed a July 2022 “Public Sector Price Sheet” for Flock products for the Fort Lauderdale Police Department in Florida. Though it was generated for one specific agency, it reflects the approximate price ranges WIRED observed in Flock purchase orders around that time from around the country.
Historically, Flock has placed agencies into one of 14 pricing “buckets” for its software, depending on their size. Agencies in “Bucket 1” have one to 15 sworn officers and could pay as little as $2,000 or as much as $115,500 for Flock software, depending on whether they get a basic package or select multiple add-ons. The costs by bucket incrementally increase until Bucket 14—which is for state and federal agencies, or local forces with more than 3,000 officers—which the sheet says gets “custom” rates.
Hardware, meanwhile, tends to be sold at flat annual rates. According to the pricing sheet, individual license plate readers and surveillance cameras cost $3,000 to $5,200 per year, not including the cost of initial installation—which can run between $150 and $2,750 upfront.
The pricing sheet puts Flock’s individual gunshot detectors at $8,500 to $35,000 annually, depending on their range. The cost for its individual drones, meanwhile, is $50,000 to $150,000 per year, and Flock’s two “mobile security trailer” offerings cost $20,000 and $25,000 annually. Fort Lauderdale police did not respond to a request for comment.
Though prices vary depending on the size of a purchase and individual negotiations with a city, Flock’s pricing appears to be comparable to its competitors. Axon recently quoted Denver $150,000 to install 50 cameras across the city and maintain them for one year, while Motorola recently charged Manti, Utah, $4,704 for a single license plate reader.
Flock also has a pricing plan for replacing damaged or stolen products—a particularly relevant concern amid a national wave of vandalism targeting Flock cameras. Per Flock contract conditions, the company retains ownership of the products it sells to cities. This means that when people damage or destroy cameras, cities are on the hook for the cost. (It also means that if a city decides to end their Flock contract, they have to give the equipment back.)
According to Flock’s website and invoices reviewed by WIRED, the company has flat rates for replacing damaged or stolen products: $800 for cameras, $500 for poles, and $1,300 for both. (This is up from its 2021 pricing, according to documents from Anderson County, South Carolina, when its replacement cost was $500 for cameras and $150 for poles.)
Some cities have gone out of their way to draw attention to the fiscal toll of replacing damaged Flock equipment—sometimes overstating the cost in the process.
Police from Winona, Minnesota, and Rutherfordton, North Carolina, have said that camera replacements cost $3,000 and $3,500 each, respectively—or $2,200 and $2,700 higher than the listed cost. And in Derby, Kansas, after a man damaged 10 Flock cameras, local police claimed that he caused $26,000 in damages. But depending on whether he damaged the poles, replacements likely would have cost $8,000 to $13,000. Police from Winona, Rutherfordton, and Derby did not respond to a request for comment.
Flock’s pricing, ultimately, is much lower than other department expenses—like police helicopters, which can cost tens of millions of dollars annually, or hiring more police officers.
Still, when compared to other technology-related expenses, Flock spending can stand out.
In Pasadena, Texas, which has a population of about 148,500, the 2026 police budget allotted $427,133 for Flock, $500,842 for body camera software, and $500,000 for "Motorola maintenance." These were, by far, the most expensive technology purchases. Most of the other purchases had budgets of less than $100,000. The Pasadena Police Department did not respond to a request for comment.
Why Some Customers Are Ditching Flock
Across the country, cities big and small have chosen to increase their Flock spending significantly over just a few years.
Savannah, Georgia, for instance, paid $33,000 for Flock in 2020 and $193,500 in 2025. Snellville, Georgia, paid Flock $5,000 in 2021 and 2022; in 2025, it paid $163,275. This year, as of August, the city has paid Flock $138,934.94. The Savannah and Snellville Police Departments did not respond to requests for comment.
However, in some cases, Flock’s pricing eventually proved to be prohibitive.
Jack Hall—the sheriff of Lorain County, Ohio—recently announced that the county would be canceling its Flock contract. Hall said that Flock planned to raise Lorain County’s two-year rate for 15 cameras by 17 percent. For him, it was too much.
Hall and the Lorain County Sheriff’s Office did not respond for comment.
Killingworth, Connecticut, also decided to end its relationship with Flock. The town paid $14,600 last year for four cameras. Killingworth first selectman Eric Couture noted “privacy concerns” related to Flock and said that it didn’t provide much to police relative to its cost.
Couture told WIRED that Flock’s cost wasn’t entirely prohibitive. But, he added, the cameras “did not add any utility” for the town’s “resident state trooper.”

India: Joint submission to GANHRI regarding review of the accreditation status of the National Human Rights Commission of India
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

We, the undersigned, are regional and international human rights nongovernmental organizations as well as individuals expressing concerns over the developments at the National Human Rights Commission of India (NHRCI).
The submitting organizations have varying degrees of direct work with the NHRCI. Most of us have been involved in advocacy to push for the NHRCI’s compliance with the United Nations Principles relating to the Status of National Institutions (The Paris Principles). We have repeatedly made submissions to the Sub-Committee on Accreditation (SCA) concerning the accreditation of NHRCI in 2023, 2024, 2025, most recently in March 2026 and now in this “Alteration of Accreditation.”
Summary:
In March 2025, the GANHRI-SCA recommended downgrading NHRCI’s accreditation and gave it one year before making a final decision. The SCA recommended that the NHRCI improve its processes and functions in line with the Paris Principles. The NHRCI challenged the downgrade before GANHRI but it was rejected in December 2025, and the NHRCI’s “Alteration of Accreditation” review was postponed from March to November 2026.
The SCA formally raised concerns about the NHRCI in 2011 and then reiterated it in its 2016, 2017, 2023, 2024 and 2025 reports to the Indian government and the NHRCI over its mandate to respond to the escalating human rights violations in India, lack of pluralism in selection and appointments of its core members, insufficient cooperation with human rights bodies, and concerns over its ability to function independent of government interference.
In March 2026, several of us wrote to your office sharing our concerns about the NHRCI’s functioning and its limited compliance with the recommendations made by the SCA.
We acknowledge that there has been an increase in the number of suo motu cases taken up by the commission, and media coverage and external communications of NHRCI’s activities appears to have improved. However, these improvements appear to be cosmetic, failing to address the core concerns regarding its mandate. For instance, the NHRCI’s redesigned website displays lots of numbers on the homepage on complaints and cases disposed, but with little context. The numbers present no clarity on deaths in police custody, judicial custody, or allegations of extrajudicial killings registered by the commission. This is important data that the website publicly disclosed earlier in keeping with the crucial oversight role the commission plays in custodial deaths. This is at a time when the United Nations Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination (CERD) found large-scale violations by law enforcement authorities, including extrajudicial killings and increased targeting of vulnerable groups.
The NHRCI had a year to implement the SCA’s recommendations but failed to address India’s deteriorating human rights situation. Various UN human rights experts and groups have raised concerns about the misuse of counterterrorism and foreign funding laws to crack down on civil society, unlawful detentions and forcible expulsions of ethnic Bengali Muslims and Rohingya refugees to Bangladesh, the arbitrary removal of millions of names from electoral rolls under the Special Intensive Revision, and allegations of extrajudicial killings and police abuses. For instance, the NHRCI did not take timely action when the police and security forces in New Delhi used excessive force against students and others peacefully protesting for educational reforms in July 2026. The authorities used batons, tear gas and pellet guns, injuring over a 100 people, and several women alleged being molested and beaten by police officers.
The NHRCI and the Indian government have repeatedly failed to implement the committee’s recommendations, as detailed below. In this context, we strongly urge GANHRI-SCA to amend the current “A” rating of the NHRCI to accurately reflect its failure to comply with the Paris Principles and address the deteriorating human rights situation in India.
Involvement of police officers in NHRCI investigations
The SCA in its 2017, 2023, 2024 and 2025 reviews noted that the NHRCI’s use of police officers “poses a concern about the perceived or real conflict of interest in having police officers seconded from the government engaged in investigations of human rights violations including those committed by police.” The SCA recommended amendments to Section 11 of the Protection of Human Rights Act (PHRA), 1993 which empowers the Indian government to appoint police officers above a certain rank for the efficient performance of the NHRCI. Till date, the NHRCI and the Indian government have not addressed this concern and have failed to undertake any legislative measures to comply with the SCA’s recommendation. The SCA observed in its 2025 review that instead of directly addressing the main concerns, the NHRCI had so far only proposed internal rules to allow them to appoint those other than police officers to form a part of their investigations. But on its website, the NHRCI clearly highlights that its Investigation Division, while “multidimensional,” comprises solely of police officers while other competent persons capable of carrying out independent investigations such as senior lawyers/retired public prosecutors, forensic experts, and experienced human rights investigators remain absent.
Such conflict of interest highlighted by the SCA is emblematic in NHRCI’s inability to hold police authorities accountable or conduct any independent inquiries into systemic police abuses. In February 2026, UN special rapporteurs urged the Indian government to launch independent inquiries into “alarming allegations of hundreds of extrajudicial killings and torture-related deaths and thousands of injuries by law enforcement officials” which disproportionately affected Muslims, Dalits, and indigenous communities like the Adivasis, especially in states such as Assam and Uttar Pradesh.
Opacity in appointments and lack of pluralism in selection criteria
The NHRCI has not incorporated any of the recommendations by the SCA to ensure it functions without any political interference. The SCA has repeatedly emphasized that the “fundamental requirement of the Paris Principles is that an NHRI is, and is perceived to be, able to operate independent of government interference.” The Indian government continues to appoint a Secretary-General who is inevitably a former civil servant whereas the SCA recommended it to amend the PHRA in such a manner that it enables the NHRCI to recruit candidates independently. The NHRCI has failed to amend the law and has instead extended the tenure of the Secretary-General three times, most recently in July 2026.
The NHRCI has not complied with the SCA’s recommendations to ensure pluralistic diversity in its leadership and functioning with two of its commissioner positions vacant since 2021 and 2018 respectively. In 2025, the SCA stated it was “concerned that the composition of the membership of the NHRC with only one woman and the composition of the staff was not sufficient to meet the pluralism requirements of the Paris Principles.” The SCA recommended that NHRCI advocate for amendments that ensure a composition representative of Indian society, including but not limited to religious or ethnic minorities, and the adequate representation of women in the institution’s decision-making body.
The NHRCI has also failed to introduce any transparency measures to the process of selection and appointment of the chairperson, who is currently appointed by the President of India, based on the recommendation by a committee that includes the Prime Minister. The SCA in its 2025 session expressed concerns about the process and recommended the NHRCI to publicly list the vacancies, have broad consultations or participation to ensure a diverse pool of candidates for the position.
Limited constructive engagement with civil society
The NHRCI has not taken any additional steps to engage with civil society organizations and human rights defenders in India despite the SCA’s recommendation reiterating constructive engagement. In its review session in 2025, the SCA stated that several civil society actors alleged NHRCI of not cooperating with them. Furthermore, NHRCI has excluded interacting with those civil society actors who are critical of their performance.
The NHRCI has failed to speak out against the Indian government’s escalating crackdown against thousands of nongovernmental organizations (NGOs), many of them working with vulnerable communities. As of September 2026, the government had canceled the foreign funding licenses of 22,493 NGOs under the Foreign Contribution Regulation Act. UN human rights experts have repeatedly urged the Indian government to repeal the FCRA and warned that it was being used to silence organizations whose priorities did not align with those of the government.
The NHRCI has failed to protect human rights defenders in the country, particularly those working with vulnerable communities or religious minorities, and on environmental rights. Most recently, it remained silent on the arrests of five Indigenous human rights defenders in Assam even after four UN experts expressed concern and urged their release in July.
Failure to address human rights violations
The NHRCI has remained conspicuously silent even as India has witnessed a worrying escalation in human rights violations over the past decade. In its 2025 report, the SCA stated it was “concerned the NHRC has not provided adequate information about how they are addressing the shrinking civic space and increased instances of targeting human rights defenders, journalists and perceived critics.”
In its August 2026 report, the CERD raised concerns over the “large-scale violations perpetrated by law enforcement officials against ethnic and ethno-religious groups, Indigenous and Tribal peoples, including Scheduled Tribes and Scheduled Castes, particularly Dalits and non-citizens.” The report should have prompted the NHRCI to strengthen its mechanisms in responding to such violations. Instead, the Indian government sought to refute the report, calling it “highly malicious.”
The NHRCI and the Indian government did not publicly acknowledge the findings of the three UN human rights experts either who raised concerns about the Election Commission’s ongoing voter lists revision across the country. Over 60 million names have been removed from the country’s electoral rolls and the UN experts highlighted a lack of transparency, potential for bias and the potential large-scale disenfranchisement of voters, particularly those from religious minority groups, despite India’s obligations under the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. The NHRCI did not take any action after receiving a letter from a civil society group in July, asking it to hold a public hearing on the large-scale removal of names from the voter rolls.
The NHRCI has remained silent on the Indian government’s discriminatory policies against religious minorities especially Muslims and Christians, increasing violence against religious minorities as well as Dalits and Adivasis, and when the authorities carry out arbitrary demolitions of Muslim homes and properties as a form of collective punishment against the community. In 2024, the Supreme Court ruled that such demolitions were illegal and in 2025, four UN experts called on Indian authorities to put an end to them.
The NHRCI has failed to act on numerous human rights violations and gender-based violence in Manipur where ethnic violence since May 2023 has killed over 300 people and displaced over 60,000.
Since 2025, Indian authorities have forcibly expelled hundreds of ethnic Bengali Muslims to Bangladesh without any due process. In 2025, the Indian government unlawfully expelled 100 Rohingya refugees to Bangladesh and then forced another 40 Rohingya refugees into the sea near Myanmar, giving them life jackets. A UN expert called the Indian authorities’ actions an “affront to human decency” in May 2025. The CERD report in August highlighted an increase in law enforcement operations like police checks involving racial profiling, arbitrary arrests and detention without due process of vulnerable communities such as Rohingya, Bengali-speaking Muslims, migrants and asylum-seekers. In 2024, the CERD called on India to end discrimination against the Rohingya community and stop arbitrarily detaining them. The committee said it was “alarmed by reports of widespread racist hate speech and harmful stereotypes against Rohingya, including by politicians and public figures.”
Over the past decade, the NHRCI has not intervened when Indian authorities have targeted students, activists, lawyers, journalists, and critics of the government under the abusive, counterterrorism law, the Unlawful Activities Prevention Act (UAPA). This includes 16 prominent activists who promoted the rights of persons from India’s most marginalized communities, accusing them of inciting violence that occurred during a Dalit meeting in January 2018 in Bhima Koregaon in Maharashtra state. The trial is yet to begin but 15 activists arrested in the case spent years in jail before they were granted bail, while 84-year-old Stan Swamy, a prominent tribal rights activist, died in custody, which a UN expert termed as “a stain on India’s human rights record.” According to reports by the US-based forensic firm Arsenal Consulting, malware was used to surveil and plant evidence on the computers of at least three accused in this case.
The NHRCI did not take any action against Delhi Police officials after they were accused of conducting biased investigations involving the arrests of activists in cases related to the February 2020 violence in Delhi following peaceful protests against the discriminatory Citizenship (Amendment) Act. The police arrested 18 student leaders and activists, most of them Muslim, under the counterterrorism law, of whom at least 11 have been granted bail. The trial has not yet begun and UN experts have called for the release of the activists, including Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam who have been repeatedly denied bail.
Indian authorities continue to restrict the rights to free expression and peaceful assembly in Jammu and Kashmir, seven years after revoking the region’s special autonomous status. There are growing restrictions on media, a number of journalists and human rights defenders have been arrested on spurious terrorism charges, and authorities regularly harass critics including through counterterrorism raids.
Signed,
Amnesty International
CIVICUS: World Alliance for Citizen Participation
CSW (Christian Solidarity Worldwide)

The Riyadh attacks and the fragility of regional security: Implications for global politics, oil markets and the world economy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:58:34 UTC
17:58:34 KST

The recent attacks on Riyadh, Saudi Arabia’s capital, particularly the strikes against King Khalid International Airport, represent a significant escalation in the security crisis affecting the Middle East. Beyond the immediate loss of life and disruption to civilian aviation, these incidents raise fundamental questions about regional deterrence, the internationalisation of the Yemen conflict, the security of global energy supplies and the resilience of the international political and economic order. According to reporting by Reuters and Al Jazeera on 12 October, 2026, a strike on Saturday killed 12 people and injured more than 300, while a subsequent attack on Sunday killed one person and injured 11. Saudi authorities and regional governments have attributed the attacks to Yemen’s Houthi movement, which is aligned with Iran. The attacks have also prompted renewed diplomatic and security cooperation among Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Turkiye and Egypt.
The significance of these developments lies not only in the immediate damage but also in their potential to connect several existing conflicts: the war in Yemen, the confrontation involving Iran and the United States, insecurity around the Red Sea and the vulnerability of Gulf energy infrastructure.
The central argument of this column is that the Riyadh attacks should be understood as both a regional security crisis and a potential international economic shock. Their ultimate consequences will depend on the scale of retaliation, the effectiveness of diplomatic intervention, the protection of maritime and energy infrastructure and the willingness of regional powers to prevent further escalation. The attacks expose the increasing interdependence of security challenges across the Arabian Peninsula. Saudi Arabia’s involvement in Yemen, the Houthi movement’s military capabilities and the broader confrontation involving Iran and the United States have created an environment in which a local conflict can generate consequences far beyond its original theatre. Reuters reported on 7 October, 2026 that Saudi Arabia had returned to a more active military role in Yemen following Houthi advances near the Red Sea coast. The renewed fighting has intensified threats to Saudi cities, airports and energy infrastructure.
Three security implications deserve particular attention.
First, the vulnerability of strategic infrastructure. Airports, oil facilities, ports and logistics centres are essential to Saudi Arabia’s security and economic development. Attacks against such facilities can disrupt transportation and commerce even when the attackers do not achieve their wider military objectives.
Second, the danger of reciprocal escalation. Saudi Arabia faces pressure to demonstrate that it can protect its territory and population. However, extensive retaliatory operations could provoke further Houthi attacks, expand the geographical scope of the conflict and increase civilian suffering in Yemen.
Third, the regionalisation of collective defence. On 12 October, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Turkiye and Egypt jointly condemned the attacks. Their declaration signalled diplomatic solidarity and support for Saudi Arabia’s legitimate defensive measures. Reuters also reported that Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye had agreed to implement collective-defence commitments under their defence arrangement.
READ: Bloomberg: Saudi Arabia disappointed by limited support from Western allies
This cooperation could strengthen deterrence, but it also raises questions about the conditions under which partners might provide intelligence, air defence, logistics or military assistance. Diplomatic solidarity should not automatically be interpreted as a commitment by every participating state to offensive military action.
The Riyadh attacks must be interpreted within the broader competition for influence among regional and international powers. Saudi Arabia remains an important US security partner because of its energy resources, strategic location and role in Gulf affairs. Repeated attacks on Saudi territory increase pressure on Washington to provide intelligence, defensive equipment and other forms of support.
Yet American policymakers face a difficult calculation. Direct military intervention against the Houthis could improve Saudi Arabia’s immediate defensive position, but it could also widen the conflict and expose US personnel, shipping and regional facilities to further attacks.
The central strategic question is whether deterrence can be restored without turning the Saudi-Houthi confrontation into a broader US-led military campaign. Reuters reported on 11 October that Washington was considering its response while Saudi Arabia sought additional support.
The Houthis are aligned with Iran, but their relationship should not be reduced to the assumption that every Houthi decision is directly controlled by Tehran. The movement has its own political interests, domestic constituencies and strategic calculations.
Nevertheless, the wider confrontation involving Iran creates opportunities for the Houthis to increase pressure on Saudi Arabia and complicate the security calculations of Riyadh’s partners.
For Iran, instability affecting Saudi infrastructure and Red Sea access could impose strategic and economic costs on its rivals. However, these possible advantages must be weighed against the danger of regional escalation and stronger international cooperation against the movement.
Iran’s role should therefore be analysed through three distinct questions: what support it provides, what influence it exercises and what decisions the Houthis make independently. These are related but not identical issues.
The joint response from Riyadh, Islamabad, Ankara and Cairo is especially significant for the future of regional security diplomacy. For Pakistan, the crisis presents a difficult policy challenge: protecting its strategic relationship with Saudi Arabia while avoiding unnecessary involvement in an expanding conflict. Pakistan must also consider the safety of its citizens in the Gulf, energy-import costs and the consequences of regional instability for its economy. Turkiye’s defence capabilities and Egypt’s strategic interests in the Red Sea add further dimensions to this emerging cooperation. If managed carefully, coordination among these states could strengthen air defence, intelligence sharing and maritime security. However, an effective regional framework would need clear limits on military commitments, credible crisis communication and diplomatic channels capable of preventing an incident from triggering a wider war.
The oil implications are among the most consequential aspects of the crisis. Saudi Arabia is a major global oil producer and exporter. Threats to its energy infrastructure can therefore influence oil prices, shipping costs, insurance premiums and expectations about future supply.
The effects are not limited to damage at a particular facility. Markets also react to the possibility that attacks could spread to production sites, refineries, pipelines, export terminals or maritime routes.

14th Bosphorus Film Festival announces documentary, short film juries
Unknown

Aise Humeyra Akgun
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
The jury members who will evaluate films competing in the documentary and short film categories of the 14th Bosphorus Film Festival, organized by the Bosphorus Culture and Arts Foundation with Anadolu as its Global Communication Partner, have been announced.
The festival, which will be held from Nov. 8-15 with the support of the Turkish Culture and Tourism Ministry’s General Directorate of Cinema, will feature director and producer Abdullah Harun Ilhan, Bahriye Kabadayi Dal and academic and director Musa Ak on its documentary film jury.
The short film jury will consist of cinematographer Emre Pekcakir, Slovenian-Italian director and screenwriter Martin Turk and Austrian actress Sarah Zaharanski.
Diverse figures in documentary cinema
Abdullah Harun Ilhan, whose work in cinema and photography has been featured at international festivals, is known for projects he has directed and produced, as well as photography exhibitions and work carried out across different regions.
Ilhan, who holds two master’s degrees in cinema, develops projects in Turkish, English and Arabic.
Bahriye Kabadayi Dal, who continues to work in documentary cinema, won the Turkish Film Critics Association (SIYAD) Best Documentary Award for her first feature-length documentary, “Devrimci Genclik Koprusu” (Revolutionary Youth Bridge).
Dal, who founded Tarcin Film in 2013, has documentaries including “Bogazici Baliklari” (Fish of Bosphorus), “Hakkari’nin Gizemli Taslari” (The Mysterious Stones of Hakkari), “Baksi, Utopyadan Gercege” (Baksi, From Utopia to Reality), “Denizlerin Koruyuculari” (Guardians of the Seas) and “Horona Duranlar” in her filmography.
Musa Ak, who completed his undergraduate and master’s studies at Erciyes University’s Faculty of Communication and earned his doctorate from Istanbul University’s Department of Radio, Television and Cinema, is known for his academic work on documentary and digital cinema.
Ak has participated in national and international festivals with documentaries including “Tuzdan Hayaller” (Dreams of Salt), “Bir Orkestranin Izinde” (Searching for ‘The Band’), “Cerde,” “Kafali,” “Tutunmak,” “Turab” and “Mada,” as well as the fiction film “Is.”
He serves as an assistant professor at Karabuk University’s Safranbolu Turker Inanoglu Faculty of Communication.
Ak is also the author of the book “Dijitallesme ve Yeni Medya Doneminde Belgesel Film Estetigi” (Digitalization and Documentary Film Aesthetics in New Media Era).
Short film jury
Emre Pekcakir, a member of the short film jury, has worked as a cinematographer on numerous short and feature-length productions.
In 2011, Pekcakir was nominated for Best Cinematographer at the Antalya Golden Orange Film Festival for “Hangi Film” and has worked on productions including “Balayi,” “Son Hasat,” “Sut Ciftligi,” “Iyi Bir Aile Degiliz” and “Mori.”
Slovenian director and screenwriter Martin Turk studied film and television directing at the Academy of Theatre, Radio, Film and Television (AGRFT) in Ljubljana.
His films have been screened at international festivals, including the Directors’ Fortnight at the Cannes Film Festival, and he has directed four feature films and numerous shorts.
Turk serves as an assistant professor of film at the University of Nova Gorica’s School of Arts.
Austrian actress and voice artist Sarah Zaharanski works across film, television, theater and radio.
Zaharanski has performed at arts institutions including Berlin’s Schaubuhne and the Salzburg Festival. Her film work includes “Woodland,” which premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF), “Soldier Monika,” which was selected for the competition section of the Torino Film Festival, and the award-winning short film “Dear Mother.”
The program of the 14th Bosphorus Film Festival and updates on the event are available on the festival’s official website and social media accounts.

Euro depreciates amid regional financial, political turmoil
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:56:28 UTC
17:56:28 KST

Bahattin Gonultas and Emir Yildirim
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
The common currency of the 21 EU member states continues to depreciate against the US dollar amid mounting financial and political uncertainty in the bloc.
Concerns have reignited in the eurozone over fears of a repeat of the 2012 debt crisis, driven by France’s deepening fiscal indiscipline, political crisis and ongoing street protests, alongside Spain’s snap elections and Italy’s debt vulnerability.
The Middle East crisis continues to drive up energy costs, adding to volatility in the global bond market, while persistent inflation has cemented the downward pressure on the euro’s value as a medium-term trend.
The euro/US dollar exchange rate has been on a gradual downward trend since testing its January high of 1.21. The exchange rate dropped to 1.11 amid ongoing developments, hitting its lowest level since May 2025.
The euro has depreciated by around 5% this year, and the currency has now come under the spotlight as a sign of persistent fragility in the financial world despite having been largely unaffected by bond market volatility in recent months.
Developments in France, the second-largest economy in the eurozone, have been driving the euro’s depreciation.
France’s 10-year bond yield hit its highest level since 2002, nearing 5% amid geopolitical risks and leading to global bond sell-offs.
France’s overall public budget deficit widened to 5.8% of gross domestic product (GDP), exceeding the EU’s 3% threshold, according to the French National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies (INSEE) and Paris.
The country has failed to post a budget surplus since 1974, while nominal growth rates have dropped below borrowing rates, dragging the country further into structural debt.
France’s total nominal debt stock hit a historic €3.6 trillion ($4 trillion), accounting for 119% of GDP and exceeding the 60% Maastricht criterion.
The spread between French and German borrowing costs reached its widest level since the major debt crisis of 2012.
Meanwhile, uncertainty in the eurozone has not been limited to France, as the crisis in Spain has also contributed.
Spain’s housing market policies brought political risks to the EU’s fourth-largest economy after Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez decided to call snap elections in November.
The US, on the other hand, is not facing global repercussions despite its historic debt burden exceeding $40 trillion and its inability to maintain spending discipline due to upcoming midterm elections.
Global capital continues to flock to the US dollar as a safe haven amid tensions in the Middle East.
Analysts say movements in the exchange rate stem directly from the euro’s weakness caused by developments in France, while the fragmented structure of national financial markets in the eurozone leaves the region vulnerable to such shocks despite sharing a common currency.
The European Central Bank’s (ECB) room for monetary policy maneuver is being limited by the financial and political turmoil.
The bank had been expected to hike rates three times next year, but these expectations have shifted to two 25-basis-point rate hikes due to the economic slowdown in the region and debt risks, alongside the loss of confidence and the widening interest rate gap between the US and Europe.
Selling pressure on the euro is expected to persist as long as structural problems remain unresolved and political tensions continue, analysts say.
While analysts think a new debt crisis is not inevitable and that France will not be driven into bankruptcy, they believe the euro is highly unlikely to strengthen against the US dollar under current conditions.
Carsten Brzeski, chief economist at ING Germany, recently said the deepening political turmoil in France reflects structural problems threatening the economic stability of the bloc. He noted that the country had already changed prime ministers six times since 2020 and urged the European Commission and the ECB to take action against Paris, as the government had managed to bring the budget deficit below the 3% goal only twice in the past two decades.
He added that political instability and uncertainty would take a toll on the economy and push France toward stagnation.
Chris Turner, head of global markets research at ING, said the euro/US dollar exchange rate would continue to be capped within the 1.10-1.15 range over the next two quarters due to the Fed’s hawkish stance and rising bond yields.
He added that further losses in the euro could be prevented by a fiscal consolidation program adopted by the French parliament, while the White House’s strategies after the midterm elections would determine the exchange rate’s direction.

Former DR Congo President Kabila joins M23 rebels in a new coalition
Kinshasa braces for potential conflict as Kabila allies with M23 rebels, challenging President Tshisekedi’s regime.
Former Congolese President Joseph Kabila has launched a new political and military coalition, including the Rwanda-backed M23 armed group, which has captured vast areas of the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).
Kabila introduced the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN) at a news conference on Monday at his residence in the eastern city of Goma, which the M23 has controlled since January 2025.
Kabila said he will head the FRN with rebel leaders, including Corneille Nangaa, the former leader of the Congo River Alliance (AFC) and the political wing of M23, serving as his deputies.
Claude Ibalanky, a coalition adviser, said the group aims to unite all resistance forces “to put an end to tyranny by any means necessary, including the use of force”.
There was no immediate response to the announcement from the DRC government.
Reporting from Goma, Al Jazeera’s Alain Uaykani said there were growing fears that fighting in eastern DRC could escalate.
“Kabila addressed the nation, explaining his plan. People are making comments across the country that this is another level of the conflict,” Uaykani explained.
Uaykani said rebels already hold Goma, Bukabu, the airports and key border crossings with Rwanda and Uganda, and that the government has been unable to push them back. Talks to resolve the conflict have also failed, with each side blaming the other.
“The government has shown no sign of defeating these people,” he said.
Uaykani noted that Kabila is a former army chief and said there were fears that government troops could defect.
“He’s still a soldier; he has led an army. People are worried that more soldiers from the government may join him as well”.
Yvon Muya, a researcher at the University of Ottawa in Canada, said the announcement increases the chances of a confrontation between Kabila and DRC President Felix Tshisekedi, and could lead to more fighting in eastern DRC.
“You don’t make an announcement like this without having prepared the actions that follow,” Muya said. “We will likely witness an escalation on the military front.”
Representatives from the DRC government and the M23 movement were expected to meet in Qatar in November for talks, but analysts warn that the new coalition could undermine the process.
Kabila led the DRC from 2001 to 2019, taking office at 29 after his father, President Laurent Kabila, was assassinated.
A DRC military court sentenced Joseph Kabila to death in absentia last year on charges of treason, war crimes and crimes against humanity, finding that he collaborated with Rwanda and M23.
Kabila has called the case politically motivated and denies the charges.
The US imposed sanctions on him earlier this year over his alleged role in funding rebel groups.
The DRC, the United States and United Nations experts accuse Rwanda of backing M23, an allegation Rwanda denies.
Tshisekedi’s second term ends in 2028, and his allies have been preparing public opinion for changes to the constitution’s two-term limit, as rebel activities intensify in the east.

Hurricane Simon hits Mexico after storms kill 6

Hurricane Simon hitting western Mexico after tropical systems kill 6
The death toll from Hurricane Simon and the remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel rose to six Tuesday after heavy rains triggered flooding and landslides along Mexico's Pacific coast, authorities said.
Hurricane Simon continued moving slowly off Mexico's Pacific coast as a Category 1 storm, bringing heavy rain to Nayarit and Sinaloa states, where authorities remained on alert for rising rivers and flooding. Over the weekend, the hurricane brought heavy rain to the southern state of Guerrero, killing one person.
While the eye of the hurricane remained offshore, its outer bands slammed communities this week between the Sierra Madre and the Pacific Ocean near Puerto Vallarta.
Simon's 90 mph strongest sustained winds made it a Category 1 storm, but the U.S. National Hurricane Center in Miami said it had technically become a small tropical cyclone. Simon was 115 miles west of Cabo Corrientes and heading west at 2 mph.
The hurricane center said the storm's intensity could fluctuate over the next few days but would likely maintain hurricane strength through Thursday, with gradual weakening forecast thereafter.
Hurricane Simon rain and flood forecast
Up to 3 inches of rain are expected from Simon across the Mexican states of Baja California Sur, Nayarit and Sinaloa by Friday, the weather service said.
Moisture associated with Simon is forecast to bring the potential for flash flooding from this evening through Friday morning to parts of Texas, New Mexico, Oklahoma, Kansas and Missouri, according to CBS News meteorologist Nikki Nolan. Rainfall could total 6 inches and perhaps 8 in some spots.
Tropical weather turns deadly
In Mexico's Baja California state, rescuers on Monday combed parts of the coastal city of Ensenada, where floodwaters swept away vehicles and damaged homes. At least four people died in the state due to the impact of post-tropical cyclone Rachel.
Resident Johana Nuriulu said the flooding began during the night, shortly after heavy rain knocked out electricity. "We heard a loud noise that sounded like ocean waves, but really loud," she said.
Nuriulu said she went outside and discovered that a nearby stream had overflowed, sending water rushing through the neighborhood. The waters inundated streets and homes, sweeping away vehicles and other belongings. "Everything was being dragged away," Nuriulu said.
Several communities were cut off by landslides and overflowing rivers elsewhere in Baja California.
In the afternoon, the Mexican military used helicopters to rescue 32 people — 22 of them foreigners — from a ranch in Ensenada. Baja California Gov. Marina del Pilar Ávila said 13 were youths.
The state Secretary of Security, Gen. Laureano Carrillo, said some of the group were missionaries meeting at the ranch and that among them were Germans and Americans.
The victims included a 13-year-old girl whose body was found Sunday, two women ages 30 and 35 and a 4-year-old boy whose bodies were recovered Monday, and an unidentified person found near a stream Tuesday, the state prosecutor's office told The Associated Press.
Five others remained missing in Baja California, including three in Ensenada and a father and son who went fishing Saturday in San Felipe, on the Gulf of California, and never returned.
According to Ávila, some 14,000 federal and state personnel had been deployed across Baja California to assist affected residents and respond to the emergency.
To the south, Simon downed trees and electricity poles, blocked roads and flooded homes in coastal towns of Guerrero state, including the major seaport of Acapulco, Gov. Evelyn Salgado said at a news conference.
A 71-year-old man died after a wall collapsed in Chilpancingo, Guerrero's capital, Salgado said.
In Puerto Vallarta, workers removed wooden panels from boarded-up storefronts and businesses reopened Monday as rains eased. The popular tourist destination's international airport suspended operations until Tuesday morning.
"Personally, I think we should remain on alert because we don't really know whether it will arrive, move elsewhere or dissipate," said Noelia Carrillo, a tourism agency worker.
U.S. impact from storms 
Rachel weakened into a post-tropical cyclone as it moved north into Southern California. The storm battered the coast with unusually large waves, which tore apart a boardwalk and smashed into homes in Long Beach. Some residents were forced to evacuate.
Las Vegas tied an all-time daily rainfall record for October when it received 1.08 inches of rain into Sunday morning, according to the U.S. National Weather Service. The record was set in 1947.
Videos posted on social media showed a torrent of water rushing through a street near the Las Vegas Strip, with a Ferris wheel and casinos in the background.
Flood advisories were mostly lifted by late Monday in Utah, Arizona and elsewhere in the Southwest.
In Utah, dozens of runners and volunteers who were part of the Moab 240 ultramarathon were evacuated Sunday after being stranded by flooding. The race goes through Canyonlands and Arches national parks.
The additional rainfall isn't associated with Rachel, but a different weather system moving across the West, forecasters said. The precipitation is expected to end by Wednesday.
Power was gradually being restored after Hurricane Isaias hit the U.S. Southeast.
At least four deaths have been linked to Isaias, the first hurricane of the Atlantic season, which came ashore as a Category 2 hurricane Friday near Destin, Florida, a Gulf Coast vacation spot filled with high-rises and tourist shops. The storm then roared into Alabama with tropical-force winds before dissipating farther north.

Montenegro provisionally closes 3 more chapters in EU accession talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13

17:46:20 KST

Talha Ozturk
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
Montenegro provisionally closed three more negotiating chapters in its accession talks with the European Union, bringing the total number of provisionally closed chapters to 21, officials announced Monday evening.
The chapters, covering economic and monetary policy, statistics, and social policy and employment, were closed during an intergovernmental conference in Luxembourg.
Prime Minister Milojko Spajic said on US social media company X that the three chapters represent key pillars of European integration: responsible economic governance, reliable policymaking and social progress.
Thanking the European Commission and all 27 EU member states, Spajic congratulated the heads and members of the working groups involved in the negotiations.
“At this point, the government of Montenegro has fulfilled literally all obligations within its competence required for the final phase of negotiations,” he said.
Spajic expressed confidence that the necessary political consensus and compromise would be reached at other levels to bring the accession process to a successful conclusion.
“We continue to move forward decisively with our European partners toward Montenegro’s full EU membership in 2028,” he added.
EU urges further reforms
EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos welcomed the progress, saying reforms under the three chapters would contribute to price stability, provide governments with reliable data for better decision-making and strengthen workers’ rights and workplace safety.
Kos noted that nearly two-thirds of all negotiating chapters have now been closed, describing the finish line as within reach.
She urged political parties in both the government and opposition to put the interests of Montenegrin citizens first, work together and implement the remaining reforms without delay.
Montenegro’s Foreign Minister Ervin Ibrahimovic also welcomed the development, describing it as an important step toward strengthening the country’s economic system, improving statistical capacities and developing labor market and social policies.
“Every closed chapter represents a concrete result of our work, but also an additional responsibility to continue decisively and with dedication to fulfill all remaining obligations on the European agenda,” Ibrahimovic said.
He noted that the latest progress followed a successful Berlin Process ministerial meeting in Przno, where participants expressed strong support for the European future of the Western Balkans, particularly Montenegro’s accession efforts.
Ibrahimovic thanked EU member states, fellow foreign ministers and Commissioner Kos for their continued support.
He reaffirmed Montenegro’s commitment to completing accession negotiations and becoming a full member of the EU, saying the closure of three additional chapters demonstrated that the country’s European future was being built through concrete results.
Montenegro is widely regarded as the frontrunner for EU membership among Western Balkan candidate countries, having made the most progress in accession negotiations and aiming to join the bloc by 2028.
Montenegro declared independence from its state union with Serbia on June 3, 2006, following a referendum held on May 21 in which 55.5% of voters supported independence.
The Balkan country applied for EU membership in December 2008 and was granted candidate status in December 2010.
Montenegro formally launched accession negotiations with the EU in June 2012, becoming one of the frontrunners in the Western Balkans’ EU integration process.
The country joined NATO in June 2017 and has since maintained EU membership as a key foreign policy priority.
Montenegro has opened all 33 negotiating chapters and, with the latest three closures, has provisionally closed 21.
The government aims to complete accession negotiations and secure full EU membership by 2028, although accession will ultimately require approval from all EU member states.

Yemeni government forces carried out nine airstrikes Tuesday targeting Houthi fighters and military equipment in the southwestern Taiz province as escalation continues to rage across the country, according to the army.
The Taiz Military Axis Media Center said warplanes belonging to the Yemeni armed forces carried out five strikes in the Al-Dhabab area and four others in Al-Misrakh district.
The strikes targeted Houthi personnel and military equipment, the center said.
It added that clashes were also ongoing between government forces and Houthi fighters on the Al-Shaqab front south of Taiz.

Yemen has been engulfed in war since the Houthis seized Sanaa and several of the country’s 22 provinces in September 2014, prompting an Arab coalition led by neighboring Saudi Arabia to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.

Government forces and their allies control the interim capital Aden, the eastern provinces of Al-Mahra and Hadramout, the southern provinces of Shabwa and Abyan, most of Lahj and Al-Dhalea, and parts of Taiz, Marib, Al-Jawf, Hajjah and Saada.

fifty oak trees and stone-paved clearing shape contemporary italian piazza by ghisellini architetti
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:45:07 UTC
17:45:07 KST

fifty oak trees and stone-paved clearing shape contemporary italian piazza by ghisellini architetti
ghisellini architetti reorganizes public square madre francesca cabrini around shaded gathering areas, layered planting, and integrated rainwater systems that reconnect the town center with the surrounding lowland landscape.
[FEATURED]
a grid of oak trees frames porphyry-paved piazza in northern Italy
Ghisellini Architetti has redesigned Public Square Madre Francesca Cabrini as a contemporary Italian piazza framed by architecture and trees. Located in a small town in the lower Lodi area of Italy, the project reinterprets the open clearings of the region’s former lowland forests, creating a defined public space enclosed by three planted edges and the existing town hall.
Ghisellini Architetti reimagines the square as a tree-lined clearing
A continuous paving surface of Italian porphyry extends from north to south, aligning with the town hall’s facade and volume. Fifty oak trees representing three species are arranged in a 7-by-7 grid, providing shade and forming sheltered green spaces around the square. Paths weave through flowers, lawns, shrubs, and shade-tolerant undergrowth, while wooden benches, drinking fountains, trash bins, and bike racks support public use. The design team at Ghisellini Architetti uses concrete monoliths to separate pedestrian areas from vehicles.
A dual-level lighting system illuminates the square after dark
A two-level lighting system combines multi-projector poles with ground-level fixtures to illuminate the square after dark. The landscape and paving also integrate rainwater management and climate-responsive measures. Permeable surfaces and lawns help replenish groundwater and reduce summer heat, while the porphyry paving directs rainfall to an underground storage system. Collected water is reused to irrigate trees, lawns, and undergrowth, with excess water gradually released into the drainage network during heavy rainfall.

name: FOREST JUMP | Public Square ‘Madre Francesca Cabrini’
architect: Ghisellini Architetti | @ghisellini_architetti
location: Public Square Madre Francesca Cabrini, Lodi, Italy

The escalation in Yemen is a turning point
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:42:55 UTC
17:42:55 KST

The escalation in Yemen is a turning point
The risk of a region-wide war is increasing, but if cooler heads prevail, a peaceful arrangement can still be reached.
Yemen is witnessing a major military escalation that has once again brought the western coast and the area around the Bab al-Mandeb strait to the forefront of regional developments. Operation Yemen’s Dawn, launched by the forces loyal to the internationally recognised Yemeni government, has produced some results.
Government forces have advanced towards the strait of Bab al-Mandeb and are now fighting against reinforced Houthi positions. Clashes continue in parts of Dhubab District and around Dhubab Airport.
The central question now is whether these military moves can bring about a lasting change in the balance of power and whether they will widen the confrontation or open the way for a new negotiating process.
Control of Bab al-Mandeb
Fighting has concentrated around Bab al-Mandeb because of its strategic position in global trade and energy flows. It is especially significant to the parties to the Yemeni conflict because control of the coastline, islands and surrounding highlands offers varying capabilities for surveillance, military deployment and threats to maritime traffic.
An advance along the coast may enable government forces to retake key positions and restrict the Houthis’ space for manoeuvre. However, it does not, by itself, guarantee the security of the strait or eliminate threats to navigation.
Even if the Houthis lose coastal positions, they could still retain their ability to launch attacks in the Red Sea. Threats to maritime traffic do not necessarily depend on direct control of the strait; they also depend on the availability of missiles, drones, launch platforms, supply networks and the ability to operate from other locations.
As operations move from the coastal strip into the highlands, particularly the Kahbub Mountains in Lahj governorate and the highlands to the west and south-west of Taiz governorate, the challenges posed by the terrain, defence, movement and supply become more severe.
In this context, three distinct levels must be differentiated: retaking coastal positions, consolidating military control over them and establishing a sustainable capacity to secure the strait and its surrounding area. Confusing these levels may lead either to an exaggerated assessment of the operation’s results or to an underestimation of the adversary’s ability to continue fighting.
Unity and cohesion
Recent statements by Dr Rashad Al-Alimi, president of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, signal a shift in objectives: from containing the Houthi threat to restoring state institutions and liberating Sanaa.
This shift gives the ongoing fighting a national dimension that goes beyond limited gains on the ground. Its success, however, remains contingent on the government forces’ ability to unify command, secure supplies and coordinate the various military formations.
Containing divisions within the components of the government—particularly over the southern issue—is essential to preserving gains and preventing the confrontation from turning into an internal conflict.
Success requires coordination among participating formations, avoidance of competition over spheres of influence and the linking of military gains to security and political governance capable of preventing fighting between factions.
This is especially important because the formations playing the most effective role in the coastal battles, the Southern Giants Brigades, originate from the southern governorates.
The regional dimension
The Houthi escalation is difficult to understand in isolation from the Iran war. Iran’s support for the group is well-known, but recent media reports have also revealed the extent of it. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps reportedly has directed Houthi movements along the coast and encouraged escalation against Saudi Arabia, with commitments to provide further support.
Control of Bab al-Mandeb is strategically important to Iran and its allies, as increased pressure there can provide more leverage in the Iran conflict.
For Saudi Arabia, involvement in the Yemen conflict is driven by direct security concerns and a desire to reduce threats to its territory and nearby maritime routes.
Against this backdrop, a Saudi response to the deadly airport attacks appears highly likely. Riyadh may be less inclined to limit itself to familiar exchanges along existing front lines and could instead target sites or capabilities of greater importance within the Houthis’ military structure. What form the response takes may reflect efforts to impose significant costs without immediately widening the confrontation into a broader regional war.
At the Gulf level, collective military participation appears less certain. The attacks could prompt an emergency GCC meeting, stronger political statements, or greater defensive coordination, but reviving a joint military campaign against the Houthis would be more difficult. Gulf states no longer share the same degree of strategic alignment over Yemen, while differences, particularly between Saudi and Emirati priorities, continue to constrain collective action.
Pakistan and Turkiye, for their part, have announced support for Saudi Arabia under the Mecca Pact, although the exact parameters of their participation are yet to be defined. The current escalation may therefore test whether these partnerships remain political and defensive frameworks or translate into practical military support, including stronger air defence deployments.
US involvement also remains possible, but any direct role would likely be limited. Previous US intervention in Yemen has focused more on deterrence, maritime security and containing threats rather than on decisively shifting the battlefield balance in favour of the government forces.
An expanding confrontation does not automatically mean that all parties seek an open war. Some may use escalation to improve their deterrence or negotiating position, although the risk of miscalculation remains.
What happens next
Developments in the Yemen war in the near future depend on the government forces’ ability to hold the positions they have retaken, secure the area around the strait and the connecting roads and remove the Houthi threat from the highlands. If these conditions are met, the balance of military and political pressure could shift, though this would not necessarily end the Houthis’ maritime threat.
However, if the advance stalls at positions that are difficult to overcome and the Houthis are able to continue using missiles and drones to conduct counterattacks, this could create a protracted confrontation. A war of attrition could have a devastating humanitarian and economic impact not just on Yemen, but across the region.
The risk of escalation and region-wide war may still push the parties to seek an understanding or an arrangement to halt the fighting. Turning military advances into a settlement, however, would require addressing broader political and security issues, including power-sharing arrangements, mutual guarantees and the security of maritime routes.
In other words, the ongoing coastal battle could become a gateway to a broader change in the course of Yemen’s crisis rather than another round in a protracted war.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Pakistan Imposes Emergency and Governor’s Rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:42:00 UTC
17:42:00 KST

On October 11, Pakistan’s federal government imposed an emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) province, which was being governed by former Prime Minister Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI).
The move, which was approved by President Asif Ali Zardari on the advice of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif following a federal cabinet meeting, marks a decisive takeover by the federal government of a province that has long been a PTI stronghold. The federal government justified the decision by pointing to a sharp surge in terror attacks across KP, alleging that the provincial administration was obstructing counterterrorism efforts, failing to maintain public order and allowing militant groups space to operate.
The federal government invoked Articles 232 and 234 of the constitution, which grant extraordinary powers to the federal government over provincial affairs.
However, the two articles address different circumstances and operate within distinct mechanisms. For instance, Article 232 empowers the federal government to declare a state of emergency when security is threatened by war or internal disturbance beyond the provincial government’s control. Under this provision, the provincial assembly continues to function, but federal laws take precedence in cases of conflict.
On the other hand, Article 234 allows the president to impose governor’s rule when a provincial government is judged unable to function in accordance with the constitution. Once implemented, the article suspends the provincial cabinet, transfers executive authority to the federal government or the governor, and permits parliament to exercise the assembly’s powers.
By deploying the two articles together, the federal government has essentially neutralized PTI’s institutional presence in the province. Article 234 has removed the PTI provincial cabinet and chief minister, which has effectively cut the party off from the province’s administrative system, official resources, and day-to-day levers of governance.
Moreover, Article 232 has shifted key legislative and public order authority to the center and provided federal authorities with stronger legal tools to enforce order, restrict street mobilization and limit any form of organized political activity.
By invoking Articles 232 and 234, the federal government has made a comprehensive effort to deny PTI any realistic prospect of regaining political or institutional influence in KP province in the near term.
This institutional confrontation is the culmination of months of friction between the federal government and PTI. The current setup in Islamabad is governed by a multi-party coalition, which is led by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif of the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) and supported prominently by the Pakistan People’s Party (PPP) under President Asif Ali Zardari. It is pertinent to mention that after having assumed power following a highly contested election in 2024, the ruling coalition in Islamabad has remained engaged in an intense political feud with Imran Khan’s party.
The latest decision indicates that the relationship between the PTI-led provincial government and the federal government had become virtually unbridgeable.
From Islamabad’s perspective, the core dispute between the two sides centered on counterterrorism policy and the provincial government’s perceived defiance of federal priorities. It is important to note that security conditions in the province have deteriorated sharply in recent months with a marked rise in militant attacks.
Information Minister Attaullah Tarar on Sunday went as far as saying that the PTI-led government had developed a nexus with terrorist groups and that a “power-sharing formula was gradually taking shape between terrorists and the PTI’s KP government, which was starting from southern districts and was ingressing further into the entire KP.”
The PTI leadership has questioned these assertions, arguing that security concerns are being leveraged to justify political measures aimed at diminishing the party’s footprint in the province. Furthermore, PTI leaders maintain that the central government refused to adopt a consultative approach to address the militancy challenge and also consistently denied party leaders access to consult with Imran Khan, who is languishing in prison.
The timing of this development is significant for many reasons. The emergency measures were imposed as the PTI prepared a long march from KP to Islamabad, the national capital, to demand Khan’s release from prison. Moreover, the provincial leadership, particularly Chief Minister Sohail Afridi, have refused to come on board the federal government’s counterterrorism policy. This stance hardened in recent months.
For decision makers in Islamabad, the provincial government had become both a political irritant and a security liability that was obstructing coordinated action against the militancy emanating from KP, which has become a threat to national security.
Following the declaration of emergency, one of the central government’s first administrative steps has been to establish a direct administrative framework for KP’s border and former tribal districts. The federal government has approved the immediate establishment of an Area Development Secretariat, which will be supervised by an Area Representative and Development Council and covers Dera Ismail Khan, Tank, Lakki Marwat, Bannu, Bajaur, Mohmand, Khyber, Kurram, Orakzai, North Waziristan, and both Upper and South Waziristan. The ADS will be responsible for restoring law and order, protecting citizens, and ensuring governance and development.
Under this arrangement, civil administration, police and military coordination have been placed under a streamlined federal framework. It has created a more direct channel for Islamabad to manage high-risk districts. Moreover, this has also arguably reduced the scope for any future provincial government to impede security operations in these areas.
The move also carries clear external implications.
On Monday, KP Governor Faisal Karim Kundi stated that the days of lack of coordination between the center and the province on terrorism related issues are over, adding that “our policies will come from Islamabad … not Kabul, Jalalabad or Kandahar.” Arguably, Kundi’s statement was meant to emphasize that the state will not entertain dialogue or local deals with militant elements. By emphasizing that policy will originate from Islamabad rather than Afghanistan, he signaled that the federal government will no longer tolerate cross-border sanctuaries and will implement security policy unilaterally.
Kundi’s statement is important as it carries clear policy-level implications. If the new administrative framework is any indication, Pakistan is set to confront Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) threats and presence in its border regions more forcefully than before, and will likely pursue an uncompromising approach toward the Afghan Taliban on issues of militancy, border management, and cross-border sanctuaries.
One can argue that while the PTI government in Peshawar had become a political problem for the center, it had also evolved, in Islamabad’s assessment, into a security challenge. The party’s resistance to the measures now being imposed in the former tribal districts was viewed as untenable by both the federal government and the military leadership.
For now, the federal government has imposed its will in the province. Whether the new direct-rule arrangement can deliver improved security and reduced terrorist threats will determine whether it ultimately gains public acceptance. The immediate challenge for Islamabad is to ensure that the policy it is seeking to implement actually produces results on the ground.

The National Transmission Network Service Provider (Private) Limited currently owns, manages and operates the national grid, including its 220kV and 132kV transmission lines. ■

AI models improve long-term flood forecasting: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:38:25 CST
17:38:25 KST

SYDNEY, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- An international research team has developed artificial intelligence (AI) models that could improve long-term flood forecasting, helping communities get warnings weeks ahead of floods.
Researchers used two decades of historical precipitation and streamflow data from the DuPage River basin in Illinois, the United States, to develop deep learning models incorporating attention mechanisms to identify patterns in rainfall and river flow, according to a statement released Tuesday by Australia's University of Technology Sydney (UTS).
By combining the models' predictions, the team improved forecasting accuracy, with the ensemble deep learning models reducing prediction errors by about 38 percent and the proposed fusion framework improving predictive performance by about 47 percent, according to the study published in the Journal of Hydrologic Engineering.
The approach remained highly accurate for forecasts up to 12 weeks ahead, said UTS Professor Amir H. Gandomi, the study's co-author, stressing that additional warning time could help communities prepare for floods.
The findings could have implications for flood risk management, including disaster preparedness, infrastructure resilience and water resource management, according to the team.
"Ultimately, the goal is not simply to predict floods more accurately, but to turn better predictions into better decisions," Gandomi said. ■

SOFIA, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Drones have attacked two merchant ships in the Black Sea off the coast of Bulgaria, and at least one of them has sunk, the country's Government Information Service said on Tuesday.
At an extraordinary meeting with the country's security council, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said one ship was attacked around 1:30 a.m. local time (2230 GMT Monday), about 18 nautical miles east of the town of Byala.
Bulgarian authorities rescued all 15 crew members aboard the vessel, including seven Ukrainian nationals and eight Azerbaijani nationals, Radev said.
The ship, named "Chelsea 3," was flying the Maltese flag, registered in Odesa, Ukraine, and Ukrainian-owned, according to Radev. The crew said three aerial drones struck the vessel.
The crew members were safely transported to the port of Varna, where five of them received medical treatment, he added.
The information service said authorities also received information about another merchant ship that was hit about 17 nautical miles east of Krapets. The vessel sank, and one crew member was rescued.
The incident marked the second drone attack on merchant ships near Bulgaria within a week. On Oct. 6, unidentified drones sank one merchant ship and set another on fire about 70 nautical miles east of Byala, within Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone.
"Another attack on merchant ships in the immediate vicinity of Bulgarian territorial waters is absolutely unacceptable," Radev said.
Bulgaria's permanent representatives to NATO and the European Union have been notified, Radev said, adding that he was due to speak with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte. ■
