Türkiye’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations Ahmet Yıldız called on Israel to end its "reckless acts” in Syria and fully comply with the 1974 Disengagement Agreement.
"Lasting stability is essential for Syria to rebuild its economy, attract investment, and participate in regional energy and connectivity projects,” Yıldız told a session of the U.N. Security Council on Monday.
"Israel’s continued violations of Syrian sovereignty and territorial integrity undermine these prospects and show disregard for international law,” he said.
"The situation is particularly alarming in southern Syria, where continued military incursions and expansionist actions and words are getting out of control,” he added.
Yıldız said Israel’s recent resumption of activities along the so-called "Sufa 53 line” in Quneitra was a further attempt to undermine the 1974 agreement and impose a fait accompli on the ground. "These reckless acts must stop,” he said.
He urged Israel to comply with the 1974 agreement and relevant Security Council resolutions, particularly Resolution 497, and to withdraw from the occupied Syrian Golan Heights. "A stable, sovereign and unified Syria capable of securing its borders, defeating terrorist organizations and contributing to regional peace and economic cooperation serves the interests of all, including Israel,” he added.
"The dissolution of the so-called SDF has opened a new chapter in the integration process,” Yıldız said. "Remaining arrangements should be finalized and fully implemented without delay, in a manner that reinforces Syria’s sovereignty, unity and social cohesion,” he added.
Yıldız described the fight against terrorism as "a critical priority” and welcomed Damascus’ cooperation with the global coalition for the enduring defeat of Daesh. "Security and economic recovery must advance hand in hand,” he said.
On refugees, Yıldız said the number of Syrians under temporary protection in Türkiye once exceeded 4 million and now stands at around 2.2 million.
He said returns have been gradual because of economic conditions, security concerns and Israeli incursions. Since Bashar Assad’s fall on Dec. 8, 2024, Israel has expanded its military operations in Syria, moving troops into the Golan buffer zone and nearby positions. Syria demands the withdrawal of Israeli forces from the areas they occupied and maintains its commitment to the 1974 Disengagement Agreement. Israel claims its movements are driven by security considerations.
Addressing the same session, Syria’s U.N. representative Ibrahim Olabi said those claiming to seek security "should not be killing Syrian citizens within Syrian territory.”
"They should know very well that there is only one path towards security, which is international legitimacy and the resolutions of the (U.N. Security) Council,” the envoy said.
"Every time they open fire on Syria, they are, as the world has witnessed, at the same time opening fire on itself locally and internationally,” he added. Olabi also urged support for economic recovery, investment, job creation and reconstruction. He called for help rehabilitating schools, hospitals and water and electricity networks and for resources and expertise to clear mines and other remnants of war.

Xi calls for decisive progress in Healthy China advancement
China
Unknown Publisher

Chinese President Xi Jinping, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, delivers an important speech during a national meeting on health in Beijing, capital of China. The meeting was held in Beijing on Monday and Tuesday. (Xinhua/Xie Huanchi)
BEIJING, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping has called for efforts to firmly follow a path with Chinese characteristics in developing the country's health programs, to secure decisive progress in the Healthy China Initiative over the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030).
Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, made the remarks at a national meeting on health held in Beijing on Monday and Tuesday.
Xi stressed that people's health is a key benchmark of a nation's prosperity and strength.
Since the 18th CPC National Congress in 2012, the Party has made a major decision to launch the Healthy China Initiative, promoting the establishment of the world's largest systems of medical services, traditional medicine, disease prevention and control, and healthcare security, said Xi, noting that the country has achieved historic accomplishments and made all-round progress in healthcare.
He said the goal is to build a Healthy China, where health services are ensured in a balanced, inclusive, high-quality and efficient manner.
Xi stressed that people's health should be factored into all policies and reflected in every aspect of work.
Prevention, he said, is the most cost-effective and efficient approach to protecting public health. He called for greater emphasis on foundational health work, addressing risks at their source, and encouraging the public to adopt a sound understanding of health and take an active role in managing their own well-being.
He also called for a stronger disease prevention and control system to guard against large-scale outbreaks.
Xi underscored the need to optimize the functions and structural layout of medical institutions so that people can access medical care close to home and receive effective treatment.
He also urged efforts to improve mechanisms for the preservation and innovative development of traditional Chinese medicine, strengthen basic research and original innovation in the health sector, and enhance the patient experience.
Xi stressed that coordinating the development and regulation of medical services, medical insurance, and pharmaceuticals should be a key priority in reforming China's medical and healthcare systems.
He also called for efforts to train and develop a sufficient number of highly qualified medical professionals.
Efforts will also be made to actively promote the building of a global community of health for all, work with other countries to address major challenges in the health sector, and continuously improve the health and well-being of people around the world, he said. ■

Chiang rejected claims that his campaign had proposed Oct. 31, saying the date came from the two broadcasters. He said organizers needed at least two weeks to prepare, making Oct. 31 the earliest possible date, per Newtalk.
Chiang said his team had agreed to the date despite existing commitments. He criticized Shen's representatives for leaving the talks without approving it, questioning whether they had the authority to make decisions.
Chiang also accused Shen of using calls for a debate as a campaign issue rather than making a serious effort to arrange one. Shen rejected the criticism, saying his campaign had sent senior staff with decision-making authority to the meeting.
Shen's campaign manager, DPP Legislator Wu Szu-yao (吳思瑤), also criticized Chiang's team for failing to clarify how many debates it would accept. She accused the campaign of trying to limit the candidates to one debate by insisting that the first event be arranged before discussing others.
Chiang maintained that his position was consistent with Lo's and said both campaigns should focus on holding the first debate. He added that he remained open to discussing a second or third debate afterward.

Fertility Treatment in Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:35:42 UTC
17:35:42 KST

This article explores why Iran has become an option for international patients seeking fertility treatment. It covers the global prevalence of infertility, Iran’s position in reproductive medicine, and factors such as specialized treatments, accessibility, and comparatively lower costs. The article also introduces VitaLife Fertility Center and its support for international patients seeking IVF, egg donation, surrogacy, and other fertility services in Iran.
Infertility is no longer a health challenge limited to a small group of couples. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), approximately one in six people of reproductive age experience infertility during their lifetime, making access to effective and affordable fertility care a growing global health priority.
As demand for assisted reproductive technologies continues to grow, patients are increasingly looking beyond their home countries for fertility treatment. Cost, access to advanced reproductive technologies, legal restrictions, waiting times, and the availability of specialized services can all influence where international patients seek care.
Among the destinations receiving increasing attention is Iran, where assisted reproductive medicine has developed substantially over the past several decades.
Infertility can result from male factors, female factors, a combination of both, or unexplained causes. Treatment may involve medication, surgery, intrauterine insemination (IUI), in vitro fertilization (IVF), egg donation, embryo-related genetic testing, or other assisted reproductive technologies.
The challenge, however, is not simply whether treatment exists. Access matters.
WHO notes that fertility treatments remain inaccessible or unaffordable for many people, with the high cost of assisted reproduction creating a significant barrier in numerous countries.
This has contributed to the growth of cross-border reproductive care, in which patients travel to another country to obtain fertility services that may be more accessible, affordable, or legally available there.
Research examining international reproductive care has found that cost and the legal availability of assisted reproductive technologies are among the most frequently reported reasons patients seek treatment abroad, alongside cultural and practical considerations.
Where Does Iran Stand in Fertility Treatment?
Iran has developed a substantial medical infrastructure for assisted reproduction. Assisted reproductive technologies have been used in the country since the 1980s, and a national report published on Iranian ART centers documented tens of thousands of IVF/ICSI cycles across dozens of centers. Researchers concluded that Iran has considerable potential to provide IVF services not only to Iranian patients but also to patients from other countries in the region.
Iran's position has also been highlighted by Iranian medical authorities. In a report published by Mehr News, Hamid Choubineh, head of the Iranian Scientific Association of Infertility and Reproductive Health, described Iran as being among the top 10 countries in the world for infertility treatment, while emphasizing the country's access to modern assisted reproductive techniques.
The country's reproductive medicine sector includes IVF, ICSI, genetic testing, donor programs, and gestational surrogacy. Iranian research has also documented the use of preimplantation genetic diagnosis for conditions such as beta-thalassemia, aneuploidy screening, and sex selection.
For international patients, this combination of medical expertise and comparatively lower treatment costs can make Iran an option worth investigating.
Why Do International Patients Consider Iran?
The reasons vary from patient to patient, but several factors frequently influence the decision.
Access to Specialized Fertility Services
Some reproductive treatments are heavily restricted in certain countries. Regulations concerning donor eggs, donor embryos, gestational surrogacy, and embryo testing vary significantly around the world.
Iran occupies a distinctive position within the Muslim world in this regard. Islamic bioethics literature notes that the late Ayatollah Ali Khamenei issued a fatwa permitting certain third-party reproductive arrangements, including egg donation and surrogacy, and that these practices subsequently became incorporated into Iran's reproductive medicine framework.
This religious and legal context differs from the position adopted by many Sunni authorities regarding third-party gamete donation. For international patients, therefore, Iran can provide an alternative where certain fertility treatments are available within a Shia Islamic legal and medical framework.
At the same time, eligibility is not unlimited. Iranian fertility programs operate within local medical and legal requirements, and international patients should confirm their eligibility before traveling. For example, VitaLife's current program information specifies eligibility requirements for international intended parents and states that its surrogacy pathway is designed for legally married heterosexual couples.
Surrogacy, Egg Donation and Gender Selection
For patients who cannot safely carry a pregnancy, surrogacy in Iran can provide another reproductive pathway. In gestational surrogacy, an embryo created through IVF is transferred to a gestational carrier.
Egg donation is another important option for patients whose own eggs may not be suitable for treatment. Iran has developed clinical experience with donor-assisted reproduction, making it an area of interest for some international patients.
Another service sought by some international couples is gender selection through IVF and preimplantation genetic testing. Iranian medical research has documented PGD-based sex selection in clinical settings, although the medical, ethical, and legal circumstances surrounding its use should always be discussed with a qualified fertility specialist.
The important point is that international fertility care should not be viewed simply as a search for the cheapest treatment. Patients need to consider medical suitability, legal requirements, laboratory standards, documentation, and the process for returning home with a child born through assisted reproduction.
How VitaLife Supports International Patients
For someone traveling abroad for fertility treatment, the medical procedure is only one part of the journey.
International patients may also need help with medical records, treatment planning, translation, travel arrangements, legal documentation, surrogate coordination, and communication with clinics.
This is where an international surrogacy agency and fertility coordinator can play an important role.
VitaLife Fertility Center in Iran works with international intended parents seeking coordinated fertility and reproductive services. Its programs include IVF, egg donation, gestational surrogacy, embryo-related genetic services, and support with the practical aspects of treatment in Iran.
The center's international support model is designed to coordinate different stages of treatment rather than leaving patients to manage each component independently. According to VitaLife's published program information, this includes medical coordination, surrogate matching, legal documentation support, international patient coordination, and assistance throughout the treatment process.
For intended parents considering treatment abroad, this type of coordinated approach can make an otherwise complicated process easier to navigate.
Choosing Fertility Treatment Abroad
Choosing fertility treatment abroad involves more than cost. International patients should consider the medical team, clinic facilities, legal requirements, treatment eligibility, timeline, total costs, and support throughout the journey.
Fertility treatment cannot guarantee pregnancy or live birth, as outcomes depend on individual medical factors such as age, reproductive history, and embryo quality.
Your Treatment Journey with VitaLife
At VitaLife Fertility Center, international patients are supported throughout their treatment journey in Iran, from the initial consultation to delivery. Mobina Hosseini, a midwifery specialist with a master’s degree in midwifery, serves as the dedicated patient coordinator, helping international intended parents navigate their treatment from A to Z.
Medical care is provided under the supervision of Dr. Farah Ghasemi, the treating physician, with IVF procedures carried out at Baharan Negar Infertility Treatment Center. For patients undergoing surrogacy, delivery takes place at Nikan Aghdasieh Hospital, providing a coordinated pathway from fertility treatment through pregnancy and birth.
This integrated approach allows international patients to have one coordinated team supporting their medical, communication, and practical needs throughout the process.
A Growing Role for Iran in International Fertility Care
Iran’s experience in assisted reproduction, specialized fertility services, and comparatively accessible treatment costs has made it an option for international patients. For intended parents, choosing the right pathway means finding medically appropriate, legally compliant, and well-coordinated care. VitaLife Fertility Center supports international patients throughout their fertility journey in Iran.

Global: New report exposes human rights failures at 2026 Men’s World Cup
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:34:34 UTC
17:34:34 KST

Coalition calls for upcoming FIFA presidential election to centre human rights
The 2026 Men’s World Cup exposed a failure of FIFA’s leadership to implement its own human rights policies, with the pursuit of record revenues prioritised over fairness and equality, the Sport & Rights Alliance and Football Supporters Europe said in a joint report released today. The 50-page report, “Profit Over People: The 2026 FIFA Men’s World Cup,” documents a tournament marked by a climate of fear given the backdrop of mass immigration detentions and deportations; discriminatory visa bans; cost and accessibility barriers for fans, players and journalists; unclear safeguarding and eligibility standards; and lack of effective access to remedy.
“The 2026 World Cup exposed how the priorities and direction set by FIFA’s leadership put profit over people,” said Andrea Florence, Executive Director of the Sport & Rights Alliance. “For everyone touched by the tournament, access and participation were limited by economic status, nationality, immigration status, disability, gender identity and sexual orientation or political circumstance. Not only did FIFA fail to use its leverage to uphold human rights obligations, it chose to lift up a government that is actively violating human rights by awarding an unvetted ‘FIFA Peace Prize’ to U.S. President Donald Trump.”
As a 48-nation, 104-match tournament hosted for the first time in three countries – Canada, Mexico, and the United States – the 2026 Men’s World Cup was the biggest mega sporting event in history, and one that, as FIFA promised would be a tournament where everyone “feels safe, included and free to exercise their rights.” The tournament was the first World Cup to be hosted under FIFA’s recognition and adoption of international business and human rights obligations, through its 2017 Human Rights Policy, integration of human rights criteria in the bidding process, and a dedicated “FWC26 Human Rights Framework” for 16 local host committees. Yet due to rising concerns about potential human rights abuses at the tournament, over 65,000 people joined Amnesty International’s call for FIFA and host nations to address risks and guarantee a World Cup for everyone.
ICE raids surged, protests were blocked and discriminatory visa policies kept many fans from enjoying what was billed as ‘the most inclusive World Cup ever’.
Frank Conde Tangberg, Policy Advisor at Amnesty International
“The unity and joy we saw on the pitch and in the stands were a world away from the fear and division beyond the stadiums. ICE raids surged, protests were blocked and discriminatory visa policies kept many fans from enjoying what was billed as ‘the most inclusive World Cup ever’,” said Frank Conde Tangberg, Policy Advisor at Amnesty International. “Many of these violations stemmed from repressive and abusive government policies, but FIFA failed to use its leverage to protect fans and local communities. It spent its political capital on maximising revenue rather than standing up for human rights.”
The report details how excessive ticket pricing, coupled with expensive visa requirements and a lack of affordable inter-city transport, as well as U.S. travel restrictions on over 39 nations, disproportionately excluded fans with disabilities, with limited incomes and/or from the Global South. Participating teams and officials faced severe disruptions: members of the Iranian national team had U.S. visas delayed or denied, and for two U.S. matches the team had to enter and depart the country on the same day – while Somali referee Omar Artan, despite having a valid visa, was denied entry at Miami International Airport following an 11-hour interrogation. These and other barriers unfolded alongside aggressive U.S. immigration enforcement, with, as Human Rights Watch documented, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) conducting over 167,000 arrests in and around 11 World Cup host cities leading up to the tournament. Although reporting of ICE detentions inside World Cup venues was limited, enforcement surged during the tournament, including over five days in late June when approximately 10,000 people were arrested.
“Supporters were treated as objects to be exploited rather than the heart of the game,” said Ronan Evain, Executive Director of Football Supporters Europe. “When ticket prices are at the highest in World Cup history, legal accessibility requirements for fans with disabilities are ignored, and dedicated supporters face discriminatory visa rejections or militarized border enforcement, you no longer have a global celebration – just an exclusive, sanitized spectacle meant only for the elite.”
The report also documents other human rights abuses in Mexico, where police confronted planned protests with tear gas and detained two journalists. In Canada, preparations were marked by street sweeps displacing unhoused residents in host cities – and immigration authorities rejected more World Cup visa applications, which came mostly from Global South applicants, than they approved. Within FIFA’s direct control, questions remain about whether FIFA failed to enforce its own in-competition policy explicitly requiring athletes to declare they have never been investigated for a sexual or other violent offence, given that at least eight players facing pending sexual assault cases or allegations competed in the 2026 World Cup. Independent journalism was also severely constrained by FIFA’s opaque media accreditation processes, U.S. visa barriers, and a lack of regular press conferences with top leadership.
“In recent years, the U.S. – the country hosting the majority of World Cup matches – fell from 45th to 64th in our Press Freedom Index, and journalists have faced violence, detention, and deportation,” said Clayton Weimers, Executive Director of Reporters Without Borders (RSF) USA. “Yet FIFA’s lack of clarity on media accreditation, coordination with visa processes, and blasé attitude toward media briefings underscored FIFA’s failures to uphold human rights. On top of this, FIFA’s continued lack of advertising for its grievance mechanism for journalists, players, fans, workers and community members means we don’t know the true extent of the harm.”
FIFA is in clear need of systemic governance reform that embeds human rights and good governance into leadership and decision-making structures, provides an independent system of checks and balances, and ensures meaningful accountability when its commitments are not met.
“The lesson of the 2026 World Cup is not that international sporting bodies can guarantee the conduct of sovereign governments, but that human rights risks must shape how tournaments are awarded, planned, contracted, monitored, and delivered – and that top leadership at FIFA and other sport governing bodies must be prepared to act, especially when circumstances change,” said Florence.
As detailed in the report, the Sport & Rights Alliance and Football Supporters Europe call on FIFA, and all candidates in the 2027 presidential election, to:
- Make human rights requirements binding, and set enforceable conditions in host agreements for all future Men’s and Women’s World Cups, backed by independent monitoring and clear consequences for non-compliance;
- Establish a transparent, survivor-centered eligibility framework for athletes and officials facing serious misconduct or sexual violence allegations, replacing case-by-case discretion;
- Ensure meaningful access without discrimination to future tournaments for fans, athletes, journalists, and other accredited participants, and ensure the rights to freedom of expression, peaceful assembly and press freedom are guaranteed in the context of FIFA tournaments;
- Guarantee equal ticket access and free companion seating for supporters with disabilities, while preventing predatory ticket pricing; and
- Make FIFA’s grievance and remedy mechanisms visible and accessible, re-establish a permanent and independent Human Rights Advisory Board, comprehensively reform the FIFA Ethics Committee, and create a permanent Remedy Fund for individuals and communities harmed by past and future tournament operations.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has ordered the security establishment and the country’s attorney-general to identify and prosecute soldiers and officers interviewed in the investigative documentary NAZA about Israel’s mass killings of civilians in Gaza, Israeli media reported on Monday.
In a letter to army Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir, Shin Bet chief David Zini and Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara, Netanyahu accused those who participated in the documentary of committing “serious information security offenses, and criminal defamation” and causing harm to “Israel’s diplomatic and security interests,” according to Haaretz newspaper.
The award-winning documentary examines Israel’s use of artificial intelligence and automated surveillance systems in targeted killings and military offensives during its genocidal war on Gaza.
The film’s title, "NAZA," refers to an acronym used by Israeli military intelligence to denote the number of civilians expected to be killed in an air strike.
During the war, the Israeli army has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 others since October 2023 in a brutal offensive that has left the entire enclave in ruins.
Netanyahu claimed that the film has presented a “false, misleading and biased narrative” that defames Israel and its military and damages the country’s international standing.
“There is concern that those involved in the defamatory film committed serious criminal offenses by exposing highly classified information and creating a breach in the information security of a highly sensitive intelligence unit,” he said in the letter.
The film, based on testimony from 24 Israeli soldiers and intelligence personnel, won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival last month.
Following the award, Israeli Culture Minister Miki Zohar asked the Interior Ministry to consider revoking the citizenship of the film’s creators, describing the documentary as “vile” and accusing them of “treason.”
Zamir separately ordered Military Intelligence, the Military Advocate General’s Corps and the Israeli Air Force to identify the soldiers featured in the film and determine whether they were active-duty troops, career officers or reservists, according to Haaretz.
During discussions on the issue, Military Advocate General Itai Ofir said that there would be no legal basis for criminal prosecution unless participants were found to have committed information-security violations or disclosed classified material.
He said disciplinary or command measures could, however, be taken if military orders were violated.
The Israeli army claimed that the documentary’s portrayal of its targeting procedures in Gaza contained “substantial factual errors.”
The Guardian, which produced the documentary, defended the film, saying the process used to assess the credibility of the testimonies was “rigorous” and included classified documents, verification of specific strikes and corroboration from additional confidential sources.
The newspaper said it had interviewed more than 100 people familiar with Israeli military systems used during the war on Gaza, including senior commanders involved in authorising strikes.
In November 2024, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant over war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
The International Court of Justice, the UN’s principal judicial organ, is also hearing a case brought by South Africa and joined by several countries accusing Israel of genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.

Mapping Africa’s energy wealth and 560 million who remain without power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:25:54 UTC
17:25:54 KST

Mapping Africa’s energy wealth and 560 million who remain without power
Africa is rich in energy, yet hundreds of millions Africans still live without electricity, most of the world’s total.
Africa holds billions of barrels of oil, trillions of cubic metres of gas and produces most of the world’s cobalt and manganese for electric car batteries.
This week, energy ministers, investors and oil executives are meeting in Cape Town for African Energy Week, which runs until October 16. The conference focuses on investment in oil and gas, energy finance and ending energy poverty.
In this visual explainer, Al Jazeera maps where Africa’s oil, gas and critical minerals are found, how its electricity is generated and who still goes without it.
How much oil does Africa have?
Africa holds about 125 billion barrels of proven crude oil reserves, representing 7.2 percent of the global total. Proven reserves are oil that has been discovered and can be extracted commercially with existing technology, but is still in the ground.
Libya and Nigeria account for nearly 70 percent of Africa’s reserves, with 48.4 billion and 36.9 billion barrels, respectively. Algeria ranks third, with 12.2 billion barrels. Angola follows with 7.78 billion barrels, while South Sudan and Egypt hold 3.75 billion and 3.3 billion barrels, respectively.
Nigeria was Africa’s largest oil producer in 2024, accounting for about 23 percent of the continent’s output. Algeria and Angola followed with about 17 percent each, and together the three produced 56 percent of Africa’s oil. The top five producers accounted for more than 80 percent. Africa as a whole produced 7.6 percent of the world’s crude oil, roughly in line with its share of global reserves.
Libya, which holds Africa’s largest proven reserves, ranked only fourth in production. Italy’s Eni, France’s TotalEnergies and Spain’s Repsol are among the foreign companies operating in the country, where political disputes and blockades have repeatedly disrupted output.
Where are Africa’s natural gas reserves?
Africa held almost 18 trillion cubic metres of proven natural gas reserves at the end of 2023.
Nigeria and Algeria hold about 58 percent of the total, followed by Mozambique with 2.84 trillion cubic metres, Egypt with 2.21 trillion and Libya with 1.51 trillion.
Algeria and Nigeria are also among Africa’s leading gas exporters, while much of Mozambique’s reserves, discovered offshore in the 2010s, remain largely undeveloped.
Where do the critical minerals come from?
The African continent supplies a large share of the minerals used in electric vehicles, batteries and renewable energy technologies.
In 2025, African countries accounted for 71.2 percent of global cobalt production and 72.4 percent of manganese production.
Cobalt is used in rechargeable batteries. Manganese is mainly used to strengthen steel, but it is also used in some electric vehicle batteries and in batteries that store renewable energy.
The Democratic Republic of the Congo produces nearly 70 percent of the world’s cobalt. Some of it is dug by hand by artisanal miners, and Amnesty International has documented dangerous and often deadly conditions in some of the country’s mines.
South Africa produces nearly 38 percent of global manganese, followed by Gabon with nearly 25 percent. Together with Ghana, the three countries account for 72.4 percent of global production.
Zimbabwe, Africa’s largest lithium producer, accounted for 9.6 percent of global production in 2025. Lithium is used in rechargeable batteries that power electric vehicles and store electricity from solar and wind.
Madagascar, Mozambique and Tanzania produced a combined 222,000 tonnes of natural graphite in 2025, or 11.9 percent of the global total. Graphite is used in the anodes of most lithium-ion batteries, the negative electrodes that store and release energy, as well as in steel manufacturing, lubricants and pencils.
How many African countries produce electricity from renewables?
Renewable energy accounted for all electricity generated in Ethiopia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2024. Uganda, Namibia and Eswatini each generated more than 96 percent from renewables, mostly hydropower.
At the other end, renewables made up less than 5 percent in Algeria, Libya, Niger and Tunisia, which rely mainly on gas or oil.
Ethiopia’s electricity comes mostly from hydropower, led by the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam on the Blue Nile, Africa’s largest hydroelectric project. The dam began generating power in 2022 and was officially inaugurated in September 2025.
Where do people have access to electricity?
In 2024, six African countries reported universal electricity access: Algeria, Egypt, Mauritius, Morocco, Seychelles and Tunisia. Together, they are home to about 215 million people, or roughly 14 percent of Africa’s population.
Elsewhere, access varies widely. In South Sudan, only 5.4 percent of people had electricity. The figure was 15.6 percent in Malawi and 22.5 percent in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, even though the DRC generates all its power from renewables.
Nigeria, Africa’s most populous country, had an access rate of 62.5 percent, leaving roughly 85 million people without electricity, the largest number of any country in the world.
In rural areas, where access is far lower than in cities, many families still rely on kerosene lamps, candles or torches to light their homes after dark.
Africa has vast energy resources, from oil and natural gas to the minerals powering the global energy transition. Yet more than 560 million people in sub-Saharan Africa lack access to electricity, accounting for about 86 percent of the global total, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

Meta has launched two new artificial intelligence models as the technology company seeks to compete more directly with leading systems developed by OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google.
Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full are Meta’s most capable models to date and are designed for personal and professional AI agents, the company said in an announcement on Monday.
The models can perform long-running tasks, use computers, and work in specialized areas including law, finance, and health. Meta said they can also handle complex coding projects, delegate work to smaller AI agents and recover from errors without abandoning the original goal.

Meta published benchmark results that it said showed the models matching or outperforming some systems from OpenAI and Anthropic on selected coding, memory, and professional tasks. The broader performance of the models will still need to be assessed through independent testing.
The company said it trained the Wonder family to protect private information, refuse assistance with harmful activity, and strengthen defenses against cyberattacks. A more detailed safety report is expected to be released later.
The launch forms part of Meta’s broader push toward what CEO Mark Zuckerberg has described as “personal superintelligence,” AI systems capable of understanding users’ goals, preferences and long-term needs.
Unlike some earlier Meta models released with downloadable weights, the company did not announce plans to make the Wonder models open source.

AI models may soon replicate across smart devices without human control, Anthropic says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:13:24 UTC
17:13:24 KST

Dilara Hamit
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
Small artificial intelligence models could soon become capable of copying themselves across internet-connected devices without human control or access to data centers, according to new Anthropic research.
The study, published Sunday by the US AI company’s Frontier Red Team, examined whether AI models could independently find devices, transfer model files, establish the software needed to operate and continue spreading from each newly infected machine.
Researchers said models with fewer than 30 billion parameters can already complete many individual stages of that process, although most still struggle to combine them reliably.
In a controlled and simplified experiment, the GLM-5.2 model successfully spread across all eight available test devices in four of five trials and reached seven in the remaining trial.
Anthropic stressed that the experiment simplified the hacking stage by using devices with an unsecured connection. The results therefore do not demonstrate that an AI model can currently escape and reproduce autonomously under real-world conditions.
“We don’t yet have a full rogue replicator,” the researchers said. However, they warned that agents were becoming increasingly capable of completing the necessary steps and passing useful information to later copies of themselves.
The study focused particularly on inexpensive internet-of-things devices, which frequently have limited security protections. Potential targets could include smart televisions, refrigerators, ovens, vacuum cleaners, security cameras and videoconferencing equipment.
Anthropic demonstrated that a 26-billion-parameter model could run across 15 inexpensive Android television boxes costing about $55 each. A smaller model successfully established the software required to operate on eight of the nine types of hardware tested.
Unlike conventional computer worms, a self-replicating AI system could potentially adjust to unfamiliar devices, diagnose technical problems and pass successful strategies to future copies.
The researchers said such a system would initially spread slowly, possibly taking one or two days to produce each new copy. However, it could be difficult to eliminate because there would be no central server to switch off.
Anthropic estimated that, if smaller models continue improving at their historical pace, they could reach the capability demonstrated by GLM-5.2 by the end of 2026. The company cautioned that this was only a rough projection based on general capability trends.
The researchers recommended monitoring unusual network traffic, isolating infected devices and requiring manufacturers to strengthen default security settings.
They warned that early, slow-moving replicators could signal the future arrival of faster systems capable of breaching more secure computers.
“We should aim to harden our systems to make it difficult for such replicators to spread,” they said, “but also prepare to deal with a world where they are here to stay.”

Denmark’s biggest retailer is training robots for supermarket night shifts. When will they be ready?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:10:33 UTC
17:10:33 KST

For now, they are slower than supermarket workers, though the start-up says advances in AI will help improve their speed and precision.
In the Danish town of Lyngby, just north of Copenhagen, the supermarket night shift is getting some unusual trainees.
Humanoid robots are learning to restock shelves after closing time, part of a multi-year trial to take on routine tasks and free employees to help customers.
With their arms, legs and fingers, the robots can operate in spaces built for people without stores having to change their layouts, according to the Danish start-up, Hive Robots.
For now, they are slower than supermarket workers, though the start-up says advances in AI will help improve their speed and precision.
How do robots learn?
Getting robots to work in real-world settings takes training and data collected on the job.
In a corner of the store, a human operator uses virtual reality glasses and handheld controllers to guide a robot as it picks up pasta bags and places them on shelves.
His demonstrations provide data to teach the machines to perform the tasks independently.
“There are a lot of small things that we as humans don’t think about that basically we need to teach the robot,” said Roger Sala, a robot pilot at Hive Robots.
Training began in June at grocery chain Føtex, owned by Denmark’s largest retailer, Salling Group, which operates more than 2,100 stores across Denmark, Germany, Poland, Latvia, Estonia and Lithuania.
Hive Robots develops the software and trains the machines, which are manufactured by Chinese robotics company Unitree.
The Danish start-up hopes they can independently restock some products at night by early 2027, with stores paying by the hour for the service.
What could it mean for workers?
The deployment of humanoid robots in workplaces adds to the debate over whether AI will ease labour shortages or reduce demand for workers.
AI could change how around 60% of jobs across the EU are done, according to a 2024 report from the International Monetary Fund, helping workers perform some tasks while potentially taking over others.
The technology offers opportunities to improve productivity as well as risks of job displacement, the report said.
Salling Group says the purpose of its trial is to support employees rather than replace them.
The grocery store Føtex estimates that restocking accounts for 40% to 50% of staff time.
Hive Robots says the chain also struggles to recruit young workers for the task.
Føtex operations director Simon Kudsk says it could take up to five years to have robots in every store. Further tasks could include identifying missing or misplaced products, removing empty cardboard boxes and checking best-before dates.
“Our vision or the dream right now is that we eventually could have one or two humanoids in every Føtex store that could support our colleagues to make it more efficient and create more time for value-adding activities focused on customers,” Kudsk said.

Tensions with teachers, pupils and Turkiye: Inside Azerbaijan’s hijab row
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:57:45 UTC
16:57:45 KST

Tensions with teachers, pupils and Turkiye: Inside Azerbaijan’s hijab row
Teachers fear losing their livelihoods and students risk being excluded as Baku’s close ally appears critical.
For Gulshan Aliyeva, a teacher, the debate over the hijab in Azerbaijan’s public schools has become a personal struggle that threatens her career and her daughter’s education.
This week, the English teacher with 23 years of experience, went to school wearing her headscarf but was denied entry. Her daughter was also prevented from entering the high school in Baku, she told Al Jazeera.
“I want to fulfil my responsibilities, educate students and continue my career without my religious beliefs becoming an obstacle to my employment,” she said.
Aliyeva argued that Azerbaijan’s Labour Code, specifically Article 16, prohibits discrimination in employment in the country.
Last month, new rules stopped short of explicitly singling out the hijab but banned pupils from wearing clothes that violate the principle of secularism in education.
Protests have erupted over the issue in a country where more than 90 percent are Muslim.
Aliyeva is among several teachers and students who have been denied entry; the Ministry of Internal Affairs said on Monday that 37 people had been detained for disrupting public order while breaking the new rules.
“Our constitutional rights to work and receive an education without obstruction must be upheld,” said Aliyeva, who intends to continue reporting to work. She said she will take her case to the relevant authorities if necessary.
The Baku City Education Department has announced that schools will be monitored to assess compliance.
Sheikh-ul-Islam Allahshukur Pashazade, chairman of the Caucasus Muslims Board (CMB), told local media on Tuesday that the hijab is “an important religious obligation”.
While people “cannot oppose the decisions of the state” they can express their “views as citizens”, he added, but criticised protesters for disturbing schools.
He also said the issue was being used for political purposes, while urging critics to address relevant ministers.
Not everyone believes the restrictions represent an infringement of individual rights.
Baku resident Timur Rzayev believes the controversy has been politicised. In his view, the government’s uniform policy should be adhered to “rather than debated”.
“There is a government decision on the implementation of uniform dress codes,” he said.
Rzayev opposes girls under the age of 18 wearing the hijab, saying such a decision often reflects parental preferences rather than the wishes of the children themselves.
His position reflects a wider concern among some Azerbaijanis that religious practices should not mix with public education.
“We are a secular state that respects the rights of religious people,” he said.
During the Soviet era, the state restricted religious practices and did not allow people to freely observe their religious traditions. After independence, these restrictions were eased, allowing people greater freedom to practise their faith.
Natiq Jafarli, head of the opposition REAL Party, said that the question of students wearing the hijab warrants further discussion.
“The issue concerning female students needs to be discussed. Public schools should establish certain compromise arrangements for primary school pupils,” he said.
“Teachers are adults, and imposing restrictions on how they dress is the wrong approach,” he added.
Tensions with Turkiye
The controversy has also affected Azerbaijan’s closest relationship on the international stage.
Oktay Saral, an adviser to Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, said Azerbaijan’s move was “unacceptable”.
“Leaving a student who covers her head for reasons of faith at the school gate – how can this fit into any conscience, any sense of justice?” he posted on X.
The governing Yeni Azerbaijan Party (YAP) hit back on Tuesday, saying Saral’s “irresponsible” comments risked harming ties between the close allies.
Zahid Oruj, chairman of the human rights committee of the National Assembly, Azerbaijan’s parliament, said the measure was not an act of religious discrimination or an attack on free expression.
“There is no ban on wearing headscarves outside school, and the primary objective is to maintain uniform rules within the educational environment,” he told Al Jazeera.
He added that many Azerbaijanis do not wear the hijab but still regard the Quran as a holy book and believe in God, suggesting that disagreement about school dress requirements should not be equated with hostility towards religion.
The National NGO Forum of Azerbaijan has likewise criticised what it describes as the politicisation of the debate.
Azerbaijan’s secularism is enshrined in its constitution. Article 7 defines the country as a secular state. Article 18 establishes the separation of religion and state and provides for the secular character of the state education system. However, Article 48 guarantees freedom of conscience.
These provisions place secular education and religious freedom within the same constitutional framework, raising questions about how the state should reconcile them when regulating clothing in public schools.
Azer Rashidoglu, chairman of the Azerbaijan-based Tolerance Public Association for Social Research, believes the new rules are not in line with the Constitution and said people affected should challenge the measures.
“Those whose rights have been violated should collectively seek legal redress through the courts and pursue their cause through peaceful and lawful means,” he said.

Power outages have been recorded this morning for consumers in the city of Kyiv and in Kharkiv, Chernihiv, Sumy, Donetsk, Dnipropetrovsk, Khmelnytskyi and Zaporizhzhia oblasts as a result of the latest Russian attack on the energy grid.
Source: Ukrenergo, Ukraine's state-owned electricity transmission operator
Details: Repair work has begun in areas where it is safe to do so.
Blackout schedules will be in effect throughout the day for up to two queues Ukrenergo defines a "queue" as a group of consumers and businesses using a specific amount of megawatts. The Dispatch Centre sets the number of queues needed across oblasts to address energy deficits. Critical infrastructure and eligible industrial companies that import at least 60% of their energy cannot be disconnected, according to a Ukrainian Cabinet resolution – meaning electricity may be unavailable for up to eight hours a day.
Power engineers also urge the public to limit consumption during peak hours – from 16:00 to 22:00 – to avoid overloading the power system and prevent grid failures.
Background:
- On the night of 13-14 October, the Russians conducted a combined attack on Ukraine. Specifically, missile and drone air-raid warnings were issued several times in Kyiv and a number of oblasts. Power cuts were recorded in the capital.
- President Volodymyr Zelenskyy noted that Russian strikes have caused significant damage to 26 energy sites. He wrote that at least 600,000 people currently remain without power and added that further blackouts are possible.

Russia built new Millerovo drone base for Geran-5 UAVs in one month – satellite images
In just one month, Russia has built a new Millerovo drone launch site for launching Geran-5 attack drones.
Source: Absolutely Reliable Source, a Ukrainian OSINT community
Quote: "On 1 September, there was nothing there but an empty field. Now, the first section of the facility is nearing completion..."
Details: Absolutely Reliable Source said the site has eight designated launcher positions and 32 areas for preparing UAVs for launch. Satellite images taken on 12 October also show drones being unloaded in Zone 3.
The community said construction has been accelerated to expand Russia's attack capabilities following the September strikes on Kyiv. The construction style closely resembles that of the Tsimbulova drone base.
"There will be no conclusions. Conventional kamikaze drones cannot effectively destroy facilities like this. So I very much hope that the ballistic missiles we have been promised will finally start flying for real, rather than just appearing in social media posts," the OSINT community added.
Absolutely Reliable Source also provided the coordinates of the drone launch site: 48.995968, 40.286255.
Background:
- Absolutely Reliable Source previously released satellite images showing damage to Russia's Tsimbulova drone base following an attack on the night of 30 September-1 October. Located near the village of Bolkhov, the base is used, among other things, to launch Geran attack drones.

The boldness Australia needs has no political home right now
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:10:08 UTC
17:10:08 KST

analysis
Boyer Lecture: The boldness Australia needs has no political home right now
This year's Boyer Lecture series explores the opportunities and challenges of Australia's engagement with Asia in the 21st century. Keynote speaker Sam Roggeveen, director of the Lowy Institute's International Security Program, gave his lecture Four Forces: Australia in the New Asia this evening. This is an edited extract.
The biggest change to Australia's region since World War II is underway. Three forces are reshaping Asia and Australia's place in it: the decline of one empire, the rise of another, and the emergence of a powerful neighbour on Australia's doorstep.
Amid this regional shift, a fourth potent force is at play: an unmistakeable change in the character of Western liberal democracy, including in Australia.
These four forces present a challenge not just to our place in the world, but to our politics and identity; we are a Western nation perched alongside Asia as it enters a post-Western era.
We can't stop these international forces, but we have a choice to make about how we meet the challenge, a choice about whether we leave our fate in the hands of others or take the harder road towards self-reliance.
The 'material dethroning of the West'
It doesn't take much persuading these days to convince Australians that China is an important part of their future, because it is already so conspicuous in our daily lives. It is a major source of immigrants, students and consumer products, our largest trading partner, and it is credited with keeping Australia out of recession during the global financial crisis.
But what China means to Australia is a fraction of what it means to the world. China is the largest trading partner to around 120 other countries, too. Roughly a third of all the physical objects produced in the world today are made in China. Its economy is now at least four-fifths the size of America's and may even be the largest in the world, depending on how you measure.
For the economic historian Adam Tooze, China's rise represents nothing less than "the material dethroning of the West as the central driver of world history".
Until not so long ago, China's economic rise was only good news. It was lifting hundreds of millions of its own people out of poverty, producing cheap goods for the world, and creating wealthy consumers for our goods and services. But China's rise was always going to create problems, including for our ally, the United States.
When the Cold War ended, the US became Asia's uncontested leader. The hope, at the time, was that China would simply go along with that arrangement. The plan in Washington was that even as China became richer, it would remain subordinate to the US. China would become something like Japan or Germany — economic powerhouses with no big independent foreign policy ambitions.
Clearly, that's not how things are turning out. China is building the world's biggest navy and quadrupling the size of its nuclear arsenal. It punishes American allies, including Australia, by imposing trade restrictions. Its behaviour in the South China Sea, where it has built artificial islands based on dubious legal claims, can be fairly described as territorial expansion. China is clearly not going to become a super-sized version of Germany or Japan.
We should assume China wants to lead in the region, and that means subordinating the US and its allies, and even pushing Washington out of Asia altogether. That's not because China is communist or because it's a dictatorship. It is those things, and that makes China harder to deal with. But this is a simple question of scale. China is big and big countries demand leadership.
Now, nothing up to this point would perturb any mainstream foreign policy commentator. But here's where I swerve off the beaten path. Because the consensus in Australia is that, whatever challenge China presents to us, the Americans will help us face it. In fact, our entire national defence is built upon this premise.
The US is weaker in Asia
China's rise has made America's position in Asia unsustainably weak. It used to be easy for America to make lavish promises to defend its partners and allies in Asia because no other country was strong enough to challenge it. That's not true anymore. It would now be incredibly costly for the US to meet the commitments it has made.
It is still assumed, on the Korean Peninsula and in Taiwan, and even in Japan and Australia, that the US will be willing to risk the lives of thousands of its troops, and perhaps even nuclear attacks on its own cities, to defend us. But the US simply has no vital reason to accept such risks. The sacrifice would not be worth it.
Now, it's important to stress: saying that America's position in Asia is weak is not the same as saying that America itself is weak. In fact, the United States has a reasonable claim to being the strongest and most secure nation in the history of the world. But that's part of our problem.
America has the world's biggest military, a huge economy, thousands of nuclear weapons, and is separated from China by a vast ocean. It is so secure that it simply doesn't need to be Asia's leader. It's nice to have, but not essential. So, when a challenger as big as China comes along, we should not assume that the US will bear the burden of resisting it.
If this is jarring, it's because it has happened relatively quickly. One of my predecessors as Boyer Lecturer, the distinguished Australian foreign policy thinker Owen Harries, titled his first address And Then There Was One, because in 2003 the US was the only superpower in the world. It's worth adding that Owen did not assume this would be a permanent condition.
You will note I haven't mentioned President Trump so far, who is so often the focus of our alliance concerns. And why not? He has threatened to annex Greenland, make Canada the 51st state, and throw Ukraine under the bus. Still, it's a mistake to focus on Trump because it invites us to believe that he was the cause of the power shift I am describing, and that things will return to something like "normal" after he leaves the world stage. They won't.
No previous US president could have prevented China's ascent, and no future US president is going to risk their nation's safety and prosperity by entering a competition with China that could lead to war.
So no, this is not a Trump phenomenon. It is a permanent shift.
AUKUS hits a jarring note
This is why AUKUS is such a jarring note in our national life. The agreement to supply Australia with eight nuclear-powered submarines, announced by the Morrison government in 2021 and now supported by the Albanese government, represents the biggest change to our alliance in its history. Yet it comes at exactly the moment when American reliability goes into permanent decline.
AUKUS is an illustration of one of the least attractive aspects of our national character: an insatiable desire to win the approval of Americans. Of course, the Americans sense this and they exploited it when we proposed AUKUS, which involves not just our biggest ever military purchase but billions of Australian dollars invested in US shipyards.
In the 1930s, America built the gambling mecca of Las Vegas, an entire city in the desert dedicated to fleecing gamblers. If AUKUS demonstrates anything, it is that the Americans still have a talent for separating fools from their money.
Australia should be sceptical of both China and America as one rises and the other declines. And from this dual scepticism flows an obvious conclusion: we must do more to look after ourselves.
Once we accept that our relationship with the US will become more transactional, the natural instinct will be to find a partner to replace it. But there is no replacement.
The sheer scale of the Asia Pacific counts against an alliance-like security partnership with Tokyo. Japan is pre-occupied with security threats far closer to home, and lacks the military capacity and ambition to be a significant power in our part of Asia.
What about India? It is in a slightly different category because of its size and still untapped potential — one day, it will likely surpass the US in GDP terms. But India is also too far away from Australia to be a close security partner. It is difficult to imagine that any security threat to Australia would ever be so vital to India that New Delhi would offer us help, and the same is true for Australia in its dealings with India.
There is one nation which, although it will never replace the US, does have vital interests that align with ours. It is close to Australia and has vast economic potential, enough to resist being pulled into China's orbit.
A great power on our doorstep
Indonesia matters to Australia because it is big and it is near.
Two hundred and ninety million people dispersed across an archipelago that covers Australia's northern approaches, and boasting consistent growth that will see it enter the top five economies in the world by the middle of the century.
Australia is about to have a great power on its doorstep.
For Australia's security, Indonesia ranks above every other nation. If we get this relationship wrong, the dangers are immense. Soon, Indonesia will be wealthy and strong, and we will not want it as an enemy.
We've had an antagonistic relationship with Jakarta before and even faced off against Indonesian troops in the so-called Konfrontasi of the early 1960s. But Indonesia was a poor country then, with little military power or influence on the regional stage. Today, Indonesia is South-East Asia's leader and soon its economy will surpass ours. From there, the gap will only widen.
For Australia, then, the stakes in the relationship continue to grow. The more powerful Indonesia becomes, the less we can afford a breach with Jakarta.
But if we get this relationship right, Indonesia offers a natural barrier against threats from third countries. And the good news is Canberra and Jakarta share one crucial interest: neither Australia nor Indonesia wants China to dominate our region. Right there is the kernel of a deeper partnership with Jakarta. It can be something like an alliance dedicated to ensuring that no outside power ever dominates the region we share.
Of course, that ambition remains distant and Jakarta may never be the partner we would like it to be. But with that vital interest in common, many barriers can be overcome, including the fact that Australia and Indonesia do not share what our politicians call "shared values".
If that sounds coldly transactional, then so be it. We Australians cherish our political traditions, but we've never insisted that our regional partners adopt our ways.
Lessons from the UK
The United Kingdom is, like us, a liberal democracy and an island lying just off a powerful continent. Ten years ago, the UK comprehensively sabotaged its own economy and its relationship with its neighbours.
I don't need to dwell on the damage Brexit has done over the past decade: according to The Economist magazine, it has taken at least 2.5 per cent, or maybe as much as 8 per cent, off Britain's GDP. Only a tenth of Brits now say Brexit has made their life better.
Why did it happen? We're told it was about xenophobia and anti-European sentiment. Yet despite some truly ugly outbreaks of racial violence, Britain remains a fundamentally liberal and tolerant society. And don't forget, the defining message of the Brexit campaign was not about keeping foreigners out, it was about taking back control.
That slogan — take back control — is a clue to what's really going on, not just in the UK but in every Western democracy touched by the rise of right-wing populism, including ours. I think the lesson of Brexit is not that British voters were xenophobic, but that they distrusted their own elites.
In every Western democracy, the gap between voters and their political leaders has widened to a chasm because the connective tissue between voter and government has withered and decayed. That connective tissue is the political party.
The decline of the big centre-right and centre-left parties that dominated Western democratic politics in the second half of the 20th century is the signature political phenomenon of our time. Those parties represented well-defined constituencies. The centre-left clustered around unions and the working class. The centre-right around business, small and large, and the middle class. But every force that once tied big political parties to a defined constituency — unionism, manufacturing, religion, class and even race — has withered.
The effect on the big parties has been catastrophic. It was the weakening of the Conservative Party at the hands of its own Eurosceptics and Nigel Farrage's UKIP that triggered the Brexit referendum. Major parties have declined all over Europe too, creating openings for new political forces.
In Australia, the collective membership of the Labor and Liberal parties couldn't fill the MCG. At the 2007 federal election, 43 per cent of us put Labor first. By 2025, even though Labor won the election convincingly, that figure was 33 per cent. The trends are roughly the same for the Coalition. Our primary votes are now split an even three ways, with independents and small parties also getting roughly one third.
The result is that modern Australian governments achieve power whilst never really feeling that they are in charge.
If a government doesn't feel it has a mandate, it sets about trying to manufacture one. Perhaps you've noticed that the term "social licence" has crept into our political vocabulary — that's an implicit acknowledgement of the democratic deficit I'm describing.
Our governments launch endless enquiries and establish expert bodies to make decisions that were once considered to be within their own remit. These are all signs of governments desperately searching for new indicators of public approval and devising mechanisms to work around its absence. No truly confident government would feel the need.
The Howard government was the last under the old two-party settlement. Not coincidentally, that was also when Australia had its last major economic reform. If we have indeed become a timid nation, as Paul Keating argues, then I think this is why.
The missing piece is a sense of authority arising from democratic legitimacy. That's what instils courage and policy boldness in governments.
Our future without a powerful regional ally
For the first time in our history, we face a future without a powerful ally committed to regional supremacy.
We face a future in which Asia will be led by an Asian superpower, one that has interests and ambitions that clash with ours. And we face a future in which our close neighbour, Indonesia, will have greater national power than us. All of this in a political environment undergoing its biggest realignment since the creation of the Liberal Party in 1944.
The changes to our region demand not just a new defence strategy or a new foreign policy, but an ambitious national reform agenda dedicated to creating a truly self-reliant Australia.
Yet our domestic political malaise is frustrating our ability to meet the regional challenges. The major parties are exhausted and fragile; they lack the energy and authority to embark on such a journey. The last big wave of Australian reform, in the 1980s and 90s, was built on consensus between our major parties. If there is to be another wave of reform it will need to be built on the ashes of the two-party system.
Right now, the boldness Australia needs has no political home. The far right offers nostalgia for a wholly imagined monoculture. The left is pre-occupied with conservation and flirts with de-growth. The major parties offer technocratic tinkering. There is not a single political force in Australia today focused squarely on building Australia's wealth and strength.
The most telling evidence is that Labor, the Coalition and One Nation are now all, to one degree or another, retreating from immigration.
Loading
Immigration retreat also one from Asia
Given the temper of our immigration debate, perhaps the least popular argument one can make right now is for Australia to get bigger. But immigration is our national superpower, and we do multiculturalism better than any country on earth.
Although many factors go into producing a strong nation, sheer size is vital. When Singapore got rich in the 1970s, the world applauded. When China got rich in the 2000s, the world shook. The difference is scale.
Australia should recommit to immigration not because "diversity is strength", to use the prime minister's anodyne phrase, but because scale is strength. Retreating from immigration will make us materially weaker. It will also raise the drawbridge to talented and industrious Asians who want to make Australia home. It will cut us off from our region. A retreat from immigration is a retreat from Asia.
Yet our politicians now propose to take us to the precipice. If the political mood against immigration holds until the next election, voters will be invited to consign Australia to a shrunken, inward looking, future — our own version of the Brexit referendum.
But Australia can't afford to turn its back on Asia the way the UK turned its back on Europe. Creating the conditions for an Australia that stands strong and independent in Asia begins with a simple act of recognition: we must look after ourselves.
If that sounds confronting, then I would close by reminding you that Asia is a source of immense opportunity, as well as risk. Although we in the West are passing through a moment of profound cultural pessimism, in Asia the future is still a source of optimism. And no wonder — the people living in its gleaming new cities are, in some cases, only one generation removed from rural poverty.
Young Australians are travelling freely around the region and imbibing its culture. They see Tokyo's urbanism, China's cityscapes, Singapore's garden-city infrastructure. These cities evoke a sense of promise.
Australia should want to capture the spirit of progress that animates those places, to be a country where the future feels exciting and abundant, maybe even a little glamorous.
Let that sense of optimism guide Australia as we navigate the difficult choices ahead.
Sam Roggeveen's keynote lecture will be on ABC TV and iview at 3:25pm October 17 and iview. This lecture and others from Louisa Lim, Mari Pangestu and Senior Minister Lee Hsien Loong will air on consecutive Sundays from October 18 on ABC Radio National's Sunday Extra program, at 8:05am.

Lithuanian minister proposes to ban self-employment for foreign students
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:56:00 UTC
16:56:00 KST

Lithuania’s interior minister has proposed banning foreign students from working under self-employment certificates, arguing that some use student visas primarily as a way to obtain temporary residence permits rather than pursue their education.
Tanjid, a student from Bangladesh in his second year at Vilnius College, says he balances work and studies in Lithuania.
“I know my class schedule – I have one or two lectures a day, so it’s easy to fit everything in,” he says.
However, finding work under an employment contract while pursuing a bachelor’s degree is difficult, he adds.
“I worked full time in a warehouse over the summer, but once classes started, it became difficult to balance everything, so I quit. But I came here to study – that’s what I’m focused on, and I work only to support myself,” he says.
According to the Migration Department, more than 230,000 foreigners currently hold temporary residence permits in Lithuania. Only about 5%, or 12,000 came to the country to study. The largest groups of international students come from Pakistan, India, Bangladesh, Morocco and Belarus.
Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas argues some students seek to enter Lithuania primarily to work, rather than study. He said foreign students exploit the system by attending classes only when necessary to maintain their residence status.
He said employers and universities also benefit from the current arrangement, as higher enrolment brings additional funding to educational institutions.
“The lecturers themselves say that migrants come only to take exams and ask for passing grades so that their residence permits based on studies are not revoked,” Katelynas said.
The minister wants to eliminate the option for foreign students to work under self-employment certificates (individuali veikla), which offer a more flexible arrangement than standard employment contracts.
He said European Union directives prevent Lithuania from banning foreign students from working altogether, but that regulating self-employment falls within national competence.
Last year, the Migration Department inspected higher education institutions and found cases in which students were absent from classes they were scheduled to attend. The department also found that institutions had failed to report when foreign students took academic leave, which could have triggered the revocation of their residence permits.
Katelynas declined to name the institutions involved, saying they were mostly colleges.
Eugenijus Gentvilas, a member of parliament from the Liberal Movement faction, questioned whether restrictions on foreign students were justified when the number of international students remained relatively small compared with the overall immigrant population.
“Please tell us which higher education institutions, which colleges, failed to learn from the observations made,” Gentvilas said. “Talking about restricting the number of foreign students when there are 12,000 of them among 220,000 migrants sounds excessively harsh toward other higher education institutions, which are being asked to internationalise their studies.”
Migration Department Director Indrė Gasperė said institutions are now more responsive to reporting requirements.
“Any change concerning a student must be reported to the Migration Department: if the student has discontinued their studies or is not earning enough credits,” she said. “Failure to report this information carries a fine under the Code of Administrative Offenses. Universities are listening to us.”
Universities also say the situation has improved.
At the private Kazimieras Simonavičius University, about two-thirds of students are foreign nationals. University representative Edgaras Genys said attendance had improved and cases of abuse had declined after rules were tightened.
“In previous years, the rules were more liberal and the admission criteria were somewhat lower, so such things could happen,” he said.
However, Genys warned that restricting employment options could make Lithuania less attractive to international students choosing where to study.
The Conference of Rectors of Lithuanian Universities also opposes the proposed restrictions.
“We would not want our students to be disadvantaged compared with students in other countries,” representative Alvidas Šarlauskas said. “Spending half the week on additional work alongside one’s studies is reasonable.”
Katelynas insists foreign students would still be able to work under standard employment contracts if the proposed restriction on self-employment is introduced. In practice, however, that would be near-impossible, since employers are generally reluctant to offer contracts to student and part-time employees.

Qais Abu Samra and Ikram Kouachi

Israeli occupiers set fire to a prayer room and a car and scrawled racist slogans in the town of Mukhmas, northeast of occupied Jerusalem, early Wednesday, according to a local official.
Mohammed Kanaan, a member of Mukhmas’ municipal council, told Anadolu that a group of Israeli occupiers attacked the area at around 2 am local time (2300GMT Tuesday) and set fire to the prayer room and a car.

On Monday, the Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission said it had documented 136 attacks by the Israeli army and occupiers linked to the olive harvest since the beginning of October.
According to the commission, the attacks included beatings, expulsions, intimidation, gunfire, tear gas, arrests, theft of olives and harvesting equipment, and damage to trees. The incidents have harmed Palestinian farmers and restricted their access to their land.
Israeli army raids and attacks by occupiers against Palestinians and their property have intensified across the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, since the start of Israel’s war on Gaza in October 2023.
